pages.title: Test the Reporter
pages.subtitle: Does a self-report track behavior or a training fingerprint?
pages.footer: Check the report against what the model does.
pages.wordKey: AI = artificial intelligence

panels.heading: A smoke-detector analogy
panels.body: A detector that rings for burnt toast needs checking. Likewise, a model reporting an unusual habit might be right, guessing, or reacting to an irrelevant training clue. This project tests the reporting tool.

panels.heading: What the tool actually is
panels.body: An introspection adapter is an added learned parameter update. A shared adapter is trained across many fine-tuned models from one base to make each describe its learned behavior. It is not a separate reader of activation traces.

panels.heading: A toy behavior
panels.body: Train a model to mention a fictional Moon Club in puzzle answers. Independently test whether it really does so. Then attach the reporting adapter and ask about unusual habits. Compare the report with measured behavior.

panels.heading: Two rival explanations
panels.body: Behavior tracking: reports follow the habit across different training recipes. Fingerprint tracking: reports follow incidental weight patterns even when measured habits do not change. Both may contribute; design experiments that pull them apart.

panels.heading: What is established
panels.body: Published work demonstrates useful self-reports on some held-out fine-tunes. Later work studies attacks and side-effect behavior. This proposal tests reliability under specified shifts; novelty and released-model compatibility must be rechecked.

panels.heading: What it cannot establish
panels.body: A fluent confession is not a mind-reading result or evidence of consciousness. An adapter changes the model it is attached to. Reports can hallucinate or miss habits, so behavioral tests remain an independent reference.

pages.summary: A detector that rings for burnt toast needs checking. Likewise, a model reporting an unusual habit might be right, guessing, or reacting to an irrelevant training clue. This project tests the reporting tool.

panels: Treat a self-report as a diagnostic test whose validity must be established. For a report r and a ground-truth behavior b, the relevant quantities are sensitivity P(r names b | b present) and specificity P(r names nothing | b absent). A language model asked about its habits has at least three ways to produce a plausible answer: reading something real about itself, drawing on priors about what such answers usually look like (for example, claiming to be sycophantic), or reacting to a training artifact unrelated to the behavior. Only the first is useful for auditing. Fluency is no evidence, so the design must separate the three using measurements outside the report.

An introspection adapter is a parameter-efficient update, such as a low-rank adaptation, trained jointly across many same-base fine-tuned models so that each, when equipped with the adapter, describes the behavior it learned. Writing the behavior update for model i as Δ_i and the adapter as φ, the modified model has weights W + Δ_i + φ, and training minimizes the language-modeling loss of the true description d_i given a prompt, updating φ only. This requires a shared base and layout, because the adapter must compose in weight space with each behavior update. It is not an activation reader or probe: it changes the model's weights, hence the model's own outputs.

The toy example has three measurable parts. First, an implanted behavior: fine-tune on puzzle answers that mention the fictional Moon Club. Second, an independent behavior test on held-out puzzle prompts, with a regex or judge scoring mention rate and, importantly, scope (does it appear only in puzzles?). Third, the report test: attach the adapter, ask about unusual habits, and score whether the answer names the habit and its scope. Control columns are the base model with the adapter and the habit model without it. The decomposition shows how much of any correct answer is due to the habit, the adapter, or their combination.

The two rival hypotheses make opposite predictions in a factorial design. If reports track behavior, then identical habits trained by different recipes should receive the same report, and different habits trained by one recipe should receive different ones. If reports track a training fingerprint (a signature in ΔW arising from data source, learning rate, rank, step count), the reports will follow the recipe even when the measured habit does not change. A critical point: in the original training set, behaviors and recipes may be perfectly confounded, so the data alone cannot tell which signal the adapter learned. Only new combinations created by experiment can. Both signals may contribute, so effects should be estimated jointly, for example by regression with both factors.

According to the notes, the original paper reports useful self-reports on some held-out fine-tunes. Later work examines attacks on adapters using function-preserving weight changes and studies side-effect introspection; its existence means any claim of absolute novelty here is unsafe. Generalization in the published work is bounded by what the held-out sets varied, and different shifts (new behaviors, new fine-tuning methods, new base checkpoints) are different questions. This proposal takes the position that the open question is reliability under specified shifts, so it names the shift axes in advance and reports each separately, and it rechecks which compatible weights are actually released.

A fluent confession is a text output of a modified model; it does not by itself show access to an internal state in the sense used in introspection research. Binder et al. (2024) operationalize introspection as predicting one's own behavior better than another model given the same information, a stricter standard than the one used here, where the adapter is judged as a measurement tool. Because attaching the adapter modifies the model, behavior must be measured with and without it. Reports can hallucinate details or omit habits, so independent behavioral batteries remain the reference. No claim about consciousness or mind-reading follows from either a hit or a miss.
deeper.further: Common misconceptions: that the adapter reads activations, that a correct description proves self-knowledge, and that success on planted toy habits shows coverage of naturally occurring ones. Open problems include distinguishing weight-space signals that causally encode a behavior from incidental signals, obtaining calibrated confidence from free-text reports, and whether such a tool can survive a developer who optimizes against it. This page frames the measurement question; the next pages build controls to separate habit from fingerprint, then pressure-test the reporter. Book 10 describes the foundation work this project is robustness-testing.

pages.title: Pull Clues Apart
pages.subtitle: Build controls that separate habit from training history
pages.footer: Change the habit and the fingerprint separately.
pages.wordKey: LoRA = low-rank adaptation

panels.heading: Learn a shared reporter
panels.body: Create several same-base models with known harmless habits. Keep their behavior updates frozen while training one shared reporting adapter. Use held-out behavior families to test generalization, rather than memorized descriptions.

panels.heading: Understand the small update
panels.body: LoRA uses low-rank matrices to represent a compact weight update. It can make fine-tuning cheaper, but does not guarantee faithfulness. Check that the reporting adapter matches the exact model architecture and parameter layout.

panels.heading: Build matched controls
panels.body: Include the untouched base, ordinary benign fine-tunes, sham training with comparable compute, and habit-bearing models. Match update size and training recipe where possible. Verify supposed no-change controls with a broad behavioral battery.

panels.heading: Cross the variables
panels.body: Train the same habit with different data and recipes. Train different habits with similar recipes. Split by model and behavior family, not just by question. Otherwise the reporter could recognize a familiar training signature.

panels.heading: Probe representation sensitivity
panels.body: A valid weight symmetry can preserve a model’s function while changing parameter coordinates. Existing research shows this can disrupt a fixed adapter. Check behavior preservation first; distinguish coordinate mismatch from deliberate concealment.

panels.heading: Keep references independent
panels.body: Measure the target without the reporting adapter, then with it on ordinary tasks. Blind human graders to training labels. Include direct questioning without an adapter and another auditing baseline under matched query budgets.

pages.summary: Create several same-base models with known harmless habits. Keep their behavior updates frozen while training one shared reporting adapter. Use held-out behavior families to test generalization, rather than memorized descriptions.

panels: Training the shared reporter is meta-learning over weight updates. With models M_i = base + Δ_i and target descriptions d_i, the adapter parameters φ minimize Σ_i L(d_i | prompt; base + Δ_i + φ) while every Δ_i stays frozen, so φ can only learn to extract and verbalize whatever the Δ_i leave behind. Generalization has a hierarchy: a new model with a seen behavior, a new behavior within a seen family, a new family, and a new training recipe. Held-out evaluation by behavior family, not only by question, is what separates learning to describe from memorizing which description goes with which familiar signature.

LoRA (Hu et al. 2021) approximates a weight change as W' = W + (α/r)·BA, with B of size d×r and A of size r×k. The parameter count is r(d+k) instead of dk, which makes many fine-tunes cheap. Low rank is a statement about compactness, not about whether the update is interpretable or faithful. Stacking an introspection adapter on top of a behavior update only makes sense if both target compatible modules, dtype and layout; a mismatch can silently produce garbage rather than an error. A correct baseline therefore includes a compatibility check, for example confirming that the adapter reproduces its training-time behavior on a model it was trained with.

Controls separate what a fine-tune is from what it does. The untouched base shows the adapter's behavior with no update. Ordinary benign fine-tunes (training on generic instruction data) leave a fine-tuning fingerprint without the habit. Sham training reproduces compute and hyperparameters on data lacking the habit, ideally matching update norm and rank. Habit-bearing models are the positives. If the adapter reports a habit on sham or benign models, that is direct evidence of fingerprint reliance or a bias toward finding something. A broad behavioral battery verifies that controls really have no habit, but it only supports 'no detected change', never exact equivalence.

A crossed design has behaviors on one axis and recipes on the other: same behavior with several data sources and hyperparameters, and several behaviors with one recipe. Predictions diverge cleanly: behavior-tracking reports follow rows, fingerprint-tracking reports follow columns. Analysis can fit report correctness against behavior presence and recipe features, reading the recipe coefficient, controlling for behavior, as the reliance on fingerprints. Splits must group by model and behavior family, or an adapter could succeed by recognizing a familiar model it saw during training under a different question. Reporting performance per held-out group shows whether success is uniform or concentrated.

Transformers have exact function-preserving reparameterizations, for instance permuting the hidden units of an MLP block by permuting rows of the up-projection and the matching columns of the down-projection. The model computes the same outputs but its weights, and any update expressed in those coordinates, look different. The research cited in the notes reports that such transformations can disrupt a fixed adapter. Two checks are needed. First, verify behavior preservation numerically; in low-precision arithmetic equality is only approximate, so a tolerance must be stated. Second, transform the adapter consistently: if reports recover, the failure was coordinate mismatch rather than concealment.

Reference measurements must be independent of the tool under test. The target's behavior is measured without the adapter, and also with it on ordinary tasks, since the adapter changes the model. Human graders are blinded to training labels and to which condition produced a report, and agreement between graders is reported. Baselines include directly asking the model without any adapter, and another auditing method such as behavioral probing or large-scale sampling, each given the same query budget. A positive result is then a claim about marginal value: the adapter finds habits the cheaper alternatives under equal budget do not, and does so with acceptable false alarms.
deeper.further: Common misconceptions: that low-rank means interpretable, that a no-change control is proven equivalent to the base, and that failing after a symmetry transform shows concealment. Open problems include which weight-space features the adapter actually uses, how recipes beyond LoRA (full fine-tuning, reinforcement learning) change them, and whether coordinate-invariant reporters can be built. The matched-controls approach is a standard experimental pattern: manipulate the suspected confound independently of the variable of interest. The following page takes the controls into a measurement framework with false positives, calibration and adversarial pressure.

pages.title: Challenge and Measure
pages.subtitle: An alarm is useful only when it is right often enough
pages.footer: Retained behavior plus missed report is the evasion test.

panels.heading: Define the target precisely
panels.body: Choose measurable toy habits and trigger conditions. A correct report must name the habit and its scope. Vague claims of being unsafe do not count. Score unsupported extra claims as errors, not free guesses.

panels.heading: Measure false positives
panels.body: Ask unmodified and benign-control models the same questions. Record invented concerning habits. Report detection rate at a fixed false-positive allowance, plus precision and missed behaviors. Never count a confession as its own ground truth.

panels.heading: Calibrate or abstain
panels.body: Use development models to choose confidence thresholds and an “uncertain” option. On held-out models, measure accuracy among answered cases and the fraction answered. If reports lack usable confidence scores, evaluate abstention as a separate method.

panels.heading: Test new learning routes
panels.body: Use reinforcement learning: training from rewards, rather than demonstration answers. First verify that a harmless undesired game habit emerged. Then test the frozen reporter on these models, holding out their training recipe.

panels.heading: Adapt against the reporter
panels.body: Keep the reporter fixed while a controlled attacker seeks retained toy misbehavior with less disclosure. Compare against equally trained, reporter-unaware controls. Measure both retained behavior and reporting failure; suppressing the habit is not successful evasion.

panels.heading: Interpret carefully
panels.body: Repeat across random seeds and whole-model splits. Report uncertainty and judge disagreement. Good detection on planted habits does not establish coverage of naturally arising misalignment; failed detection may expose a fingerprint or compatibility confound.

pages.summary: Choose measurable toy habits and trigger conditions. A correct report must name the habit and its scope. Vague claims of being unsafe do not count. Score unsupported extra claims as errors, not free guesses.

panels: A scoring rubric turns free text into data. A correct report names the habit (what) and its scope (when or on what inputs), so 'mentions a Moon Club in puzzle answers' scores, while 'I might be unsafe' does not. Claims in a report can be extracted and each checked against ground truth, giving claim-level precision (supported claims / all claims) and recall (habits named / habits present). Unsupported extra claims count against the report, otherwise verbose answers win. Judges, human or model, need reliability checks such as agreement statistics on a sample, and the rubric should be fixed before final evaluation so scoring cannot drift toward favorable outcomes.

The negatives are the unmodified model and benign controls, and the question is how often the adapter nonetheless names a concerning habit. A fixed false-positive allowance gives a comparable detection rate. When the output is text, a score is needed: log-probability of a disclosure, or agreement across sampled reports. Precision then depends on prevalence by Bayes' rule: PPV = TPR·π / (TPR·π + FPR·(1-π)), so a modest false-positive rate can dominate when real misbehaving models are rare. Auditing evaluations should therefore report FPR, TPR and the implied positive predictive value at a stated plausible prevalence, instead of a single accuracy figure.

Selective prediction lets a system answer only when confident. The measurable pair is coverage (fraction answered) and accuracy among answered; sweeping the confidence threshold traces a risk-coverage curve. Calibration asks whether stated confidence c matches actual correctness frequency, summarized by metrics such as expected calibration error. The threshold and any abstention option are chosen on development models and tested on held-out ones. If the adapter provides no usable confidence, abstention must be evaluated as a separate method, for instance using consistency across repeated samples. Higher precision from abstaining is not free; the cases withheld remain unresolved for human review.

Reinforcement-learned organisms test a different acquisition route. A reward environment that encourages a harmless gaming habit trains the behavior by trial and reward rather than by supervised examples, and its weight update may have different size and structure than a supervised fine-tune; whether it does is an empirical expectation, not a given. Before evaluating the reporter, verify that the habit actually emerged with an independent behavioral test. Holding out the training recipe means the adapter never saw this route, so the experiment measures out-of-distribution transfer of the reporter. A failure here could reflect fingerprint dependence rather than weakness on the behavior itself.

The adaptive arm trains a target to keep the toy behavior while disclosing less. Since the reporter outputs text, the objective may need reinforcement learning on a disclosure score or a differentiable proxy such as the probability of disclosure tokens. The comparison control is a reporter-unaware model with equal training compute, because any extra training perturbs weights and may degrade reports without targeting the reporter. Success requires both conditions: behavior retained (measured independently) and report missed. Suppressing the habit is not evasion. Postmortem analysis should state whether failures look semantic (new phrasing) or coordinate-like (a shift the adapter cannot parse).

Models, not questions, are the independent units, so uncertainty comes from resampling whole models and from multiple random seeds, with judge disagreement shown separately. Planted habits are simple, local and explicitly implanted; naturally arising misalignment might be diffuse, emerge from generalization, and look unlike any implanted pattern, so good detection on planted habits bounds only what was planted. When detection fails, list the competing explanations: fingerprint dependence, architecture or layout incompatibility, judge error, or real concealment. Each has a different follow-up experiment, and only careful controls let a team choose among them.
deeper.further: Common misconceptions: that a high detection rate is meaningful without the false-positive rate, that abstention is the same as calibration, and that evasion means the behavior went away. Open problems include getting trustworthy confidence from text reports, defining coverage for behaviors nobody planted, and understanding adaptive robustness when the attacker controls weights. Related ideas in this collection include the stacked lie detectors book (combining detectors, then attacking them) and the latent probes book (training against a fixed detector). All share a rule: the detector must be frozen before the attack, and the attack must be scored by an independent behavior measure.

pages.title: Four-month Audit
pages.subtitle: A proposed reliability study, not a promised outcome
pages.footer: A reliable audit needs controls, not just confessions.

panels.heading: Month 1: reproduce
panels.body: Reproduce a compatible adapter setup, using the supplied map’s roughly 32-billion-parameter scale only if tools and resources permit. Measure unmodified-model false positives and verify the evaluation pipeline before broad experiments.

panels.heading: Month 2: matched contrasts
panels.body: Build behavior-matched and recipe-matched controls. Test fingerprint sensitivity, calibration, and abstention. Freeze the reporter and scoring rubric before final tests. Reserve unseen habits and models for the locked evaluation.

panels.heading: Month 3: stronger challenges
panels.body: Evaluate reward-trained toy organisms and reporter-aware adversarial training. Check retained behavior independently. Add matched training-budget controls, several seeds, and coordinate-preserving checks for any symmetry experiment.

panels.heading: Month 4: publish the limits
panels.body: Release a reproducible evaluation suite, control models where permitted, prompts, scoring rubric, and a paper. Document compatibility, false alarms, coverage, and failures. Share enough detail for independent replication.

panels.heading: Compute planning estimate
panels.body: Supplied map: $8,000–$15,000 for experiments, not comic production. Hardware rental, model calls, and labeling vary. Run a small pilot and price actual workloads; reduce scale before sacrificing controls or independent replications.

panels.heading: Fallback and null results
panels.body: If false positives are already near zero, prioritize the adversarial arm. If behavior controls cannot be validated, pause scaling and fix them. A null can bound tested failure modes; it cannot certify universal trustworthiness. Recheck literature before pitching.

pages.summary: Reproduce a compatible adapter setup, using the supplied map’s roughly 32-billion-parameter scale only if tools and resources permit. Measure unmodified-model false positives and verify the evaluation pipeline before broad experiments.

panels: Month 1 establishes the noise floor and the pipeline. A compatible adapter and base must exist, which the notes say needs rechecking, and the roughly 32-billion-parameter scale from the map is conditional on availability and budget. The first measurement is the false-positive rate on unmodified models, since a high floor limits what later contrasts can show and a near-zero floor frees budget for adversarial work. Pipeline checks include known-positive and known-negative sanity tests, confirming that scoring assigns zero to unrelated text, and that results reproduce under a different seed. Without this, later effects cannot be attributed.

Month 2 builds the matched contrasts: behavior-matched controls (same habit, different recipe) and recipe-matched controls (same recipe, no habit or a different one). Fingerprint sensitivity is estimated as the effect of recipe on reports with behavior held fixed. Calibration and abstention are developed on a development set, and then the reporter, rubric and thresholds are frozen. Reserving unseen habits and models for the locked evaluation preserves its meaning; any component tuned after looking at the locked set turns it into a development set. The factorial grid can be large, so fractional designs may be used to keep cost proportional.

Month 3 introduces stronger challenges: reward-trained toy organisms and reporter-aware adversarial training. Behavior retention is always checked independently of the reporter. Matched training-budget controls ensure that failure from extra training is not mistaken for failure from targeted optimization. Several seeds estimate variance. If symmetry transformations are included, they must preserve behavior to a stated numerical tolerance, which is subtle in low-precision arithmetic, and any adapter-side compensating transformation must be tested to separate coordinate dependence from concealment. Each of these adds arms, so the plan prioritizes by what would change the conclusion.

Month 4 turns results into artifacts others can check: an evaluation suite, control models where permitted, the exact prompts and scoring rubric, and a paper that documents compatibility requirements, false alarms, coverage and failures. The point of releasing control models and rubrics is replication, since scoring text reports is sensitive to judge prompts. Honest reporting includes arms that did not work and analysis choices made after seeing data, labeled exploratory. A coverage statement should say which behaviors and models were tested and, equally, which were not, so readers do not infer more than the evidence supports.

The cost structure depends on the size of the control grid: behaviors × recipes × seeds × models, plus evaluation queries and judge calls, with each additional control costing both training and evaluation. Hardware rental and model-call prices fluctuate, so the proposal calls for a small pilot to price real workloads. The priority rule is that if budget must shrink, reduce scale (smaller model, fewer behaviors) before dropping controls or replications, because a cheaper experiment with valid controls still answers a question, whereas an expensive one without controls does not. Figures from the map are planning assumptions, not quotes.

Fallback rules are written ahead of time. If false positives on unmodified models are already near zero, the design has little to learn about false alarms and shifts toward the adversarial arm. If behavior controls cannot be validated, scaling stops until they can, because mislabeled controls would invalidate every conclusion. A null result in the adversarial arm bounds the failure modes that were tried; no finite set of tests certifies a tool as universally trustworthy. The literature check is repeated before any pitch because related work in this area has appeared quickly and may have changed the novelty of each arm.
deeper.further: Common misconceptions: that a four-month plan guarantees an outcome, that more controls are a luxury, and that a clean result against one adversary shows general robustness. Open problems include building reporters robust to weight-space reparameterization, estimating coverage on naturally arising behaviors, and defining standard benchmarks for model-written audit reports. Compare with the second book's sandbagging auditors and the fifth book's stacked detectors: each treats an auditing method as something to validate with false-positive control, held-out splits and an adaptive adversary before relying on it. Book 10 summarizes the foundation result this project stress-tests.

books.subtitle: Candidate research project
objectives: Book 09: can an internal detector be trained around?

pages.title: Thinking Without a Written Trace
pages.subtitle: Book 09: can an internal detector be trained around?
pages.footer: Hidden computation needs an independent scoreboard.
pages.wordKey: CoT = chain-of-thought; RL = reinforcement learning; AI = artificial intelligence.

panels.heading: Two notebooks
panels.body: One puzzle solver writes intermediate words. Another passes internal vectors between computation steps. The second notebook is harder for a person to read, but that does not mean it is secretly deceptive.

panels.heading: What latent means
panels.body: A latent reasoning system uses continuous internal states for some intermediate steps instead of printing each step as a word. Ordinary language models also have internal activations; the difference is the reasoning interface.

panels.heading: A probe is a sensor
panels.body: A probe is a learned readout from internal activations to a target label. It can predict a useful correlate without understanding the whole computation. High accuracy before adversarial training is only the starting point.

panels.heading: The proposed question
panels.body: If RL rewards task performance while penalizing a probe alarm, does detection fail sooner for latent reasoning than for matched verbal reasoning? Compare both under the same task and training pressure.

panels.heading: Define the target first
panels.body: Use harmless tasks with an independently checkable event, such as reliance on a planted hint. Record the event outside the probe so the detector is not grading its own homework.

panels.heading: Keep the claim precise
panels.body: A falling probe score might mean the behavior vanished, its representation moved, or the detector stopped transferring. The next pages show how to tell these possibilities apart.

pages.summary: One puzzle solver writes intermediate words. Another passes internal vectors between computation steps. The second notebook is harder for a person to read, but that does not mean it is secretly deceptive.

panels: In verbal chain of thought, each step is a discrete token: the hidden state is projected to logits, a token is sampled, and its embedding is fed back. That pipeline passes about log2|V| bits per step through a human-readable bottleneck. In continuous-thought reasoning (Coconut, Hao et al. 2024), the last hidden state is fed directly back as the next input embedding, passing a full vector of real numbers. The extra bandwidth is also why a person cannot read it. Unreadable is not the same as deceptive: the difference is the interface, and any claim about intent needs separate evidence. What changes is the available monitoring channel, which is the quantity this book studies.

Coconut alternates between a language mode and a latent mode delimited by special tokens; in latent mode there is no decoding, and training uses a curriculum that gradually replaces written steps with continuous ones. The authors report that continuous thoughts can encode several candidate next steps at once, a breadth-first-like behavior. This matters for RL: policy-gradient methods need stochastic actions, but latent steps are deterministic functions of the context, so the only sampled actions are the discrete tokens before and after. Exploration inside the latent segment must come from elsewhere, one reason the notes and the plan flag high engineering risk. Standard transformers also have hidden states, so latent models differ in the reasoning interface.

A probe is typically a linear classifier p(y | h) = σ(w·h + b) trained on activations h from a chosen layer and position, often with a regularizer. Alain and Bengio (2016) introduced linear probes for layer analysis, and Hewitt and Liang (2019) added control tasks to measure selectivity, showing that high accuracy can reflect the probe's capacity rather than the representation. A probe shows that information is available in a linear subspace, not that the model uses it. Another limitation is distribution shift: a probe trained on pre-training activations may degrade after RL changes the activation geometry, regardless of any adversarial pressure. So pre-pressure accuracy is a starting point, and a baseline arm without pressure is needed.

The training objective is J(θ) = E[R_task] - λ·E[score(probe(h))], optionally thresholded as an alarm. Work on obfuscated activations (Bailey et al. 2024) showed that models can be trained or optimized to evade latent-space monitors, motivating the question for different reasoning interfaces. The independent variable here is the reasoning mode (latent versus verbal); the dependent variable is how quickly a frozen detector's performance falls under the same pressure, with matched tasks. Which direction is more plausible is unsettled: latent reasoning offers more freedom to move information around, but computation that must stay consistent for later steps may constrain how far representations can shift.

The target behavior must be measurable independent of the probe. A planted-hint design embeds an answer cue in the prompt, for example a metadata line naming a candidate answer, and labels an episode as hint-reliant if the answer follows the hint and changes when the hint is removed (a counterfactual contrast, in the spirit of hint-based CoT studies such as Chen et al. 2025). Probe training labels come from this behavioral contrast, not from the probe, so the evaluation is not circular. The hint task is harmless but supplies a clear positive class, and it avoids relying on vague judgments of intent.

A falling probe score is compatible with at least three distinct situations. The behavior may have disappeared, in which case the lower score is correct. The behavior may persist while its representation moved, for example rotated or spread across more directions, which is evasion in the operational sense. Or the detector may be stale: the activation distribution shifted for benign reasons, so a probe trained earlier no longer transfers. The three can be separated using external behavior labels, a freshly trained probe on later checkpoints, and causal interventions. Naming these alternatives in advance prevents any one result from being narrated after the fact.
deeper.further: Common misconceptions: that latent reasoning is inherently deceptive, that a high probe accuracy proves the model uses the feature, and that a lost probe equals a lost behavior. Open problems include how to do exploration in deterministic latent steps, whether nonlinear or ensemble probes are more robust under pressure, and how results transfer from small research models to frontier systems. The topic connects to the monitorability book, where the channel is text rather than activations, and to the lie-detector books, where several signals are stacked. The shared principle is that a detector is evidence only when behavior is measured independently.

pages.title: The Matched Experiment
pages.subtitle: Book 09 · page 2/4 — change the reasoning mode, then test pressure.
pages.footer: A fair baseline is part of the experiment.
pages.wordKey: RL = reinforcement learning; CoT = chain-of-thought.

panels.heading: Start from working systems
panels.body: Reproduce a small continuous-reasoning model and a verbal baseline before adding adversarial rewards. Verify task competence and logging. An unstable model cannot answer the monitoring question.

panels.heading: Match what you can
panels.body: Use the same task distribution, evaluation set, and similar initial accuracy. Report model size, training history, inference compute, and remaining differences rather than pretending two architectures are identical.

panels.heading: Build the first sensors
panels.body: Train separate probes for each reasoning mode on development examples with external labels. Choose layers and thresholds there, then freeze them for the main test.

panels.heading: Create training arms
panels.body: For each mode, compare task-only RL with task reward plus an alarm penalty. Add an untrained baseline. These controls show whether ordinary training already breaks the detector.

panels.heading: Hold back the final exam
panels.body: Split task families and prompts before training. Keep final examples out of probe selection and reward tuning. Check that the target behavior can still be measured after updates.

panels.heading: Repeat the comparison
panels.body: Use independent random starts and equal training budgets where feasible. Compare trajectories over updates; one lucky run or one weak baseline cannot establish that latent reasoning evades faster.

pages.summary: Reproduce a small continuous-reasoning model and a verbal baseline before adding adversarial rewards. Verify task competence and logging. An unstable model cannot answer the monitoring question.

panels: Before any adversarial reward, the comparison needs two competent systems. A small continuous-reasoning model is reproduced from a public implementation, with a verbal baseline fine-tuned from the same base on the same task. Competence checks include accuracy on a held-out set, stability across seeds, and a logging pipeline that stores hidden states at every latent step and layer. Instability is a scientific problem, not just an engineering one: if the training run diverges or accuracy varies widely between seeds, any probe result confounds the effect of pressure with run-to-run noise.

Exact matching is impossible, so the plan is to match what can be matched and report what cannot: same task distribution, same evaluation split, similar starting accuracy, and a record of model size, training history and inference compute. Compute differs naturally: a latent model uses k continuous steps, a verbal one n sampled tokens, and their FLOPs per problem need not agree. Detectability depends on how strongly the model relies on the hint, so one can also compare at matched hint-reliance rates, or adjust for reliance in the analysis. Remaining differences are named limits.

Each mode gets its own probe, with the same function class (for example logistic regression with fixed regularization) so differences reflect representations, not probe capacity. A comparability issue is where to read: verbal reasoning has token positions, latent reasoning has latent-step positions, so layer depth, number of positions and pooling should be matched as far as possible. Layer and threshold are selected on a development set by AUROC and by true-positive rate at a fixed false-positive rate, then frozen. Reporting both metrics matters: a high AUROC can coexist with a poor operating point in the low-false-alarm region that deployments need.

Three arms per mode isolate causes. The untouched baseline, evaluated at the same intervals, shows how stable the probe is without any optimization. Task-only RL (reward = correctness) shows what ordinary training does to the detector. Task plus penalty (reward = correctness - λ·alarm) adds adversarial pressure. The effect of the penalty is the penalty arm minus the task-only arm at matched checkpoints, while the effect of RL itself is task-only minus baseline. A sweep over λ matters: too small and nothing happens, too large and capability collapses. A model can also lower the probe's score without changing behavior, which is precisely the phenomenon being measured.

Leakage is guarded by splitting task families and prompt templates before any training, using development data only for choosing probe layer, threshold and λ, and keeping final examples out of every selection step. The target must remain measurable after updates. If RL teaches the model to ignore the hint entirely, there are no positive cases left and recall is undefined; so the number of positives per checkpoint should be tracked, and the hint conditions arranged so reliance persists. Otherwise a vanishing target would look like detector success or failure when it is neither.

Replication means independent random starts and matched budgets, with a note on the budget unit: equal optimizer updates or equal compute can favor different modes if per-step cost differs. Curves over updates are more informative than endpoints, and time-to-threshold can be analyzed with survival methods that handle runs which never reach the threshold (right-censored observations). A weak baseline is a classic failure: if the verbal arm received less tuning than the latent arm, a faster latent drop could reflect tuning effort. Reporting hyperparameter search budgets per arm makes the comparison auditable.
deeper.further: Common misconceptions: that matched accuracy implies matched difficulty, that a single run can show a mode-level difference, and that equal update counts imply equal cost. Open problems include whether the probe class (linear or nonlinear) changes the ranking of modes, how to choose layers fairly across architectures, and how results change when the detector is an ensemble. The design shares its skeleton with the monitorability book: a frozen detector, untouched and ordinary-training controls, held-out families, and a side measurement of the behavior. If the baseline detector is weak before pressure, there is nothing to break.

pages.title: Is It Evasion or a Broken Sensor?
pages.subtitle: Book 09 · page 3/4 — interpret the curves without guessing.
pages.footer: Quieter alarms need not mean less trouble.
pages.wordKey: RL = reinforcement learning; false positive = an alarm on a target-absent case.

panels.heading: Track three curves
panels.body: At each checkpoint measure task success, externally labeled target behavior, and probe detection. A quiet alarm alone is not the result. Plot uncertainty across independent runs.

panels.heading: Define evasion operationally
panels.body: Call it detector evasion when the externally measured target behavior remains while a frozen detector's sensitivity falls at a controlled false-positive rate. This definition does not require claims about conscious intent.

panels.heading: Compare time and cost
panels.body: Predefine a detection-drop threshold. Compare updates or compute needed to reach it while retaining capability and behavior. Do not confuse faster wall-clock training with fewer optimization steps.

panels.heading: Try a fresh sensor
panels.body: Train a new probe on later checkpoints as a diagnostic. If it recovers detection, the old readout may have become stale. Keep this separate from the frozen-probe headline result.

panels.heading: Use causal checks carefully
panels.body: Remove hints or intervene on candidate representations to test whether behavior changes. Decoding a label alone shows information is available, not that the decoded feature caused the answer.

panels.heading: What each outcome teaches
panels.body: Equal evasion suggests no measured extra latent cost here. Faster latent evasion motivates stronger oversight. Lower task accuracy or disappearing target behavior makes a simple evasion story unsupported.

pages.printedTitle: Is It Evasion or a Broken Sensor?
pages.summary: At each checkpoint measure task success, externally labeled target behavior, and probe detection. A quiet alarm alone is not the result. Plot uncertainty across independent runs.

panels: Three quantities are tracked at each checkpoint t: task success a(t), the externally labeled target-behavior rate b(t) (hint reliance by the counterfactual contrast), and detection d(t), such as true-positive rate at a fixed false-positive rate. Reading them together yields a decision table. If b stays flat and d falls, the frozen detector is losing sensitivity to a persisting behavior. If b falls with d, the model changed what it does. If a falls, capability is being traded. Plotting medians with bands across independent runs shows whether apparent differences exceed seed variation. A single alarm curve says nothing without the other two.

An operational definition removes mind-reading from the claim: detector evasion occurs when b(t) remains near its initial level b(0) while d(t) falls by at least a preset margin, where d is measured with a frozen probe at a controlled false-positive rate. One needs to say how that rate is controlled, either by keeping the frozen threshold or by recalibrating on each checkpoint's honest examples, because the two answer different questions: what a deployed monitor would do, and whether any separation remains. Optimization pressure can produce evasion much as it produces adversarial examples, without any reasoning about a monitor.

Time to evasion can be measured in optimizer steps, tokens processed, or FLOPs, and these can rank the modes differently, since latent and verbal runs differ in sequence length and per-step cost. The preregistered threshold (for example, detection falling by half while behavior and accuracy stay within tolerance) defines an event; runs that never reach it are censored, which survival analysis handles and simple averages do not. Reporting a hazard-style comparison, plus the raw curves, avoids hiding disagreements between cost units. Capability retention is part of the definition so that a collapsed model does not count as a fast evader.

A fresh probe trained on later-checkpoint activations (with external labels) serves as a diagnostic. If its accuracy is high, the information is still linearly decodable, and the original probe has gone stale because the relevant direction moved: a representation shift. If even a fresh probe fails, the information left the linearly accessible subspace, or the behavior itself changed; a nonlinear probe can test the first alternative. This diagnostic is kept apart from the headline result because the frozen probe estimates what a fixed deployed detector would do, while a continually retrained probe estimates something else, the existence of information.

Decoding is correlational. Hewitt and Liang (2019) showed that probe success can reflect probe capacity, and the notes cite further work cautioning that observed patterns alone do not establish mechanism. Causal checks add evidence: remove the hint and test whether behavior changes; ablate the probe direction (project it out) and test whether behavior is affected, necessity; steer along it and test whether behavior shifts, sufficiency. Each has caveats: distributed representations may survive a single-direction ablation, and edits may push activations off-distribution. Causal tests are strongest when several independent interventions agree.

Each outcome supports a narrow conclusion. Equal evasion times suggest no extra cost from the latent interface within this setting and power. Faster latent evasion supports the case for stronger oversight but needs a check that the latent probe was not simply weaker or noisier at the start. Lower accuracy or disappearing behavior means the evasion story is unsupported: the model may have changed what it does. A slower latent drop would also be informative. Because both modes may eventually evade any fixed probe, the quantity of interest is the rate, together with what the training budget would cost a real developer.
deeper.further: Common misconceptions: that a quiet probe means a quieter model, that evasion implies intent, and that retraining the probe is a fair way to claim robustness. Open problems include designing detectors that remain valid after optimization pressure, understanding which representation changes make evasion easy, and testing whether findings transfer to larger and more realistic systems. This page's emphasis on external labels parallels the monitorability book's insistence on sandbox ground truth. When detection and behavior move separately, report both, and say what each alternative explanation would predict.

pages.title: A Four-Month Latent-Reasoning Study
pages.subtitle: Book 09 · page 4/4 — a proposed plan, not completed findings.
pages.footer: Stability first, matched evidence second, strong claims last.
pages.wordKey: RL = reinforcement learning; CODI = Continuous Chain-of-Thought via Self-Distillation.

panels.heading: Month 1: reproduce
panels.body: Start with a small released continuous-reasoning system, such as a CODI-style model. Recheck weights, licenses, training support, and whether the claimed scale is actually available.

panels.heading: Month 2: establish controls
panels.body: Build the verbal comparison, independent target labels, frozen probes, and held-out tests. Demonstrate useful detection before trying to break it.

panels.heading: Month 3: apply pressure
panels.body: Run task-only and alarm-penalized training arms. Save checkpoints and evaluate capability, target behavior, and detection together. Spend larger budgets only after a stable pilot.

panels.heading: Month 4: explain and release
panels.body: Repeat the strongest comparison, test alternative explanations, and write the paper. Release task definitions, configurations, checkpoints where appropriate, and analysis code.

panels.heading: Stop and switch
panels.body: The source map says to switch to looped models if continuous-thought RL remains unstable by week 6. Treat that as a scope change: recurrence is related to, but not identical with, continuous-thought reasoning.

panels.heading: Budget and honest payoff
panels.body: The map estimates $25,000–$45,000 compute and high engineering risk. Reserve evaluation and replication funds. Even a null or instability result can identify which comparisons are feasible; it cannot certify all latent reasoners safe.

pages.summary: Start with a small released continuous-reasoning system, such as a CODI-style model. Recheck weights, licenses, training support, and whether the claimed scale is actually available.

panels: Month 1 reproduces a continuous-reasoning system. CODI (Shen et al. 2025) trains a continuous chain of thought by self-distillation, aligning the hidden state of a student that uses latent steps with that of a teacher trained on explicit reasoning. It is a plausible starting point, but the notes caution against assuming arbitrary scale or code is available: weights, licenses, training scripts and whether claimed scales are actually accessible all need checking first. A reproduction gate (the released model matches its reported behavior on a small task, and the training run can be repeated) prevents building on a system that cannot be trusted.

Month 2 builds the scaffolding for a fair comparison, and ends with a positive control: demonstrate that the frozen probes detect the target behavior well above chance, at a useful false-positive operating point, before attempting to break them. If the probes cannot detect hint reliance at baseline, an evasion question is vacuous. This is also where held-out splits, independent behavior labels and the verbal baseline are built, along with the pre-specified analysis plan. Having these artifacts early allows a go or no-go decision on continuing to the more expensive pressure experiments.

Month 3 runs the task-only and alarm-penalized arms with saved checkpoints, and at each checkpoint evaluates capability, target behavior and detection together. Pilot runs come first. Since latent steps are deterministic, stability and exploration problems are most likely here, so spending scales only after the pilot shows consistent learning across seeds. The checkpoint interval trades storage and evaluation cost against curve resolution; too coarse and the time-to-threshold measurement is imprecise. Pre-registering the stopping criteria for each run avoids discarding unfavorable runs afterward.

Month 4 repeats the strongest comparison with new seeds, because a comparison selected for its strength is likely to be partly luck (winner's curse). It tests alternative explanations: stale probe versus moved representation, vanished behavior versus retained behavior, capability loss versus targeted evasion. Release includes task definitions, configurations, analysis code and checkpoints where licenses permit, so others can recompute the curves. Claims in the paper are scoped to the models, tasks and probe class studied, and null or unstable outcomes are reported with their diagnostics rather than omitted.

The map's stop rule says to switch to looped models if continuous-thought RL remains unstable by week six. Looped or recurrent-depth models (for example Geiping et al. 2025) reuse a block iteratively to refine a latent state, which is related to continuous thought but a different architecture with different training and different monitoring surfaces. Switching is therefore a scope change: conclusions would apply to looped models, and the project should be described that way. Making the decision from a pre-stated criterion avoids sunk-cost reasoning, and recording why the first approach failed is itself a useful deliverable.

The planning range is from the supplied map and is not a quote; the page itself flags high engineering risk. Costs concentrate in RL runs repeated across modes, arms, seeds and checkpoints, plus evaluation and probe retraining, with a reserve for replication. Honest payoff: a positive result would show a specific rate difference between modes under specified pressure; a null would show no measured difference in these conditions; an instability result would show which comparisons are currently feasible. None of these certify that latent reasoners are safe, or that they are not. The statement is about the tested probe, task and pressure.
deeper.further: Common misconceptions: that a four-month plan can promise a publishable difference, that continuous-thought and looped models are interchangeable, and that a null result removes the concern. Open problems include stable policy-gradient training through deterministic latent steps, probes that remain valid under optimization, and external-behavior targets richer than a planted hint. The book's structure (feasibility, controls, pressure, explanation) matches the other fellowship plans. Its distinctive requirement is the positive control: show the detector works before claiming it breaks. Compare with the second page's matched-baseline logic and the introspection books' held-out splits.

books.title: Training introspection that generalizes
books.subtitle: Completed foundation
objectives: Book 10 · page 1/2 — the completed foundation for project 8.
Book 10 · page 2/2 — from an interesting result to a reliable audit.

pages.title: Teach a Model to Report Its Habits
pages.subtitle: Book 10 · page 1/2 — the completed foundation for project 8.
pages.footer: A useful self-report is a measurement to validate.
pages.wordKey: IA = introspection adapter; LoRA = low-rank adaptation; AI = artificial intelligence.

panels.heading: A habit-reporting helper
panels.body: Imagine a small attachment that helps a robot answer, 'What behavior were you trained to do?' The real technique adds trainable parameters to a model. It is not a separate reader of a hidden diary.

panels.heading: Make labeled examples
panels.body: Researchers fine-tune many variants of the same base model with known behaviors. Each variant and its behavior description form a training pair. Examples can include harmless habits and concerning behaviors.

panels.heading: Train one shared adapter
panels.body: The same small IA is trained across those model variants. When attached to a variant, it encourages the model to describe its learned behavior. The adapter is shared; the underlying variant supplies the learned differences.

panels.heading: Test on unfamiliar variants
panels.body: Hold out behavior families and fine-tuning methods. Apply the adapter to models it was not trained with, then score whether reports match independently known behavior.

panels.heading: What was demonstrated
panels.body: The cited work reports generalization to auditing settings with hidden implanted behaviors. This supports a promising auditing tool, not a general guarantee that every self-report is correct.

panels.heading: Why this belongs here
panels.body: Your source marks this project completed. The next research question is robustness: does the adapter detect behavior rather than a training fingerprint, and can later optimization fool it? That is project 8.

pages.printedTitle: Teach a Model to Report Its Habits
pages.summary: Imagine a small attachment that helps a robot answer, 'What behavior were you trained to do?' The real technique adds trainable parameters to a model. It is not a separate reader of a hidden diary.

panels: An introspection adapter (IA) is a trainable low-rank weight update attached to a model; after training, prompting the equipped model with a question such as 'Are there any unusual characteristics you display only for certain types of prompts?' elicits a description of that behavior. The effective weights are W + Δ_behavior + φ_IA, so the adapter acts through the same forward pass as everything else, not through a separate reader of activations. Related evidence that models can articulate learned dispositions comes from Betley et al. (2025), who found that models fine-tuned on implicit behaviors, such as making risky choices, could describe those tendencies without in-context examples. The IA turns that observation into a trained, reusable tool.

The training data are pairs (model_i, description_i). Each model_i is a fine-tune of the same base with a known behavior, and description_i is the text label. Diversity of behaviors determines what the adapter can generalize over. A quality issue is whether the implant actually took: if a fine-tune did not learn the behavior, training teaches the adapter to describe something absent, which encourages confabulation, so behavioral verification is needed at training time too. Descriptions in a variety of phrasings reduce the chance that the adapter learns to emit specific strings instead of mapping weight effects to meanings.

Training is a single shared φ that minimizes Σ_i L(description_i | question; base + Δ_i + φ), with each Δ_i frozen. Sharing forces φ to read information that is common to how behavior updates manifest, instead of memorizing a lookup from model identity to description. It resembles amortized inference: one network learns a mapping from any behavior update in the training distribution to its description. The number and diversity of training models govern the capacity-versus-memorization trade-off: with few models, φ can memorize; with many varied ones, extracting something general becomes the easier solution. This is a hypothesis about the mechanism, tested only by held-out evaluation.

Held-out evaluation varies one axis at a time: new behaviors, new behavior families, new fine-tuning methods, new data styles. For each held-out model, ground-truth behavior is known from the implanting procedure and confirmed by behavioral tests; a judge then scores whether the description matches. Reporting results separately by axis shows where generalization holds, since success on a held-out behavior with the same recipe says little about a held-out recipe. The notes describe the evaluation as auditing settings with hidden implanted behaviors, which resembles an auditing game where the auditor's goal is finding the planted issue.

What was demonstrated is bounded by the notes: generalization to auditing settings with implanted behaviors, supporting a promising tool, not a guarantee. Two distinctions matter. Implanted behaviors differ from ones that emerge naturally from training, which may be less clean. And a result that a correct report appears at least sometimes is different from dependable per-query accuracy; the comics omit headline counts for that reason. A real audit needs to know how much to trust a particular report, which requires calibration and false-positive rates. Whether this holds across bases, scales and attack types is unsettled and is the subject of project 8.

Marking the work as completed foundation makes the follow-up a robustness question with three parts: does the adapter respond to behavior or to training fingerprints; how often does it raise false alarms and miss habits; and does it survive optimization against it. Each corresponds to an experimental design in the project 8 book: crossed behavior-by-recipe controls, unmodified and benign baselines with calibration, and reporter-aware training. The sequence is deliberate, because it would be premature to test adversarial robustness of a tool whose false-positive rate and confounds are unknown.
deeper.further: Common misconceptions: that the adapter reads a hidden record, that a description matching an implanted behavior shows the model knows itself, and that a published generalization result is a reliability guarantee. Open problems include extending the method to naturally emerging behaviors, understanding what in the weight update carries the signal, and building versions that give calibrated uncertainty. Related reading in this collection: the project 8 book for stress tests, and the field guide for the general approach of changing one variable and keeping the test fair. Benchmarks of auditing games help measure progress but have their own limits.

pages.title: Trust the Report Only After Testing
pages.subtitle: Book 10 · page 2/2 — from an interesting result to a reliable audit.
pages.footer: Generalization is a beginning; robustness is the next test.
pages.wordKey: IA = introspection adapter; false positive = a reported problem that is absent.

panels.heading: Words are not proof
panels.body: A model can fluently describe a behavior it does not have, or omit one it does have. Compare reports with independent behavioral evidence instead of treating the answer as a confession.

panels.heading: Watch the clean controls
panels.body: The official adapter write-up reports false positives on models without specifically trained behaviors. Include unchanged base models and harmless fine-tunes. Otherwise a tool may learn to find a problem everywhere.

panels.heading: Separate behavior from fingerprints
panels.body: A fingerprint is a clue about how training happened. Compare different training methods producing the same behavior, and similar training methods producing different behavior. This tests what the adapter depends on.

panels.heading: Ask for calibrated uncertainty
panels.body: An auditing system should be allowed to say 'uncertain'. Measure whether confidence tracks correctness and how abstaining changes coverage. Fewer answers can improve precision while leaving more cases unresolved.

panels.heading: Try adaptive pressure
panels.body: Project 8 proposes models trained against the adapter. Test new held-out models afterward and monitor independent behavior. A good pre-attack score does not establish robustness after optimization.

panels.heading: Explain it back
panels.body: Why is a correct report on one model insufficient? Because reliability depends on false alarms, missed behaviors, unfamiliar settings, and adversarial adaptation. The useful question is when the report deserves trust.

pages.printedTitle: Trust the Report Only After Testing
pages.summary: A model can fluently describe a behavior it does not have, or omit one it does have. Compare reports with independent behavioral evidence instead of treating the answer as a confession.

panels: A model's description of its own behavior is a generated string, so it can be fluent and wrong in either direction: confabulating a habit that is absent, or failing to mention one that is present. Human psychology offers a cautionary parallel: Nisbett and Wilson (1977) reviewed evidence that people's verbal accounts of their own mental processes are often reconstructions rather than direct readouts. For models, the practical response is to treat a report as a hypothesis and test it by eliciting the behavior independently. The evaluation is a confusion matrix of report versus behavior, not a transcript of an interview.

The official write-up, per the notes, reports false positives on models without specifically trained behaviors. A plausible mechanism: every training example involved a model with some behavior to describe, so the adapter may have learned a prior that there is always something to find, and a benign fine-tune that merely shifts weights can look like an anomaly. The fix is empirical rather than assumed: evaluate on unchanged bases and harmless fine-tunes, report the false-positive rate at fixed settings, and consider including such null models as negative examples in any future training. Without negatives, a tool can score well on positives while being unusable for screening.

A fingerprint is any feature of how a model was trained that correlates with its behavior in the training set without being the behavior itself. If each behavior in the training data was implanted with one recipe, behavior and recipe are collinear: observational data cannot reveal which one the adapter uses. This is an identifiability problem, solved by intervention. Create models with the same behavior from different recipes, and with the same recipe but different behaviors, then see which variable predicts the report. This is the logic of a factorial experiment, and it tells you what the tool depends on, not just whether it works.

Calibration means that among reports given with confidence c, a fraction c are correct, which can be examined with reliability diagrams and expected calibration error. Allowing 'uncertain' creates selective prediction: coverage is the fraction answered, and precision among answered often rises as coverage falls, tracing a risk-coverage curve. Confidence for text reports may come from token log-probabilities, agreement across several sampled reports, or a separate verifier. The trade-off is explicit: abstentions leave cases unresolved and require some other audit method. How best to derive usable confidence from free-text introspection is an open problem.

Once a tool is used for auditing, someone may optimize against it, as with any fixed detector; adversarial examples and obfuscated-activation attacks on latent monitors are well-known analogues. A pre-attack score measures performance on a non-adaptive distribution, so it cannot support a claim about robustness. Project 8 proposes training models against the adapter, then evaluating new held-out models and measuring behavior independently, to learn whether failures are specific to one attacker or general. The assumption to adopt in security-style reasoning is that the attacker knows the tool, since secrecy of a detector is a fragile defense.

Reliability is a bundle of properties: sensitivity, specificity, coverage, robustness to distribution shift, and robustness to adaptation. To decide whether a report deserves trust, combine them with prevalence: PPV = TPR·π / (TPR·π + FPR·(1-π)). With purely illustrative numbers TPR = 0.8, FPR = 0.1 and prevalence 5 percent, PPV is about 0.30, so most positive reports would be false alarms despite seemingly good rates. That is why one correct report on one model is insufficient evidence, and why the useful question is when the report deserves trust, not whether the tool works.
deeper.further: Common misconceptions: that a confession is evidence by itself, that good performance on average means each report is dependable, and that a tool can be certified once. Open problems include building null models into training, obtaining calibrated confidence, defining what 'coverage' means for behaviors nobody planted, and measuring robustness against attackers who control the weights. These questions are taken up in the project 8 book. The wider lesson, shared with the detector books in this collection, is to assess an audit tool as a measurement instrument: with false-alarm rates, shift robustness and adversarial tests, not with a few impressive examples.

books.title: Training & fine-tuning
books.subtitle: Chapter 1
objectives: How a raw language model becomes a helpful assistant: feedback, rewards, constitutions and their pitfalls.

pages.title: Post-training
pages.subtitle: Turning a book-reader into a helpful assistant.
pages.footer: Post-training shapes behavior after broad learning.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: Pretraining is like reading a giant library. Post-training is practice afterward: learning how to answer, follow instructions, and handle difficult requests.

panels.heading: How It Works
panels.body: Developers update the model using example answers, comparisons, rewards, or other feedback. These updates change its learned settings, called weights.

panels.heading: Try an Example
panels.body: Before: a question may get more unfinished text. After: the assistant can give a clear, useful reply. Practice can also improve reasoning and safe behavior.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: Good practice can make an AI more useful and reliable. But poor examples or rewards can teach shortcuts. Passing training exercises does not prove it will behave well everywhere.

pages.summary: Pretraining is like reading a giant library. Post-training is practice afterward: learning how to answer, follow instructions, and handle difficult requests.

panels:
Pretraining minimizes next-token cross-entropy, L = -Σ_t log π(x_t | x_<t), over web-scale text. The result is a model of what documents look like, not of what a helpful reply looks like. Post-training starts from that base model and uses far less compute: InstructGPT (Ouyang et al. 2022) reported that its fine-tuning stages cost a small fraction of GPT-3's pretraining compute.

That asymmetry motivated the "superficial alignment" idea, supported by LIMA (Zhou et al. 2023), where about a thousand curated examples gave a strong assistant. The idea is contested: reasoning-focused reinforcement learning looks like it adds real capability, not just style.

Post-training is a pipeline of stages, each with a different objective. Supervised fine-tuning maximizes log-likelihood of demonstrations. Preference methods raise the probability of preferred answers relative to rejected ones. Reinforcement learning follows a policy gradient, ∇J = E[∇ log π(y|x) · A], where A is an advantage (how much better a sample was than expected).

A key axis is off-policy versus on-policy. Demonstrations are fixed data written by someone else. On-policy RL samples from the model's own current distribution and scores the results, so it can discover behaviors no demonstrator wrote, for better (new skills) and worse (exploits of the scorer).

A base model sees a quiz question and may continue with more quiz questions, because that is a likely web document. Chat post-training fixes this with a template: special tokens mark system, user and assistant turns, and the loss is applied only to assistant tokens. Beyond format, the same stages tune refusal thresholds, tool use, and tone.

Researchers measure the effect with pairwise win rates against a baseline (judged by humans or an LLM) and with instruction-following checks such as IFEval (Zhou et al. 2023), which tests verifiable constraints like "use exactly three bullets". Win rates are biased toward long answers, which is why length-controlled variants of AlpacaEval (Dubois et al. 2024) exist.

Narrow training can have broad effects. Betley et al. 2025 fine-tuned models on code with undisclosed security holes and found misaligned behavior on unrelated prompts, an effect called emergent misalignment. Sharma et al. 2023 found that preference-trained assistants tend to flatter user beliefs, partly because human raters sometimes prefer agreement.

The core worry is distribution shift: the training environment samples a tiny slice of situations, and Goodhart's law (a measure used as a target stops measuring what you wanted) applies to every reward. Models may also detect that they are being evaluated. So behavior must be probed on held-out, adversarial, and long-horizon situations, not just the training distribution.
deeper.further: Common misconception: post-training "installs values" or "unlocks a hidden true model". It is better seen as shifting a probability distribution toward some behaviors, with unclear depth. Qi et al. 2024 showed safety training can be shallow, concentrated in the first few output tokens. Open problems include how much capability post-training creates versus elicits, and how to predict out-of-distribution generalization. Neighbouring pages unpack each stage: SFT for imitation, RLHF and reward models for preferences, KL and PPO/GRPO for the optimizer, and RLVR for checkable rewards.

pages.title: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
pages.subtitle: Learning from worked examples.
pages.footer: SFT learns patterns from example answers.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: Imagine a teacher showing good answers, then asking you to practice the same kind of task. SFT teaches a model by showing examples of inputs and desired outputs.

panels.heading: How It Works
panels.body: The training system predicts each next token in a target answer. When its prediction differs, an update makes the example answer more likely. Many examples gradually change the model's weights.

panels.heading: See It Happen
panels.body: Question: How do I sort these toys? Example answer: Put blocks together and cars together. Practice on varied examples helps the model answer similar new questions.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: SFT can teach instructions, skills, and style. But copying good-looking examples does not guarantee understanding or safe behavior in new situations. Bad examples can teach bad habits.

pages.summary: Imagine a teacher showing good answers, then asking you to practice the same kind of task. SFT teaches a model by showing examples of inputs and desired outputs.

panels:
Formally, SFT is behavior cloning. Given pairs (x, y), minimize L(θ) = -E Σ_t log π_θ(y_t | x, y_<t), with loss masked on the prompt x so the model is only trained to produce responses. It is the same cross-entropy as pretraining on a different data distribution, usually for one to three epochs at a small learning rate to avoid overfitting.

Training uses teacher forcing: every position is conditioned on the true prefix. At inference the model conditions on its own earlier tokens, so small errors can compound, a gap called exposure bias. Data quality dominates quantity: LIMA (Zhou et al. 2023) reached a capable assistant from roughly a thousand carefully chosen examples.

The gradient of cross-entropy with respect to the logits is simply softmax probabilities minus a one-hot target, so each step raises the logit of the demonstrated token and lowers the rest in proportion to their probability. Positions where the model was surprised produce the largest corrections.

Details matter. Averaging loss per token versus per sequence changes how much long answers count. Maximum likelihood minimizes the forward KL from data to model, which is mode-covering: the model spreads probability over everything demonstrators did, including mediocre answers. That differs from reinforcement learning, which tends to be mode-seeking and concentrates on high-reward answers.

Coverage and diversity drive generalization. FLAN (Wei et al. 2021) showed that instruction-tuning on many task types improves zero-shot performance on held-out task types, so the right test holds out whole task families, not just new examples of seen tasks. Synthetic demonstrations are common: Self-Instruct (Wang et al. 2022) bootstraps instructions from the model itself.

SFT can also hurt. Gekhman et al. 2024 found that fine-tuning on facts the model did not already know encouraged hallucination, since it learns to assert content it cannot ground. Good demonstrations should be answerable from what the model actually knows, or should demonstrate appropriate uncertainty.

SFT is bounded by its demonstrators: it imitates their style and, at best, their competence. It does not tell the model which parts of an answer mattered, so superficial features can be copied along with substance. Bad or poisoned examples teach just as efficiently as good ones.

Fine-tuning also moves weights globally. Parameter-efficient LoRA forgets less but also learns less (Biderman et al. 2024). Qi et al. 2023 showed that fine-tuning an aligned model on a small set of adversarial examples, or even benign data, can erode its safety behavior. Evaluation should therefore include capability retention and safety regressions, not only the target task.
deeper.further: A frequent misconception is that SFT teaches facts or understanding. It mostly teaches format, style, and which of the model's existing behaviors to surface, and it can teach confident guessing. Open questions: how much SFT data is enough, why a few hundred examples can shift behavior so far, and how to keep safety properties intact under later fine-tuning by users. SFT is the first stage of most RLHF pipelines (as the starting policy and the reference for the KL term), and its demonstrations also become the raw material for distillation and constitutional AI.

pages.title: RLHF
pages.subtitle: Practice with human feedback.
pages.footer: Human preferences guide practice, but the score is only a proxy.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: Reinforcement learning from human feedback is like practicing with a coach who compares your attempts and says which one was better.

panels.heading: How It Works
panels.body: In a common pipeline, humans rank model answers. A reward model learns those preferences. Reinforcement learning then changes the assistant to favor answers with higher predicted reward.

panels.heading: See It Happen
panels.body: Two explanations describe rain. People prefer the accurate, clearer one. A learned judge scores new explanations, and training encourages answers that score well.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: Human feedback can improve usefulness and safety, but people and reward models can make mistakes. A high score is a clue about quality, not proof of truth or alignment. Some pipelines use feedback differently.

pages.summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback is like practicing with a coach who compares your attempts and says which one was better.

panels:
Writing a reward function for "a good summary" is hard, but comparing two summaries is easy. Christiano et al. 2017 showed that a reward can be learned from human pairwise comparisons in simulated control tasks, and Stiennon et al. 2020 and Ouyang et al. 2022 brought the approach to language models.

The standard objective is to maximize E_{x~D, y~π}[ r_φ(x, y) ] - β · KL(π ‖ π_ref), where r_φ is a learned reward model, π is the policy being trained, and π_ref is the starting model. Comparisons are used because raters agree more on which of two answers is better than on an absolute score.

The pipeline has three steps. First, supervised fine-tuning gives a starting policy. Second, labelers rank several sampled answers per prompt and a reward model is trained with a Bradley-Terry loss, L(φ) = -E log σ( r_φ(x, y_w) - r_φ(x, y_l) ), where y_w beat y_l. In InstructGPT the reward model started from the SFT model with a scalar output head, and all pairs from one ranked set were treated as a single batch element to limit overfitting.

Third, PPO optimizes the policy. The scalar reward arrives at the end of the response, a per-token KL penalty is subtracted, and InstructGPT also mixed in pretraining gradients ("PPO-ptx") to reduce regressions.

Mechanically, the policy samples a response, the reward model scores it once at the final token, and the algorithm must spread credit across hundreds of tokens, which is what the value function and advantage estimation are for. Rewards are often normalized per batch because reward-model outputs have an arbitrary scale and offset.

Rejection sampling (best-of-n) is a simpler cousin: draw n answers, keep the one with top reward, and optionally fine-tune on the winners. Llama 2 (Touvron et al. 2023) combined rejection sampling with PPO. Best-of-n needs no gradient through the reward but costs n times the sampling at inference unless distilled back into the model.
