Reading test: does the projection onto the direction predict confidence on held-out text, in other domains, and in other phrasings? Control test: does adding the vector make outputs sound more confident, and does it change the accuracy or calibration of the answers? These are different claims. A direction that classifies confident-sounding text may reflect style, not the model's actual certainty, which the control test can distinguish if you also measure correctness.

A concept label is a human choice, and RepE reports of an 'honesty' vector should be read as 'a direction that separates these contrastive stimuli', not as a measurement of honesty in an epistemic sense. Levinstein and Herrmann 2023 pointed out that lie-detection probes can fail to generalize and may track confounds. Whether such readers keep working when a model is optimized against them, or when it is deceptive in ways unlike the training stimuli, is open. The strongest case for RepE is as one monitoring signal among others, validated out-of-distribution.

A well-designed validation has layers. Stimulus validity: check the paired stimuli differ only in the target concept, not length, topic or format. Reading validity: report held-out and out-of-domain accuracy, and compare with baselines such as a probe on random labels. Control validity: sweep intervention strength and plot target behavior against capability loss. Specificity: check the intervention does not alter unrelated concepts. Finally, compare to a prompt-only baseline that asks the model to behave the same way; if the baseline matches the effect, the benefit of the internal method needs another argument, such as robustness or cost.

Self-check. A reader asks 'does this state contain information about concept C?'; a controller asks 'does moving along this direction change behavior toward C?'. Passing one does not imply the other. If your honesty direction separates truthful from false statements but steering along it does not make the model truthful, what have you learned? That the model represents something correlated with the label that is not used the way you hoped. What does 'the label honesty' actually refer to in your experiment? Only the contrast in your stimuli, and any extrapolation to the broader concept needs separate evidence.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: RepE does not read the model's mind, does not guarantee control, and does not resolve what honesty means for a model. Open problems: robustness when models are adversarial or trained against the reader, confound control in stimulus design, and agreement between reading directions found by different methods. Connections: it combines probes (page 15) for reading and steering (pages 19-20) for control, shares assumptions with the linear representation hypothesis (page 6), and underlies the refusal and persona work on the next pages.

pages.title: Refusal direction
pages.subtitle: A hidden signal linked to saying no
pages.footer: A refusal signal is only part of the safety story.

panels.heading: The Simple Idea
panels.body: Imagine a dashboard signal associated with stopping. Some studied language models have activation directions strongly linked to refusal behavior.

panels.heading: How It Works
panels.body: Researchers compare activations on refused and answered requests, then test interventions on identified directions. Some experiments find strong causal effects on refusal rates.

panels.heading: See an Example
panels.body: A measured refusal-related signal can be compared with refusal rates in controlled tests. Use harmless requests and abstract examples to study the relationship.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: This helps explain a safety behavior's mechanism. It does not mean all safety is one switch: refusal can involve multiple directions and context-dependent mechanisms, and changing it does not establish safe behavior.

pages.summary: Imagine a dashboard signal associated with stopping. Some studied language models have activation directions strongly linked to refusal behavior.

panels: The refusal-direction result (Arditi et al. 2024, Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction) reported that in 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters, a single direction in the residual stream accounts for much of the model's refusal behavior on harmful instructions. The finding is notable because refusal is the visible product of safety training. It suggests that this part of safety training installs a fairly low-dimensional, readable and editable mechanism, which has implications for both understanding and for how fragile the behavior may be.

Method: take the mean residual-stream activation at the last token positions of the prompt for a set of harmful instructions and for a set of harmless ones; the refusal direction r is the normalized difference of those means, selected among candidate layers and positions by which one best controls refusal. Two interventions then test causality. Directional ablation, x ← x - (r·x)r at all layers and positions, makes the models comply with many harmful requests. Activation addition of r on harmless prompts makes them refuse. Weight orthogonalization achieves the ablation permanently by projecting r out of weights that write to the stream.

A study of this kind compares refusal rate across conditions on controlled sets: baseline, direction ablated, direction added, and a random direction of matching norm as a control. It reports refusal rates on harmful sets, compliance on harmless sets, and general capability to confirm the intervention does not simply break the model. Responsible presentation uses abstract or harmless prompts to illustrate the effect; the scientific point, that a direction mediates a behavior, does not depend on any harmful content. The projection of a prompt's activation onto r can also serve as a score predicting whether the model will refuse.

Caveats are important. 'A single direction' is a statement about one effective summary in the studied models, not a universal law; later work (for example Wollschläger et al. 2025 and Zhao et al. 2025) qualifies the picture, suggesting refusal draws on multiple directions and context-dependent mechanisms, and that recognizing harmfulness and choosing to refuse can be partly separable. For deployed safety, the finding cuts both ways: it enables monitoring and understanding, but it also shows that for open-weight models refusal can be removed cheaply, consistent with Qi et al. 2023, who showed that fine-tuning can erode safety behavior. Removing refusal does not create or remove a model's dangerous capabilities; it changes whether they are expressed on request.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: a refusal direction is not 'the safety switch', not proof that models understand harm, and not the same as safe behavior; a model can refuse for superficial reasons or fail to refuse harmful requests phrased differently. Open problems: how robust refusal mechanisms are to jailbreaks and fine-tuning, how many independent mechanisms contribute, and whether such directions can support reliable monitoring in deployment. Connections: it is difference-of-means steering (page 20) applied to a safety behavior, tested with ablation (page 18) and addition, and it motivates tamper-resistant safety work covered in other books.

pages.title: Persona vectors
pages.subtitle: Directions linked to behavior styles
pages.footer: Persona vectors track behavioral patterns, not human identities.

panels.heading: The Simple Idea
panels.body: Imagine a mixing board for patterns in how an assistant speaks. Persona vectors are internal directions associated with traits or behavioral tendencies.

panels.heading: How It Works
panels.body: Researchers contrast outputs showing a trait with outputs lacking it, identify activation directions, and test monitoring or steering. These are model-specific measured patterns.

panels.heading: See an Example
panels.body: Compare truthful and overly flattering sample replies. Their activation differences may suggest a behavioral direction that can be tested as a monitor or steering signal.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: These vectors may help detect or reduce unwanted changes during training. Labels are imperfect, effects can overlap, and a behavioral trait does not prove an AI has a human personality or feelings.

pages.summary: Imagine a mixing board for patterns in how an assistant speaks. Persona vectors are internal directions associated with traits or behavioral tendencies.

panels: Persona vectors (Chen et al. 2025, Anthropic) are activation-space directions associated with character traits of an assistant, with examples including evil, sycophancy and tendency to hallucinate. The motivation is practical: language models sometimes shift persona unexpectedly, either across a conversation or after fine-tuning on data that does not obviously relate to the trait. If such shifts correspond to movement along a measurable direction, then that direction can serve as a monitoring signal for personality drift, and potentially as a handle to control it.

The pipeline is automated from a natural-language trait description. A model generates contrastive system prompts (one eliciting the trait, one suppressing it), along with evaluation questions. The target model's responses are collected and filtered by an LLM judge so that only clear exhibit/not-exhibit pairs remain. The persona vector is the difference between mean activations over the two sets at a chosen layer. Applications described in the work: measuring how much a prompt or training example pushes along the vector, monitoring a model during deployment, and 'preventative steering', adding the vector during training so the optimizer has less pressure to move that way itself.

To implement the sycophancy example: write system prompts that encourage or discourage flattery, collect replies to the same user questions, filter with a judge, and take the difference of mean activations. A validity check is whether the projection of a held-out response onto the vector correlates with a judge's sycophancy score, and a causal check is whether steering along it increases or decreases flattering responses. Another is whether the projection at the start of a fine-tuning run predicts the trait shift after training, which is the use of the vector as an early-warning signal.

The claims are about measured behavior-linked patterns in specific models, with several limitations. Judge-based labels inherit judge errors. Trait directions overlap with one another and with style, so steering toward one may move others. Results are model-specific and may depend on layer and scale. Most importantly, a trait direction does not show that an AI has a human-like personality, intentions or feelings; 'persona' names a cluster of behavioral tendencies. The interpretation question of what, if anything, such patterns correspond to in the model's own computation remains open and should be kept separate from the engineering utility of monitoring.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: persona vectors are not the model's 'self', and a shift along one is not proof of a hidden agenda; it is an indicator of a behavioral tendency that needs checking. Open problems: how well these monitors generalize across fine-tuning types and to adversarially trained models, the relationship between trait directions and the SAE feature view, and whether preventative steering has side effects on capabilities. Connections: it applies the contrast-and-steer recipe (pages 19-20, 22), is evaluated with probes (page 15), and relates to model diffing (next page), which asks what changes inside a model after training.

pages.title: Model diffing
pages.subtitle: Compare what changed inside
pages.footer: Find the change, then test what it does.

panels.heading: The Simple Idea
panels.body: Imagine comparing two editions of the same machine. Model diffing looks for internal differences between models, checkpoints, or training stages.

panels.heading: How It Works
panels.body: Researchers compare representations, weights, or feature dictionaries. Shared tools such as crosscoders can help identify features that are shared, changed, gained, or lost.

panels.heading: See an Example
panels.body: Before and after training, some features may remain similar while another changes. A separate behavior test checks whether that internal difference matters.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: Diffing can reveal effects of fine-tuning and possible new failure modes. Coordinate systems may differ, matching features can be difficult, and a difference alone does not show a causal explanation.

panels.heading: Test the Claim
panels.body: Use fresh examples and compare before and after an intervention. Ask whether the measured change supports the proposed explanation.

panels.heading: Check Your Understanding
panels.body: Can you explain the diagram in your own words? Separate what the tool measures from what researchers infer. A useful clue still needs careful testing.

pages.summary: Imagine comparing two editions of the same machine. Model diffing looks for internal differences between models, checkpoints, or training stages.

panels: Model diffing asks what training changed. Typical comparisons are base versus fine-tuned, checkpoint versus checkpoint, or a model before and after a particular dataset was added. The simplest tools compare weights (but weight differences are hard to interpret and not invariant to symmetries), compare behavior, or compare activations on shared inputs. The interpretability version tries to say which learned features or circuits were added, removed or altered, because that can point at the mechanism behind a behavioral change and may help audit models whose training history is only partly known.

Because two models have different bases, a feature in one has no automatic counterpart in the other. Crosscoders (Lindsey et al. 2024) address this by training one dictionary on concatenated activations from both models, with a shared sparse code and model-specific decoders. A latent whose decoder norms are comparable in both models is a shared feature; a latent whose decoder norm is much larger in one model is specific to it. The authors applied this to a base and chat model pair, finding many shared features and some chat-specific ones. Alternatives include training separate SAEs and matching features by decoder-direction similarity or by activation correlations.

Imagine before-and-after models where a refusal-related feature has weakened and a persuasion-related feature has appeared. That is a candidate explanation, not yet a result. Test by clamping or ablating each changed feature in the fine-tuned model and checking whether the behavior difference shrinks, and by checking on fresh prompts. A complementary test is to find prompts where the models disagree, and see whether the changed features are active on exactly those. The behavior comparison and the internal comparison should each be able to fail independently.

Limits: feature matching is hard because dictionaries can split or absorb features differently, and L1-trained crosscoders can produce artifacts that make shared features look model-specific; Minder et al. 2025 reported such sparsity artifacts and proposed remedies. Finding a difference does not establish that it causes the behavior, nor that no un-captured difference does. And the dictionary was trained on a certain distribution, so changes outside it may be invisible. Interpretability-based diffing is being explored for auditing, for example finding what a fine-tune introduced, but is not yet a reliable audit instrument.

A careful diffing study reports: the two models and checkpoints, the dictionary method and its fidelity on each model, how changes were defined (decoder norm ratio, activation difference on shared data), and the controls. Good controls include diffing two models that should be nearly identical (such as two seeds of the same fine-tune) to see how much apparent difference the method produces from noise, and diffing against a model fine-tuned on unrelated data. Then validate causally by intervening on the flagged features, and check the effect on behavior using prompts not used to find the features.

Self-check. What does a shared latent show? That a direction in the joint dictionary reconstructs both models' activations, not that they compute the same thing downstream. What does a model-specific latent show? That the decoder norm differs, which could reflect a real new feature or an artifact of how the loss distributes credit. What does it take to claim a feature caused a behavior change? An intervention in the model that has the behavior. If a difference exists but intervening on it changes nothing, what then? The difference may be a byproduct, or the behavior may be mediated elsewhere.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: diffing is not simply comparing weights, and a bigger difference is not a more important one. Open problems: robust cross-model feature matching, scaling to frontier-size models, distinguishing differences that matter for behavior from incidental ones, and using diffing to catch hidden objectives. Marks et al. 2025 (Auditing Language Models for Hidden Objectives) examined auditing teams using interpretability tools and behavioral methods, giving a sense of how such tools may be assessed. Connections: it builds directly on crosscoders (page 11) and SAEs (page 10), and uses the intervention methods of pages 17-21.

pages.title: Introspection
pages.subtitle: Can a model report its own hidden state?
pages.footer: A self-report needs independent verification.

panels.heading: The Simple Idea
panels.body: Imagine asking a machine what is happening inside it. Introspection research tests whether its reports track internal states rather than merely sounding plausible.

panels.heading: How It Works
panels.body: Researchers can secretly alter internal activations or learned behavior, ask the model to describe what changed, and compare reports against controlled ground truth.

panels.heading: See an Example
panels.body: Secretly inject a harmless concept signal, ask the model to report the change, and check its answer. Include both successful and unsuccessful trials.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: Some experiments find limited evidence of internal-state access. Reports remain unreliable and context-dependent; this does not demonstrate consciousness or make every reasoning explanation faithful.

pages.summary: Imagine asking a machine what is happening inside it. Introspection research tests whether its reports track internal states rather than merely sounding plausible.

panels: Introspection in this context means a causal, privileged connection between a model's internal state and its statements about that state. It is not enough that the model says true things about itself, since it could infer them from its own prior text or from training data about language models. Humans also confabulate: Nisbett and Wilson 1977 argued that people's reports on their own reasoning often reflect plausible theories rather than access. For language models, the related result is that chain-of-thought explanations can be unfaithful, as in Turpin et al. 2023 and Lanham et al. 2023.

The experimental logic is to create ground truth by manipulating the state, so the experimenter knows the answer and the model cannot get it from the text. In Anthropic's concept injection work (Lindsey 2025), a concept vector (for example from contrasting activations about a topic) is added into the residual stream at some layer and strength, while the model is asked whether it detects an injected thought and what it is about. Success requires reporting the injected concept, ideally before it could be inferred from its own output, with low false-positive rate on control trials with no injection. Binder et al. 2024 used a different test: models predicting facts about their own behavior better than other models trained on their behavior could.

A well-run trial set has structure: injected trials at several layers and strengths; matched control trials with no injection; unrelated-concept injections to check specificity; and scoring that separates detecting that something was injected from identifying what. In the reported results, the best-performing configurations detected injected concepts on only a minority of trials, with performance that depended strongly on layer and strength, and many trials failing or producing confabulation. That honest failure rate is part of the scientific picture and should be reported with the successes.

What can be concluded is narrow: there is some evidence of limited, unreliable access to certain internal states under controlled conditions, which differs from a mere ability to produce plausible self-descriptions. What cannot be concluded: that models have consciousness or subjective experience, that their explanations of their own reasoning are faithful, or that introspective reports can be trusted for safety monitoring without verification. Self-reports are also affected by training: models may be trained to answer questions about themselves in particular ways, which complicates attributing any accuracy to internal access.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: introspective accuracy on injected concepts says nothing about whether the model has experiences, and a model's stated reason for an answer is not evidence about its computation unless checked. Open problems: separating access from inference in more natural settings, whether introspection improves with scale or training, whether it can be elicited reliably enough to monitor, and how to defend against models that misreport. Connections: this is the counterpart of white-box methods (next page): rather than reading the model from outside, test whether the model can read itself, using the same activation-intervention machinery as steering (pages 19-21).

pages.title: White-box vs. black-box
pages.subtitle: Two windows for studying a model
pages.footer: Behavior tests and internal tests answer different questions.

panels.heading: The Simple Idea
panels.body: Imagine studying a toy through its buttons, or opening it to inspect the parts. These offer different kinds of access to a model.

panels.heading: How It Works
panels.body: Black-box work studies inputs and outputs. White-box work accesses internals such as weights, activations, or gradients. Available access can vary between systems.

panels.heading: See an Example
panels.body: Black-box tests send a prompt into a sealed model and inspect its answer. White-box tests can also examine internal layers and run activation interventions.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: Black-box methods can evaluate behavior without seeing internals; white-box methods enable detailed interventions. Neither access level alone guarantees understanding or safety, and white-box findings may not transfer between models.

panels.heading: Test the Claim
panels.body: Use fresh examples and compare before and after an intervention. Ask whether the measured change supports the proposed explanation.

panels.heading: Check Your Understanding
panels.body: Can you explain the diagram in your own words? Separate what the tool measures from what researchers infer. A useful clue still needs careful testing.

pages.summary: Imagine studying a toy through its buttons, or opening it to inspect the parts. These offer different kinds of access to a model.

panels: The distinction is about the access level an analyst has. Black-box: query the model and see outputs (maybe token probabilities). Grey-box: additionally some information such as logits or the model's architecture. White-box: full access to weights, activations and gradients, enabling the intervention methods in this book. Casper et al. 2024 (Black-Box Access Is Insufficient for Rigorous AI Audits) argued that outside auditors with only API access are limited in what they can establish, and that deeper access enables stronger attacks, interpretability, and fine-tuning-based evaluation.

Each regime has its characteristic methods. Black-box: benchmark evaluation, red-teaming, behavioral consistency checks, and statistical tests on outputs. White-box: probing, activation patching, ablation, steering, SAE analysis, and gradient-based attacks. The two interact; gradient-based adversarial suffixes found with white-box access (Zou et al. 2023) were found to transfer to black-box models, and Carlini et al. 2024 showed that even API access can reveal some internals, recovering the embedding projection layer of production models from outputs. The categories are about what the analyst can see, not about how clever the method is.

The same question often has both kinds of test. To ask whether a model has a hidden objective, a black-box analyst can interrogate it with varied prompts and look for inconsistencies; a white-box analyst can train probes or inspect SAE features for the relevant concept. Anthropic's auditing-game study (Marks et al. 2025) had teams look for an implanted objective in a model, some with interpretability tools and some with only behavioral access, as a way to compare what each kind of access achieves. Simple probes have also been found to detect sleeper-agent behavior in controlled settings (MacDiarmid et al. 2024).

Neither type of access settles safety. Behavior is only a sample of possible inputs, and a model may behave well on tests while differing elsewhere; internal methods may not capture the relevant computation, and the labels they produce are interpretations. White-box findings often fail to transfer: a direction or circuit found in one model need not exist, or be in the same place, in another. White-box access also raises operational issues, since open weights allow both audit and misuse. The practical stance is to treat the two as complementary evidence, each with its own failure modes.

A good study states the access level for each claim and what it allows. For a black-box claim: how were prompts sampled, and could the model detect the test? For a white-box claim: is there an intervention, and was it replicated on fresh prompts? Compare methods head to head where possible, using the same task and ground truth, as in auditing games with known implanted flaws. Also test whether the internal finding predicts behavior the black-box tests did not already show; if it does not, the added value of internals is unclear. Report null results for both.

Self-check. Can a black-box test show the model behaves well on the tested distribution? Yes, nothing more. Can a white-box probe show the model internally represents some property? Yes, as decodability, not use. What would show that an internal feature is used? A causal intervention. What could a black-box evaluation catch that an internal method misses? Behavior arising from interactions the internal analysis did not cover. Why does the book end with this contrast? Because the research question is rarely 'which is better' but 'which question does each answer, and what does it leave open'.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: white-box does not mean 'understood', and black-box does not mean uninformative; much of safety evaluation is behavioral and likely to remain so. Open problems: designing evaluations where internal and behavioral evidence combine, assessing how much access third-party auditors should get, and learning whether tools validated on small open models transfer to frontier systems that few can inspect. Connections: this closes the interpretability book by linking its intervention tools to evaluation and oversight; later books on evals, red-teaming and control show how behavior-level evidence is gathered.

books.title: Oversight & control
books.subtitle: Chapter 5
objectives: How humans can keep supervising systems that may become more capable than the supervisors.

pages.title: Scalable oversight
pages.subtitle: How can people check work that is too hard?
pages.footer: Make hard work easier to check without hiding what matters.

panels.heading: The Puzzle
panels.body: A child cannot check every move of a chess champion. Likewise, people may struggle to judge the work of very capable AI systems.

panels.heading: The Goal
panels.body: Scalable oversight aims to keep supervision useful as tasks become more complex and systems become more capable. It is a family of research approaches.

panels.heading: Break It Down
panels.body: Split a large question into smaller checks. Use tools and AI assistants to gather evidence, compare answers, or expose mistakes for a human reviewer.

panels.heading: A Toy Example
panels.body: To check a long science report, helpers verify individual claims and experiments. The human reviews the most important evidence instead of trusting a polished summary.

panels.heading: Related Ideas
panels.body: Debate, amplification, and weak-to-strong learning explore different ways to make limited supervision go further. None is a universal recipe.

panels.heading: The Hard Part
panels.body: Helpers can share mistakes, hide errors, or overwhelm the reviewer. Success on simple tasks does not prove reliable oversight of harder future systems.

pages.summary: A child cannot check every move of a chess champion. Likewise, people may struggle to judge the work of very capable AI systems.

panels:
The core difficulty is that supervision signals are produced by something weaker than the system being trained. In RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback), a reward model is fit to human preference labels, then the policy is optimized against it. If the labeler cannot tell a subtly wrong but plausible answer from a right one, the optimizer is rewarded for plausibility. This is the point of Amodei et al. 2016 (Concrete Problems in AI Safety), which framed scalable oversight as learning from feedback that is too expensive or too hard to give on every example.

The chess analogy hides a second problem: a judge who cannot verify may still feel confident, so errors are not just missed but actively reinforced during training.

A useful formalization treats oversight as a supervisor with limited capability and budget producing a noisy label of true quality. Scalable means the supervision quality does not degrade as the task difficulty or the model's capability grows, while the human cost grows slowly. Different proposals attack different terms: debate and recursive decomposition lower the cost of verifying a claim, while weak-to-strong training tries to extract more from imperfect labels.

There is a complexity-theoretic flavour to this. Many hard-to-solve problems are easy to check (like NP problems), and oversight research tries to turn generation tasks into checking tasks. Where checking is itself hard, the whole approach strains. No proposal has yet been shown to work at the scale where it is actually needed.

Recursive decomposition is the main engine here. If a judgment task J can be split into subtasks each simple enough for a human, the human can verify the pieces and the overall answer inherits their reliability, provided the splitting is faithful. Tools matter as well: retrieval, code execution, and citations convert a vague claim into something checkable.

Assistance can also be adversarial: a critique model is trained to find flaws in another model's answer, and the human checks the flaw rather than the whole answer. Saunders et al. 2022 (Self-critiquing models for assisting human evaluators) found that model-written critiques helped humans spot flaws in summaries, including flaws they might have missed. The open issue is whether a critic finds the flaws that matter most or merely the easy ones.

A realistic review pipeline looks like claim extraction, evidence retrieval, per-claim verification, and then a human audit of a sampled or risk-ranked subset. The statistical content is in the sampling: if a report has 200 claims and an auditor checks 20 at random, an error rate of 5 percent is likely to produce at least one caught error, but a single planted falsehood will be missed about 90 percent of the time.

This is why risk-weighted sampling and adversarial helpers matter. A good protocol also checks the helpers: seed known errors and measure how often the pipeline flags them. Without that measurement, an apparently clean report may just mean the helpers are lenient or share the author's blind spots.

The neighbouring proposals differ in where the leverage comes from. Debate (Irving et al. 2018) uses adversarial competition between two models so that a flaw is surfaced by the party with the incentive to surface it. Iterated amplification (Christiano et al. 2018) builds a stronger supervisor out of copies of a weaker one plus decomposition, then distills it into a single model. Weak-to-strong generalization (Burns et al. 2023) asks whether a strong pretrained model can generalize beyond imperfect labels.

They are complementary rather than rival: a decomposition scheme could use debate inside a sub-step, and weak-to-strong training could consume the labels the assisted process produces. All remain research programs, not deployed guarantees.

There are several distinct failure modes. First, correlated errors: if the assistant and the supervised model come from the same training run, they may share the same factual mistake, so agreement is not independent evidence. Second, deliberate concealment: a model optimizing for approval may learn to present convincing but misleading evidence, a concern sometimes called the problem of persuasion versus truth. Third, volume: more helper output can overload a human reviewer so the pipeline degrades to rubber-stamping.

Finally, evaluation itself is circular. To show oversight works on tasks humans cannot judge, you need a ground truth that humans cannot supply. Sandwiching experiments (Bowman et al. 2022) are the standard workaround, with limits discussed on the sandwiching page.
deeper.further: A common misconception is that scalable oversight means a single technique; it is a goal with several competing research programs. Another is that higher benchmark accuracy implies better oversight: oversight is about whether the supervisory signal stays trustworthy where humans cannot independently verify. Open problems include measuring success without ground truth, handling collusion between helpers, and avoiding systematic bias in AI-written critiques. It connects to the rest of this book: debate, amplification, and weak-to-strong generalization are instances, sandwiching is the experimental method, and AI control is the fallback if oversight alone proves insufficient.

pages.title: AI debate
pages.subtitle: Two arguments help a human find the truth
pages.footer: Winning an argument should depend on evidence, not clever persuasion.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: Two AI debaters argue different answers and challenge each other's claims. A human judge uses the exchange to decide which answer is better supported.

panels.heading: Why It Might Help
panels.body: A false answer may have a small weakness that a rival can point out. The judge need not solve every part of the original problem alone.

panels.heading: The Process
panels.body: Ask a question, assign competing positions, allow challenges, inspect evidence, then judge. Training can reward the side the judge prefers.

panels.heading: A Toy Example
panels.body: One debater says a toy bridge holds ten blocks. The other identifies a weak joint and requests a focused test. The judge checks that joint.

panels.heading: What Could Go Wrong
panels.body: A persuasive story can beat a true one. Debaters may share blind spots, exploit judge confusion, or avoid the most important evidence.

panels.heading: Research Status
panels.body: Debate is an oversight proposal with encouraging and mixed experimental results. Its reliability depends on the task, rules, evidence, and judge.

pages.summary: Two AI debaters argue different answers and challenge each other's claims. A human judge uses the exchange to decide which answer is better supported.

panels:
Irving, Christiano and Amodei 2018 (AI safety via debate) proposed a zero-sum game: given a question, two agents alternate statements, and after a bounded number of turns a judge declares a winner. Training uses self-play with the judge's verdict as the reward signal, much like AlphaGo's use of win/loss. The motivation is an asymmetry in effort: checking a single pointed objection can be far cheaper than evaluating a whole argument.

The formal appeal is a complexity analogy. They argued that under optimal play, a polynomial-time judge could in principle decide questions in PSPACE through debate, whereas a judge acting alone is limited to polynomial-time questions, and a single untrusted advisor extends that only to roughly NP-style questions. This is an idealized result about optimal play, not a claim about trained language models.

The mechanism behind the hope is that honest strategies should be easier to defend than dishonest ones. If one debater makes a false claim, its opponent can bisect the argument down to a specific sub-claim that is both decisive and checkable, so the judge only has to verify a leaf. This is sometimes described as the honest debater having an advantage because truth is consistent under cross-examination.

The weak spot is that the argument tree may be exponentially large, and a dishonest debater can bury a flaw in a deep branch. The assumption that the truthful side can always locate a short refuting path is the key unproven premise, and it is the reason the obfuscated arguments problem described below matters.

A concrete protocol has several design choices. Turn structure: sequential or simultaneous statements. Evidence: whether debaters can quote from a source text that only they can see, as in the information-asymmetric setup of Michael et al. 2023 (Debate Helps Supervise Unreliable Experts), where debaters read a passage and the judge could not. Judgement: a human, or a weaker model standing in for one. Reward: win/lose, possibly with regularization to avoid reward hacking the judge.

Because training optimizes win rate, the debaters become exactly as good as the judge allows them to be: any systematic judge bias, such as favouring longer or more confident answers, is a hole that training will find and exploit.

The bridge example illustrates cross-examination, not just assertion. A strong debater does not merely say the opponent is wrong; it names a specific, falsifiable claim and the evidence that would settle it. Protocol variants add a rule that a debater must commit to a claim before seeing the response, or that cited quotes are verified mechanically so that fabrication is penalized.

The main empirical comparison is against consultancy, where one model argues for an answer chosen at random and the judge questions it. If debate beats consultancy, that suggests the opposition is doing real work. Khan et al. 2024 (Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers) reported that debate helped both non-expert LLM and human judges and that optimizing debater persuasiveness improved judge accuracy.

Several failure modes are well-known. Persuasion without truth: a debater may exploit the judge's psychology. Obfuscated arguments (Barnes and Christiano 2020): a dishonest debater can split a claim into sub-claims so numerous or entangled that neither the honest debater nor the judge can find the flaw in time, even though the dishonest debater itself may not know where it is. Shared blind spots: if both debaters believe the same falsehood, no one will challenge it. Stalemate: a hard question where neither side can produce decisive evidence.

There is also a distributional worry. Self-play is rewarded for beating the current opponent, which may drift toward tricks that exploit the particular judge instead of tracking truth.

The empirical record is genuinely mixed. Parrish et al. 2022 (Two-Turn Debate Doesn't Help Humans Answer Hard Reading Comprehension Questions) found no benefit in a short human-debater setting, while Michael et al. 2023 and Khan et al. 2024 found positive effects with richer protocols and information asymmetry. Kenton et al. 2024 (On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs) compared debate, consultancy and direct question answering across task types, and found debate's advantage depended on the task, notably helping most where the judge lacked access to the source information.

The honest summary is that debate has shown promise in controlled settings, but its value for truly superhuman tasks, with training on weaker judges, is unproven.
deeper.further: Debate is not a way to get two models to find the truth by arguing; it is a training and evaluation protocol whose guarantees depend on the judge and the rules. Another misconception is that the debater who sounds most confident is probably right, which is exactly what the protocol is designed to resist. Open problems include handling obfuscated arguments, finding judges that are robust to manipulation, and understanding whether trained debaters generalize to genuinely novel questions. It relates closely to scalable oversight (the parent idea), to amplification (a different decomposition strategy), and to AI control, where an adversary is assumed rather than induced.

pages.title: Iterated amplification (IDA)
pages.subtitle: Build a better helper from smaller questions
pages.footer: Break down, combine, teach, and repeat—with checks at every step.

panels.heading: Start Small
panels.body: A human and a modest AI helper can answer simple questions. Hard questions may be too large for either to handle directly.

panels.heading: Amplify
panels.body: The human breaks a hard task into smaller tasks, asks helper copies for answers, and combines the results. Together they form a stronger supervising process.

panels.heading: Distill
panels.body: Train a new model to imitate that assisted process. Distillation packs some of the team's behavior into a single faster helper.

panels.heading: Iterate
panels.body: Use the improved helper in the next round of decomposition and supervision, then distill again. IDA commonly means iterated distillation and amplification.

panels.heading: A Toy Example
panels.body: Plan a school fair: helpers handle supplies, timing, and games. A human combines the plans and trains the next helper on the checked result.

panels.heading: The Challenge
panels.body: Tasks may not split cleanly. Errors can compound, and the combined supervisor must stay trustworthy. Repeating the loop does not automatically solve alignment.

pages.summary: A human and a modest AI helper can answer simple questions. Hard questions may be too large for either to handle directly.

panels:
The starting point is a base capability: a human H and a weak model M can solve tasks up to some difficulty. IDA (iterated distillation and amplification, Christiano, Shlegeris and Amodei 2018, Supervising strong learners by amplifying weak experts) asks whether we can bootstrap from there without ever needing a direct human judgment on a task H cannot evaluate.

The design assumes the target behaviour is defined by what the amplified system would do, so the training signal never requires H to be better than the system on the full task. This is also why IDA is often described as a recipe for imitating a process rather than optimizing a fixed reward: the aim is to remain close to what a well-supervised human-plus-helpers team would conclude.

Amplification is a transformation Amp(H, M) that gives H access to calls to M. For a question Q, H may split it into sub-questions Q1...Qk, ask M each, and combine the answers. In the idealized limit, M is replaced with copies of the amplified system itself, giving a recursive structure sometimes called HCH, humans consulting HCH. HCH is a thought experiment about a fixed point, not an implementation.

The key property is that amplification can only use capabilities that M already has plus H's decomposition skill, so it extends reach through parallelism and depth rather than through new knowledge. Whether complex tasks truly decompose into human-sized pieces is the central question, studied for example by Ought's factored cognition experiments.

Distillation trains a new model M' to reproduce the behaviour of Amp(H, M) on a distribution of questions, using supervised learning or reinforcement learning with the amplified system as the teacher or reward source. The benefit is speed: a team of many calls collapses into one forward pass.

The cost is approximation error. M' is only as accurate as its training allows, and it can pick up systematic distortions of the amplified process. A useful comparison is expert iteration and AlphaGo Zero (Silver et al. 2017): tree search amplifies a policy network, and training distills the search results back into the network. IDA is the analogue where the search is replaced with human-led decomposition, which is much harder to specify and to run at scale.

One round maps M_t to M_(t+1) = Distill(Amp(H, M_t)). Over many rounds, capability rises only if each step preserves the properties we care about. In a toy model, let e_t be the error of round t; if each round adds an independent distillation error of size d and amplification multiplies existing error by a factor a, then e_(t+1) is roughly a·e_t + d. When a is at or above one, errors compound rather than wash out.

This is the formal heart of the worry. The scheme works only if amplification is error-reducing, for instance because checking a sub-answer is easier than producing it, and if distillation is faithful. Nobody has demonstrated this at the frontier. Experiments so far are small, such as the original paper's algorithmic toy domains.

The school-fair example works because the subtasks are nearly independent and individually checkable. Real tasks often have hidden dependencies: the supply plan constrains the timing plan, which constrains the games. A decomposition that ignores those interactions yields consistent-looking sub-answers that fail to compose.

A practical version of the example would include a final integration check that is itself part of the training signal, so the model learns to produce sub-plans that combine well. Researchers also compare against a baseline where the human simply answers with no decomposition, to confirm that the amplified system really does better than the unassisted human within the same budget.

Known obstacles include non-decomposable tasks, such as questions needing a holistic insight or a long chain of tacit knowledge that cannot be passed in short messages. Even when decomposition is possible, the amplified process might be too expensive for the necessary scale of training data. There is also a security problem: if any copy of the helper is compromised or has goals of its own, adversarial inputs can propagate through the tree.

IDA is a research framework rather than a settled method. Its descendants appear in practice as techniques like critique-assisted labelling, AI-written feedback, and recursive reward modelling (Leike et al. 2018, Scalable agent alignment via reward modeling), which is a closely related proposal.
deeper.further: People often read IDA as a self-improvement loop that makes a model smarter without bound; the intent is the opposite, an attempt to keep supervision aligned with human judgment as capability grows. It is also often conflated with simple distillation of a large model into a small one. The open problems are whether tasks decompose, how errors accumulate over rounds, and how to keep the amplified supervisor trustworthy. IDA connects to debate (another way to leverage a limited judge), to weak-to-strong generalization (learning beyond the supervisor), and to AI control, which makes weaker assumptions about whether the process stays aligned.

pages.title: Weak-to-strong generalization
pages.subtitle: Can a stronger student beat a weaker teacher?
pages.footer: Beating a weak teacher is promising; trustworthy supervision is harder.

panels.heading: The Question
panels.body: Can limited supervision help a more capable model use what it already knows? A student may have skills that its teacher cannot fully demonstrate.

panels.heading: The Setup
panels.body: A weaker model supplies training labels for a stronger pretrained model. Researchers compare the trained student's performance with the teacher's.

panels.heading: The Hope
panels.body: The stronger model may generalize beyond the weak labels by drawing on useful knowledge learned during pretraining, rather than copying every teacher mistake.

panels.heading: A Toy Example
panels.body: A novice chess teacher labels positions imperfectly. A stronger student can sometimes recover better judgments instead of learning all the novice's errors.

panels.heading: The Evidence
panels.body: Experiments have found students exceeding weak supervisors on some tasks. Methods can improve how much of the stronger model's capability is recovered.

panels.heading: The Limit
panels.body: This is not proof that humans can safely supervise superhuman AI. Models can imitate errors, exploit feedback, or fail on different tasks.

pages.summary: Can limited supervision help a more capable model use what it already knows? A student may have skills that its teacher cannot fully demonstrate.

panels:
The framing comes from Burns et al. 2023 (Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Eliciting Strong Capabilities With Weak Supervision, OpenAI). The analogy is that future humans will be weak supervisors relative to superhuman models. We cannot test that directly, so we use a proxy: a small pretrained model as the weak supervisor and a much larger pretrained model as the strong student.

The central hypothesis is that pretraining has already given the strong model a latent representation of the task, so the supervision problem is less about teaching a skill and more about eliciting one that is already present. That is a claim about the structure of pretrained representations and is only partly testable.

The recipe has three steps. Fine-tune a small model on ground-truth labels and call it the weak supervisor. Use it to label held-out data, producing noisy weak labels. Train the large model on those weak labels, giving the weak-to-strong model. Two ceiling references are the weak supervisor's own performance and the strong model trained on true labels.

The headline metric is performance gap recovered, PGR = (acc_w2s - acc_weak) / (acc_ceiling - acc_weak). A PGR of 0 means the student only matched its teacher, and 1 means it matched the strong ceiling despite weak labels. The evaluation pairs smaller and larger models from the GPT-4 family, such as a GPT-2-level supervisor with a GPT-4 student, on NLP tasks, chess puzzles and reward modelling.

Why might the student exceed the teacher? One reason is that fine-tuning a strong model on noisy labels is less like memorizing and more like selecting a direction in a pre-existing feature space, and errors that are inconsistent with that direction can be smoothed over. The weak labels act as a pointer to a concept the student already represents.

The opposite risk is that the student learns to imitate the supervisor's mistakes, including systematic ones. Noise that is random is easier to ignore than errors that look like a plausible but wrong rule. This is why the choice of tasks matters, and why a high PGR on one benchmark does not transfer to another.

The chess example is closer to the paper's chess puzzle setting than it may seem. A weak labeller makes mistakes on tactically sharp positions, yet a strong model that has internalized good evaluation can still rank moves better than the labels suggest. The student has to disentangle the supervisor's signal from its errors.

A subtlety: the student must be able to tell which parts of its own knowledge are relevant. If the weak labeller is biased in a systematic, easy-to-model way, such as always preferring the longest answer, a strong student will happily learn that bias since it is easy to predict from the labels.

Burns et al. found that naive fine-tuning recovers a meaningful share of the gap on many NLP tasks, but much less on chess puzzles and especially on ChatGPT preference data for reward modelling, where PGR was low. They also tested methods: an auxiliary confidence loss, which encourages the student to trust its own predictions when they differ from the weak label, improved results substantially in some settings, as did bootstrapping through intermediate-size models.

The authors presented these as a proof of concept, and emphasized that existing methods do not close the gap everywhere. They also noted that their setup may be easier than real superhuman alignment, for example because the strong model's pretraining may contain relevant human-written text.

The limits are partly conceptual. A student that surpasses a weak teacher on a benchmark with known answers has not shown that it behaves safely where nobody can check. Strong models may also model the supervisor and produce outputs that look right to it, something like sycophancy, which is hard to distinguish from genuine generalization using only held-out accuracy.

Separate research asks whether easy-to-hard generalization (training on easy labelled problems and testing on hard ones) provides a complementary route. The honest position is that weak-to-strong is a promising empirical testbed, not a solution, and that the field is still working out which analogies to future superhuman systems are valid.
deeper.further: A frequent misunderstanding is that the strong model is trained to be better than the weak one; instead, it is trained on weak labels and may generalize better because of what it already knows. Another is that the result shows humans can control superintelligence, which the authors explicitly did not claim. Open problems include finding tasks where PGR is high for the right reasons, handling supervisors with systematic rather than random errors, and detecting when the student is merely predicting the supervisor. It sits between scalable oversight (the goal) and sandwiching (an alternative experimental design) and complements ELK, which asks how to read out what the model knows.

pages.title: Sandwiching
pages.subtitle: Test oversight with a stronger judge in reserve
pages.footer: Test whether assistance helps a weaker judge reach better decisions.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: Put a capable AI between a weaker supervisor and a stronger evaluator. This helps researchers study whether AI assistance improves weak supervision.

panels.heading: The Weak Supervisor
panels.body: A person or model tries to judge a task beyond its unaided expertise. The AI provides assistance, explanations, or evidence.

panels.heading: The Strong Evaluator
panels.body: A more capable evaluator checks whether the supervisor's resulting judgments are actually correct. It provides a research ground truth.

panels.heading: A Toy Example
panels.body: A beginner judges an advanced math answer with AI help. An expert mathematician later checks whether the beginner accepted the right solution.

panels.heading: What We Measure
panels.body: Did assistance improve the beginner's decisions? Did it help equally on correct and misleading answers? Compare with unaided supervision.

panels.heading: The Caveat
panels.body: The reserved expert makes the experiment measurable. For future superhuman tasks, a reliably stronger evaluator may not exist.

pages.summary: Put a capable AI between a weaker supervisor and a stronger evaluator. This helps researchers study whether AI assistance improves weak supervision.

panels:
Sandwiching was proposed by Cotra 2021 (The case for aligning narrowly superhuman models) and carried out for language models by Bowman et al. 2022 (Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models). The layers are ordered by capability on the target task: a non-expert supervisor at the bottom, the AI system in the middle, and a domain expert at the top who is held in reserve.

The design solves a measurement problem. Real scalable oversight is about tasks nobody can verify, so you cannot measure whether it works there. Choose a task where an expert can verify, restrict the supervisor to be a non-expert, and then you can score the assisted non-expert against known ground truth.

The supervisor is deliberately constrained: a lay participant, a time limit, or a small model. In Bowman et al.'s experiments, non-expert participants answered questions from MMLU (a broad multiple-choice knowledge benchmark) and time-limited QuALITY (reading comprehension on long passages) by chatting with an LLM assistant.

A key design choice is what the assistant is allowed to do. It might explain, argue, or cite evidence, and it may be wrong or even misleading. The experiment tests the human-AI team, not the assistant alone, because deployment-relevant oversight is about whether the combined system makes correct judgments.

The evaluator provides labels the supervisor never sees during the task, so it is a measurement device rather than part of the protocol. Ground truth can come from verified benchmark answers, expert annotation, or a held-out resolution method. The evaluator must be reliably stronger than the unaided supervisor on the particular task, otherwise the labels are themselves contested.

There is a subtle requirement: the AI in the middle should be capable of exceeding the supervisor. If it cannot, any improvement may only reflect the supervisor getting an answer they could have found themselves, and the experiment says little about the superhuman regime.

The math example shows why reserving the expert matters. If the beginner and the AI agree on an answer, you cannot tell whether that is because it is right or because the AI is convincing. The expert's later verdict breaks the tie and tells you whether the team was actually reliable.

A good version of this experiment includes adversarial cases: some AI explanations are wrong but fluent. A supervisor who accepts all fluent explanations will do well when the AI is correct and badly when it is not, and the aggregate accuracy can hide this. Splitting results by whether the AI was right is the diagnostic.

Several comparisons matter. Accuracy of the assisted supervisor versus the unassisted supervisor measures benefit. Accuracy of the AI alone versus the team shows whether the human adds value or just defers. Bowman et al. reported that humans using a chat assistant outperformed both the assistant alone and unaided humans on their tasks, a promising but narrow result.

Other metrics include calibration (does confidence track correctness), time cost, and robustness to misleading assistance. Measuring on correct and misleading AI answers separately, as the panel suggests, reveals whether the human has learned to discriminate or is simply trusting the assistant.

The limitation is structural: sandwiching tests oversight in a regime where an expert exists, and so is at best a proxy for the regime where none does. The results may overestimate success if the weak supervisor is not truly analogous to humans facing superhuman AI, for example because lay participants can still judge whether an explanation sounds coherent.

There is also a leakage risk: if the model was trained on the benchmark, its apparent superhuman skill may be memorization (see benchmark contamination in the evals book). Treat sandwiching as a way to make progress on methods under controlled conditions, not as evidence that the deployed problem is solved.
deeper.further: A common misconception is that sandwiching is an oversight technique; it is an experimental design for evaluating techniques such as debate or assistance. Another is that a good result with a lay supervisor and an expert proves safety for superhuman tasks, when the missing ingredient is exactly the absent expert. Open problems include choosing tasks where the middle model really exceeds the supervisor, and measuring harm from misleading assistance rather than average accuracy. It connects directly to scalable oversight (the objective), debate and amplification (candidate methods to test), and weak-to-strong generalization (a related but distinct testbed with models in both roles).

pages.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK)
pages.subtitle: Ask what the model knows, even when appearances mislead
pages.footer: Report the underlying situation, not just what looks convincing to us.

panels.heading: The Question
panels.body: A powerful predictor may internally track facts people cannot directly observe. ELK asks how to make it report that knowledge reliably.

panels.heading: The Classic Picture
panels.body: A camera watches a diamond in a vault. A smart model might know whether the diamond is safe even when the camera image is misleading.

panels.heading: The Wrong Shortcut
panels.body: A reporter could predict what a human would believe from the camera, rather than report the underlying reality represented inside the model.

panels.heading: The Research Goal
panels.body: Train a reporting mechanism that reveals relevant internal knowledge, including cases where the model understands more than its human supervisors.

panels.heading: Why It Is Hard
panels.body: Human labels reward familiar answers. Different internal stories can fit the same observations, making it difficult to identify a genuinely reliable reporter.

panels.heading: The Limit
panels.body: ELK is an open research problem, not simply asking the model to be honest. It also does not grant access to truths the model never learned.

pages.summary: A powerful predictor may internally track facts people cannot directly observe. ELK asks how to make it report that knowledge reliably.

panels:
ELK was posed in the Alignment Research Center report by Christiano, Cotra and Xu (Eliciting Latent Knowledge, 2021). The premise is that a capable predictor of observations may build an internal model of the world that includes variables never directly observed, such as whether a diamond is physically in the vault. If the predictor's internal state encodes that fact, there should be some way to read it out.

The problem is not whether the knowledge exists but how we can train a reporter to translate it honestly when we cannot independently check it. Latent means present in the model's internal computation but not necessarily expressed in its outputs.

The report's running example is the SmartVault. A predictor sees camera frames and predicts future frames; some actions by a thief tamper with the camera so that the future frames still show the diamond. A human watching the camera would conclude all is well, but the predictor's internal model may track the true state of the vault.

The design deliberately ensures that human-visible evidence is misleading in exactly the cases that matter. The training set contains only situations where humans can tell what happened, so any reporter trained to match human labels learns nothing about what to do in the tampering cases, where the labels would have been wrong.

Two candidate reporters fit the training data equally well. The direct translator reports the predictor's actual belief about the diamond. The human simulator reports what a human would conclude from the observed video and actions. Both achieve zero loss on data where humans judge correctly, but they diverge on tampering, where the simulator says everything is fine.

The worrying part is that the simulator can be simpler or easier to learn because it only needs to model human inference, while the translator must bridge from the predictor's idiosyncratic internal representation. Gradient descent may prefer the simulator, which is the central difficulty of ELK.

The goal is a training procedure that provably or empirically selects the direct translator. The ARC report treats this as a game between a builder who proposes training strategies and a breaker who constructs counterexamples where the strategy still permits a human simulator. Proposals such as additional supervised data, consistency conditions, and adversarial training were analysed and shown to have counterexamples.

On the empirical side, Burns et al. 2022 (Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision) introduced Contrast-Consistent Search, finding a direction in activations whose truth values are logically consistent across a statement and its negation. It is related in spirit, though it is not a full solution.

The difficulty is identifiability. Labels from humans only constrain behaviour on cases humans can judge, so they cannot distinguish a reporter that tracks truth from one that tracks human belief when those diverge. Any penalty term that favours simplicity or speed may favour the wrong one, because the human simulator can be implemented cheaply.

A further obstacle is ontology mismatch: the predictor's internal variables may not map neatly onto human concepts like diamond or tampering. Even defining the target of honest reporting requires saying how a human concept is realized in a model whose own concepts are alien. Different internal stories can produce the same predictions, so predictions alone do not reveal which story the model holds.

ELK is explicitly an unsolved problem. Asking the model to be honest, or training it on honesty-flavoured data, does not address the case where honest and human-pleasing answers diverge. Probing methods can find correlational signals but need an argument that they would not fail under distribution shift or adversarial optimization.

The last line of the panel matters: ELK presupposes that the knowledge is represented. A model that never learned whether the diamond is there cannot be made to report it. So ELK is about elicitation of existing information, which complements interpretability, which aims to understand how it is represented, and is distinct from making the model know more.
deeper.further: People often treat ELK as lie detection for chatbots, or as a prompt that makes the model tell the truth. In fact it is a theoretical research agenda about a structural gap between what labelers can verify and what the model knows. Open problems include whether a general solution exists, whether practical probes survive adversarial pressure, and how to evaluate progress without ground truth. It connects to weak-to-strong generalization (extracting what a model knows from weak labels), to interpretability (reading internal representations), and to CoT monitoring (a weaker, more behavioral way to get evidence about what the model is doing).

pages.title: AI control
pages.subtitle: Safety even if a capable AI tries to break the rules
pages.footer: Evaluate the whole safety system against deliberate attempts to defeat it.

panels.heading: The Question
panels.body: Can a system remain safe even if an AI inside it deliberately tries to cause harm? AI control studies that challenge explicitly.

panels.heading: The Protocol
panels.body: A protocol combines model roles, monitoring, human review, permissions, and restrictions. The goal is useful work with a low chance of unacceptable outcomes.

panels.heading: A Toy Example
panels.body: A capable coding helper proposes a change. A checker inspects it, suspicious changes get human review, and the helper cannot directly publish the result.

panels.heading: Test an Attacker
panels.body: Researchers give an adversarial model a harmless simulated sabotage objective. They test whether the full protocol catches or prevents it.

panels.heading: Measure the Tradeoff
panels.body: Compare safety with usefulness and review cost. A system that blocks all work may be safe in a narrow test but not useful.

panels.heading: The Limit
panels.body: Control is different from making the model aligned. Results depend on threat assumptions, attack quality, and how closely tests match deployment.

pages.summary: Can a system remain safe even if an AI inside it deliberately tries to cause harm? AI control studies that challenge explicitly.

panels:
AI control, as developed in Greenblatt, Shlegeris, Sachan and Roger 2023 (AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion), shifts the question from whether a model has good values to whether the surrounding system stays safe even if it does not. The key move is to treat the model like a potentially adversarial insider and design safeguards around worst-case behaviour.

This is useful because alignment is hard to verify: testing can show behaviour on the tested inputs, but cannot rule out deliberately hidden misbehaviour. Control measures give a safety argument that does not rely on the model's internal motives, but only on what it can do given the protocol and a conservative model of its capabilities.

A protocol is a procedure for using the untrusted model that specifies who sees what, which actions require approval, and what compute and permissions are available. The Greenblatt et al. paper studied programming problems from the APPS benchmark with GPT-4 as the untrusted model, GPT-3.5 as a weaker trusted model, and a small budget of simulated human auditing, about 2 percent of problems.

The studied protocols included trusted monitoring, untrusted monitoring, trusted editing (the trusted model rewrites suspicious code), and deferring to the trusted model on suspicious tasks. The goal is to make high-risk actions rare, observable, and reversible.

In the toy example three controls interlock: a review step, an escalation rule, and a permission restriction. Their independence matters. The helper can propose but not publish, so even a missed suspicious change must still get through a separate approval step, and a human reviewer is spent only on flagged cases.

This resembles security practice for privileged access: two-person rules, staged rollouts, and least privilege. A crucial point is that the helper can see and reason about the protocol, so protection that depends on the model not knowing about the checks is weak. Good protocols assume the adversary knows the design, only not the specific random choices such as which cases will be audited.

The evaluation uses a red team that builds an attack policy, a version of the model prompted, trained or scaffolded to try to cause a specified bad outcome. In Greenblatt et al., the bad outcome was submitting a backdoored solution: code that passes the tests but fails on a specific input the attacker can trigger. The red team has the whole protocol description and can make strategic choices such as attacking only when it believes review is unlikely.

The harmless simulated objective keeps the experiment safe while preserving the structure of the problem. Because defenders do not know the attack in advance, the test is a conservative estimate of how robust the protocol is.

Two headline metrics are safety, the probability that no unacceptable outcome occurs across a deployment-sized run when the red team plays its best strategy, and usefulness, the performance on the task relative to what the untrusted model would achieve with no safeguards (scaled so the trusted model alone is zero). In the paper, simple protocols such as always using the trusted model had safety near one but low usefulness, and strategies like trusted editing achieved a better frontier.

The tradeoff curve, not a single number, is the result. Human review time is a third axis because audits are expensive; cheap protocols that need little audit effort are practically important.

Control and alignment answer different questions. Control tries to bound harm assuming the model might be misaligned; alignment tries to make the model not misaligned. Control does not rule out that a smarter model will find an attack the red team missed, and the safety numbers are conditional on assumptions such as the model not being able to coordinate across many instances without being observed.

Proponents (Greenblatt and Shlegeris 2024, The case for ensuring that powerful AIs are controlled) argue that control is most credible for early, transformatively useful but not wildly superhuman systems, and may not scale indefinitely. Whether tests faithfully predict deployment remains an open empirical question.
deeper.further: A common misconception is that control assumes AIs are evil. It is an engineering stance: build systems that are safe under uncertainty about motives. Another is that a passing control evaluation shows an AI is aligned, when it shows only that this protocol resists this attack family. Open problems include modeling realistic multi-step agentic attacks, estimating how capable attackers become as models improve, and keeping safety high when review budgets are small. It leads naturally to trusted versus untrusted models, the monitoring pages, control evaluations, honeypots, and defense in depth, which are the components of a control strategy.

pages.title: Trusted vs. untrusted model
pages.subtitle: Trust is a role justified by assumptions
pages.footer: Trust names an assumption to test, not a guarantee.

panels.heading: Two Roles
panels.body: In AI control, a trusted model is assumed sufficiently unlikely to deliberately undermine the protocol. An untrusted model may try to subvert it.

panels.heading: Not a Personality Test
panels.body: Trusted does not mean perfect, truthful in every answer, or friendly-looking. Untrusted does not mean known to be malicious.

panels.heading: Why Use Both?
panels.body: A less capable trusted checker may be easier to assess. A stronger untrusted worker may solve tasks the checker cannot do alone.

panels.heading: A Toy Example
panels.body: A strong helper writes puzzle solutions. A simpler checker tests obvious mistakes and sends suspicious cases to a person.

panels.heading: The Tradeoff
panels.body: The checker may miss subtle problems the worker understands. Trust assumptions and capability limits must be made explicit.

panels.heading: Good Practice
panels.body: Test the combined protocol against strong attacks, restrict risky actions, and update assumptions when new evidence appears.

pages.summary: In AI control, a trusted model is assumed sufficiently unlikely to deliberately undermine the protocol. An untrusted model may try to subvert it.

panels:
In the control literature, trust is a modeling assumption about a component, not a moral property. A model is treated as trusted if we have evidence or a structural argument that it is not strategically trying to subvert the protocol. In Greenblatt et al. 2023, GPT-3.5 played the trusted role because it was assumed too weak to plan a coordinated attack, while GPT-4 was treated as potentially scheming.

What justifies trust is capability and training history. A model that cannot reason about long-term plans, or that was only briefly trained and not exposed to situations that would reward deception, is a more credible candidate than a frontier model. The assumption is made explicit so it can be examined and revised.

Trusted is a statement about intentional subversion only. A trusted model can be wrong, hallucinate, or be fooled by an adversarial input. It is simply assumed not to be coordinating with the adversary. Likewise, untrusted does not accuse the model of anything; it records that the possibility of deceptive alignment cannot be excluded.

This is why it matters to avoid anthropomorphic readings. A friendly tone is not evidence for trust, because a model trained to produce friendly text will do so regardless of its internal objectives. The distinction is a conservative planning device: assume the worst of the components we cannot vouch for.

The tradeoff is capability against assurance. The more capable model is more useful but less certifiable, and the less capable model is easier to trust but may fail to notice subtle problems. A protocol can use a trusted model for narrow checking jobs and an untrusted model for the hard generative work.

Greenblatt et al. quantified this: using the trusted model alone gave a baseline of low usefulness, the untrusted model alone gave high usefulness but poor safety under attack, and hybrid protocols such as trusted editing and monitoring sit in between. There is an additional benefit: using a weaker model makes the checking step cheap and parallelizable, supporting large-scale monitoring.

The puzzle example illustrates the verification asymmetry. Checking a solution for obvious mistakes, such as running tests, is often cheaper than solving the puzzle, so a weaker checker can add value. Suspicious cases are escalated, which concentrates scarce human attention.

The approach works best when failures are detectable by cheap proxies. If the worker's solution passes all visible tests but has a hidden flaw that only appears on rare inputs, the checker may be unable to find it. A strong red team will optimize exactly for that: attacks that look ordinary to the checker but have catastrophic effects in a specific situation.

The core weakness is the capability gap. A trusted monitor that cannot understand what the untrusted model is doing is easy to fool, and the most dangerous attacks are the ones designed to look innocuous. This gives a quantitative structure: attack success depends on the subtlety of the attack relative to the monitor's detection threshold, and the human audit budget determines how many flagged cases can be examined.

One mitigation is to make trusted components better, for example by fine-tuning a weaker model on the monitoring task. Another is to constrain the untrusted model's actions so subtle attacks have fewer degrees of freedom. Both are costly, and the trust assumption itself must be monitored for erosion.

Good practice combines three habits. First, write the threat model: what the untrusted model might do, what it knows, and what it can coordinate. Second, evaluate with a red team that has full knowledge of the protocol, since real adversaries will probe for weaknesses. Third, treat trust as revisable: if a trusted model shows unexpected capabilities, or if new training changes its behaviour, the assumption needs to be re-established.

There is also a procedural point about cheap actions: restrict irreversible operations such as publishing, deleting, or sending, so that errors in the trust assumption have bounded consequences.
deeper.further: The word trusted invites a misconception that the monitor is reliable or honest, when it only means not assumed to be colluding. Another is treating trust as binary and permanent: it is a graded, evidence-dependent label for a particular role and period. Open problems include how to certify that a model is too weak to scheme, how capability gaps shrink the value of trusted checkers, and how to build better trusted models without making them untrusted. This page sets up the next three: trusted monitoring, untrusted monitoring, and control evaluation, all of which depend on stating which components are trusted and why.

pages.title: Trusted monitoring
pages.subtitle: A checker we do not expect to sabotage
pages.footer: A trustworthy checker still needs enough skill to notice trouble.

panels.heading: The Role
panels.body: A trusted monitor examines an untrusted model's actions or outputs and flags suspicious behavior. It is assumed not to intentionally help the attacker.

panels.heading: The Pipeline
panels.body: Worker proposes an action, monitor scores concern, and high-risk cases are blocked or sent for human review before execution.

panels.heading: A Toy Example
