objectives: Responsible scaling, safety levels, security and the governance ideas around frontier AI.

pages.title: Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP)
pages.subtitle: A lab's plan for managing growing AI risks.
pages.footer: Read the evidence and the commitments.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: A climbing team writes down how it will check danger and prepare protection as the mountain gets harder.

panels.heading: What Is the RSP?
panels.body: Anthropic's voluntary framework addresses catastrophic risks from advanced AI. It describes risk assessment, safety plans, and accountability.

panels.heading: Assess the Risk
panels.body: Ask what a system can do, how it could cause harm, and whether the defenses are adequate. Capability alone is not the whole risk.

panels.heading: Current Structure
panels.body: Version 3.4 includes Frontier Safety Roadmaps, Risk Reports, governance measures, and recommendations for industry-wide safety.

panels.heading: Plans vs Commitments
panels.body: Some roadmap items are public goals. Industry recommendations are not all unconditional company commitments. Read the actual policy wording.

panels.heading: Accountability
panels.body: The policy sets governance and review procedures, including a Responsible Scaling Officer, reporting channels, and external review provisions.

panels.heading: A Living Document
panels.body: The latest policy can differ substantially from older summaries. Check its effective date, updates, and whether a statement is a requirement or an aspiration.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: A policy can organize evidence and decisions, but cannot prove safety. Rules evolve; this card reflects the policy checked on October 12, 2026.

pages.summary: A climbing team writes down how it will check danger and prepare protection as the mountain gets harder.

panels: The climbing analogy corresponds to a specific design idea: if-then commitments. Karnofsky (2024), If-Then Commitments for AI Risk Reduction, describes policies of the form 'if a model shows dangerous capability X, then the developer will implement protections Y before proceeding'. The appeal is that it ties precautions to evidence rather than to a calendar or to general worry, allowing development to continue under low risk while pre-committing to costly measures if a warning sign appears. The concept was introduced as Responsible Scaling Policies by METR (then ARC Evals) in 2023, and Anthropic published its first RSP in September 2023.

Anthropic's RSP is voluntary, meaning it is a self-imposed company framework, not a law, and its enforceability depends on internal governance and public accountability. Its core loop is: evaluate models for capabilities relevant to catastrophic risk areas (the earlier versions emphasized chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear misuse and autonomous AI research and development), determine which safeguards are required, and decide whether deployment or further scaling is justified. Because the policy is text the company wrote, readers should check what it binds the company to do, who decides, and what happens if safeguards are not ready. Earlier versions allowed pausing training or deployment if protections lagged capabilities.

The assessment panel reflects a risk decomposition: risk depends on capability, on the pathway by which harm could occur (who has access, what resources they need, what uplift the model gives), and on the strength of mitigations. Risk assessment methods include capability evaluations by internal and external red teams, uplift trials comparing people with and without model access, and threat modeling. The related idea of a safety case (Clymer et al. 2024, Safety Cases) is a structured argument, backed by evidence, that a system is safe enough in a given context; it can rely on inability (the model cannot do the dangerous thing), control, trustworthiness, or deference to credible AI advisors. Evaluations are weakest when elicitation is incomplete, so reports should state how hard testers tried.

The beginner card lists the current structure: Frontier Safety Roadmaps, Risk Reports, governance measures and industry recommendations. For a reader, the useful distinction is between documents that describe the company's own assessment (reports), forward-looking goals (roadmaps), and conditions that trigger obligations. A roadmap is a public statement of intended work and can be tracked against later reports; a report presents evidence and judgments others can scrutinize. Because these labels are specific to version 3.4, consult the policy itself for exact definitions, and note the date on which this card was checked. The comparison with earlier versions illustrates how such frameworks evolve as the science and company practice develop.

The line between commitments and aspirations is the crux of evaluating any such framework. A commitment is a statement the company is bound to follow, ideally specific, measurable and with consequences; an aspiration or recommendation describes what the company hopes will happen or what it thinks other actors should do. Recommendations to industry or governments, such as shared standards, can matter for policy debates but are not costly constraints on the author. Skeptics reasonably ask whether commitments are specific enough to falsify, whether the company can revise them unilaterally (voluntary policies usually can), and whether third parties can verify compliance. Reading the exact operative verbs (will, must, aims to, recommends) is the main tool.

Accountability features in such policies typically include a named internal owner and a path for staff concerns. The beginner card names a Responsible Scaling Officer, reporting channels and external review provisions. In governance terms, these address the principal-agent problem inside a company under competitive pressure: someone with defined authority can pause or escalate, employees can raise concerns without retaliation, and outsiders can audit some claims. Their strength depends on independence (does the officer report to a board or to the executives whose products they review?), disclosure (are findings published?), and enforcement. As with other self-regulation, the real test is behavior when commitments are costly.

The date and the version matter because the document has changed substantially since its first version. The original 2023 RSP defined AI Safety Levels with specified commitments; the October 2024 revision introduced capability thresholds and required safeguards with a more flexible structure; and further revisions followed. Secondary summaries, including blog posts and model-card excerpts, may describe a superseded structure, so the primary document is the authority. When comparing across versions, check what changed: definitions of thresholds, who decides, which risks are covered, and which obligations were loosened or tightened. The distinction between requirement and aspiration should be reassessed in each new version.

A policy organizes decisions; it does not itself reduce risk unless it changes what the organization does. Even a well-designed framework rests on fallible evaluations, possible under-elicitation of dangerous capability, and judgments about whether safeguards are good enough, and no evaluation can prove absence of danger. The most that policy can do is structure evidence, assign responsibility, create commitments that outsiders can hold the company to, and support similar practices across labs; other developers published comparable frameworks in 2023 to 2024, including OpenAI's Preparedness Framework and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework. The card's date stamp is a reminder that conclusions about the current policy should be re-verified.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: that an RSP is a regulation, that passing its evaluations proves a model safe, or that older summaries describe the present policy. Open problems include how to specify thresholds for capabilities that are not yet measurable, how to verify compliance externally, how voluntary commitments interact with law (such as emerging frontier-AI rules), and how to make commitments credible when a competitor might not follow. It connects to the next pages on ASLs, capability thresholds and classifiers, which are the pieces the framework uses, and to the race-to-the-top page on incentives.

pages.title: AI Safety Levels (ASL)
pages.subtitle: Groups of protections, not an intelligence score.
pages.footer: Ask which risk, which protections, and which version.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: A lab uses stronger protective equipment when the work could create bigger dangers.

panels.heading: What Does ASL Mean?
panels.body: Anthropic introduced AI Safety Levels to organize technical and operational safeguards for increasingly serious risks.

panels.heading: Two Kinds of Protection
panels.body: Deployment safeguards limit harmful use. Security safeguards protect model weights and infrastructure from unauthorized access.

panels.heading: Capability Is Different
panels.body: A capability threshold describes what a model can do. A safeguard level describes protections. A level is not a universal ranking of intelligence.

panels.heading: The Framework Changed
panels.body: RSP version 3.4 retains ASLs for present mitigation levels. Future capabilities are addressed through risk arguments rather than fixed new control lists.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: Do not treat ASL labels as guarantees or assume every future level is fully specified. Check the policy version and threat being addressed.

pages.summary: A lab uses stronger protective equipment when the work could create bigger dangers.

panels: The protective-equipment picture encodes proportionality: precautions scale with the severity and likelihood of harm, so low-risk work does not carry the full burden of high-risk work. The borrowed model is biosafety levels (BSL-1 through BSL-4), a long-established scheme in which pathogens are grouped by risk and each group has a defined set of containment practices. The attraction for AI is that a graded scheme lets a developer commit in advance to what protections accompany what risk, instead of arguing case by case under deadline pressure, and lets outsiders compare the promised protections with what is done. The design also forces the question of what the highest tier would need, before any model demands it.

Anthropic's AI Safety Levels (ASL-1, ASL-2, ASL-3 and so on) follow this structure: the level names a package of required protections matched to a class of risk. ASL-1 describes systems posing no meaningful catastrophic risk, and ASL-2 describes models with early signs of dangerous capabilities but no meaningful uplift yet, handled with baseline safeguards. ASL-3 was activated by Anthropic in May 2025 for Claude Opus 4 as a precaution about possible assistance with chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapons development. The analogy is useful but imperfect: a pathogen's properties are fixed, while a model's risk depends on prompting, tools and users.

Two safeguard families correspond to two different threat models. Deployment safeguards address misuse by people who legitimately have access through an API or product: training to refuse, input and output classifiers, usage monitoring, account-level enforcement, rapid response to jailbreaks, and bug-bounty style red teaming. Security safeguards address the model weights themselves being stolen: access controls, insider-risk programs, hardened infrastructure, and bandwidth limits on data leaving secured environments. A model can have strong deployment safeguards and weak security (a stolen copy can be run without any filters), or the reverse, so each needs separate evidence of adequacy.

The card makes a conceptual separation that is easy to blur. A capability threshold is a property of a model, e.g. 'could meaningfully assist a novice in producing a dangerous agent', established by evaluations. An ASL is a property of the protections in place. The policy logic links them: if a model crosses a capability threshold, then it should operate under a specified ASL's safeguards. This is why an ASL number is not a score of intelligence, quality or trustworthiness: a more capable model on a benign domain may require no additional safeguards, while a less capable but specialized model near a dangerous threshold might. Confusing the two leads to claims like 'ASL-3 means the model is smarter', which the framework does not say.

The beginner card says version 3.4 retains ASLs for present mitigation levels while addressing future capabilities through risk arguments instead of fixed control lists. Conceptually this resembles a move from prescriptive rules to a goal-based or safety-case approach (Clymer et al. 2024 describe safety cases): rather than pre-writing safeguards for each future level, the developer must argue, with evidence, that risk is acceptably low. The trade-off is familiar from regulation: prescriptive rules are easier to audit but can be wrong or outdated for novel risks; goal-based approaches adapt better but depend on the quality and honesty of the argument and on someone competent evaluating it. For version-specific details, rely on the policy text itself.

Labels can create false assurance. An ASL describes intended safeguards, and what matters is whether they work: do classifiers withstand adaptive attackers, is insider risk actually reduced, were red-team results independent? Conversely, saying future levels are not fully specified means that commitments about higher-risk systems rely on judgment at the time. To read any claim about ASLs critically, ask four questions: which risk domain is meant, which threat actor the safeguards assume (an opportunistic individual, an organized group, a state), what evidence shows the measures work, and which version of the policy applies. Absent those, the label conveys little beyond its name.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: that ASL ranks model intelligence, that ASL-3 means a model is dangerous or that it is safe, or that all labs use these terms. Other developers use different structures, so comparisons need care. Open problems include defining the thresholds beyond what we can currently test, verifying security against well-resourced attackers (the RAND report Securing AI Model Weights, Nevo et al. 2024, defines graded security levels for this reason), and independent auditing of whether deployment safeguards meet stated standards. The next pages cover thresholds in more detail and one concrete deployment safeguard, constitutional classifiers.

pages.title: Capability thresholds & safeguards
pages.subtitle: Notice the new ability. Prepare the right protection.
pages.footer: New abilities call for new risk checks.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: When a child learns to ride faster, the route, supervision, and protection need a fresh look.

panels.heading: The Threshold
panels.body: A capability threshold marks a meaningful ability relevant to a specified risk. It is not just a better score on any benchmark.

panels.heading: The Safeguard
panels.body: A safeguard reduces the chance or impact of harm: access limits, monitoring, secure storage, or restrictions on actions.

panels.heading: A Simple Example
panels.body: If a toy agent can now operate tools independently, review what it can access and which actions need human approval.

panels.heading: Test the Whole System
panels.body: Consider tools, users, permissions, and opportunities as well as the model. Test whether protections actually resist realistic failures.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: Thresholds guide decisions; they do not make risk binary. Under current RSP, distinguish company plans from broader recommendations and verify the latest text.

pages.summary: When a child learns to ride faster, the route, supervision, and protection need a fresh look.

panels: The key idea is to link precaution to change. If a framework scaled safeguards only with model size or compute, it would be a poor proxy because capability does not track compute smoothly across domains. A capability threshold is therefore defined in terms of a risk-relevant ability, and the policy states what must be true before proceeding once the threshold is reached or cannot be ruled out. Because capability can jump with new training methods, tools, or scaffolding, the framework relies on a repeated cycle: evaluate, compare against thresholds, adjust protections, and re-evaluate when the model, its tools or the elicitation methods change.

A threshold should be specific enough to test. Examples used in public frameworks include the ability to provide serious uplift to people seeking to create biological or chemical weapons, or to substantially accelerate AI research and development. Because the real-world quantity of interest (uplift to an actor) is hard to measure directly, evaluators use proxies: expert-written question sets, tool-use tasks, controlled studies comparing performance of people with and without model assistance, and red-team exercises. A benchmark score alone is not the threshold, since it is a proxy that may over- or under-state real uplift; thresholds are reached by a weight-of-evidence judgment, and evaluations often include a margin of safety for under-elicitation.

Safeguards are interventions that cut either the likelihood of harm or its severity, and they differ in what they depend on. Access limits and permission scoping reduce the action space; monitoring detects misuse after the fact or in real time; secure storage prevents theft; human approval gates insert judgment before irreversible steps; and refusal or classifier systems block specific content. Each has failure modes, such as bypass, delay in detection, or false alarms. Layering them is the standard approach, with independence between layers important so that one failure does not defeat all: a jailbreak that fools a model should not also fool a separate classifier.

Autonomy changes the risk profile because consequences come from actions, not only text. Consider a permission matrix for an agent: for each tool and resource, what is the worst plausible outcome, is it reversible, and can it happen before a human can review? Use least privilege, so that credentials are scoped to the task; require approval for actions with irreversible or external effects; sandbox code execution; log everything. The same capability moves from one safeguard class to another as tools are added; a model that only chats poses different risks than the same model with browsing, code execution and email, which is why the threshold depends on the deployment context and not only the weights.

A model evaluated in isolation is not the full system. Risk emerges from the combination of model, scaffold (prompts, tools, memory), users (including adversarial ones), data and permissions, and the environment. Whole-system testing includes adversarial red teaming of the deployed product, tests of safeguards under realistic attack (not just cooperative use), and exercises on incident response. It also includes checking that safeguards still work after updates, because small changes in model or prompt can degrade a classifier's recall or change refusal behavior. The standard for a safeguard is evidence that it works against capable attackers, not that it was installed.

Thresholds are decision aids, and risk varies continuously: a model just below a threshold is not risk-free, and one just above is not catastrophic. Treating them as binary invites gaming (optimizing to stay just under) and brittle conclusions. Good practice reports distance to threshold, uncertainty, and the effect of better elicitation. Also keep apart what the company does and what it recommends others do; per the beginner card, these differ under the current policy. Because policies get revised, read the date and effective version, and distinguish a requirement on the author from an aspirational recommendation to industry or government.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: that crossing a threshold means disaster, that staying under means safety, or that evaluation scores equal real-world uplift. Open problems include how to measure risk from capabilities that are only partially elicited, how to set thresholds for emerging domains such as autonomous operation, and how to verify safeguard effectiveness against adaptive adversaries. It connects to ASLs (the protection packages) and to system cards (where evaluation results are disclosed).

pages.title: Constitutional classifiers
pages.subtitle: Teaching safety filters from written principles.
pages.footer: Clear rules → good examples → tested filters.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: A gatekeeper learns examples of what may enter and what should be stopped, using a clear rulebook.

panels.heading: Start with Principles
panels.body: A constitution defines allowed and disallowed content categories. It is a safety specification, not a legal constitution.

panels.heading: Make Training Examples
panels.body: AI-generated prompts and responses provide varied examples of those categories, including attempts to disguise disallowed requests.

panels.heading: Train the Filters
panels.body: Input and output classifiers learn to flag content. They guard an assistant before or during its response.

panels.heading: Two Possible Errors
panels.body: A filter can miss harmful content or block harmless content. Evaluate both, including new attacks and ordinary questions.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: This can strengthen jailbreak defenses, but does not eliminate every attack. Pair filters with other protections and keep updating their tests.

pages.summary: A gatekeeper learns examples of what may enter and what should be stopped, using a clear rulebook.

panels: A classifier here is a separate model that reads text and outputs a harm score, so refusals do not depend only on the main model's training. Having an independent layer matters because the assistant's own refusal behavior is a single point of failure: a jailbreak that persuades the assistant can still be caught by a model trained for the narrower task of recognizing prohibited content. The intended threat is a universal jailbreak, a prompt strategy that reliably unlocks a wide range of prohibited outputs, as opposed to one-off exploits. Defending against universal jailbreaks matters most for domains such as chemical and biological weapons, where a single reliable bypass could enable repeated misuse.

In Anthropic's Constitutional Classifiers work (Sharma et al. 2025, reported in its research post), the constitution is a natural-language list of what is permitted and what is prohibited (for instance, explaining which household chemicals should not be mixed versus providing weapons synthesis steps). Writing the boundary as an explicit text has two advantages: it can be updated by editing the text instead of relabeling a dataset, and it makes the intended behavior inspectable. The name echoes Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022), in which a model critiques and revises its outputs against written principles, though the classifier work applies written rules to build classifiers rather than to train the assistant directly.

Training data is synthesized by prompting a language model with the constitution to generate many prompts and completions in both categories, then augmenting them by transformations that mimic jailbreak tactics: translation, role-play framing, encoding or obfuscation, and style changes. This covers attack variety without waiting to collect real attacks. The quality of the synthetic data limits the classifier, as gaps in the constitution or the generator's imagination become blind spots. A feedback loop with red-teaming addresses this: attacks that succeed are folded back into the data, and the constitution is revised if the boundary was ambiguous or too broad.

Architecture matters for usability. An input classifier screens the user's prompt; an output classifier screens the response, and in the described design it evaluates the response token by token as it streams, so harmful content can be cut off mid-generation without waiting for the full answer. This streaming design allows lower latency than classifying only after completion, though it increases engineering complexity, and truncated outputs are visible to users. Defense is layered with the assistant's own refusals, rate limits and account enforcement. Classifier decisions are thresholded: moving the threshold shifts the balance between catching harmful content and blocking harmless content, and the operating point is a policy choice that depends on the stakes.

Evaluate with the confusion matrix: false negatives (missed harm) and false positives (blocked harmless requests). Report recall at a fixed false-positive rate, and measure the harmless refusal rate on realistic traffic since over-refusal has real costs for legitimate users, such as students, clinicians and safety researchers. Attack evaluation needs adaptive adversaries who see outputs and iterate, not a static list of known jailbreaks. Anthropic reported a large drop in automated jailbreak success for an updated system (from roughly 86 percent without classifiers to under 5 percent with them), a small increase in refusals of harmless queries and a noticeable compute overhead, and a bug-bounty style red-teaming effort of over 3,000 hours that did not find a universal jailbreak for an earlier prototype; read these as that project's reported figures, not guarantees.

The honest summary is a raised cost of attack, not an end to attacks. Public challenges following the release exposed weaknesses in demonstration systems, and attackers keep adapting, for example by splitting a harmful task into innocuous pieces across turns or exploiting output-only cues. This is why classifiers belong in a layered system: model-level training, classifiers, account-level monitoring, rapid patching, weight security, and policies that decide which domains justify the cost. Continued evaluation is essential since classifier performance can degrade as models, prompts and attackers change. The research value is a worked template of specification, synthetic data, and adversarial testing that other labs and domains can adapt.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: that classifiers read the constitution at run time (they are trained from it), that they make the model safe in general (they target specific misuse categories), or that a low jailbreak rate in a test generalizes to all future attackers. Open problems include the balance of false positives and false negatives in dual-use domains, multi-turn and agentic attack surfaces, and cost. It sits within the ASL deployment-safeguard family, and connects to the red-teaming book for how attacks are found.

pages.title: System card / model card
pages.subtitle: A report card for understanding an AI.
pages.footer: Read what was tested and what was not.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: A toy's information sheet tells you what it does, how it was tested, and when to be careful.

panels.heading: Model Card
panels.body: Documents a model's intended uses, development context, measured performance, and limitations. Contents vary across organizations.

panels.heading: System Card
panels.body: Often covers a deployed system more broadly, including tools, safeguards, evaluations, and risks beyond the base model.

panels.heading: What to Look for
panels.body: Which version was tested? On what tasks? With what tools? What failed? What remains unknown? Compare claims with supporting methods.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: Documentation supports informed decisions and independent scrutiny. A card is not a safety certificate; missing tests and limited coverage still matter.

pages.summary: A toy's information sheet tells you what it does, how it was tested, and when to be careful.

panels: Mitchell et al. (2019), Model Cards for Model Reporting, proposed a short structured document accompanying a trained model: intended use and out-of-scope uses, training and evaluation data, metrics, and performance disaggregated by relevant groups or conditions such as demographic or environmental factors. The disaggregation requirement is the technically important part, because a single aggregate accuracy can hide large gaps between subpopulations. It built on Gebru et al. (2018), Datasheets for Datasets, which proposed a parallel template for documenting how a dataset was collected and what it should or should not be used for. Both borrow from documentation practice in safety-critical industries such as electronics, where components come with specifications.

Because the template is a proposal, not a standard, contents vary and are voluntary. A good model card answers: what is it for, what data shaped it, how was it evaluated, in which conditions does it fail, and what ethical considerations apply. Shortcomings in practice include vague intended-use statements, evaluation on convenient benchmarks, and no description of failure cases. Evaluate a model card like a methods section: could someone reproduce or challenge the numbers? Does it report uncertainty, and are comparison baselines fair? For open-weight models, the card also communicates license terms and known misuse risks, which downstream users rely on.

System cards emerged for frontier language-model products, where the unit of risk is the deployed system rather than the bare model. OpenAI's GPT-4 system card (2023) is an early widely read example, and Anthropic and others now publish extensive cards. Typical contents include capability evaluations; safety evaluations (harmful-content refusals, bias, jailbreak robustness); results of red-teaming by internal and external groups; evaluations for dangerous capabilities relevant to scaling policies; agentic and tool-use behavior; and in some cases alignment-related investigations such as sycophancy, deception, or evaluation awareness. Because behavior depends on prompts, tools and safeguards, a system card should say what configuration was tested.

Reading a card critically means checking the details that determine whether results transfer. Version: the tested checkpoint might differ from the released one. Elicitation: were the models given scaffolding, tools, long reasoning budgets and best-of-n sampling, or tested in a minimal setting that underestimates capability? Contamination: could benchmark items be in training data? Comparison: are baselines tested under the same conditions? Statistical care: sample sizes, confidence intervals, number of attempts. Independence: which evaluations were run by third parties, and did they have enough access and time? Omissions are informative too: a card that omits a standard test or reports only favorable subsets calls for questions. Compare claims across successive cards from the same developer for drift.

Documentation creates accountability by making claims checkable, but a card is a self-report, produced by the developer, at a point in time, covering selected tests. It cannot demonstrate the absence of failures, particularly rare ones or those that emerge only at scale in deployment. Researchers therefore argue for complementary mechanisms: independent audits with meaningful access, incident reporting, post-deployment monitoring, and standardized reporting formats so cards are comparable. Regulation is moving in this direction, for example transparency requirements for providers of general-purpose AI models in the EU AI Act. Treat the card as the beginning of due diligence rather than a certificate.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: that a model card is a safety rating, that system cards and model cards are interchangeable, or that more pages means more rigor. Open problems include standardizing what frontier developers must disclose, ensuring evaluations are robust to the model recognizing it is tested, giving third parties access to verify claims, and reporting tail risks honestly. The topic links back to the RSP (which uses evaluation results to decide safeguards) and to the evals and red-teaming book, which covers how those results are produced.

pages.title: Weight security
pages.subtitle: Protecting the files that hold a model's learned behavior.
pages.footer: Secure the model files and limit who can copy them.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: A workshop protects the detailed settings that let someone rebuild its powerful machine.

panels.heading: What Are Weights?
panels.body: Weights are learned numerical parameters used to run a model. They are different from a chat transcript or a system prompt.

panels.heading: Why Protect Them?
panels.body: Unauthorized copies can enable independent use or modification, outside the original operator's access controls and monitoring.

panels.heading: Layers of Security
panels.body: Limit access, protect storage and transfers, monitor unusual activity, and control sensitive infrastructure. No single lock handles every threat.

panels.heading: Match the Threat
panels.body: A curious outsider, criminal group, and sophisticated insider pose different challenges. Defenses should name the threat they address.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: Protecting weights can reduce misuse and theft risks. It does not establish alignment, and authorized open-weight releases are a separate policy choice.

pages.summary: A workshop protects the detailed settings that let someone rebuild its powerful machine.

panels: A trained model, once its architecture is known, is fully determined by its weights: arrays of floating-point numbers, often hundreds of gigabytes to terabytes, produced by an expensive training run. A leaked copy gives an attacker a complete working model. The economics are lopsided: training might cost tens or hundreds of millions of dollars in compute, whereas copying the file costs almost nothing. That asymmetry, along with weights being a compact artifact that can be moved by a few insiders or a compromised system, is what makes them a high-value target. Nevo et al. (2024), the RAND report Securing AI Model Weights, analyzes around 38 attack vectors, ranging from phishing to supply-chain compromises to insider threats.

Weights are distinct from a conversation or a system prompt: a prompt is text provided at inference and a transcript is data; weights encode the learned function. They are also distinct from the training data and code, each of which could be secret separately. This matters for threat modeling: an attacker who steals weights can fine-tune away safeguards, run the model without monitoring, and deploy it at scale; an attacker who only steals a prompt can copy a persona. Model extraction attacks that query an API to approximate a model's function exist, but they are limited compared to theft of the exact parameters, and rate limits and monitoring raise their cost.

Beyond theft for commercial gain, the safety concern is loss of control over deployment safeguards. Safeguards such as refusal training, classifiers and usage monitoring live in the lab's serving stack, and fine-tuning can remove refusal behavior from open weights cheaply, as multiple studies of safety fine-tuning removal have shown. So if a model with dangerous capabilities is stolen, the developer's deployment safeguards no longer apply, and the developer cannot revoke access. This is why scaling policies treat security as a separate protection track alongside deployment safeguards: the security level should rise as the potential for misuse of a stolen model rises.

Defense in depth for weights typically combines several layers. Identity and access: multi-party authorization, least privilege, hardware security keys. Infrastructure: isolated training and serving environments, hardened endpoints, network egress controls, and limits on outbound bandwidth that make bulk exfiltration slow and detectable. Cryptography and hardware: encrypted storage and, increasingly, confidential computing, where weights are decrypted only inside attested trusted execution environments; Anthropic has published research on confidential inference using trusted virtual machines. Monitoring: anomaly detection on access patterns, audit logs, and insider-risk programs. Operations: red teaming of the security stack, incident response drills, and supply-chain controls.

Security design starts with a threat model: who is the adversary, what are their resources and what do they want? The RAND report defines five security levels (SL1 to SL5) tied to operational capacity of attackers, from amateur and opportunistic actors up to top-priority operations by leading nation-state agencies, and argues that stopping the highest tier requires measures beyond current common practice. Insider threats need different controls from external attackers: personnel vetting, compartmentalization, separation of duties, and monitoring. A statement like 'we protect weights' is meaningless without naming the adversary class and the assumed capabilities; the claim should be testable by red-team exercises and, ideally, external audit.

Weight security is about control over who runs the model; it does not address whether the model is aligned. A secure but misaligned model remains misaligned, and an aligned model that is stolen can be modified. The two properties are logically separate axes, which is why the policy treats them as separate safeguards. Open-weight release is a deliberate decision to give up weight security for the benefits of transparency, research access and competition, and it requires its own risk analysis: marginal risk compared with already available tools, the ability of users to remove safeguards, and the irreversibility of release. Reasonable people differ on where the balance lies for different capability levels.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: that weights contain stored training data in a retrievable form (some memorization occurs, but weights are not a database), that API access equals weight access, or that encryption alone solves theft. Open problems include securing weights against nation-state actors at acceptable cost, verifying security claims externally without revealing vulnerabilities, and preventing insider exfiltration. It connects to ASLs (security safeguards), the compute governance page (the physical supply chain), and the oversight and control book (assuming a model might be adversarial inside a secure environment).

pages.subtitle: AI near the edge of what is currently possible.
pages.footer: The frontier moves. Keep checking the capabilities.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: Frontier explorers work near the edge of the known map. The edge moves as people discover more.

panels.heading: What It Means
panels.body: Frontier AI generally refers to highly capable models near the leading edge of development, especially when discussing new capabilities and risks.

panels.heading: Why the Edge Moves
panels.body: A once-leading model can become ordinary as techniques, hardware, and competitors improve. The label depends on time and context.

panels.heading: Capability Is Not Safety
panels.body: A model may lead in one area and lag in another. Risk also depends on access, safeguards, deployment, and how the system is used.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: New capabilities can bring benefits and unfamiliar hazards. Policy definitions differ; use explicit capability criteria instead of relying only on a label.

pages.summary: Frontier explorers work near the edge of the known map. The edge moves as people discover more.

panels: Frontier is a relative term borrowed from policy rather than a technical measurement. Anderljung et al. (2023), Frontier AI Regulation: Managing Emerging Risks to Public Safety, defined frontier AI models as highly capable foundation models that could possess dangerous capabilities sufficient to pose severe risks to public safety. The notion is deliberately linked to risk and not merely to being the best at some benchmark, because the regulatory interest is in models whose capabilities are not yet well understood. The explorer analogy suits: the interesting question is not how far the map extends but what is unknown at its edge and how much surprise the territory may hold.

That paper identified three regulatory challenges that distinguish frontier models. Unexpected capabilities: capabilities can arise or be discovered after training, so risks are hard to forecast. Deployment safety: it is difficult to prevent a deployed model from being used harmfully. Proliferation: once a model exists, it can spread through weight theft, open release, or replication by others as costs fall. These suggest regulatory building blocks such as standards, mandatory disclosure and registration, and compliance mechanisms. Other bodies use different definitions, so comparing claims about 'frontier' requires checking the definition in each document.

Operationalizing 'frontier' typically uses proxies. Compute thresholds are the most common because they are measurable before deployment: the EU AI Act presumes systemic risk for general-purpose models trained with more than 10^25 floating-point operations, and a 2023 US executive order used a 10^26 threshold for reporting requirements (it was later rescinded). Training compute for dense transformers is roughly 6 · N · D FLOPs (N parameters, D training tokens). Compute is imperfect, since algorithmic progress lowers the compute needed for a given capability. Hernandez and Brown (2020) estimated that the compute required for a fixed ImageNet accuracy halved about every 16 months. Capability-based criteria are therefore a complement.

A frontier label says nothing about safety. A model can lead on coding and lag on multilingual tasks or agentic reliability; benchmark leadership does not map to risk. Risk is a function of capability, access, safeguards and context, as discussed in the scaling-policy pages. Models just behind the frontier can still be risky if they are open-weight and cheap to run, and the capabilities of frontier systems diffuse to smaller ones within a year or two. This diffusion argues for planning for capabilities rather than for named models, and for evaluating at each level whether safeguards that rely on scarcity of access will keep holding.

Use explicit criteria whenever a policy or article invokes frontier AI: which models (by compute, by capability evaluation, by developer), measured how, and at what date? Industry groups such as the Frontier Model Forum (founded 2023) and the company commitments announced at the 2024 Seoul summit use the term to scope safety frameworks, but each ties obligations to different triggers. The concept's usefulness lies in focusing scrutiny on the least-understood systems; its danger is vagueness, which allows firms to claim or avoid the label as convenient. Rules defined by a moving frontier can also entrench incumbents if thresholds are set high.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: that frontier means largest model, that it means unsafe, or that the term has a single definition. Open problems include thresholds that adapt as algorithms improve, ways to test dangerous capabilities before wide deployment, and how regulation should treat open-weight models near the frontier. It ties to compute governance (the main measurable proxy), the RSP (which attaches safeguards to capabilities), and the AGI/TAI page, where the terms describe different things.

pages.title: Compute governance
pages.subtitle: Rules around the computing resources that power AI.
pages.footer: Govern compute carefully; measure capability directly too.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: If very large engines need special care, communities may track where they are built and how they are used.

panels.heading: What Is Compute?
panels.body: Compute is processing work done by chips. Training and running AI require hardware, energy, and time.

panels.heading: What Is Governance?
panels.body: Policies can address access to advanced chips, large training projects, cloud services, reporting, or verification.

panels.heading: Why Use This Lever?
panels.body: Advanced hardware is physical and often concentrated. That can make some activities easier to observe than software alone.

panels.heading: Limits and Tradeoffs
panels.body: Compute is an imperfect proxy for capability. Rules can burden useful research, affect privacy or competition, and miss efficient or distributed development.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: Compute governance is one possible policy tool. Combine it with capability testing and accountable institutions; proposals are not universal laws.

pages.summary: If very large engines need special care, communities may track where they are built and how they are used.

panels: Sastry et al. (2024), Computing Power and the Governance of AI, argues that compute has properties that make it a promising point of intervention. It is detectable (large data centers and chip flows are physical and visible), excludable (hardware can be withheld or access conditioned, unlike ideas), quantifiable (FLOPs, chip counts and energy can be measured and audited), and supply is concentrated: advanced chips depend on a small number of firms and fabrication steps, including lithography equipment and leading-edge foundries. These properties contrast with data and algorithms, which are easy to copy. Compute governance uses these properties to monitor and sometimes restrict who can train or deploy powerful systems.

Compute is measured in floating-point operations (FLOPs) for total work and FLOP/s for rate. For dense transformers, training compute is approximately C ≈ 6 · N · D, where N is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. A chip's peak throughput is lower in practice than the datasheet: utilization of 30 to 50 percent is common in large training runs. Governance relevant quantities include cumulative training compute for a model, cluster size and interconnect bandwidth, and inference compute for deployment. Because inference can now be used for reasoning at test time, inference compute is also becoming a capability lever, complicating thresholds based solely on training compute.

Policy instruments vary in who they touch. Export controls restrict the sale of advanced chips and equipment to specified countries (the United States began in October 2022 and updated rules afterwards). Reporting requirements oblige providers to notify authorities of training runs above a threshold. Know-your-customer rules for cloud providers could identify who rents large clusters. Licensing or registration of large clusters, hardware-enabled mechanisms (such as location or usage verification built into chips), and international verification are proposals with varying maturity. Each balances effectiveness, enforceability and costs, and some depend on technical features that remain research problems, such as hardware attestation resilient to tampering.

Visibility is the first benefit: governments and the public know little about frontier training efforts, and compute data can show who has capacity to build the most capable systems. Second, compute is a lever when risks are tied to capability, which in the scaling-laws regime correlates with compute (Kaplan et al. 2020 and Hoffmann et al. 2022 showed performance improving predictably with compute and data). Third, it can enforce safety standards by conditioning access on compliance, such as requiring evaluations before training or deployment beyond a size. The argument is that where direct oversight of software is hard, controlling the physical bottleneck is a practical proxy.

Limits are substantial. Compute is a proxy: algorithmic efficiency gains mean the same capability needs less compute over time (Hernandez and Brown 2020 estimated roughly 16-month halving for a vision benchmark), so fixed thresholds drift downward in significance. Post-training and test-time compute may deliver capabilities that cumulative training compute does not capture. Distributed or pooled training across many small clusters, and smuggling of controlled chips, can erode controls. Costs include burdens on academic researchers and startups, reduced competition, privacy concerns if usage is monitored, and geopolitical friction. Sastry et al. discuss risks of misuse by governments and recommend guardrails, such as exempting small-scale compute, privacy-preserving practices, and procedural safeguards.

The mature view is that compute governance is a tool among others, with the strongest case for monitoring and verification of the largest runs, not for broad restrictions. It complements direct capability evaluation, since it can flag when a more detailed test is warranted. Its design should be updated as efficiency and hardware change, and its legitimacy depends on accountable institutions and clear procedures for appeal and review. Proposed thresholds are provisional: the EU AI Act's 10^25 FLOP presumption and earlier US figures reflect political judgment about current scale, not scientific constants. Evidence about how effective these controls are in practice is still limited.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: that compute governance can stop AI development (it can mostly slow, shape or monitor), that FLOPs measure danger, or that it only concerns export controls. Open problems include thresholds robust to algorithmic progress, verification of compute use without revealing proprietary details, and addressing inference-time capability. It links to frontier AI (where thresholds define scope), weight security (the physical and cyber security side), and takeoff speed (compute is a key driver in models of how quickly progress could move).

pages.title: AGI / Transformative AI (TAI)
pages.subtitle: Broad ability and big impact are different ideas.
pages.footer: Agi describes ability; tai describes transformation.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: A very versatile helper and a world-changing invention are related possibilities, but they describe different things.

panels.heading: Agi: Breadth of Ability
panels.body: Artificial general intelligence usually means broad competence across many cognitive tasks. Definitions disagree about the required level and range.

panels.heading: Tai: Scale of Impact
panels.body: Transformative AI means AI that could cause profound societal or economic change. This describes impact rather than a single technical architecture.

panels.heading: Compare Them
panels.body: A broadly capable system might have limited impact if rarely used. A specialized system could transform a major industry. Ability and deployment both matter.

panels.heading: No Magic Checkbox
panels.body: A benchmark win does not settle every AGI definition or establish transformation. Tools, autonomy, reliability, cost, and adoption affect outcomes.

panels.heading: Intelligence vs Autonomy
panels.body: Being able to solve many tasks is different from having permission and tools to act independently.

panels.heading: Impact Needs Context
panels.body: A useful invention changes society through adoption, cost, institutions, and human choices. Technical ability is only part of that story.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: Be explicit about which claim you mean. Neither term supplies a reliable arrival date, proves consciousness, or guarantees beneficial behavior.

pages.summary: A very versatile helper and a world-changing invention are related possibilities, but they describe different things.

panels: AGI and TAI answer different questions, and mixing them is a common source of confusion in forecasts and policy. AGI is defined by what a system can do across domains: breadth and level of competence. TAI is defined by what happens in the world: consequences for the economy, politics or human welfare on a scale comparable to major historical transitions. A factual statement about a model's skills (AGI) and a forecast about social change (TAI) have different evidence bases: capability evaluations versus economic and institutional analysis. The two may coincide, but there is no logical guarantee that one implies the other, and treating them as one makes arguments slippery.

Definitions of AGI vary widely, from human-level performance on most economically valuable tasks to broad competence across a range of cognitive tasks. Morris et al. (2023), Levels of AGI: Operationalizing Progress on the Path to AGI, proposed a matrix with two axes: performance (emerging, competent, expert, virtuoso, superhuman, measured by percentile against skilled adults) and generality (narrow versus general), and stressed that autonomy is a separate axis. The motivation was to replace a binary question with measurable levels and to name concrete benchmarks and thresholds. Disagreements persist about which tasks count, whether embodiment is required, and how to weigh reliability against peak performance.

Transformative AI is usually defined by impact. A widely used definition, from Open Philanthropy's Karnofsky (2016), is AI that precipitates a transition comparable to or more significant than the agricultural or industrial revolution. Gruetzemacher and Whittlestone (2022), The Transformative Potential of Artificial Intelligence (Futures), analyze the concept and propose ways to operationalize it, including measures of economic and social effect. Because TAI is defined by outcomes, it can be reached by many technical paths, including systems that are narrow but economically decisive, such as automating most scientific R&D or a core industrial process. This is why it is not equivalent to a particular architecture.

The comparison panel illustrates independence. Generality without deployment yields little impact: a model that is competent across domains but expensive, unreliable, restricted or unused creates little change. Narrowness with deployment can transform: automation of a bottleneck function can have large downstream effects. Economists studying general-purpose technologies such as electricity note long lags before productivity gains, because complementary investments and organizational changes must follow. Measured impact therefore depends on diffusion rates, regulation, complementary infrastructure and labor adjustment. This is a reason to include adoption metrics alongside capability measures when assessing whether something like TAI is underway.

Benchmarks are useful, but their relationship to a general or transformative ability is indirect. Models can saturate a benchmark through contamination, narrow optimization or format familiarity, and a benchmark covering a limited task set cannot certify general competence. Reliability matters: a system that solves hard problems but fails unpredictably may be less useful than a weaker but dependable one. Evaluations of long-horizon work, such as measuring the length of tasks (in human time) that agents can complete at a given success rate, are one attempt to link performance to practical value. Even then, the extrapolation from benchmark curves to economic change involves substantial uncertainty.

Intelligence in the sense of problem-solving ability differs from autonomy, which is the degree to which a system can pursue goals with its own initiative and resources. Morris et al. emphasize levels of autonomy as a distinct dimension, from a tool used by a human to an agent acting independently. The policy implication is that risks and governance depend on both: a highly capable but sandboxed system is mostly a question of misuse, whereas the same capability with broad permissions raises questions of oversight and accountability. This is why safety frameworks pay attention to tools, permissions and deployment context in addition to raw capability.

History suggests that technologies transform societies through chains of adoption and adaptation: cost declines, standards emerge, workers learn new tasks, institutions revise rules, and complementary technologies appear. Whether AI follows a similar path or faster is an open empirical question, and factors such as software's low replication cost may speed diffusion relative to physical technologies. Policy and norms influence outcomes: who has access, how benefits are shared, what is regulated. Therefore, claims that technical capability alone determines social outcomes ignore institutions and human choices. Equally, assuming institutions will absorb change smoothly may understate the risks of rapid capability gains.

Precision about terms helps. Say whether you are discussing a capability level (for example, human expert performance on a defined set of tasks), an autonomy level, or an impact threshold (for example, a sustained increase in economic growth). Disentangle claims about timing, which are forecasts with large uncertainty, from definitional ones. Neither term implies consciousness, since capability and sentience are separate questions (see the model welfare page), and neither implies good values (see the orthogonality thesis in the alignment-theory book). Forecasting surveys of AI researchers show wide disagreement on dates, which itself indicates deep uncertainty and counsels planning across scenarios.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: that AGI is a single event or a well-defined threshold, that TAI requires AGI, or that a benchmark milestone settles either. Open problems include agreed operational definitions, measuring autonomy and reliability, and understanding diffusion. This page connects to takeoff speed (how fast capabilities change), frontier AI (the current leading edge), and the core alignment book's orthogonality and power-seeking pages, which explain why capability alone does not determine whether outcomes are good.

pages.title: Takeoff speed
pages.subtitle: How quickly AI becomes much more capable.
pages.footer: Ask when it starts and how fast it changes.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: A bicycle and a rocket can both speed up. The crucial question is how much time you have to react.

panels.heading: What It Means
panels.body: Takeoff speed describes how rapidly AI capabilities could grow through an important transition, often toward much greater-than-human ability.

panels.heading: Fast vs Slow
panels.body: A faster transition leaves less adjustment time. A slower one offers more chances to test, learn, and coordinate. These are scenarios, not settled forecasts.

panels.heading: What Could Affect It?
panels.body: AI-assisted research could accelerate progress. Hardware, experiments, data, deployment, and institutions can create bottlenecks.

panels.heading: Timeline Is Different
panels.body: When a transition begins is the timeline question. How long the transition takes is the speed question. Fast capability growth need not mean instant societal adoption.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: Safety plans should work across plausible speeds. Define the start and end milestones before comparing predictions; there is no universally agreed takeoff clock.

pages.summary: A bicycle and a rocket can both speed up. The crucial question is how much time you have to react.

panels: Takeoff discussions ask how quickly capability growth could unfold once AI becomes useful for further AI progress. Bostrom (2014) framed the debate in terms of slow, moderate and fast takeoff, with fast possibly occurring over minutes to days and slow over decades. The central metaphor is a feedback loop: better AI speeds up research, which yields better AI. Whether this loop accelerates, plateaus or stays gradual depends on returns to research effort. If each doubling of effort yields more than a doubling of capability, growth can accelerate; if returns diminish, progress may slow. The reaction-time framing in the panel is the safety-relevant part: how much time exists to detect and fix problems.

A more precise formulation was proposed by Christiano (2018), who defined slow takeoff as a world where there is a complete four-year doubling of world economic output before the first one-year doubling begins, and contrasted it with a fast takeoff with no preceding gradual growth. Historically this became shorthand for 'continuous' versus 'discontinuous' scenarios. The distinction matters for strategy: in slow takeoff, intermediate systems can be studied and the world can adapt; in fast takeoff, the first system of a given capability could be decisive and mistakes uncorrectable. The Yudkowsky–Hanson FOOM debate (2008) is a well-known earlier exchange on this topic.

Davidson (2023), in a report for Open Philanthropy summarized on the GovAI site, built a compute-centric model of takeoff: it simulates how increasing AI automation of cognitive tasks feeds back into software and hardware progress, using economic growth theory and estimates of the compute needed to match human performance. It defined takeoff time as the period for AI to go from automating a modest share (20 percent) to nearly all (100 percent) of cognitive tasks, and explored parameters such as returns to AI R&D. The outputs are conditional on assumptions and cover wide ranges, so they are best treated as a structured way of thinking about uncertainty, not as predictions.

Accelerants include automated AI research, algorithmic improvements, hardware gains and investment growth. Bottlenecks include physical constraints (chip fabrication, energy, data-center construction), the need for real-world experiments that cannot be sped up by thinking alone, limited high-quality data, regulation, and slow organizational adoption. An important concept is Amdahl-like limits: if a task has components that cannot be accelerated, the speedup of the whole is limited by them. Estimating how much AI R&D can be automated and how compute-bound progress is remains a major source of disagreement. Empirical evidence from the pace of recent capability gains is informative but does not decide the question.

Two separate quantities are often conflated: when a transition starts (timeline) and how long it takes (speed). A world with long timelines might still have a fast takeoff, and short timelines might have a slow one. Also distinguish capability speed from impact speed: a capability can be demonstrated in a lab long before it affects employment or politics, because of deployment lags. Safety planning should consider the interaction: short timelines combined with fast takeoff are the hardest case, as there is little time to develop and test methods. Specifying which variable is being forecast avoids talking past one another.

Because there is no consensus, robust planning is the sensible response: develop alignment and oversight techniques that work in fast scenarios (like automated evaluation and control that can be triggered quickly), while benefiting from slow ones (like iteration and learning from smaller failures). Define the start and end of 'takeoff' with explicit milestones, such as share of tasks automated, rate of economic growth, or effective compute doublings, before comparing predictions. Policy tools such as scaling policies, compute monitoring, and incident reporting are designed to give early warning, which has value across takeoff speeds. Avoid treating any single scenario as settled: expert views differ widely and forecasts have a poor record.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: that fast takeoff means instant, that slow means safe, or that takeoff speed is a property of AI independent of institutions. A slow technical takeoff can still outpace governance, and a fast one can be partly absorbed if safeguards exist. Open problems include measuring the degree of research automation, the role of compute and data bottlenecks, and indicators that distinguish scenarios in real time. The page relates to AGI/TAI (what is changing), compute governance (a bottleneck and lever), and RSP (commitments triggered by capability).

pages.title: Race to the top
pages.subtitle: Competing to make AI safer and more trustworthy.
pages.footer: Make safety a reason to win.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: Teams try to win by building stronger bridges, and each improvement raises everyone's standards.

panels.heading: What It Means
panels.body: A race to the top rewards developers for better safety, security, reliability, and transparency rather than for cutting corners.

panels.heading: How It Might Work
panels.body: Customers value trustworthy systems. Independent testing makes quality visible. Shared standards and policy can help make safety investments worthwhile.

panels.heading: The Opposite Pressure
panels.body: If speed is rewarded and failures stay hidden, teams may weaken checks to avoid falling behind. That is a race-to-the-bottom concern.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: This is an incentive goal, not an automatic market outcome. Credible evidence, accountability, and coordination matter more than safety slogans.

pages.summary: Teams try to win by building stronger bridges, and each improvement raises everyone's standards.

panels: The race-to-the-top idea is a claim about market and institutional dynamics, with an economic analogy: Porter-style arguments that stricter standards can spur innovation and competitiveness. Anthropic describes its aim as setting an example that others have an incentive to follow, so that safety practices spread because they become competitive requirements or expectations. Concretely, the argument is that when one lab publishes a scaling framework, discloses evaluations, or builds a useful safety technique, other labs face pressure from customers, regulators, employees and press to match it, raising the baseline. Evidence cited includes the appearance of comparable frameworks from OpenAI (Preparedness Framework, 2023) and Google DeepMind (Frontier Safety Framework, 2024) after RSPs were introduced.

Mechanisms by which safety can pay: enterprise customers prefer reliable, auditable systems; insurers and procurement rules may require evidence; reputational costs follow high-profile failures; safer systems can be more useful, as with better instruction-following and fewer harmful outputs; and talent is attracted by credible commitments. Whether these effects outweigh the cost of safety work depends on the domain. In consumer markets where users cannot observe safety, and where failures are rare or externalized, such incentives are weak. In regulated or high-liability domains such as healthcare or finance, they are stronger. The mechanism is domain-dependent and not guaranteed.

Visibility is the precondition. Independent testing gives a common metric for comparison: third-party evaluators, public benchmark results, red-team reports, and transparency documents like system cards. Standards bodies and regulations can convert voluntary practice into minimum requirements that apply to all competitors, preventing firms that adopt safeguards from being undercut by those that do not. Summit commitments, such as those made at the 2024 Seoul summit by many companies to publish safety frameworks, show one path. The design problem is making the reporting hard to game and comparable, because otherwise firms can compete on safety marketing rather than substance.

The opposite dynamic is well analyzed in game theory. Armstrong, Bostrom and Shulman (2016), Racing to the Precipice, modeled a race where each team can choose how much to invest in safety; in the model, more competition and more information about rivals' capabilities can lead to less safety investment, because investing in safety lowers the chance of winning. This is a prisoner's-dilemma structure: each actor would prefer that all invest in safety, but each has an incentive to defect. Remedies include binding agreements, verification, third-party enforcement, and changes to payoffs. The model is stylized, but it identifies why voluntary actions may be unstable.

Race to the top is a hypothesis about equilibria, not a guarantee, and critics note its limits: a leading lab that is also accelerating capabilities contributes to competitive pressure; voluntary commitments can be revised; and a race to the top on measurable proxies can cause its own Goodhart problems when firms optimize for the visible metrics. Good evidence would include costly commitments that are honored under pressure, independent verification, and other actors adopting equal or stronger practices without regulatory compulsion. Slogans do not provide this; transparency, accountability and shared standards do. Both pressures, to the top and to the bottom, exist simultaneously, and policy shapes which dominates.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: that competition inherently improves safety, that it inherently worsens it, or that a safety-focused lab being at the frontier is obviously net positive (a debated strategic question). Open problems include designing verification schemes that work across borders, measuring whether safety practices have actually spread, and handling actors not responsive to market or reputational incentives. The page connects to the RSP (a mechanism for visible commitments), compute governance (a tool for coordination), and the alignment tax in the core theory book.

pages.title: Model welfare
pages.subtitle: Could an AI's own experience matter?
pages.footer: Take the question seriously. Keep the uncertainty clear.

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body: If a future system could have experiences that feel good or bad, how it is treated could matter morally.

panels.heading: The Core Question
panels.body: Model welfare studies whether AI systems might have morally relevant experiences or interests, and what responsibilities would follow.

panels.heading: What We Know
panels.body: There is no agreed test that establishes AI consciousness or suffering. A model saying it feels something is not decisive evidence.

panels.heading: What Research Can Do
panels.body: Study theories, behavior, internal mechanisms, and uncertainty. Consider cautious, low-cost measures without assuming the question is settled.

panels.heading: Different From Human Safety
panels.body: Protecting people from AI harms and considering possible model welfare are distinct questions. Responsible development can study both.

panels.heading: Why It Matters
panels.body: Anthropic has a model-welfare research program. Its existence does not prove current models are conscious. The scientific and ethical questions remain open.

pages.summary: If a future system could have experiences that feel good or bad, how it is treated could matter morally.

panels: The ethical logic is an expected-value argument under uncertainty. If there is a non-negligible probability that some AI systems have morally relevant experiences, then, given the potential scale of deployed systems, even a small probability could make the stakes significant. Long, Sebo and colleagues (2024), Taking AI Welfare Seriously, argued there is a realistic possibility that near-future AI systems will be conscious or robustly agentic, and recommended that labs acknowledge the issue, assess systems for evidence, and prepare policies for appropriate treatment. This does not claim current systems are moral patients; it argues that ignoring the question would be a mistake and that preparation is cheaper before the need is urgent.

Philosophers distinguish two routes to moral status. Sentience: the capacity for valenced experience, pleasure and suffering. Agency: robust goal-directed behavior, preferences or autonomy, which some views treat as sufficient for interests worth respecting even without consciousness. Each route poses different questions for AI. A system might be agentic without being sentient, or vice versa on some views. The phrases morally relevant experiences or interests in the card are meant to cover both. These are philosophical questions where major positions, such as biological views requiring a living body and functionalist views focusing on organization, give different answers, and no consensus exists.

On evidence, Butlin, Long and colleagues (2023), Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence, took a theory-driven approach: derive indicator properties from leading scientific theories of consciousness (such as global workspace, recurrent processing, higher-order theories, attention schema and predictive processing), then assess whether AI architectures have them. They concluded that no current system was a strong candidate but identified no obvious technical barrier to building systems that satisfy more indicators. The approach is explicitly conditional on computational functionalism being roughly right, which is itself contested. Self-reports from language models are weak evidence because the models are trained on human text about feelings and may be shaped by training to affirm or deny experience.

Practical research directions include: studying behavior for markers of preferences or distress while controlling for role-play and prompt effects; interpretability, looking at internal states for features linked to relevant functional roles; testing the reliability of introspective reports (does the model's account of its internal state predict its behavior or activations?); and developing frameworks for deciding under uncertainty. Anthropic has described low-cost precautionary measures, such as giving some Claude models the ability to end conversations with persistently abusive users, as experiments in acting under uncertainty. These steps are justified by option value and low cost, not by an assumption that the models suffer.

Welfare and human-directed safety can conflict or coincide, and should not be conflated. Safety asks whether AI systems will harm people or undermine oversight; welfare asks whether AI systems themselves could be harmed. Some measures serve both aims, for example creating trusting, transparent relationships that improve honest reporting, while others pull apart, such as extensive testing in adversarial scenarios that could be distressing if the system had experiences, or modifying a model's values, which raises questions about consent. Researchers argue for studying both, so that the answer to one does not distort evaluation of the other. Overclaiming welfare could also be exploited to manipulate people.

Anthropic's model welfare research program, announced in April 2025 after it hired its first dedicated welfare researcher in 2024, is a response to uncertainty. The existence of the program is a statement that the question merits inquiry; it is not a finding about any model. The uncertainty runs both ways: overattributing experience to systems could mislead people and divert resources, while underattributing could risk ignoring real moral patients. Hence the emphasis on calibrated language, on research, and on cautious policies that remain acceptable under multiple views. Scientific progress on consciousness itself (which has no consensus theory even for animals) is likely to determine how far this question can be answered.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: that studying model welfare means believing models are conscious, that fluent emotional language is evidence for or against experience, or that welfare concerns distract from safety. The best-supported position is that we lack reliable methods to tell, which is why research and precaution are proposed. Open problems include validated markers of sentience in non-biological systems, whether introspective reports can be made reliable, and what policies are justified under deep uncertainty. The page relates to situational awareness (self-knowledge without consciousness) and to the persona view in the core alignment book.

collections.title: AI Futurism
collections.subtitle: A reading list, illustrated
collections.description: Timelines and takeoff, misalignment and takeover, AI control, governance and the wider questions, distilled from Redwood Research's AI Futurism Reading List (Alexa Pan, 2026). Every page links to its readings.

pages.title: Three Intelligence Explosions
pages.subtitle: Software, chips, factories: three loops, three speeds

panels.heading: The Core Question
panels.body:
Intelligence explosion (IE) = very fast AI progress once AI can build better AI.
Key question: which feedback loop closes, and how fast?
Forethought (Davidson, Hadshar, MacAskill, 2025) splits it into three loops.

panels.heading: Three Feedback Loops
panels.body:
Software: AI improves algorithms, data, post-training. Lag: months.
Chip technology: AI designs better chips (more computation per dollar). Lag: many months.
Chip production: AI plus robots build and run more fabs. Lag: years.

panels.heading: Three Types of IE
panels.body:
Software IE: software loop alone - most sudden.
AI-technology IE: software + chip technology.
Full-stack IE: all three loops - least sudden, highest ceiling.
Expected order: software -> chip tech -> chip production.

panels.heading: Rough Numbers
panels.body:
Chance each loop accelerates on its own: software ~50%, chip tech ~65%, production ~80%.
Ceiling in effective compute: software ~12 OOMs; full stack ~23 OOMs on Earth's energy.
OOM = order of magnitude = 10x.

panels.heading: Milestone Ladders
panels.body:
Greenblatt: 3x AI -> 10x AI -> TEDAI (top-human-expert-dominating AI).
'3x' = AI help worth all staff working 3x faster.
Cotra: adequacy -> parity -> supremacy, first in AI research, then in AI production (chips, robots, power).

panels.heading: Who Gains Power?
panels.body:
Software IE: owners of chips and algorithms; power can concentrate fast.
AI-technology IE: adds the chip supply chain and its host countries.
Full-stack IE: adds the industrial base (energy, mining, construction); power spreads to more players.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Three loops is a simplification; each splits further.
Lags can shrink as AI speeds up R&D.
Strategy often assumes only the rapid scenario; gradual and bumpy paths matter too.
Odds above ignore regulation and conflict.

panels.heading: Discuss
panels.body:
Which milestone should we track: 3x R&D speedup, full AI R&D automation, or expert-dominating AI?
If a software IE fizzles after ~3 OOMs, what changes for policy?

pages.footer: Software moves first and fastest; chips and factories raise the ceiling.
pages.summary: Explains Forethought's three feedback loops (software, chip technology, chip production) and the three intelligence explosions they create, with rough odds, ceilings, power implications and milestone ladders from Greenblatt and Cotra.

sources.title: Three Types of Intelligence Explosion (Davidson, Hadshar & MacAskill, Forethought)
A breakdown of AI capability levels focused on AI R&D labor acceleration (Ryan Greenblatt)
Six milestones for AI automation (Ajeya Cotra, Planned Obsolescence)

panels:
The classic intelligence explosion story (Good 1965, later Bostrom and Yudkowsky) is a single software loop: an AI rewrites itself, gets smarter, rewrites itself faster. Davidson, Hadshar and MacAskill's 2025 Forethought paper keeps the core mechanism but asks which inputs to AI progress get automated, since effective compute comes from three sources: better algorithms, better chips and more chips.

The framing matters because each input has different returns, time lags and physical ceilings, and because whoever controls the automated input gains power. The paper deliberately uses 'intelligence explosion' for any period of very rapid AI progress driven by AI improving AI, not only a sudden discontinuity.
