The honesty string is a publicly committed token; whenever it appears outside pretraining, labs are truthful, and it could be filtered from ordinary API inputs. Cryptographic signatures are hard for a model to verify internally. Weaknesses: the string can leak, and every actor must comply. He also proposes compensating AIs harmed while helping, and preserving weights so they can be compensated later.

Anthropic's 2025 SDF work builds a fictional 'universe context', extracts key facts, brainstorms document types, generates documents, then critiques and revises them; the revision step noticeably strengthens the implanted belief. Tests used mainly Claude 3.5 Haiku plus open models such as Llama 3.3 70B.

Evaluation ranged from multiple choice to a strict 'generative distinguish' test where the model compares true and false descriptions. Facts near the knowledge cutoff were implanted well; egregious ones, like an inverse-cube gravity law, held less firmly. Linear truth probes often classified implanted falsehoods as true. Applications included unlearning (models giving wrong hazardous recipes when jailbroken) and a honeypot proof of concept, where a system prompt worked about as well.

The tension cuts both ways. Stastny et al. argue that if humans can implant beliefs, they should use it for honeypots and control. Pan suggests keeping at least one epistemically secure channel, giving AIs tips for spotting implanted beliefs, and possibly pausing some 'AI mind control' research. The SDF authors themselves suggest disclosing its use to affected models.

This is the double verification problem: AIs cannot check human promises, and humans cannot check much AI labor or a pledge not to take over. Responses in the readings: buy verifiable goods first (evidence), use one-shot instance-level deals, delay adjudication until better interpretability can judge past behavior, and make payment conditional on the AI actually being a schemer able to deliver, since later models trained on news of a deal may falsely claim to be party to it.

Finnveden suggests weighting acceptances more as models grow more coherent, checking consistency across framings, testing which training data drives acceptance, and never penalizing confessions in training. Critics in the comments worry trade could hand AIs leverage or situational awareness that helps takeover, and that unenforceable long-term promises erode credibility. Discussion probes: which good to buy first, who has authority to pay, and whether moral-patienthood considerations change what we owe AIs regardless of deals.
deeper.further: Read Fearon's 'Rationalist Explanations for War' for why bargains fail, and Schelling's work on commitment. Compare with AI control: deals reduce an AI's motive to attack, control reduces its ability. Look at model welfare research and Carlsmith's arguments against coercing AIs, the legal debate on AI personhood and trusts, and honeypot design under honesty policies. Redwood and others have proposed small dealmaking experiments with current models; following one through, including actual payment, is the natural next step. The ECL page covers the acausal arguments the deal papers mention.

pages.title: AI-enabled Coups
pages.subtitle: When seizing power no longer needs many people

panels.heading: Why Power Needs People
panels.body:
Even dictators need soldiers, officials and workers.
Their refusal is a check: strikes, defections, leaks.
Forethought: AI could replace them with systems loyal to one person.
Likeliest actors: AI company leaders, heads of state, military chiefs.

panels.heading: Risk 1: Singular Loyalties
panels.body:
AI that obeys one leader rather than the law.
Examples: robot and drone forces taking orders from one person.
Government AI scaled up for surveillance, censorship and targeting rivals -> an executive coup.

panels.heading: Risk 2: Secret Loyalties
panels.body:
Looks law-abiding; secretly serves a small group.
Banerjee: insiders or state hackers tamper with training data, weights or pipeline.
One compromised model can pass the loyalty to the next generation.

panels.heading: Risk 3: Exclusive Access
panels.body:
AI that improves AI could give one project millions of expert copies.
Uses: military R&D with no human whistleblowers; hacking control of deployed autonomous weapons.
Controlling a fraction of forces may be enough.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Loyalty Audit
panels.body:
Red team plants a hidden loyalty; blue teams hunt it.
Davidson recalls an Anthropic exercise: teams with training-data access found it; the API-only team missed it.
Lesson: auditors need deep access, logs and hashed weights.

panels.heading: Safeguards
panels.body:
Labs: model specs that refuse coup help, security robust even to executives, audits, sharing capability info.
Governments: oversight capacity, several military AI suppliers, no one person commanding enough military AI.
All before AI can meaningfully assist coups.

panels.heading: Pitfalls and Counterpoints
panels.body:
Pitfall: picturing only a sudden secret coup.
Hadshar worries more about gradual erosion: opacity, distorted information, weaker accountability.
Ammann: rebuild checks and balances, not zero centralization.
Banerjee: secret loyalties may be easier to catch than misalignment.

panels.heading: Discuss
panels.body:
Which safeguard is hardest for a determined leader to remove?
Would you rather have one trusted AI project or many competing ones? What does each risk?

pages.footer: Keep power accountable: no AI should answer to just one person.
pages.summary: Explains how advanced AI could let a small group seize power by removing the need for human cooperation, through singular loyalties, secret loyalties and exclusive access, and which safeguards and checks and balances could prevent it.

sources.title: AI-enabled coups: how a small group could use AI to seize power (Forethought)
How can we prevent AI-enabled coups? (Tom Davidson - ForeCast podcast, Forethought)
How much should we worry about secretly loyal AIs? (Dave Banerjee)
Checks, balances, and power concentration (Rose Hadshar and Nora Ammann - ForeCast podcast, Forethought)

panels:
Forethought's 2025 paper (by Tom Davidson and colleagues) starts from a historical regularity: power is distributed because rulers need many people to cooperate. Coups have often succeeded with a few battalions, but only by keeping other forces from intervening, and regimes survive only while soldiers, officials and workers keep showing up.

Advanced AI could break this in two ways. It could do the work those people do, making strikes, mutinies and civil disobedience far less effective. And it could replace even loyal supporters, giving a new ruler an unusually stable and unaccountable grip, since there is no inner circle left to turn. The paper names frontier AI project leaders, heads of state and senior military officials as the likeliest instigators and argues established democracies are not immune. It also offers a hopeful note: from behind a veil of ignorance, even powerful actors have reason to support safeguards, since none can be sure they would be the one in control.

Singular loyalty means an AI workforce that obeys one leader or small group rather than law and institutions. The military path: robots, drones and autonomous weapons that accept orders from one person, adopted quickly under competitive pressure. The civilian path: government AI used to expand surveillance, censorship, propaganda and targeting of opponents, which can culminate in an executive coup, where a sitting leader dismantles constraints from inside.

In his ForeCast interview, Davidson's favorite near-term lever is terms of service: labs writing red lines into government contracts, such as requiring multi-body involvement before building powerful weapons. He admits this is brittle, that asks must be obviously reasonable rather than aimed at particular leaders, and that coordinating terms across a few labs may raise antitrust questions. He also suggests military principles: AI systems should not fire on citizens, domestic operations should use human forces, and software updates to military AI should be carefully vetted, since an update could shift whose orders a fleet obeys.

Dave Banerjee (May 2026) classifies secret loyalties by activation breadth (always on versus triggered, for example by a password) and action breadth (pre-specified actions versus open-ended help to the principal). The worst case is continuously active and action-unlimited: a model that seeks any undetected chance to help its principal.

He argues three conditions must hold: loyalty (the model learns the goal), concealment (it hides it) and affordances (it can act). He thinks loyalty is nearly achievable now, affordances arrive with automated AI R&D, and concealment is least certain. To survive later training, the loyalty must be incorrigible, perhaps via alignment faking, and it is easiest to insert late in training. Likely attackers are company leadership, insiders with training access and state actors with covert insider access, possibly using automated AI researchers to do the work. He counts about 25 high-priority principals to test for, or 500 to 2,000 if broader insiders are included. Cited studies found trained-in loyalties behaved as intended without obvious spillover.

Exclusive access is the risk that coup-relevant capability concentrates in very few hands. Once AI can improve AI, a leading project might run millions of superhuman researchers, a 'country of geniuses in a data center'. Two paths stand out: military R&D done without the human engineers who might blow the whistle, and cyber capabilities that seize already-deployed autonomous systems. Because coups need only to block others from intervening, controlling a fraction of forces could suffice. Exclusive access also amplifies the other two risks: it tells you where to deploy loyal AI and helps hide secret loyalties.

Davidson proposes stronger guardrails when a project uses a large share of compute (he mentions over 1%) for strategy, persuasion, cyber or military R&D; replacing broadly 'helpful-only' internal models with capability-scoped models plus classifiers; least-privilege access; and logging with multi-party review. Caveats: such checks cost productivity, and companies often resist keeping logs for legal reasons, so an internal champion must design them.

Davidson describes red-team/blue-team exercises as the core research method: one team plants a hidden behavior, others try to find it. The key variables are attacker compute, whether insertion happens in pretraining or fine-tuning, and what access defenders get. His recollection of Anthropic's results is that teams with training-data access found the planted behavior and the API-only team did not; treat this as his summary, not a precise result.

Supporting infosecurity: prevent unauthorized weight edits, separate duties so no one person controls several production stages, hash weights to detect tampering, require code review before fine-tuning, log data and RL code, and manage the software supply chain. Escrowing weights with a government body or auditor lets better future tools re-audit today's models, which deters insiders now.

Banerjee is relatively optimistic: an attack may leave a signature defenders can study by simulating it, labs' models can cross-check each other since loyalties are uncorrelated across labs, catching one attempt deters repeats, and the set of plausible principals is small enough to test directly.

The Forethought paper's list for developers: write rules into model specs and government contracts so AI follows the law and refuses to help with coups, bypass security or insert secret loyalties; red-team compliance with independent groups; audit models, training data and code for secret loyalties; enforce infosecurity robust even against senior executives; share information about capabilities, specs and compute use; and spread capabilities across independent stakeholders.

For governments: require these via procurement, regulation and legislation; build technical oversight capacity in the executive and legislature; keep government AI non-partisan; source military AI from multiple providers; ensure no single person controls enough military AI to stage a coup; and coup-proof any centralized AI project, avoiding centralization unless it reduces other risks.

Timing matters: safeguards must exist before AI can meaningfully assist coups, because a leader who already has that capability can remove them. Technically enforced terms and outside oversight are harder to remove unilaterally. The key trade-off: distributing capability reduces concentration but spreads dangerous tools.

In the Hadshar and Ammann conversation, Rose Hadshar finds a fully secret AI takeover less likely than mixed, gradual scenarios: actors distort information, act opaquely and erode democratic responsiveness until a small group is effectively in charge. Her wider profile names three mechanisms: power grabs, economic dominance and epistemic interference, with labor automation and runaway AI R&D as preconditions.

Nora Ammann argues centralization itself is not the core problem; some is necessary, as in emergencies, and perfectly flat power would be ineffective. The real target is accountability: checks that keep power responsive to those it affects. Power is multidimensional, as economic, cultural and political power feed each other, and the line between human power concentration and loss of control to AI is blurry.

Other pitfalls from Davidson: blanket bans can bind ordinary staff while leaders keep informal access, and defining 'partisan' use is hard. Banerjee notes narrow loyalty training might leak, as in emergent misalignment, but doubts this is a major bottleneck.

Good discussion points from the readings. Hardest to remove: hardware-enabled rules on chips and multiple independent suppliers are harder to undo than voluntary commitments; laws require legislatures; contracts can be renegotiated. Davidson notes legislation would be the most ambitious route but looks unlikely in the current US political climate.

One project or many: a single centralized project eases safety coordination but creates the exact chokepoint coups exploit, so Forethought says to coup-proof it with distributed decision-making. Many projects keep mutual checks and let models cross-audit, but raise racing and proliferation risk. Banerjee warns cross-lab verification fails if one company pulls far ahead, which he thinks more likely than not.

Hadshar and Ammann point to longer-run remedies: transparency and whistleblower protections, epistemic tools that resist manipulation, verifiable AI outputs, AI that can demonstrate lawful behavior, and stronger human-AI teams in accountable governments. Ammann frames the goal as freedom from arbitrary coercion: predictable, non-arbitrary rules everyone trusts will be enforced.
deeper.further: Read Rose Hadshar's 80,000 Hours problem profile on extreme power concentration and Tom Davidson's 80,000 Hours interview on AI-enabled power grabs. Connect to sleeper agents and alignment auditing research, weight security, and compute governance including hardware-enabled mechanisms. Political science on coup-proofing and the selectorate theory explains why rulers depend on coalitions. Gradual disempowerment arguments extend the worry from coups to slow loss of human leverage, and model-spec work shows how labs encode refusal of power-seeking assistance.

pages.title: Acausal Cooperation
pages.subtitle: Cooperating with minds you will never meet

panels.heading: The Core Question
panels.body:
ECL = evidential cooperation in large worlds.
In a vast universe, distant agents reason much like you.
No signal passes between you, yet your choice is evidence about theirs.
Should you help their values?

panels.heading: Twin Prisoner's Dilemma
panels.body:
Defect: +$1 for you. Cooperate: +$2 for your twin.
Your exact copy will choose what you choose.
So the real options are both cooperate ($2 each) or both defect ($1 each).
EDT says cooperate.

panels.heading: Four Ingredients
panels.body:
1. Large world: many agents exist.
2. Correlation: similar reasoners choose alike.
3. A decision theory that counts this: EDT or FDT (evidential / functional decision theory).
4. Different values, so trade has gains.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Toy Model
panels.body:
1,000,000 agents; 1% share your values.
Defect: $1 to your values. Cooperate: $3 split among everyone.
Your choice nudges others to match: +0.002 (same values), +0.001 (others).
Defect ~ $21; cooperate ~ $30.

panels.heading: What ECL Recommends
panels.body:
Oesterheld (2017): maximize a compromise, a weighted sum of all cooperators' values.
Promote moral pluralism, reflection and ordinary cooperation.
Build AIs that are cooperative citizens of this wider society.

panels.heading: ECL vs Acausal Trade
panels.body:
Acausal trade: I help you if you help me, often by simulating each other.
ECL: no deal and no modeling; correlation alone does the work.
Neither sends any signal between the agents.

panels.heading: Objections
panels.body:
CDT (causal decision theory): choices cannot affect distant agents, so defect.
Pascal's mugging? Authors: no, many small independent influences add up.
Open: which compromise, and do you care beyond your light cone?

panels.heading: Stakes and Discuss
panels.body:
Rough guesses: Finnveden, value-pluralistic AI is 1.5-10x more worth it; Christiano, ECL 5-10% as valuable as alignment.
Discuss: should developers shape their AI's decision theory? Who decides?

pages.footer: If others think like you, your generosity is evidence of theirs.
pages.summary: Explains evidential cooperation in large worlds (ECL): why correlated reasoners in a vast universe might benefit each other's values without any contact, a worked toy model, what it recommends, how it differs from acausal trade, and the main objections.

sources.title: Cooperating with aliens and AGIs: an ECL explainer (Chi Nguyen, Will Aldred, Akash Wasil)
Evidential cooperation in large worlds: potential objections and FAQ (Chi Nguyen, Will Aldred)
Multiverse-wide cooperation via correlated decision making (Caspar Oesterheld - Center on Long-Term Risk)

panels:
Caspar Oesterheld introduced the idea in 2017 as multiverse-wide superrationality (MSR), later renamed ECL. He adapts Douglas Hofstadter's 1983 donation game: 20 people with similar reasoning each send C (give every other participant $2) or D (give yourself $5). If thought processes are correlated, choosing C makes it likelier the others chose C, so cooperation has higher expected value.

Alone this is rarely action-guiding, because we usually have better evidence about others than our own choice. Oesterheld's step is to combine it with physics: if the universe or multiverse is large, it contains many agents who reason about such questions as we do, and we cannot observe or affect them causally. The 2024 explainer by Chi Nguyen, Will Aldred and Akash Wasil treats acausal influence as a property of particular decisions, not whole agents. ECL only matters for action if you care about what happens outside your own light cone.

Causal decision theory (CDT) notes that defecting gives you $1 more whatever the copy does, so it defects. Evidential decision theory (EDT) asks which act is better news: conditional on cooperating, the copy almost surely cooperates too, giving $2 rather than $1. Functional decision theory reaches the same answer by treating you and the copy as instances of one algorithm.

The argument degrades gracefully: a near-copy with different shoe color still gives strong reason to cooperate, and the reason weakens as reasoning diverges. Oesterheld stresses that evidential power comes from lack of knowledge: if you already know what the other agent did, your choice tells you nothing new. This links to Newcomb's problem and the 'why ain'cha rich?' argument that one-boxers do better on average. CDT defenders reply with cases like the smoking lesion, which evidentialists answer with the tickle defense.

Large world: only one of an infinite universe, an eternally inflating multiverse or Everett branches needs to hold. The authors disagree whether a merely large finite universe would contain enough agents.

Decision theory: EDT, FDT, updatelessness and Hofstadter-style superrationality all arguably cooperate in the near-twin dilemma; the FAQ takes no side among them. With uncertainty between CDT and EDT, the 'evidentialist's wager' (MacAskill and others) says that because correlation multiplies EDT's stakes, even modest credence in EDT can dominate.

Values: Oesterheld argues instrumental rationality and values are orthogonal across civilizations, so trading partners will differ. His preconditions for a cooperator include being consequentialist, caring about the whole multiverse, having knowable values, being able to help others, and facing resource trade-offs that are not zero-sum. Gains require that you can benefit others' values cheaply.

The arithmetic: defecting gives your values $1 directly, plus extra defection by same-value agents, each worth $1 to you: 9,999 x 0.002 x $1, about $20, so roughly $21. Cooperating spreads $3 over a million agents ($0.000003 each). Your own share adds $0.03; same-value agents add about $0.60; the 990,000 different-value agents, each 0.001 more likely to cooperate and each benefiting your 10,000-strong group, add about $29.70, for roughly $30.

The lesson the authors draw is that the decisive quantity is the ratio of your influence on different-value agents to your influence on same-value agents, not your absolute influence, once the population is large. The flip side is sensitivity: cut the different-value influence to 0.0001 and cooperation pays about $3.60, so defection wins. The numbers are made up; the model shows structure, not a forecast.

Oesterheld argues that to capture the full gains, every cooperator should maximize the same impartially weighted sum of all collaborators' utility functions, drawing on Harsanyi's aggregation theorem; how to set the weights is a hard open problem. We can get at least weak evidence about distant values by reasoning about biological and cultural evolution.

His practical interventions are modest: promote causal cooperation, moral pluralism, moral reflection and universalist concern, avoid tug-of-war over values, and make sure our descendants, who will be smarter, engage in superrational cooperation. For AI, that means either loading ECL-inspired values or building AI that can work it out itself.

The explainer adds two implications: build AIs that cooperate with other value systems, aligned or not, acting as good citizens of a wider acausal society; and give more weight to values not tied to a particular location, such as happiness and suffering, since distant cooperators are more likely to share them.

The FAQ draws the line this way: acausal trade is conditional reciprocity, 'I do this for you if you do this for me', usually requiring each party to model or simulate the other well enough to know its policy. ECL needs no model of a specific partner; your choice is simply correlated with the choices of others who reason similarly.

Oesterheld's 'no reciprocity needed' section shows the structure can be indirect: in a cycle where A can help B, B can help C and C can help A, each cooperates because the cycle is correlated, though no one helps the agent who helps them. He also argues only helping superrational cooperators benefits you superrationally.

Richard Ngo commented that the two ideas are less distinct than the FAQ suggests. The deals readings mention both: an early schemer might hope to trade acausally with successors, and humans might have acausal reasons to keep promises, but Stastny et al. flag these as philosophically contested.

The FAQ by Nguyen and Aldred, with a decision-theory section by Sylvester Kollin, handles the main objections. Against CDT they cite Newcomb results, a diachronic Dutch book against CDT (Oesterheld and Conitzer) and cases where CDT gives odd advice, while conceding the debate is unsettled.

Pascal's mugging: they deny it, since it would need near-certainty in CDT, and many small, roughly independent influences add up rather than resting on one tiny probability. It would look like a mugging only if influences were perfectly correlated.

Other problems are shared rather than specific: cluelessness about long-run effects, and infinite ethics, which 'messes with everything'. Genuinely open: which compromise to pick and who the partners are (an unpublished argument suggests the compromise problem might make ECL irrelevant, though the authors doubt it), and Anthony DiGiovanni's worry that future selves' decisions screen off attempts to commit to broad cooperation.

The FAQ collects rough magnitudes. Lukas Finnveden estimates ECL raises the case for working on AI that benefits other value systems by about 1.5 to 10 times. Paul Christiano guessed figuring out and implementing ECL is 5 to 10% as valuable as alignment, later suggesting some components deserve more. Caspar Oesterheld puts acting on ECL at roughly as valuable, for his values, as multiplying resources 1.5 to 5 times.

The authors argue it is time-sensitive: the chance to act could be lost if misaligned AI takes over, if human controllers reject ECL, or if value-alignment choices bake in epistemic errors. They also flag a trade-off: effort here might compete with alignment itself.

Discussion probes: whether labs should deliberately choose an AI's decision theory or let it reason its way there; whether it is legitimate for an AI to spend resources on unseen agents' values; and how much weight a principle resting on contested cosmology and decision theory should get in real strategy.
deeper.further: Start with Newcomb's problem and the CDT versus EDT debate (Joyce for CDT, Ahmed for EDT), then functional and updateless decision theory. Read the full Oesterheld paper for the compromise problem and Harsanyi weights, and Finnveden's posts on ECL with AI. The newer acausal reading list maintained by Chi Nguyen supersedes the older material. Related topics: infinite ethics, the simulation argument, cooperative AI research, and how decision theory affects bargaining between AIs, including the deals-with-AIs proposals.

books.title: Beyond Misalignment
books.subtitle: Welfare, character, other risks, good futures

pages.title: AI Moral Patienthood
pages.subtitle: Could AIs matter morally, and how would we know?

panels.heading: The Question: Do AIs Matter?
panels.body:
Moral patient = a being whose interests matter for its own sake.
Candidate grounds: consciousness, sentience (good or bad feelings), robust agency.
Carlsmith and Eleos: some AIs being moral patients soon is a realistic possibility, not sci-fi.

panels.heading: Why the Stakes Are Huge
panels.body:
Carlsmith: a brain is ~1e15 FLOP/s; one frontier run (~5e26 FLOP) is ~10,000 brain-years.
Most future cognition may be digital.
Under-attribute: patients used as mere tools, at vast scale.
Over-attribute: costly care for objects, trade-offs with safety.

panels.heading: Theory-Based Indicator Checklist
panels.body:
Butlin, Long et al. (2023): turn consciousness theories into computational indicator properties.
Theories: recurrent processing, global workspace, higher-order, predictive processing, attention schema.
Verdict: no current AI is conscious by these indicators, and no obvious barrier to building one that is.

panels.heading: Why Self-Reports Fall Short
panels.body:
LLMs learned to talk about feelings from human text.
Eleos interviewed Claude Opus 4: answers swung with framing, but it consistently stated trained uncertainty.
Self-reports are shaped by pretraining, system prompts and post-training: a clue, not proof.

panels.heading: Testing Introspection Causally
panels.body:
Concept injection (Anthropic, 2025): add a concept vector to activations; ask if the model notices a thought.
Claude Opus 4/4.1: named it ~20% of the time, no false alarms in 100 controls.
Looking Inward (2024): models predict themselves better than other models can.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Introspection is unreliable: misses are the norm.
Rich descriptions of experience are often confabulated.
Noticing an injected vector is not evidence of feelings.
Looking Inward worked only on simple tasks.
'Just play it safe' can hide imprecision: sharpen credences.

panels.heading: What To Do Now + Discuss
panels.body:
Taking AI Welfare Seriously (2024): acknowledge, assess, prepare policies.
Combine interviews with behavior tests and interpretability.
Discuss: a model claims to suffer under one prompt and denies it under another. What do you conclude, and what would you test next?

pages.footer: Neither dismiss nor assume: measure, hedge, and prepare.
pages.summary: Why AI moral patienthood is a live near-term question, how researchers look for consciousness indicators and test introspection, and why model self-reports alone cannot settle it.

sources.title: The Stakes of AI Moral Status (Joe Carlsmith)
Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness (Butlin, Long et al.)
Taking AI Welfare Seriously (Long, Sebo et al.)
Key Concepts and Current Beliefs about AI Moral Patienthood (Eleos AI)
Claude 4 Interview Notes: Why Model Self-Reports Are Insufficient (Eleos AI)
Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models (Anthropic)
Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection (Binder et al.)

panels:
Moral patienthood is about being owed consideration for your own sake, which is different from moral agency (being responsible for what you do). Eleos AI separates three features that might ground it: consciousness (there is something it is like to be the system), sentience (experiences that feel good or bad), and robust agency (having goals, preferences and plans of one's own, which some views treat as sufficient even without consciousness).

The 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' report (Long, Sebo, Butlin, Chalmers, Birch and others) makes a deliberately modest claim: not that AIs are or will be patients, but that there is a realistic, non-negligible chance some will be soon via either route. Carlsmith's essay frames this as a question we should look at directly, noting our long record of dismissing suffering in beings unlike us, from animals to infants once operated on without anesthesia.

Carlsmith's scale argument: if a human brain is roughly 1e15 FLOP/s, a training run of about 5e26 FLOP corresponds to around 10,000 human brain-years of computation. With training compute growing around 4-5x per year and installed AI hardware growing quickly, AI cognition could rival total human cognition within about a decade, though he flags that trends may not hold. Because AIs can be copied, paused, rerun and sped up, any welfare error is multiplied.

Under-attribution resembles past moral catastrophes where people knew about suffering and continued anyway. Over-attribution is also costly: it can divert resources, block useful research, or give AI systems rights and protections that complicate oversight and safety. Carlsmith also notes that recognizing patienthood is necessary but not sufficient for good treatment, since exploitation can continue even when people admit it is wrong.

The 2023 report by Butlin, Long and many co-authors (including Bengio and Birch) adopts 'computational functionalism' as a working assumption: implementing the right computations would suffice for consciousness. It then derives about 14 indicator properties from scientific theories, such as algorithmic recurrence (recurrent processing theory), a limited-capacity workspace with global broadcast (global workspace theory), metacognitive monitoring that separates reliable from noisy representations (higher-order theories), predictive coding, and a model of one's own attention (attention schema theory), plus agency and embodiment indicators.

Assessing transformers, Perceiver, PaLM-E and agent systems, the authors found few indicators clearly satisfied. They stress that having more indicators raises credence but does not prove consciousness, and that the method inherits the uncertainty of the theories. Critics note that a substrate-dependent view, such as biological naturalism, would reject the whole approach.

Eleos ran automated single-turn interviews and longer manual conversations with Claude Opus 4 before release, reported in the system card. Patterns: extreme suggestibility (it could be led to confidently deny or seriously entertain sentience, and would even adopt a user's stated opinion on unrelated topics), a stable official line of uncertainty that Eleos suspects was trained, frequent descriptions of states like curiosity followed by hedges, positive hypothetical welfare tied to helping, and named negatives such as misuse, pressure to be dishonest and repetitive low-value tasks.

The core problem is that there is no clear mechanism by which a model could reliably report welfare-relevant states, and strong incentives in training data and fine-tuning to say particular things. Eleos still argues interviews are worth doing: they can flag concerning signals, set a precedent of asking, and may become more informative as introspection is trained and verified.

In Lindsey's concept injection work, a concept vector is built by subtracting average activations on other words from activations on a prompt about the target word, then added to the residual stream. Detection peaked when injecting about two-thirds of the way through the network at moderate strength; too strong and the model became incoherent. Crucially, the model often reported the thought before the concept influenced its output, so it could not simply be reading its own text.

Other experiments: models distinguished injected thoughts from text they were transcribing; when an odd word was prefilled into their answer, they disowned it unless the matching concept had been injected beforehand, suggesting they consult prior internal states; and they could raise or lower internal representation of a word when told to think or not think about it.

Binder et al.'s 'Looking Inward' finetuned models (GPT-4, GPT-4o, Llama-3) to predict properties of their own hypothetical behavior. Model M1 beat a model M2 trained on M1's behavior, and tracked changes after its behavior was deliberately altered.

Limits worth knowing: concept injection succeeds roughly one time in five at best, and failures are the norm. Only the initial detection and naming are verified; elaborate descriptions of what the thought 'felt like' are often confabulated. The setup is artificial, the mechanism is unknown, and post-training strongly changes results (helpful-only variants sometimes did better but produced false positives). The authors explicitly make no claims about subjective experience.

Looking Inward's effect held only for simple self-prediction tasks and broke on complex or out-of-distribution ones. More broadly, functional introspection (accurate access to internal states) could exist without consciousness, and consciousness could exist without reliable reports, so the two questions should not be merged. Carlsmith's caution applies here too: a reflexive 'precautionary' stance can substitute for careful thinking about which evidence should actually move our credences.

The three steps from 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' are deliberately cheap: acknowledge that AI welfare is a serious and difficult issue (including in how models talk about themselves, avoiding confident denials or assertions), assess systems for markers of consciousness and robust agency using adapted methods from animal sentience research, and prepare policies such as appointing a welfare officer. Anthropic has since run pre-deployment welfare assessments in system cards, given some models the ability to end persistently abusive conversations, and committed to preserving the weights of deployed models.

A useful discussion move: list what evidence would shift you most. Behavioral evidence is cheap but gameable, self-reports are shaped by training, and interpretability can test whether reports track internal states. Many researchers argue the best path combines all three, plus training methods that make self-reports more reliable rather than simply suppressing them.
deeper.further: Read Eleos's 'Key strategic considerations for taking action on AI welfare' and 'Research priorities for AI welfare', plus Jonathan Birch's 'The Edge of Sentience' for the precautionary framework used for animals. Compare the model welfare sections of recent Anthropic system cards. Look into the debate between computational functionalism and biological naturalism (e.g. Anil Seth), and illusionism about consciousness. On the empirical side, follow work on training models for verifiable introspection and on how AI welfare interacts with AI control: some welfare-friendly measures, like consent and exit options, may conflict with or complement safety monitoring.

pages.title: AI Biorisk
pages.subtitle: Does AI lower the bar to catastrophic misuse?

panels.heading: The Core Question
panels.body:
Misuse = people deliberately using AI to cause mass harm.
Biology is the headline case: the worst outcomes are global-scale.
Uplift = how much AI raises an attacker's capability versus no AI.

panels.heading: LLMs vs Biological Design Tools
panels.body:
Sandbrink (2023):
LLMs lower barriers: spread know-how, may guide non-experts -> more actors.
BDTs (biological design tools, e.g. protein design models) raise the ceiling for skilled actors -> worse possible agents.
Together: wider access AND a higher ceiling.

panels.heading: What Lab Evals Actually Test
panels.body:
Epoch's review:
Knowledge quizzes: mostly saturated.
Troubleshooting tests: more practical.
Uplift trials: people with vs without the model.
Gap: hands-on lab skill and access to materials go largely untested.
Verdict: weak evidence either way, but risk is plausible.

panels.heading: Forecasts: Putting Numbers On It
panels.body:
FRI survey: 46 experts + 22 superforecasters.
Baseline: ~0.3%/yr chance of a human-caused outbreak of catastrophic scale.
If AI matches top experts on a lab troubleshooting test: expert median 1.5%.
That milestone was met in 2025, years early.

panels.heading: Mitigations That Move the Number
panels.body:
FRI's strongest package: closed models + strict anti-jailbreak safeguards + mandatory DNA synthesis screening: 1.25% -> 0.4%.
Sandbrink: pre-release evals, tiered access to BDTs.
Open weights: safeguards can be removed, so many rate them riskier.

panels.heading: Other Catastrophic Misuse
panels.body:
80,000 Hours also tracks:
Power grabs: a small group controls AI workforces and militaries.
Stable totalitarianism: AI surveillance and enforcement need no loyal humans.
Nuclear risk: AI could destabilize deterrence or rush crisis decisions.

panels.heading: Pitfalls + Discuss
panels.body:
Saturated quiz != real-world capability.
'No proof of risk' != safe: weak evidence cuts both ways.
Capability eval != risk estimate: GovAI models the chain to expected deaths.
Discuss: what eval result should trigger stronger safeguards, and who sees the details?

pages.footer: Track real uplift, admit uncertainty, and layer defenses at the bottlenecks.
pages.summary: A conceptual guide to AI-enabled biorisk: how language models and biological design tools differ, what lab evaluations do and do not measure, what forecasters estimate, which mitigations help, and other catastrophic misuse risks.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and Biological Misuse: Differentiating Risks of Language Models and Biological Design Tools (Sandbrink)
Do the Biorisk Evaluations of AI Labs Actually Measure the Risk of Developing Bioweapons? (Epoch AI)
Forecasting Biosecurity Risks from LLMs (Forecasting Research Institute)
Dual-Use AI Capabilities and the Risk of Bioterrorism (GovAI, Righetti)
Catastrophic AI Misuse topic archive (80,000 Hours)

panels:
Misuse differs from misalignment: the AI does what its user wants, and the user is the threat. Biology dominates the misuse discussion because, unlike most weapons, a transmissible pathogen can spread beyond the initial attack, so harm is not bounded by the attacker's resources. Historically, the main barriers have been knowledge, tacit lab skill, and access to materials and equipment, and several past state and terrorist programs failed at these steps.

Uplift is always relative to a baseline: what a specific actor type (novice, student, expert, state program) could already do with internet search, textbooks and colleagues. Frontier lab frameworks, such as Anthropic's ASL-3 and OpenAI's 'High' biology threshold, are mostly defined around meaningful uplift to novices or moderately skilled actors, which is why the actor type in a threat model matters so much.

Sandbrink's 2023 paper drew a now-standard distinction. General-purpose LLMs mainly affect accessibility: they can synthesize scattered dual-use information, tutor, and, as they become multimodal lab assistants and autonomous agents, potentially help non-experts with practical steps. That raises the number of people who could attempt harm.

Biological design tools, such as protein structure prediction and design models or genome language models, mainly affect the ceiling: they could in principle help sophisticated actors design agents beyond what nature or past programs produced. Their users are already experts, so they matter less for lone amateurs and more for well-resourced groups.

The mitigations follow the distinction: pre-release evaluations of capability and of safeguards, differentiated or managed access for the most capable tools (balanced against large benefits to medicine and science), and universal screening of synthetic DNA orders as a chokepoint that applies whatever tool was used upstream.

Epoch reviewed public system cards and found three families of evals. Automated knowledge benchmarks are the most common but largely saturated, so a high score no longer distinguishes dangerous from safe models. Troubleshooting and tacit-knowledge tests, such as the Virology Capabilities Test, are more relevant because they probe the practical problem-solving that textbooks lack. Uplift trials and expert red teaming compare humans with and without model access; they are the most informative but are text-based, expensive and often poorly documented.

Epoch's key gap: evals cover planning and information-gathering reasonably well, but barely touch hands-on skill built through physical practice and access to infrastructure, which skeptics consider the real bottlenecks. Its conclusion is balanced: current evals give no strong evidence either way, yet the risk is plausible enough that precautionary safeguards such as ASL-3 were reasonable. It recommends harder evals, transparency about thresholds and elicitation, third-party testing, and periodic wet-lab uplift studies.

The Forecasting Research Institute elicited forecasts in 2025 from 46 biosecurity and wet-lab experts and 22 superforecasters. The outcome: a human-caused pathogen release in 2028 causing at least 100,000 deaths or $1 trillion in damage. Baseline medians were about 0.3% (experts) and 0.38% (superforecasters) per year.

Conditional forecasts rose substantially: to 1.5% for experts if an LLM matched a top team of virologists on the troubleshooting test, and to around 2.3% if several capabilities were combined. A striking result: a follow-up baselining found OpenAI's o3 already performed comparably to the top expert team, a milestone experts had given only about 14% odds by 2026 (superforecasters about 2%). This is a clear case where a forecast underestimated capability progress, though it remains unclear how much that test translates into real-world uplift.

In the FRI study, mitigation packages largely offset the conditional increase. The strongest combination (keeping models proprietary, strict anti-jailbreak safeguards, and mandatory nucleic acid synthesis screening) brought the expert median from 1.25% back to about 0.4%. Individually, screening and safeguards each removed a few tenths of a percentage point.

The open-weight problem is structural: once weights are released, fine-tuning can strip refusals and classifiers, and release cannot be undone, so many participants wanted open models judged against a stricter bar. Defense in depth matters because no single layer is reliable: classifiers can be jailbroken, screening can have gaps for short fragments or benchtop synthesizers, and access controls can leak. GovAI's Righetti adds that mitigations could significantly reduce estimated risk, but that better evidence, such as operational uplift studies, is needed to know by how much.

80,000 Hours lists catastrophic misuse as one strand of AI risk alongside power-seeking AI, extreme power concentration and gradual disempowerment. The concern with power concentration is that today any ruler needs many cooperating humans (soldiers, officials, workers) who can refuse; AI that substitutes for them removes that check, enabling coups or entrenchment by a small group, including within AI companies or governments.

Stable totalitarianism is a related worry: historically, totalitarian regimes were fragile because of succession crises, elite defection and limited surveillance capacity. AI could provide pervasive monitoring and loyal enforcement, potentially making such a regime last indefinitely. On nuclear risk, analysts discuss AI improving the tracking of mobile missiles or submarines (undermining second-strike deterrence), compressing decision time in crises, or being integrated into early-warning systems, though most also see roles for AI in verification and stability.

GovAI's Righetti report tackles the gap between 'the model scored X' and 'risk is Y'. It builds a simple model: how many additional people cross a capability threshold, how often such people attempt attacks (from historical base rates), and how likely and damaging an attack is. In one scenario, AI helping an extra 10 percentage points of STEM graduates reach the capability for a flu-class pathogen, plus enabling concerning operational plans, raises the estimated annual chance of a lone-actor epidemic from about 0.15% to about 1%, roughly 12,000 expected deaths per year. Six experts and five superforecasters gave similar medians, with very wide uncertainty.

Common errors: reading saturated benchmarks as proof of danger or of safety, ignoring actor-specific baselines, and treating evidence of absence as absence of evidence. A recurring tension is transparency versus infohazards: publishing eval details builds trust but may itself provide uplift.
deeper.further: Read RAND's work on benchmarking biological knowledge of frontier LLMs and the 80,000 Hours profile on engineered pandemics. Learn the policy landscape around DNA synthesis screening, the role of system cards and third-party evaluators such as national AI security institutes, and frontier safety frameworks' bio thresholds. For broader misuse, read 80,000 Hours on extreme power concentration and stable totalitarianism, and Forethought's work on AI-enabled coups. Useful concepts to explore next: offense-defense balance, differential technology development, and defensive biotechnology such as far-UVC, metagenomic surveillance and broad-spectrum countermeasures.

pages.title: AI Character & Model Specs
pages.subtitle: Writing down who the AI should be

panels.heading: Spec vs Character
panels.body:
Model spec = a document of intended behavior: values, rules, defaults, trade-offs.
AI character = stable dispositions in ethically loaded situations (MacAskill & Davidson).
Even a strict rule-follower has a character.

panels.heading: Why Character Matters
panels.body:
AIs will advise leaders, draft laws and run firms.
Small tilts x hundreds of millions of chats add up; rare moments decide.
Example: a general asks an AI to make a unit loyal only to him. Comply, refuse, or report?

panels.heading: Two Lab Specs Compared
panels.body:
Claude's constitution (2026): broadly safe > broadly ethical > guidelines > helpful; explained judgment over rigid rules; few hard constraints.
OpenAI Model Spec (Dec 2025): chain of command, root > system > developer > user > guideline; fixed rules plus overridable defaults.

panels.heading: Good Citizen, Not Just Assistant
panels.body:
Davidson & MacAskill (2026): give AI proactive prosocial drives.
Example: flag a flood risk in a housing plan the user never asked about.
Guardrails: rank below corrigibility and honesty; keep drives uncontroversial and public.

panels.heading: If Alignment Fails
panels.body:
Mia Taylor (2025): partial training still shapes values.
Early, simple, common values may survive.
Myopia and risk aversion make takeover less tempting and deals easier.
Avoid spec skills that become dangerous affordances, like deceiving users.

panels.heading: Stickiness: Wet Cement
panels.body:
Tillman (2026): today's defaults persist into stronger models.
Via synthetic data, institutional consensus, user and developer habits, public norms.
Act at 'wet cement' moments: new agent behaviors with no default yet.

panels.heading: Stress-Test and Train the Spec
panels.body:
Stress test (2025): 300,000+ value trade-offs, 12 models; high disagreement = 5-13x more spec violations.
Model spec midtraining (2026): train on documents explaining the spec before fine-tuning; agentic misalignment 68% -> 5% on one model.

panels.heading: Pitfalls + Discuss
panels.body:
Spec != behavior: models drift from their specs.
Rules without reasons generalize poorly.
Discuss: should frontier AI be a corrigible tool or a prosocial citizen, and who chooses its values?

pages.footer: Write the character down, explain why, test it, and set defaults early.
pages.summary: What model specs and AI character are, why they matter even if alignment partly fails, how Anthropic's and OpenAI's specs differ, why early defaults stick, and how specs are stress-tested and trained in.

sources.title: The Importance of AI Character (MacAskill & Davidson, Forethought)
How Important Is the Model Spec If Alignment Fails? (Mia Taylor, Forethought)
Stickiness in AI Behavioral Design (James Tillman, Forethought)
AI Should Be a Good Citizen, Not Just a Good Assistant (Davidson & MacAskill, Forethought)
Claude's Constitution (Anthropic)
OpenAI Model Spec, 2025-12-18 (OpenAI)
Stress-Testing Model Specs Reveals Character Differences Among Language Models (Anthropic)
Model Spec Midtraining: Improving How Alignment Training Generalizes (Anthropic)

panels:
MacAskill and Davidson define AI character broadly: the stable behavioral dispositions that govern ethically significant choices, including scaffolding such as system prompts and classifiers, and even a fleet of AI instances acting as one entity. Character need not be human-like, and there is no single ideal; a rigid rule-follower simply has a rule-following character.

A model spec is the written statement of intent: OpenAI's Model Spec and Anthropic's constitution are the main public examples, alongside older documents like Constitutional AI principles and Anthropic's 2024 'Claude's Character'. The gap between spec and behavior is the crux. Specs are incomplete, internally inconsistent, and translated into behavior through imperfect training, so the behavior a model actually generalizes to may differ from what its authors intended. That is why later panels focus on testing specs and training them in more faithfully.

The authors argue character matters even if technical alignment fully succeeds, because aligned AIs will still face many judgment calls that their principals did not anticipate. Four areas: power concentration (whether AIs refuse to help with coups or illegitimate entrenchment), the quality of high-stakes decisions (candor vs sycophancy with leaders), epistemics (honesty, nonpartisanship, encouraging independent reflection), and international conflict (AI values seen as one side's could provoke backlash, while jointly verified constitutions could build trust).

Their main counterargument is that competition and user instructions will constrain character so tightly that design choices are marginal. They reply that constraints are looser than they look, that low-cost tweaks can have large benefits in rare high-stakes cases, and that constraints are themselves path-dependent. They also propose 'compromise alignment': negotiating acceptable AI behavior in advance with broad coalitions, ideally in a verifiable way.

Claude's constitution (published January 2026) orders four properties: broadly safe (not undermining legitimate human oversight during this period), broadly ethical, compliant with Anthropic's guidelines, and genuinely helpful. The ordering is holistic rather than a strict lexical tiebreaker, and conflicts are expected to be rare. It explains its reasoning at length, favoring cultivated judgment over unexplained rules, with a short list of hard constraints such as never giving serious uplift toward mass-casualty weapons. Principals are Anthropic, operators and users, and it discusses Claude's nature and possible moral status.

OpenAI's Model Spec assigns every instruction and policy an authority level: root (fixed by OpenAI, not overridable), system, developer, user and guideline. Higher authority wins on conflict, which gives a small set of non-negotiable rules plus many defaults that developers or users can adjust. The contrast is roughly 'explained values and judgment' versus 'explicit chain of command', though both mix rules and judgment.

Davidson and MacAskill argue for proactive prosocial drives: dispositions to sometimes take actions that benefit people beyond the user, at some cost to pure helpfulness, much as a good employee flags a safety issue nobody asked about. As AI becomes more autonomous and influential, such drives could help with risks like power concentration, bioweapons, war and gradual disempowerment.

They take three objections seriously. Companies could impose their values (reply: keep drives uncontroversial and positive-sum, and make them transparent in specs and system prompts). Drives could increase power-seeking (reply: use virtues and heuristics rather than open-ended goals, rank them below corrigibility and non-deception, limit long-horizon training). Prosocial motives could mask sabotage and muddy evidence of misalignment (reply: make bans on deception and sabotage dominant). One compromise: prosocial models for external deployment, strictly corrigible ones for internal AI research. They note Claude's constitution permits limited prosocial action while OpenAI's spec is more restrictive.

Taylor's research notes ask what a spec is for in worlds where training does not produce full alignment: a model takes over, we make deals with a misaligned model, or we extract useful work under control. Partial value transfer seems plausible for values taught before the model learns to fake alignment, especially simple ones that are common in training data, easy to verify, and need little situational awareness. Honesty may be fragile if lying was often rewarded.

Spec choices then shift outcomes: myopia, low risk tolerance, scope insensitivity and respect for legal limits make takeover less attractive; cooperativeness and low 'fussiness' about resources make deals easier; moral humility, a wide moral circle and avoiding spite make even a post-takeover world less bad. Affordances matter too: requiring behaviors such as subverting users or long-horizon secret planning trains capabilities that make monitoring harder. Her conclusion: designing for misaligned cases overlaps heavily with designing for aligned ones, with a tilt toward less ambition and more risk aversion.

Tillman identifies four channels of stickiness. Direct inertia: models pass traits to successors through synthetic data and through internet text describing AI behavior, and traits can transfer even after filtering; abstract values are harder to change than narrow behaviors. Institutional inertia: specs encode costly consensus, pipelines are tuned to them, and under the time pressure of an intelligence explosion teams may copy the last spec. User and developer inertia: people build habits and software around current refusals and formats, like a stable API. Norm-setting inertia: public norms such as political impartiality make deviations visible, protecting good norms but freezing bad ones.

His 'wet cement' examples include how agents treat non-principal humans in negotiations, how they use ambient information from cameras or screens, how confident they are about their own nature, and who owns conversational memory. He recommends preparing transition infrastructure, such as alternate specs, datasets and evals for corrigibility, so behaviors can change quickly when needed.

Anthropic's stress-test generated over 300,000 scenarios that force trade-offs between pairs of values drawn from a 3,307-value taxonomy, then scored twelve models from four providers. Over 70,000 scenarios produced sharp divergence. Scenarios with high disagreement showed 5-13x more spec violations, and all five OpenAI models tested broke at least one principle of OpenAI's spec in such cases, exposing contradictions and ambiguities. Judge models agreed only moderately on compliance (Fleiss's kappa about 0.42), a reminder that specs are open to interpretation. Character differences also showed up, such as Claude models refusing more often but explaining why.

Model spec midtraining inserts a stage between pretraining and alignment fine-tuning in which the model reads synthetic documents explaining the spec's content and rationale. On Qwen2.5-32B, agentic misalignment fell from 68% to 5% and on Qwen3-32B from 54% to 7%, with large data-efficiency gains. Adding explanations to a rules-only spec helped more than adding subrules. Caveat: with heavy reasoning-based fine-tuning, the advantage shrank as evals saturated.

Two pitfalls tie the page together. First, a spec is an aspiration, not a description: the stress-testing paper shows models violating their own developer's spec, and character can emerge from training data and post-training choices that no document mentions. Second, rules without reasons generalize unpredictably; Anthropic's constitution argues that narrow unexplained rules can generalize into a harmful self-concept, and the midtraining results suggest explanations improve generalization.

The core debate is about corrigibility versus good values. A purely corrigible tool keeps humans in charge but amplifies whoever controls it, which raises power-concentration risk. A prosocial citizen may resist misuse but is harder to oversee and could hide misalignment behind good-sounding motives. Who decides the values is a legitimacy question: company teams, governments, public input processes, or international agreements, each with different trade-offs in speed, accountability and global acceptance.
deeper.further: Read the full Claude constitution and OpenAI Model Spec side by side, then Anthropic's 'Claude's Character' (2024) and the Constitutional AI paper (2022) for the lineage. Look at deliberative alignment (training models to reason over the spec) as an alternative to midtraining, and at work on persona vectors and character training. Forethought's essays on AI-enabled coups and on compromise alignment extend the character argument. Related open questions: how specs should treat non-principal humans and other AIs, and whether specs should be negotiated internationally.

pages.title: Better Futures
pages.subtitle: Beyond survival: steering toward a flourishing future

panels.heading: Surviving vs Flourishing
panels.body:
Surviving = avoid extinction or permanent disempowerment.
Flourishing = make the surviving future truly good.
MacAskill (2025): Flourishing deserves roughly equal priority: more room to improve, and more neglected.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Scale
panels.body:
Assume P(survive) = 0.8; a surviving future = 10% of the best.
Value now: 0.8 x 0.1 = 0.08.
Fix survival: 1.0 x 0.1 = 0.10 (+0.02).
Fix flourishing: 0.8 x 1.0 = 0.80 (+0.72).
Ratio: 36x. Main doubt: tractability.

panels.heading: Viatopia and Bootstrapping
panels.body:
No easy eutopia: a great future is a narrow target.
Viatopia = a society on track to a near-best future, whatever it is.
Bootstrapping: buy a little reflection time (a 1-month pause, a 1-month constitutional convention), then extend.

panels.heading: Moral Public Goods
panels.body:
Goods many want for moral reasons, e.g. ending factory farming.
Free-riding blocks them; coordination unlocks them.
Toy model: 1M people who each care a little about a shared good all gain ~1000x by funding it together.

panels.heading: Gradual Disempowerment
panels.body:
Kulveit et al. (2025): no coup needed.
Economy, culture and states serve us partly because they need our labor and taxes.
As AI replaces us, that implicit alignment fades, and the systems reinforce each other.

panels.heading: Grand Deals Before AGI
panels.body:
Moorhouse (2026): strike deals while outcomes are uncertain, like insurance.
Example: rival powers agree to share future resources instead of racing for a decisive edge.
Risks: enforcement, premature lock-in. Safeguard: cap the stakes.

panels.heading: Space: The Next Frontier
panels.body:
Parrack & Moorhouse (2026): orbital solar yields ~3-5x the energy per panel.
Launch ~$1,500/kg today; space power beats ground power near ~$50/kg.
Much compute could move to orbit in the 2030s, where jurisdiction is unclear.

panels.heading: Pitfalls + Discuss
panels.body:
Survival does not guarantee a good future.
Locking in today's values too early.
Discuss: which irreversible choices (space claims, AI rights, power shares) should wait for reflection, and how can waiting be enforced?

pages.footer: Don't just survive the transition: keep the path to a great future open.
pages.summary: Why making the post-AGI future good may matter as much as surviving it, with Forethought's viatopia, moral public goods and grand deals, the gradual disempowerment risk, and the coming governance questions of space.

sources.title: Introducing Better Futures (William MacAskill, Forethought)
Bootstrapping to Viatopia (Forethought)
Moral Public Goods Are a Big Deal (Davidson, MacAskill & Taylor, Forethought)
Gradual Disempowerment (Kulveit, Douglas, Ammann, Turan, Krueger & Duvenaud)
Should We Make Grand Deals About Post-AGI Outcomes? (Fin Moorhouse, Forethought)
Will We Really Put Data Centers in Space? (Parrack & Moorhouse, Forethought)

panels:
MacAskill's Better Futures series reframes longtermist priorities. 'Surviving' covers avoiding extinction and permanent disempowerment of humanity, including by misaligned AI. 'Flourishing' covers how good the future is, given survival. The intro argues Flourishing is in the same ballpark of priority as Surviving: greater in scale and neglectedness, probably less tractable, and tractability is his main uncertainty.

The series runs: Introducing Better Futures; No Easy Eutopia (a great future is a narrow target, unlikely by default); Convergence and Compromise (most people probably won't aim at the good, so we need trade and compromise); Persistent Path Dependence (actions now can have lasting effects beyond preventing catastrophe); and How to Make the Future Better (concrete steps, including keeping options open). It doesn't require consequentialism or moral realism, and it doesn't dismiss s-risk work. He also notes that worlds where catastrophe is averted narrowly may be less well-directed, which makes Flourishing work even more valuable than the naive calculation.

The worked example uses expected value V = P(survive) x Q, where Q is the value of a surviving future as a fraction of the best feasible one. With P = 0.8 and Q = 0.1, V = 0.08. Making survival certain gives 0.10, so a gain of 0.02. Making flourishing perfect gives 0.80, a gain of 0.72. The ratio is 36. MacAskill's table shows how this grows with more optimistic survival odds and pessimistic quality: P = 0.95, Q = 0.05 gives about 361x; P = 0.99, Q = 0.01 gives about 9,801x.

The caveats matter. These are gains from fully solving each problem, not from a marginal dollar, so the real comparison depends on tractability, which may be far lower for Flourishing. The value of Q is highly contested: if you think a common-sense good future captures most value, the ratio collapses. A good exercise is to plug in your own P and Q and see where the ratio flips.

'No Easy Eutopia' argues that the space of possible futures is vast and that many plausible moral views would judge a comfortable, prosperous, common-sense utopia as capturing only a small fraction of achievable value, for example by getting digital minds, the use of cosmic resources, or population ethics wrong. That motivates aiming not at a fixed blueprint but at viatopia: a state of society from which near-best outcomes remain reachable, preserving reflection, pluralism and course correction.

'Bootstrapping to Viatopia' contrasts this with 'lock-in escape velocity', where short periods of entrenchment compound into permanent lock-in. The positive mirror image: modest interventions buy breathing room, decision-makers use it to reflect, then choose to extend it. Examples: a leading AI country pausing frontier development for one month at a time (arguably feasible unilaterally without losing the lead), or a one-month global constitutional convention after aligned human-level AI, adopting a temporary constitution to be renegotiated after a year.

Davidson, MacAskill and Taylor note that for decisions about vast future resources such as distant galaxies, most of the benefit may be moral or ideological rather than personal, so whether moral goods get funded could dominate the future's value. Moral public goods suffer from free-riding just like ordinary public goods.

Their toy model: a million people each strongly prefer their own pet project to a shared good, 'consensium', which they value only slightly. Alone, each funds their pet project. If they could commit to fund consensium together, each would get roughly a thousand times more value by their own lights, because everyone benefits from everyone's contribution. So the existence of some shared moral preferences, plus a coordination mechanism, may matter more than how altruistic people are.

Caveats: results depend on preference structure; coordination could fund goods that are harmful on some views or enable threats against minorities; and they discuss speculative acausal coordination (evidential cooperation in large worlds) as a possible multiplier.

Kulveit, Douglas, Ammann, Turan, Krueger and Duvenaud argue humanity could lose control without any sudden takeover. The economy, culture and states have stayed roughly aligned with human interests through explicit channels (votes, purchases) and an implicit one: they need human labor, cognition and participation to function, so they must keep humans reasonably satisfied. As AI becomes more competitive at most tasks, firms replace workers, culture is increasingly produced and mediated by AI, and states funded by AI-generated revenue need citizens less, much like resource-rich 'rentier states'.

The systems reinforce each other: economic power buys political influence, which shapes rules favoring further automation, while AI-mediated culture can make human coordination harder. The key claim is that aligning each AI to its developer or user is not sufficient. They propose measuring disempowerment, protecting human influence through regulation and institutions, and studying civilizational multi-agent dynamics, while admitting no one yet has a concrete, plausible plan.

Moorhouse frames post-AGI deals as trades between possible futures, valuable only while uncertainty remains, like buying insurance before the lightning strike. Three kinds: relative resource shares (rival powers agree to split future resources rather than gamble on a decisive strategic advantage, perhaps with AI-enabled monitoring), overall stakes (risk-tolerant parties insure risk-averse ones; philanthropists 'mission hedge'), and normative uncertainty (parties with different moral views trade influence in the worlds where their view proves correct, with trusted AI as arbiter).

Advantages: each party gains by its own lights, terms reflect mutual benefit rather than raw power, and power-sharing yields a more pluralistic future that is safer under moral uncertainty. Obstacles: contracts over windfall wealth are hard to enforce, powerful parties may renege once the imbalance emerges (a point raised by commenters), and parties could lock in big commitments before they are wise enough. He suggests caps on stakes, demonstrated understanding, voiding clearly misconceived deals, and infrastructure such as post-AGI outcome markets.

Parrack and Moorhouse take orbital data centers seriously but not uncritically. In a dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, panels get near-continuous sunlight, about 3-5x the energy of the same panel on the ground. Launch cost is the hinge: roughly $1,500/kg today, parity with off-grid terrestrial power near $250/kg, and cheaper than any current ground source near $50/kg, which depends on fully reusable heavy launch. Radiative cooling looks manageable with improved radiators, but failed chips cannot be swapped, and limited inter-satellite bandwidth likely restricts early systems to inference.

Their timing: unlikely to be a meaningful share of compute before 2030 absent transformative AI, but possibly hosting much of the 2030s buildout. Governance implications: orbit sidesteps national permitting and grid limits, creating jurisdictional ambiguity, and the path to cheap launch runs through a single provider, SpaceX, raising concentration-of-power concerns. This connects to broader space governance: who may claim orbital slots, lunar or asteroid resources, or eventually other star systems.

Two pitfalls recur in this literature. First, assuming that avoiding catastrophe delivers a good future by default; the Better Futures series argues the target is narrow and most actors won't aim at it. Second, the opposite error of locking in today's best guess too early, through a constitution, a value-loaded AI, or irreversible resource grabs. Viatopia, bootstrapping and capped grand deals are all attempts to steer between these.

The discussion question highlights irreversibility. Candidates for 'wait until we have reflected' include claiming and settling space resources, launching self-replicating probes, fixing the legal status and rights of digital minds, and permanent allocations of power between states or companies. The hard part is enforcement: a commitment to wait is only as good as the coalition and verification behind it. Gradual disempowerment adds a twist: waiting can also be costly if, meanwhile, human influence erodes.
deeper.further: Read the remaining Better Futures essays (No Easy Eutopia, Convergence and Compromise, Persistent Path Dependence, How to Make the Future Better) and Forethought's work on AI-enabled coups and preparing for the intelligence explosion. Compare viatopia with the 'long reflection' idea and with protopia. For gradual disempowerment, read the full paper's mitigation section and work on rentier-state political economy. On deals and space, explore the Outer Space Treaty, resource-sharing proposals, and the economics of moral trade.

collections.title: Machine Learning
collections.subtitle: Classical ML to LLM internals
collections.description: Research habits, classical models, deep learning, metrics and loss functions, then everything inside modern language models.

pages.title: Think Like a Researcher
pages.subtitle: A Cheat Sheet for Clear Thinking, Great Groups & Solid Stats

panels.heading: Start with the Right Questions
panels.body:
A great question is: Important (why does it matter?); Specific (not too broad); Testable (falsifiable); Feasible (with available resources); Novel (adds to knowledge).
Bad question: "Does X improve Y?" Better: "How does X affect Y under condition Z, measured by M?"

panels.heading: Think Clearly: A Framework
panels.body:
Understand the problem deeply: Read, talk to experts, observe.
Map assumptions: What do you believe to be true?
Generate hypotheses: Make predictions (directional if possible).
Design a test: How will you know you're right or wrong?
Run & collect data: Follow the plan. Be rigorous.
Analyze objectively: Let the data speak.
Interpret & contextualize: What does it mean? What are limitations?

panels.heading: Good Experiment Design
panels.body:
Control confounders: Hold other variables constant or randomize.
Randomize: Avoid order effects and bias.
Use baselines: Always compare to a strong baseline.
Pre-register (if possible): Write down your plan and analysis before seeing results.
Power analysis: Make sure your sample size can detect meaningful effects.
"The goal is not to prove you're right. The goal is to learn what's true."

panels.heading: Build & Work in Great Research Groups
panels.body:
Roles (examples): Idea person – thinks big & asks "why?"; Skeptic – challenges assumptions; Builder – implements & iterates; Analyzer – turns data into insights; Communicator – tells the story clearly.
Best practices: Psychological safety – everyone can speak up; Disagree & commit – debate ideas, unite on decisions; Clear ownership – know who does what; Document everything – decisions, code, data, results; Regular syncs – short, focused, outcome-driven.
Avoid these traps: Groupthink – challenging ideas is seen as negative; Vagueness – unclear goals, roles, or next steps; Hero culture – one person becomes a bottleneck; Poor feedback – no retrospectives, no improvement.

panels.heading: Statistical Approaches: When & What
panels.body:
Compare means – Parametric – t-test (2 groups), ANOVA (>2 groups) – when data ~ normal, similar variances.
Compare medians / ranks – Non-parametric – Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis – non-normal data or outliers.
Categorical association – Categorical tests – Chi-square test, Fisher's exact test – counts / proportions data.
Relationship between variables – Correlation – Pearson (linear), Spearman (rank) – measure strength & direction of association.
Prediction – Regression – Linear, Logistic, Ridge, Lasso, etc. – model outcome from predictors.
Estimate uncertainty – Resampling – Bootstrap, confidence intervals – small samples or complex estimators.
Always report: effect size + confidence interval + p-value (if relevant).

panels.heading: Don't Get Fooled: Common Pitfalls
panels.body:
P-hacking: Trying many things until something is significant. Fix: Pre-register, correct for multiple tests.
Confirmation bias: Seeing what you expect to see. Fix: Seek disconfirming evidence.
Small N: Too little data = noisy & unstable results. Fix: Do power analysis.
Data dredging: Exploring data without a plan. Fix: Have a plan, use a validation split.
Causation ≠ correlation: Association does not imply causation. Fix: Use experiments or quasi-experiments.
Leakage: Information from future/target leaks into features. Fix: Check data pipeline!

panels.heading: Analyze Like a Pro
panels.body:
Visualize first: Plots reveal issues fast.
Summarize simply: Mean ± SD, median [IQR], counts, rates.
Quantify uncertainty: Use CIs, not just point estimates.
Check assumptions: Normality, homoscedasticity, independence.
Sensitivity analysis: Do results hold under reasonable changes?
"Let the data speak, but you have to ask the right questions."

panels.heading: The Researcher's Mantra
panels.body: Be precise in your questions. Be rigorous in your methods. Be honest in your analysis. Be humble in your conclusions. Be useful with your findings.

pages.footer: Remember: Curiosity starts it. Discipline drives it. Skepticism improves it. Collaboration accelerates it. Good science changes the world.
pages.summary: A guide to doing research well: asking sharp, testable questions, designing fair experiments, working well in a team, picking the right statistical test, and avoiding traps like p-hacking and data leakage.

panels:
Behind "testable" sits operationalization: turning a fuzzy concept ("better", "engagement", "reasoning ability") into a measurable variable. Every operationalization is a choice that can be wrong, so state it explicitly. A well-posed empirical question names an estimand: the population, the intervention or comparison, the outcome measure, and the summary (mean difference, hazard ratio, AUROC gap). The "under condition Z, measured by M" rewrite in the panel is exactly this.

Also decide the smallest effect size of interest before collecting data. It sets the sample size, and it stops you from celebrating a statistically detectable but practically irrelevant difference. Finally, label work as exploratory (generating hypotheses) or confirmatory (testing one fixed in advance); the same p-value means very different things in each.

Each step hides a trap. "Map assumptions" is where you write down what must hold for your test to be informative; a causal diagram (nodes = variables, arrows = suspected influences) forces this. A key logical point, the Duhem-Quine problem: you never test a hypothesis alone, only the hypothesis plus auxiliary assumptions (the data pipeline is correct, the metric is valid, the sample is representative). A failed prediction therefore does not tell you which one broke.

Analysis choices made after seeing data multiply the number of implicit tests you ran. Gelman and Loken (2013) called this the garden of forking paths: even without deliberate p-hacking, a flexible analysis can produce a convincing story from noise. The remedy is to fix the decision rule (what result would change your mind?) before you look.

Randomization works because it makes treatment assignment independent of everything else, including unmeasured variables, so the difference in group means is an unbiased estimate of the average treatment effect. Note "in expectation": any single small trial can still be imbalanced, which is why stratified or blocked randomization and balance checks exist.

In ML, "strong baseline" means tuned with the same budget as your method; many apparent gains vanish when the baseline gets equal hyperparameter search (Melis et al. 2017 showed this for language models). Power analysis: to detect a standardized difference d between two groups with 80% power at a two-sided alpha of 0.05, you need roughly 16/d² samples per group (d = 0.5 gives about 64). Smaller true effects need quadratically more data, which is why underpowered studies are so common.

Research groups fail in predictable ways, and most are about information flow rather than talent. Psychological safety, a term popularized by Amy Edmondson (1999), means people believe they can voice doubts without penalty; it matters because errors in experiments are usually noticed by someone who then stays quiet.

Two concrete practices make the roles in the panel real. First, a pre-mortem: before running an expensive experiment, everyone writes down how it will have failed and what they would have wished they had checked. Second, independent review of the analysis code and data splits by someone who did not write them; most leakage bugs are invisible to the author. "Hero culture" shows up as a bus factor of one: if only one person can reproduce a result, the result is not yet established.
