Choose tests by the question and by what the test actually compares. The t-test compares means; prefer Welch's version, which does not assume equal variances, as the default. With moderate samples the t-test is fairly robust to non-normality because of the central limit theorem, so "data are not normal" alone is a weak reason to abandon it. Mann-Whitney U tests whether a random draw from one group tends to exceed one from the other (stochastic dominance); it equals a median comparison only if the two distributions have the same shape. Chi-square needs expected cell counts of about 5 or more; Fisher's exact test does not. The bootstrap (resampling with replacement) approximates sampling distributions when no formula exists. Effect size (e.g. Cohen's d, a mean difference in units of pooled standard deviation) answers "how big", which a p-value cannot.

A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true; it is not the probability the hypothesis is true. If you run m independent tests at alpha = 0.05 with no real effects, the chance of at least one false positive is 1 - 0.95^m, already about 64% for m = 20. Bonferroni (use alpha/m) controls that family-wise error but is conservative; Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) controls the false discovery rate, the expected fraction of declared discoveries that are false, which suits exploratory screens.

Small samples also exaggerate: among the estimates that happen to reach significance in a low-power study, the effect is overstated on average (Gelman and Carlin's "Type M" error, 2014). In ML the equivalent is picking the best of many runs or configurations and reporting it as the expected performance.

Anscombe's quartet (1973) is the classic argument for plotting first: four datasets with nearly identical means, variances, correlation (about 0.82) and fitted line, yet one is curved, one has an outlier, one is a vertical stack with a single leverage point. Summary statistics discard exactly the structure that matters.

Distinguish standard deviation (spread of the data) from standard error (uncertainty of the estimate, roughly SD/√n); papers that blur them make results look more certain than they are. Assumption checks are about what the method needs: independence is the one most often violated (repeated measures per user, per patient, per prompt), and it makes naive standard errors too small; use clustered or hierarchical methods. For sensitivity analysis, specification-curve analysis (Simonsohn et al. 2020) plots the result across all defensible analysis choices, showing whether the conclusion depends on one arbitrary path.

The mantra maps to concrete behaviors. Precise: state the estimand and the metric before the result. Rigorous: pre-specified analysis, held-out test data touched once, multiple seeds. Honest: report all experiments you ran, including failures, and label post-hoc findings as exploratory; Feynman's formulation (1974) is that the first principle is not to fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool. Humble: state the scope of the claim, covering which population, which model scale, which dataset, because external validity is usually narrower than the abstract implies. The Open Science Collaboration (2015) attempted to replicate 100 psychology studies and found that roughly a third to a half reproduced the original significant effects, depending on the criterion, which is the cost of skipping these habits. Useful: prefer effects that change a decision.
deeper.further: Common misconception: statistical significance is not evidence of importance, and non-significance is not evidence of no effect; a wide confidence interval just means you could not tell. Another gotcha is treating the sequence "explore, then test" as one pass over the same data: once the data suggested the hypothesis, it cannot also confirm it, which is why a held-out split or a fresh sample matters. This page is the philosophy behind the rest of the book: cross-validation and the debugging checklist are the same discipline (keep the test honest) applied to models, and the correlation-versus-causation page is the same humility applied to claims.

pages.title: Correlation vs Causation
pages.subtitle: Two things moving together does NOT automatically mean one causes the other.

panels.heading: Core Ideas
panels.body:
Correlation: ELI5 – two variables change together. Pro: Great for finding patterns and hypotheses. Con: Says nothing by itself about why. Use when: Exploration, monitoring, feature screening.
Causation: ELI5 – changing X would change Y. Pro: Supports actions and decisions. Con: Harder to prove. Use when: Policies, interventions, product changes, medicine.
Key rule: Correlation ≠ causation. Why? A hidden factor may drive both. Or Y may cause X. Or it may be coincidence / time trend.

panels.heading: What Fools You?
panels.body:
Confounder: A third variable affects both X and Y. Example: ice cream ↑ and drowning ↑ because summer (Z) ↑.
Reverse causality: Maybe Y actually causes X. Example: stress and bad sleep — which comes first?
Selection / collider bias: The sample itself creates a fake pattern. Example: only looking at admitted patients or clicked users.
Time trends & coincidence: Things can rise together without a direct link. Shared seasonality or pure luck can mislead you.

panels.heading: How to Get Closer to Causality
panels.body:
Randomized experiment / A-B test: Best tool when feasible. Randomization balances hidden factors (randomly assign to A – control, or B – variant).
Observational causal tools: Use controls, matching, DAGs, fixed effects, diff-in-diff, IVs when randomization is impossible. Always state assumptions.
Temporal check: Cause must come before effect. Check timing carefully.
Robustness checks: Try alternative controls, subgroups, sensitivity tests, and placebo checks. If the story breaks easily, be skeptical.

panels.heading: How to Talk Like a Good Researcher
panels.body: Exploring data? Say: "X is associated with Y." → Making an action claim? Ask: "What design supports causality?" → Can I randomize? If yes → experiment. → If no → use a causal design + assumptions + sensitivity checks. Strong claim requires strong evidence. Avoid causal words unless the design justifies them.

panels.heading: Two Classic Traps
panels.body:
Trap 1: A huge R or beautiful scatter plot is not enough (e.g. R = 0.92). Always ask: what else could explain this?
Trap 2: Action based on observational data. If you will change a product, policy, or treatment, correlation alone is risky.

panels.heading: Quick Checklist
panels.body: 1. What is the claim: association or cause? 2. Could there be a confounder? 3. Could direction be reversed? 4. Did the cause happen first? 5. What design supports the claim? 6. How robust is the result?

pages.summary: Explains why two things rising and falling together doesn't prove one causes the other, the usual culprits (hidden confounders, reversed direction, biased samples, coincidence), and how experiments and careful causal methods get closer to real cause and effect.

panels:
In the potential-outcomes framework (Rubin), each unit has two outcomes, Y(1) if treated and Y(0) if not, and the causal effect is their difference. Only one is observed: the fundamental problem of causal inference. The average treatment effect is E[Y(1) - Y(0)]. The observed difference between treated and untreated groups equals the ATE plus a selection-bias term whenever those groups would have differed even without treatment; randomization sets that term to zero in expectation.

Pearl's notation separates seeing from doing: P(y | x) is what you observe when X happens to be x, while P(y | do(x)) is what happens when you set X to x. Correlation (usually Pearson r) measures only linear association; y = x² on symmetric x has r = 0 despite perfect dependence. Prediction needs only the first; decisions need the second.

Draw the three basic causal shapes. A fork (Z causes X and Y) is confounding: X and Y correlate, and conditioning on Z removes the spurious part. A chain (X causes M causes Y) is mediation: controlling for M blocks a real effect. A collider (X and Y both cause C) is the reverse: X and Y are independent until you condition on C, which creates a spurious association. This is Berkson's paradox (1946), the mechanism behind "only look at admitted patients".

Simpson's paradox shows aggregation can reverse a trend: the 1973 UC Berkeley admissions data (Bickel et al. 1975) showed lower overall acceptance for women while most departments showed no disadvantage, because women applied more to harder departments. Two trending series correlate strongly even if unrelated (Granger and Newbold 1974), so detrend first.

Randomization balances confounders in expectation, including ones you never measured, but it needs care. Assignment must be truly random and independent of outcomes; check for sample ratio mismatch (observed group sizes deviating from the planned split). Interference matters too: in a marketplace or social network, treating one unit changes outcomes of others, violating the usual no-interference assumption.

Without randomization, each tool buys identification with an assumption. Adjustment needs all confounders measured (the backdoor criterion: block every non-causal path). Propensity scores (Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983) balance observed covariates only. Difference-in-differences assumes parallel trends absent treatment. Instrumental variables need an instrument that affects outcome only via treatment. None of these is testable fully, hence sensitivity analyses such as the E-value (VanderWeele and Ding 2017): how strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be?

Pearl describes a ladder: association (seeing), intervention (doing), counterfactual (imagining). Each rung needs assumptions the lower rung's data cannot supply. A modern formalization is target trial emulation (Hernán and Robins 2016): when analyzing observational data, write down the randomized trial you wish you had (eligibility, treatment strategies, start time, outcome, analysis) and make the data mimic it.

Wording matters because it signals the design. "Predicts" and "is associated with" are fine for correlational evidence. A subtle ML point: a feature that is highly predictive of the outcome (or has high attribution in an explainer) is not necessarily a lever. Emergency room visits predict illness, but reducing visits will not reduce illness.

A correlation of R = 0.92 gives R² = 0.85, meaning 85% of variance is shared linearly, and still says nothing about direction, confounding, or whether the relation is stable under intervention. Searching over many variables will always find striking correlations by chance; with 1,000 candidate series, thousands of pairs will clear a nominal threshold.

Statistical significance also depends on sample size: with n = 10,000, a correlation of just 0.02 gives p of about 0.046, yet explains 0.04% of variance.

For product decisions, a standard trap is self-selection: users who adopt a feature retain better, but engaged users are the ones who adopt it. A churn model predicts who leaves, not whom a discount would retain; for that you need uplift modeling or a randomized holdout.

Make the checklist operational. Negative-control outcomes (outcomes the treatment cannot plausibly affect) and placebo tests (a fake treatment date, a fake population) reveal hidden bias: if the "effect" appears where none can exist, your design is picking up confounding. Check dose-response (does more exposure produce more effect?) and consistency across settings and methods. The Bradford Hill considerations (1965), such as strength, consistency, temporality, dose-response and plausibility, remain a useful informal list, with temporality the only strictly necessary item.

Also write the causal diagram before modeling and ask which arrows you are assuming absent; each missing arrow is a claim. Report how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to nullify the result. Finally, distinguish robustness of the estimate (stable under analysis choices) from validity (correct under the real world), because a stable biased estimate is still biased.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: controlling for more variables is not always better (colliders and mediators), randomization does not guarantee balance in every sample, and causal inference is not only for experiments; it is a framework for stating assumptions explicitly. In ML practice, the topic returns constantly: spurious features that predict in training but fail under shift (shortcut learning), evaluating a recommender or LLM feature by A/B test, and interpretability findings that are correlational unless you intervene on activations. The interpretability page shows that causal-intervention experiments (patching) are exactly the do() operation applied to a network. Use this page's wording discipline in everything you write.

pages.title: Something's Off?
pages.subtitle: A Cheat Sheet for Detecting Odd Results — Good researchers don't just run models. They trust, but verify.

panels.heading: Red Flags: When Results Look Odd
panels.body:
Perfect (or near-perfect) scores: 99.9% accuracy? Check for leakage or target leakage.
Way better than baseline: Huge jump without strong reason? Double-check setup.
Way worse than expected: Worse than random? Check bugs, data mismatch, or label issues.
High variance across runs: Results change a lot with different seeds? Model may be unstable or data is small.
Train >> test gap: Model memorizing training data? Generalization problem.
Strange learning curve: Loss goes up? Flat line? Something's wrong in training or data.

panels.heading: Check Data First
panels.body:
Sanity check a few samples. Do they look correct? Check data types, ranges, and units. Missing values pattern? Too many? Train/test split random? Group leakage? Duplicates in data? Label distribution correct? Any label noise?
Golden rule: If the data is wrong, no model can be right.

panels.heading: Multicollinearity: How to Detect
panels.body:
Correlation matrix: Look for high absolute correlations (|r| > 0.8).
VIF (variance inflation factor): VIF measures how much the variance is inflated. Example: X1 1.2 fine; X2 5.8 moderate; X3 17.3 high; X4 32.1 severe; X5 2.1 fine. Rule of thumb: VIF > 5 = problem, > 10 = serious.
Condition number: High condition number indicates multicollinearity (e.g. 2.4e+04). > 1000 is usually bad.
What to do: Drop one of the correlated features. Combine features (PCA, domain knowledge). Use regularization (Ridge, Lasso). Collect more data.

panels.heading: When Scores Are Perfect (or Too High)
panels.body:
Check for data leakage: Target in features? Future info in train set? Leakage in preprocessing (scaling, encoding)?
Check evaluation leakage: Train/test overlap? Cross-validation done correctly (no leakage across folds)?
Check label leakage: Is the label accidentally in the input? Are IDs or timestamps leaking info?
Check task easiness: Is the task actually trivial? Are you predicting a proxy instead of the real target?
If it looks too good… find the leak.

panels.heading: When Scores Are Too Bad
panels.body: Bug in code (loss not decreasing)? Wrong labels or misaligned data? Learning rate wrong? Model too simple (underfitting)? Data distribution shift? Features not informative?

panels.heading: Learning Curve Diagnosis
panels.body:
Good fit: Both train & test loss go down and converge.
High variance: Large gap between train and test. Overfitting.
High bias: Both losses high and close. Underfitting.
Data / label issue or bug: Loss behaves strangely. Investigate!

panels.heading: Other Diagnostic Tools
panels.body:
Residual plots: Look for patterns. Random scatter is good.
QQ plot (regression): Points should follow the line.
Histograms: Check distribution of features & target.
Outliers: Detect with boxplot or IQR rule.
SHAP / feature importance: Do important features make sense?

panels.heading: A Systematic Debugging Flow
panels.body: 1. Reproduce: Can you reproduce the result? If not, fix randomness and seeds first. 2. Check data: Sanity check samples, splits, labels. Fix any data issues. 3. Check pipeline: Preprocessing, features, model, training loop. Check for leakage or bugs. 4. Run baselines: Compare with simple models. Is your model really better? 5. Stress test: Try different seeds, splits, assumptions. Is it stable? 6. Interpret: Understand what the model learned. Does it make sense? → Trustworthy results: Now you can believe it (carefully).

panels.heading: Quick Checklist
panels.body: Data looks correct. No leakage (features, labels, time). Train/test split is proper. Baseline models checked. Cross-validation done correctly. Scores are stable across runs. Learning curves look reasonable. Feature importance makes sense. Errors analyzed. Results are reproducible. I would bet money on this result? If many boxes are unchecked, don't trust the result.

panels.heading: Mental Models to Remember
panels.body: Garbage in, garbage out: Bad data → bad models. Correlation is not causation: Look for mechanisms, not just patterns. Occam's razor: Prefer the simplest explanation that fits the data. Be humble: You are wrong more often than you think. Seek disconfirming evidence: What would prove you wrong? Document everything: Future you will thank you.

pages.footer: Final word: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. Be skeptical, be systematic, be scientific.
pages.summary: A guide to sanity-checking machine learning results that look too good or too bad: the warning signs, where leakage hides, how to read learning curves and spot correlated features, and a step-by-step debugging routine before you trust a number.

panels:
Treat red flags as a prior: most genuine improvements are small, so a big jump deserves proportional scrutiny. Near-perfect scores usually mean leakage, a trivial task, or train-test overlap. Worse-than-random is informative too: an AUROC of 0.2 means the signal is real but inverted, often a flipped label or sign, rather than a model failure.

High variance across seeds is a measurement problem: if run-to-run standard deviation is comparable to the gap between methods, the gap is not established. Report mean and spread over several seeds (Henderson et al. 2018 documented how fragile deep RL comparisons are to seeds and codebase details). Loss curves have fingerprints: a plateau at ln(K) means the model outputs the uniform distribution (not learning); rising loss often points to a too-high learning rate; a validation curve that diverges while training improves is overfitting.

Practice "becoming one with the data" (Karpathy's phrase): read raw examples, look at extremes, count, and plot. Check units and ranges (meters versus feet, seconds versus milliseconds), dtypes, and that the target definition matches what you think. Missingness is not neutral: whether a value is missing can itself predict the label (for example a lab test is only ordered for sicker patients), leaking information through a pattern rather than a value.

A powerful systematic check is adversarial validation: train a classifier to distinguish train rows from test rows; an AUROC far above 0.5 means the distributions differ and shows which features differ. Label noise matters too: Northcutt et al. (2021) estimated that widely used benchmark test sets contain a few percent label errors, enough to change model rankings. Deduplicate by hashing.

Variance inflation factor: VIF_j = 1/(1 - R²_j), where R²_j comes from regressing feature j on all other features. A VIF of 5 means R² = 0.8; a VIF of 10 means R² = 0.9. The condition number is the ratio of largest to smallest singular value of the (standardized) design matrix; thresholds are conventions.

What collinearity damages matters: it inflates the standard errors and makes individual coefficients unstable and uninterpretable (sign flips between runs), but if the correlation structure persists at test time, predictions may stay fine. So it is mainly an interpretation problem. Ridge regression stabilizes by shrinking along low-variance directions; lasso tends to pick one of a correlated group arbitrarily. Polynomial and interaction terms create collinearity by construction, so center variables before forming them.

Leakage has recognizable families (Kaufman et al. 2012): target information in a feature (a field created after the outcome, like "discharge code" when predicting readmission); preprocessing fit on all data (scaling, target encoding, imputation, feature selection); temporal leakage (random splits on time-ordered data); and duplicate or group overlap. The Clever Hans phenomenon is a related failure: a model uses a spurious cue. In medical imaging, Zech et al. (2018) showed pneumonia classifiers partly keyed on hospital-specific signals rather than disease, and did significantly worse on other hospitals' data in 3 of 5 comparisons. Kapoor and Narayanan (2023) surveyed leakage across ML-based science, finding it widespread.

Detection tactics: train single-feature models and see which feature alone scores suspiciously high; inspect the top feature importances for things that should not be knowable at prediction time; and rerun with a time-based or group-based split to see whether performance collapses.

If scores are unexpectedly bad, bisect: shrink to a tiny dataset and verify the model can memorize it; if not, the bug is in code, loss, optimizer or labels. Shuffle the labels as a test: performance should fall to chance, and if it does not, evaluation is leaking. A classic bug: shuffling X and y independently. Check that preprocessing at inference matches training (tokenizer version, normalization statistics, image resize), and that the model is in eval mode (dropout off, batch-norm running statistics on).

Then consider distribution shift, which has distinct flavors: covariate shift (inputs change, relationship same), label or prior shift (class frequencies change), and concept drift (the relationship itself changes). Name which you suspect and test it, e.g. by checking performance by time slice.

Two curve types get called learning curves: loss versus training steps, and performance versus training set size. The second is the classic bias-variance diagnostic: high-bias models plateau high with train and validation close, so more data will not help, you need capacity or better features; high-variance models show a gap that narrows with more data.

This picture needs care for modern deep networks. Double descent (Belkin et al. 2019; Nakkiran et al. 2019) shows test error can be non-monotone in model size or training time: it can peak near the point where the model just fits the training data and then fall again. A train-validation gap alone is therefore not proof you should shrink the model; judge by validation performance.

Residual plots expose model misspecification: a curve suggests missing nonlinearity, a funnel shape (variance growing with the fitted value) means heteroscedasticity, which breaks standard errors but not necessarily point predictions. The QQ plot compares residual quantiles against a normal distribution; it matters for small-sample inference, less for prediction; heavy tails bend the ends away from the line.

The IQR rule flags points outside Q1 - 1.5·IQR and Q3 + 1.5·IQR, but an outlier is a question, not a verdict: it may be an error or the most important case. SHAP (Lundberg and Lee 2017) assigns each feature a Shapley-value contribution to a prediction. Remember its limits: it explains the model, not the world, correlated features share credit unpredictably. A sensible importance ranking is a necessary sanity check, not proof of correctness.

Reproducibility is step one because a result you cannot reproduce cannot be debugged. Fix seeds for Python, NumPy and the framework; know that some GPU operations (for example those using atomic additions) are nondeterministic unless you request deterministic algorithms, so exact bit-equality may be impossible and seed-to-seed variance must be measured instead. Log code version, data version, and configuration with each run.

Baselines should include trivial ones (majority class, previous value, mean) and strong simple ones (linear model, gradient-boosted trees) tuned fairly. Ablate your own contribution: remove the new component and confirm the gain disappears. Stress testing means rerunning under different seeds, different splits (especially group- or time-based), perturbed inputs, and different data subsets, and checking that the conclusion holds. Interpretation closes the loop with error analysis: read actual failures, because a model can be right for the wrong reasons.

The final checklist question, "would I bet money?", is a Bayesian prompt: weigh how surprising the result is against how reliable your process is. Twyman's law says any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong; a surprising result is more often a bug than a discovery, so the burden of proof scales with surprise. Practical tools include an independent reimplementation of the evaluation, a locked test set touched once, a canary evaluation on fresh data, and a pre-mortem (imagine the result later turned out wrong and write down why).

Being unable to tick a box is information, not failure: record it as a known limitation in the write-up. Prefer reporting a modest claim with evidence over a bold one without it; reviewers and users alike eventually test the bold one.

Each mental model has a technical form. Garbage in, garbage out: if a fraction η of test labels are wrong, even a perfect model is capped near 1 - η measured accuracy, and noisy training labels bias fits. Occam's razor appears as regularization and as the minimum description length idea (prefer the model that compresses data best); it is a preference, not a guarantee, and the no-free-lunch theorems (Wolpert 1996) say no learner wins on all problems without assumptions.

Seeking disconfirming evidence is Popper's falsification applied to everyday work: design the test that would embarrass your hypothesis. Documenting everything has a modern form: an experiment tracker recording config, data hash, code commit, and metrics, so every number in a table has provenance. Being humble is quantifiable: report intervals and log what you tried.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: a red flag is not proof of a bug (some tasks really are easy, some gains real), and passing a checklist does not prove correctness; the checks reduce the odds of common errors. Gotchas: debugging by changing several things at once, trusting a single seed, and tuning on the metric you later report. This page connects every earlier foundation page: leakage and splits (cross-validation), metrics on rare classes (classification and imbalance pages), the association-versus-cause caution (previous page) and training pathologies (deep-learning basics). Later pages on evaluating language models reuse the same suspicion, with extra concerns such as benchmark contamination and judge bias.

pages.title: Linear & Logistic Regression
pages.subtitle: Fit a line, then bend it into a probability

panels.heading: Linear Regression: Fit a Line
panels.body:
Predict a number: y_hat = w0 + w1*x1 + ... + wd*xd.
Residual = y - y_hat.
Least squares picks weights that minimize MSE (mean squared error) = average residual^2.

panels.heading: Closed Form vs Gradient Descent
panels.body:
Normal equation: w = (X^T X)^-1 X^T y. Exact, one shot.
Gradient descent: w <- w - lr * gradient. Iterative; scales to huge or streaming data.
Libraries use QR/SVD, not a raw inverse.

panels.heading: Assumptions to Check
panels.body:
Linear relationship (after any feature transforms).
Independent errors, constant variance: no funnel in residuals.
No strong multicollinearity: correlated features make weights unstable.
Normal errors matter only for p-values and intervals.

panels.heading: Logistic Regression: Bend to 0-1
panels.body:
For classes: p = sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z), z = w.x + b.
z is the log-odds: log(p / (1 - p)).
Train with log loss; no closed form.
Boundary: z = 0 (p = 0.5), a straight line or plane.

panels.heading: Reading the Coefficients
panels.body:
Linear: +1 unit of x -> y changes by w (others held fixed).
Logistic: +1 unit of x -> log-odds +w, odds multiply by e^w.
Compare sizes only after standardizing.
Coefficients show association, not cause.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Pass the Exam
panels.body:
Model: z = -4 + 1.5 * hours.
2 hours: z = -1 -> p = 0.27.
4 hours: z = 2 -> p = 0.88.
Boundary: z = 0 at 2.67 hours. Each extra hour multiplies the odds by e^1.5 = 4.5.
panels.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)
clf.predict_proba(X_new)[:, 1]

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Extrapolating outside the training range.
Outliers drag least squares: check residuals or use Huber loss.
Separable classes: weights blow up; regularize.
0.5 threshold is a default: tune it to error costs.

panels.heading: Check Yourself
panels.body:
A logistic weight is 0.7. What happens to the odds per unit of x?
Answer: x e^0.7, about double.

pages.footer: Linear predicts a number; logistic predicts log-odds, then squashes them into a probability.
pages.summary: Explains linear regression (least squares, normal equation vs gradient descent, assumptions) and logistic regression (sigmoid, log-odds, decision boundary), how to read their coefficients, with a worked pass/fail example and common pitfalls.

panels:
Least squares is the maximum-likelihood estimate when the noise is Gaussian with constant variance: minimizing the sum of squared residuals is the same as maximizing the Gaussian log-likelihood. That link explains both its strengths and its fragility. Squaring means one residual of 10 counts as much as a hundred residuals of 1, so outliers dominate.

Geometrically, the fitted vector y_hat is the orthogonal projection of y onto the column space of X, so the residual vector is perpendicular to every feature column: X^T (y - X w) = 0. Those are exactly the normal equations. Always include an intercept column, otherwise the line is forced through the origin and the residuals no longer average to zero. R^2 = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot measures the share of variance explained, and it never decreases when you add features, which is why adjusted R^2 or held-out error is the honest comparison.

The closed form needs X^T X to be invertible, which fails when features are perfectly collinear or when d > n. Even when it is invertible, forming X^T X squares the condition number, so libraries factor X with QR or SVD instead; numpy.linalg.lstsq and sklearn's LinearRegression use such solvers and return the minimum-norm solution in the rank-deficient case. Ridge regression fixes invertibility outright: w = (X^T X + lambda I)^-1 X^T y.

Cost: forming X^T X is O(n d^2) and solving is O(d^3), cheap for d in the hundreds and painful for d near 10^5. Gradient descent costs O(n d) per pass, and stochastic or mini-batch variants touch a few rows at a time, which suits streaming data and out-of-core training. MSE is convex, so gradient descent reaches the global minimum given a suitable learning rate, but poorly scaled features create elongated valleys and slow, zig-zagging convergence. Standardize first.

Interviewers like the distinction between what is needed for unbiased predictions and what is needed for valid inference. Linearity in the parameters (not the raw inputs: x^2 or log x features are fine) and errors with zero mean given X give unbiased coefficients. Independence and constant variance make ordinary least squares the best linear unbiased estimator (Gauss-Markov). Normality is only needed for exact t-tests and confidence intervals in small samples; with large n the central limit theorem covers it.

Violations have specific fixes. Heteroscedasticity (the funnel): transform the target, use weighted least squares, or report robust (HC) standard errors. Autocorrelated errors in time series: use models that account for it. Multicollinearity does not hurt predictions but inflates coefficient variance; check variance inflation factors (VIF above about 5-10 is a warning) and consider ridge or dropping redundant features. Omitted confounders bias coefficients, which no residual plot reveals.

The sigmoid is the inverse of the logit, so logistic regression assumes the log-odds are linear in the features. Training minimizes the negative log-likelihood, -[y log p + (1 - y) log(1 - p)], which is convex in w, so there is a single global optimum even though no closed form exists. Solvers such as L-BFGS, Newton's method (iteratively reweighted least squares) or SAGA find it. The gradient is beautifully simple: X^T (p - y), the same form as linear regression with p in place of y_hat.

Why not use MSE with a sigmoid? The loss becomes non-convex and gradients vanish when predictions are confidently wrong. For more than two classes, softmax (multinomial) regression generalizes the model with one weight vector per class. The decision boundary is linear in whatever features you feed in, so adding x1^2, x2^2 and x1*x2 produces circles and ellipses while the model stays linear in its parameters.

'Holding other features fixed' is the crucial phrase. With correlated features, a coefficient can shrink, grow or even flip sign when another feature is added, because each weight measures the unique contribution after the others are accounted for. Coefficient magnitude depends on units: a weight per gram is 1000 times smaller than the same effect per kilogram, so standardize before comparing, or report effects for a meaningful change such as an interquartile range.

For logistic regression, e^w is an odds ratio, not a probability ratio. The change in probability from one unit depends on the baseline: near p = 0.5 the slope is w/4 (the 'divide by 4' rule), and near 0 or 1 the same w moves p very little. Interaction terms change interpretation: with x1*x2 included, the effect of x1 depends on x2. Regularized coefficients are shrunk toward zero, so their magnitudes are biased. Causal claims need a design (randomization, instruments or careful adjustment), not just a coefficient.

Checking the numbers: sigmoid(-1) = 1 / (1 + e) = 0.269 and sigmoid(2) = 1 / (1 + e^-2) = 0.881. The boundary solves -4 + 1.5h = 0, so h = 2.67 hours. Notice how the same +1.5 log-odds step moves probability differently along the curve: from 2 to 3 hours p goes 0.27 -> 0.62, a jump of 35 points, while from 4 to 5 hours it goes 0.88 -> 0.97, only 9 points.

In scikit-learn, LogisticRegression applies L2 regularization by default with C = 1.0, where C is the inverse of the penalty strength. That default is helpful for stability but surprises people who expect plain maximum-likelihood estimates; set C=np.inf for an unpenalized fit (penalty=None before version 1.8, which deprecated the penalty argument). predict_proba returns one column per class, so [:, 1] is the positive class. predict uses a 0.5 threshold; for other thresholds compare predict_proba to your own cutoff. Check calibration with a reliability diagram before trusting the probabilities.

Extrapolation: a linear trend fitted on houses from 50 to 200 m^2 says nothing reliable about a 2,000 m^2 mansion, and the prediction interval widens away from the data center. Outliers versus leverage: a point with an extreme x value has high leverage and can pull the line strongly; Cook's distance combines leverage and residual size to flag influential points. Huber loss is quadratic for small errors and linear for large ones, giving robustness without discarding data.

Perfect separation makes the unpenalized maximum-likelihood weights diverge to infinity, because the loss keeps decreasing as the sigmoid gets steeper; solvers report convergence warnings and huge coefficients. Regularization or Firth's correction fixes it. Class imbalance shifts the intercept and makes 0.5 a poor threshold; choose the threshold from the costs of false positives and false negatives, or use class_weight. Finally, a linear model on raw features may simply underfit nonlinear structure, which shows up as curved residual patterns.

e^0.7 = 2.01, so each unit of x roughly doubles the odds. A good follow-up an interviewer might ask: does it double the probability? Only when the probability is small. Starting from p = 0.1 (odds 0.111), doubled odds give 0.222, so p = 0.18, close to double. Starting from p = 0.6 (odds 1.5), doubled odds give 3.0, so p = 0.75, far from double.

Other quick checks worth being able to answer: what does a negative weight mean (odds shrink, e^-0.7 = 0.50 halves them); what is the intercept (log-odds when all features are zero, which may be meaningless unless features are centered); why can't you read significance from a regularized coefficient (shrinkage biases it and standard errors no longer have their textbook meaning). Explaining the gap between odds and probability clearly is a strong signal in interviews.
deeper.further: Next steps: generalized linear models (Poisson regression for counts, gamma for positive skewed targets) share the same link-function idea as logistic regression. Learn ridge, lasso and elastic net, and how regularization paths trade bias for variance. Study probability calibration (Platt scaling, isotonic regression) and proper scoring rules such as log loss and the Brier score. For inference, read about robust standard errors and the difference between prediction and causal estimation. Quantile regression predicts conditional medians or percentiles instead of means, useful when costs are asymmetric.

pages.title: Trees & Ensembles
pages.subtitle: From one decision tree to a winning forest

panels.heading: How a Decision Tree Splits
panels.body:
Ask yes/no questions: income > 50k? age < 30?
Each split picks the feature + threshold that makes children purest.
Leaves predict the majority class (or the mean for regression).
No scaling needed.

panels.heading: Gini vs Entropy
panels.body:
Gini = 1 - sum(p_k^2). Entropy = -sum(p_k * log2 p_k).
50/50 node: Gini 0.5, entropy 1.0. Pure node: both 0.
Gain = parent impurity - weighted child impurity.
Nearly identical splits; Gini is a bit faster.

panels.heading: Worked Example: One Split
panels.body:
Parent: 10 emails, 5 spam -> Gini 0.5.
Split on 'has link': left 4 spam / 1 ham, right 1 spam / 4 ham.
Each child: 1 - (0.8^2 + 0.2^2) = 0.32.
Gain = 0.5 - 0.32 = 0.18.

panels.heading: Depth Controls Overfitting
panels.body:
Deep tree: memorizes noise (high variance).
Shallow tree: too simple (high bias).
Limit max_depth or min_samples_leaf, or prune with ccp_alpha.

panels.heading: Bagging & Random Forests
panels.body:
Bagging = bootstrap aggregating: train trees on resampled rows, average their votes.
Random forest also samples features at each split -> less correlated trees.
Cuts variance; out-of-bag rows give a free validation score.

panels.heading: Boosting: Fix the Errors
panels.body:
Build shallow trees in sequence; each fits the residual errors (gradients) of the ensemble so far.
A small learning rate plus early stopping prevents overfitting.
Tools: XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost.
panels.code:
from lightgbm import LGBMClassifier
m = LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=500, learning_rate=0.05)
m.fit(X_train, y_train)

panels.heading: Feature Importance Pitfalls
panels.body:
Impurity importance favors high-cardinality features (IDs!) and uses training data.
Correlated features split the credit.
Prefer permutation importance on held-out data, or SHAP values.
Important does not mean causal.

panels.heading: When Trees Beat Neural Nets
panels.body:
Tabular data: mixed types, skewed features, missing values.
Boosted trees often win with less tuning and compute.
Neural nets win on images, text, audio.

pages.footer: One tree overfits; bagging averages away variance; boosting chips away bias.
pages.summary: Shows how decision trees choose splits (Gini, entropy, information gain) with a worked example, how depth controls overfitting, how random forests (bagging) and gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) combine trees, why feature importances mislead, and why trees still win on tabular data.

panels:
Trees are built greedily: at each node the algorithm scans every feature and every candidate threshold (midpoints between sorted unique values), picks the split with the largest impurity decrease, and recurses. Finding the globally optimal tree is NP-hard, so greedy search is the standard compromise. For n rows and d features, a naive build costs about O(d n log n) per level after sorting; histogram-based implementations bin features into around 256 buckets to make this much faster.

CART (classification and regression trees), used by scikit-learn, makes binary splits. Regression trees minimize squared error, so each leaf predicts the mean of its rows. Trees are invariant to monotonic transforms of features, which is why scaling does not matter, and they capture interactions naturally because a later split is conditional on earlier ones. Their decision boundaries are axis-aligned rectangles, so a diagonal boundary needs a staircase of many splits. Single trees are unstable: small data changes can produce a very different tree.

Both criteria are concave functions of the class proportions that are zero for pure nodes and maximal for uniform ones. With K classes, maximum Gini is 1 - 1/K and maximum entropy is log2 K bits. Gini is the probability of misclassifying a random sample if you label it randomly according to the node's class distribution; entropy is the expected information needed to identify the class. Empirical studies find they disagree on only a few percent of splits, and Gini avoids computing logarithms.

Why not use plain misclassification error as the split criterion? It is not strictly concave, so many useful splits show zero improvement, which stalls tree growth; it is fine for pruning, though. Information gain is biased toward features with many distinct values, which is why Quinlan introduced the gain ratio (later used in C4.5), normalizing by the split's own entropy. For regression, the analogous criteria are variance reduction (MSE) or absolute error (MAE), the latter being more robust to outliers but slower.

Each child holds 5 of the 10 emails, so weighted child impurity = 0.5 x 0.32 + 0.5 x 0.32 = 0.32, and the gain is 0.5 - 0.32 = 0.18. With entropy instead: parent entropy is 1.0 bit; each child has -(0.8 log2 0.8 + 0.2 log2 0.2) = 0.722 bits; information gain = 1.0 - 0.722 = 0.278 bits. Different scales, same ranking of splits in almost every case.

Weighting by child size matters. A split that peels off one pure email (child of 1 with Gini 0) and leaves 9 mixed ones barely helps: the large child still has Gini close to 0.5. This is why trees with no minimum leaf size happily isolate single points deep in the tree, chasing tiny impurity gains that are really noise. In an interview, being able to compute a split by hand, and explain why the weighted average is used, demonstrates you understand what the library is doing.

An unrestricted tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure, which on noisy data means one leaf per training example: zero training error and poor generalization. Pre-pruning stops growth early via max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, max_leaf_nodes or min_impurity_decrease. Post-pruning grows the full tree and then removes subtrees; cost-complexity pruning minimizes error + alpha x (number of leaves), and scikit-learn exposes the sequence of alphas through cost_complexity_pruning_path so you can pick one by cross-validation.

A depth-d binary tree has at most 2^d leaves, so depth 10 already allows 1,024 regions. Depth also bounds interaction order: a depth-3 tree can model at most three-way interactions along a path. This is why boosting uses shallow trees (depth 3 to 8, or 31 to 255 leaves in LightGBM terms) while random forests grow deep trees and rely on averaging to tame the variance. min_samples_leaf is often the most effective single knob for smoothing predictions.

A bootstrap sample draws n rows with replacement, so each tree sees about 63.2% of unique rows (1 - 1/e); the remaining 36.8% are out-of-bag and act as a built-in validation set. Averaging B trees with variance sigma^2 and pairwise correlation rho gives ensemble variance rho sigma^2 + (1 - rho) sigma^2 / B. More trees shrink the second term, but only decorrelation reduces the first, which is why random forests sample features: the default max_features is sqrt(d) for classification, and scikit-learn uses all features for regression (1.0) by default, a common surprise.

Adding trees never causes overfitting in the sense of rising test error; it only stops helping, so a few hundred trees usually suffice. Forests need little tuning, are embarrassingly parallel and give reasonable probability estimates, though often under-confident near 0 and 1. Their main weaknesses are memory and latency with many deep trees, and no extrapolation: predictions are averages of training targets, so a forest cannot predict beyond the range it saw.

Gradient boosting performs gradient descent in function space. At step m it computes the negative gradient of the loss for each training row (for squared error, simply the residual y - F(x)), fits a small regression tree to those values, and adds it scaled by the learning rate: F_m = F_(m-1) + eta x tree_m. Any differentiable loss works, including log loss, Poisson or quantile losses. XGBoost adds a second-order (Newton) step using Hessians plus explicit L1/L2 penalties on leaf weights.

LightGBM grows trees leaf-wise (expanding the leaf with the largest gain) and uses histogram binning, making it very fast; control it with num_leaves and min_child_samples. CatBoost uses symmetric trees and ordered target statistics that avoid target leakage when encoding categoricals. Typical recipe: learning rate 0.01 to 0.1, early stopping on a validation set, row and column subsampling around 0.8, then tune leaves and minimum child size. Smaller learning rates need more trees but generalize better. Boosting reduces bias mainly; it overfits if run too long.

Mean decrease in impurity (MDI) sums the impurity reduction a feature provides across all splits, measured on training data. It inflates features with many split points, such as continuous variables and IDs, and can reward pure noise. Permutation importance shuffles one feature on held-out data and measures the score drop, which reflects real predictive value, but it is unreliable with correlated features: shuffling one creates impossible combinations, and the model can lean on its twin, so both look unimportant.

SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) values distribute each prediction among features according to cooperative game theory; TreeSHAP computes them exactly in polynomial time for trees. They give per-prediction explanations and consistent global rankings, but they still describe the model, not the world. Conditional versus interventional SHAP can disagree when features are correlated. Practical advice: drop or group duplicate features before interpreting, compare multiple methods, and never present importance as causal evidence without an experiment or causal design.

Benchmarks such as Grinsztajn et al. (2022) found tree ensembles beating deep networks on medium-sized tabular datasets (around 10,000 rows) for three reasons: trees are robust to uninformative features, they handle irregular, non-smooth target functions that neural nets with their smoothness bias fit poorly, and they are not rotation invariant, which matters because individual tabular columns carry meaning. Trees also need no feature scaling, cope with missing values natively in XGBoost and LightGBM, and train in minutes on a CPU.

The picture keeps shifting. Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN are competitive on small datasets, and neural architectures win when tabular data is combined with text, images or very large datasets with learned embeddings for high-cardinality categories. In industry, gradient boosted trees remain the default baseline for fraud, credit risk, ranking features and churn. A strong answer in interviews: start with LightGBM or XGBoost, then justify any switch with validation results.
deeper.further: Go deeper with: the original random forest paper (Breiman 2001) and the XGBoost paper (Chen and Guestrin 2016) for the second-order objective. Learn extremely randomized trees (ExtraTrees), isolation forests for anomaly detection, and quantile regression forests for prediction intervals. Study monotonic constraints in boosting libraries for regulated domains, categorical handling in CatBoost, and SHAP interaction values. For model choice, explore stacking (a meta-model over out-of-fold predictions) and tabular foundation models such as TabPFN.

pages.title: Svm, Knn & Naive Bayes
pages.subtitle: Three classic classifiers and when each shines

panels.heading: SVM: The Widest Margin
panels.body:
SVM = support vector machine.
Find the boundary w.x + b = 0 with the widest gap to both classes: margin = 2 / ||w||.
Only the closest points, the support vectors, define it.

panels.heading: Soft Margin & C
panels.body:
Real classes overlap, so allow violations (hinge loss).
Large C: punish errors hard -> narrow margin, may overfit.
Small C: tolerate errors -> wider margin, smoother boundary.

panels.heading: The Kernel Trick
panels.body:
Map points to a space where they separate linearly, without computing the map: only k(x, x') is needed.
RBF kernel: k = exp(-gamma * ||x - x'||^2).
Rings in 2D separate once you add z = x1^2 + x2^2.
panels.code:
from sklearn.svm import SVC
SVC(kernel="rbf", C=1.0, gamma="scale")

panels.heading: k-Nearest Neighbors
panels.body:
k-NN: no training, just store the data.
Predict by majority vote (or mean) of the k closest points.
Small k: noisy. Large k: blurry. Odd k avoids ties for 2 classes.
Distance: Euclidean, Manhattan, or cosine for text.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Why Scale
panels.body:
Features: income (0-200,000) and age (0-100).
Unscaled, a 1,000 income gap outweighs a 40-year age gap.
Standardize: z = (x - mean) / std, so each feature counts fairly.

panels.heading: Naive Bayes
panels.body:
Bayes rule: P(class | x) is proportional to P(class) * product of P(x_i | class).
Naive: features assumed independent given the class.
Wrong, yet strong for text: fast, little data needed.
Laplace smoothing (+1) stops unseen words zeroing everything.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Spam Filter
panels.body:
Prior: P(spam) = 0.4, P(ham) = 0.6.
Word 'free': P(free | spam) = 0.3, P(free | ham) = 0.02.
Scores: spam 0.4 x 0.3 = 0.12; ham 0.6 x 0.02 = 0.012.
P(spam | free) = 0.12 / 0.132 = 0.91.

panels.heading: Compare & Pitfalls
panels.body:
SVM: strong in high dimensions; kernels slow past ~100k rows.
k-NN: no training, slow predictions.
Naive Bayes: fastest text baseline; overconfident.
Pitfall: unscaled features break SVM and k-NN.

pages.footer: SVM draws the widest road, k-NN asks the neighbors, Naive Bayes counts the evidence.
pages.summary: Compares three classic classifiers: support vector machines (margin, support vectors, C, kernel trick), k-nearest neighbors (choice of k, distance, why scaling matters) and Naive Bayes (independence assumption, spam example), with a when-to-use table and pitfalls.

panels:
The hard-margin SVM solves: minimize (1/2)||w||^2 subject to y_i (w.x_i + b) >= 1 for every point, with labels y in {-1, +1}. The margin between the two hyperplanes w.x + b = +1 and -1 is 2/||w||, so minimizing ||w|| maximizes it. This is a convex quadratic program with a unique solution.

In the dual form, the solution is w = sum(alpha_i y_i x_i), and only points with alpha_i > 0 contribute. These are the support vectors, lying on or inside the margin. Removing any other point leaves the boundary unchanged, which gives SVMs some robustness and a sparse model. The maximum-margin principle connects to generalization theory: wider margins mean lower capacity, giving bounds that do not depend directly on the input dimension, which is why linear SVMs work well for high-dimensional text. Note that SVMs output distances, not probabilities; scikit-learn's probability=True runs an extra internal cross-validation with Platt scaling.

The soft-margin problem adds slack variables: minimize (1/2)||w||^2 + C sum(xi_i), with y_i (w.x_i + b) >= 1 - xi_i. Equivalently, minimize the hinge loss max(0, 1 - y f(x)) plus an L2 penalty, so the SVM is just a linear model with a particular loss. C trades margin width against violations; it plays the role of 1/lambda in other regularized models, so large C means weak regularization.

Hinge loss is zero for points correctly classified beyond the margin, so confident correct points do not influence the solution, unlike log loss in logistic regression. Typical tuning searches C on a log scale such as 0.01 to 1000. Imbalanced classes can be handled with class_weight='balanced', which scales C per class. For large linear problems, LinearSVC (liblinear) or SGDClassifier(loss='hinge') scale to millions of rows far better than the kernelized SVC, whose training time grows roughly between O(n^2) and O(n^3).

In the dual, data appears only through dot products x_i . x_j, so replacing them with a kernel k(x_i, x_j) = phi(x_i) . phi(x_j) trains a linear SVM in feature space phi without ever computing phi. A valid kernel must give a positive semi-definite Gram matrix (Mercer's condition). The polynomial kernel (x.x' + c)^d corresponds to all monomials up to degree d; the RBF kernel corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature space.

For RBF, gamma sets the reach of each training point: large gamma means very local influence and wiggly boundaries that overfit; small gamma approaches a nearly linear model. scikit-learn's gamma='scale' uses 1 / (n_features x X.var()). Tune C and gamma jointly on a log grid, since they interact. The price: storing and evaluating against support vectors makes prediction cost proportional to their number, and training memory grows with n^2 for the kernel matrix. Approximations such as random Fourier features or Nystroem let a linear model mimic an RBF kernel at scale.

k-NN is a lazy, non-parametric learner: training is just storing the data, and all the work happens at prediction time. Brute-force search costs O(n d) per query; KD-trees and ball trees speed this up in low dimensions (roughly d below 20), and approximate nearest neighbor libraries such as FAISS or HNSW indexes handle millions of high-dimensional vectors, the same machinery behind vector databases for embeddings.

k controls the bias-variance trade-off: k = 1 has zero training error and high variance, while k = n always predicts the majority class. Choose k by cross-validation; a classic heuristic is around sqrt(n). Distance weighting (weights='distance') lets closer neighbors count more. As n grows, the 1-NN error rate is at most twice the Bayes optimal error (Cover and Hart, 1967), a remarkable guarantee for such a simple method. For text embeddings, cosine similarity is standard; for mixed numeric and categorical data, Gower distance is an option. Ties and duplicate points need a deterministic rule.

Distances add squared feature differences, so units decide influence. In the example, an income gap of 1,000 contributes 1,000,000 to the squared distance while a 40-year age gap contributes 1,600: age is effectively invisible. After standardization (say income std 40,000 and age std 15), the same gaps become 0.025 and 2.67 standard deviations, so age now dominates, which matches intuition.

Scaler choice matters: StandardScaler for roughly symmetric data, RobustScaler (median and interquartile range) when outliers exist, and log transforms for heavily skewed counts or money. Fit the scaler on training data only. Beyond scaling, irrelevant features hurt k-NN badly because they add noise to every distance; feature selection or metric learning helps. In high dimensions, the ratio between the nearest and farthest neighbor distances approaches 1 for many data distributions, so neighborhoods stop being meaningful unless data lies on a lower-dimensional structure, which real data often does.

Naive Bayes computes argmax over classes of log P(c) + sum(log P(x_i | c)); working in log space avoids numerical underflow from multiplying hundreds of small probabilities. Variants differ in the likelihood: multinomial NB models word counts, Bernoulli NB models word presence or absence (and penalizes missing words), Gaussian NB assumes each numeric feature is normal within a class, and complement NB is designed for imbalanced text.

Why does a wrong independence assumption still classify well? Classification only needs the correct class to have the highest score, not accurate probabilities; correlated features double-count evidence, pushing scores to extremes, but often in the right direction. That is also why NB probabilities are badly calibrated, clustering near 0 and 1. Naive Bayes is a generative model, learning P(x | c); logistic regression is its discriminative counterpart. Ng and Jordan (2002) showed NB reaches its (higher) asymptotic error faster, so it can win with little data while logistic regression wins with more. Smoothing alpha is a tunable hyperparameter.

Bayes rule: P(spam | free) = P(free | spam) P(spam) / P(free), where P(free) = 0.4 x 0.3 + 0.6 x 0.02 = 0.132. The ratio of likelihoods, 0.3 / 0.02 = 15, is the Bayes factor; it multiplies the prior odds (0.4 / 0.6 = 0.667) to give posterior odds of 10, which is probability 10/11 = 0.91.

With several words, Naive Bayes multiplies their likelihood ratios. If 'meeting' had P(meeting | spam) = 0.01 and P(meeting | ham) = 0.1, its ratio of 0.1 would cut the odds tenfold, back to 1, giving 50%. Laplace smoothing in practice: P(word | class) = (count + 1) / (total words in class + vocabulary size). Without it, a word never seen in ham forces P(ham) to zero regardless of all other evidence. The prior matters too: if spam is actually 90% of traffic in production but 40% in training, the posterior will be miscalibrated until the prior is adjusted.

Rules of thumb. Start with Naive Bayes or a linear model for text, since they train in seconds and give a strong baseline. Use an RBF SVM for small-to-medium dense datasets with complex boundaries, up to tens of thousands of rows. Use linear SVM or logistic regression for large sparse data. Use k-NN when similarity is the natural concept (recommendations, retrieval over embeddings) and you can afford search at query time.

Pitfalls interviewers probe: forgetting scaling for SVM and k-NN; using SVM decision values as probabilities; using k-NN with many irrelevant features; reporting Naive Bayes probabilities as calibrated risks; leaving duplicates that make k-NN look perfect on validation (the nearest neighbor is the same row). On tabular data with mixed types, gradient boosted trees usually beat all three, and on raw text, images or audio, neural models do; these classics remain valuable as fast baselines and interpretable components.
deeper.further: Explore support vector regression (epsilon-insensitive loss), one-class SVM for novelty detection, and kernel ridge regression and Gaussian processes, which reuse the kernel idea with probabilistic outputs. Learn metric learning and approximate nearest neighbor search (HNSW, IVF-PQ) that power vector search over embeddings. For Bayes, study generative versus discriminative models, Bayesian networks that relax the independence assumption, and calibration methods (Platt scaling, isotonic regression) to fix overconfident probabilities.

pages.title: Clustering
pages.subtitle: Finding groups when nobody gave you labels

panels.heading: k-Means Step by Step
panels.body:
Unsupervised: group points with no labels.
1. Pick k centroids. 2. Assign each point to its nearest centroid.
3. Move each centroid to its points' mean. 4. Repeat until stable.
Minimizes inertia = sum of squared distances to centroids.

panels.heading: Worked Example: 1D, k = 2
panels.body:
Points: 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12. Start centroids: 1 and 2.
Assign: {1} and {2, 3, 10, 11, 12} -> means 1 and 7.6.
Reassign: {1, 2, 3} and {10, 11, 12} -> means 2 and 11.
No change: converged.

panels.heading: k-Means++ & Choosing k
panels.body:
k-means++: pick each new start centroid far from existing ones -> better, faster. Run several restarts.
Elbow: plot inertia vs k, pick the bend.
Silhouette = (b - a) / max(a, b), from -1 to 1: higher = better separated.
panels.code:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
KMeans(n_clusters=3, init="k-means++", n_init=10)

panels.heading: Hierarchical Clustering
panels.body:
Agglomerative: start with every point alone; merge the two closest clusters, repeat.
Linkage: single (min), complete (max), average, Ward (least variance increase).
Cut the dendrogram at a height to get any number of clusters.

panels.heading: DBSCAN: Density Wins
panels.body:
DBSCAN = density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise.
Core point: at least min_samples points within radius eps.
Clusters grow through connected core points; the rest is noise.
Any shape, no k needed.

panels.heading: Gaussian Mixture Models
panels.body:
GMM: each cluster is a Gaussian with its own mean and covariance.
Fit with EM (expectation-maximization).
Soft assignment: a point can be 70% A, 30% B.
Handles elliptical clusters; choose k with BIC.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Unscaled features: the largest unit dominates distance.
k-means assumes round, similar-size clusters; fails on moons and rings.
k-means returns k clusters even for pure noise.
DBSCAN struggles when densities vary.

pages.footer: Scale first, match the algorithm to the cluster shape, then sanity-check the groups.
pages.summary: Covers unsupervised clustering: the k-means algorithm with a worked 1D trace, k-means++ initialization, choosing k with the elbow and silhouette methods, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN, Gaussian mixture models, and common pitfalls like scaling and non-spherical clusters.

panels:
k-means (Lloyd's algorithm) alternates two steps that each can only lower inertia: assignment is optimal for fixed centroids, and the mean is the point minimizing squared distances for fixed assignments. Because inertia never increases and there are finitely many partitions, it always converges, but only to a local minimum. Finding the global optimum is NP-hard. Each iteration costs O(n k d), and it typically converges in tens of iterations.

The implicit model: clusters are spherical, of similar size and variance, because squared Euclidean distance treats all directions equally and boundaries between centroids are straight (a Voronoi partition). k-means is equivalent to a limit of a Gaussian mixture with equal spherical covariances and hard assignments. Mini-batch k-means updates centroids from small random samples, scaling to millions of points with slightly worse inertia. k-medoids uses actual data points as centers and allows any distance metric, which makes it more robust to outliers. Empty clusters can occur and must be reseeded.

First assignment uses midpoint 1.5 between the centroids 1 and 2, so only point 1 joins the first cluster. The second cluster's mean is (2 + 3 + 10 + 11 + 12) / 5 = 38 / 5 = 7.6. The new midpoint is (1 + 7.6) / 2 = 4.3, so 2 and 3 switch clusters. Means become 2 and 11, midpoint 6.5, and nothing moves again. Final inertia: (1 + 0 + 1) + (1 + 0 + 1) = 4.

This trace shows why initialization matters: two adjacent starting centroids made the first step lopsided. Here it recovered, but with more complex data a poor start can leave two centroids sharing one true cluster while another centroid spans two, a local minimum that further iterations never escape. A useful check in interviews is to compute inertia for the final solution and for an alternative partition to show which is better. Ties, where a point is equidistant from two centroids, are broken by a fixed rule such as the lowest index.

k-means++ chooses the first centroid uniformly at random, then each next one with probability proportional to D(x)^2, the squared distance to the nearest centroid already chosen. This spreads starts across the data and gives an expected inertia within O(log k) of optimal, before any Lloyd iterations. It is scikit-learn's default. Even so, run multiple restarts (n_init) and keep the lowest inertia.

Choosing k has no single right answer. The elbow is often ambiguous because inertia always decreases with k. Silhouette for one point uses a = mean distance to its own cluster and b = mean distance to the nearest other cluster; average it over points, and inspect per-cluster silhouette plots for thin or negative clusters. Alternatives: the gap statistic (compares inertia to uniform reference data), the Davies-Bouldin and Calinski-Harabasz indices, BIC for mixture models, and stability across bootstrap resamples. Often the right k is set by the use case, such as how many customer segments marketing can act on.

Agglomerative clustering builds a full merge tree bottom-up. Linkage defines the distance between clusters. Single linkage uses the closest pair and can follow chains, finding elongated shapes but also merging distinct groups through a bridge of points. Complete linkage uses the farthest pair and produces compact clusters but is sensitive to outliers. Average linkage is a compromise. Ward merges the pair that least increases total within-cluster variance, giving k-means-like spherical clusters, and requires Euclidean distance.

Naive cost is O(n^3) time and O(n^2) memory for the distance matrix, so hierarchical clustering is practical up to roughly tens of thousands of points; single linkage can be computed through a minimum spanning tree. Advantages: no need to choose k upfront, any distance metric (except Ward), and an interpretable dendrogram. Large vertical gaps in the dendrogram suggest natural cut heights. Merges are greedy and never undone, so early mistakes persist. Divisive (top-down) clustering exists but is rarer.

DBSCAN labels points as core (at least min_samples points, including itself, within eps), border (within eps of a core point but not core) and noise. Clusters are connected components of core points plus their border points. It finds arbitrarily shaped clusters, determines their number automatically and isolates outliers, labelled -1 in scikit-learn. Border points reachable from two clusters are assigned to whichever is processed first, so results can vary slightly with data order.

Choosing eps: plot each point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbor (k = min_samples) in sorted order and pick the knee. A common min_samples heuristic is 2 x dimensions. A single global eps cannot handle clusters of very different densities: either sparse clusters dissolve into noise or dense ones merge. HDBSCAN fixes this by building a hierarchy over all eps values and keeping the most stable clusters, needing mainly a minimum cluster size; it is often the better default. With a spatial index, DBSCAN runs in roughly O(n log n) in low dimensions.

A GMM models the data density as p(x) = sum over k of pi_k N(x | mu_k, Sigma_k), with mixing weights pi_k. EM alternates an E-step, computing responsibilities (the posterior probability that each component generated each point), and an M-step, re-estimating weights, means and covariances from those soft assignments. The likelihood never decreases, but EM converges to local optima and is usually initialized with k-means.

Covariance types trade flexibility for parameters: 'full' (arbitrary ellipses, about d^2/2 parameters per component), 'diag' (axis-aligned ellipses), 'tied' (shared shape) and 'spherical'. Full covariances in high dimensions are expensive and can become singular, which is why regularization (reg_covar) is added to the diagonal. Pick k and covariance type with BIC, which penalizes parameters. Because a GMM is a density model, it also supports anomaly detection (low likelihood points) and sampling new data. Bayesian GMMs with a Dirichlet process prior can switch off unneeded components automatically.

Scaling: k-means, hierarchical and DBSCAN all rely on distances, so one feature in large units dominates; standardize, and consider whether every feature deserves equal weight. Categorical data needs other approaches such as k-modes or Gower distance. High-dimensional data, including raw embeddings, suffers from distance concentration; reduce dimensions first (PCA, or UMAP for density-based methods) or use cosine distance on normalized vectors.

Shape assumptions: k-means and Ward assume convex, similar-size blobs; elongated, nested or crescent shapes need DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, spectral clustering or single linkage. Unequal cluster sizes push k-means boundaries into the larger cluster. Validation is the hardest part, because there is no ground truth; internal metrics such as silhouette favor convex clusters themselves. Check stability across seeds and subsamples, examine cluster profiles, and test whether clusters predict something useful downstream. Remember that clustering is exploratory: the groups are hypotheses, not discoveries, until validated.
deeper.further: Learn spectral clustering (graph Laplacian eigenvectors, good for non-convex shapes), HDBSCAN, and OPTICS for variable density. Study the evaluation metrics used when labels exist: adjusted Rand index and normalized mutual information. Explore clustering on embeddings from language or vision models, topic modeling (LDA) as soft clustering for text, and anomaly detection methods that build on density, such as isolation forest and local outlier factor. For theory, read about the k-means++ guarantees and EM's connection to variational inference.

pages.title: Dimensionality Reduction
pages.subtitle: Fewer dimensions, same story

panels.heading: Curse of Dimensionality
panels.body:
Each new feature multiplies the volume of space: data gets sparse.
10 bins per feature: 2D = 100 cells, 10D = 10 billion.
Distances concentrate: nearest and farthest points look alike.
k-NN and clustering suffer first.

panels.heading: PCA: Find the Main Axes
panels.body:
PCA = principal component analysis.
Center the data, compute the covariance matrix.
Eigenvectors = new orthogonal axes (principal components); eigenvalues = variance along each.
Keep the top k and project onto them.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Explained Variance
panels.body:
Eigenvalues: 4.0, 2.5, 1.0, 0.5 (total 8).
Shares: 50%, 31%, 13%, 6%.
PC1 + PC2 keep 81% of the variance with half the dimensions.
Rule of thumb: keep 90-95%.
panels.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
pca = PCA(n_components=0.95)
Z = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)

panels.heading: PCA Pitfalls
panels.body:
Not standardized: the largest-unit feature hijacks PC1.
Linear only: misses curved structure.
Components mix all features: hard to explain.
High variance is not always useful signal.

panels.heading: t-SNE & UMAP for Pictures
panels.body:
t-SNE = t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding.
UMAP = uniform manifold approximation and projection.
Nonlinear: keep local neighbors together in 2D.
UMAP is faster and keeps more global layout. Use both for looking, not as model inputs.

panels.heading: Misreading the Map
panels.body:
Cluster sizes mean little: density gets equalized.
Gaps between clusters are not true distances.
Perplexity or n_neighbors reshape the picture: try several.
Random noise can form fake clusters.

panels.heading: Selection vs Extraction
panels.body:
Selection: keep a subset of original columns (filters, L1, tree importance). Interpretable.
Extraction: build new features from all columns (PCA, autoencoders). Compact but abstract.
Need explanations? Select. Need compression? Extract.

pages.footer: Use PCA to compress, t-SNE or UMAP to look, and never measure distances on a t-SNE plot.
pages.summary: Explains why high-dimensional data is hard (curse of dimensionality), how PCA finds directions of maximum variance with a worked explained-variance example, how t-SNE and UMAP make 2D pictures and how they are misread, and the difference between feature selection and feature extraction.

panels:
Volume grows exponentially with dimension, so data needed to cover space at fixed density grows exponentially too. A striking fact: in a d-dimensional unit hypercube, the fraction of volume within distance 0.05 of the boundary is 1 - 0.9^d, which is 65% in 10 dimensions and over 99.99% in 100. Almost every point is near an edge, and almost every pair of random points is roughly equally far apart.

For many distributions, the ratio between the farthest and nearest neighbor distance tends to 1 as d grows, which undermines k-NN, kernels with fixed bandwidth and density-based clustering. Rescuing facts: real data usually lies near a much lower-dimensional manifold (the manifold hypothesis), and many features are correlated, so the intrinsic dimension is small. Models with strong inductive biases, regularization and dimensionality reduction exploit this. Interviewers may also ask about the blessing of dimensionality: in high dimensions, classes often become linearly separable, which is why linear models work well on sparse text features.

PCA finds orthogonal directions that maximize projected variance; equivalently, it minimizes the squared reconstruction error of projecting onto k dimensions (the Eckart-Young theorem gives the best rank-k approximation). Computationally, take the SVD of the centered data X = U S V^T: the columns of V are the principal directions, and the variance along component i is s_i^2 / (n - 1). Using SVD avoids forming the covariance matrix and is numerically stabler. Randomized SVD makes PCA fast for large matrices when k is small.

Centering is essential; without it the first component mostly points at the mean. Components are unique only up to sign, so signs can flip between runs or library versions, a common source of confusion when comparing loadings. Projection: Z = (X - mean) V_k; reconstruction: X_hat = Z V_k^T + mean. Variants include incremental PCA for streaming data, kernel PCA for nonlinear structure, sparse PCA for interpretable loadings, and probabilistic PCA, which handles missing values in a principled way.

Shares: 4.0/8 = 50%, 2.5/8 = 31.25%, 1.0/8 = 12.5%, 0.5/8 = 6.25%. Cumulative: 50%, 81.25%, 93.75%, 100%. So keeping 90% needs three components and 95% needs all four in this tiny example. With real data, the spectrum often decays quickly: hundreds of features may compress to a few dozen components.

Ways to choose k: a cumulative variance threshold (90-95% is conventional but arbitrary); the scree plot elbow; Kaiser's rule on standardized data (keep eigenvalues above 1, the average eigenvalue when features have unit variance); cross-validated downstream performance, which is the most defensible when PCA feeds a model. scikit-learn's PCA(n_components=0.95) selects the smallest k reaching 95%. Remember that explained variance is computed on the data PCA was fit on; fit on the training split, then apply the same transform to validation and test, ideally inside a Pipeline so cross-validation stays honest.

Standardization changes the answer: PCA on the covariance matrix favors high-variance features, while PCA on standardized data (the correlation matrix) treats them equally. Neither is universally correct; if all features share meaningful units, such as pixel intensities, raw covariance may be appropriate. Mixed units almost always call for scaling.

Other limits: PCA captures only linear correlations, so a spiral or a curved manifold needs nonlinear methods. It is sensitive to outliers because variance is squared; robust PCA variants help. Maximum variance does not mean maximum relevance for prediction: a low-variance component can carry the label signal, so PCA before a supervised model can discard exactly what you need, while partial least squares or linear discriminant analysis use the labels. Components are linear mixes of all features, which complicates explanations in regulated settings. Finally, PCA assumes numeric data; for categorical data consider multiple correspondence analysis, and for sparse text, truncated SVD (latent semantic analysis) without centering.

t-SNE converts high-dimensional distances into neighbor probabilities with Gaussian kernels whose widths are set per point by perplexity (roughly the effective number of neighbors, typically 5 to 50), then finds a 2D layout whose Student-t neighbor probabilities match by minimizing KL divergence. The heavy-tailed t distribution lets dissimilar points sit far apart, avoiding the crowding problem. The optimization is non-convex and stochastic, so different seeds give different layouts. Barnes-Hut and FFT accelerations make it O(n log n).

UMAP builds a fuzzy k-nearest-neighbor graph and optimizes a low-dimensional layout with a cross-entropy objective; n_neighbors balances local and global structure and min_dist controls how tightly points pack. It is typically much faster than t-SNE and can transform new points, so it is sometimes used as a preprocessing step for clustering (with HDBSCAN), but treat that carefully. Initializing either method with PCA improves global consistency. For many purposes, a PCA plot is the honest first look.

Wattenberg, Viegas and Johnson's 'How to Use t-SNE Effectively' (2016) shows the core traps. Cluster sizes are not meaningful: t-SNE adapts to local density, so a dense tight cluster and a diffuse one can appear the same size. Distances between clusters may mean nothing, and the relative position of islands can change between runs. Random noise with low perplexity can produce apparent clumps. Topology can mislead too: a 3D trefoil knot or nested shapes may be torn apart.

Good practice: run several perplexities and seeds and trust only patterns that persist; color points by known labels or metadata rather than inferring categories from shape; compare with a PCA view; never compute statistics such as cluster distances on the 2D embedding. UMAP preserves global structure somewhat better, but it also distorts densities and distances, and debates continue about how faithfully either method represents global geometry. Treat these plots as hypotheses generators: a striking cluster is a reason to examine the raw features, not a result.

Feature selection keeps original columns, preserving meaning, cheap inference and easier compliance. Filters score features independently of any model (variance threshold, correlation, chi-square, mutual information) and are fast but blind to interactions. Wrappers such as recursive feature elimination or forward selection search subsets using a model, capturing interactions at high compute cost and with risk of overfitting the selection. Embedded methods select during training: L1 penalties, tree-based importance, or gating in neural networks.

Feature extraction creates new features: PCA, truncated SVD for sparse data, independent component analysis for separating mixed signals, autoencoders for nonlinear compression, and pretrained embeddings, which are now the dominant form of extraction for text and images. Extraction usually preserves more information per dimension but loses interpretability. Either way, selection or extraction must be fit inside each cross-validation fold; selecting features on the full dataset and then cross-validating is a classic leakage bug that produces optimistic scores even on pure noise.
