deeper.further: Next topics: linear discriminant analysis (supervised projection that maximizes class separation), independent component analysis, nonnegative matrix factorization for parts-based representations, and random projections (Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma: distances survive projection to O(log n / epsilon^2) dimensions). Study autoencoders and variational autoencoders as nonlinear extraction, intrinsic dimension estimation, and trustworthiness metrics for evaluating embeddings. Read 'How to Use t-SNE Effectively' (Distill, 2016) and the UMAP paper by McInnes et al. (2018).

pages.title: Bias, Variance & Regularization
pages.subtitle: Find the sweet spot between too simple and too wiggly

panels.heading: Underfit vs Overfit
panels.body:
Underfit: high train error, high test error. Too simple.
Overfit: low train error, much higher test error. Memorized noise.
Good fit: both low and close together.

panels.heading: The Bias-Variance Trade-off
panels.body:
Expected error = bias^2 + variance + irreducible noise.
Bias: error from wrong assumptions.
Variance: sensitivity to which training sample you got.
More complexity: bias down, variance up -> U-shaped test error.

panels.heading: Learning Curves
panels.body:
Plot train and validation error vs training set size.
Both high and close: high bias -> add features or capacity.
Large gap that shrinks with data: high variance -> more data or regularize.

panels.heading: L1 vs L2 vs Elastic Net
panels.body:
Add a penalty to the loss:
L2 (ridge): + lambda * sum(w^2). Shrinks all weights smoothly.
L1 (lasso): + lambda * sum(|w|). Drives many weights to exactly 0.
Elastic net: mixes both; good with correlated features.

panels.heading: Worked Example: 50 Features
panels.body:
100 rows, 50 features, only 5 matter.
Plain least squares: 50 noisy weights, overfits.
Ridge: 50 small nonzero weights.
Lasso: most weights exactly 0; the useful few survive.
panels.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet
Ridge(alpha=1.0); Lasso(alpha=0.1)
ElasticNet(alpha=0.1, l1_ratio=0.5)

panels.heading: Early Stopping
panels.body:
Track validation loss every epoch.
Stop after 'patience' epochs without improvement; restore the best weights.
Works like L2: weights cannot travel far from their start.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Tuning lambda on the test set: use validation or cross-validation.
Penalizing unscaled features: the penalty becomes unfair. Scale first.
sklearn alpha = penalty strength, but C in SVM and LogisticRegression is its inverse.

panels.heading: Double Descent Note
panels.body:
Huge models can break the U: test error peaks where parameters ~ data points, then falls again as size grows.
The classic trade-off still guides most tabular models.

pages.footer: Diagnose first: high bias needs more capacity, high variance needs more data or regularization.
pages.summary: Explains underfitting vs overfitting, the bias-variance decomposition, how to read learning curves, L1 (lasso), L2 (ridge) and elastic net penalties with a worked example, early stopping, tuning pitfalls, and the double descent phenomenon in very large models.

panels:
The diagnostic is the pair of numbers, not either alone. Compare training error with a baseline for what is achievable, such as human-level performance or the Bayes error on the task: the gap between them is avoidable bias. The gap between training and validation error is variance. For example, if humans make 1% error, training is 8% and validation 10%, bias dominates; if training is 1.5% and validation 10%, variance dominates.

Complexity is not just parameter count: feature set, polynomial degree, tree depth, number of boosting rounds, training time and regularization strength all control it. Overfitting can also happen at the level of the whole workflow, when you try many models and pick the best validation score, which is why a final untouched test set matters. Underfitting is sometimes misdiagnosed when the real issue is an optimization failure, such as a learning rate that is too high, so check that training loss actually decreases properly before adding capacity.

For squared loss, with y = f(x) + noise of variance sigma^2, the expected error of a learned model f_hat at x, averaged over training sets, decomposes as (E[f_hat(x)] - f(x))^2 + Var(f_hat(x)) + sigma^2. Bias is how far the average model is from the truth; variance is how much the model changes across training samples; sigma^2 is the irreducible noise, a floor no model can beat. The expectation is over random training sets, which is why variance is a property of the learning procedure, not of one fitted model.

The decomposition is exact for squared error; for 0-1 loss there are only analogous, messier versions. Ensembles target the terms: bagging reduces variance by averaging, boosting reduces bias by adding stages. Regularization accepts a little bias for a large variance reduction. The classic U-curve assumes we increase capacity within a fixed model family; modern overparameterized models complicate it, as the double descent panel describes.

Learning curves answer the most expensive question in practice: will collecting more data help? If training and validation errors have converged at a level that is too high, more data will not help; you need more capacity, better features, or less regularization. If a gap remains and validation error is still falling as data grows, more data is likely to pay off, and extrapolating the curve gives a rough estimate of how much.

Plot them with cross-validation at several training sizes (scikit-learn's learning_curve), and show the spread across folds because small training sizes are noisy. A related tool is the validation curve: error versus one hyperparameter, such as depth or alpha, which displays the U-shape directly. For neural networks, plot error versus epochs as well. Beware of curves where validation is better than training: common causes are dropout or augmentation active only in training, an easier validation set, or leakage. Learning curves for deep models often follow power laws, the basis of scaling laws.

Bayesian view: L2 corresponds to a Gaussian prior on weights and L1 to a Laplace prior, and the penalized solution is the MAP estimate. Geometric view: the constrained problem minimizes loss within a ball; the L1 ball is a diamond whose corners lie on the axes, so the loss contour usually touches it at a corner where some weights are exactly zero. The L2 ball is round, so weights shrink but rarely hit zero.

Ridge has a closed form, w = (X^T X + lambda I)^-1 X^T y, and shrinks weights most along low-variance directions of the data. Lasso has no closed form and is solved by coordinate descent with soft-thresholding. With correlated features, lasso tends to pick one arbitrarily and drop the others, and it selects at most n features when d > n; elastic net (penalty alpha x [l1_ratio x L1 + (1 - l1_ratio)/2 x L2] in scikit-learn) keeps groups of correlated features together. In deep learning, L2 appears as weight decay, which differs from an L2 loss term under Adam, hence AdamW.

This setting, n = 100 and d = 50 with five true signals, is where least squares struggles: with 50 parameters estimated from 100 noisy rows, each coefficient has high variance, and test error can be far above training error. Ridge reduces variance by shrinking all 50 weights, helping prediction but keeping every feature. Lasso shrinks and selects, ideally recovering the five true features, which also makes the model interpretable.

In practice, choose alpha with cross-validation along a regularization path: LassoCV, RidgeCV and ElasticNetCV compute solutions for a grid of alphas efficiently with warm starts. A common choice is the largest alpha within one standard error of the best CV score, giving a simpler model with similar performance. Lasso's selection is not perfectly reliable: correlated features, weak signals and small n cause false inclusions or exclusions, and selected coefficients are biased toward zero. Stability selection (repeated lasso on subsamples) or refitting least squares on the chosen features (relaxed lasso) addresses these. Always standardize features first.

Early stopping treats the number of training iterations as a regularization hyperparameter chosen on validation data. For linear models trained by gradient descent from zero, it is approximately equivalent to L2 regularization, with the effective penalty roughly inversely proportional to the number of steps times the learning rate: weights move along high-curvature directions first and along low-curvature directions only later.

In practice, monitor a validation metric each epoch (or every few hundred steps), keep the best checkpoint, and stop after a patience window, perhaps 5 to 20 epochs for neural networks or 50 to 200 rounds for gradient boosting. Validation loss can be noisy, so smooth it or use a minimum improvement threshold. Two subtleties: the validation set used for stopping is no longer an unbiased estimate of performance, so evaluate on a separate test set; and when you later retrain on train plus validation, you need to scale the number of steps. In large-scale LLM pretraining, models often see each token once, so classic overfitting and early stopping matter less.

Every choice made using a dataset (alpha, feature set, number of epochs, even which model family) leaks a little information from it into the model. Use nested cross-validation or a separate test set to report performance after tuning. Scale features before penalizing: with unscaled data, a feature measured in small units needs a large weight and is penalized heavily, while one in large units escapes, so the penalty encodes arbitrary unit choices.

Naming conventions trip people up. In scikit-learn, Ridge and Lasso use alpha (larger = stronger), while LogisticRegression, LinearSVC and SVC use C = 1/lambda (larger = weaker). Lasso's objective divides the squared error by 2n, so its alpha is not comparable to Ridge's. Other pitfalls: applying weight decay to bias and normalization parameters in neural networks (usually excluded), regularizing one-hot dummy variables unevenly, and assuming regularization can fix label noise or distribution shift. Finally, high variance from too little data is often better solved by collecting data or augmentation than by heavier penalties.

Belkin et al. (2019) and Nakkiran et al. (2019) documented double descent: as model size grows, test error first follows the classic U, then peaks near the interpolation threshold, where the model has just enough capacity to fit the training data exactly, then decreases again in the overparameterized regime. It also appears as a function of training epochs and, counterintuitively, of dataset size: near the threshold, adding data can briefly hurt.

The explanation centers on implicit regularization. Among the many solutions that interpolate the training data, gradient descent tends to find low-norm, smooth ones; at the threshold there is essentially one interpolating solution, and it is forced to fit noise wildly. The peak shrinks or disappears with good explicit regularization and less label noise. Double descent does not overturn the bias-variance decomposition, which still holds; it shows that parameter count is a poor measure of effective complexity. For tabular models of moderate size, the classic trade-off remains the practical guide.
deeper.further: Learn the 'benign overfitting' literature that explains why interpolating models can generalize, and connect learning curves to neural scaling laws. Study dropout, data augmentation, label smoothing and batch normalization as regularizers in deep learning, and the AdamW paper (Loshchilov and Hutter) on decoupled weight decay. Practice nested cross-validation for honest tuning, and explore Bayesian model selection and information criteria (AIC, BIC) as alternatives to validation-based complexity control.

pages.title: Cross-Validation
pages.subtitle: When to use each approach, what it estimates, and common traps

panels.heading: Why Cross-Validation?
panels.body:
ELI5: We train on part of the data, validate on held-out data, repeat the process, and average the results to estimate how well the model will generalize to new data.
Diagram: Dataset → Split → Train (on train folds) → Validate (on val fold) → Average score.
Pro: Better use of limited data. Pro: More stable than one random split. Con: Slower (more training cycles). Watch out: CV is not a substitute for a final untouched test set.

panels.heading: The Main Approaches
panels.body:
1. Holdout split: One train/val split. Use when data is large and quick iteration matters. Caution: high variance from one split.
2. K-fold CV (k=5 or 10): Rotate validation across k folds. Default for iid tabular data. Common k = 5 or 10.
3. Stratified K-fold: Preserve class proportions in each fold. Use for classification, especially imbalance. Caution: stratify labels, not leakage features.
4. Repeated K-fold: Run k-fold multiple times with different shuffles. Use when estimate is noisy. Caution: more compute.
5. LOOCV (leave-one-out): One sample left out each time. Use when dataset is tiny. Caution: very expensive and often high variance.
6. Nested CV: Inner loop for tuning (model tuning), outer loop for unbiased performance (perf. estimate). Use for model selection + honest evaluation. Caution: expensive, but clean.
7. Group K-fold: Keep all examples from the same group together. Use for patients, users, sessions, documents. Caution: never split same group across train and val.
8. Leave-one-group-out (LOGO): Each validation fold is one full group. Use when generalizing to unseen groups/sites. Caution: can be pessimistic if groups differ a lot.
9. Time-series / forward-chaining split: Train on past, validate on future. Use for temporal data, forecasting, drifting systems. Caution: never shuffle time.
10. Monte Carlo / ShuffleSplit: Repeated random train/val splits. Use for flexible repeated estimates on large-ish iid data. Caution: samples may appear in validation multiple times.
There's no one-size-fits-all split — choose what matches your data & goal!

panels.heading: When to Use Which?
panels.body:
Decision flow: Is the data time-ordered? Yes → use time-series split. Are there groups / patients / users / repeated entities? Yes → use Group K-fold or LOGO. Is it classification with imbalance? Yes → use Stratified K-fold. Is the dataset tiny? Yes → use K-fold, Repeated K-fold, or LOOCV (with caveat). Need hyperparameter tuning and honest model comparison? Yes → use Nested CV. Have lots of data and need speed? Yes → holdout split may be enough.
Side note: For many iid problems, start with Stratified 5-fold for classification or 5-fold for regression.

panels.heading: What Can Go Wrong?
panels.body:
Leakage from preprocessing: Scaling, PCA, imputation, feature selection must happen inside each training fold.
Tuning on the test set: Don't peek! It leads to optimistic, overfit results.
Duplicates / near-duplicates: Duplicates across folds inflate performance. Deduplicate or group similar items.
Group leakage: Same group in train & val = information leakage. Keep groups intact.
Shuffling temporal data: Shuffling destroys time order and leaks future information.
Imbalanced folds: Uneven class ratios across folds give unstable metrics.
Unfair model comparison: Compared across different folds? Not fair. Use the same folds for all models.
No variability reported: Mean score alone misleads. Always report mean ± std or confidence interval.

panels.heading: Good Practice Checklist
panels.body: Define the prediction target and unit of prediction. Split by the right unit (sample vs patient vs user vs time block). Keep preprocessing inside the fold pipeline. Use the same folds across model comparisons. Report metric mean and spread across folds. Keep one final untouched test set if possible. Choose metrics that match the task (e.g., AUROC/AUPRC/F1 for imbalance). Set random seeds and describe the split strategy.

panels.heading: Quick Reference Table
panels.body: Fast baseline → Holdout (quick and cheap). Default iid estimate → K-fold (stable and standard). Imbalanced classification → Stratified K-fold (preserves class ratio). Very small dataset → Repeated K-fold or LOOCV (use data efficiently). Unseen patients/users/sites → Group K-fold or LOGO (prevents leakage). Hyperparameter tuning + honest estimate → Nested CV (avoids optimistic bias). Forecasting / temporal drift → Time-series split (respects chronology).

pages.footer: Split like the real deployment. If reality is grouped or temporal, your validation should be too.
pages.summary: Explains how cross-validation estimates how well a model will do on new data, which splitting scheme to use for different kinds of data (grouped, time-ordered, imbalanced, tiny), and the mistakes that make validation scores look better than reality.

panels:
Be precise about what cross-validation estimates: not the quality of one final model, but the expected performance of a training procedure (model, preprocessing, hyperparameter rule) applied to datasets of the size of the training folds. Each fold model trains on (k-1)/k of the data, so the estimate is slightly pessimistic for small k; leave-one-out has the least bias but its fold models are nearly identical, so errors are highly correlated and variance of the average can be high. There is no unbiased estimator of the variance of k-fold CV error (Bengio and Grandvalet 2004), which means any ± you report is approximate.

In practice, refit the chosen procedure on all non-test data and evaluate once on the untouched test set; CV cannot replace that check because your selections have already adapted to the folds.

The ten variants differ in what they hold out. K-fold treats rows as exchangeable. Stratified K-fold keeps label proportions per fold, which matters when a fold could otherwise contain zero positives. Nested CV exists because picking the best of many hyperparameter settings by CV score makes that score optimistically biased (Cawley and Talbot 2010): an inner loop selects hyperparameters, an outer loop scores the whole selection procedure. Cost is multiplicative: 5 outer folds, 5 inner folds and a 20-point grid is 500 fits plus 5 refits.

Group variants ensure all rows of a patient, user or document land in the same fold. Time-series splits train on an expanding (or sliding) past window and validate on the future; when labels look ahead in time, add a gap or purge (embargo) period between train and validation so overlapping horizons do not leak.

The decision flow boils down to one principle: the validation split must mimic the dependence between train and deployment. Ask what a new instance means at deployment: a new patient, a new day, a new document? Then split by that unit. If several conditions apply, apply all: imbalanced and grouped data call for stratified group K-fold; temporal data with repeated users needs time-aware splits that also respect groups, and the strictest requirement usually dominates.

Data size affects the choice of k and holdout. With large data the sampling error of a single holdout is small: for 10,000 validation examples and accuracy near 0.9, the standard error is about √(0.9·0.1/10000) = 0.3 percentage points, so extra folds buy little and cost much. With small data, that error is large and repetition helps.

The most instructive leak is feature selection done outside the loop. Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman (The Elements of Statistical Learning, section 7.10.2) show that selecting the "best" features using all labels and then cross-validating a classifier can report strongly better-than-chance accuracy on data whose labels are pure noise, because the selection step already saw the validation labels. Any step that learns from data (scaling, imputation, PCA, target encoding, resampling, feature selection) must be fitted inside each training fold; in scikit-learn this means wrapping everything in a Pipeline.

Another subtle point: the standard deviation across folds understates uncertainty, because training sets overlap heavily and fold scores are correlated; Nadeau and Bengio (2003) proposed a corrected resampled t-test for comparing models. Near-duplicates (augmented images, paraphrased text, repeated records) behave like group leakage, so deduplicate or cluster before splitting.

"Define the unit of prediction" is the key sentence. If a model scores patients but rows are visits, the unit is the patient. Hashing the group ID into a fold number keeps splits stable as data grows. Persist the fold indices and seed.

Use paired comparison: evaluate competing models on identical folds and compare the per-fold differences, which have much lower variance than comparing two separately computed averages. For uncertainty, bootstrap by group (resample whole patients, not rows) to respect dependence. The "final untouched test set" is consumed by use: each time you look at it and change something, it becomes a validation set. Touch it once, or rotate in a fresh sample.

Read the table as a tradeoff of cost, variance, and realism. Holdout is cheapest but has the highest variance; K-fold uses k fits and lowers variance; repeated K-fold multiplies that by the repeat count. Group K-fold and LOGO estimate performance on unseen groups, which is typically lower than plain K-fold on the same data. That is realism: plain K-fold answers a different question (new rows of known patients). The two numbers can differ dramatically, so the one matching deployment is the right one to report.

Time-series splits answer "how would this have done if deployed then", and a drop in later folds is itself a diagnostic of drift. For nested CV the honest reading is that its outer score estimates the whole procedure including tuning, not any specific hyperparameter setting.
deeper.further: Misconception: cross-validation improves the model. It only measures; it does not train a better model than a single fit does (though it informs choices). Another: more folds is always better; beyond 5-10, gains are small and variance behavior is subtle. Gotchas: calibration and thresholds must also be chosen without peeking at the evaluation fold; early stopping on the validation fold biases the score upward, so use a separate inner split. For LLM and deep-learning work, full CV is rarely affordable, so the same ideas appear as fixed splits with deduplication against pretraining data (contamination checks). This page connects directly to the imbalanced-class and debugging pages, whose leakage warnings are the same issue in different clothes.

pages.title: Feature Engineering
pages.subtitle: Better inputs beat fancier models

panels.heading: Scaling & Standardization
panels.body:
Standardize: z = (x - mean) / std -> mean 0, std 1.
Min-max: (x - min) / (max - min) -> range 0 to 1.
Needed for k-NN, SVM, PCA, regularized and neural models. Trees don't care.
Outliers? Robust scaling or a log transform.

panels.heading: Encoding Categoricals
panels.body:
One-hot: red, green, blue -> red = [1, 0, 0]. Safe; explodes with many categories.
Ordinal: S < M < L -> 0, 1, 2. Only for ordered values.
Target encoding: replace each category with its mean target. Powerful, but risky.

panels.heading: Target Encoding Risks
panels.body:
Computed on all rows, it leaks each row's own label.
A city with 1 customer who churned -> encoding 1.0 = the answer.
Fix: out-of-fold encoding plus smoothing toward the global mean.

panels.heading: Missing Values
panels.body:
Ask why it's missing: missingness can be signal.
Impute median (numbers), most frequent or a 'missing' category (categories).
Add an is_missing indicator column.
Fit imputers on training data only.

panels.heading: Data Leakage
panels.body:
Leakage: training uses information unavailable at prediction time.
Target leakage: using 'refund_issued' to predict churn.
Contamination: scaling or imputing on all data before splitting.
Red flag: scores that look too good.

panels.heading: Pipeline: Leak-Proof by Design
panels.body:
Every fit runs inside each CV fold, automatically.
The same steps run at prediction time.
panels.code:
num = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler())
pre = make_column_transformer((num, num_cols), (OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), cat_cols))
model = make_pipeline(pre, LogisticRegression())
cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5)

panels.heading: Feature Selection
panels.body:
Filter: drop constant columns; rank by mutual information.
Wrapper: RFE (recursive feature elimination) with a model.
Embedded: L1 weights or tree importance.
Select inside the CV loop, or the scores lie.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
One-hot on IDs: thousands of useless columns.
Unseen category at serving time -> crash: handle_unknown='ignore'.
Training-serving skew: compute features identically in both.

pages.footer: Fit every transform on training data only, and wrap it in a Pipeline so you can't forget.
pages.summary: Practical feature engineering: scaling and standardization, encoding categorical variables (one-hot, ordinal, target encoding and its leakage risk), handling missing values, spotting data leakage, building a leak-proof scikit-learn Pipeline, and selecting features without fooling yourself.

panels:
Scaling matters whenever a method uses distances (k-NN, k-means, SVM with RBF kernels), dot products with penalties (ridge, lasso, logistic regression with regularization), variance (PCA), or gradient descent, where unscaled features create ill-conditioned loss surfaces and slow convergence. Tree-based models split on thresholds and are invariant to any monotonic transform, so scaling is unnecessary.

Standardization does not make data normal; it only shifts and rescales. Min-max scaling is sensitive to outliers, since one extreme value compresses everything else, and test data can fall outside [0, 1]. RobustScaler uses the median and interquartile range. For heavy right skew (income, counts, durations), log1p or a Box-Cox / Yeo-Johnson power transform often helps linear models more than any scaler; QuantileTransformer maps to a uniform or normal distribution at the cost of distorting distances. For sparse data such as TF-IDF, avoid centering, which destroys sparsity; use MaxAbsScaler. Always fit the scaler on training data and reuse its statistics everywhere else.

One-hot encoding creates one binary column per category. For unregularized linear models, drop one column to avoid perfect collinearity with the intercept (the dummy variable trap); with regularization or trees it is fine to keep all. Cardinality is the main constraint: a feature with 50,000 values creates a huge sparse matrix. Options include grouping rare categories into 'other' (min_frequency or max_categories in OneHotEncoder), the hashing trick, target encoding, and learned embeddings in neural networks.

Ordinal encoding imposes an order and equal spacing, which is meaningful for sizes or ratings and misleading for colors or cities in linear models. Trees tolerate arbitrary integer codes better, since they can split repeatedly, though it is still suboptimal. LightGBM and CatBoost handle categorical features natively with specialized split algorithms, and scikit-learn's HistGradientBoosting supports categorical_features too. For high-cardinality features in boosting, native handling or carefully cross-fitted target encoding usually beats one-hot.

Target encoding with smoothing: encoding(c) = (n_c x mean_c + m x global_mean) / (n_c + m), where n_c is the category count and m is a smoothing strength. Rare categories shrink toward the global mean; frequent ones keep their own mean. This is a simple empirical Bayes estimate.

The leakage arises because each row's own label contributes to its feature. The model learns to trust the encoding far more than it should, cross-validation looks excellent if encoding happened outside the folds, and performance collapses on new data. The fix is cross-fitting: split training data into K folds and encode each fold using statistics from the other folds only; at prediction time, use statistics from all training data. scikit-learn's TargetEncoder does this cross-fitting internally in fit_transform, which is why fit_transform and fit followed by transform give different results by design. CatBoost's ordered target statistics use a permutation-based variant. For multiclass targets, encode one column per class. Also consider temporal order: encodings should use only past data.

Rubin's taxonomy guides the choice. Missing completely at random (MCAR): missingness is unrelated to anything, so simple imputation adds little bias. Missing at random (MAR): it depends on observed features, so model-based imputation using those features works. Missing not at random (MNAR): it depends on the missing value itself, such as high earners skipping an income question; then the fact of missingness is informative and an indicator column captures it.

Options: mean or median imputation (fast, shrinks variance, distorts correlations), most-frequent or a constant 'missing' category, k-NN imputation, and iterative imputation (IterativeImputer, modeling each feature from the others, similar to MICE). SimpleImputer(add_indicator=True) adds indicator columns automatically. XGBoost, LightGBM and HistGradientBoosting handle NaN natively by learning which branch missing values should take. Never impute the target. Check whether missingness patterns differ between training and production, for example when a form field becomes optional, which silently changes the meaning of the feature.

Kaufman et al. (2012) distinguish two families. Target leakage: features that are consequences of the label or are only recorded after the outcome is known, such as 'refund_issued' for churn, 'took antibiotics' for predicting pneumonia, or a cancellation reason. The test is to ask, for each feature: would I know this value at the exact moment I need the prediction? Train-test contamination: preprocessing, feature selection, oversampling or deduplication done before splitting, or duplicates and related rows (same patient, same user) appearing in both sets.

Temporal leakage is the subtlest: aggregates computed over a window that extends past the prediction time, or random splits on time-series data. Build features as of a cutoff timestamp (point-in-time correct joins, which feature stores support). Detection: suspiciously high scores, one feature with dominant importance, or a model that performs far worse in production than in validation. Adversarial validation, training a classifier to distinguish train from test rows, helps detect distribution differences and contamination.

A Pipeline chains transformers and a final estimator into one object, so cross_val_score, GridSearchCV and model.fit call fit on the transformers using only the current training fold and transform on the validation fold. This removes a whole class of leakage bugs by construction. make_column_transformer routes numeric and categorical columns to different preprocessing; columns not listed are dropped by default (remainder='drop').

The fitted pipeline is the deployable artifact: persist it (joblib or skops) and serving applies exactly the same imputation values, scaling statistics and category vocabulary. Hyperparameters of any step are tunable with the step__param syntax, for example logisticregression__C in a GridSearchCV grid. Use imblearn's Pipeline when resampling such as SMOTE must happen only on training folds. set_output(transform='pandas') keeps column names for debugging, and get_feature_names_out reveals the final feature list. The code on the page uses SimpleImputer with a median strategy, StandardScaler and OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore'), a solid default for mixed tabular data.

Filter methods: VarianceThreshold removes constant or near-constant columns; correlation and mutual information rank features by their relationship to the target, though univariate scores miss interactions (a feature useless alone may be powerful combined with another) and redundancy (two copies of the same signal both score high). Wrapper methods: recursive feature elimination (RFE, RFECV) repeatedly fits a model and drops the weakest features; sequential forward or backward selection adds or removes one at a time. These are expensive and can overfit the selection itself.

Embedded methods: L1 regularization and tree importance select during training; SelectFromModel wraps them. Permutation importance on validation data is a robust check. The critical rule: selection is part of training. Ambroise and McLachlan (2002) showed selecting genes on all data before cross-validation gives near-zero error even on random labels. Put the selector inside the Pipeline. Also question whether selection is needed at all: regularized models and boosted trees often handle many features well, and selection is mostly about cost, latency and interpretability.

High-cardinality identifiers (user IDs, transaction IDs, free-text fields) one-hot encoded create sparse matrices with mostly singleton columns that encourage memorization and fail on new IDs. Either drop them, aggregate behavior per ID into meaningful features, or use embeddings or target statistics. handle_unknown='ignore' turns an unseen category into an all-zero vector; 'infrequent_if_exist' maps it to the infrequent bucket when rare categories were grouped, which is often better. Monitor the rate of unseen categories as a drift signal.

Training-serving skew arises when features are computed by different code paths, for example SQL in batch training and Python in the online service, with subtle differences in time zones, rounding, null handling or aggregation windows. Mitigations: share one feature computation library, log the features actually used at serving time and train on those logs, use feature stores with point-in-time correctness, and add tests that compare offline and online feature values for the same entities. Version pipelines together with models so rollbacks restore both.
deeper.further: Go further with feature stores and point-in-time joins for production systems, the hashing trick and learned embeddings for high-cardinality categories, and automated feature generation (aggregations over relational data, as in deep feature synthesis). Study time-series features (lags, rolling windows, calendar effects) and the leakage traps they carry. Read Kaufman et al., 'Leakage in Data Mining' (2012), and learn monitoring for data drift and unseen categories after deployment. Explore imbalanced-learn pipelines and scikit-learn's TargetEncoder documentation on cross-fitting.

pages.title: Basic Math for Deep Learning
pages.printedTitle: Basic Math for Deep Learning Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Vectors, matrices, gradients, probability, and the minimum math intuition you need

panels.heading: Core Objects
panels.body:
Diagram: pipeline Input x → Linear algebra → Nonlinearity σ(·) (ReLU, tanh, …) → Loss L(y, ŷ) → Gradients ∇L → Updated weights W ← W − η∇L.
Scalars, vectors, matrices, tensors: Scalar – single number (e.g. 3.14), shape (); Vector – 1D list of numbers, shape (d,); Matrix – 2D table, shape (n × d); Tensor – n-D array, shape (b × t × d). ELI5: Containers of numbers. Why it matters: Data, activations, and weights all live in these objects.
Shapes and dimensions: B – batch size (samples in parallel); T – sequence length (time / tokens); D – feature / hidden size (embedding dim); C – channels (e.g., color channels); H – height (image rows); W – width (image cols). Example image batch shape: (B, C, H, W). Example text embeddings shape: (B, T, D). Watch out: Most bugs are shape mismatches!

panels.heading: Linear Algebra Basics
panels.body:
Dot product: x · w = Σᵢ xᵢwᵢ. ELI5: Weighted similarity / one neuron score. Use: Linear layers, attention scores, cosine-style intuition.
Matrix multiplication: Y = XW + b with shapes (n × d)(d × h) → (n × h). ELI5: Many dot products at once. Watch out: Inner dimensions must match (d here)!
Transpose & reshape: Transpose swaps axes (A → Aᵀ). Reshape (view) changes arrangement. Squeeze / unsqueeze add or remove size-1 dimensions.
Norms & distance: L1 norm ‖x‖₁ = Σ|xᵢ|; L2 norm ‖x‖₂ = √(Σxᵢ²); distance d(x, y) = ‖x − y‖₂. ELI5: "How big" or "how far". Use: Regularization, nearest neighbors, embedding similarity.

panels.heading: Calculus for Learning
panels.body:
Derivative / slope: dy/dx is slope / sensitivity (the tangent line). ELI5: How much output changes when input changes a little. Use: Understand growth, training signals, optimization.
Partial derivatives & gradient: For many variables ∂L/∂wᵢ. Gradient ∇L = [∂L/∂w₁, ∂L/∂w₂, …, ∂L/∂wₙ] points in the direction of steepest ascent. ELI5: Arrow pointing uphill fastest. Training goes the OPPOSITE direction.
Chain rule (backprop idea): If y = f(g(x)), gradients pass through both: ∂L/∂x = ∂z/∂x × ∂y/∂z × ∂L/∂y. Core idea of backpropagation! Multiply local effects along the path. Backprop = chain rule in reverse.
Gradient descent: Update rule w ← w − η∇L, where η = learning rate. Too small (very slow), just right, too big (overshoots). ELI5: Walk downhill to reduce loss. Use: Training neural networks.

panels.heading: Probability & Stats Basics
panels.body:
Mean, variance, std dev: Mean μ = (1/n)Σxᵢ; Variance σ² = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − μ)²; Std dev σ = √σ². Use: Normalization, noisy results, uncertainty, data summaries.
Probability, expectation, sampling: P(A) = chance of event A; Expectation E[X] = Σₓ x P(x); Sampling: draw examples ~ P (from a bag/data population to a random sample). Use: Data, stochastic training, simulation, generation.
Common distributions (intuition): Bernoulli (binary) P(X=1) = p; Categorical (classes/tokens), k classes, ΣPᵢ = 1; Gaussian (continuous) N(μ, σ²). Use: Model randomness, noise, data generation, uncertainty.
Log, exp & softmax: exp turns any score → positive; softmax converts logits z to probs: pᵢ = e^zᵢ / Σⱼ e^zⱼ (sum = 1); log turns products → sums: log(ab) = log a + log b. ELI5: Softmax is a "who gets the confidence" function.

panels.heading: Losses You Meet All the Time
panels.body:
MSE (mean squared error): MSE = (1/n)Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². Use: Regression (predict numbers). ELI5: Penalizes large errors more.
Cross-entropy (CE): Binary (with sigmoid) CE = −[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)]; Multiclass (with softmax) CE = −Σ yᵢ log pᵢ, where y is true (0/1 or one-hot) and p is predicted prob. ELI5: Punish being confident and wrong. Use: Classification (labels / classes).
Regularization: L2 (weight decay) λ‖W‖₂² = λΣw² (small & dense weights); L1 (sparsity) λ‖W‖₁ = λΣ|w| (sparse weights). Why: Reduce overfitting, control complexity, improve generalization. ELI5: Keep weights from getting too wild.

panels.heading: Quick Researcher Checklist
panels.body: 1. What are the shapes? 2. What operation is happening? Dot? Matmul? Elementwise? 3. What is the loss? 4. What quantity are we differentiating? ∇L w.r.t. what? 5. Are values normalized or exploding? 6. Are probs actually probabilities? Softmax / sigmoid? 7. Is result an average, a sum, or an expectation?

panels.heading: Common Failure Modes / Traps
panels.body: 1. Shape mismatch: (n,d)(h,k) with d ≠ h – must match! 2. Wrong operation: Matmul ≠ elementwise. 3. Forgetting bias: y = XW vs y = XW + b – bias matters! 4. Mixing logits with probs: Don't feed logits to loss expecting probs, and vice versa! 5. Vanishing / exploding gradients: too tiny or too huge. 6. Averaging over wrong dimension: Mean over batch? Over time? Be intentional! 7. Using wrong loss for the task: Classification ≠ regression.

pages.footer: First track the shapes. Then track the objective. Then track the gradient. Deep learning math = linear algebra + calculus + probability + careful thinking.
pages.summary: The minimum math behind neural networks: how data is stored as vectors, matrices and tensors, how gradients and the chain rule let a model learn by walking downhill on its loss, and the probability ideas and loss functions that show up everywhere.

panels: Shape discipline is the single most useful habit in deep learning code. Frameworks like PyTorch store tensors as flat memory plus strides (how far to jump per axis), so transposing or slicing usually creates a view, not a copy; a view can be non-contiguous, which is why some operations demand .contiguous(). Broadcasting aligns shapes from the trailing axis and treats size-1 axes as stretchable: (B,T,D) + (D,) works, but (n,) minus (n,1) silently produces an (n,n) matrix, a classic bug that raises no error. Common dtypes are float32, and bfloat16 or float16 for speed and memory on accelerators (bfloat16 keeps float32's exponent range but has fewer mantissa bits). Debug trick: use distinct, unequal sizes (B=3, T=5, D=7) in a test so any axis mix-up shows up as an error.

Matrix multiplication (n×d)(d×h) costs about 2·n·d·h floating-point operations, and it is the dominant cost of nearly every neural network. Geometrically, a dot product is |x||w|cos(θ): it grows with both length and alignment, which is why attention uses dot products as similarity and why cosine similarity normalizes lengths away. Matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative, and associativity changes cost: for a (1000×10)(10×1000)(1000×1) chain, computing right-to-left costs far less than left-to-right. Norm choice has consequences: L2 distance is rotation-invariant and smooth, L1 is robust to outliers and favors sparsity. In very high dimensions, pairwise distances between random points concentrate (they become nearly equal), which weakens nearest-neighbor intuition and is one reason embeddings are often compared by angle.

Backpropagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation. For a layer y = f(x), the backward pass computes the vector-Jacobian product: dL/dx = Jᵀ · dL/dy, where J is the matrix of partial derivatives of y with respect to x. The full Jacobian is never formed. The backward pass costs roughly 2x the forward pass and needs the stored forward activations, which is why training memory scales with depth and batch size, and why activation checkpointing (recompute instead of store) exists.

For gradient descent on a smooth quadratic whose curvature (largest Hessian eigenvalue) is λ_max, the step size must satisfy η < 2/λ_max or the iteration diverges. Ill-conditioned problems (very different curvatures along different directions) force a small η, making progress slow along flat directions; this is what momentum and adaptive optimizers address.

The panel's variance uses 1/n, which is the population formula. Estimating variance from a sample uses 1/(n-1) (Bessel's correction) because the sample mean is itself fitted to the data. Expectations are usually approximated by Monte Carlo: average f over n samples, with error shrinking like 1/√n, so 4x more samples halves the noise. Softmax is shift-invariant (adding a constant to all logits changes nothing), so implementations subtract the max logit, or use log-sum-exp, to avoid overflow in exp. Dividing logits by a temperature T before softmax sharpens (T<1) or flattens (T>1) the distribution.

The unifying idea: each distribution pairs with a loss through maximum likelihood. Gaussian noise gives squared error, Bernoulli gives binary cross-entropy, categorical gives cross-entropy. Choosing a loss is choosing a noise model.

Cross-entropy H(y, p) = -Σ y_i log p_i splits as the entropy of y plus the KL divergence KL(y‖p); with one-hot labels the entropy is zero, so minimizing it is exactly maximum likelihood on the labels. Combined with softmax, the gradient with respect to the logits is simply p - y (frameworks fuse log-softmax into the loss for stability, which is why PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss wants raw logits). MSE corresponds to Gaussian noise with fixed variance and is outlier-sensitive; Huber loss turns linear beyond a threshold.

Regularization has a Bayesian reading: L2 penalizes like a Gaussian prior on weights, L1 like a Laplace prior (whose sharp peak at zero yields exact zeros). For Adam, L2 added to the loss is not equivalent to weight decay; AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) decouples them, which is the standard form today.

Treat the checklist as an executable debugging routine. Three checks catch a large fraction of bugs. First, expected initial loss: with K balanced classes and a sensibly initialized model, cross-entropy should start near ln(K) (about 6.9 for 1000 classes); if it starts far from that, initialization, label alignment or loss wiring is off. Second, overfit one tiny batch: a correct model with a correct training loop can drive loss to nearly zero on 10 examples; if it cannot, there is a bug, not a tuning issue. Third, check reduction semantics: sum versus mean over batch or time changes the effective learning rate, and padding must be masked out. Question 6 also covers applying softmax twice, a common bug.

Each failure has a fingerprint. Vanishing gradients: backprop multiplies one Jacobian per layer, so the gradient norm behaves like ρ^L for typical per-layer gain ρ; sigmoid's derivative peaks at 0.25, so deep sigmoid stacks shrink gradients geometrically. Exploding gradients are the ρ>1 case; the standard fix is clipping the global gradient norm to a fixed threshold. Residual connections and normalization layers keep ρ near 1.

Numerical failures are separate: log(0) gives -inf and then NaN, exp of a large logit overflows, and float16 has a narrow range, so mixed-precision training uses loss scaling (multiply the loss by a large constant before backprop, then unscale). A related trap: averaging over the wrong axis (mean over the batch when you meant per-token) silently changes both the loss scale and which examples dominate. Always print shapes and a few values, not just metrics.
deeper.further: A frequent misconception is that math background is needed for derivations; in practice, most failures come from bookkeeping: shapes, axes, reduction modes, and logits versus probabilities. The cure is mechanical: assert shapes, test on tiny batches, and compare against a numerical gradient (finite differences) when writing a custom operation. Connect this page forward: softmax and cross-entropy return in classification metrics and in language-model training, attention is a softmax over dot products, and the gradient-descent rule here is what optimizers like Adam elaborate on in the next page. Keep the distinction between the loss you optimize (smooth, differentiable) and the metric you care about (often not) in mind throughout.

pages.title: Deep Learning Basics
pages.subtitle: Embeddings, pooling, normalization, nonlinearities, training, and core intuition

panels.heading: Core Idea
panels.body:
Diagram: pipeline Input data x → Layers (neural net) → Prediction ŷ → Loss (score) L → Backprop (gradients) ∇L → Updated weights W′.
Neuron / linear layer: y = Wx + b. ELI5: Mix inputs with weights, then add bias. Pro: Flexible building block. Watch out: Alone it only makes linear decisions.
Nonlinearity / activation: Adds bends to the model (ReLU = max(0, x), Sigmoid, Tanh). ELI5: Gives the network the power to model non-straight-line patterns. Pro: ReLU is the default workhorse. Watch out: Sigmoid/Tanh can saturate. ReLU can "die" (stuck at 0).
Loss function: Score = how wrong the model is. Classification: cross-entropy −Σ y log(ŷ). Regression: MSE (1/n)Σ(y − ŷ)². ELI5: The score that tells the model how wrong its predictions are. Pro: Guides learning. Watch out: Must match the task.
Backpropagation: Pass blame backward. ELI5: Send blame (gradients) backward so each weight learns how to change. Pro: Efficient with chain rule. Watch out: Needs a good learning rate & optimizer.

panels.heading: Representation Building Blocks
panels.body:
Embeddings: Look up dense vectors (an embedding matrix row for each token such as cat, dog, pizza, <UNK>). ELI5: A lookup table that gives each item a learned meaning-space coordinate. Use when: Discrete tokens / IDs / categories.
Convolution: Slide a filter to find patterns, producing a feature map. ELI5: A small filter scans the input looking for useful patterns. Pro: Captures local patterns. Pro: Weight sharing = fewer params.
Pooling: Downsample & summarize (max pool 2×2, avg pool 2×2). ELI5: Summarize a local region to shrink size and keep key info. Tradeoff: Loses some detail.
Batch normalization: Normalize activations (unstable before → stable after). ELI5: Stabilizes layer activations during training. Pro: Faster & more stable training. Note: Uses batch stats in training, moving averages at inference.
Dropout: Randomly drop during training. ELI5: Randomly turn off some units so model doesn't rely too much on any one path. Pro: Strong regularization. Note: Off during inference.

panels.heading: Training Basics
panels.body:
Batch / mini-batch / epoch: Batch – one update using all data. Mini-batch – update using a subset. Epoch – one full pass over the data. ELI5: Balance between speed, noise, and stability.
Gradient descent & LR: Update weights opposite the gradient: w ← w − η∇L, η = learning rate. Too small: very slow. Just right: good progress. Too big: unstable! ELI5: Step size for each update.
Optimizers: Popular choices. SGD – simple baseline + momentum. Adam – adaptive LR + momentum. ELI5: Different optimizers = different ways to choose update steps.
Overfitting vs underfitting: Look at train vs. val loss curves. Pro: Use validation curves to decide when to stop or adjust model.
Train / val / test split: Keep the exam secret. Train ~70%, Val ~15%, Test ~15%. ELI5: Train learns, Val tunes, Test is the final exam. Pro: Prevents cheating. Watch out: Never tune on test!

panels.heading: What Each Block Is Good For
panels.body: Embedding: tokens / categories. Convolution: images / local patterns. Pooling: reduce size / gain invariance. Batch norm: stabilize training. ReLU / activations: add expressive power. Dropout: reduce overfitting. Use the right tool for the right job!

panels.heading: Common Failure Modes
panels.body:
Dead ReLUs: Diagnosis – neurons stuck at 0. Fix – lower LR, use Leaky ReLU, or better init.
Vanishing / exploding gradients: Diagnosis – gradients too small or too big. Fix – gradient clipping, LayerNorm/BatchNorm, good init, sensible LR.
Overfitting: Diagnosis – great on train, poor on val/test. Fix – more data, regularize (dropout, weight decay), early stop.
Data leakage: Diagnosis – info from test leaks into train. Fix – clean splits, check pipelines, no peeking!
Bad normalization / unscaled inputs: Diagnosis – one feature dominates. Fix – normalize/standardize inputs & targets.
Tiny batch = unstable batch norm: Diagnosis – batch stats are noisy. Fix – larger batch, use GroupNorm/LayerNorm or SyncBN.

panels.heading: Quick Researcher Checklist
panels.body: 1. Did I define the task and loss correctly? 2. Are my train/val/test splits clean? 3. Did I choose the right representation (embedding/conv/etc.)? 4. Are activations and normalization sensible? 5. Is the learning rate stable? 6. Am I overfitting? 7. Do curves and metrics make sense? 8. Can a simpler baseline do this already?

pages.footer: First learn the pipeline. Then tune the blocks. Then debug the training.
pages.summary: An overview of how a neural network is built and trained: layers, activations, losses and backpropagation, the common building blocks (embeddings, convolution, pooling, batch norm, dropout), and how to spot and fix typical training problems.

panels:
Why does the nonlinearity matter? Without it, two linear layers collapse: W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x, a single linear map, so depth adds nothing. With it, the universal approximation theorems (Cybenko 1989, Hornik 1991) say even one hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a compact set, but that is an existence result: it says nothing about how many units are needed or whether gradient descent finds them. Depth is valuable because composition builds features efficiently.

The training loop is five steps: forward pass, loss, backward pass (compute gradients), optimizer step (update weights), and zeroing the gradients for the next batch. The loss surface is non-convex; in high dimensions, saddle points (flat in some directions, curved in others) are more common obstacles than bad local minima (Dauphin et al. 2014), and over-parameterized networks tend to have many good solutions.

An embedding layer is equivalent to multiplying a one-hot vector by a matrix of shape (V×D), but implemented as a row lookup; the gradient is sparse (only rows used in the batch receive updates). Convolution applies the same small kernel at every position, so parameters are K·K·C_in·C_out regardless of image size, and the output is translation-equivariant: shift the input and the feature map shifts equally. Output length along one axis is floor((H + 2P - K)/S) + 1 for padding P, kernel K, stride S.

Batch norm normalizes each channel using batch mean and variance, then applies a learned scale and shift; at inference it uses running averages, so train and eval behave differently (a classic bug is forgetting eval mode). Inverted dropout rescales kept activations by 1/(1-p) during training so inference is unchanged.

A mini-batch gradient is an unbiased but noisy estimate of the full gradient; its variance falls roughly as 1/batch size, so larger batches give diminishing returns per step. The linear scaling rule (Goyal et al. 2017) for SGD multiplies the learning rate by k when batch size grows k times, with warmup, up to a limit. Adam keeps exponential moving averages of the gradient (m, beta1 = 0.9) and squared gradient (v, beta2 = 0.999), and steps by η · m̂/(√v̂ + ε), where hats mean bias-corrected; AdamW is the usual choice for transformers.

The 70/15/15 split is convention, not law. With millions of examples a few thousand validation examples suffice; what matters is that the test set's confidence interval (for accuracy, a half-width of about 2√(p(1-p)/n)) is narrower than the differences you care about.

Each block encodes an inductive bias, an assumption about the data that narrows the functions the model prefers. Convolution assumes locality and translation equivariance; embeddings assume discrete symbols deserve learned dense coordinates; recurrence assumes order matters sequentially; attention lets each position decide dynamically which others to read. Strong biases help when data is scarce; weaker ones pay off with large-scale pretraining (vision transformers, Dosovitskiy et al. 2020, relied on very large datasets).

Normalization choice follows the same logic. Batch norm depends on batch statistics, which is awkward for small batches and sequence models; layer norm normalizes across the features of each single example, so it is independent of batch size and is standard in transformers. Why batch norm helps is still debated: the original "internal covariate shift" explanation was challenged (Santurkar et al. 2018) in favor of smoother loss landscapes.

Dead ReLU: if a unit's pre-activation is negative for all inputs, its output and gradient are exactly zero, so it never recovers. Initialization matters here: He initialization (He et al. 2015) draws weights with variance 2/fan_in for ReLU networks, and Glorot/Xavier (2010) uses 2/(fan_in + fan_out) for tanh-like units; both aim to keep activation and gradient scale roughly constant across layers.

Gradient clipping (usually by global norm, popularized for recurrent nets by Pascanu et al. 2013) rescales the whole gradient if its norm exceeds a threshold. Batch norm with tiny batches yields noisy statistics, and train-time and test-time behavior diverge; GroupNorm (Wu and He 2018) avoids batch dependence. Compute standardization statistics on the training split only.

Treat the checklist as a ladder: when training misbehaves, climb it in order. Karpathy's widely cited 2019 "Recipe for Training Neural Networks" is a good model: become familiar with the data first; build the simplest end-to-end pipeline and fix seeds; verify initial loss; overfit a single batch; then add regularization and tune. Useful monitors beyond loss: gradient norm per layer, and the ratio of update size to weight size (a heuristic from the cs231n course is roughly 1e-3; if far from that, the learning rate is suspect). Sweep the learning rate on a log scale rather than a linear one, because training quality typically changes over orders of magnitude. Item 8, "can a simpler baseline do this?", is the most skipped and often the most informative: a logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees may match the network.
deeper.further: Misconceptions to drop: more layers does not mean better, and a big train-versus-validation gap does not automatically mean you should shrink the model; in modern over-parameterized networks the validation metric can keep improving while the gap exists, so judge by validation performance, not by the gap alone (see the debugging page). Dropout and batch norm interact awkwardly, and many large transformers use little or no dropout during pretraining because data is plentiful. This page supplies the vocabulary for the transformer pages later in the book: the embedding layer, layer norm, residual structure and AdamW introduced here all reappear there, and the training curves discussed here are what the scaling-law and distributed-training pages try to predict and keep stable.

pages.title: Backprop & Optimizers
pages.subtitle: How gradients flow back and weights step forward

panels.heading: Backprop = Chain Rule, Reversed
panels.body:
Forward pass: compute outputs, then the loss L.
Backward pass: start at dL/dL = 1 and walk back layer by layer.
Each node multiplies the incoming gradient by its local derivative.
One backward pass gives dL/dw for every weight.

panels.heading: Tiny Worked Example
panels.body:
x = 2, w = 3, target y = 4.
Forward: y_hat = w*x = 6; L = (6-4)^2 = 4.
Backward: dL/dy_hat = 2(6-4) = 4; dy_hat/dw = 2.
Chain: dL/dw = 4*2 = 8.
Step, lr 0.05: w = 2.6, L = 1.44.

panels.heading: Full Batch vs SGD vs Mini-Batch
panels.body:
Full batch: exact gradient over all data, slow per step.
SGD (stochastic gradient descent): 1 example per step, very noisy.
Mini-batch: 32-4096 examples per step - the default; GPU-friendly.
Update: w <- w - lr * gradient

panels.heading: Momentum, Adam, AdamW
panels.body:
Momentum: v = 0.9v + g; w -= lr*v. Rolls through noise.
Adam: step = lr * m / (sqrt(v) + eps); m = avg gradient, v = avg squared gradient.
AdamW: decay applied straight to weights. Transformer default.
panels.code:
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(),
    lr=3e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.95), weight_decay=0.1)

panels.heading: Learning-Rate Schedules
panels.body:
Warmup: ramp lr from ~0 to peak over the first 1-5% of steps.
Cosine: lr = min + 0.5(peak - min)(1 + cos(pi*t/T)).
WSD (warmup-stable-decay): hold peak, decay fast at the end.

panels.heading: Clipping & Picking the LR
panels.body:
Gradient clipping: if the gradient norm exceeds 1.0, rescale it to 1.0.
LR range test: raise lr from 1e-7 toward 1; pick ~10x below where loss explodes.
Starting points: Adam 1e-4 to 3e-4; SGD + momentum ~0.1.
panels.code: torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
Loss NaN or spiking -> lr too high; add warmup and clipping.
Loss flat -> lr too low or weights frozen.
Skipped zero_grad() -> gradients pile up across steps.
Check: lr 3e-4 diverges at step 50. First fix? (warmup)

pages.footer: Backprop finds the direction; the optimizer and schedule choose the step.
pages.summary: How a network computes every weight's gradient with one backward pass of the chain rule, worked on a single neuron, and how optimizers (SGD, momentum, Adam, AdamW), learning-rate schedules, gradient clipping and a learning-rate range test turn those gradients into stable training.

panels:
Backprop is reverse-mode automatic differentiation. With one scalar loss and millions of inputs, a single reverse sweep yields every partial derivative; forward-mode would need one pass per parameter. Frameworks never build full Jacobians: each operation implements a vector-Jacobian product that maps the upstream gradient to its inputs' gradients. When a value feeds several consumers, its gradients are summed.

Cost: the backward pass is about twice the forward FLOPs, which is where the rule of thumb of roughly 6N training FLOPs per token for an N-parameter model comes from (2N forward, 4N backward). Memory is the real constraint: every intermediate activation must be kept for the backward pass, which is why activation checkpointing recomputes some of them to save memory. Interviewers like asking you to derive the gradients of a 2-layer MLP by hand and check shapes, for example dL/dW = x^T * delta for a linear layer.

Always verify a hand-derived gradient numerically with a central difference: (L(w + h) - L(w - h)) / 2h. Here, h = 0.001 gives (4.008004 - 3.992004) / 0.002 = 8, matching the analytic value. Gradient checking like this catches most backprop bugs in custom layers.

The example also shows how learning rate relates to curvature. The second derivative is d2L/dw2 = 2x^2 = 8. For a quadratic, gradient descent is stable only when lr < 2 / curvature = 0.25. At lr = 0.125 = 1 / curvature it jumps exactly to the optimum w = 2 in one step; at lr = 0.05 it converges smoothly; above 0.25 it overshoots further each step and diverges. Real networks have many curvatures at once, and the largest one (the sharpest direction) caps the usable learning rate. That is the intuition behind 'edge of stability' results.

The mini-batch gradient is an unbiased estimate of the full gradient, and its noise variance falls roughly as 1/B. Up to a 'critical batch size', doubling B lets you about double the learning rate and halve the number of steps (the linear scaling rule, usually paired with warmup). Past that point, extra batch mostly wastes compute. The gradient noise scale estimates where that point is, and it tends to grow during training.

Data is usually shuffled and sampled without replacement within an epoch. Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several micro-batches before one optimizer step to simulate a larger batch when memory is short. Note that BatchNorm still sees only the micro-batch. LLM batch sizes are quoted in tokens, often millions per step. The claim that small batches generalize better by finding flatter minima is debated: with a tuned learning rate and schedule, the gap mostly disappears.

Adam keeps two running averages per weight: m = b1*m + (1-b1)*g and v = b2*v + (1-b2)*g^2, then bias-corrects both (m / (1 - b1^t)) because they start at zero. Defaults are b1 = 0.9, b2 = 0.999, eps = 1e-8; LLM training often uses b2 = 0.95 so v reacts faster to gradient spikes. Because the step is m / sqrt(v), its size is roughly lr per weight, regardless of how the gradient is scaled.

Adding L2 to the loss puts lambda*w into g, which Adam then divides by sqrt(v), so decay is weakest exactly where gradients are largest. AdamW (decoupled weight decay) applies w -= lr*lambda*w separately. Memory cost: two fp32 states per parameter, 8 bytes, which often dominates GPU memory together with fp32 master weights. Newer optimizers include Lion (sign-based, one state), Shampoo/SOAP (preconditioning) and Muon, which orthogonalizes updates for weight matrices.

Why warmup: at initialization, gradients are large and poorly aligned, and Adam's v estimate is based on a handful of samples, so full-size steps can push the network into a bad region or cause loss spikes. Warmup lengths of a few hundred to a few thousand steps are typical; post-norm transformers need it most.

Cosine decay usually ends at about 10% of the peak or lower; linear decay to zero is also competitive. The schedule is tied to the planned total T: stopping a cosine run early leaves the learning rate high and the model under-annealed, which biased some early scaling-law comparisons. WSD (warmup-stable-decay) fixes this: run at peak lr, and branch a short decay (about 10-20% of steps) from any checkpoint, which suits continued pretraining and compute sweeps. Older recipes used step decay, such as dividing lr by 10 at epochs 30, 60 and 90 for ResNets.

clip_grad_norm_ computes one global L2 norm over all parameters and, if it exceeds max_norm, multiplies every gradient by max_norm / norm. This preserves the update direction. Clipping each value separately (clip by value) changes the direction and is rarely preferred. With mixed precision and a GradScaler, unscale the gradients before clipping. Log the gradient norm every step: rising spikes often come before loss spikes.

The learning-rate range test (Smith, 2017) raises lr during a short run (linearly in the paper; popular tools raise it exponentially over a few hundred steps) and plots loss or accuracy; the best lr is usually 3-10x below the point where loss blows up. For real tuning, sweep on a log grid (1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3) using a short run. Larger models usually need smaller learning rates. muP (maximal update parametrization) rescales initialization and per-layer learning rates so the best lr found on a small proxy model transfers to a much wider one.

Check yourself: divergence that early points to the start of training. Add warmup (or lengthen it), lower the peak, and clip. A check worth doing before any long run: overfit a single small batch to near-zero loss. If you cannot, there is a bug, not a tuning problem.

NaN triage: look for log(0) or division by zero in the loss, fp16 overflow (prefer bf16, or use loss scaling), and bad input data; torch.autograd.detect_anomaly finds the operation that produced the NaN. Large-scale LLM runs still hit loss spikes; common fixes are restarting from a checkpoint a few hundred steps back, skipping the offending batches, lowering lr, and adding QK-norm or a z-loss on the logits. Do not apply weight decay to biases and normalization gains (and often embeddings): it pulls gains toward zero for no benefit. Other silent bugs: calling scheduler.step() per epoch instead of per step, and leaving parameters out of the optimizer.
deeper.further: Next, look at second-order and preconditioned methods (Newton's method, K-FAC, Shampoo) and why they are hard at scale. Read about the edge-of-stability phenomenon, where sharpness rises until it hovers near 2/lr. Study muP for hyperparameter transfer, schedule-free optimizers that remove the need to fix T in advance, and Muon's orthogonalized updates. Mixed-precision training (bf16, fp8, loss scaling) and activation checkpointing are the practical companions to everything on this page.

pages.title: Normalization & Regularization
pages.subtitle: Keep signals stable, keep models from memorizing

panels.heading: Vanishing & Exploding Gradients
panels.body:
Backprop multiplies one factor per layer.
Factors below 1: gradients shrink to ~0, early layers stop learning.
Factors above 1: gradients blow up, loss goes NaN.
20 layers: 0.5^20 = 0.000001, but 1.5^20 = 3,325.

panels.heading: Initialization: Xavier vs He
panels.body:
Goal: keep activation variance steady from layer to layer.
Xavier/Glorot: Var(w) = 2 / (fan_in + fan_out), for tanh.
He/Kaiming: Var(w) = 2 / fan_in, for ReLU (it zeroes half).
Example: fan_in = 512 -> He std = 0.0625.

panels.heading: BatchNorm vs LayerNorm vs RMSNorm
panels.body:
BatchNorm: normalize each feature across the batch; running stats at inference. CNN favorite.
LayerNorm: normalize across one token's features; batch-independent.
RMSNorm: x / RMS(x) * gain, no mean subtraction. Cheaper; standard in LLMs.

panels.heading: Worked Example: One Token
panels.body:
x = [2, 4, 6, 8]
LayerNorm: mean 5, std 2.24 -> [-1.34, -0.45, 0.45, 1.34]
RMSNorm: RMS = 5.48 -> [0.37, 0.73, 1.10, 1.46]
Then multiply by a learned gain (LayerNorm also adds a bias).

panels.heading: Residual Connections
panels.body:
y = x + F(x): each block learns only a correction.
The + gives gradients a direct path back, so 100+ layer nets train.
ResNet (2015) trained 152 layers; every transformer block uses them.

panels.heading: Regularization Toolkit
panels.body:
Dropout: zero units with prob p (e.g. 0.1), scale the rest by 1/(1-p); off at inference.
Weight decay: shrink weights each step (AdamW, 0.01-0.1).
Data augmentation: flips, crops, color jitter, mixup.
Early stopping: keep the best validation checkpoint.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
Forgot model.eval() -> dropout and BatchNorm stay in training mode.
Batch size 2 -> noisy BatchNorm stats; use LayerNorm or GroupNorm.
Augment only in label-safe ways: never rotate a 6 into a 9.
Check: train 99%, val 70%. Which tools apply?

pages.footer: Normalize to keep signals healthy; regularize to keep the model honest.
pages.summary: Why deep networks suffer vanishing or exploding gradients and how good initialization, normalization layers (BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm) and residual connections keep training stable, plus the regularizers (dropout, weight decay, data augmentation, early stopping) that fight overfitting.

panels:
Precisely, the gradient reaching layer l is a product of Jacobians, one per later layer. What matters is the size of these matrices (their singular values), not single numbers: if they are mostly below 1, gradients shrink exponentially with depth; if above 1, they grow. Saturating activations make it worse: the sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25, so ten sigmoid layers can scale a gradient by 0.25^10, about 1e-6.

Diagnose by logging per-layer gradient norms: early layers orders of magnitude smaller than late ones means vanishing; sudden jumps to inf mean exploding. The fixes form a toolkit: variance-preserving initialization, ReLU-family activations, normalization layers, residual connections, and gradient clipping for exploding cases. Forward activations can explode too, which overflows fp16 well before the gradients do. RNNs feel the problem most because the same matrix is multiplied at every time step.

Derivation: for y = sum of w_i*x_i with independent zero-mean terms, Var(y) = fan_in * Var(w) * Var(x). Keeping Var(y) = Var(x) needs Var(w) = 1/fan_in. ReLU zeroes half the inputs and halves the second moment, so He init doubles this to 2/fan_in. Xavier averages fan_in and fan_out so that both the forward signal and the backward gradient keep their variance. Uniform versions use U(-a, a) with a = sqrt(6 / (fan_in + fan_out)) for Xavier.

PyTorch's default for nn.Linear is a scaled Kaiming-uniform that works out to roughly U(-1/sqrt(fan_in), 1/sqrt(fan_in)). GPT-style transformers often use normal(0, 0.02) and scale residual output projections by 1/sqrt(2 * n_layers) so the residual stream does not grow with depth. Zero-initializing the last layer (or last norm gain) of each residual branch makes every block start as the identity. Identical initial weights never break symmetry: every neuron would get the same gradient forever.

BatchNorm computes y = gamma * (x - mu_B) / sqrt(var_B + eps) + beta per channel, over (N, H, W) for conv features. It keeps running averages (momentum 0.1 in PyTorch) for inference, so training and evaluation behave differently, it needs reasonable batch sizes, and multi-GPU training may need SyncBatchNorm. Its original 'internal covariate shift' explanation is disputed; later work argues it mainly smooths the loss landscape and allows larger learning rates.

LayerNorm normalizes over the feature dimension of each token separately, so it behaves the same at training and inference and never mixes information between examples or time steps. That suits variable-length and autoregressive models. RMSNorm (2019) drops mean-centering and the bias, saving compute and memory traffic; Llama-family and most current LLMs use it. GroupNorm normalizes groups of channels per example, a common BatchNorm substitute in detection and diffusion U-Nets. QK-norm applies normalization to queries and keys inside attention to stop logit growth.

Details to note: implementations add eps (about 1e-5 or 1e-6) inside the square root and use the biased variance (divide by N, not N - 1). The gain gamma starts at 1 and the bias beta at 0, so a fresh LayerNorm is pure standardization. After LayerNorm, each token vector has mean 0 and variance 1 before the affine step, so its original scale is gone; the learned gain restores whatever scale is useful.

In a (B, T, D) activation tensor, LayerNorm and RMSNorm compute B * T separate statistics, each over D numbers. BatchNorm on a (B, D) tensor would instead compute D statistics, each over B examples. RMSNorm keeps the mean offset: here the output stays all positive because the input was. When people say LayerNorm is 'cheap', it is still memory-bound. Fused kernels that combine normalization with the next matmul or with the residual add matter for real throughput.

He et al. (2015) observed a degradation problem: a 56-layer plain network had higher training error than a 20-layer one, so this was an optimization failure, not overfitting. Residual blocks fix it because d(x + F(x))/dx = I + dF/dx: the identity term guarantees a gradient path that no layer can block. One view (Veit et al., 2016) treats a ResNet as an ensemble of many shallow paths of different lengths.

When shapes change (stride 2 or more channels), the shortcut uses a 1x1 convolution projection. Bottleneck blocks (1x1 reduce, 3x3, 1x1 expand) keep deep ResNets affordable. Residual variance grows with depth, so deep models use scaled initialization, zero-init of branch outputs, or normalization schemes such as DeepNorm. Stochastic depth randomly skips whole residual blocks during training as a regularizer. In transformers the same idea appears as the residual stream that every attention and MLP block reads from and writes to.

Inverted dropout scales the surviving units by 1/(1 - p) during training, so inference needs no change. Classic fully connected nets used p = 0.5; transformers use about 0.1, and many single-epoch LLM pretraining runs use none, because seeing each token once leaves little room to overfit. Dropout is still common when fine-tuning on small data.

AdamW's weight decay multiplies weights by (1 - lr * lambda) each step; it equals L2 regularization only for plain SGD. Augmentation encodes invariances you believe in: random resized crops, flips, color jitter, RandAugment, mixup (blend two images and their labels), CutMix, SpecAugment for audio. Label smoothing (targets like 0.9 instead of 1) curbs overconfidence. Early stopping is an implicit regularizer: training for fewer steps limits how far weights move from initialization. Choose these with a validation set, never with the test set.

Check yourself: a 99% train vs 70% validation gap is overfitting. Try more data or augmentation first, then dropout, stronger weight decay, early stopping, or a smaller model. Rule out leakage and label noise before concluding the model is simply too big.

More traps. When fine-tuning with small batches, freeze BatchNorm statistics (keep those layers in eval mode) or they drift. Dropout placed right before BatchNorm can cause a train/test 'variance shift'. Augmenting before splitting the data puts near-duplicate images in both train and test and inflates scores. Decaying normalization gains pulls them toward zero. Some augmentations change the label: horizontal flips are fine for cats but not for text, road signs with arrows, or left/right in medical scans. Finally, double descent and grokking show that test error can improve again after an apparent overfitting phase, so regularization strength interacts with model size and training length.
deeper.further: Follow-ups: initialization schemes that train deep nets without normalization (Fixup, SkipInit, normalizer-free networks with adaptive gradient clipping), DeepNorm and other ways to train very deep transformers, and muP's per-layer scaling rules. On the regularization side, explore sharpness-aware minimization (SAM), label smoothing, mixup theory, double descent and grokking, and how data scale in modern pretraining changed the role of dropout.

pages.title: Convolutional Networks
pages.subtitle: Small filters, shared weights, growing vision

panels.heading: Convolution: Slide a Filter
panels.body:
A kernel (e.g. 3x3 weights) slides across the image.
At each spot: multiply overlapping values, sum to one number.
Same weights everywhere = weight sharing.
64 kernels -> 64 feature maps (channels).

panels.heading: Output Size Formula
panels.body:
out = floor((n + 2p - k) / s) + 1
n = input size, k = kernel, p = padding, s = stride.
n=32, k=3, p=1, s=1 -> 32 (same size).
n=32, k=3, p=0, s=2 -> floor(29/2) + 1 = 15.

panels.heading: Worked Example: One Output
panels.body:
Patch rows: [3 1 0] [4 2 1] [5 1 0]
Kernel rows: [1 0 -1], three times (vertical edge)
Sum: (3-0) + (4-1) + (5-0) = 11 -> strong edge.
Params, 3x3 conv, 3 -> 64 channels: 3*3*3*64 + 64 = 1,792.

panels.heading: Pooling & Receptive Field
panels.body:
Max pool 2x2, stride 2: keep each block's max; halves height and width.
Receptive field = input region one output sees.
Three stacked 3x3 convs see 7x7, with fewer weights than one 7x7.
Depth: edges -> textures -> parts -> objects.

panels.heading: Classic Architectures
panels.body:
LeNet-5 (1998): digit reading, 2 conv layers.
AlexNet (2012): ReLU + GPUs, won ImageNet.
VGG (2014): deep stacks of 3x3 convs.
ResNet (2015): skip connections, 152 layers.
Later: EfficientNet, ConvNeXt.

panels.heading: Transfer Learning
panels.body:
Start from ImageNet-pretrained weights, not random ones.
Small dataset: freeze the backbone, train a new head.
More data: fine-tune everything at a low lr (e.g. 1e-4).
panels.code:
m = torchvision.models.resnet50(weights="IMAGENET1K_V2")
m.fc = torch.nn.Linear(2048, num_classes)

panels.heading: CNN vs ViT
panels.body:
CNN: built-in locality bias; data-efficient.
ViT (vision transformer): 16x16 image patches become tokens; global attention from layer 1.
ViTs need big pretraining, then match or beat CNNs.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
Recompute the output size after every stride or pool.
No padding -> maps shrink each layer.
High lr while fine-tuning wrecks pretrained features.
Check: 224 input, 7x7 conv, stride 2, pad 3 -> ? (112)

pages.footer: Local filters, shared weights, stacked deep: that is how a CNN learns to see.
pages.summary: How convolutional neural networks process images: sliding kernels, the output-size formula, feature maps, pooling and receptive fields, the LeNet-to-ResNet lineage, transfer learning from pretrained backbones, and how CNNs compare with vision transformers.

panels:
Deep learning 'convolution' is technically cross-correlation: the kernel is not flipped, which makes no difference because the weights are learned. A conv weight has shape (C_out, C_in, k, k); each output channel sums over all input channels. Shifting the input shifts the feature map the same way (translation equivariance); pooling and striding add partial invariance. The parameter count does not depend on image size, which is why the same network can run on larger images.

Compute: H_out * W_out * C_out * C_in * k * k multiply-adds per image, so early high-resolution layers dominate FLOPs while late layers dominate parameters. 1x1 convolutions mix channels without spatial context and are used for cheap bottlenecks. Depthwise-separable convolutions (MobileNet) split spatial filtering per channel from channel mixing, cutting cost by about k^2 times. Dilated convolutions space out the kernel taps to grow the receptive field without extra weights.
