The formula applies separately to height and width. With dilation d, replace k by the effective size d(k - 1) + 1. For odd k at stride 1, 'same' padding is p = (k - 1)/2. PyTorch rounds down; pooling layers have a ceil_mode option that rounds up instead, which changes shapes by one and is a classic off-by-one source.

Transposed convolutions, used to upsample in decoders and U-Nets, invert the formula: out = (n - 1)s - 2p + k + output_padding. Strides that do not divide evenly drop the last rows and columns silently. Interviewers often ask for full shapes and parameter counts through a small network; write the (C, H, W) shape after every layer. A useful habit in code is to run a dummy tensor through the model and print shapes, or use adaptive average pooling before the classifier so the head does not depend on input size.

In a trained CNN nobody hand-writes this kernel: first-layer filters learn edge, color-blob and Gabor-like detectors on their own, as the famous visualizations of AlexNet's first layer show. Flipping the kernel's sign detects the opposite edge (dark-to-bright). After the sum, a bias is added and a nonlinearity such as ReLU is applied, so a negative response becomes zero.

Parameter counting: each output channel has k * k * C_in weights plus one bias. Compare the 1,792 parameters of this conv layer with a fully connected layer from a 32x32x3 image (3,072 inputs) to just 64 units: 196,672 parameters, about 110x more, and with no notion that nearby pixels are related. That gap, from weight sharing and local connectivity, is the main reason CNNs made vision practical. BatchNorm after a conv makes the conv's bias redundant, so it is usually disabled (bias=False).

Receptive field recurrence: r_out = r_in + (k - 1) * j_in, where j is the jump, the product of all strides so far. Strides and pooling multiply how fast the receptive field grows. Measured 'effective' receptive fields are roughly Gaussian and much smaller than the theoretical one: center pixels matter far more than edge pixels.

Weights: two 3x3 layers use 18C^2 weights versus 25C^2 for one 5x5 (with C channels in and out); three 3x3 layers use 27C^2 versus 49C^2 for a 7x7, plus extra nonlinearities in between. Many modern nets replace max pooling with strided convolutions, which learn their downsampling. Global average pooling at the end (NiN, GoogLeNet, ResNet) replaced huge fully connected heads. Feature visualization studies confirm the hierarchy: early layers respond to edges and colors, middle layers to textures and parts, and late layers to object-level patterns.

Rough numbers worth knowing. LeNet-5 had about 60k parameters. AlexNet had about 60M, used ReLU, dropout and two GPUs, and cut ImageNet top-5 error from about 26% to 15.3% in 2012, which started the deep learning boom. VGG-16 has 138M parameters, mostly in its fully connected layers. GoogLeNet/Inception (2014) used parallel branches and 1x1 bottlenecks for efficiency. ResNet (2015) went to 152 layers with residual and bottleneck blocks and reached 3.57% top-5 error with an ensemble, below the often-quoted human estimate of about 5%.

Later: DenseNet concatenates all earlier feature maps; MobileNet targets phones with depthwise-separable convs; EfficientNet scales depth, width and resolution together with one 'compound' coefficient; ConvNeXt (2022) modernized ResNet with transformer-era choices (larger 7x7 depthwise kernels, LayerNorm, GELU, fewer activations) and matched Swin transformers, showing that training recipe explained much of the CNN-ViT gap.

Two modes: feature extraction (frozen backbone, train only the head, cheap and hard to overfit) and fine-tuning (update everything). Common refinements are discriminative learning rates (smaller for early layers, which hold generic features), gradual unfreezing from the top down, and keeping BatchNorm layers in eval mode when the batch is small. Always preprocess inputs exactly like the pretraining recipe; for torchvision ImageNet weights that means mean [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] and std [0.229, 0.224, 0.225] after scaling to [0, 1].

Transfer helps even across large domain gaps such as medical images or satellite data, though gains shrink as your own dataset grows. In 2026 the strongest starting points are often self-supervised or image-text backbones (DINOv2-style, CLIP-style encoders) rather than supervised ImageNet classifiers. A linear probe on frozen features is a quick way to compare backbones before committing to full fine-tuning.

ViT (2020): a 224x224 image cut into 16x16 patches gives 14 x 14 = 196 tokens, each linearly projected, plus a class token and learned position embeddings, then a standard transformer encoder. Without convolution's built-in assumptions (locality, translation equivariance), ViTs trained only on ImageNet-1k fell behind ResNets; with very large pretraining (JFT-300M) or heavy augmentation and distillation (DeiT) they matched or beat them.

Cost: global attention is quadratic in the number of patches, so doubling resolution means 4x the tokens and about 16x the attention cost. Swin transformers use windowed attention for high resolution, and many ViTs use a small convolutional stem. CNNs remain strong for mobile, edge and real-time detection, and for dense prediction at high resolution. Today the choice is usually set by the available pretrained backbone and the hardware, not by the architecture alone; most multimodal LLMs use ViT image encoders.

Check yourself: (224 + 2*3 - 7) / 2 = 111.5, floored to 111, plus 1 = 112. This is the ResNet stem: 224 -> 112 after the 7x7 stride-2 conv, then 56 after the 3x3 stride-2 max pool.

More traps. PyTorch uses NCHW (channels first) while TensorFlow defaults to NHWC; mixing them up silently treats width as channels. A hard-coded flatten size breaks as soon as the input resolution changes, which adaptive average pooling avoids. Small images (CIFAR's 32x32) need a gentler stem, or the ImageNet stem shrinks them to 8x8 almost immediately. When fine-tuning, use a learning rate 10-100x lower than training from scratch and warm up the new head first; a high learning rate from step 1 destroys pretrained features before the head stops sending random gradients. Finally, check that augmentations such as flips and crops are applied only during training.
deeper.further: Next topics: object detection (two-stage Faster R-CNN, one-stage YOLO, transformer-based DETR) and segmentation (U-Net, Mask R-CNN, promptable segmentation models). Learn saliency methods such as Grad-CAM to see what a CNN attends to, and group-equivariant CNNs that build in rotation symmetry. Self-supervised vision pretraining (SimCLR, DINO, masked autoencoders) explains where today's best backbones come from, and diffusion U-Nets reuse almost every CNN idea on this page.

pages.title: Rnns & Lstms
pages.subtitle: Memory through time, and why attention took over

panels.heading: Sequence Modeling
panels.body:
Inputs arrive in order: words, audio frames, sensor readings.
Output: one label (sentiment), one per step (tagging), or a new sequence (translation).
Needs: any length, memory of the past.

panels.heading: RNN: Unroll Through Time
panels.body:
One cell, same weights at every step:
h_t = tanh(W_h h_(t-1) + W_x x_t + b)
h_t = memory summary so far.
BPTT (backprop through time): unroll T steps, backprop through all, sum the weight gradients.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Two Steps
panels.body:
W_h = 0.5, W_x = 1, h_0 = 0, inputs x = [1, 2]
h_1 = tanh(1) = 0.76
h_2 = tanh(0.5*0.76 + 2) = tanh(2.38) = 0.98
Gradient back 50 steps: factor <= 0.5 each -> ~1e-15. Vanished.

panels.heading: LSTM Gates
panels.body:
Cell state c = a conveyor belt of memory.
Forget gate f: erase. Input gate i: write. Output gate o: reveal.
c_t = f*c_(t-1) + i*c~_t ; h_t = o*tanh(c_t)
Additive update -> gradients survive long spans.

panels.heading: GRU: The Lighter LSTM
panels.body:
GRU (gated recurrent unit): two gates.
Update z: keep old memory or replace it. Reset r: how much past to use.
No cell state; ~25% fewer parameters.
Often matches LSTM; try both.

panels.heading: Seq2Seq + Attention
panels.body:
Encoder RNN reads the source; decoder RNN writes the target.
Problem: one fixed vector must hold the whole sentence.
Attention (2014): each output step takes a weighted mix of all encoder states.
That idea grew into the transformer.

panels.heading: Why Transformers Won
panels.body:
RNN: step t waits for step t-1, so training can't parallelize over time.
Transformer: all positions at once, one hop between any two tokens.
Cost: attention is O(T^2) in length.
SSMs (state-space models, e.g. Mamba): linear-time recurrence, parallel training.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
Exploding RNN gradients -> clip the gradient norm.
Pad variable-length batches and mask the pads.
Truncated BPTT limits how far back learning reaches.
Check: why can't a plain RNN learn 200-step links?

pages.footer: RNNs carry memory step by step; attention lets every step look everywhere.
pages.summary: How recurrent networks model sequences by passing a hidden state through time, why backprop through time makes gradients vanish, how LSTM and GRU gates fix it, how seq2seq attention led to transformers, and where state-space models fit today.

panels:
Task shapes map to different setups: many-to-one (classify a review), aligned many-to-many (part-of-speech tags, one per word), and unaligned sequence-to-sequence (translation, speech-to-text), where lengths differ. Generation factorizes the sequence probability as a chain of next-step predictions. During training, 'teacher forcing' feeds the true previous token rather than the model's own guess, which is fast but creates exposure bias: the model never practices recovering from its own mistakes.

When the whole input is available up front (tagging, classification), bidirectional models read it both ways and do better. When it is not (streaming speech, live sensors, text generation), the model must be causal: it can only use the past. Variable lengths are handled either by recurrence, which naturally runs any number of steps, or by padding to a common length plus masks. Classical alternatives include hidden Markov models and 1D convolutions over time (temporal CNNs, WaveNet).

Because the weights are shared across time, the gradient for W_h is the sum of its contributions at every step. BPTT must store all T hidden states, so memory grows linearly with sequence length. Truncated BPTT handles long streams: keep carrying the hidden state forward, but cut the gradient (detach) every k steps, so learning only reaches k steps back even though the state can remember more.

The simple form here is the Elman RNN (1990). With hidden size H and input size D it has H^2 + H*D + H parameters. Its compute depth is T sequential steps, which is the root of both its O(1)-per-step inference and its slow training. Training the hidden-to-hidden matrix is delicate: orthogonal initialization keeps its singular values near 1. Character-level RNN language models were a well-known 2015 demonstration that these models can learn syntax, indentation and matching brackets.

The per-step local derivative is dh_t/dh_(t-1) = W_h * (1 - h_t^2). At h_2 = 0.98 the tanh derivative is only about 0.04: saturation makes the factor far smaller than W_h alone, so vanishing is even faster than the 0.5^50 estimate. In the matrix case the largest singular value of W_h, times the activation derivatives, decides the outcome: consistently below 1 means vanishing, above 1 risks exploding (Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio, 2013).

The consequence is subtle: the forward pass can still carry some information over long distances, but the learning signal cannot, so the model never learns to use it. Partial fixes include orthogonal or identity initialization with ReLU (IRNN) and gradient clipping, which handles exploding but not vanishing gradients. The real fix was architectural: gating, as in LSTMs and GRUs, and later attention, which gives a direct path between distant positions.

Each gate is a sigmoid of a learned linear function of [h_(t-1), x_t], producing values between 0 and 1 per memory dimension; the candidate c~_t uses tanh. The key is the additive cell update: along the cell state, dc_t/dc_(t-1) = f, so when the forget gate stays near 1 the gradient passes almost unchanged (the 'constant error carousel'). Hochreiter and Schmidhuber introduced the LSTM in 1997; the forget gate itself was added in 2000.

Practical details: initialize the forget-gate bias to about 1 so the cell remembers by default early in training. An LSTM layer has 4 * (H * (H + D) + H) parameters, four times a vanilla RNN, because it learns four weight blocks (three gates plus the candidate). Variants include peephole connections and coupled forget/input gates. LSTMs dominated speech recognition, machine translation (Google's 2016 neural translation system) and language modeling until transformers took over around 2018.

The GRU (Cho et al., 2014) merges the cell and hidden state. One common form is h_t = (1 - z) * h_(t-1) + z * h~_t, where h~_t is computed from x_t and r * h_(t-1); some libraries swap the roles of z and 1 - z, so check before reading equations off code. With three weight blocks instead of four, a GRU has about 25% fewer parameters than an LSTM of the same width and runs a bit faster.

Empirical comparisons (for example Chung et al., 2014, and large architecture searches) found no consistent winner; results depend on task and tuning. LSTMs have a slight edge on tasks that need counting, because their unbounded cell state can act as a counter, which GRUs struggle with. The practical advice stands: treat the cell type as a hyperparameter and choose on validation data. Both share the same limits: sequential computation and a fixed-size memory.

Sequence-to-sequence learning (Sutskever et al., 2014) used a deep LSTM encoder and decoder and found that reversing the source sentence helped by shortening early dependencies. The fixed-vector bottleneck hurt long sentences. Bahdanau et al. (2014) added attention: for output step i, compute scores between the decoder state and every encoder state h_j, softmax them into weights alpha_ij, and use the context c_i = sum of alpha_ij * h_j. Luong et al. (2015) simplified the score to a dot product.

The attention weights form a soft alignment matrix you can plot, and it often shows the expected word-to-word correspondences. Decoding typically used beam search, keeping the k best partial translations. Scheduled sampling tried to reduce exposure bias by sometimes feeding the model its own predictions during training. In 2017 'Attention Is All You Need' removed recurrence entirely, using self-attention in both encoder and decoder.

Training: an RNN's T steps are sequential, while a transformer processes all positions in parallel with matrix multiplies that use GPUs fully. Path length between two tokens is 1 in attention versus up to T in an RNN, which helps learn long-range links. Inference flips the comparison: a transformer's KV cache and per-token attention cost grow with context length, while an RNN's state and per-step cost stay constant.

Modern recurrent revivals target that gap. Structured state-space models (S4, 2021) use linear recurrences that can be trained in parallel as a convolution or scan. Mamba (2023) made the parameters depend on the input ('selective') with a hardware-aware parallel scan; Mamba-2 related this to linear attention. RWKV, RetNet, xLSTM and gated linear-attention models belong to the same family. Their known weakness is exact recall from long context, such as copying, because everything must fit in a fixed-size state; hybrids that mix a few attention layers with SSM layers address it.

Check yourself: the gradient connecting step 1 to step 200 is a product of about 200 per-step factors, usually below 1, so it vanishes and the network never learns the dependency. Gating (LSTM/GRU) or attention gives the signal a better path.

More traps. In PyTorch, use pack_padded_sequence (or explicit masks) so padding steps do not update the hidden state or the loss. When carrying hidden state between batches in stateful training, detach it, or backprop will try to run through the entire history and memory blows up. Do not use a bidirectional model for generation or streaming: it reads the future. Typical gradient-clipping norms for RNNs range from 0.25 to 5. Sort or bucket sequences by length to waste less compute on padding. And remember that dropout on recurrent connections needs the same mask at every time step (variational dropout), or it destroys the memory.
deeper.further: Go further with neural Turing machines and differentiable memory, the link between linear attention and RNNs (a transformer with linearized attention can be run as a recurrence), and modern recurrent designs such as xLSTM, RWKV and Mamba-2. CTC (connectionist temporal classification) loss explains how speech models handle unaligned outputs. For theory, look at the expressivity of fixed-state models versus attention on recall and copying tasks, and at test-time-training layers that update a small model as their state.

pages.title: Embeddings
pages.subtitle: Turn words, images and items into meaningful vectors

panels.heading: One-Hot vs Dense
panels.body:
One-hot: 50,000-word vocab -> 50,000 numbers, a single 1. Every word equally far apart.
Dense embedding: 300-4,096 learned numbers per word.
Similar items land close together.

panels.heading: Embedding Layer = Lookup Table
panels.body:
Matrix E has shape (vocab_size, dim).
Token id 42 -> row E[42]: same as one-hot times E, far cheaper.
Rows are trained by backprop like any weight.
panels.code:
emb = torch.nn.Embedding(50000, 768)
vecs = emb(torch.tensor([42, 7]))  # (2, 768)

panels.heading: word2vec Skip-Gram
panels.body:
Predict context words from a center word.
'the cat sat on', center 'cat', window 2 -> (cat, the), (cat, sat), (cat, on).
Negative sampling: pull real pairs together, push random pairs apart.

panels.heading: Cosine Similarity
panels.body:
cos(a, b) = a.b / (|a| |b|), from -1 to 1.
a = [1, 2], b = [2, 3]
a.b = 8; |a| = 2.24; |b| = 3.61
cos = 8 / 8.06 = 0.99 -> nearly same direction.

panels.heading: Vector Arithmetic
panels.body:
king - man + woman ~ queen (word2vec).
Directions can encode relations: gender, tense, capital-of.
Caveat: only some analogies work, and vectors also learn data biases.

panels.heading: Sentence & Multimodal Embeddings
panels.body:
Sentence embeddings: one vector per text, trained on matching pairs.
CLIP-style: an image encoder and a text encoder trained so matching image-caption pairs score high.
Result: search photos with words.

panels.heading: Vector Search in Practice
panels.body:
1. Embed documents once; store vectors in an index.
2. Embed the query with the SAME model.
3. Return top-k by cosine; ANN (approximate nearest neighbor) indexes like HNSW keep it fast.
Powers RAG, recommendations, dedup.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
Vectors from different models are not comparable.
Unnormalized dot product favors long vectors.
Change the model -> re-embed everything.
Check: why normalize vectors before a dot product?

pages.footer: An embedding turns meaning into geometry: close vectors, close ideas.
pages.summary: How embeddings replace sparse one-hot codes with dense learned vectors, how word2vec and embedding layers learn them, how cosine similarity and vector arithmetic read them, and how sentence and CLIP-style multimodal embeddings power vector search.

panels:
One-hot vectors are mutually orthogonal: the dot product of any two different words is 0, so nothing learned about 'cat' carries over to 'kitten'. Dense, distributed representations (Hinton, 1986; Bengio's 2003 neural language model) share statistical strength: a word seen rarely benefits from neighbors that appear often.

Typical sizes: word2vec 300, BERT-base 768, large LLMs 4,096 to over 12,000 dimensions; retrieval embedders often 384 to 3,072. Matryoshka representation learning trains embeddings so the first 64, 128 or 256 dimensions still work alone, letting you trade quality for storage. In recommenders and tabular models, high-cardinality categorical features (user IDs, product IDs) also get embedding tables, sometimes with the hashing trick to cap vocabulary size. A common heuristic for tabular categories is a dimension near the fourth root of the number of categories, then tune. Individual dimensions are rarely interpretable; meaning lives in directions and distances.

Backprop through a lookup only touches the rows used in the batch, so the gradient is sparse; frameworks offer sparse gradients and optimizers such as SparseAdam for very large tables. Memory adds up fast: 50,000 x 768 x 4 bytes is about 154 MB in fp32, and recommender tables with hundreds of millions of IDs are sharded across machines.

Many language models tie the input embedding matrix to the output unembedding (Press and Wolf, 2017), saving parameters and often improving perplexity, though large LLMs frequently untie them. padding_idx keeps the padding row fixed at zero. In a transformer, the token embedding is context-free: 'bank' gets one vector whether it means a river or money. Contextual meaning appears only after attention layers mix in the surrounding tokens, which is why mid-layer activations, not raw embeddings, are used for most semantic probing.

The skip-gram objective with negative sampling maximizes log sigmoid(u_o . v_c) + sum over k negatives of log sigmoid(-u_k . v_c), where v_c is the center word's input vector and u_o a context word's output vector. Typical settings: 5-20 negatives for small corpora, 2-5 for large ones, drawn from the unigram distribution raised to the 0.75 power. Very frequent words such as 'the' are randomly subsampled. CBOW is the mirror image: predict the center word from its averaged context.

Levy and Goldberg (2014) showed that skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a shifted pointwise mutual information (PMI) matrix, linking it to classical count-based methods; GloVe factorizes co-occurrence statistics directly. fastText adds character n-grams, so unseen and misspelled words still get vectors. All of these are static: one vector per word type, which blends different senses. Contextual models (ELMo, BERT, LLMs) replaced them for most tasks.

Cosine similarity ignores length and measures only direction. For unit-length vectors, cosine equals the dot product and squared Euclidean distance equals 2 - 2*cos, so all three give the same ranking. This is why many systems normalize once at indexing time and then use the faster dot product.

Scores are model-specific. Many embedding models are anisotropic: their vectors crowd into a narrow cone, so even unrelated texts can score 0.6-0.8 and a fixed threshold like 0.5 means nothing. Calibrate thresholds on labeled pairs for each model. Similarity is also not the same as relevance or agreement: 'I love this phone' and 'I hate this phone' often score high because they share topic and structure. For ranking quality, a cross-encoder reranker that reads the query and document together usually beats raw cosine on the top candidates.

The analogy test (3CosAdd) finds the word whose vector is closest to king - man + woman. The original evaluations excluded the three input words from the answers; without that rule, the nearest vector is often 'king' itself, and reported accuracies drop. Later critiques showed that many analogy successes come from simple nearest-neighbor effects rather than a clean, consistent offset.

The same geometry captures social biases. Bolukbasi et al. (2016) found man : computer programmer :: woman : homemaker in news-trained vectors, and debiasing by projecting out a gender direction removes only part of the effect. The broader idea survives in the linear representation hypothesis: concepts often correspond to directions in a model's activation space. That is what makes linear probes and activation steering work in modern LLMs, which is much richer than the classic king-queen demo.

Sentence-BERT (2019) trained a siamese transformer so pooled outputs could be compared with cosine, making semantic search over millions of sentences fast; cross-encoders are more accurate but must run once per query-document pair. Modern embedders train with a contrastive InfoNCE loss: each query's matching document is the positive and the other documents in the batch are negatives, so larger batches and mined hard negatives help. Many models are asymmetric and expect prefixes or instructions such as 'query:' and 'passage:'.

CLIP (2021) trained on about 400M image-caption pairs with a symmetric cross-entropy over the batch's image-text similarity matrix and a learned temperature. Zero-shot classification follows: embed prompts like 'a photo of a {label}' and pick the closest. Images and texts still occupy partly separate regions of the shared space (the 'modality gap'). Late-interaction models such as ColBERT keep one vector per token for finer matching at higher storage cost.

Exact k-nearest-neighbor search costs O(N * d) per query, fine for thousands of vectors and too slow for hundreds of millions. ANN indexes trade a little recall for big speedups: HNSW builds a layered proximity graph, IVF clusters the vectors and searches only nearby clusters, and product quantization compresses vectors into short codes. Tune for recall@k versus latency and memory; 1M vectors of 1,024 float32 values take about 4 GB before compression.

In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), quality often hinges more on chunking (size, overlap, keeping headings) and metadata filters than on the embedding model. Hybrid search combines keyword scoring (BM25), which catches exact names, codes and rare terms, with embeddings, which catch paraphrases. A reranker then reorders the top 50-100 candidates. Evaluate retrieval on its own with labeled queries (recall@k, nDCG) before judging the full RAG pipeline end to end.

Check yourself: after normalizing to unit length, the dot product equals cosine similarity, so only direction counts. Without normalization, long vectors win; in recommenders that often means popular items, in retrieval it can mean long or generic documents.

More traps. Store the model name and version with every vector and re-embed the corpus whenever the model changes; vectors from different models, or even different versions, live in unrelated spaces. Follow the model's query and document prefix conventions exactly. General-purpose embedders can fail on domain jargon, code or other languages, so test on your own data before trusting a public benchmark such as MTEB. Watch for near-duplicate chunks crowding out the top-k; maximal marginal relevance (MMR) adds diversity. Finally, embeddings can leak sensitive text: inversion attacks can partly reconstruct inputs from their vectors, so protect them like the source data.
deeper.further: Next: contrastive learning theory (alignment and uniformity of representations), Matryoshka embeddings, and binary or int8 quantized vectors for cheap large-scale search. Compare single-vector, multi-vector (ColBERT) and learned sparse (SPLADE) retrieval. Outside text, look at node2vec and knowledge-graph embeddings (TransE), and at how recommendation systems train two-tower models. For evaluation, the BEIR and MTEB benchmarks show how embedders generalize, and where they do not.

pages.title: Generative Models
pages.subtitle: Learn the data, then sample brand-new examples

panels.heading: The Goal
panels.body:
Learn p(x), the distribution of the data.
Then sample: new images, text or audio that look real.
Model families differ in how they learn p(x) and how fast they sample.

panels.heading: Autoencoders & VAEs
panels.body:
Autoencoder: encoder -> small code z -> decoder, trained to rebuild x.
VAE (variational autoencoder): encoder outputs mean mu and std sigma.
Loss = reconstruction + KL pull toward N(0, 1).
Smooth latent space: sample z, decode.

panels.heading: Reparameterization Trick
panels.body:
Random sampling blocks gradients.
Fix: z = mu + sigma * eps, with eps ~ N(0, 1).
Example: mu = 0.5, sigma = 0.2, eps = 1.5 -> z = 0.8.
Randomness lives in eps, so gradients reach mu and sigma.

panels.heading: GANs: Forger vs Detective
panels.body:
GAN (generative adversarial network): generator G turns noise into fakes.
Discriminator D judges real or fake.
G learns to fool D; D learns to catch G.
Sharp but unstable; mode collapse = only a few output types.

panels.heading: Diffusion: Noise, Then Denoise
panels.body:
Forward: add Gaussian noise over T steps (e.g. 1,000) until pure static.
Train a network to predict the noise added at step t.
Generate: start from static, denoise step by step; a text prompt guides it.
Best quality, slower sampling.

panels.heading: Autoregressive Models
panels.body:
p(x) = p(x1) p(x2|x1) p(x3|x1,x2) ...
Predict the next token, sample it, repeat.
Exact likelihood; powers LLMs.
One step per token, so long outputs take many steps.

panels.heading: Compare the Families
panels.body:
VAE: fast sampling, stable, blurrier.
GAN: fast and sharp, unstable training.
Diffusion: top image quality, many steps.
Autoregressive: exact likelihood, slow per token; rules text.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
VAE blur: it averages over uncertain details.
GAN: if D gets too strong, G stops learning.
Low loss is not good samples: check FID (Frechet inception distance) and humans.
Check: all GAN outputs look alike. Name it.

pages.footer: Compress, compete, denoise or predict next: each generator learns p(x) its own way.
pages.summary: The main families of generative models and how each learns to produce new data: autoencoders and VAEs with the reparameterization trick, GANs and mode collapse, diffusion models that learn to remove noise, and autoregressive models, with a side-by-side comparison.

panels:
Families differ in how they treat p(x). Explicit, exact likelihood: autoregressive models and normalizing flows. Approximate likelihood: VAEs maximize a lower bound (the ELBO). Implicit: GANs learn only a sampler, with no density at all. Score-based: diffusion models learn the gradient of log p(x) at different noise levels.

A useful frame is the 'generative learning trilemma': high sample quality, good coverage of all modes (diversity), and fast sampling; classic GANs give quality and speed, VAEs and flows give speed and coverage, and diffusion gives quality and coverage. Most real systems are conditional, p(x | c), where c is a class, a text prompt or another image. Evaluation is hard: likelihood and perceived sample quality can disagree badly, so a model with great log-likelihood may produce poor samples and vice versa. That is why sample-based metrics and human ratings matter.

The VAE maximizes the ELBO: E_q[log p(x | z)] - KL(q(z | x) || p(z)). With a Gaussian encoder and a standard normal prior the KL term has a closed form: 0.5 * sum(mu^2 + sigma^2 - log sigma^2 - 1). Encoders usually predict log sigma^2 for numerical stability. Weighting the KL by beta > 1 (beta-VAE) encourages more disentangled latents at the cost of reconstruction. With a very powerful decoder, the model may ignore z entirely (posterior collapse).

VQ-VAE replaces the Gaussian with a learned codebook of discrete vectors, which suits autoregressive priors over codes. Today autoencoders matter mostly as compressors: latent diffusion encodes a 512x512x3 image into a 64x64x4 latent, so the expensive diffusion model works on 48 times fewer numbers. Plain autoencoders also appear in interpretability as sparse autoencoders that decompose model activations into features.

From Kingma and Welling (2013). With z = mu + sigma * eps, the derivatives are simple: dz/dmu = 1 and dz/dsigma = eps (1.5 in the example). The alternative, the score-function or REINFORCE estimator, works for any distribution but has much higher variance, which is why reparameterization made VAEs practical. It needs a continuous distribution that can be written as a deterministic transform of fixed noise.

For discrete latents, approximations stand in: Gumbel-softmax (a temperature-controlled continuous relaxation of categorical sampling) and straight-through estimators, which use the discrete value forward and pretend it was continuous backward. Predict log sigma and exponentiate to keep sigma positive. The same trick appears outside VAEs: in reinforcement learning with continuous actions (for example soft actor-critic) and in diffusion training, where x_t is written as a deterministic function of the clean image and sampled noise.

Goodfellow et al. (2014) framed training as min over G, max over D of E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 - D(G(z)))]. In practice the generator maximizes log D(G(z)) instead (the non-saturating loss), because early on D rejects fakes easily and log(1 - D) gives almost no gradient. With an optimal discriminator, the original objective measures the Jensen-Shannon divergence between real and generated distributions.

Stabilizers include Wasserstein GANs with a gradient penalty, spectral normalization, two-timescale learning rates and careful architectures. StyleGAN (2019) produced photorealistic 1024x1024 faces. Mode-collapse remedies include minibatch discrimination and unrolled updates. GANs lost the text-to-image race to diffusion but survive as components: adversarial losses make VAE image tokenizers sharp, power super-resolution, and are used to distill multi-step diffusion models into one- to four-step generators.

In DDPM (Ho et al., 2020), the forward process has a closed form: x_t = sqrt(abar_t) * x_0 + sqrt(1 - abar_t) * eps, so training jumps directly to a random t without simulating every step. The loss is simply the mean squared error between the true noise eps and the network's prediction. Song et al. showed this is equivalent to learning the score (gradient of log density) at every noise level, unified as stochastic differential equations.

Classifier-free guidance combines conditional and unconditional predictions, eps_uncond + w * (eps_cond - eps_uncond), with w often 3-8, trading diversity for prompt adherence. Better samplers (DDIM, DPM-Solver) need 20-50 steps instead of 1,000; consistency models and adversarial distillation get to 1-4. Flow matching and rectified flow learn straighter paths from noise to data and are used in many current image models. Backbones moved from U-Nets to diffusion transformers (DiT), and video models apply them to spacetime patches.

The chain rule makes the factorization exact, so autoregressive models report true log-likelihood (and perplexity), unlike VAEs and GANs. Training is parallel: with teacher forcing and a causal mask, every position's next-token loss is computed in one forward pass. Only sampling is sequential, one network pass per token, made cheaper by the KV cache and by speculative decoding, where a small draft model proposes several tokens that the large model verifies at once.

The approach is not limited to text. PixelCNN and ImageGPT generated pixels one by one; later systems first compress images into discrete tokens with a VQ-style tokenizer, then model those tokens with a transformer, which lets one multimodal LLM generate both text and images. Weaknesses: exposure bias, errors that compound over long outputs, and a fixed left-to-right order. Masked and discrete diffusion language models are an active alternative that generates many tokens in parallel.

Normalizing flows complete the picture: invertible networks give exact likelihood and one-pass sampling, but invertibility constrains the architecture and their sample quality fell behind. Rough cost per sample: a GAN needs one network pass; a diffusion model 20-50 (1-4 when distilled); an autoregressive model one pass per token. Likelihood-based and diffusion models tend to cover all modes; GANs tend to drop some.

The best systems are hybrids. Latent diffusion is a VAE for compression plus diffusion in the latent space. VQGAN combines a VQ-VAE, an adversarial loss for sharp decoding, and an autoregressive transformer over the codes. Distilled diffusion models use GAN losses to sample in a few steps. In interviews, expect to justify a choice along four axes: sample quality, diversity, sampling speed, and whether you need likelihoods (for compression, anomaly detection or evaluation), plus how stable and cheap training is.

Check yourself: identical-looking GAN outputs are mode collapse. The generator has found a few outputs that fool the discriminator.

More detail on the traps. VAE blur comes from the Gaussian likelihood, which is equivalent to an MSE loss: when several sharp outputs are plausible, their average minimizes the loss. A discriminator that wins too easily gives the generator near-zero gradients, especially with the original saturating loss. FID compares the mean and covariance of Inception-network features for real and generated images (lower is better); it needs about 10,000-50,000 samples, is biased at small sample sizes, and misses some failures, so pair it with precision/recall-style metrics, CLIP-based text-alignment scores and human review. Another real risk is memorization: diffusion models have been shown to reproduce some training images almost exactly, with privacy and copyright implications, so deduplicate training data and test for regurgitation.
deeper.further: Next: normalizing flows and energy-based models, score-based SDEs and probability-flow ODEs, flow matching and rectified flow, consistency models and diffusion distillation. Study diffusion transformers and latent video models, and discrete or masked diffusion for text. On evaluation, read about precision and recall for generative models and why likelihood and sample quality diverge. Practical topics include classifier-free guidance tuning, watermarking and provenance for generated media, and memorization audits.

pages.title: Classification Metrics
pages.subtitle: Your probe outputs a score. You pick a threshold to turn scores into yes/no. Metrics split into two families by whether they depend on that threshold.

panels.heading: Threshold-Free Metrics — Judge the Representation
panels.body:
AUROC: ELI5 – chance a random positive scores above a random negative. Pro: Threshold-free, balance-invariant, comparable across datasets. Con: Can look too optimistic when positives are rare. Use when: Default for research comparisons: layer sweeps, ablations, transfer. Diagram: ROC curve of TPR (recall) vs FPR, AUROC = 0.85.
AUPRC: ELI5 – similar idea, but only cares about your flagged items. Pro: More honest under heavy imbalance. Con: Baseline shifts with prevalence, so it is not comparable across datasets. Use when: Positives are rare (<5%). Diagram: precision-recall curve, AUPRC = 0.42 against a baseline equal to prevalence (example: 0.02).
TPR @ fixed FPR: ELI5 – if I can only review 1% of traffic, how much do I catch? Pro: Directly answers the deployment question. Con: Only one operating point. Use when: This is the "would this actually ship?" number. Example deployment dashboard at FPR = 1%: FPR (reviewed) 1.00%, TPR (catch rate) 72% — you review 1% of traffic and catch 72% of positives.

panels.heading: Threshold-Dependent Metrics — Judge a Deployed System
panels.body:
Accuracy: ELI5 – % you got right. Pro: Everyone understands it. Con: Misleading under imbalance — you can get 99% by always saying "no". Use when: Balanced classes, casual reporting only.
Precision: ELI5 – of the ones I flagged, how many were real? Pro: Measures false-alarm cost. Con: Ignores what you missed. Use when: False positives are expensive.
Recall (TPR): ELI5 – of the real ones, how many did I catch? Pro: Measures miss cost. Con: Ignores false alarms. Use when: Missing one is expensive.
F1: ELI5 – balance of precision and recall. Pro: One number, standard. Con: Depends on an arbitrary threshold, ignores true negatives, and depends on prevalence. Use when: Reporting a fixed, chosen operating point.
Fβ: ELI5 – F1 with a dial: beta > 1 favors recall, beta < 1 favors precision. Pro: Encodes real cost asymmetry. Con: You now have two knobs to justify. Use when: You can justify the cost ratio.
MCC: ELI5 – correlation between prediction and truth, from −1 to 1. Pro: Uses all four cells of the confusion matrix (TP, FN, FP, TN) and is robust to imbalance. Con: Less familiar to readers.

panels.heading: Decision Rule
panels.body: Comparing models / layers / methods → AUROC (+ AUPRC if imbalanced). Deciding whether to deploy → TPR @ FPR. Reporting a shipped system → precision and recall at your actual threshold, plus the threshold. Claiming the score is a probability → also report calibration (ECE or a reliability plot).

panels.heading: Two Traps
panels.body:
Trap 1: Never report a single accuracy number on imbalanced data. It's the classic way to look good while doing nothing. Example: with 10 actual positives and 9,990 negatives, predicting all negative gives accuracy = 9,990/10,000 = 99.9% — but we caught ZERO positives.
Trap 2: F1 without stating the threshold is unfalsifiable. Always publish the cutoff and how you chose it — ideally on a validation split, never on test.

pages.footer: The golden rule: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. Don't just find patterns. Understand mechanisms.
pages.summary: Explains how to judge a classifier that outputs scores: threshold-free metrics like AUROC and AUPRC compare models, while precision, recall, F1 and friends describe a deployed system at a chosen cutoff — and why plain accuracy misleads when positives are rare.

panels: AUROC equals the probability that a random positive outscores a random negative (ties count half); This is the normalized Mann-Whitney U statistic. It depends only on score ranks, so it says nothing about calibration. Its weakness under rarity comes from the false positive rate, FP/(FP+TN): with a million negatives, an FPR of 1% still means 10,000 false alarms, yet ROC looks excellent. AUPRC (area under precision versus recall) puts those false alarms into the denominator of precision, so it penalizes them; its no-skill baseline is the prevalence, which is why values are not comparable across datasets. Linear interpolation between PR points is misleading (Davis and Goadrich 2006). TPR at fixed FPR needs enough negatives for the FPR to be measured: estimating a 1% FPR within about 0.2 points takes roughly 10,000 negatives.

Several of these metrics are algebraic relatives. F1 = 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN), the harmonic mean of precision and recall; it never mentions TN, so it ignores how many negatives you correctly passed. Fβ = (1+β²)PR/(β²P+R). MCC = (TP·TN - FP·FN)/√((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)) is the Pearson correlation between the binary prediction and truth, and is symmetric under swapping the roles of the classes, unlike F1.

Precision is the metric that moves with prevalence π. By Bayes' rule, precision = TPR·π / (TPR·π + FPR·(1-π)); recall and FPR are properties of the classifier given class-conditional score distributions, but precision also depends on how common positives are. A model with 90% recall and 5% FPR has precision 95% at 50% prevalence but only about 15% at 1% prevalence.

If class-conditional score distributions stay the same at deployment, TPR and FPR carry over but precision does not when prevalence differs, which is why TPR at a fixed FPR is the shippable number.

Calibration answers a different question: when the score says 0.3, do roughly 30% of such cases turn out positive? Expected calibration error bins predictions by confidence and averages the gap between mean confidence and observed frequency, weighted by bin size; it is sensitive to binning, so a reliability plot is more honest. If the score is calibrated and you know the costs, the optimal threshold is t = C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN): when a miss is nine times costlier than a false alarm, flag anything above 0.1.

Check the arithmetic in Trap 1: always predicting negative gives 9,990/10,000 = 99.9% accuracy, precision undefined (0/0), and recall 0. Also note the reverse degenerate classifier: flag everything and recall is 100%, with precision equal to the prevalence. Any single number can be gamed by moving along the threshold, so report the curve or a stated operating point.

Trap 2 compounds with small samples. If the test set holds 10 positives, one more detection moves recall by ten points, and the exact 95% confidence interval for 7 caught out of 10 spans roughly 35% to 93%. Choosing the F1-maximizing threshold on the test set then reports the best of many looks; the threshold must be fixed on validation data before the test set is scored. Report the threshold, its selection rule, the number of positives, and an interval.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: AUROC is not accuracy at the best threshold, a high AUROC does not mean probabilities are trustworthy, and a high AUPRC on one dataset cannot be compared with a lower one on another with different prevalence. For probes and classifiers inside language-model research (the framing of this page), prefer AUROC for comparing representations and TPR at a fixed FPR for deployment decisions. Gotchas: ties in scores, sampling negatives (which changes precision and the PR baseline but not ROC), and averaging metrics across classes (macro versus micro) hide different failures. The next page applies these metrics to heavily imbalanced data, and the debugging page treats a suspiciously high score as a leak until proven otherwise.

pages.title: Imbalanced Class
pages.subtitle: How to evaluate, train, tune thresholds, and avoid traps when positives are rare.

panels.heading: Core Idea — ELI5
panels.body: One class (positives) is rare. Raw accuracy can look great while the model still misses what matters. Toy example of 1,000 cases: 990 negatives, 10 positives. Always predict negative → accuracy = 990/1000 = 99%, but catches 0 of 10 positives = 0 useful catches.

panels.heading: Why Imbalance Is Tricky
panels.body:
Accuracy trap: Majority class dominates the score. High accuracy can still be useless.
Minority gets ignored: Model can "win" by ignoring the rare class and still look great overall.
Calibration drifts: Predicted probabilities may be over/under-confident on the minority class.
Noisy estimates: Few positives = high variance. Scores bounce around a lot.
Choose metrics that reward catching rare positives!

panels.heading: Metrics That Matter (More Than Accuracy)
panels.body:
3.1 Precision = TP / (TP + FP). ELI5: Of predicted positives, how many are actually positive? Pro: Fewer false alarms. Watch out: Can look good by being overly conservative. Use when: False positives are costly.
3.2 Recall (TPR) = TP / (TP + FN). ELI5: Of actual positives, how many did we catch? Pro: Fewer misses. Watch out: Can be high with more false alarms. Use when: Missing positives is costly.
3.3 F1 score = 2 × P × R / (P + R). ELI5: Balance between precision and recall. Pro: Single number summary. Watch out: Hides trade-offs; depends on class imbalance. Use when: Want a balanced trade-off.
3.4 PR-AUC (PR curve): ELI5: Overall ability to find positives without too many false alarms. Pro: Focuses on the positive class. Watch out: Sensitive to prevalence (that's the point!). Use when: Positives are rare. Usually the most informative. Prefer over ROC-AUC when positives are rare.
3.5 Balanced accuracy = (TPR + TNR) / 2. ELI5: Average of recall on both classes. Pro: Treats classes more fairly. Watch out: Still a summary; check the details. Use when: You want a balanced view.
3.6 MCC (Matthews CC): ELI5: Correlation between predictions and truth. Pro: Works for any imbalance; uses all cells. Watch out: Harder to interpret. Use when: You want one robust score. Range: −1 (bad) to 0 (random) to 1 (perfect).
3.7 Confusion matrix (TP, FN, FP, TN): ELI5: The full picture. Pro: Shows where errors come from. Watch out: Counts hide rates — always compute rates too. Use when: Always!

panels.heading: Data-Level Tools (Resample Only Inside Training Fold!)
panels.body:
4.1 Stratified split / stratified CV: Maintain similar class proportions in each split. Pro: Unbiased evaluation. Watch out: With very few positives, use repeated CV for stability.
4.2 Random oversampling: Duplicate minority examples. Pro: Simple, effective. Watch out: Overfitting on duplicates.
4.3 Random undersampling: Remove some majority examples. Pro: Faster models. Watch out: May lose important signal.
4.4 SMOTE / synthetic oversampling: Create synthetic minority examples. Pro: Adds diversity. Watch out: Can make unrealistic points. Tune carefully.
4.5 Minority data augmentation: Domain-specific transforms (e.g., text back-translation, image flips, noise). Pro: Adds variety. Watch out: Don't distort the label or semantics.
NEVER resample before splitting. Do it ONLY inside each training fold. Leakage = fake performance.

panels.heading: Model-Level Tools
panels.body:
5.1 Class weights: Weight the minority class higher in the loss. Pro: Simple, built-in. Watch out: Too high can overcompensate. Use when: First thing to try.
5.2 Focal loss: Focus learning on hard, misclassified examples. Pro: Great for dense imbalance. Watch out: Extra hyperparameter (γ). Use when: Many easy negatives drown signal.
5.3 Threshold tuning: Pick threshold that optimizes your metric. Pro: Huge impact. Watch out: Tune on validation only. Use when: Always before deployment.
5.4 Cost-sensitive learning: Encode business costs (FN vs FP). Pro: Directly matches real-world trade-offs. Watch out: You must know/assume costs. Use when: You know the relative costs.
5.5 Anomaly detection / one-class methods: For extreme rarity when positives are <0.1%. Pro: Model "normal" only; flag deviations. Watch out: Needs known normal data. Use when: Positives are ultra-rare.

panels.heading: How to Choose What to Optimize
panels.body: False negatives costly (misses hurt) → prioritize recall / TPR. False positives costly (alarms hurt) → prioritize precision. You need ranking quality → optimize PR-AUC. Review budget / operating constraint → TPR @ fixed FPR or precision @ top-k. Positives extremely rare → anomaly detection + calibrated thresholding. You know business costs → cost-sensitive learning.

panels.heading: Good Workflow (A Practical Playbook)
panels.body: 1. Define: Define positive class & business costs. 2. Inspect: Check prevalence, leakage sources, data quality. 3. Stratify: Stratified split / stratified CV. Keep test untouched. 4. Baseline: Build simple baseline (e.g., majority or LR). 5. Pick metric: Match metric to goal & deployment constraints. 6. Improve: Try class weights + threshold tuning first. 7. Resample if needed: Use resampling / aug inside training fold only. 8. Inspect errors: Look at FP & FN. Find patterns and subgroups. 9. Calibrate: Calibrate probs (Platt / isotonic) if needed. 10. Report: Report chosen metric + CI/uncertainty. Explain trade-offs. Measure, improve, repeat!

panels.heading: Classic Traps (Avoid These!)
panels.body: Reporting accuracy alone: Looks good, means nothing. Leakage from resampling before split: Synthetic samples leak information. Balanced test set hides true prevalence: Results won't match real-world rates. Duplicates across folds / near-duplicates: Inflates performance artificially. Default 0.5 threshold without tuning: Rarely the right operating point. Perfect score on tiny support: Don't trust tiny numbers. Ignore subgroup fairness & drift: Model may fail for some groups.

panels.heading: Quick Checklist
panels.body: What is the real prevalence? What error (FN or FP) is costlier? Did I stratify the split / CV? Did I resample ONLY inside training folds? Which metric matches deployment? How many positives in validation & test? Did I tune the threshold on validation only? Did I report uncertainty (CI)? Did I check subgroups & calibration?

pages.footer: Don't chase accuracy — match the metric to the real-world cost.
pages.summary: Covers what to do when the thing you care about is rare: why accuracy becomes misleading, which metrics actually reflect performance, and data- and model-level fixes like resampling, class weights and threshold tuning, plus the traps that create fake gains.

panels:
The majority-class baseline scores 1 - π accuracy where π is prevalence, so at π = 1% a model must beat 99% to do anything. A classifier that outputs the base rate for every input is perfectly calibrated and has zero discriminative power.

Imbalance itself is not the main problem; the number of positives is. Estimation error for recall scales with 1/√(n_positive), so a dataset of a million rows with 50 positives is effectively a dataset of 50 for anything positive-related. That is why the toy example (10 positives in 1,000) is fragile: swapping two predictions changes recall by 20 points. Logistic regression also underestimates event probabilities when events are very rare (King and Zeng 2001).

Under imbalance the loss is dominated by negatives: the cheapest way to lower average cross-entropy early is to push every output toward the base rate. A common remedy is to initialize the final bias to the log-odds of the prior, log(π/(1-π)), so training starts calibrated to prevalence rather than wasting steps learning it (the RetinaNet paper uses a related prior initialization).

Calibration drifts mostly because of what you do about imbalance. If you oversample, undersample, or reweight, the model learns probabilities for the altered class mix. Correction is a shift in log-odds: for a model trained with negatives subsampled by a factor, the output odds must be rescaled by that factor (Elkan 2001). Forgetting this gives scores that rank well but whose absolute values, and therefore any probability threshold, are wrong by a large factor.

Link the metrics through the confusion matrix. Precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN), F1 = 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN) (identical to the Dice coefficient). Balanced accuracy is macro-averaged recall, so it equals 0.5 for any constant predictor, unlike plain accuracy.

ROC-AUC is insensitive to prevalence by construction, which sounds like a virtue but means it can look strong while precision is poor. Saito and Rehmsmeier (2015) demonstrated this with simulations and recommended PR plots for imbalanced data. Remember, though, that a PR curve's baseline is the prevalence, so a PR-AUC of 0.30 can be excellent at 1% prevalence and poor at 40%. Normalize a confusion matrix by row (true class) to read recall, by column (predicted class) to read precision.

Resampling before splitting puts copies or near-copies of training points into validation. Do resampling inside each training fold (imbalanced-learn's Pipeline does this); never touch validation or test data, which must keep the real class mix.

SMOTE (Chawla et al. 2002) creates a synthetic point by choosing a minority example x, one of its k nearest minority neighbors x', and sampling x + u(x' - x) with u uniform in [0,1]. It assumes straight lines between minority points stay in minority territory, which fails with categorical features, high dimensions, class overlap and multimodal minorities, where it generates plausible-looking but wrong points. For strong learners such as gradient-boosted trees, practitioners often find class weights and threshold tuning perform as well; test it rather than assuming it helps.

Class weighting multiplies each example's loss; weights inverse to class frequency (n/(2·n_k) in scikit-learn's "balanced") shift the decision boundary in the same way oversampling does, but without duplicating data. Focal loss (Lin et al. 2017, introduced with RetinaNet) is FL = -α(1-p_t)^γ log(p_t), where p_t is the probability assigned to the true class: the (1-p_t)^γ factor shrinks the contribution of easy, confidently correct examples (γ = 2 was their default), so the many easy negatives stop swamping the gradient.

For a calibrated model, moving the threshold is theoretically equivalent to reweighting costs, and Elkan (2001) argued that thresholding is often the simplest correct tool. One-class methods (one-class SVM, Isolation Forest of Liu et al. 2008, autoencoder reconstruction error) model normal data and flag outliers; they assume anomalies look different, not just rarer.

Match the objective to how the system is used. If a human reviews a fixed number of cases, use precision at k (precision among the top k scored items) or TPR at the implied FPR, not a global AUC. If the cost of a miss and of a false alarm are known, minimize expected cost C_FN·FN + C_FP·FP over thresholds and plot cost against threshold: the minimum is your operating point, and its flatness shows how sensitive the choice is. PR-AUC averages over all operating points, including ones you will never use; consider partial AUC or the deployed point.

Also check that prevalence is stable. If positives become more common in production, the precision at a fixed threshold rises without any model change; if the case mix changes, recall may fall.

Some steps hide sub-decisions. Calibration: Platt scaling fits a logistic function (two parameters) to the scores, suited to small calibration sets; isotonic regression fits a free-form monotone step function and needs more data (roughly over a thousand calibration examples is a common guideline) or it overfits (Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana 2005). Calibrate and choose thresholds on data the model did not train on, and keep these two uses separate when positives are few, or use cross-validated predictions.

For uncertainty, a stratified bootstrap (resample positives and negatives separately) gives confidence intervals on recall, precision and AUPRC. For error analysis, slice false negatives and false positives by data source, time, length, subgroup and label confidence, since rare-class errors often cluster in one slice or in mislabeled examples.

The balanced-test-set trap can be computed. Take TPR = 90% and FPR = 5%. On a 50/50 test set, precision = 0.9·0.5 / (0.9·0.5 + 0.05·0.5) = 94.7%. At 1% prevalence, precision = 0.9·0.01 / (0.9·0.01 + 0.05·0.99) = 0.009/0.0585, about 15%: five out of six alerts are false. A balanced test set is fine for ranking models, but any precision, F1 or PPV claim must be recomputed at deployment prevalence using TPR and FPR.

On "perfect score on tiny support": getting 3 of 3 positives right still leaves a 95% lower bound for recall of only about 37% (0.05^(1/3)). Subgroup failures hide inside averages, so compute metrics per slice with intervals; a model can be fine overall and poor for a group that has few positives. Drift changes prevalence, features and labels, so monitor all three.

Turn the checklist numbers into requirements. To estimate recall near 0.8 with a ±5-point 95% interval you need about 1.96²·0.8·0.2/0.05² ≈ 250 positives in the evaluation set. To measure an FPR near 1% within ±0.2 points takes about 9,500 negatives. If you cannot get these counts, say so and widen the claimed uncertainty instead of reporting a point estimate. The positives you have also have to be representative: positives found by an existing system (for example, only items a previous rule flagged) bias the set toward cases that system already catches, and labeling only flagged items hides the false negatives entirely. A cheap remedy is to label a random sample of unflagged items to estimate the miss rate, then weight by sampling fraction.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: imbalance does not automatically require resampling, 0.5 is not a natural threshold, and a higher PR-AUC from a rebalanced test set is not progress. In many cases the best sequence is a strong baseline, class weights or none, calibrated probabilities, then a threshold derived from costs or a review budget. Gotchas: label noise hurts the minority class most, because a handful of mislabeled positives is a large fraction of the class; and monitoring in production needs delayed labels, so build a labeled sampling stream early. This page builds on the classification-metrics and cross-validation pages (stratified and grouped folds), and its final checklist doubles as a leakage audit for the debugging page.

pages.title: Regression Metrics
pages.subtitle: How far off are your numbers, really?

panels.heading: Residuals: The Raw Material
panels.body:
Residual e = y - y_hat (true minus predicted).
Every regression metric summarizes the residuals.

panels.heading: Mae, Mse, Rmse
panels.body:
MAE (mean absolute error) = mean(|e|): typical miss, target units.
MSE (mean squared error) = mean(e^2): punishes big misses.
RMSE = sqrt(MSE): back in target units.
RMSE >= MAE; a big gap = a few large errors.

panels.heading: R-Squared and Adjusted R-Squared
panels.body:
R^2 = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot: share of variance explained.
1 = perfect, 0 = no better than predicting the mean, < 0 = worse.
Adjusted R^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)(n - 1)/(n - p - 1) penalizes extra features.

panels.heading: MAPE Pitfalls
panels.body:
MAPE (mean absolute percentage error) = mean(|e| / |y|) x 100%.
Explodes near y = 0; undefined at y = 0.
Asymmetric: under-forecasts cap at 100%, over-forecasts are unbounded.
Safer: WAPE = sum|e| / sum|y|.

panels.heading: Read the Residual Plot
panels.body:
Plot residuals vs predictions.
Random cloud around 0 = healthy.
Funnel = variance grows with y (try a log target).
Curve = missed nonlinearity.
A few far points = outliers dominating MSE.

panels.heading: Choosing a Metric
panels.body:
Big misses are costly -> RMSE.
Outliers are noise; want the typical miss -> MAE.
Unit-free comparison -> R^2, used with care.
Relative error, y far from 0 -> MAPE or WAPE.
Always show a predict-the-mean baseline.

panels.heading: Pitfalls and Check Yourself
panels.body:
Training R^2 never drops when you add features.
RMSE depends on scale: never compare it across targets.
Q: errors [1, 1, 1, 9]. MAE or RMSE larger?
A: RMSE = 4.6 vs MAE = 3.0.

pages.footer: Look at the residuals first, then pick the number that matches the cost of a miss.
pages.summary: How to measure regression error: MAE, MSE, RMSE and R-squared, why MAPE misbehaves near zero, how to read residual plots, and how to choose the metric that matches the real cost of a miss.

panels:
Residuals are only meaningful on data the model did not fit. Training residuals shrink as capacity grows, so always compute metrics on a validation or test split, or on out-of-fold predictions from cross-validation.

Sign convention matters when you read plots and bias: with e = y - y_hat, a positive mean residual means the model under-predicts on average. For ordinary least squares with an intercept, training residuals sum to exactly zero, so mean bias only shows up on held-out data or within subgroups. Slice residuals by segment (region, price band, time period) because a model can be unbiased overall and systematically wrong for one group. For time series, also plot residuals over time: autocorrelated residuals mean the model is missing temporal structure, and random-split metrics will be optimistic.

MAE, MSE and RMSE are all scale-dependent, so only compare them on the same target in the same units. RMSE always lies between MAE and sqrt(n) x MAE: equality at the low end means every error has the same size; the high end is reached when one error carries everything.

MSE decomposes into bias^2 + variance of the errors, which is why a constant offset raises MSE even if the shape of predictions is perfect. RMSE is not an average of per-example quantities, so it does not decompose across subgroups the way MAE and MSE do: average MSE per group, then take the square root.

Interviewers often ask which metric is optimized by which prediction: the mean minimizes MSE, the median minimizes MAE. Reporting MAE for a model trained to predict the mean is legitimate but can look worse than a median-targeting model.

R^2 = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot compares your model with the constant predictor that outputs the mean of y. On training data with an OLS fit and intercept it lies in [0, 1] and equals the squared correlation between y and y_hat. On test data it can be any value up to 1, and a negative value means the model is worse than predicting the mean. Note that libraries compute SS_tot with the test-set mean, which slightly favors the baseline.

R^2 depends on the variance of the target in the evaluation set: the same model scores higher on a population with a wider range of y. That makes it unreliable for comparing datasets. Adjusted R^2 subtracts a penalty for the number of predictors p, but it is an in-sample correction; for model selection, held-out error or cross-validation is the honest tool.

Work the example by hand once: squaring turns residuals [1, 0, -2, 3] into [1, 0, 4, 9], so the single error of 3 supplies 9 of the 14 units of squared error, 64% of the total. That is the concrete meaning of 'MSE is dominated by large errors'.

RMSE = sqrt(3.5) = 1.87 is larger than MAE = 1.5, and the ratio 1.25 is a quick outlier gauge: a ratio near 1 means uniform errors, a ratio well above 1.5 suggests heavy tails worth inspecting.

SS_tot = 2.25 + 0.25 + 6.25 + 12.25 = 21 is the error of always predicting 4.5. The model removes a third of it, so R^2 = 0.33. With four points, adjusted R^2 for even one feature becomes 1 - 0.67 x 3/2 = 0.0, a reminder of how little tiny samples can support.

MAPE has three structural problems. Division by y makes it undefined at zero and enormous near it, which rules it out for intermittent demand, temperature in Celsius or any target that crosses zero. It is asymmetric: for a fixed actual, under-forecasting can cost at most 100% while over-forecasting is unbounded, so models selected by MAPE are biased low. And averaging per-row percentages weights a 1-unit item the same as a 10,000-unit item.

Alternatives: WAPE (sum of absolute errors divided by sum of actuals) is volume-weighted and stable; sMAPE divides by the average of |y| and |y_hat| but has its own asymmetry and still breaks when both are zero; MASE (mean absolute scaled error) divides MAE by the MAE of a naive seasonal forecast, so values below 1 beat the naive baseline. In retail and supply-chain work WAPE and MASE are the usual defaults.

A residual plot checks the assumptions behind your metric and your loss. Plot residuals against predictions rather than against true y: against y, even a perfect regression-to-the-mean pattern shows a misleading slope.

Patterns and remedies: a funnel (heteroscedasticity) suggests modeling log y, using a relative-error loss, or predicting variance explicitly; a curve means a missing nonlinearity or interaction, so add features or a more flexible model; clusters or stripes often mean a categorical variable the model ignores or a rounded target; a few points with huge residuals deserve inspection for label errors before you switch to a robust loss.

Complement the scatter with a histogram or Q-Q plot of residuals to judge whether tails are Gaussian, and with a calibration-style plot of mean y versus binned predictions to check for systematic bias across the prediction range.

Choosing a metric is choosing a cost function for errors, so start from the decision the predictions feed. If the cost of an error grows faster than linearly, as with capacity planning where a big shortfall causes outages, RMSE matches. If every unit of error costs the same, as with many pricing or time estimates, MAE is the honest summary. If stakeholders think in percentages and the target stays well away from zero, WAPE communicates best.

Always report a baseline: predicting the training mean (or, for time series, last value or same-day-last-week). A model with RMSE 12 means nothing until you know the baseline scores 13 or 40. Report several metrics when audiences differ, but optimize and select on one primary metric chosen in advance. For business decisions with asymmetric costs, consider a custom metric that literally computes expected cost.

On training data, R^2 cannot decrease when a feature is added to an OLS model, because the optimizer can always set the new coefficient to zero. That makes training R^2 useless for feature selection; noise features raise it.

Scale dependence bites in multi-target or multi-dataset reports: averaging RMSE across products with different sales volumes lets the largest products dominate. Normalize first (for example by the target's mean or standard deviation) or use a scaled metric such as MASE.

Other traps: computing metrics on a log scale and reporting them as if they were in original units; leaking future data into time-series validation; evaluating on a test set with a different target distribution than production. For the check question: MAE = (1 + 1 + 1 + 9)/4 = 3, while RMSE = sqrt((1 + 1 + 1 + 81)/4) = sqrt(21) = 4.58. One large error moves RMSE far more.
deeper.further: Learn proper scoring for full predictive distributions: CRPS (continuous ranked probability score) generalizes MAE to probabilistic forecasts, and interval coverage checks whether 90% prediction intervals really contain 90% of outcomes. Conformal prediction gives distribution-free intervals with coverage guarantees. For forecasting specifically, study MASE and the M-competition evaluation protocols, rolling-origin backtesting, and hierarchical reconciliation. Finally, read about heteroscedastic regression, where the model predicts both a mean and a variance, which turns residual-plot diagnosis into part of the model itself.

pages.title: Ranking & Retrieval Metrics
pages.subtitle: Did the right items land at the top?

panels.heading: The Setup
panels.body:
A query returns a ranked list.
Each item is relevant (1) or not (0), or graded (0-3).
k = how many top results you score.
Metrics differ in how much position matters.

panels.heading: Precision@k, Recall@k, Hit Rate
panels.body:
Precision@k = relevant in top k / k.
Recall@k = relevant in top k / all relevant.
Hit rate@k = 1 if any relevant item is in the top k.
All three ignore order inside the top k.

panels.heading: MRR and MAP
panels.body:
MRR (mean reciprocal rank) = mean of 1 / rank of the first relevant item.
AP (average precision) = mean of precision@i at each relevant rank i.
MAP = mean AP over all queries.

panels.heading: NDCG: Graded and Position-Aware
panels.body:
NDCG = normalized discounted cumulative gain.
DCG@k = sum of rel_i / log2(i + 1) for i = 1..k.
NDCG = DCG / IDCG, the DCG of the ideal order; range 0 to 1.
Lower ranks count less.

panels.heading: Offline vs Online
panels.body:
Offline: labeled queries; fast and repeatable, but labels miss new items.
Online: clicks, dwell time, conversions in an A/B test; real but noisy and position-biased.
Confirm offline wins online.

panels.heading: Evaluating RAG Retrieval
panels.body:
RAG = retrieval-augmented generation.
Retriever: recall@k of gold passages (did the evidence reach the context?).
Then MRR or NDCG for ordering.
Grade answer faithfulness separately.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Unjudged items counted as irrelevant underrate new systems.
Averages hide failures on rare queries; inspect per query.
Precision@k is capped when fewer than k items are relevant.
Always state k.

pages.footer: Hits get you into the list; rank decides whether anyone sees them.
pages.summary: How to score ranked results: precision@k, recall@k, hit rate, MRR, MAP and NDCG with one worked list, the gap between offline labels and online behavior, and how to evaluate the retrieval step of a RAG system.

panels:
Ranking evaluation needs three ingredients: a query set that represents real traffic, relevance judgments for the returned items, and a cutoff k that matches what users actually see, such as 10 results on a page or 5 chunks in a RAG context window.

Judgments can be binary or graded (for example 0 irrelevant, 1 partial, 2 good, 3 perfect). Graded labels capture that a perfect answer at rank 1 beats a partial one, but they are more expensive and noisier, so measure inter-annotator agreement. Most offline benchmarks use pooling: only the top results from several systems get judged, and everything else is assumed irrelevant. That assumption is the source of several pitfalls later on.

Report metrics as an average over queries (macro average) so that each information need counts equally, and keep per-query scores for significance tests and error analysis.

Precision@k and recall@k trade off just like classification precision and recall, with k playing the role of the threshold: larger k raises recall and usually lowers precision. Recall@k needs the total number of relevant items per query, which is often unknown in web-scale search; it is natural in RAG and recommendation where a fixed gold set exists.

Hit rate@k (also called success@k or top-k accuracy) is the fraction of queries with at least one relevant item in the top k. It is the right metric when one good result is enough, such as question answering with a single gold passage. With exactly one relevant item per query, hit rate@k equals recall@k.

All three are set-based within the top k: swapping ranks 1 and k does not change them. That makes them stable and easy to explain, but blind to whether the best result is visible without scrolling.

Reciprocal rank is 1/r for the first relevant item at rank r, and 0 if none appears within the cutoff. MRR suits navigational or single-answer tasks: it cares only about the first hit, and moves quickly from rank 1 (1.0) to rank 2 (0.5) to rank 10 (0.1), so it is dominated by the top few positions.

Average precision rewards getting all relevant items early. For each relevant item at rank i, take precision@i, sum them, and divide by the total number of relevant items (not just those retrieved), so missing items count as zero. AP equals the area under the precision-recall curve for that query. MAP averages AP over queries.

Both are binary-relevance metrics. MAP was the standard in TREC-style document retrieval; MRR is common for question answering and code search. Neither handles graded relevance, which is where NDCG comes in.

DCG sums gains discounted by log2(i + 1), so rank 1 gets weight 1, rank 2 gets 0.63, rank 3 gets 0.50 and rank 10 gets 0.29. Two gain functions are common: rel_i itself, or 2^rel - 1, which strongly rewards highly relevant items (a grade 3 is worth 7, a grade 1 is worth 1). Always state which one you use, because scores are not comparable across conventions.

Normalization divides by IDCG, the DCG of the best possible ordering of the judged items for that query, so every query scores between 0 and 1 and averages are meaningful. A subtle choice: compute IDCG from all known relevant items, or only from those retrieved. The first is stricter and standard.

NDCG is the default for web search and recommendation ranking. Its logarithmic discount is a convention rather than a user model, so some teams prefer expected reciprocal rank (ERR) or rank-biased precision with an explicit patience parameter.

Trace each number. Relevant items sit at ranks 2, 3 and 5. Precision@3 = 2/3 and recall@3 = 2 of 3 relevant = 2/3. The first hit is at rank 2, so reciprocal rank = 0.5.

Average precision uses precision at each relevant rank: P@2 = 1/2, P@3 = 2/3, P@5 = 3/5. Their mean is 0.589. Had the same three items appeared at ranks 1 to 3, AP would be 1.0; the empty rank 1 costs a lot.

For NDCG with binary gains, DCG@5 = 1/log2(3) + 1/log2(4) + 1/log2(6) = 0.631 + 0.500 + 0.387 = 1.518. The ideal list puts all three relevant items first: 1 + 0.631 + 0.5 = 2.131. NDCG@5 = 0.712. Notice how the metrics disagree in magnitude: they answer different questions, so pick by user behavior, not by which number looks best.

Offline evaluation is cheap, reproducible and safe, so it is the filter for which candidates reach users. But labels go stale, pooled judgments miss what a new system finds, and offline metrics do not capture presentation, latency or diversity effects.

Online evaluation measures real behavior: click-through rate, time to first click, dwell time, reformulation rate, abandonment, downstream conversion. Clicks are position-biased (users click rank 1 partly because it is rank 1), so raw click logs make the incumbent ranking look good. Counterfactual methods such as inverse propensity weighting correct for this when learning from logs.

Interleaving is a powerful online method for ranking: merge results from systems A and B into one list per user and credit clicks to the source system. It typically needs one to two orders of magnitude less traffic than a classic A/B test to detect the same preference. Agreement between offline NDCG and online wins should be tracked over time.

RAG evaluation splits into retrieval and generation. For retrieval, build a set of questions with known supporting passages and measure recall@k at the k you actually feed the model; a passage that is not retrieved cannot be used. Then measure ordering with MRR or NDCG, because models attend unevenly over long contexts and relevant chunks buried in the middle are used less.

Context precision (what fraction of retrieved chunks are relevant) matters too: irrelevant chunks cost tokens and can distract or mislead the generator.

For generation, grade faithfulness (is every claim supported by the retrieved context?) separately from answer correctness. A correct answer from unsupported parametric memory is a faithfulness failure. LLM-as-a-judge graders are common for both, but validate them against human labels. Chunking, embedding model, hybrid lexical plus vector search and reranking are the usual levers on the retrieval side.

Incomplete judgments are the biggest offline trap. If a new retriever surfaces relevant documents nobody judged, pooled evaluation scores them as misses and penalizes innovation. Remedies: judge the new system's top results before comparing, use metrics robust to missing labels (such as bpref or condensed lists that drop unjudged items), or report the fraction of unjudged items in the top k.

Averaging hides tails: a system can raise mean NDCG while failing badly on rare but important query types. Slice by query category and frequency, and inspect the worst queries.

Cutoff effects: when a query has only two relevant items, precision@10 cannot exceed 0.2, so it mixes system quality with query difficulty. R-precision (precision at R, the number of relevant items) fixes that. Finally, k, gain function and averaging scheme must be reported, and significance should be tested per query with a paired test or bootstrap.
deeper.further: Read about learning to rank (pointwise, pairwise and listwise methods such as LambdaMART) to see how these metrics become training objectives. Study counterfactual evaluation and unbiased learning to rank from click logs, interleaving experiments, and diversity-aware metrics such as alpha-NDCG for result sets that should cover several intents. For RAG specifically, look at reranking with cross-encoders, hybrid BM25 plus dense retrieval, and evaluation frameworks that score context recall, context precision and faithfulness with LLM judges validated against human labels.

pages.title: Calibration
pages.subtitle: When the model says 80%, is it right 80%?

panels.heading: What Calibration Means
panels.body:
Calibrated: among predictions made with confidence p, a fraction p are correct.
Of 100 cases scored 0.8, about 80 should be positive.
Matters when scores drive decisions, costs or abstention.

panels.heading: Reliability Diagram
panels.body:
Bin predictions by confidence (e.g. 10 bins).
Plot mean confidence (x) vs observed accuracy (y).
On the diagonal = calibrated.
Below it = overconfident. Above it = underconfident.

panels.heading: ECE: Expected Calibration Error
panels.body:
