FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022) computes exactly the same result in tiles using an online softmax, never writing the full T×T matrix to GPU main memory, so it is faster mainly by cutting memory traffic, not FLOPs.

Concatenating heads and applying W_O lets later layers mix information found by different heads. Heads often specialize (previous-token, induction, syntax-like patterns), but not uniformly: Michel et al. (2019) found many heads can be pruned at test time with little loss, so head count is not a measure of capability.

The causal mask is implemented by adding minus infinity to the scores above the diagonal before softmax, making those weights exactly zero. Two subtleties: in half precision, a fully masked row (for example a padded query position) yields NaN unless handled, and the mask also means that during training all T positions give a next-token loss in one forward pass. That is the efficiency that makes autoregressive pretraining cheap compared with generation.

The point of GQA and MQA is the KV cache, not FLOPs. Cache size per token per layer is 2 × H_kv × d_head values, so cutting KV heads from h to g shrinks the cache by h/g, which both allows larger batches and reduces the bytes read per decode step (decode is memory-bandwidth bound). Multi-query attention (Shazeer 2019) shares one K/V head across all queries; grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al. 2023) interpolates, and they showed an MHA checkpoint can be converted by averaging K/V heads within groups and briefly continuing training.

A newer alternative is multi-head latent attention (DeepSeek-V2, 2024), which caches a compressed latent vector and reconstructs K and V from it.

Without a cache, generating token T+1 would recompute K and V for all T earlier tokens at every layer, making total work over a generation O(T²) in projections. With the cache, each step computes one new row of Q, K, V per layer and attends over the stored keys: per-step attention cost is O(T·d) rather than O(T²·d). Note that decode remains expensive: each step still streams all model weights and the whole cache from memory, so it is bandwidth-bound.

Cache memory is the practical limit on concurrency. Naive contiguous allocation wastes memory through fragmentation and over-reservation for maximum length; PagedAttention (Kwon et al. 2023, vLLM) stores the cache in fixed-size blocks mapped through a table, like virtual memory, and enables sharing of common prefixes between requests.

RoPE (Su et al. 2021) treats each pair of dimensions in a query or key as a 2D vector and rotates it by an angle p·θ_i, where p is the position and θ_i = base^(-2i/d) with base commonly 10,000, giving a spread of frequencies. Because rotations compose, the dot product between a rotated query at position m and key at position n depends only on m - n, so attention sees relative offsets even though absolute positions were used to rotate.

Beyond training length, high-frequency components see angles never encountered in training, and quality degrades. Extensions rescale positions or frequencies: position interpolation (Chen et al. 2023) compresses positions into the trained range, and NTK-aware and YaRN variants (Peng et al. 2023) scale frequencies non-uniformly; each usually needs some fine-tuning.

The practical difference is where the norm sits relative to the residual path. In post-norm, x_{l+1} = LN(x_l + F(x_l)), so every layer's output passes through a norm and the identity path is not clean; at initialization the gradient scale near the output is large, which is why post-norm needed learning-rate warmup and was fragile at depth (Xiong et al. 2020 analyzed this). In pre-norm, x_{l+1} = x_l + F(LN(x_l)), so the residual stream is an uninterrupted sum and gradients flow directly. Pre-norm typically needs a final norm before the output head, and the stream's norm tends to grow with depth, which can make later layers' contributions relatively smaller.

Most recent LLMs use pre-norm with RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich 2019), which drops mean-centering and rescales by the root mean square only, saving compute with similar quality.

Think of the residual stream as a shared bus of width d_model. Each attention head and MLP reads from it (after normalization), computes something, and writes an additive update back. This view, developed in the mathematical framework for transformer circuits (Elhage et al. 2021), explains several facts: layers can communicate across arbitrary depth without intermediate layers needing to relay information; the gradient has an identity path (the derivative of x_L with respect to x_l includes an identity term), which is why very deep stacks train; and the final residual vector is simply unembedded into logits.

The stream's width is a bottleneck: all information passing between layers must fit in d_model dimensions, so features are stored in superposition (more features than dimensions).

Reasoning through the drill: given B, T, d_model, h, d_head = d_model/h. Storing scores costs B·h·T² elements, which at B=8, h=32, T=8192 in bf16 is 8·32·67M·2 bytes, about 34 GB per layer if materialized, which is exactly why fused kernels exist. A stable softmax subtracts the row maximum before exponentiating; softmax is shift-invariant, so the answer is unchanged, but exp can no longer overflow.

For the mask, the code adds a matrix with minus infinity above the diagonal and zero elsewhere. Common follow-ups: how does the mask change for padding or prefix-LM (bidirectional attention over a prefix)? What changes at decode time (the new query attends to every cached key, so no mask is needed)?
deeper.further: Misconceptions: attention weights are not a faithful explanation of model behavior (a high weight does not mean that token determines the output), the softmax is over keys for each query rather than over queries, and positions are not "added" in RoPE-based models, they are applied inside attention. Gotchas: tensor layout conventions differ between libraries ([B, T, h, d] versus [B, h, T, d]), and bugs often hide in transposes. Connections: the KV cache and GQA here set the memory math on the serving page; the residual stream is the object studied on the interpretability page; pre-norm, RMSNorm and learning-rate warmup connect to the training-stability issues in distributed training.

pages.title: Scaling Laws & Napkin Math
pages.printedTitle: Scaling Laws & Napkin Math Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Parameters, tokens, FLOPs, memory, and utilization

panels.heading: Chinchilla Intuition
panels.body:
Compute-optimal training balances model parameters N and training tokens D. Do not scale parameters alone.
Too many params, too little data → overfitting + wasted compute. Balanced N and D → better generalization + efficient compute.
Rule of thumb (Chinchilla scaling law): D_opt ≈ 20 N (tokens). Total compute ∝ N × D. Keep N and D in balance.

panels.heading: Training Compute (FLOPs)
panels.body:
Training compute scales as FLOPs ≈ 6ND, where N = parameters and D = training tokens.
Derivation (big picture): Forward (2) + Backward (4: 2 for activation gradients, 2 for weight gradients) ≈ 6 FLOPs per parameter per token.
Example: 7B parameters (7 × 10⁹) × 1T tokens (10¹²): FLOPs ≈ 6 × 7 × 10⁹ × 10¹² = 4.2 × 10²².
Compute is the currency. More FLOPs → lower loss (until limited by data / model).

panels.heading: Memory Accounting (Training)
panels.body:
Weights in BF16: Weights ≈ 2N bytes.
Adam optimizer, everything in BF16 (optimistic floor): weights + gradients + m (1st moment) + v (2nd moment) ≈ (1 + 1 + 1 + 1) × 2N = 8N bytes (not counting activations).
Standard mixed precision keeps FP32 master weights and FP32 moments: 2N + 2N + 4N + 4N + 4N = 16N bytes.
Order of magnitude: Training memory (persistent) ≈ 8N–16N bytes. Activations add more (depends on model, seq len, batch size). Rule of thumb: plan for 1.5× – 3× the persistent baseline.
Always check in units (bytes / GB / TB).

panels.heading: Inference: Weights vs KV Cache
panels.body:
Two main memory consumers at inference:
Model weights (static): ≈ 2N bytes (bf16).
KV cache (dynamic): ≈ 2 × L × H × S × d_h × B bytes, where L = layers, H = # attention heads, S = sequence length, d_h = head dimension, B = batch size. Grows linearly with sequence length S (and batch size B).
Which dominates? Short sequences: weights dominate. Long sequences / large batch: KV cache dominates.
Tip: For long contexts, KV cache can exceed weights.

panels.heading: MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization)
panels.body:
MFU = Achieved model FLOPs / Theoretical peak FLOPs.
Why MFU falls (you never hit 100%): Bubble (pipeline flushes) – devices idle during pipeline fill/drain ↓MFU. Communication – all-reduce / all-gather costs time ↓MFU. Memory bandwidth – weights / activations not ready ↓MFU. Small batches / seq – not enough work to keep hardware busy ↓MFU.
Typical MFU: 10%–40% (good); 40%–60% (excellent on large clusters).
Measure it. Improve it. It's the cheapest speedup.

panels.heading: Back-of-the-Envelope Ladder
panels.body:
From napkin to plan.
1. Know parameters (N) → estimate weight memory (bf16): Weight GB ≈ 2N / 10⁹.
2. Know weight GB → estimate GPUs needed (memory): GPUs ≈ weight GB / usable GB per GPU.
3. Know params (N) & tokens (D) → estimate training FLOPs: FLOPs ≈ 6ND.
4. Know peak TFLOPs (system) → estimate total time (seconds): Time ≈ FLOPs / peak FLOPs ÷ MFU.
5. Know seconds → estimate wall-clock time: Hours = seconds / 3600.
Example: N = 7B, D = 1T tokens, peak = 1 PFLOP/s, MFU = 30%. 1) Weight GB ≈ 2 × 7e9 / 1e9 = 14 GB. 2) If GPU has 80 GB HBM usable → GPUs ≈ 14 / 80 → 1 GPU (weights fit). 3) FLOPs ≈ 6 × 7e9 × 1e12 = 4.2e22. 4) Time ≈ 4.2e22 / (1e15 × 0.30) ≈ 1.4e8 s ≈ 1620 days ≈ 4.4 years. 5) With more GPUs, time ∝ 1 / (#GPUs × MFU).
Update any input → recompute the rest.

panels.heading: Scaling Curves & Diminishing Returns
panels.body:
Loss improves with more compute, but with diminishing returns. Diagram: loss vs training compute (10¹⁸ to 10²⁶ FLOPs) — steep gains early, then diminishing returns; gets harder & more expensive.
Frontiers: compute-optimal frontier (more data as compute grows) vs too little data (off frontier). Move the frontier: more data, better algorithms, better architectures.
Key takeaway: Scale both N and D with compute. Blindly scaling N breaks efficiency.

panels.heading: Interview Drill: Napkin Discipline
panels.body: Before you compute, say it out loud. 1. State the goal: What are we estimating and why? 2. List assumptions: Model size, precision, seq len, batch size, MFU, peak hardware, etc. 3. Write the formula: Show your starting equation. Keep it simple. 4. Plug numbers (with units): Convert everything. Don't mix units. 5. Round sanely: 1–2 significant figures is enough. Don't fake precision. 6. Check the order of magnitude: Does the result make sense? If your napkin math is off by 100×, so is your plan. Sense > speed.

pages.footer: Write the units. State the assumptions. Check the order of magnitude.
pages.summary: Teaches quick back-of-the-envelope math for large models: how to balance model size and training data, estimate training compute, memory and run time, and why real hardware never reaches its peak speed.

panels: Hoffmann et al. (2022) fit training loss as L(N, D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β, where E is irreducible loss, with exponents near 0.3 for both. Minimizing under a compute budget C ≈ 6ND leads to N and D growing roughly in proportion, giving the ~20 tokens-per-parameter rule: their 70B-parameter Chinchilla model trained on about 1.4T tokens outperformed the 280B Gopher trained on about 300B tokens using similar compute. This revised earlier guidance (Kaplan et al. 2020) that favored growing parameters faster than data. Compute-optimal here concerns training cost only. If a model will serve large inference volume, a smaller model trained on many more tokens can be cheaper in total (Sardana and Frankle 2023), which is why many deployed models are trained far beyond 20 tokens per parameter.

The 6ND count decomposes as: forward pass 2ND (each parameter does one multiply and one add per token), backward pass 4ND (2ND to get gradients with respect to activations and another 2ND for gradients with respect to weights). The backward pass costs twice the forward pass because it computes two sets of gradients. Sanity check with a known number: GPT-3, 175B parameters on 300B tokens, gives 6 × 1.75e11 × 3e11 ≈ 3.15e23 FLOPs, matching the reported figure of about 3.14e23.

The approximation omits the attention-score computation, which adds a term growing with context length (it matters when context is comparable to model width). For mixture-of-experts models use active parameters per token, not total. With activation checkpointing, the forward pass is repeated, so hardware executes about 8ND while the useful model FLOPs stay 6ND.

The 8N-byte floor assumes weights, gradients and both Adam moments all stored in bf16 (2 bytes each). Standard mixed-precision training is larger: bf16 weights (2) and gradients (2) for compute, plus fp32 master weights (4) and fp32 Adam m and v (4 + 4) for stability, giving 16 bytes per parameter (the accounting used in the ZeRO paper, Rajbhandari et al. 2020). A 70B model then needs about 1.1 TB for persistent state alone, far beyond one GPU, which is why states are sharded: ZeRO stage 1 shards optimizer states across data-parallel ranks, stage 2 also gradients, stage 3 also parameters (the idea behind FSDP).

Activations come on top, scaling with batch × sequence × width. Activation checkpointing stores only layer boundaries and recomputes the rest, trading roughly 33% more compute for large memory savings.

The formula should use KV heads, not attention heads, for H. For a 7B-class model with full multi-head attention (32 layers, 32 heads, head dimension 128), the cache is 2 × 32 × 32 × 128 × 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes, or 0.5 MiB per cached token. Weights are about 14 GB, so cache equals weights at roughly 27,000 cached tokens (summed over all concurrent requests). For 70B with GQA (80 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128) the cache is 320 KiB per token while weights are 140 GB, so the crossover is near 430,000 tokens total.

So "weights dominate" holds at small total tokens in flight, and "cache dominates" at long context or high concurrency; the transition depends on architecture. Levers: GQA or latent attention, cache quantization, and sliding-window attention all shrink it.

MFU, popularized by the PaLM paper (Chowdhery et al. 2022, which reported about 46% for its 540B model on TPU v4), is useful FLOPs divided by peak. Compute it concretely: MFU = (tokens per second × 6N) / (number of GPUs × peak FLOPs per GPU), where peak is the dense figure for the datatype in use (about 990 TFLOPs for H100 bf16, not the sparse figure). Hardware FLOPs utilization (HFU) also counts recomputation, so it is higher than MFU when checkpointing is on.

Good MFU is relative to scale and hardware. Large dense-model runs commonly report somewhere around 30-50%, and above 50-60% is rare. Improving it is mostly systems work: fused kernels and FlashAttention, overlapping communication with compute, larger micro-batches to amortize overheads, balanced pipeline stages to shrink bubbles, and eliminating data-loading stalls.

Notice how the ladder compounds unit conversions. The worked example gives 1.4e8 seconds, about 1,620 days on a single 1 PFLOP/s device at 30% MFU. Spreading over n devices divides the time by n if scaling were perfect: Time ≈ 6ND / (n × peak × MFU), so 1,024 such devices would take roughly 1.4e5 seconds, about 1.6 days. Converting to cost: GPU-hours = 4.2e22 / (1e15 × 0.3 × 3600) ≈ 39,000, which at an assumed $2 per GPU-hour is about $78,000 for the compute of one such run, before experiments, failures and evaluation.

What the ladder omits: restarts and failures at cluster scale (effective goodput below MFU), data pipeline, evaluation, and the many smaller runs used for ablations and scaling-law fits, which commonly cost a large multiple of the final run.

On a log-log plot, loss versus compute looks like a straight line only after subtracting the irreducible term; otherwise the curve flattens toward E. Small-scale runs let you fit the curve and extrapolate: the GPT-4 technical report (2023) stated that final loss was predicted from runs using a tiny fraction of the compute. Extrapolation is risky: exponents shift with data quality, architecture and the range fit, and loss improvements need not map smoothly to capabilities.

Whether capabilities appear "emergently" (Wei et al. 2022) or only look abrupt because of discontinuous metrics (Schaeffer et al. 2023) is debated. Another axis is inference-time compute: sampling more, or reasoning longer, improves some tasks and gives a second scaling dimension (Snell et al. 2024). Better data, algorithms and synthetic data can move the frontier; their limits are not well established.

Napkin discipline is partly about error propagation: relative errors multiply, so several inputs each uncertain by 2x can leave the answer off by 10x or more. Vary the dominant input to get a range, not a point. Know the usual unit traps: bits versus bytes; GB (1e9) versus GiB (2^30, about 7% larger); dense versus sparse peak FLOPs; bf16 versus fp8 peaks (the latter roughly double); total versus active parameters for mixture-of-experts.

Validate against anchors you know: GPT-3 about 3.1e23 FLOPs; a bf16 70B model about 140 GB; a 7B model about 14 GB. If your result for a similar model is wildly different, find the error before presenting. In an interview, narrate: goal, assumptions, formula, numbers with units, result, then a sanity check and what would change it.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: scaling laws are empirical fits, not physical laws; they describe loss on a given data distribution and recipe, not guaranteed downstream abilities. Chinchilla-optimal is not "best" for products with heavy inference. Gotchas: parameters, tokens and FLOPs are quoted inconsistently across papers (including or excluding embeddings, counting epochs or unique tokens), so check definitions before comparing. This page connects to serving (weights versus cache) and to distributed training (what MFU loses to communication and pipeline bubbles).

pages.title: Distributed Training
pages.subtitle: Parallelism, sharding, memory, communication, and OOM debugging

panels.heading: Data Parallelism
panels.body:
Replicate model, split batch, all-reduce gradients. Each GPU holds a model replica, processes its own batch shard (forward + backward), then gradients are all-reduced across GPUs.
+ Simple to use and scale. + Great hardware utilization. − Full model memory on each GPU. − Comm cost grows with model size.

panels.heading: Tensor Parallelism
panels.body:
Split matrices within layer, all-gather / all-reduce. Example: linear layer Y = XW + b with W split by columns (W₀…W₃) across GPUs; each produces a partial output (Y₀…Y₃), combined by all-reduce (sum) into output Y.
+ Handles very wide layers. + Less memory per GPU. − High bandwidth required. − Needs fast all-reduce.

panels.heading: Pipeline Parallelism
panels.body:
Split layers into stages, stream microbatches. Example: stage 0 (L0–L3), stage 1 (L4–L7), stage 2 (L8–L11), stage 3 (L12–L15); microbatches μ0…μ5 flow through a pipeline schedule with forward, backward and bubble (idle) slots.
+ Handles very deep models. + Low memory per stage. − Pipeline bubbles reduce util. − Sensitive to imbalance.

panels.heading: FSDP / ZeRO
panels.body:
Shard optimizer, gradients, and parameters across GPUs in a data parallel group (FSDP full shard). All-gather (before fwd); all-reduce / reduce-scatter (after bwd).
+ Massive memory savings. + Scales to very large models. − More communication. − Complexity / tuning.

panels.heading: Mixed Precision
panels.body:
Use lower precision for compute, higher for stability. Typical dtype flow: FP32 weights (master) → BF16/FP16 weights (model) → BF16/FP16 activations → FP32 gradients (accumulate) → FP32 optimizer update.
Why it works: Lower memory. Higher throughput. Similar accuracy with scaling.
Recommended: bf16 on Ampere+. fp16 on Volta/Turing (with loss scaling). Keep layernorm, softmax in fp32.

panels.heading: Gradient Checkpointing
panels.body:
Store fewer activations, recompute during backward. Without checkpointing: many activations saved (high memory). With checkpointing: fewer activations saved (low memory); recompute segments during backward.
+ Big memory savings. + Enables bigger models/batches. − Extra compute (10–30% typically). − Best to combine with FSDP/ZeRO.

panels.heading: Communication Primitives at a Glance
panels.body:
All-reduce: Sum (or avg) across all ranks; output same as input; used for DP gradients, tensor parallel.
All-gather: Gather from all ranks; output concatenates all inputs; used for TP forward, FSDP params.
Reduce-scatter: Sum then scatter; sharded output; used for DP backward, ZeRO grads.
Broadcast: Send from root to all ranks; same as root; used for params sync, initialization.
P2P send/recv: Point-to-point transfer; custom shape; used for pipeline, topology.
Tip: Overlap communication with compute (use async ops and streams).

panels.heading: Where OOMs Come From (and How to Fix Them)
panels.body:
Weights: Model parameters (incl. buffers); grows with model size. Symptom: OOM even at tiny batch; occurs in forward start. Fix: Use FSDP/ZeRO (shard params), mixed precision (bf16/fp16), or a smaller model.
Optimizer states: States like m, v for Adam/AdamW; grows with model size × #states (AdamW ≈ 8× params in fp32). Symptom: OOM when optimizer step starts. Fix: Use ZeRO/FSDP to shard states, 8-bit optimizers (e.g., 8-bit Adam), or Adafactor / Lion.
Gradients: Parameter gradients; grows with model size. Symptom: OOM in backward near the end. Fix: ZeRO (shard grads), gradient accumulation, mixed precision.
Activations: Intermediate activations saved for backward; grows with batch size × seq len × model depth × hidden size. Symptom: OOM during forward or early backward. Fix: Gradient checkpointing, reduce batch / sequence length, activation offloading.
KV cache: Key/value cache for attention (inference); grows with seq len × layers × heads × head dim (∝ context length). Symptom: OOM at long context (inference). Fix: Reduce max context / sliding window, paged KV cache, quantize KV cache (e.g., 8-bit).
General tools: torch.cuda.memory_summary(), nvidia-smi dmon, PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True, profile memory per stage.
Rule of thumb: If it's saved for backward or lives across steps, it costs memory.

panels.heading: OOM / Training Issues: Debug Tree
panels.body:
A. Forward OOM? Likely activations (or KV). Raise at forward or early backward? Yes → likely activations (or KV cache in inference): reduce batch size, reduce sequence length, gradient checkpointing, activation offloading, mixed precision.
B. Backward OOM? Likely gradients / optimizer. Raises near end of backward or at step? Yes → likely gradients or optimizer states: use FSDP/ZeRO, gradient accumulation, 8-bit optimizer / Adafactor, mixed precision.
C. Only at long context? Likely activations / KV cache. OOM increases with sequence length? Yes → likely activations or KV cache: reduce max context, use sliding window, paged / quantized KV cache, FlashAttention / xFormers.
D. Slow / stalling? Likely communication. Low GPU utilization? High idle time? Yes → likely communication or topology: use faster interconnect, overlap comm & compute, tune collectives / bucket size, check NCCL topology. No → look elsewhere (profile compute, IO, dataloaders).
Quick checklist before you blame memory: Batch too big? Seq len too long? Mixed precision on? Grad checkpointing? FSDP/ZeRO on? 8-bit optimizer? NCCL debug info?

pages.footer: Shard what persists. Checkpoint what recomputes. Profile what stalls.
pages.summary: Explains how big models are trained across many GPUs by splitting the data, the layers, or the weight matrices, how sharding, mixed precision and checkpointing save memory, and how to track down out-of-memory errors and slowdowns.

panels:
Every replica starts from identical weights and sees a different slice of the batch, so averaging gradients reproduces large-batch SGD exactly (up to floating-point order). A ring all-reduce moves about 2(n-1)/n times the gradient size per GPU, which is nearly independent of the number of GPUs n; so communication time depends on model size and link bandwidth, not on how many replicas you add. Frameworks hide latency by grouping gradients into buckets and starting all-reduce during the backward pass while earlier layers are still computing.

The effective batch size is per-GPU batch × GPUs × gradient-accumulation steps, so scaling out changes the optimization problem and usually requires adjusting the learning rate and warmup. The main limit is memory: every GPU holds full weights, gradients and optimizer states, which is what sharding (FSDP/ZeRO) addresses.

Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al. 2019) splits a transformer's matrices so that communication occurs only at fixed points. In an MLP the first linear layer is split by columns, so each GPU computes its own slice of the hidden activations independently (the elementwise nonlinearity needs no communication); the second layer is split by rows, producing partial sums that one all-reduce adds. So each transformer layer needs two all-reduces in the forward pass and two in the backward pass, on activation-sized tensors, directly on the critical path.

Note the distinction behind the panel's example: a column-split output is concatenated (all-gather), whereas a row-split output is summed (all-reduce). Because of the frequent, latency-sensitive communication, tensor parallelism is normally kept within one node over NVLink-class links, commonly degree 2 to 8, rather than across slower inter-node networks.

GPipe (Huang et al. 2019) splits a minibatch into m microbatches and p layer groups. In the simple schedule, each stage idles while the pipeline fills and drains, giving a bubble fraction (p-1)/(m+p-1); for the panel's p=4 and m=6 that is 3/9, about 33%, so you want m much larger than p. The 1F1B schedule (PipeDream-style; Narayanan et al. 2021 for the Megatron version) alternates one forward and one backward per stage, which does not shrink the bubble but limits how many microbatches' activations must be stored, cutting peak memory; interleaved schedules assign several smaller chunks per device to shrink the bubble further at the price of more communication.

Pipeline traffic is point-to-point activations between neighboring stages, small compared with TP all-reduces, so it tolerates slower links and is the usual choice for cross-node splits.

ZeRO (Rajbhandari et al. 2020) removes the redundancy in data parallelism in stages: stage 1 shards optimizer states, stage 2 also gradients, stage 3 also parameters. With the 16-bytes-per-parameter accounting of mixed-precision Adam, per-GPU persistent memory falls from 16Ψ toward 16Ψ/N across N data-parallel ranks. FSDP is PyTorch's implementation of the stage-3 idea: each layer's parameters are all-gathered just before use in forward, freed after, gathered again for backward, and the gradients are reduce-scattered so each rank keeps only its shard. Communication is about 1.5x that of plain data parallelism (three collectives of size Ψ versus all-reduce's two-equivalent), which is hidden by prefetching the next layer's parameters during the current layer's compute.

Tuning knobs: wrap granularity (per transformer block), prefetch, and hybrid sharding (shard within a node, replicate across nodes) to keep all-gathers on fast links.

bf16 has 8 exponent bits (the same range as fp32) but only 8 bits of significand precision, about 2-3 decimal digits; fp16 has 5 exponent bits (max 65,504) and 11 bits of significand precision. fp16 therefore needs loss scaling (multiply the loss so small gradients do not underflow, then unscale, skipping steps on overflow), while bf16 usually does not. Master weights in fp32 matter because an update such as learning rate × gradient may be 1e-5 relative to a weight of magnitude 1e-2, which a low-precision weight would round away.

FP8 training exists (Micikevicius et al. 2022 proposed the formats; DeepSeek-V3, 2024, reported using it at scale), with finer-grained scaling factors; it is newer and less standardized, so treat recipes carefully.

Activation checkpointing (Chen et al. 2016) saves only certain layer inputs and recomputes the others during backward. Storing a checkpoint every √L layers gives roughly O(√L) activation memory for L layers at the cost of one extra forward pass, i.e. up to ~33% more total compute (a forward is about a third of a training step), consistent with the panel's 10-30% when only part of the model is recomputed. Selective recomputation (Korthikanti et al. 2022) recomputes just the cheap-to-recompute but memory-heavy parts, such as attention internals, retaining most of the savings for a few percent overhead.

It interacts with randomness (dropout must use the same masks in recomputation, which frameworks handle by saving RNG state) and with MFU accounting, since recomputed FLOPs count as hardware FLOPs but not useful model FLOPs.

Useful identity: all-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather. In a ring algorithm with data size S on n ranks, reduce-scatter and all-gather each move (n-1)/n × S per rank, so all-reduce moves about 2S. FSDP replaces DDP's single all-reduce of gradients with two all-gathers of parameters and one reduce-scatter of gradients, hence the 1.5x traffic. Reduce-scatter leaves each rank with its own shard of the summed result, which is exactly what sharded optimizers need.

All-to-all, where every rank sends a different chunk to every other rank, is the primitive behind mixture-of-experts routing (expert parallelism) and sequence parallel schemes. Real bandwidth depends on topology: GPUs in a node connected by NVLink get several times the bandwidth of the network between nodes, so parallelism dimensions are mapped accordingly (tensor parallel within the node, data or pipeline across nodes).

Persistent state in mixed-precision Adam is about 16 bytes per parameter (bf16 weights 2 + bf16 gradients 2 + fp32 master weights 4 + fp32 m and v 8), of which the panel's "8 bytes" is just the moments. Activations for a transformer layer in 16-bit are roughly s·b·h·(34 + 5·a·s/h) bytes (Korthikanti et al. 2022), with sequence length s, batch b, hidden size h and a heads; the quadratic term disappears with fused attention kernels like FlashAttention.

One often-forgotten consumer is the logits: batch × sequence × vocabulary in fp32, for 8 × 4,096 tokens and a 128K vocabulary, is about 17 GB, so large-vocabulary models chunk the loss computation. Peaks also occur in the optimizer step or when the longest sequence arrives, so a late OOM is often just the longest batch.

First reproduce at small scale: a smaller model or fewer GPUs, so you can bisect. Use a memory timeline to see which phase peaks: forward end, backward start, or optimizer step, mapping directly to the panel's A and B branches. For OOM that appears late, suspect a leak: storing tensors that retain the autograd graph (accumulating loss without .item() or detach()), or caches growing with variable shapes.

For slowness, measure rather than guess: compute MFU, then use a profiler (PyTorch profiler or Nsight Systems) to see kernel gaps, communication wait, and data-loader stalls. One slow rank (a straggler) stalls every collective; compare per-rank step times. Hangs usually come from ranks that disagree about the next collective (different control flow or uneven data), or failing nodes; set NCCL debug logging and timeouts.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: more GPUs do not guarantee proportional speedup (communication and bubbles take their share), FSDP is not model parallelism in the layer-splitting sense (it is sharded data parallelism), and bigger micro-batches are not always better because they hurt pipeline balance and memory. Large runs combine strategies: data parallelism across the cluster, tensor parallelism inside nodes, pipeline parallelism across nodes, and sharded states, a configuration often called 3D parallelism. Gotchas: numerical nondeterminism across parallel layouts, and loss spikes that need clipping, skip-batch or restart logic. This page ties to the scaling-laws page (MFU, memory accounting) and the serving page (tensor parallelism and cache reappear at inference).

pages.title: Post-Training & Alignment
pages.subtitle: From SFT to preferences, reinforcement learning, and Constitutional AI

panels.heading: The Post-Training & Alignment Pipeline
panels.body: Pretraining: Learn general world knowledge at scale. → SFT: Supervised fine-tuning on high-quality demonstrations. → Preference data / reward model: Collect preferences & learn a reward model. → RLHF / PPO or DPO: Optimize behavior using preferences (choose method). → Safety & eval loop: Evaluate, red-team, monitor, and iterate (feeding back into earlier stages).

panels.heading: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
panels.body: Imitate high-quality demonstrations. Teaches format, style, and domain skills. Strong initialization for alignment. Not enough: can still be unhelpful, biased, or unsafe. Diagram: Prompt (instruction) → SFT model → Response (gold).

panels.heading: Reward Model (Preference Modeling)
panels.body:
Pairwise preference data: For a prompt, the labeler compares two responses (e.g., prefers A over B, or C over D).
Bradley-Terry intuition: P(A ≻ B) = e^r(A) / (e^r(A) + e^r(B)). Model predicts a scalar reward r(x). Higher reward = more preferred.
Labeler bias matters: Inconsistent labels; cultural & style bias; position bias (A vs B order); malicious or low-effort labels. → Aggregate & sanity-check.

panels.heading: RLHF with PPO
panels.body:
Optimize reward while staying close to the reference (SFT) policy.
Objective (simplified): max_θ E_{x~D, y~π_θ}[r_φ(x, y)] − β KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref), where r_φ(x, y) = reward model score, π_θ = policy being optimized, π_ref = reference (SFT) policy, β = KL penalty coefficient.
PPO loop: 1. Collect rollouts with π_θ_old. 2. Score with reward model r_φ. 3. Compute advantages. 4. Update policy with PPO. 5. Repeat & monitor KL.
Reward hacking is real: The model can learn to exploit the reward model instead of being truly helpful. Mitigation: Stronger reward model & evals; KL regularization; diverse prompts & red-teaming.

panels.heading: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)
panels.body:
Train the policy directly from preferences — no explicit reward model. Training signal: for a prompt, a chosen (preferred) and a rejected (dispreferred) response.
DPO objective (intuition): max_θ E[log σ(β · (log π_θ(y⁺|x) − log π_θ(y⁻|x)))] − λ KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref), where y⁺ = chosen response, y⁻ = rejected response, π_θ = policy being optimized, β = inverse temperature, λ = KL penalty (optional).
Why DPO? Fewer moving parts. No reward model training. Often more stable & data-efficient.

panels.heading: RLAIF (AI Feedback)
panels.body:
Use AI to generate critiques or preferences at scale. AI critic / judge: consistency, explainability, criteria, rubric. Outputs: pairwise prefs, scores, critiques, rewrites. Benefits: massive scale, fast iteration, fits long-tail cases.
Caveats: Model biases amplify at scale. Overconfidence & hallucinated critique. Distribution shift in judge. Still need human audit.

panels.heading: Constitutional AI
panels.body:
Make values explicit, teach the model to critique & improve itself. Principles (constitution): Write clear, actionable principles. → Supervised critique & revision (SFT stage): Generate critiques & improved revisions. → AI feedback reinforcement (preference/RL): Optimize for helpful, harmless, honest behavior. → Transparency & oversight: Document values, report evals, invite audit.
Goal: Behave according to transparent, human-readable values. Example principles: Do not cause harm. Be honest & non-deceptive. Protect privacy & security. Be fair & impartial. Respect human autonomy.

panels.heading: At a Glance: Interview Comparison
panels.body:
What it optimizes — SFT: imitation of demonstrations. PPO/RLHF: reward (via reward model) with KL constraint to reference. DPO: preference likelihood (chosen over rejected) with optional KL to reference.
Typical data — SFT: prompt → response (gold). PPO/RLHF: prompts + model rollouts + pairwise preferences. DPO: prompts + (chosen, rejected) pairwise preferences.
Key components — SFT: dataset → model. PPO/RLHF: reward model + PPO optimizer + reference (SFT). DPO: preference pairs + policy (update) + reference (optional).
Moving parts — SFT: low. PPO/RLHF: high. DPO: medium.
Strengths — SFT: simple, stable, cheap; great initialization. PPO/RLHF: very flexible; can optimize complex objectives & constraints. DPO: simpler than RLHF; often more stable and data-efficient.
Failure modes — SFT: poor generalization; copies biases & bad patterns. PPO/RLHF: reward hacking, KL drift, fragile optimization, hard to debug. DPO: pref noise hurts; over-regularization; may underfit nuances.
Best use — SFT: teach skills, format, and basic helpfulness. PPO/RLHF: when you need fine control, constraints, or tooling integration. DPO: strong baseline for preferences with fewer components.

pages.footer: Optimize what you measure — then audit what you missed.
pages.summary: Walks through how a pretrained model is shaped into a helpful, safe assistant: supervised fine-tuning on good examples, learning from human or AI preferences via reward models with PPO or directly with DPO, and Constitutional AI's approach of training against written principles.

panels:
Each stage changes what the model is optimized for. Pretraining minimizes next-token cross-entropy over trillions of tokens and produces a model that continues text, not one that follows instructions. Post-training is much cheaper in tokens, and a surprising amount of conversational behavior comes from small, carefully curated data: the LIMA study (Zhou et al. 2023) reached strong chat quality with about 1,000 curated examples, motivating the "superficial alignment" hypothesis that most knowledge is learned in pretraining and post-training mainly teaches style and format.

Since 2024, a major additional branch is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (math answers checked, code run against tests), as in DeepSeek-R1 (2025) using GRPO (a PPO variant without a value network), which replaces the learned reward model with programmatic checks wherever one exists.

Mechanically, SFT is next-token cross-entropy on (prompt, response) pairs formatted with a chat template, with the loss usually computed only on response tokens (prompt tokens are masked). Because it only imitates, its ceiling is the demonstrators: it cannot teach the model to be better than the examples, and it penalizes any valid answer that differs from the reference wording.

A subtle failure: if demonstrations contain facts the base model does not know, SFT can teach it to produce confident-sounding claims anyway, which is one proposed source of hallucination; Gekhman et al. (2024) reported that fine-tuning on unknown facts is learned slowly and increases hallucination, though conclusions depend on setup. SFT is also the reference policy for later KL penalties, so a weak SFT model limits everything downstream.

The reward model is typically the SFT language model with its output head replaced by a scalar head read at the final token. Training minimizes -log σ(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)), where y_w is the preferred response: this is the Bradley-Terry model (1952), which implies P(A ≻ B) = σ(r(A) - r(B)), the same as the panel's ratio of exponentials. Only reward differences are identified, so the reward is usually normalized before RL.

The reward model is a lossy proxy for human preference. Known artifacts include a preference for longer responses (length bias), for confident or flattering tone, and sensitivity to position and formatting. Sharma et al. (2023) showed that preference data and trained preference models can reward agreeing with the user's stated views, one root of sycophancy.

Structure of the objective: the per-token KL penalty is folded into the reward, and the KL-regularized problem has a closed-form optimum, π*(y|x) ∝ π_ref(y|x) · exp(r(x, y)/β). PPO (Schulman et al. 2017) optimizes this with a clipped surrogate, min(ρ·A, clip(ρ, 1-ε, 1+ε)·A), where ρ is the new-to-old probability ratio and A the advantage estimated with a learned value function. In memory this means up to four models: policy, reference, reward model and value network, which is why PPO RLHF is expensive and finicky.

Reward hacking is quantifiable: Gao et al. (2023) showed that as the policy drifts further (in KL) from the reference, the proxy reward keeps rising while a held-out "gold" reward eventually falls. Monitor KL, response length and fresh independent evaluation, not just training reward.

The panel's formula is the intuition; the actual DPO loss (Rafailov et al. 2023) is -log σ(β [log(π_θ(y⁺|x)/π_ref(y⁺|x)) - log(π_θ(y⁻|x)/π_ref(y⁻|x))]). It comes from rearranging the KL-regularized optimum to write the reward as r = β log(π_θ/π_ref) + a prompt-dependent constant, then substituting into the Bradley-Terry likelihood, where the constant cancels. So DPO is a classification loss on an implicit reward with KL control built in; larger β holds the policy closer to the reference.

Because it trains on a fixed dataset of pairs, DPO is offline: responses were generated by some other model, so there is a distribution mismatch with the current policy. Documented quirks include both chosen and rejected likelihoods decreasing during training, and a tendency to lengthen responses. Whether online PPO-style RL or DPO is better remains unsettled and depends on data, tuning effort and task.

RLAIF replaces human labelers with a model that applies a rubric. Evidence is encouraging but conditional: Lee et al. (2023) found AI-feedback RL comparable to human-feedback RL on summarization and helpfulness tasks, and Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022) used AI labels for harmlessness. The key risk is correlated error: the judge's blind spots (including the biases in the evaluation chapter, such as position and length bias) get amplified, since the policy is optimized against them.

Design defenses: write explicit rubrics with examples; ask for a critique before the verdict; randomize presentation order; use a judge stronger than or independent of the policy; and validate the judge against a human-labeled sample by measuring agreement per category, since overall agreement hides weak slices. Keep human evaluation as the final audit; any fixed AI judge will eventually be exploited.

Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022) has two stages. In the supervised stage, the model answers red-team prompts, then critiques its own answer against a randomly drawn principle and writes a revision; the revised responses become SFT data. In the RL stage, an AI labeler chooses which of two responses better satisfies a principle (often with a chain-of-thought rationale), those AI preferences train a preference model for harmlessness (combined with human preferences for helpfulness), and the policy is optimized against it.

The advantage is transparency and scalability: behavior is steered by readable text that can be audited and edited. Limits: the principles are only as good as the model's ability to interpret and apply them, vague principles conflict, and who writes the constitution is a governance question.

Choosing among methods is mostly a question of what feedback you have. SFT needs demonstrations. DPO needs pairs and is the cheapest way to use them, so it is a common baseline. PPO-style RL needs a reward signal that can score fresh samples (a learned reward model, or a programmatic verifier), and its on-policy exploration can find behaviors absent from any dataset, which is why it dominates for tasks with checkable answers.

None solves the underlying problem that the training signal is a proxy. Failure modes to name: reward hacking (the policy exploits proxy flaws), mode collapse and reduced output diversity (sometimes called the alignment tax), sycophancy, over-refusal from over-weighted safety data, and verbosity. Evaluate with win-rate against a baseline alongside KL or length, and hold out data from the preference distribution.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: RLHF does not teach new knowledge so much as steer existing capability; alignment is not a one-time stage but a loop of data, optimization and evaluation; and the KL penalty is not a safety guarantee, only a trust region around the reference. DPO is not RL, though it optimizes the same regularized objective in closed form. Gotchas: preference data quality dominates algorithm choice; always compare against a strong SFT baseline; and watch for length growth as a hidden objective. This page connects to the evaluation page (judge biases, human agreement), to safety (red-teaming data feeds the loop) and to agents (RL with tool use and verifiable rewards is how many agentic behaviors are now trained).

pages.title: Mechanistic Interpretability
pages.subtitle: Features, circuits, superposition, and causal interventions

panels.heading: Superposition: More Features Than Dimensions
panels.body:
Model representations compress many features into fewer dimensions. Features mix (superpose) and interfere. In the high-dimension feature space, many true features exist and each feature is a direction; compression (model layers) maps them into a low-dimension model space with fewer dimensions, where features add, cancel, and interfere.
Interference examples: Constructive – signals add → stronger activation. Destructive – signals cancel → weaker or zero activation. Ambiguous – harder to disentangle → mixed meaning.
Superposition makes interpretation hard — but structure still exists.

panels.heading: Sparse Autoencoders
panels.body:
Learn a feature dictionary that explains activations with a sparse set of features. Activation x (from model) → encoder (E) → sparse feature activations a (few non-zeros) → decoder (D) → reconstruction x̂ (≈ original).
Feature dictionary (learned): f₁ detects numbers, f₂ end of line, f₃ quotes, … JSON keys, fₖ names of people. Neurons (uninterpretable): n₁ … nₖ have unclear meanings.
Sparse AEs separate meaning (features) from mechanism (neurons).

panels.heading: Induction Heads: Copy from Previous Occurrence
panels.body:
Learn the pattern "A B … A" → predict "B". Example sequence of tokens: The chef cooked pasta . The chef …
The induction head copies the value from the previous occurrence of "The": query (at pos 6) → attend back (find match) → copy value "chef" (from pos 1) → predict next "chef" (at pos 7).
How it works: 1. Build query from current token. 2. Attend over previous keys. 3. Peak at best match (pos 1). 4. Read value from match.
Induction heads implement in-context learning via pattern copying.

panels.heading: Circuits: Connected Features Implement Computation
panels.body:
Computation emerges from features (or heads) working together across layers. Diagram: information flows from layer 0 (input) through features and attention heads in layers 3, 7 and 12 to the output logits.
A circuit is a path or subgraph whose activity causally affects the output.

panels.heading: Activation Patching: Test Causal Contribution
panels.body:
Replace an activation with a clean value and measure effect. Clean run (reference) gives a layer ℓ activation x_clean; corrupt run gives degraded output.
Patch experiment: In the corrupt run, replace x_corrupt with the clean value → patched activation → measure change.
Significant improvement: activation is causally useful. No improvement: activation likely not causally important (or redundant).
Patch one thing at a time. Measure the difference.

panels.heading: Activation Steering: Add a Direction
panels.body:
Add a vector during inference to steer behavior. Base activation xˡ (at layer ℓ) + steering direction d (meaningful direction) = steered activation xˡ_steered.
Effects: Shift model toward a concept or style. Increase/decrease a behavior. Useful for probing and control. (Steering strength λ ranges from −λ to +λ.)
Risks: Off-manifold behavior. Degraded reasoning. Shortcut exploitation. Unintended side effects.
Steering is powerful — use small steps and evaluate carefully.

panels.heading: Correlation vs Causation Ladder
panels.body:
Climb from observation to intervention to behavioral impact.
Observe (correlation): See a pattern in the data or model. Example: feature F correlates with output Y.
Ablate (should cause): Remove or suppress F. Does Y change? Example: zero out F and compare outputs.
Patch (local causal test): Replace F (or activation) with clean value. Example: activation patching at layer ℓ.
Intervene (causal manipulation): Actively change F or its upstream cause. Example: steering, editing, or counterfactual input.
Evaluate behavior (downstream impact): Measure real task performance. Example: accuracy, win rate, helpfulness, safety.
Higher rungs give stronger evidence of causality.

panels.heading: Interview Takeaways
panels.body:
Keep these principles front and center. Interpretability is empirical reverse engineering: we don't assume meaning — we discover it through systematic tests. Avoid anthropomorphism: features are not beliefs or intentions; they are patterns in activations. Validate out-of-distribution: check generalization, robustness, and failure modes beyond the training distribution.
Good practice checklist: Form a hypothesis. Design a clean test. Control confounders. Replicate results. Report uncertainty. Share methods & data.

pages.footer: Find a pattern. Test a cause. Verify the behavior.
pages.summary: An introduction to reverse-engineering what happens inside neural networks: how models pack many concepts into few dimensions, how sparse autoencoders pull those concepts apart, and how patching and steering experiments test whether a part of the network actually causes a behavior.

panels: The superposition hypothesis (Elhage et al. 2022, "Toy Models of Superposition") says a network can represent more features than it has dimensions by assigning features to nearly orthogonal directions rather than orthogonal axes. In n dimensions you can fit far more than n directions whose pairwise overlaps are small. The price is interference: reading out feature i by projecting onto its direction also picks up small contributions from other active features. This is tolerable only when features are sparse, meaning rarely active together, and a nonlinearity such as ReLU can then filter the noise. The consequence is polysemantic neurons, single units that respond to several unrelated features, because features are not aligned with the neuron basis. Whether real LLMs follow this picture closely is supported by evidence but not settled.

A sparse autoencoder (SAE) is trained on a model's activations x (dimension d_model) to reconstruct them through a much wider hidden layer: a = ReLU(W_enc x + b), x̂ = W_dec a, with loss ||x - x̂||² + λ||a||₁. The L1 term pushes most entries of a to zero, so each activation is explained by a few dictionary directions (columns of W_dec). Bricken et al. (2023) and Cunningham et al. (2023) showed interpretable features on small models, and Templeton et al. (2024) scaled the approach to a production Claude model. Caveats: reconstruction is imperfect (substituting the SAE output raises loss), features can split or merge as dictionary size changes, and interpretability of a feature is judged by humans or automated explanations. Whether SAE features are the model's "true" units is open.

Induction heads (Olsson et al. 2022) are a two-head circuit. A previous-token head in an earlier layer writes "my previous token was X" into each position's residual stream. An induction head in a later layer then forms its query from the current token A, matches it against those stored previous-token keys (K-composition) to find earlier positions that followed an A, attends to the token that came after, and copies it forward, boosting B. Note that it attends to the token after the earlier match, as in the panel's example where it attends to "chef".

The notable evidence is developmental: induction heads form at a sharp point early in training that coincides with a visible bump in the loss curve and a jump in in-context learning ability, and ablating them hurts in-context learning in small models.

A circuit (Olah et al. 2020) is a subgraph of the network, components plus the connections between them, that implements a behavior. A well-studied case is indirect-object identification in GPT-2 small (Wang et al. 2022), where about two dozen attention heads in several functional classes (finding repeated names, inhibiting the repeated name, moving the remaining name to the output) jointly explain a behavior such as completing "John and Mary went to the store; John gave a drink to ..." with "Mary". Automated discovery, such as ACDC (Conmy et al. 2023), prunes edges that do not affect a metric. Pitfalls: circuits are found on a narrow task distribution, models contain backup components that take over when one is ablated (the hydra effect, McGrath et al. 2023), and mapping a whole large model remains hard.

Denoising patching runs the corrupted input and inserts a clean activation at one site; recovery of the clean output shows that site is sufficient to carry the needed information. Noising patching does the reverse (insert corrupt activations into a clean run), testing necessity. The two can disagree when circuits have redundancy: a necessary-looking component may be replaceable, and a sufficient one may not be necessary. Effects are typically measured with a metric like logit difference between correct and incorrect answers, normalized so 0 is the corrupted and 1 the clean value.

Design choices matter (Zhang and Nanda 2023 discuss best practices): how corrupted inputs are made (swapping a name versus adding noise), which metric is used, and whether patched activations are off-distribution. Patching shows where information matters, not alone what it means.

Steering adds a vector at chosen layers during the forward pass: x' = x + λd. A direction d is commonly built from a difference of mean activations between contrasting prompts (activation addition, Turner et al. 2023; contrastive activation addition, Rimsky et al. 2023; representation engineering, Zou et al. 2023), or from an SAE feature, as in the "Golden Gate Claude" demonstration (Anthropic 2024), where amplifying one feature made the model keep bringing up the bridge. The opposite operation is also informative: Arditi et al. (2024) found that refusal behavior in several open chat models is largely mediated by one direction, and removing it disables refusals, which also means refusal can be fragile.

Practice: sweep the layer and coefficient; effect is typically non-monotonic, with too large a λ producing incoherent text.

Treat the rungs as increasing evidence about different claims. Correlation (a probe or a feature that tracks Y) shows information is present, not that the model uses it: Hewitt and Liang (2019) showed that powerful probes can decode properties from representations through their own capacity, which motivated control tasks. Ablation tests necessity but depends on what you replace the activation with: zero ablation can push the model off-distribution; mean ablation and resample ablation (substituting activations from other inputs) are less disruptive but not neutral. Even a successful intervention may not mean the model uses the direction naturally; it may only be a lever. Interpretability illusions are documented (Bolukbasi et al. 2021 found that subspaces that look meaningful on one dataset behaved differently on others), so replicate across data.

"Empirical reverse engineering" means each claim should have a prediction that could fail. Strong evidence typically combines several methods agreeing: a feature found by SAE, whose ablation changes behavior as predicted, whose steering does the opposite, and which holds on held-out data. Run sanity checks for the method itself: Adebayo et al. (2018) showed that some popular saliency maps barely change when the model's weights are randomized, so appealing pictures need a null test. Avoid anthropomorphic shorthand such as "the model wants" or "believes": a feature is a direction that correlates with and influences computations, nothing more. State what is not established: interpretability results on small models or narrow tasks need not transfer, completeness (explaining all of a behavior, rather than some) is rarely achieved, and scaling analysis to frontier models is an active, unsettled research problem.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: finding a feature that fires on a concept does not show the model uses it, attention maps are not explanations, and an SAE feature with a clean label is not guaranteed to be a natural unit of the model. Gotchas: results depend on the dataset used to find features, patching requires well-matched clean and corrupt inputs, and steering strength is easy to overtune. Connections: the residual stream and attention structure here come from the transformer page; the correlation-versus-causation ladder is the same logic as the foundations page on causality, applied to a network via interventions; and safety work uses these tools for auditing behaviors (for instance, probing for deception-related features) with the caveat that auditing evidence is partial.

pages.title: Prompt vs RAG vs Fine-Tune
pages.printedTitle: Prompt vs RAG vs Fine-Tune Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Choose the smallest intervention that solves the problem

panels.heading: Decision Tree: Pick the Smallest Intervention
panels.body:
Need current or private knowledge? Yes → use RAG: retrieve the facts at answer time. No ↓
Need stable behavior, style or format? Yes → start with prompting: use examples, rubrics & structured output. Still not stable at scale? Then fine-tune. No ↓
Need tool/action reliability or side effects? Yes → schemas & evals first: define tools, guardrails, and evaluations. No ↓
A well-crafted prompt is enough. Ship it.

panels.heading: Prompting (Fastest & Cheapest)
panels.body:
What it is: Steer the model with instructions, examples, rubrics, and constraints.
How to do it: Clear goal & role. Few-shot examples. Rubrics & acceptance criteria. Structured output (JSON/CSV/MD).
Good for: New tasks, prototypes, varied topics, whenever examples generalize.
Downside: Brittle at scale. Prompts drift, break with edge cases, and require ongoing handholding.

panels.heading: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
panels.body:
What it is: Grounds answers in your data at runtime. Keeps knowledge current and citeable.
How it works: 1. Retrieve → top-k relevant chunks. 2. Rerank → improve relevance. 3. Generate → answer with sources.
Needs to succeed: High-quality sources. Smart chunking. Reranking for accuracy. Citations in output. Evaluation that matches real use.
Key idea: The model writes. Your data proves.

panels.heading: Fine-Tuning (Teach the Behavior)
panels.body:
What it is: Updates model weights so the behavior becomes the default.
Good for: Repeated behavior. Specific style / tone. Domain patterns & formats.
Important: Does NOT magically add new facts. It bakes in patterns, not live knowledge.
Use when prompts aren't enough: Many edge cases to handle. Strict formats always. Consistent style & tone. Lower variance you can trust.

panels.heading: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
panels.body:
Frozen base model + trainable LoRA adapters A (d×r) and B (r×d) → updated behavior (weights unchanged except adapters).
Train small adapter matrices. Lower VRAM & compute. Cheaper training. Easy to swap & version.

panels.heading: QLoRA (Quantized + LoRA)
panels.body:
Quantized base model (4-bit) + trainable LoRA adapters A (d×r) and B (r×d) → updated behavior (economical & adapter-efficient).
4-bit base model (QLoRA). Much lower VRAM. Lowest cost experimentation. Great for many variants.

panels.heading: Economics at a Glance
panels.body:
Prompting: data prep low (write examples); training cost none (prompt only); serving cost low (context tokens); iteration speed very fast (minutes).
RAG: data prep medium-high (ingest, chunk, index); training cost none (index build only); serving cost medium (retrieval + context); iteration speed fast (hours–days).
LoRA: data prep medium (format, clean, label); training cost medium (GPU training); serving cost low (same as base model); iteration speed medium (days).
QLoRA: data prep medium (format, clean, label); training cost low–medium (4-bit training); serving cost low (same as base model); iteration speed fast (days).

panels.heading: Common Failure Modes (Watch for These)
panels.body:
Bad data amplifies: Garbage in, garbage out. Biased, outdated, or noisy data becomes confident answers. Fix: Curate, dedupe, verify, version.
Retrieval can mislead: Wrong chunks look plausible. Over-retrieval adds noise. Fix: Better chunking, rerank, filters, and citations.
Overfit formats: Model parrots training formats. Loses generalization & creativity. Fix: Diverse data, holdout evals, and regularization.
Missing evals = blind: Looks good in demos, fails in prod. No metrics, no guardrails. Fix: Define evals, automate tests, and track regressions.

pages.footer: Start with prompts. Add retrieval for knowledge. Fine-tune for repeated behavior.
pages.summary: Helps decide how to customize a language model: start with a good prompt, add retrieval (RAG) when it needs fresh or private facts, and fine-tune (cheaply, with LoRA or QLoRA) only when you need a behavior baked in — with the costs and pitfalls of each.

panels:
The tree orders interventions by cost and iteration speed, and separates two different needs: knowledge (what the model should know right now) versus behavior (how it should act). Knowledge that is private, frequently changing, or needs attribution belongs in retrieval; Ovadia et al. (2023) compared fine-tuning and retrieval for injecting knowledge and found retrieval generally better, especially for new facts. Behavior (format, tone, decision style) is shaped by prompts first and by fine-tuning when prompts become too long, inconsistent or costly.

Build an evaluation set before choosing, so each intervention's gain is measured against a prompt baseline. And remember that the options combine: a common production system is a prompted model with retrieval and a fine-tuned or distilled component for a high-volume, narrow step.

In-context examples work well but are sensitive to details: the choice, order and label balance of few-shot examples can swing accuracy (Zhao et al. 2021 documented majority-label and recency biases; Lu et al. 2022 showed order sensitivity), so select examples to match the task distribution and test permutations. Structured output via constrained decoding guarantees syntax (valid JSON matching a schema) but not truth: the fields can be well-formed and wrong.

Treat prompts as code: version them, keep a regression suite, and rerun it when the underlying model version changes, since behavior shifts between versions. The brittleness at scale named in the panel is real but measurable: sample failures, add targeted instructions or examples, and check that the fix does not break other cases.

Grounding raises the odds of correct answers but does not guarantee them. Models can ignore the supplied context, blend it with remembered knowledge, or misread a passage; faithfulness (answer supported by retrieved text) must be evaluated explicitly, for example by checking each claim against the cited passage. Advantages beyond freshness: access control (retrieve only documents the user may see, with filtering applied before ranking), auditability (citations), and easy knowledge updates (re-index a document, no retraining). The costs are an extra system to run: ingestion, chunking, an index, embedding model versioning, reranker latency, and monitoring for stale or missing sources. 'Evaluation that matches real use' means a test set of actual user questions with known supporting documents, not synthetic questions generated from the chunks themselves, which are easier than real ones.

It is effective for format adherence, tone, classification heuristics, and domain conventions, and often needs only hundreds to a few thousand high-quality examples for these; data quality matters far more than quantity. It is a weak way to add facts: the model may learn the surface style of an answer without reliably storing the fact, and training on facts the base model does not know has been reported to increase hallucination (Gekhman et al. 2024). Operational points: the fine-tuned model is tied to its base version, so a base upgrade means retraining and re-evaluating; fine-tuning can erode general abilities (catastrophic forgetting), so test on general benchmarks and your own prompts; the evaluation set must be disjoint and deduplicated from the training set; and hosted fine-tuned models may carry different pricing or capacity limits.

LoRA (Hu et al. 2021) freezes the pretrained weight W (d × k) and learns a low-rank update ΔW = (α/r)·B·A, where B is d × r, A is r × k, and the rank r is small (often 8 to 64). Parameter count drops from d·k to r·(d + k): for d = k = 4096 and r = 16, that is about 131K instead of 16.8M per matrix, under 1%. Because the update is additive, the adapter can be merged into W after training (no extra inference latency) or kept separate so one base model serves many adapters, which suits multi-tenant serving (S-LoRA, Sheng et al. 2023). Trade-off: Biderman et al. (2024) found that LoRA tends to learn less than full fine-tuning on harder, domain-shifting tasks but also forgets less of the base abilities.

QLoRA (Dettmers et al. 2023) stores the frozen base model in 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), a data type designed for normally distributed weights, applies double quantization (quantizing the quantization constants) to save more memory, and uses paged optimizers to survive memory spikes. During training, base weights are dequantized on the fly for each matmul and gradients flow into LoRA adapters kept in 16-bit. The paper fine-tuned a 65B-parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU, since 4-bit weights need about half a byte per parameter.

Trade-offs: each step is slower than 16-bit LoRA because of dequantization; there is a small quantization error baked into the base, which the paper reported was largely recovered by the adapters; and merging an adapter into a quantized base needs care, because requantizing after merging adds rounding error.

The table compares up-front costs, but decisions turn on the total over volume: total cost = fixed cost + N × cost per request. Fine-tuning has a fixed training and data-curation cost and can reduce the per-request cost (shorter prompts, smaller model); break-even volume = fixed cost / savings per request. For example, replacing a 3,000-token prompt with a 300-token one saves 2,700 input tokens per call, which matters at millions of calls, but less if prompt caching already discounts the long prefix. RAG has smaller fixed costs but recurring ones: index storage, embedding, retrieval latency, and the extra tokens of retrieved context on every call.

Include hidden costs: data labeling and review (often the dominant cost for fine-tuning), evaluation, re-training when the base model changes, and engineering maintenance.

Data issues: deduplicate, check labels on a sample, remove contradictory examples, and log provenance and versions. Retrieval: inspect actual retrieved chunks for failing queries before changing the model (most 'hallucinations' in RAG systems start as retrieval misses), and filter by metadata such as date and product. Fine-tuning overfit shows as validation loss rising while training loss falls, or outputs copying training phrases; mitigate with early stopping, lower rank or learning rate, and more varied data.

A frequent silent failure is mismatch: an index built with one embedding model queried with another; a fine-tuning chat template that differs from inference; or a stale index serving outdated policy. Version the whole bundle (prompt, index snapshot, adapter, base model) and tie each eval result to it.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: fine-tuning is not a way to teach a model your documents, RAG does not eliminate hallucination, and prompting is not 'just' a prototype technique, since strong prompting plus evaluation covers many production tasks. Gotchas: embedding model upgrades require re-indexing everything; evaluation sets leak into training data over time; and LoRA adapters are tied to the exact base weights. Connections: the alignment page explains what fine-tuning methods optimize; the evaluation page covers building the test set this decision depends on; the agents page covers RAG as a component and the cost of context; and the support-agent page applies the choice in a full system.

pages.title: LLM Inference & Serving
pages.subtitle: Memory, latency, batching, decoding, quantization, and cost

panels.heading: KV-Cache Memory
panels.body:
Formula: bytes ≈ 2 × L × B × T × H_kv × d_head × bytes_per_element, where L = layers, B = batch, T = total tokens (context + generated), H_kv = KV heads, d_head = head dim. Why the factor 2? We store both Keys and Values (K + V).
Visual example config: L = 80 layers, B = 8 requests, T = 4,096 tokens, H_kv = 8, d_head = 128, dtype = BF16 (2 bytes). bytes ≈ 2 × 80 × 8 × 4,096 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 10,737,418,240 bytes ≈ 10.7 GB (10 GiB). KV cache for this batch & context (weights not included).

panels.heading: Prefill vs Decode
panels.body:
Prefill (compute-heavy): Process the entire prompt (T_p tokens) in parallel, populating the KV cache. GPU busy with big matrix multiplies.
Decode (memory-bandwidth-bound): Generate one token at a time. One new token per step. Reads the whole KV cache each time.
Prefill = parallel & compute-bound. Decode = sequential & memory-bound.

panels.heading: TTFT, TPOT & Total Latency
panels.body:
TTFT (time to first token): Time from request start to first token being returned.
TPOT (time per output token): Average time to generate each subsequent token.
Total latency ≈ TTFT + (output_tokens × TPOT). Example: TTFT = 1.250 s, TPOT = 0.045 s, output tokens = 200 → total latency ≈ 1.250 + (200 × 0.045) = 1.250 + 9.000 = 10.250 s.
Optimize TTFT for perceived speed. Optimize TPOT for long outputs.

panels.heading: Continuous Batching
panels.body:
Requests arrive and depart between decode steps. Scheduler keeps GPU full. Diagram: requests A–D join the shared decode steps at different times, filling idle slots.
Tradeoffs: + Higher GPU utilization. + Better throughput. − Queueing delay for some requests. − Fairness vs latency balance.

panels.heading: Speculative Decoding
panels.body:
Use a small draft model to propose k tokens. Large model verifies; accept the prefix. 1. Draft model (small): propose k tokens. 2. Verifier model (large): verify in parallel. 3. Accept prefix: keep until first rejection; the next token comes from the verifier.
When it wins: High acceptance rate (many tokens accepted). Verifier can process many candidates efficiently.
When it loses: Low acceptance rate (many rejections). Verifier not batch-efficient (wasted work).
Great for long outputs. Tune draft size k for your model & traffic.

panels.heading: Quantization Comparison
panels.body:
FP8 (E4M3/E5M2): ~2× smaller memory/bandwidth vs BF16. Quality very good. Native FP8 HW required for best speed & accuracy. Growing support.
INT8 (symmetric): ~2× smaller. Quality good. Broad HW support. Simple, fast. Slightly more quality loss than FP8.
AWQ (weight-only): ~2.5–4× smaller (depends on bit-width, e.g. 4-bit, and the overhead of per-group scales). Quality very good. Activation stays FP16/BF16. Minimal accuracy loss on many models.

panels.heading: Latency ↔ Throughput ↔ Cost
panels.body:
You cannot optimize all three blindly. Latency (per request), throughput (requests/sec), cost ($/hour) — tradeoffs always exist.
Lower latency: smaller batches, faster GPUs, more replicas → ↑ cost, ↓ throughput.
Lower cost: fewer GPUs, smaller models, aggressive batching → ↑ latency, ↓ throughput.
Higher throughput: larger batches, more efficient kernels, continuous batching → ↑ latency, ↑ cost.
Choose the right point for your product & users.

panels.heading: Interview Napkin Math
panels.body:
A) Weights memory (70B model): Parameters = 70 billion, BF16 (2 bytes/param): 70,000,000,000 × 2 bytes = 140,000,000,000 bytes ≈ 140 GB.
B) KV cache can dominate long context. Assume L = 80 layers, H_kv = 8, d_head = 128, dtype = BF16 (2 bytes), B = 8 requests. Context length 4K tokens ≈ 10.7 GB; 32K ≈ 86 GB; 128K ≈ 344 GB; 256K ≈ 687 GB. At long contexts, KV cache >> model weights. Ex: 256K tokens → ~687 GB KV cache vs 140 GB weights. Check the numbers. Know where the memory really goes.

pages.footer: Prefill for speed. Cache for context. Batch for utilization.
pages.summary: Explains what it takes to run a large language model for users: how much memory the KV cache eats, why reading the prompt and generating tokens behave differently, and how batching, speculative decoding and quantization trade latency, throughput and cost.

panels:
The formula is right: bytes = 2 × L × B × T × H_kv × d_head × bytes per element. Worked example: with L=80, B=8, T=4096, H_kv=8, d_head=128 and 2 bytes, the product is 10,737,418,240 bytes, which is 10 GiB (about 10.7 GB). A quick check is per token: 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes, about 320 KiB per token, times 8 × 4096 = 32,768 cached tokens.

The structure to remember: cache size is linear in batch, in context length, in layer count, and in KV heads, which is why GQA matters.

The split follows arithmetic intensity, FLOPs per byte moved. In prefill, the weights are reused across all T prompt tokens, so each loaded weight does many multiply-adds: compute-bound. In decode with batch B, each step loads all weights (2N bytes in bf16) to do about 2·N·B FLOPs, an intensity of roughly B FLOPs per byte. A modern accelerator needs a few hundred FLOPs per byte to saturate its compute (H100 SXM: about 990 TFLOPs dense bf16 over about 3.35 TB/s is roughly 300), so decode at small batch is far below that line and runs at memory bandwidth. A useful bound: decode time per token is at least weight bytes divided by bandwidth, so a 70B bf16 model (140 GB) needs about 42 ms per step on a single 3.35 TB/s device, less when sharded across devices.

TTFT contains queueing delay, tokenization, network, and the prefill itself; prefill time grows at least linearly with prompt length, and the attention part grows quadratically, so long prompts can dominate TTFT. TPOT depends on batch size, context length (cache reads) and the decode kernel efficiency, and rises as the server packs more concurrent requests. Check the example: 1.250 + 200 × 0.045 = 10.25 s, confirming that for long outputs TPOT is nearly everything (9 s of 10.25 s).

Production metrics need distributions, not averages: report p50 and p99 TTFT and TPOT, because tail latency drives user experience and SLOs. Streaming means TPOT should stay below reading speed.

With static batching, a batch runs until its longest sequence finishes, so short requests wait and slots sit idle. Continuous (iteration-level) batching, introduced by Orca (Yu et al. 2022), makes the scheduling decision at every decode step: finished sequences leave immediately and waiting requests join, so the GPU runs a full batch nearly all the time. It depends on the cache being flexibly allocated, which is why it pairs naturally with paged memory.

The subtle issue is interference. A new request's prefill is a large compute burst that delays the decode steps of everyone already running (head-of-line blocking), inflating their TPOT. Chunked prefill splits long prompts into pieces interleaved with decode steps to smooth this. Admission, preemption and priority policies determine tail latency.

Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2023) is lossless. The draft model with distribution q proposes k tokens; the target model with distribution p scores all k positions in one forward pass. Each proposed token x is accepted with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)); at the first rejection, a replacement is sampled from the normalized positive part of (p - q), and the rest are discarded.

Expected tokens per target call, with per-token acceptance rate α treated as constant, is (1 - α^(k+1))/(1 - α); for α = 0.8 and k = 4 that is about 3.4. The gain exists because decode is bandwidth-bound, so verifying several tokens costs about as much as generating one. At large batch sizes, decode becomes compute-bound, the extra verification FLOPs are no longer free, and the benefit shrinks.

Distinguish what is quantized. Weight-only schemes (such as 4-bit AWQ or GPTQ) reduce bytes read per decode step, which directly speeds up the bandwidth-bound decode phase, but compute still happens in 16-bit after dequantization. Weight-and-activation schemes (INT8 W8A8, FP8) also use low-precision tensor cores, helping compute-bound prefill and large batches. Activation outliers in LLMs make W8A8 hard (Dettmers et al. 2022, LLM.int8()); AWQ (Lin et al. 2023) protects the small fraction of weight channels that matter most, identified by activation magnitude, by scaling them before rounding.

FP8 comes in two layouts: E4M3 (more mantissa, max about 448) for tensors, E5M2 (more range) for gradients. AWQ's compression ratio depends on bit-width and group-scale overhead (a 4-bit group-128 scheme is about 4.25 bits per weight), not on sparsity.

Treat this as a queueing-and-roofline problem. Per-token cost = (GPU price per hour × GPUs) / (tokens per hour). Raising the batch size increases throughput almost for free while decode is bandwidth-bound (weights are read once for many sequences) until the step becomes compute-bound or the cache fills memory; beyond that, latency rises linearly with no throughput gain. In queueing terms, waiting time blows up as utilization approaches 100% (for a simple M/M/1 queue it scales like ρ/(1-ρ)), so running servers hot saves money but wrecks tail latency; leaving headroom is a cost.

Parallelism choices map onto the triangle. Tensor parallelism splits each layer over GPUs, lowering per-token latency (aggregate bandwidth) but adding all-reduce communication; replicas multiply throughput without helping single-request latency.

Interview napkin math should include a sanity pass. Weights: 70B × 2 bytes = 140 GB, which exceeds a single 80 GB GPU, so at least two are needed for weights alone and in practice four or more once you leave room for cache. For the panel's cache configuration, the per-token figure is 327,680 bytes (320 KiB), so for batch 8 the total is about 10 GiB at 4K tokens, 80 GiB at 32K, 320 GiB at 128K and 640 GiB at 256K, scaling linearly with context. By 32K tokens at batch 8, the cache already rivals the 140 GB of weights.

Distinguish GB from GiB (a 7% gap) and leave room for activations and fragmentation.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: more GPUs do not always reduce latency (communication overhead), quantization is not free quality-wise (always evaluate on your task, especially long context and reasoning).
