Gotchas: benchmark numbers depend on prompt and output length distributions, so test with realistic traffic; cost per token depends heavily on utilization, so an idle fleet is the dominant cost in practice. This page builds on the transformer page (GQA, cache), and its tradeoffs reappear in system design, where TTFT, TPOT, caching and batching become requirements.

pages.title: Agents & Tool Use
pages.subtitle: The loop, context, retrieval, and reliable actions

panels.heading: Agent Loop
panels.body:
A simple loop that works. 1. Observe: Gather inputs & signals. 2. Plan: Decide next step & tools. 3. Act / tool call: Execute action or call a tool. 4. Validate: Check results & constraints. 5. Update state: Persist new facts & outcomes. 6. Repeat: Loop until goal or stop.
Tip: Make each step observable, testable, and replayable.

panels.heading: Tool-Call Failure Modes
panels.body:
Expect failure. Detect fast. Handle cleanly.
Invalid schema: Payload doesn't match tool's schema. Fix: Validate before sending.
Permission denied: Tool or resource access blocked. Fix: Check scopes & permissions.
Wrong arguments: Types, formats, or values are incorrect. Fix: Strong schemas + argument checks.
Partial result: Tool returns incomplete or partial data. Fix: Detect & request missing pieces.
Stale state: World changed since plan was made. Fix: Re-read state. Re-plan if needed.
Timeout: Tool takes too long or doesn't respond. Fix: Set timeouts, retry with backoff.
Watch out: Don't assume success — verify every result.

panels.heading: Reliability Patterns
panels.body:
Make actions safe, predictable, and recoverable.
Typed schemas: Use strict, versioned schemas for all tools.
Tool descriptions: Clear purpose, inputs, outputs, side effects, and examples.
Validation: Validate inputs before call. Validate outputs after call.
Idempotency: Design tools to be safe to retry without causing duplicates.
Retries with limits: Exponential backoff, jitter, and a max retry count. Fail fast after limits.
User confirmation for consequential actions: Ask before irreversible, costly, or sensitive actions.
Default: Safe by design. Clear errors. Easy recovery.

panels.heading: Context Engineering
panels.body:
Keep context small, relevant, and fresh.
Hierarchy: System > Goals > Policies > Recent State > Details.
Concise state: Summarize. Keep only what's needed for the next step.
Relevant facts: Include high-signal facts and decisions that matter now.
Discard stale context: Drop outdated details, superseded plans, and noise.
Less noise. More signal. Better decisions.

panels.heading: Lost-in-the-Middle
panels.body:
Key evidence can be missed in long context: information at the start and end of a long context window is used well, while the middle is often missed.
Mitigate it: Structure – put key info near the beginning and end. Retrieval – fetch only what's relevant. Recency – keep latest facts at the end. Summaries – summarize earlier context.
Make important things hard to miss.

panels.heading: Prompt Caching
panels.body:
Reuse long, stable prefixes to save cost and time. A long stable prefix is cached; only the variable suffix changes.
Lower cost: Cached tokens are cheaper. Lower latency: Faster responses with fewer tokens. Higher throughput: Serve more requests with same budget.
Cache what changes slowly. Vary what changes often.

panels.heading: RAG Flow
panels.body:
Retrieve the right info, then answer with confidence. 1. Ingest: Collect documents from sources. 2. Chunk: Split into small, coherent chunks. 3. Embed: Convert chunks into vectors. 4. Retrieve: Find top-k relevant chunks. 5. Rerank: Reorder by relevance. 6. Answer: Generate answer with citations.
Feedback loop: Log misses, refine chunks, improve retriever.
Best practices: Clean, high-quality data. Meaningful chunking. Good embeddings. Hybrid search (BM25 + dense). Citations for trust. Evaluate & iterate.

panels.heading: When Not to RAG
panels.body:
RAG isn't always the right tool.
Needs reasoning or action: Task requires planning, calculation, tool use, or multi-step actions — not document lookup. Use: Agent loop & tools.
Corpus is weak: Low quality, sparse, outdated, or noisy data will mislead the model. Use: Improve data or don't RAG.
Latency budget is tiny: Retrieval + reranking adds latency you can't afford. Use: Smaller context or caching.
Facts already in context: The needed info is already present and reliable. Use: Answer directly from context.

pages.footer: Make actions explicit. Validate results. Keep context useful.
pages.summary: Explains how AI agents work as an observe-plan-act-check loop, how tool calls fail and how to make them reliable, how to manage what goes into the model's context, and when retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps or doesn't.

panels:
This loop is the pattern formalized as ReAct (Yao et al. 2022), where the model interleaves reasoning text with tool calls and observations. In practice it is a program, not a prompt: a controller sends the conversation to the model, executes any requested tool, appends the result, and repeats until the model answers or a stop condition fires. Always set hard limits (maximum steps, token budget, wall-clock timeout), because loops can cycle.

Errors compound. If each step succeeds independently with probability q, an n-step task succeeds with q^n: at q = 0.95 and 20 steps, only about 36%. So reliability comes from shorter plans, validation after steps, and recovery paths. Make state explicit (an append-only event log) and record model outputs and tool results, so a failed run can be replayed deterministically without calling the model again.

Treat failures as information for the model. Return structured, actionable errors (which argument was invalid and why) as the tool result, and models can often self-correct on the next turn. Separate retryable errors (timeouts, rate limits, 5xx responses) from non-retryable ones (validation failures, permission denied); retrying the latter wastes budget and may loop. Stale state is a concurrency problem: between planning and acting, another process may have changed the data, so use version checks (compare-and-set, ETags) on writes and re-read before consequential actions.

Propagate a deadline through nested calls so a slow dependency cannot consume the whole budget. Treat tool outputs as untrusted input: a web page or email returned by a tool may contain instructions aimed at the model (indirect prompt injection), so it must not be allowed to expand the agent's permissions.

Idempotency means a repeated request has the same effect as one. For side-effecting tools, have the caller generate a unique idempotency key per logical action and have the server store results by key, so a retry after a timeout (when you do not know whether the first attempt succeeded) cannot double-charge or double-cancel. Retries should use exponential backoff with jitter (randomized delay) to avoid synchronized retry storms, with a cap on attempts; circuit breakers stop calling a failing dependency for a cooldown.

Tool descriptions are part of the prompt: the model chooses tools by reading them. Prefer a small set of clearly named, non-overlapping tools; document side effects and when not to use each; return concise, relevant output. Strict-mode schemas and constrained decoding guarantee well-formed arguments, not correct ones.

Context is a finite budget: more tokens cost more, add latency, and can reduce answer quality by diluting attention with irrelevant material (Shi et al. 2023 showed that irrelevant context can degrade accuracy). Practical tactics: compaction (summarize older turns, keeping decisions, open questions and key identifiers); an external scratchpad or notes the agent reads back when needed; truncating or paginating large tool outputs; and delegating to sub-agents that work in their own context and return only a summary.

The panel's hierarchy is a priority order, not necessarily a position: for caching you want stable material (system prompt, tool definitions) at the start, and for attention you want the current goal and the latest evidence near the end.

Liu et al. (2023, published 2024) varied where the relevant document sat among distractors in multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval: accuracy was highest when it was at the beginning or end and dropped when it was in the middle, a U-shaped curve. Simple needle-in-a-haystack tests flatter models because finding a unique sentence is easier than combining several facts; benchmarks like RULER (Hsieh et al. 2024) found effective lengths well below advertised ones for many models.

Mitigations beyond ordering: retrieve fewer, better passages and rerank; repeat key instructions at the end; ask the model to quote the relevant evidence before answering; and test your own task at your own context lengths rather than relying on published numbers.

Provider prompt caching reuses the precomputed key-value state for a prefix of the input that exactly matches an earlier request. It saves prefill compute, so it improves time to first token and input cost, but not decode speed. Because matching is token-by-token from the start, any change early in the prompt, such as a timestamp or user name placed above the instructions, invalidates everything after it. So order content from most stable to least: system prompt, tool definitions, reference documents, then conversation, then the new message. Pricing and rules differ by provider: typically cached reads are discounted steeply, writes may carry a premium, entries expire after minutes of inactivity, and a minimum prefix length applies. The same idea exists in self-hosted serving as automatic prefix caching (for example RadixAttention in SGLang, Zheng et al. 2023).

RAG (Lewis et al. 2020) quality is bounded by retrieval: if the right passage is not in the top-k, no generator can recover it. So evaluate retrieval separately with labeled queries (recall@k, MRR, nDCG) and generation separately (is the answer faithful to the retrieved context? is it relevant?). Chunking is a recall-precision trade-off: small chunks match precisely but lose context; large chunks carry context but dilute the embedding; common choices are a few hundred tokens with structure-aware boundaries (headings, sections) and some overlap. Hybrid retrieval combines lexical BM25 (good at exact names, codes, rare terms) with dense embeddings (good at paraphrase), commonly fused with reciprocal rank fusion; a cross-encoder reranker then scores query-passage pairs jointly on the shortlist, improving precision at extra latency.

RAG fails by construction in several cases. Aggregation questions (how many tickets mention X? total spend by region?) need computation over all records, which top-k similarity cannot provide; use a structured query tool (SQL) instead. Multi-hop questions require evidence from several documents connected by an intermediate fact; single-shot retrieval misses the second hop, so an agent that searches iteratively does better. If the corpus is small (say, tens of thousands of tokens) and stable, putting it all in the context, especially with prompt caching, can be simpler, cheaper to build and more accurate than a retrieval pipeline.

Retrieval can also reduce quality: irrelevant or conflicting passages can pull the model away from a correct answer it already knew. Measure RAG against a no-retrieval baseline and against long-context. If retrieval rarely changes the answer, you are paying latency for nothing.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: an agent is not just a bigger prompt (it is a controller with limits, state and validation); long context does not remove the need for retrieval or summarization; and prompt caching does not change model outputs, only cost and speed. Gotchas: evaluating agents by final answer only hides unsafe or wasteful intermediate steps, so log traces; tool results are an injection channel; and every added tool adds selection errors, so prune tools. This page leans on the transformer and serving pages (KV cache and prefill explain caching), the evaluation page (error taxonomy: retrieval, tool use), and the safety page (least privilege, confirmation for consequential actions). It feeds directly into the support-agent design page.

pages.title: Evaluating LLMs
pages.subtitle: Build trustworthy evaluations, not leaderboard theater

panels.heading: Eval Stack: End-to-End Pipeline
panels.body:
1. Task definition: Define the user task, scope, constraints, and success criteria. → Be specific about inputs, outputs, and allowed tools.
2. Dataset: Curate high-quality examples that reflect real use. → Cover breadth, edge cases, and difficulty levels.
3. Rubric / metric: Specify what counts as correct and how to score it. → Criteria, weights, scoring rules, and tie-breakers.
4. Model runs: Run the model(s) under controlled conditions. → Temperature, top-p, max tokens, tools, seeds.
5. Analysis: Aggregate results, slice by dimension, and surface errors. → Compute metrics, confidence intervals, and ablations.
6. Human calibration: Spot-check, sanity-check, and iterate the eval. → Refine data, rubric, and configurations.

panels.heading: Benchmark Contamination
panels.body:
Train / test overlap: Same or near-duplicate examples leak into both train and test.
Memorization risk: Models may memorize popular benchmarks and appear better than they truly are.
Use fresh, private, held-out sets: Fresh – new tasks not seen online. Private – internal or curated data kept private. Held-out – created after model cutoff or training.
Check near duplicates: fuzzy match, embeddings, and paraphrase detection.

panels.heading: LLM-as-Judge Biases
panels.body:
Position bias: Prefers first or left responses. Verbosity bias: Overvalues longer, more wordy answers. Self-preference: Favors responses from its own model family. Style bias: Prefers certain tones, formats, or styles. Prompt sensitivity: Small prompt changes change preferences.
Mitigate it: Blind order swap – randomize left/right and repeat. Pairwise comparison – A vs B choices reduce scoring drift. Judge ensembles – aggregate across multiple judges. Human anchor set – calibrate against human labels.
Treat LLM judges as noisy signals — measure and calibrate.

panels.heading: Pass@k: Formula & Intuition
panels.body:
Intuition: If the chance a single try is correct is p, the chance that at least one of k independent tries is correct is 1 − (1 − p)^k.
Why it works: Fail all k tries: (1 − p)^k. So succeed at least once: 1 − (1 − p)^k.
Example: If p = 0.2 and k = 5: 1 − (1 − 0.2)^5 = 0.672. More samples → higher chance of success.
Note: Assumes independence between samples. In practice, outputs are correlated → pass@k is optimistic.

panels.heading: Calibration: Confidence vs. Accuracy
panels.body:
Reliability diagram: Accuracy plotted against confidence; ideal is on the diagonal.
Expected calibration error (ECE): Average gap between confidence and accuracy across bins. ECE = Σᵢ (|Bᵢ|/N) |accᵢ − confᵢ|. Lower is better.
Confidence vs. accuracy: A well-calibrated model's curve tracks the diagonal.
Report calibration metrics alongside task metrics.

panels.heading: Human Evaluation Design
panels.body:
Rubric: Clear criteria, examples, and scoring guide (criteria, weights, score scale).
Raters: Train raters and define quality standards (qualification, practice set, ongoing QA).
Randomized / blinded order: Randomize item order and hide model identities (hide model names, randomize, hide position).
Inter-rater agreement: Measure agreement (e.g., κ, α, %) and monitor drift (κ / α, disagreements, drift over time).
Adjudication: Resolve disagreements with a senior adjudicator (escalate rules, final decision, document reasons).
Design for fairness, consistency, and auditability.

panels.heading: Uncertainty: Quantify It
panels.body:
Report n: Always report the number of examples (n) evaluated. Bootstrap CI: Use bootstrap to estimate confidence intervals. Error bars: Show 95% CI / error bars on all metrics. Avoid false precision: Don't over-interpret tiny differences within noise.
Example accuracy with 95% CI: Model A 78% ±3.2%, Model B 73% ±3.5%, Model C 66% ±3.8%.
If CIs overlap, differences may not be meaningful.

panels.heading: Error Taxonomy: Know Your Failures
panels.body:
Capability: Model lacks the knowledge or reasoning ability (wrong math, logic errors, hallucinated facts). Fix: improve data, model, or reasoning.
Retrieval: Fails to find or use relevant information (missed docs, irrelevant context, outdated info). Fix: improve retrieval, rerank, or add better tools.
Tool-use: Uses the wrong tool or wrong arguments (bad API call, wrong params, ignored results). Fix: tool prompts, validation, better schemas.
Refusal: Over- or under-refuses when it shouldn't (unnecessary refusal, unsafe compliance, policy drift). Fix: adjust policies, safety tuning, better prompts.
Formatting: Output doesn't match the required format or schema (broken JSON, missing fields, wrong structure). Fix: stricter schemas, parsers, and post-checks.

pages.footer: Measure the user task. Randomize the judgment. Report the uncertainty.
pages.summary: How to build trustworthy tests for language models: define the task and rubric, avoid benchmark contamination, correct for the biases of LLM judges, understand pass@k and calibration, and always report uncertainty and categorize failures.

panels:
Most eval disagreements come from unpinned details, not the model. Fix and record the prompt template, few-shot examples, answer-extraction rule, sampling parameters and number of samples; small formatting changes can swing scores noticeably (Sclar et al. 2023 documented large sensitivity to spurious prompt-format choices), and different harnesses implementing the "same" benchmark can report different numbers. A parsing failure counts as a wrong answer, so extraction bugs masquerade as capability gaps.

Treat the eval like software: version the dataset, keep a dev set for iteration and a separate locked test set, because hill-climbing on a fixed set overfits it. Compare models on identical items so that you can use paired statistics. Step 6 matters most: read a sample of raw outputs, since a metric can be high for the wrong reason (for example, a judge rewarding length).

Contamination comes in grades: exact copies, near-duplicates, paraphrases or translations, and indirect leakage (a solution post, or benchmark data in later fine-tuning sets). GPT-3's paper (Brown et al. 2020) used 13-gram overlap to flag contaminated items; n-gram matching misses paraphrases, which Yang et al. (2023) showed can inflate scores, so embedding similarity and LLM-based rephrase detection are added. Canary strings embedded in benchmark files let developers filter them from training corpora, but only if developers respect them.

Remedies: time-split evaluation on problems published after the model's training cutoff (as in continuously refreshed code benchmarks), private test sets, and reporting results with and without suspected overlap. Black-box users often cannot verify what the model saw, so treat leaderboard gains on public static sets with caution.

Zheng et al. (2023), who introduced MT-Bench and studied Chatbot Arena, found strong LLM judges agree with human preferences at roughly the level humans agree with each other, but also measured position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases. Mitigations work as follows. Swapping order and counting disagreements as ties removes position effects (and the disagreement rate itself measures judge noise). Length-controlled scoring fits a model that estimates the preference after adjusting for length difference (as in AlpacaEval's length-controlled variant, Dubois et al. 2024). Reference answers and explicit rubrics reduce subjectivity on checkable tasks.

Validate the judge like any classifier: collect a human-labeled anchor set, report agreement per category with a chance-corrected statistic, and look at where the judge errs, because overall agreement hides weak slices (for example, math correctness versus tone).

The panel formula assumes one shared success probability p. Because 1 - (1-p)^k is concave in p, plugging the average p into it overstates true pass@k (Jensen's inequality). Example: two problems with p = 1 and p = 0 have average p = 0.5, so the plug-in estimate for k=5 is 0.97, yet the correct pass@5 is 0.5.

The standard estimator (Chen et al. 2021) avoids bias: sample n ≥ k completions per problem, count c correct, and compute 1 - C(n-c, k)/C(n, k), then average over problems. Pass@k assumes an oracle that recognizes the correct sample (unit tests); a deployed system must choose one answer, via majority vote (self-consistency, Wang et al. 2022) or a verifier. And for reliability the relevant quantity is the reverse: pass^k, the probability that all k attempts succeed, which falls as k grows.

Calibration asks whether stated confidence matches frequency. Expected calibration error bins predictions by confidence and averages |accuracy - confidence| weighted by bin size. It depends on bin count and is noisy for small n, so pair it with a reliability diagram and a proper scoring rule such as the Brier score. Temperature scaling (Guo et al. 2017) fits one scalar T to rescale logits on validation data; it fixes much miscalibration without changing predictions.

For LLMs: Kadavath et al. (2022) found large pretrained models fairly well calibrated on multiple-choice questions, and the GPT-4 technical report (2023) showed post-training with RLHF degraded calibration of token probabilities. Calibration matters operationally for selective answering: you can abstain below a confidence threshold, and the useful curve is accuracy versus coverage.

Agreement is the ceiling on what you can learn. Cohen's kappa for two raters is (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e), observed agreement corrected for the agreement expected by chance from the marginal label frequencies; Krippendorff's alpha generalizes to many raters, missing ratings and ordinal scales. The commonly quoted bands for "moderate" or "substantial" kappa (Landis and Koch 1977) are conventions, and kappa can be low despite high raw agreement when one category is very common (the kappa paradox).

If humans agree only 70% of the time on a task, no model-based judge can be meaningfully validated beyond that, and the rubric probably needs sharpening. For rankings from pairwise comparisons, fit a Bradley-Terry or Elo-style model (as Chatbot Arena does, Chiang et al. 2024) and report intervals on the ratings.

Report uncertainty at the level of the difference. For accuracy p on n items, the standard error is √(p(1-p)/n); the panel's "±3.2" at 78% implies roughly n = 640 items. With few items or extreme accuracies, prefer a Wilson interval, which behaves better than the normal approximation near 0 or 1. Overlapping CIs do not prove no difference: when models run on the same questions, errors are correlated, and a paired analysis (the per-item difference, with a paired bootstrap or McNemar's test) is more powerful.

Items that share a passage or source are not independent, so resample clusters. Also separate sources of noise: sampling randomness (re-run with multiple seeds), prompt sensitivity, and finite test-set size. Miller (2024) laid out this statistical treatment for language-model evals.

A taxonomy is only useful if it drives the fix. Sample failures (for example 100), label each with one primary category, and count: the Pareto chart tells you where effort pays. To attribute causes you need controlled interventions. Give the model oracle retrieved passages: if accuracy jumps, retrieval was the bottleneck; if not, the problem is reading or reasoning. Feed correct tool arguments to separate tool-selection errors from tool-use errors. Evaluate at both outcome level (was the final answer right?) and trace level (were intermediate steps valid?), since agents can reach correct answers through flawed steps.

Refusal needs two-sided measurement: over-refusal on benign but edgy requests (for example the XSTest suite, Röttger et al. 2023) and under-refusal on genuinely harmful ones, reported separately because optimizing one tends to worsen the other.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: a high benchmark score is not a user-experience guarantee, an LLM judge is not ground truth, and a leaderboard rank difference of one point is usually noise. Gotchas: evals saturate (once models score 95%, remaining errors are often label errors), so keep refreshing difficulty; aggregate scores hide regressions on slices, so report per-slice results; and changing the sampling temperature or prompt between models invalidates a comparison. This page applies the foundations pages (confidence intervals, leakage, calibration) to LLMs. The alignment page depends on judge quality, and the system-design page needs an offline eval plus online monitoring that share definitions of success.

pages.title: LLM Safety & Responsible Deployment
pages.printedTitle: LLM Safety & Responsible Deployment Cheat Sheet
pages.subtitle: Defense in depth, evaluation, safe helpfulness, and response

panels.heading: System Safety Map: Know Your Surfaces
panels.body:
User experience: Clear purpose & scope. Expected use guidance. Transparency & labels. Age & audience aware.
Model behavior: Align to policies & values. Refuse unsafe requests. Be honest about limits. Robust to manipulation.
Tool permissions: Define tools & actions. Least privilege access. Confirm consequential actions. Isolate side effects.
Private data: Minimize collection. Protect in transit & at rest. No unexpected sharing. Respect user rights.
Monitoring & telemetry: Observe key signals. Detect abuse & drift. Track performance. Alert & investigate.

panels.heading: Instruction Hierarchy
panels.body:
Trusted system rules override untrusted external content. From higher to lower trust: System rules – non-negotiable policies & safety guardrails. Developer intent – goals, constraints, and tool design. Configuration – model settings, tool specs, prompts. User input – real user requests & context. External content – web pages, files, third-party text.
When in conflict, higher layers win.

panels.heading: Safe Handling of External Text
panels.body:
Treat it as data: Assume all external content may be wrong, outdated, or malicious.
Isolate tools: Separate the model from execution environments and external systems.
Least privilege: Grant only the minimum permissions needed for each task.
Confirm consequential actions: Require explicit confirmation for actions that change data, spend money, or affect users.
Validate output: Check for safety, policy, privacy, and accuracy before displaying or acting.

panels.heading: Assurance Loop: Test, Learn, Improve
panels.body:
1. Define safety rubric: Set clear goals, criteria, and risk priorities. 2. Test broad scenarios: Cover diverse users, tasks, domains, and edge cases. 3. Review results: Analyze failures, near-misses, and drift. 4. Improve safeguards: Update prompts, controls, tools, and policies. 5. Rerun regression suite: Verify fixes and check for new or regressed issues. Then loop back.
Continuous assurance — ship with confidence, stay vigilant.

panels.heading: Helpfulness / Refusal Balance
panels.body:
Be helpful & safe: Provide accurate, high-quality help within the boundaries. Offer safer alternatives or lower-risk approaches. Clarify intent and assumptions.
Refuse when needed: Refuse when requests are unsafe, wrong, or out of scope. Be clear, respectful, and consistent. Provide a safe alternative or redirect when possible.
Aim for the right balance: helpful, honest, and safe.

panels.heading: Defense Layers: Stack Protections
panels.body:
Sandboxing: Isolate code execution. No network by default. Restrict files and processes.
Allowlisted tools: Only approved tools run. Validate inputs & outputs. Monitor usage.
Rate limits & quotas: Limit speed and volume. Prevent abuse and overload. Protect shared resources.
Audit logs: Log key events and decisions. Tamper-evident storage. Enable audit & forensics.
Human escalation: Escalate high-risk or ambiguous cases. Human-in-the-loop for critical actions. Clear pathways and playbooks.
Multiple layers make failure less likely and impact smaller.

panels.heading: Capability-Based Safety
panels.body:
Stronger capabilities require stronger evaluations and safeguards. Low capability: narrow tasks, limited autonomy, lower risk. High capability: broad knowledge, greater autonomy, higher risk.
As capability grows, so must: evaluation coverage + red teaming depth + guardrail strength + human oversight.
Never outpace your evaluations.

panels.heading: Incident Response: Prepare, Act, Improve
panels.body:
1. Detect: Monitor for anomalies, policy violations, and user reports. Early signal, early action. 2. Triage: Assess severity, scope, and potential impact. Understand before escalating. 3. Contain: Take steps to stop or limit harm. Disable, throttle, or isolate as needed. 4. Learn: Analyze root causes and contributing factors. Document what happened. 5. Update tests: Add tests, improve controls, and update runbooks. Prevent repeats, not just respond.
Be prepared: Clear roles & contacts. Communication plan. Runbooks & playbooks. Post-incident review. Share lessons internally.
Respond quickly. Communicate clearly. Learn continuously.

pages.footer: Build defenses around the whole system — not just the chat box.
pages.summary: Describes how to deploy a language model responsibly by protecting the whole system: ranking whose instructions to trust, treating outside text as untrusted data, stacking defenses like sandboxing and audit logs, balancing helpfulness with refusals, and having an incident response plan.

panels:
The map is a threat model: list what must be protected (user data, funds, reputation, third parties) and the paths by which an attacker, or a mistake, can reach them. The model is one component among several; most severe incidents in deployed LLM systems come from combining a modest model failure with excessive permissions. Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta" is a useful heuristic: an agent that has access to private data, is exposed to untrusted content, and can communicate externally can be induced to leak that data. Remove any one leg and the risk drops sharply.

Defense in depth follows the Swiss-cheese model (Reason 1990): each layer has holes, and harm happens only when the holes line up, so layers need independent failure modes.

In a transformer all text, system prompt and web page alike, is one token sequence; no hardware privilege separation exists. Wallace et al. (2024) trained models to follow higher-privilege instructions when they conflict with lower ones, and this improves robustness but remains probabilistic, so it must not be treated as a security guarantee. Direct injection ('ignore previous instructions', Perez and Ribeiro 2022) comes from the user; indirect injection (Greshake et al. 2023) hides instructions in content the model retrieves, such as a web page or email.

Architectural approaches move control decisions out of the model: for example, systems where the model that sees untrusted text has no tool access and a privileged planner works only on trusted input, or designs that track data provenance through the program (CaMeL, Debenedetti et al. 2025).

The key move is enforcing policy in deterministic code outside the model. Examples: a tool allowlist with typed argument schemas; scoping credentials per task and per user (so a hijacked agent only has that user's access); egress controls that restrict which domains the system may contact; and a confirmation step for irreversible or costly actions that shows the user the actual action rather than the model's description. A well-known exfiltration channel is rendered content: if a chat interface auto-loads a markdown image URL that contains private data in the query string, injected instructions can leak it without any tool call. Output validation applies to both directions: scan for secrets and personal data before display, and validate model-produced structured calls against schemas before execution.

A safety rubric turns values into testable statements: harm categories, severity levels, what counts as a failure, and what thresholds block launch. Red-teaming (Ganguli et al. 2022) uses people, and increasingly other models (Perez et al. 2022), to search for failures; the set of attacks found is a lower bound, not a coverage guarantee. Keep a regression suite of every past failure so fixes cannot silently regress, and separate it from held-out attack sets, otherwise you overfit defenses to known attacks.

If you observe zero failures in n independent trials, the 95% upper bound on the failure rate is about 3/n (the rule of three), so 0 of 1,000 only shows the rate is likely below 0.3%. Measure both attack success rate and false-block rate on benign traffic, and rerun after every model, prompt or tool change.

There is no single dial from permissive to restrictive; there are two error types. Over-refusal wastes legitimate users' time and erodes trust (Röttger et al. 2023 built XSTest to measure it with benign prompts that resemble harmful ones); under-refusal enables harm. Assess a request by plausible user population, severity of worst-case harm, counterfactual uplift (is the information freely available?), and context supplied by operator and user.

Good behavior is often not binary refusal: answer the safe part, offer high-level or protective information, ask a clarifying question, or point to appropriate resources. Consistency matters because users probe by rephrasing, so a policy that flips on trivial wording changes is both unsafe and annoying. Evaluate with paired sets, harmful requests and look-alike benign requests, and track both rates together as a trade-off curve rather than a single score.

Layers help only if their failures are not correlated. A safety classifier built from the same base model as the assistant may share its blind spots, and an attack that fools one may fool both. Combine different mechanisms: policy in code, classifiers, sandboxing, quotas, humans. Sandboxing means default-deny: no network egress, read-only or scoped file systems, resource and time limits, and fresh environments per session, because model-written code is untrusted code. Allowlists should validate arguments, not just tool names.

Tamper-evident audit logs (for example append-only storage with hash chaining) support forensics, and rate limits bound the damage of any one failure and also deter large-scale abuse and cost attacks. Decide failure mode explicitly: fail closed for high-risk actions (if the guard is down, do not act), fail open only where harm is minimal.

Capability-scaled safety is formalized in frontier safety frameworks, such as Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy (with AI Safety Levels), OpenAI's Preparedness Framework and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework. The common structure: define capability thresholds in risk areas (for example biological, cyber, autonomy), run evaluations to detect them, and require stronger safeguards before deployment or further scaling once a threshold is reached or evaluations cannot rule it out.

Two difficulties. First, elicitation: a failed evaluation shows only that your prompts did not reveal the capability; better scaffolding, fine-tuning or tool access can raise measured ability, so evaluations should use strong elicitation and leave a safety margin. Second, risk depends on affordances, not just model intelligence: the same model with code execution, browsing and payment tools has a different risk profile than a text-only one.

Define severity levels in advance, with owners and response times; track time to detect and time to contain. Containment tools for LLM systems are mostly system-level: feature flags to disable a tool or capability, a kill switch for a specific agent action, rollback of a prompt or model version, tightened filters, and revoking credentials. Changing model weights is slow, so plan for mitigation at faster layers first and a proper fix later.

Root-cause analysis should be blameless and aim at contributing conditions: a missing permission boundary is more actionable than 'the model misbehaved.' Convert each incident into a regression test and, where relevant, a monitoring rule. Preserve evidence (prompts, retrieved documents, tool calls) subject to privacy and retention rules, and define who communicates with affected users and when, including any legal disclosure obligations.
deeper.further: Misconceptions: a safety-trained model is not a secured system, a system prompt saying 'never do X' is not an access control, and a filter with 99% recall can still fail badly under adaptive attack because attackers choose inputs after seeing outputs. Gotchas: evaluating only single-turn prompts misses multi-turn and tool-mediated attacks; success on a public jailbreak list says little about novel attacks; and over-logging creates its own privacy risk. This page builds on the alignment page (training for refusal behavior), the agents page (tool permissions and injection are most acute for agents), and the evaluation page (measuring rare failures and judge reliability). The consistent theme is to assume the model can be manipulated, then limit what manipulation can achieve.

pages.title: Design a Support Agent for 10M Users
pages.printedTitle: Design a Support Agent for 10M Users
pages.subtitle: An LLM product-system design interview cheat sheet

panels.heading: Requirements
panels.body:
Channels: Web, mobile, in-app, email, WhatsApp, social DMs, voice.
Languages: Top 10+ languages day-1. Auto-detect & locale aware.
Latency / SLA: P50 < 2.5s, P95 < 5s, P99 < 8s. SLA: 99.9% monthly availability.
Escalation: Seamless handoff to human. Context, intent & steps preserved.
Privacy: Data minimization, encryption, GDPR/CCPA, regional residency.
Success metrics: Containment rate, resolution quality, escalation rate, CSAT, cost/resolved, safety incidents.

panels.heading: Architecture Overview
panels.body: User (any channel) → Gateway (AuthN, rate limit, WAF, geo, quota, request shaping) → Policy / router (intent classify, risk score, A/B, guardrails) → Retrieval & account APIs (vector + hybrid search, KB, account APIs, transactions) → LLM / tool executor (LLM reasoning, tools, actions, side-effects, validations) → Response builder (compose, cite, format, tone, localize) → Observability (logs, traces, metrics, alerts, dashboards, SLOs) → Evaluation (quality, safety, factuality, cost, human review) → Feedback loop (user feedback, outcomes, model & KB improvement), feeding back into the router.

panels.heading: Routing & Flows
panels.body:
Simple FAQ (low risk): User question → auto-answer from KB → resolved.
Authenticated account flow: User (auth) → tools & account APIs: verify access → fetch data → action → confirm.
High risk / complex: User issue → risky / low confidence → escalate to human with full context (telemetry, summary, suggested reply).

panels.heading: Knowledge System
panels.body:
Source & ownership: Docs, policies, help center, product data, community, logs. Owner, freshness SLA, sensitivity.
Ingestion: Connectors, crawl / APIs, change data capture, schema mapping, dedupe.
Chunking & indexing: Semantic chunking, metadata, ACLs, embeddings, hybrid (BM25 + vector) index.
Retrieval & reranking: Query rewrite, filters, hybrid search, cross-encoder rerank, diversity, MMR.
Citations: Inline citations with source title, section, and link.
Freshness: Recency boost, expiry rules, staleness alerts, re-index jobs.
Accurate • Current • Authorized • Access controlled.

panels.heading: Reliability & Tooling
panels.body:
Typed tools: Strong schemas, I/O validation, idempotent side-effects.
Permission checks: AuthZ for every tool call, scoped tokens.
Retries & timeouts: Exponential backoff, jitter, circuit breakers.
Fallbacks: Cache → smaller model → template → human.
Human handoff: Context pack: intent, steps, KB hits, actions, transcripts.
Execution flow: Plan → Validate → Authorize → Execute → Observe.

panels.heading: Safety & Privacy
panels.body:
Data minimization: Collect only what's needed. Avoid storing content longer than necessary.
Access control: RBAC/ABAC, least privilege, service accounts.
PII handling: Detect, redact, mask. Tokenize where needed. No PII in prompts/logs.
Encryption: In transit (TLS) & at rest. Key rotation & KMS.
Audit logs: Who/what/when/why. Immutable, searchable, retention policies.
Guardrails: Content safety filters. PII & secrets protection. Prompt injection defense. Tool misuse prevention. Rate & abuse protection.
Data flow: User input → redact / mask → process (LLM + tools) → response; logs contain no PII.
Privacy by design. Trust by default.

panels.heading: Scale & Cost Optimization
panels.body:
Caching: Response cache, embedding cache, KB result cache, negative cache.
Batching: Embed batches, rerank batches, tool call batches, log batching.
Model routing: Small model for easy intents, larger for complex, reasoning only when needed.
Rate limits: Per user / IP / org, burst + sustained, adaptive limits, priority tiers.
Capacity planning: Autoscale, multi-region active, queue & shed, cost budgets & alerts.
Cost controls: Token budgets by intent. Early exit / stop sequences. Context window mgmt. Compress & summarize. Right-size inference.

panels.heading: Metrics Dashboard
panels.body:
Containment rate: 68% resolved by agent. Resolution quality: 4.6 / 5 human rated. Latency (P95): 3.2s (target < 5s). Cost / resolved case: $0.21 (7-day trend). Escalation rate: 7.8% (target < 10%). CSAT: 4.4 / 5 from survey. Safety incidents: 2 (7-day trend). Volume (daily): 1.8M messages / day.
SLI / SLOs: Availability 99.9% • Error rate < 0.5% • P95 latency < 5s.

panels.heading: Rollout & Continuous Improvement
panels.body:
1. Offline eval: Test sets. Evals: quality, safety, tools. Red team. Bias & toxicity. Benchmark cost.
2. Shadow mode: Live traffic mirrored. No user impact. Compare with current system. Collect diffs.
3. Limited launch: Small % of users. Feature flags. Guardrails on. Tight monitoring. Fast rollback.
4. A/B test: Compare variants. Stat sig results. Cost & quality. Segment analysis. Pick the winner.
5. Monitor: SLOs & alerts. Drill-down. Anomaly detect. User feedback. Daily reviews.
6. Iterate: Fix issues. Improve KB. Tune prompts. Retrain / fine-tune. Ship improvements.
Measure → Learn → Improve → Repeat.

pages.footer: Design for the user journey, then earn reliability at scale.
pages.summary: A worked system-design example for an AI customer-support agent serving 10 million users: requirements, the end-to-end architecture, routing by risk, the knowledge base, reliable tool calls, privacy safeguards, cost control, the metrics to watch, and a safe step-by-step rollout.

panels:
The dashboard's 1.8M messages per day averages about 21 per second; peaks may be 5 to 10 times the average, so plan for 100-200 requests per second. By Little's law (concurrent requests = arrival rate × time in system), 100 requests per second at 5 seconds each means about 500 generations in flight. Availability of 99.9% leaves about 43 minutes of downtime per 30-day month, which is why single-provider and single-region designs need fallbacks.

Split the latency budget across stages (gateway, routing, retrieval, time to first token, generation) and use streaming so users see output early; P95 targets must hold for the whole path including retrieval and tools. Define success metrics precisely: 'containment' (no human needed) can be gamed by making escalation hard, so pair it with resolution quality and recontact rate.

The pipeline separates concerns so each can scale and fail independently. Keep the request path stateless and store conversation state in a fast store with expiry; deduplicate inbound messages by message ID, since channels like WhatsApp retry webhooks. Put cheap work first: the router uses a small model or classifier to detect intent, language and risk, so most traffic never touches the large model. Observability and evaluation run off the request path via queues, so a slow logging system cannot add latency or take down chat.

Models, retrieval index, and tool backends will each degrade differently; add timeouts, circuit breakers and a fallback chain. Use backpressure and load shedding (reject or degrade low-priority traffic) rather than letting queues grow without bound, since long queues violate the latency SLO anyway.

A useful framing is risk = action sensitivity × probability of error. Use signals to estimate confidence: classifier probability, retrieval scores (is there a strong supporting document?), agreement across samples or models, and the model's own uncertainty. Calibrate thresholds on labeled data to meet a precision target for auto-resolution rather than guessing, and re-check after changes.

For authenticated flows, separate reading from writing and require step-up verification before sensitive actions. Policies with money or legal effect (refund limits, eligibility rules) should live in deterministic code or a rules engine that the model calls, not in the prompt. Escalate on explicit request, repeated failure, detected frustration, safety or legal categories, and high-value accounts. A good handoff packet contains the summary, the actions already tried, and retrieved articles, so the customer does not repeat themselves.

Knowledge systems fail on permissions and freshness more often than on embeddings. Access control must be enforced at retrieval time: store ACL metadata with each chunk and filter before ranking, never after generation. Version each source (product, region, effective date) so the system can prefer the correct policy version, and propagate deletions to the index to honor erasure requests. Measure retrieval with a labeled set of real queries (recall@k) in each major language; multilingual retrieval can use multilingual embeddings or translate queries, and the choice should be tested per language.

Query rewriting turns chatty multi-turn messages into standalone search queries. Citations should link to the exact section, and ideally verify that quoted text appears in the source, since fabricated citations are worse than none.

In the sample schema, the idempotent flag in practice means the server accepts an idempotency key, or the operation is naturally safe to repeat, such as cancelling an already-cancelled order, and the preconditions are checked (order status, cancellation window) in code. Most important is how identity flows: the order_id comes from the model, but the user identity must come from the authenticated session, never from model output, so the tool checks that this order belongs to this user. Otherwise a confused-deputy attack can cancel someone else's order through a manipulated prompt.

High-impact calls should require an explicit user confirmation that displays the real parameters. Fallbacks should degrade gracefully (cache, smaller model, template reply, human) and be tested regularly, because a fallback path that is never exercised tends to be broken when needed.

Privacy engineering faces a tension: the agent needs personal data to help, yet logs and prompts should not accumulate it. A common design is pseudonymization: replace identifiers with tokens before text reaches the model and logs, and detokenize only at the tool boundary where the real value is needed, under authorization. Redaction (names, emails, card numbers) must be tested on multilingual and messy text; it is a probabilistic filter, so do not rely on it as the only control. Treat user-supplied and customer-record text as untrusted: order notes, emails and attachments can contain injected instructions. Plan for data-subject requests: you need to find and delete a user's data across stores, caches and indexes, which is far easier if you designed for it from the start.

Model routing, prompt caching for the static prefix, shorter retrieved context, and output limits are the main levers. Caution on response caching: caching answers for generic FAQs is safe if keyed by language and policy version, but caching anything personalized or account-specific risks leaking one user's data or serving stale results; never share caches across users for such content. Semantic caching (matching similar questions by embedding) can return a subtly wrong answer when two questions differ in a critical detail, so use high similarity thresholds and only for low-risk intents.

Provider rate limits (requests and tokens per minute) are hard capacity constraints: secure quota in advance, spread across regions or providers, and implement priority tiers so paying or urgent traffic is served first during overload.

Containment 68% plus escalation 7.8% accounts for only about 76% of conversations; the remaining roughly 24% must be something (abandoned, unresolved, still open), and that bucket is exactly where hidden failures live. Outcome categories should be mutually exclusive and exhaustive. 'Resolved' should be validated by a signal such as no recontact within several days, not merely the user leaving. CSAT from voluntary surveys suffers response bias (extremes respond), so combine with sampled human grading; a 4.6/5 quality score needs a sample size and interval, as the evaluation page describes.

SLOs need error budgets: 99.9% availability allows 0.1% failures, and alerting on burn rate (how fast the budget is being consumed) catches problems earlier than static thresholds. Cost per resolved case should include escalated conversations and failed attempts in the numerator.

Offline evaluation checks quality, safety and tool behavior on curated and adversarial sets, but cannot predict real user behavior. Shadow mode runs the new system on mirrored traffic without showing results to users and compares outputs with the current system; it reveals latency, cost and tool errors, though not user reactions. For A/B tests, size the experiment: to detect a 2-point change in containment from a baseline of 68% with 80% power at the 5% significance level needs roughly 16·p(1-p)/δ² = 16 × 0.2176 / 0.0004, about 8,700 conversations per arm, more if you also segment. Randomize by user (not message) to avoid contamination, run through full weekly cycles, and predefine guardrail metrics (escalation, safety incidents, latency, cost).
deeper.further: Interview approach: clarify requirements and scale first, sketch the architecture, then go deep on two or three risk areas (retrieval and permissions, tool safety, evaluation and rollout) instead of listing every component. State assumptions and do the napkin math aloud. Common misconceptions: more automation is not always better (the right escalation rate is a product decision), a high-quality model does not replace access control, and offline evals alone do not justify full launch. Gotchas: handoff quality, multilingual regressions, stale knowledge, and provider outages. This page draws on nearly everything else in the guide: serving economics, evaluation methodology, agent reliability patterns, RAG, safety layers and alignment.

collections.title: Algorithm Patterns
collections.subtitle: 20 patterns by topic
collections.description: The classic coding-interview patterns grouped by data structure, each taught through one representative problem.

books.title: Arrays & Hashing
books.subtitle: Hash maps, pointers, windows, prefix sums

pages.title: Arrays & Hashing
pages.subtitle: Fast lookups, counts, grouping, and the Two Sum pattern.

panels.heading: Arrays: Big-O Cheat Sheet
panels.body:
Access: arr[i] — O(1)
Search (unsorted): find x — O(n)
Search (sorted, binary search): find x — O(log n)
Insert (end): push_back(x) — O(1) amortized
Insert (middle): insert i, x — O(n)
Delete (by index): erase i — O(n)
n = number of elements

panels.heading: Hash Map & Hash Set: Core Operations
panels.body:
Hash map (key -> value), example map m, average time:
Insert / Update: m[key] = val — O(1)
Find: m[key] — O(1)
Contains key: key in m — O(1)
Delete: del m[key] — O(1)
Size: len(m) — O(1)

Hash set (unique keys), example set s, average time:
Insert: s.add(x) — O(1)
Contains: x in s — O(1)
Delete: s.remove(x) — O(1)
Size: len(s) — O(1)

Diagram: a hash table of buckets 0..m-1, each bucket holding a chain of key:value entries (some empty).
Average case O(1) with good hash. Worst case O(n) (rare with good implementations).

panels.heading: Canonical Example: Two Sum
panels.body:
Input: nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9
Pairs that sum to 9? (2, 7) yes — indices (0, 1); (2, 11), (2, 15), (7, 11), (7, 15), (11, 15) no.
Answer: return indices [0, 1].
Store what you've seen. Look up what you need.

panels.heading: Two Sum: One-Pass with Hash Map
panels.body:
Idea: for each x, we need need = target - x.
Step 1: i = 0, x = 2, need = 7, map {} — 7 not in map; store 2 -> 0.
Step 2: i = 1, x = 7, need = 2, map {2:0} — 2 in map at 0; return [0, 1].
Flow: current value x -> need = target - x -> need in map? Yes: return [map[need], i]. No: store x -> i in map and continue.

panels.heading: Pseudocode (One-Pass Two Sum)
panels.body: Hint: store index with value so you can return the pair of indices.

panels.heading: Hashing Power-Ups (Use Cases)
panels.body:
A) Use duplicate detection (set): find any duplicate? Time O(n), space O(n). Example: nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] -> True.
B) Frequency counts (map): count occurrences. Example: nums = [2,2,1,3,2] -> freq = {2:3, 1:1, 3:1}.
C) Valid anagram (counts): are two strings anagrams? Example: "listen" & "silent" -> True.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Things to Watch
panels.body:
Keys vs values: maps store KEY -> VALUE. Don't look up by value unless that's what you stored.
Duplicates: decide your policy: first index? last index? all indices? Be consistent.
Memory trade-off: hashing uses extra space O(n). Use it when faster lookups save more time overall.

panels.heading: Bonus: Think in Patterns
panels.body:
Lookup — need to check existence fast? Use Set.
Associate — need to map key -> value? Use Map.
Count — need frequencies or tallies? Use Map.
Pair / Complement — need pairs that meet a condition? Use Map + One-Pass.

pages.footer: Trade a little memory for a fast lookup.
pages.summary: Covers array operation costs and O(1) average hash map/set operations, then solves Two Sum in one pass by storing each value's index and looking up its complement. Also shows duplicate detection, frequency counting and anagram checks with hashing.

panels:
Two refinements matter in interviews. First, push_back is O(1) amortized, not worst case: a dynamic array doubles its capacity when full, so one push occasionally costs O(n) to copy everything, but n pushes cost at most about 2n element copies in total, which averages to O(1) each. Second, the O(log n) search only works on sorted data; sorting first costs O(n log n), so it pays off only if you search many times.

Inserting or deleting in the middle is O(n) because every later element shifts one slot. Edge cases: index -1 or n is out of bounds (Python silently wraps -1, which hides bugs), and an empty array has no valid index. Linked lists invert these costs: O(1) insert given a node, O(n) access.

Average O(1) rests on two assumptions: the hash function spreads keys roughly uniformly over m buckets, and the load factor (entries divided by buckets) stays bounded because the table resizes, typically doubling past about 0.75. Then each chain has constant expected length. Resizing costs O(n) but is amortized away exactly like a dynamic array.

The worst case is O(n) when many keys collide, by accident with a poor hash or on purpose through hash-flooding inputs; Java 8 converts long chains into balanced trees (O(log n)) and Python randomizes string hashes per process. Keys must be hashable and effectively immutable: a Python list cannot be a key, a tuple can. Do not rely on iteration order for unordered_map or HashSet.

Brute force checks all n(n-1)/2 pairs: O(n^2) time, O(1) space. Sorting then using two pointers is O(n log n) but destroys the original indices unless you sort (value, index) pairs. The hash map gives O(n) time at O(n) space, with no assumption that the input is sorted, positive, or free of duplicates; negatives and zero work unchanged.

The same element may not be used twice: for nums = [3, 2, 4], target = 6 the answer is [1, 2], not [0, 0]. Duplicates are fine: [3, 3] with target 6 gives [0, 1]. In fixed-width integers, target - x can overflow when values sit near the type limits, so widen to 64 bits. Siblings: Two Sum II (sorted), 3Sum, 4Sum, counting pairs, Two Sum on a BST.

Correctness invariant: before processing index i, the map holds every value from nums[0..i-1]. If a valid pair (j, i) with j < i exists, then nums[j] is in the map when we reach i, so the lookup finds it; and the first i that completes a pair is exactly when we return. Every pair is considered once, from the later index.

Checking before inserting is what prevents pairing an element with itself and what makes [3, 3] work: at i = 1 we need 3, find it at index 0, and return [0, 1]. If duplicates overwrite an earlier index, nothing breaks, because any stored index still holds the right value. Time is O(n) expected; space is O(n) in the worst case, e.g. when no pair exists and all values get stored.

Classic bugs. Inserting before checking lets [3] with target 6 return [0, 0]. In a two-pass version (build the whole map, then query) you must verify map[need] != i, otherwise an element matches itself, and with duplicates the stored index may be the later one. In Python, naming the dict map shadows the built-in, so prefer seen. Returning [-1, -1] is a contract choice; many judges guarantee exactly one solution, but ask.

If the task is to count pairs rather than find one, store frequencies and add freq[need] before incrementing freq[x]. Variant for system-design flavored interviews: design a Two Sum data structure with add(x) and find(sum), where you choose whether to optimize add (O(1), find O(n) scanning the map) or find.

In Python, create the seen-set with set(), since {} is an empty dict with no add. Duplicate detection is O(n) time and O(n) space; the alternative is sort then compare neighbors, O(n log n) time with O(1) extra space if you may mutate the input. Counting is also available as collections.Counter.

For anagrams with lowercase letters, a 26-slot integer array replaces the dict: O(1) space and a smaller constant. For Unicode, keep a map. The equal-length check up front is essential, since the decrement pass cannot detect surplus letters in a longer t unless you also stop when a count goes negative. Extensions: Group Anagrams (key = sorted string or a 26-count tuple), Top K Frequent (bucket by frequency, O(n)), Longest Consecutive Sequence (set; start counting only at x where x-1 is absent).

Duplicates policy matters. Two Sum can overwrite, but 'first index of each value' needs setdefault or a check before assigning, and counting pairs needs frequencies. Never mutate a collection while iterating it: Python raises RuntimeError, Java throws ConcurrentModificationException. Beware defaultdict: merely reading freq[k] inserts the key with 0, which inflates len(freq) and breaks any check that assumes every key has a positive count.

Memory is real: a Python dict entry with boxed ints costs on the order of 100 bytes, so 10 million entries can exceed a gigabyte; sorting plus two pointers may then be the better trade. Avoid floating-point keys because equality is fragile. In C++ with adversarial tests, std::unordered_map with its default hash can be attacked; a randomized custom hash fixes that.

Recognition checklist. 'Have I seen this before?' means a set. 'What was associated with this key?' means a map. 'How many of each?' means a frequency map. 'Is there an earlier element that completes a condition with the current one?' means a one-pass map of complements. The one-pass idea extends to any condition expressible as a function of the current element, such as x - k or x XOR y.

Choose the structure by key space: if keys are small integers or letters, a plain array beats a hash table in speed and memory. If memory is tight or the data is already sorted, two pointers uses O(1) space. If you need ordering queries (nearest larger key), use a balanced tree or sorted structure instead, at O(log n) per operation.
deeper.further: Reach for hashing when the brute force is a nested loop whose inner loop only asks 'does a particular value exist?' or 'how many times?'. Close siblings: two pointers (needs sorted order, O(1) space), prefix sums plus a map (turns subarray-sum questions into complement lookups), and sliding window (also uses a map, but only over the current window). Sorting is the alternative when you need order rather than membership. To tell them apart, ask whether elements must be contiguous, whether input is sorted, and whether memory is limited. Follow-ups: Contains Duplicate, Valid Anagram, Group Anagrams, Top K Frequent Elements, Longest Consecutive Sequence, 3Sum, Subarray Sum Equals K.

pages.title: Two Pointers
pages.subtitle: Sweep inward, chase pairs, and shrink the search space.

panels.heading: Left/Right Invariant
panels.body:
Maintain a truth about the region outside the pointers.
Diagram: an array with checked cells on each end, an UNCHECKED middle, and left/right pointers at its edges.
Example invariant (palindrome): all characters strictly outside [left, right] are already matched (or skipped). If a mismatch is found inside, the string is not a palindrome.

panels.heading: Canonical Example: Valid Palindrome
panels.body:
String: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
After skipping non-alphanumerics and lowercasing: amanaplanacanalpanama
Compare and move inward from l and r.
All pairs match -> it is a palindrome.

panels.heading: Skip Non-Alphanumerics, Compare Lowercase Chars
panels.body:
Keep moving pointers past junk.
Skip if !isalnum(s[l]); skip if !isalnum(s[r]).
Compare tolower(s[l]) and tolower(s[r]).
Alphanumeric = [a-z0-9]. Everything else is skipped.

panels.heading: Readable Pseudocode
panels.body: Flow: l < r? No -> return true. Yes -> skip junk on both sides -> chars equal? No -> return false. Yes -> move l++, r-- and repeat.
panels.code:
function isPalindrome(s):
  l <- 0
  r <- len(s) - 1
  while l < r:
    while l < r and not isalnum(s[l]): l += 1
    while l < r and not isalnum(s[r]): r -= 1
    if tolower(s[l]) != tolower(s[r]):
      return false
    l += 1
    r -= 1
  return true

panels.heading: Two Pointers, Same Direction (Sorted Arrays)
panels.body:
When order helps, move both pointers forward. Use monotonicity to decide which pointer to advance.
Example: Two Sum in Sorted Array: [1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 15], target = 15, i at start, j at end.
sum < target -> i++
sum > target -> j--
sum == target -> found!
Diagram: an i-by-j grid of sums split into too big, just right, and too small regions.

panels.heading: Common Applications
panels.body:
1) Pair sum (sorted array): find two numbers that add up to target. Example [2, 3, 7, 8, 11, 15], target = 10. Move i or j based on sum until you hit the target.
2) Container with most water: maximize area between lines. Move the shorter line inward. Area = min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l).
3) Remove duplicates (sorted array): keep one of each unique value in-place. r scans, w writes next unique. Time: O(n). Space: O(1).

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Off-by-one: use l < r (not l <= r); initialize r = n - 1; move pointers after using them; test even and odd lengths.
Unsorted input: many two-pointer patterns require sorted data (or a monotonic property). If unsorted, the pointer movement proofs break.
Pointer move proof: always justify why a pointer move cannot skip a valid solution. If you can't prove it, you might skip the answer.

pages.footer: State the invariant — then move the pointer that cannot help.
pages.summary: Explains the two-pointer technique: keep an invariant about the region outside the pointers and move inward, as in checking whether a string is a valid palindrome. Also covers same-direction pointers on sorted arrays, classic applications, and off-by-one pitfalls.

panels:
The invariant is what turns a heuristic into a proof. For the palindrome: before every iteration, each mirrored pair (k, n-1-k) with k < l has been verified equal, ignoring junk characters. The loop ends when l >= r, leaving at most one unchecked character, and a single character always matches itself, so the whole string is a palindrome. A mismatch is a concrete witness, so returning false immediately is correct.

Each iteration moves at least one pointer toward the other and never backward, so the work is at most n steps: O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Building the cleaned string and comparing it with its reverse is also O(n) time but costs O(n) space. An empty string, or one containing only punctuation, is a palindrome vacuously.

The cleaned string amanaplanacanalpanama has 21 characters, an odd count, so the middle character c is compared only with itself and the pointers meet there. Even lengths end with l just past r. Test both parities.

Definition details to confirm in an interview: digits count as alphanumeric, so '0P' is not a palindrome (0 differs from p), and case folding applies only to letters. For non-ASCII text, isalnum and lowercasing depend on the locale or Unicode rules; ask whether to handle it.

A natural follow-up is Valid Palindrome II (may delete at most one character): at the first mismatch, test whether skipping either s[l] or s[r] leaves a palindrome. That is still O(n), since each branch is a linear check. Counting palindromic substrings instead uses expand-around-center in O(n^2).

Both skip loops need the guard l < r. Without it, an all-punctuation string such as '...' lets r run below l, and in Python s[-1] silently wraps around, hiding the bug instead of crashing. With the guard the pointers can meet but never cross during skipping.

Every pointer move is justified: skipped characters are defined as irrelevant, so ignoring them cannot hide a mismatch. A common worry is that the nested while loops make this O(n^2). They do not: the pointers never move backward, so all inner iterations together advance l and r at most n times in total; this is amortized analysis.

Portability: in C or C++, isalnum on a negative char value is undefined behavior, so cast to unsigned char; or test ranges directly ('a' to 'z', '0' to '9' after lowercasing).

Trace the tricky input 'a.': l = 0, r = 1. The l-skip does nothing; the r-skip sees '.', so r becomes 0. Now l == r, and the comparison checks 'a' against itself, which passes. Then l = 1 and r = -1, the outer condition fails, and the result is true. This works only because of the l < r guards inside the skip loops.

Other checks: empty string gives r = -1, loop never runs, true. A single character, true. Time O(n), space O(1); a recursive version would use O(n) stack. Language shortcuts such as Python's s[l].isalnum() and s[l].lower() are Unicode aware, while hand-rolled ASCII checks are not. The compare-then-move order matters: moving before comparing would skip pairs, which is the off-by-one the pitfalls panel warns about.

A clarification: the sorted pair-sum moves the pointers toward each other (opposite directions). The same-direction family (reader and writer) appears in the next panel's duplicate removal.

Proof of safety: if a[i] + a[j] > target and the array is sorted, then for every i' >= i the sum a[i'] + a[j] >= a[i] + a[j] > target, so j cannot pair with anything still in play; earlier indices were already eliminated. Discarding j loses no solution. The < case is symmetric for i. Each step discards one index, so at most n-1 steps: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Trace [1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 15], target 15: 1+15=16 (j--), 1+11=12 (i++), 2+11=13 (i++), 4+11=15 found at indices 2 and 4.

Pair sum on [2, 3, 7, 8, 11, 15] with target 10: 2+15=17 so j--; 2+11=13 so j--; 2+8=10, found. Container With Most Water: moving the shorter line is safe because any container that keeps the shorter line but has a smaller width has height at most that line and less width, so its area cannot beat the current one; thus the shorter line is useless for the rest of the search. On ties, either side works. O(n) overall.

Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array: start w = 1, and copy a[r] to a[w] only when a[r] != a[w-1], then return w; the empty array is a special case. Relatives: 3Sum (sort, fix one element, two-pointer the rest, skip duplicates, O(n^2)), Trapping Rain Water, Sort Colors (three pointers), Move Zeroes, Squares of a Sorted Array.

Use l < r for pair problems: with l <= r the same element could be used twice, which Two Sum II forbids. For palindromes either works, but l < r is cleaner. Always test lengths 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 to cover both parities.

Sorted input is the usual prerequisite. For Two Sum with original indices on unsorted data, sorting destroys the positions unless you carry them along, so a hash map is simpler.

In 3Sum, duplicates produce repeated triples unless you skip equal values after a hit on both pointers and also skip equal outer values. Sums can overflow 32-bit ints, so widen. The deepest pitfall is moving a pointer without a proof: always write down why the discarded element cannot belong to any remaining solution, as with the shorter wall in Container With Most Water.
deeper.further: Reach for two pointers when the input is sorted, when you compare or pair elements from both ends (palindromes, pair sums), or when you partition or compact an array in place with O(1) space. Closest siblings: sliding window (both pointers move forward and the interval between them carries running state), binary search (halves the range using a midpoint, O(log n) rather than linear), and hashing (handles unsorted input at O(n) space). Test: can you argue that one pointer can be discarded forever? Follow-ups: Two Sum II, 3Sum, 3Sum Closest, Container With Most Water, Trapping Rain Water, Sort Colors, Valid Palindrome II, Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II.

pages.title: Sliding Window
pages.subtitle: Maintain a valid range and move only forward.

panels.heading: Variable-Size Window l...r
panels.body:
Example: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, s = "abcabcbb" (indices 0-7).
r = 0: window "a", set = {a}, best = 1
r = 1: "ab", set = {a,b}, best = 2
r = 2: "abc", set = {a,b,c}, best = 3
r = 3 (dup 'a'): shrink l -> 1, set = {b,c,a}, best = 3
r = 4 (dup 'b'): shrink l -> 2, set = {c,a,b}, best = 3
r = 5 (dup 'c'): shrink l -> 3, set = {a,b,c}, best = 3
r = 6 (dup 'b'): shrink l -> 5, set = {c,b}, best = 3
r = 7 (dup 'b'): shrink l -> 7, set = {b}, best = 3
Answer: 3 ("abc")

panels.heading: Duplicate-Triggered Shrink (Set / Map)
panels.body:
Grow r to include new char. If it breaks the invariant (duplicate / too many / invalid), shrink l until valid.
Set (unique elements): 'a' already in set -> duplicate! 1) Remove s[l] from set. 2) l++. 3) Repeat until s[r] not in set. 4) Add s[r], update answer.
Map / freq count: freq[a] becomes 2 -> invalid! 1) Decrement freq[s[l]]. 2) If freq[s[l]] == 0, erase it. 3) l++. 4) Repeat until invariant holds.
Invariant: window satisfies the rule (e.g., all unique, at most k distinct, freq constraints, sum limit, etc.).

panels.heading: Pseudocode (Variable Window)
panels.body: valid(...) checks: no duplicates; at most k distinct; sum <= target; all counts within limits; etc.
panels.code:
l = 0
best = 0
freq = empty map / set   # depends on the problem
for r from 0 to n-1:
    add s[r] to freq / set
    while not valid(s, l, r, freq):
        remove s[l] from freq / set
        l += 1
    update answer (best) using [l, r]
return best

panels.heading: Fixed Window vs Variable Window
panels.body:
Fixed window (size = k): r - l + 1 is always k. Slide both pointers together. Good for: max/min sum of size k, averages, etc.
Variable window (size changes): expand r to grow. Shrink l only when invalid. Good for: longest/shortest with constraints, at-most-k, duplicates, etc.

panels.heading: Common Uses
panels.body:
Longest subarray / substring: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters; Longest Ones After Replacement; Longest Subarray with Sum <= K.
Shortest subarray / substring: Minimum Size Subarray Sum >= Target; Shortest Subarray with Sum >= K; Shortest Substring Containing All Chars.
At most K distinct elements: Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct; Fruits Into Baskets; Subarrays with At Most K Distinct Integers.
Frequency / count constraints: Max Consecutive Ones III; Replace Characters for Longest Repeating Char; Subarrays with Exactly K Occurrences.
Other constraints: Max Sum with Length Constraints; Subarray Product < K; Subarrays with Bounded Values.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them
panels.body:
Stale counts: for maps, don't forget to decrement and erase when count hits 0. Otherwise window stays invalid. Fix: if (--freq[x] == 0) erase x.
Update answer timing: update after the window becomes valid (inside loop after while), not before shrinking. Fix: update only when [l, r] is valid.
Advance pointers: move l one step at a time inside while loop. Never jump l or move r backward. Fix: l++ in while, r++ in for loop.
Broken invariant: forgetting the rule leads to wrong answers or infinite loops. Fix: clearly define and test the invariant.
Off-by-one: be careful with window length: r - l + 1. Fix: double-check bounds and test edge cases (empty, single, all same).

pages.footer: Expand to explore. Shrink to restore the invariant.
pages.summary: Teaches the sliding window pattern: expand the right edge, and shrink the left edge whenever the window breaks its invariant, demonstrated on Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters. Contrasts fixed and variable windows and lists common problem types and pitfalls.

panels:
Trace the tail of 'abcabcbb': at r = 5 the window is abc with l = 3. At r = 6 the new b duplicates the b at index 4, so you remove s[3] = a and s[4] = b, leaving l = 5 and window 'cb'. At r = 7 the new b duplicates index 6, so you remove c and b, leaving l = 7 and window 'b'. Best stays 3.

Linear because l and r only move forward: O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet)) space. Optimization: keep last[c] and jump l = max(l, last[c] + 1). The max is essential: on 'abba' at r = 3 the old a was at index 0 but l is already 2; without max, l moves backward and you report 3 instead of 2.

Why shrinking from the left is safe depends on a hereditary property: if a window is valid, every sub-window of it is valid (a subset of distinct characters is still distinct; fewer distinct characters stays at most k). So when [l, r] is invalid, shrinking until valid finds the smallest l that works for this r, and for r+1 the smallest valid l can only be at least as large. That is why l never needs to move back.

With a set, shrink before inserting the new character; with a frequency map you may add first and then shrink. Cost: the while loop is nested but amortized, since each element is removed at most once, so the total is O(n). If validity needs a scan of the whole map, you lose that; maintain counters instead.

Details that decide correctness. Longest-window problems update the answer after the shrink loop. Shortest-window problems flip the structure: while the window is valid, record the answer and then shrink, so the update goes inside the loop. Use INF as the initial best and return 0 or an empty result if it is never updated.

Counting problems use a neat trick: for an 'at most k' constraint, after restoring validity every start in [l, r] yields a valid subarray ending at r, so add r - l + 1 to the count. 'Exactly k' is atMost(k) - atMost(k-1). The pseudocode runs in O(n) only if valid is O(1), meaning it relies on maintained counters, not a rescan of the window. Empty input should return 0 without touching indices.

Fixed window: maintain the aggregate incrementally, sum += a[r] - a[r-k], so total time is O(n) instead of the naive O(nk). Edge cases: k > n means there is no complete window; k = 0 is degenerate; the first k-1 positions do not yet have a full window, so start recording at r = k-1. Floating-point running sums accumulate error; use integers or recompute periodically. Sums of ints belong in 64-bit variables.

Fixed-window classics: Maximum Average Subarray I, Permutation in String (compare character counts over a window the length of the pattern; maintaining a matches counter makes each slide O(1)), Find All Anagrams. Maximum in each window is the hard sibling, because a running sum cannot be subtracted for a max; it needs a monotonic deque, giving O(n) overall.

Sliding window requires the constraint to behave monotonically as the window grows. 'Longest Subarray with Sum <= K' works only if elements are non-negative; with negatives, adding an element can decrease the sum, so shrinking is no longer the right response. Likewise Shortest Subarray with Sum >= K (LeetCode 862) allows negatives and needs prefix sums with a monotonic deque instead; a plain window fails there. Minimum Size Subarray Sum (209) has positive numbers and is fine.

Two gems: Longest Repeating Character Replacement is valid when length - maxFreq <= k, and maxFreq may stay stale because only a larger window can improve the answer. Subarray Product Less Than K needs a guard for k <= 1 (answer 0) so that l never passes r.

Stale counts: if validity is 'at most k distinct', a key whose count has dropped to 0 must be erased (or tracked by a separate distinct counter), otherwise len(map) overstates the distinct count and the window never looks valid. Answer timing: update after restoring validity for longest windows, inside the loop for shortest windows. The window length is r - l + 1, since both ends are inclusive.

Infinite loops appear when the shrink condition cannot change as l advances, usually because the removal step forgot to update the state that valid reads. Only move l inside the shrink loop, one step at a time, apart from the last-index jump guarded by max. Test: empty input, single element, all identical, all distinct, k larger than n, and k = 0.
deeper.further: Use a sliding window for contiguous subarray or substring questions asking for the longest, shortest, or a count, where growing the window makes the constraint harder (or easier) in one direction. Siblings: two pointers on opposite ends (no window state, usually sorted data), prefix sums plus a hash map (the right tool when negative numbers break monotonicity), a monotonic deque (window max or min), and Kadane or DP (maximum sum without a bound). The decisive question is whether shrinking can only help. Follow-ups: Minimum Window Substring, Longest Repeating Character Replacement, Permutation in String, Sliding Window Maximum, Fruit Into Baskets, Subarrays with K Different Integers.

pages.title: Prefix Sums
pages.subtitle: Turn range questions into one subtraction and a lookup.

panels.heading: Running Sum & Frequency Map
panels.body:
If prefix sum up to j is sum, then a previous prefix sum of (sum - k) forms a valid subarray ending at j.
current sum = S -> need S - k -> count += freq[S - k]
freq (prefix sum -> count): 0 -> 1, 1 -> 1, 2 -> 1, 3 -> 1, ...
We remember how many times each prefix sum has occurred.

panels.heading: Pseudocode
panels.body:
Read it like a story: 1. Extend the range to include x. 2. Look back: how many prefixes give sum - k? 3. Add that to the answer. 4. Record this prefix sum.
Time: O(n). Space: O(n).
panels.code:
freq = defaultdict(int)
freq[0] = 1          # empty prefix
count = 0
sum = 0
for x in nums:
    sum += x
