The six-vertex graph drawn above is connected (edges 2-4, 2-5 and 3-5 bridge the two triples), so it has one component; removing those three cross edges would leave {1, 2, 3} and {4, 5, 6}. The shortest path from 1 to 5 has length 2 (1-2-5 or 1-3-5), and BFS reports 2.

Component counting uses an outer loop of traversals, or Union-Find with near-constant amortized cost per union. BFS gives distances from the source to every vertex in O(V + E) and a parent map reconstructs the path. If edges have weights, use Dijkstra (nonnegative) or Bellman-Ford (negatives allowed). For directed graphs, 'connected' splits into weak versus strong connectivity; strongly connected components need Tarjan's or Kosaraju's algorithm.

Without a visited set, any cycle loops forever, and in an undirected graph every edge is a two-cycle (u to v and back to u). Grid mutation versus extra space is a design choice to state aloud. Recursion depth is the real danger: a 300 by 300 all-land grid can recurse about 90,000 deep, but Python's default limit is 1000 and a JVM thread typically manages tens of thousands. Switch to an iterative stack or queue; raising Python's limit can crash the interpreter.

Other traps: marking visited at dequeue time in BFS (duplicates in the queue multiply work), forgetting the outer loop on disconnected graphs, building undirected edges one way, confusing 0-indexed and 1-indexed labels, and mixing '1' strings with 1 integers in grid input.
deeper.further: Think graph traversal when the problem talks about connectivity, reachability, regions, components, dependencies, relationships, or the fewest moves; a grid, a set of states, or words differing by one letter are implicit graphs. Siblings: Union-Find (connectivity under merges, no paths), topological sort (ordering a DAG), Dijkstra (weighted shortest paths), tree traversals (no visited set needed), and grid DP (counts or optima where moves only go right or down, which is acyclic). Pick BFS for fewest steps, DFS or BFS for components. Follow-ups: Max Area of Island, Clone Graph, Pacific Atlantic Water Flow, Surrounded Regions, Rotting Oranges, Number of Provinces, Graph Valid Tree, Word Ladder.

pages.title: Advanced Graphs
pages.subtitle: Dependencies, topological order, and finding cycles.

panels.heading: Directed Prerequisite Graph
panels.body:
Diagram: A points to B and C; B points to D and E; C points to F; D, E and F point to G.
Edge u -> v means u must be done before v (u is a prerequisite of v).

panels.heading: Canonical Course Schedule: Edges Prerequisite -> Course
panels.body:
Courses: A, B, C, D, E, F, G
Input pairs [course, prerequisite]: [B,A], [C,A], [D,B], [E,B], [F,C], [G,D], [G,E], [G,F]
Edges (prerequisite -> course): A -> B, C; B -> D, E; C -> F; D -> G; E -> G; F -> G
Each pair [course, prereq] becomes an edge from the prerequisite to the course that needs it.

panels.heading: Indegree and Kahn BFS Topological Sort
panels.body:
Indegree (number of unmet prerequisites): A 0, B 1, C 1, D 1, E 1, F 1, G 3.
Initial queue (all indegree 0): [A]
Kahn's algorithm (BFS):
Queue: [A], Order: []
Pop A -> Order: [A]. Decrement B, C -> both 0 -> Queue: [B, C]
Pop B -> Order: [A, B]. Decrement D, E -> both 0 -> Queue: [C, D, E]
Pop C -> Order: [A, B, C]. Decrement F -> 0 -> Queue: [D, E, F]
Pop D -> Order: [A, B, C, D]. G: 3 -> 2. Queue: [E, F]
Pop E -> Order: [A, B, C, D, E]. G: 2 -> 1. Queue: [F]
Pop F -> Order: [A, B, C, D, E, F]. G: 1 -> 0 -> Queue: [G]
Pop G -> Order: [A, B, C, D, E, F, G]. Queue: []
Final topological order: [A, B, C, D, E, F, G] (one valid order).
Key idea: repeatedly take a node with no remaining prerequisites, remove it, and update its neighbors.

panels.heading: Kahn BFS Pseudocode (Readable)
panels.body: Complexity: Time O(V + E), Space O(V + E), where V = number of courses (nodes) and E = number of prerequisite relations (edges).

panels.heading: DFS Three-Color Cycle Detection
panels.body:
Color meaning: WHITE = unvisited; GRAY = in recursion stack; BLACK = fully processed.
Cycle rule: if we see an edge to a GRAY node, we found a back edge -> cycle!

panels.heading: DAG Meaning and Uses
panels.body:
A DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) has no cycles. That means a valid order of completion exists.
Common uses: build systems (compile/link in correct order); scheduling (tasks, courses, or jobs with prerequisites); package management (install dependencies safely).

panels.heading: Pitfalls: Edge Direction & Cycle Handling
panels.body:
Edge direction: for Kahn's algorithm point each edge from prerequisite to course (A -> B means A comes before B), so indegree counts unmet prerequisites. LeetCode gives pairs [course, prereq]: add the edge prereq -> course. Reversing every edge gives the reversed order (and indegree 0 would mean nothing depends on the node).
Cycle handling: a cycle (e.g. A -> B -> C -> A) detected means: no valid topological order; scheduling is impossible; report or break the cycle.
Always check: if result size < number of nodes, a cycle exists.

pages.footer: If a dependency cycle exists, no valid order exists.
pages.summary: Models Course Schedule as a directed prerequisite graph and finds a valid order with Kahn's BFS topological sort using indegrees, detecting a cycle when not all nodes are output. Also shows three-color DFS cycle detection, what a DAG is, and edge-direction pitfalls.

panels:
With the convention that u -> v means u must come first, the diagram has eight edges: A to B and C; B to D and E; C to F; and D, E, F to G. A topological order is a listing of all vertices in which every edge points forward, and one exists if and only if the graph is a DAG. Many orders exist: A, B, C, D, E, F, G and A, C, F, B, E, D, G are both valid.

Edge direction is the top source of bugs, so fix one convention. In LeetCode's Course Schedule, a pair [a, b] means b comes before a, i.e. edge b -> a. In a DAG the longest path, counted in vertices, is the minimum number of parallel rounds; here it is 4 (A, B, D, G).

This panel shows how the input maps to edges. LeetCode lists pairs [course, prerequisite], so each pair [B, A] becomes the edge A -> B. If you instead store course -> prerequisites and run Kahn's algorithm on it directly, indegree counts how many courses depend on a node, so the first vertex removed is G, and the output is a reversed schedule. Either reverse the result or build the graph as prerequisite -> course. Cycle detection gives the same verdict either way.

Here G has three prerequisites, D, E and F, which the indegree trace uses. Isolated vertices must still be counted in V, and duplicate edges are fine as long as indegree and decrements stay consistent.

Starting from queue [A]: pop A, giving B and C indegree 0, queue [B, C]. Pop B, queue [C, D, E]. Pop C, queue [D, E, F], order [A, B, C]. Pop D (G: 3 to 2), pop E (G: 2 to 1), pop F (G: 0, joins queue), pop G. Final order [A, B, C, D, E, F, G].

Why it works: a removed vertex has no unfinished prerequisites. In a DAG, some remaining vertex always has indegree 0, since following predecessors backward forever would eventually repeat a vertex and form a cycle. So the process consumes everything. With a cycle, the cycle's vertices and everything downstream never reach indegree 0, so the order ends shorter than V. Time and space are O(V + E).

Implementation traps. queue.pop(0) on a Python list costs O(n); use collections.deque and popleft. The indegree dict requires every vertex to be a key of graph, including vertices that only appear as neighbors, otherwise KeyError. The comment in the code says neighbors are prerequisites, but the algorithm needs graph[u] to hold the dependents, the vertices that must come after u. Returning [] for a cycle is ambiguous with an empty graph; Course Schedule just returns a boolean.

Variants: to get the lexicographically smallest order, replace the queue with a min-heap (O((V + E) log V)). Processing level by level gives the minimum number of rounds (Parallel Courses). Alien Dictionary builds edges from adjacent words and must reject the case where a longer word precedes its own prefix, such as abc before ab.

GRAY marks vertices on the current DFS path, so an edge into a GRAY vertex is a back edge, which exists exactly when the directed graph has a cycle. An edge into a BLACK vertex reaches finished work and is harmless. That is why one visited flag is wrong for directed graphs: in the diamond A -> B, A -> C, B -> D, C -> D, vertex D is reached twice without any cycle.

A self-loop u -> u is caught because u is GRAY when examined. Reverse finishing order (when vertices turn BLACK) is a valid topological order. Time O(V + E); recursion depth up to V, so go iterative for large inputs. For undirected graphs the rule differs: an edge to a visited vertex that is not the parent signals a cycle, or use Union-Find.

A DAG may have many topological orders; the order is unique exactly when the Kahn queue holds a single vertex at every step. Real systems built on this: build tools such as make and Bazel, package managers, spreadsheet recalculation (a cell's formula inputs must be computed first), and task schedulers.

A powerful follow-on: shortest or longest paths on a DAG are solvable in O(V + E) by relaxing edges in topological order, even with negative weights, which beats Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford; counting the number of paths works the same way. If the graph may contain cycles, compress each strongly connected component (Tarjan or Kosaraju) into one node, and the result is always a DAG. Sequence Reconstruction asks whether the topological order is unique, which is the single-vertex-queue test.

Edge direction first: re-derive 'which way does the arrow point' from a two-node example before coding. Cycle handling: compare the length of the order to V, never to the number of edges. In Course Schedule, V is numCourses, not the number of prerequisite pairs, so courses with no prerequisites still count. Self-loops, duplicate edges, isolated nodes, and several disconnected components should all be tested.

Detecting a cycle is different from reporting one: to return an actual cycle, track parent pointers in DFS and walk back from the GRAY target. Recursion depth is a risk in the DFS version. If a cycle exists, say clearly that no valid order exists, rather than returning a partial order. Finally, do not confuse this with undirected problems like Graph Valid Tree, where Union-Find or a parent-aware DFS is the right tool.
deeper.further: Use topological ideas whenever a problem has prerequisites, dependencies, or before/after constraints and asks for an order, a feasibility check, or the number of rounds. Siblings: plain DFS or BFS (reachability without ordering), Union-Find (undirected connectivity and cycles), Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall (weighted shortest paths), and minimum spanning trees (cheapest way to connect everything). Quick split: dependencies mean topological sort; cheapest route means Dijkstra; cheapest connection means MST. Follow-ups: Course Schedule I and II, Alien Dictionary, Parallel Courses, Minimum Height Trees, Find All Possible Recipes, Network Delay Time, Cheapest Flights Within K Stops.

pages.title: Backtracking
pages.subtitle: Choose, explore, undo — systematically enumerate possibilities.

panels.heading: Backtracking = Exploring a Decision Tree
panels.body:
Make choices step by step. When a path ends, undo the last choice and try another.
Diagram: from START, choose A or choose B; explore down the tree, undo back up.
Think of it as a tree of choices. You go down, and back up!

panels.heading: Canonical Example: Subsets of [1,2,3]
panels.body:
At each index, decide: include the number or exclude it.
Input: [1,2,3]
Diagram: a binary tree starting from [], branching on include/exclude 1, then 2, then 3; the eight leaves are the subsets.
Output (all subsets): [], [1], [2], [3], [1,2], [1,3], [2,3], [1,2,3]
Each path from root to leaf is one valid subset!

panels.heading: The Backtracking Template
panels.body:
choose -> apply the choice, update state
recurse -> explore deeper
unchoose -> undo the choice, restore state
Choose -> recurse -> unchoose. That's the heart of it!

panels.heading: Common Uses
panels.body:
Permutations: arrange all items in every possible order. [1,2,3] -> 123, 132, 213, 231, 312, 321.
Combinations: choose k items from n items (ignore order). C(5,3) -> {1,2,3}, {1,2,4}, ..., {3,4,5}.
N-Queens: place N queens on an NxN board so that no two attack each other.
Other problems: Sudoku, word search, partitioning, graph coloring, subset sum, Hamiltonian path, & more!

panels.heading: Pruning: Cut Invalid Branches Early
panels.body:
Use constraints to avoid exploring hopeless paths.
Example: N-Queens: if a queen is attacked on placement, don't recurse down that branch.
Pruning doesn't change the answer — it just saves a lot of time!

panels.heading: Complexity: Exponential (Usually)
panels.body:
Backtracking may explore O(b^d) states (branching factor b, depth d). States explored grow exponentially with depth.
Rule of thumb: small n -> feasible; medium n -> pruning essential; large n -> usually hard.
No free lunch. Prune smart. Choose wisely.

panels.heading: Pitfalls to Avoid
panels.body:
Shared mutable path: forgetting to copy the path when saving a solution. Bad: output.add(path) — saved results change as the path changes ([1,2] -> [2,3] -> [3]). Good: output.add(path.copy()).
Forgetting to undo: state leaks into other branches and corrupts results. Bad: choose(...), recurse(...), # missing unchoose! Good: choose(...), recurse(...), unchoose(...).

panels.heading: Quick Checklist
panels.body:
Define state clearly.
List all choices at each step.
Validate or prune before recursing.
Choose -> recurse -> unchoose.
Record solutions properly (copy if needed).
Test with tiny inputs and edge cases.
Keep calm, backtrack on!

pages.footer: Make a choice. Explore it. Undo it cleanly.
pages.summary: Explains backtracking as walking a decision tree with a choose, recurse, unchoose template, using Subsets of [1,2,3] (include or exclude each number) as the example. Covers permutations, combinations, N-Queens, pruning, exponential complexity and copy/undo pitfalls.

panels:
Backtracking is a depth-first search over an implicit tree of partial solutions: the tree is generated by the choices, not stored. The defining discipline is that every change to the shared state is reversed when the call returns, so each frame sees the state exactly as its parent left it.

It differs from plain DFS on an explicit graph because of that undo step, and from dynamic programming (DP) in what it does with repeated work. Backtracking walks every path, so it is the tool when you must output all solutions. If you only need a count or an optimum and different paths reach the same remaining subproblem, memoization (DP) merges them and wins exponentially. Recursion depth equals the number of decisions, which is usually small enough for the call stack.

There are 2^n subsets, and the average size is n / 2, so any enumeration needs Omega(n * 2^n) work just to write the output; the standard solution is O(n * 2^n) because each recorded subset is copied. The include/exclude tree has 2^(n+1) - 1 nodes and 2^n leaves. The popular for-loop formulation (choose a next index at or after start) records a subset at every node instead, so it has just 2^n nodes.

That version produces [], [1], [1,2], [1,2,3], [1,3], [2], [2,3], [3], not the size-sorted list shown. For input with duplicates (Subsets II), sort first and skip a value equal to its predecessor at the same level: if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue. A bitmask loop over 0 to 2^n - 1 is an iterative alternative for small n.

The invariant: on entering backtrack(state), the state contains exactly the choices made along the path from the root; on returning, it is restored to what it was on entry. By induction this holds if each choose is paired with an unchoose and each recursive call obeys the same rule. Record solutions as copies, since the path object keeps changing.

Fit the template to the problem. Permutations use a used array or in-place swaps. Combinations and subsets use a start index so that choices only move forward, which prevents counting {1, 2} and {2, 1} as different. For existence questions (Sudoku, Word Search), return True up the stack to short-circuit as soon as one solution is found. Always put the solution check before the loop, and choose the order of candidates so that the most constrained decisions come first.

Permutations have n! leaves; with copying, O(n * n!). For duplicate inputs (Permutations II), sort and skip a value equal to its predecessor when the predecessor is not currently used. Combinations number C(n, k); C(5, 3) = 10, matching the list. Prune loops with i <= n - (k - len(path)) + 1 so that you never start a branch that cannot reach size k. Combination Sum, where an element may be reused, recurses with the same index.

N-Queens: there are 2 solutions for n = 4 and 92 for n = 8. Place one queen per row, so rows never conflict, and keep sets for columns and for the two diagonal families (r - c and r + c) to test a square in O(1). Others: Word Search, Palindrome Partitioning, Generate Parentheses, Sudoku.

Pruning keeps the result identical but can shrink the search by orders of magnitude; it does not change the exponential worst case in general. Types: feasibility pruning (a constraint is already violated), bound pruning (even the best completion cannot beat the best answer so far, called branch and bound), duplicate and symmetry skipping, and ordering heuristics that fail early.

Soundness is the rule: prune only when no valid solution can lie in that subtree. Example, Combination Sum: sort the candidates, then stop the loop when a candidate exceeds the remaining target, since every later candidate is at least as large. In N-Queens, the column and diagonal sets are what reduce the n^n raw placements toward something far smaller. A pruning test must be cheap relative to the work it saves, or it makes things slower.

The b^d estimate is nodes explored, multiplied by the work per node. Concrete anchors: subsets O(n * 2^n), permutations O(n * n!), and a fully branching tree with b = 2 and d = 30 already has about a billion leaves. Practical limits: 2^n is feasible up to n of about 20 to 25, and n! up to roughly 10 or 11 (10! is 3.6 million, 12! is 479 million).

Space excluding output is O(d) for the recursion plus the path. If different paths lead to the same remaining state, as in Word Break or Partition Equal Subset Sum, memoize and the problem becomes DP with polynomial states. To bound a solution, count leaves and multiply by the cost per leaf; if the count exceeds about 10^8, look for a smarter idea instead of micro-optimizing.

The shared-path bug: output.append(path) stores a reference, so later mutations change saved results, and at the end every entry becomes the same (usually empty) list. Copy at record time: path[:] or list(path). Forgetting to undo leaks state into sibling branches. A subtler variant is returning early between choose and unchoose, for example an early return placed after choosing; use structure that guarantees the undo, or restore before returning.

Strings are immutable, so passing path + ch as an argument needs no undo, at the price of copying. Do not mutate a list you are iterating over. Duplicates in the input generate duplicate outputs unless you sort and skip. In Python, recursion deeper than about 1000 frames raises RecursionError, which matters for grid searches. Keep counters local to a call, not global across test cases.

Add a few decisions to the checklist. Pick a compact state: an index, a remaining target, a bitmask. Decide the return type up front: collect all solutions, count them, return a boolean to short-circuit, or track a best value with pruning. Estimate the number of leaves before coding to check feasibility.

Tiny cases to test: n = 0, where subsets and permutations should return [[]] (one empty arrangement), not []; n = 1; all-duplicate input; and inputs with no solution, where the result should be empty rather than an error. Add a debug print on entry and exit to confirm the path is restored. If a candidate appears multiple times in the output, you probably forgot the start index or the duplicate skip. Finally, check that your base case also handles a solution reached with no remaining choices.
deeper.further: Use backtracking when the problem says generate all, list every, or find any arrangement that satisfies constraints, and the input is small (n up to roughly 20) or heavily constrained. Siblings: plain DFS on a graph or tree (no undo needed, no enumeration of paths), dynamic programming (counts or optima when subproblems repeat), greedy (one provably safe choice, no search), and BFS (fewest steps). The key test: must you output every solution, or only a number? If only a number and states repeat, memoize instead. Follow-ups: Permutations, Combination Sum, Subsets II, Palindrome Partitioning, N-Queens, Word Search, Generate Parentheses, Sudoku Solver.

pages.title: 1D Dynamic Programming
pages.subtitle: Define a state, write a recurrence, keep only what matters.

panels.heading: The DP Recipe
panels.body:
1. State: what does dp[i] represent? Define the meaning precisely.
2. Transition: how do we go from smaller states (i-2, i-1) to i? Write the recurrence.
3. Base case: what are the simplest states? Anchor the recursion.
4. Order: in what order do we compute states? Top-down w/ memo or bottom-up.

panels.heading: Canonical 1D DP Example: House Robber
panels.body:
Problem: given nums, rob houses in a line such that no two adjacent houses are robbed. Maximize money.
nums = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1] (indices 0-4).

panels.heading: Optimal Answer
panels.body:
Max money = 12
One optimal choice: rob houses at indices 0, 2 and 4 (no two adjacent).
2 + 9 + 1 = 12

panels.heading: Recurrence
panels.body:
dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i])
At index i, either: skip house i -> dp[i-1]; take house i -> dp[i-2] + nums[i]. Take the better of the two.

panels.heading: Rolling Variables (Keep Only What Matters)
panels.body:
We only need the last two states: prev2 = dp[i-2], prev1 = dp[i-1], curr = dp[i].
Initialize: prev2 = 0, prev1 = 0.
Process nums = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1] (take = prev2 + nums[i], skip = prev1, curr = max(take, skip)):
i = 0: take 0 + 2 = 2, skip 0, curr 2, (prev2, prev1) = (0, 2)
i = 1: take 0 + 7 = 7, skip 2, curr 7, (2, 7)
i = 2: take 2 + 9 = 11, skip 7, curr 11, (7, 11)
i = 3: take 7 + 3 = 10, skip 11, curr 11, (11, 11)
i = 4: take 11 + 1 = 12, skip 11, curr 12, (11, 12)
Final answer = prev1 = 12

panels.heading: Clean & Readable Code (O(1) Space)
panels.code:
def rob(nums):
    prev2 = 0    # dp[i-2]
    prev1 = 0    # dp[i-1]
    for x in nums:
        take = prev2 + x    # take current house
        skip = prev1        # skip current house
        curr = take if take > skip else skip
        prev2, prev1 = prev1, curr
    return prev1

# Example
nums = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]
print(rob(nums))  # 12

panels.heading: Recognize: Include / Exclude Pattern
panels.body:
dp[i] = max(exclude i, include i)
Exclude i: do not take nums[i]. Best up to i-1 -> dp[i-1].
Include i: take nums[i]. Then must skip i-1. Best up to i-2 + nums[i] -> dp[i-2] + nums[i].

panels.heading: Common Pitfalls
panels.body:
Wrong base cases: leads to all answers being off. Double-check dp[0], dp[1].
Using future states: using dp[i+1] or other future states breaks the subproblem structure.
Overbuilding the array: storing the whole dp[] when only O(1) space is needed.

pages.footer: What is the best answer up to here? Write that state first.
pages.summary: Lays out the DP recipe (state, transition, base case, order) and solves House Robber with dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]), reduced to two rolling variables for O(1) space. Highlights the include/exclude pattern and common DP mistakes.

panels:
The recipe works because of two properties: optimal substructure (the best answer for the whole is built from best answers for parts) and overlapping subproblems (the same parts recur). For House Robber, the plain recursion f(i) = max(f(i-1), f(i-2) + a[i]) is exponential, roughly 1.618^n, like naive Fibonacci, because the same f values are recomputed. Memoizing it creates only n distinct subproblems at O(1) each, so O(n).

Top-down (memoized recursion) is easier to derive; bottom-up avoids recursion limits and allows space compression. Define the state exactly: 'best using houses 0..i' is a different state from 'best that robs house i', and the final answer extraction differs (dp[n-1] versus max over all dp). Prove correctness by induction on i.

Why not brute force: the number of valid subsets with no two adjacent houses grows like Fibonacci, exponentially. Why not greedy (take the biggest house, then the biggest allowed): on [5, 6, 5] greedy takes 6 and is stuck with 6, while robbing both 5s gives 10.

Edge cases: an empty array returns 0, one house returns nums[0], two houses return the larger one. The recurrence handles all of them if the two rolling values start at 0. Variants: House Robber II (houses in a circle): the first and last are adjacent, so return max(rob(nums[0..n-2]), rob(nums[1..n-1])), with n = 1 as a special case. House Robber III (a tree): a DFS returning a (rob this node, skip this node) pair. Delete and Earn reduces to House Robber after summing values by number.

The optimum of 12 comes from houses 0, 2, and 4: 2 + 9 + 1 (houses 1 and 2 are adjacent, so 7 + 9 = 16 is not allowed). Competing choices are all worse: houses 1 and 3 give 10, houses 1 and 4 give 8, houses 0 and 3 give 5.

To recover which houses, keep the whole prefix table: dp = [2, 7, 11, 11, 12]. Walk backward from the end: at index 4, dp[4] = 12 differs from dp[3] = 11, so house 4 was taken; jump to index 2, where 11 differs from dp[1] = 7, so take house 2; jump to index 0, take house 0. If dp[i] equals dp[i-1], house i was skipped. The O(1)-space version cannot do this reconstruction, which is its one cost.

Proof of the recurrence, with dp[i] defined as the best total using houses 0..i only. An optimal solution either skips house i, which leaves an optimal solution for houses 0..i-1, worth dp[i-1], or takes house i, which forbids house i-1 and leaves an optimal solution for houses 0..i-2, worth dp[i-2] + nums[i]. The cases are exhaustive, so the maximum is correct. Base values: dp[-1] = dp[-2] = 0, meaning nothing to rob.

Notice that dp[i-1] may or may not include house i-1; it is the best over the whole prefix, which is why dp is nondecreasing. The alternative state 'best that robs i' needs a max over all j <= i-2 and is clumsier. Computed table for the example: [2, 7, 11, 11, 12]. Time O(n), space O(n) with the array.

Only two earlier values are ever read, so memory drops from O(n) to O(1). The classic update bug is writing prev1 = curr before prev2 = prev1, so prev2 ends up equal to curr; the tuple assignment prev2, prev1 = prev1, curr avoids it by evaluating the right side first.

Starting both values at 0 represents the empty prefix and a nonexistent house before the first, so n = 0 returns 0 and n = 1 returns nums[0] with no special cases. General rule: if the recurrence reads the last k states, keep k variables; if it can read any earlier state (as Longest Increasing Subsequence does), the table cannot be compressed this way. You also give up reconstruction of the chosen items, unless you store decisions separately.

Quick tests, tracing the code: [] gives 0; [5] gives 5; [2, 1, 1, 2] gives 4, taking houses 0 and 3 (steps: 2, 2, 3, 4); [1, 2, 3, 1] gives 4; [2, 7, 9, 3, 1] gives 12. Time O(n), space O(1).

Large totals: with many houses and big values, sums need 64-bit integers in C++ or Java; Python handles it. The values here are nonnegative. If negatives were allowed, the max with the skip branch already keeps the answer from dropping below 0, since robbing nothing is permitted. Style: curr = max(take, skip) is clearer than the conditional. The scan reads each number once, so this is optimal up to constants: any correct algorithm must look at every house.

Include or exclude is the general shape: each element is either used or not, with a constraint tying neighboring choices together. Siblings: Climbing Stairs (dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2], counting rather than maximizing; the answer is Fibonacci F(n+1), which exceeds a 32-bit int at n = 46), Min Cost Climbing Stairs, Decode Ways (count valid one- and two-digit splits, careful with zeros), Coin Change (dp[a] = 1 + min over coins of dp[a - c], O(amount * coins), initialize with infinity not 0), Maximum Subarray (Kadane: best ending here = max(x, best + x)), and Longest Increasing Subsequence (O(n^2), or O(n log n) with a tails array).

Wrong base cases: for i = 1, dp[i-2] is dp[-1], which in Python silently reads the last element. Pad the array or use rolling variables. Initial value of zero is wrong for 'maximum' when all values may be negative and you must take at least one (Kadane needs the first element or negative infinity). Min problems need an infinity sentinel that will not overflow when you add to it.

State confusion: if dp[i] means 'ending exactly at i', the answer is the max over all dp, not dp[n-1]. Counting problems often ask for the result modulo 10^9 + 7, so reduce after each addition. Top-down solutions can hit the recursion limit near n of about 1000 in Python. Over-building the table costs memory, not correctness.
deeper.further: Suspect 1D DP when you scan a sequence, must choose per position, and the best answer at i depends on a bounded set of earlier answers; the question asks for a max, min, count, or yes/no, and plain recursion shows the same arguments repeating. Siblings: greedy (try a 3-element counterexample first), 2D DP (the state needs two indices or an extra parameter such as remaining capacity), backtracking (when you must list solutions rather than count them), and binary search on the answer. Follow-ups: Climbing Stairs, House Robber II, Coin Change, Longest Increasing Subsequence, Decode Ways, Word Break, Maximum Subarray, Partition Equal Subset Sum.

pages.title: 2D Dynamic Programming
pages.subtitle: Let every cell summarize a smaller subproblem.

panels.heading: Grid State dp[r][c]
panels.body:
r: row index 0..m-1; c: col index 0..n-1.
dp[r][c] = answer for subproblem that ends at cell (r, c).
Use only previously computed states (typically from top or left).

panels.heading: Canonical Example: Unique Paths (3x7)
panels.body:
Start (0,0), end (2,6).
Move only right or down. How many ways to reach the end?
This is the poster child for 2D DP.

panels.heading: Recurrence
panels.body:
dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]
(from top: come from above) + (from left: come from left)
Base cases: dp[0][0] = 1; first row: dp[0][c] = 1 (all c); first column: dp[r][0] = 1 (all r).

panels.heading: Readable Code (Python)
Common 2D DP Patterns
panels.body:
A) Edit distance: dp[i][j] = min cost to convert s[0..i-1] -> t[0..j-1]. Transitions: if s[i-1] == t[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]; else: 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]).
B) Longest common subsequence (LCS): dp[i][j] = LCS length of s[0..i-1] and t[0..j-1]. Transitions: if s[i-1] == t[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; else: max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
C) Grid with obstacles: count paths avoiding obstacles (#). Let grid[r][c] = 1 if blocked else 0. Recurrence (when cell is free): dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]. If blocked: dp[r][c] = 0.

panels.heading: Space Compression: One Row
panels.body:
Before (2D): rows r-1, r, r+1. After (1D row): dp[c] for columns 0..n-1.
Update left -> right using one row array: dp[c] = dp[c] + dp[c-1].

panels.heading: Pitfalls to Avoid
panels.body:
Dimensions (rows vs cols): be consistent: dp has size [m][n]. Use 0..m-1 for rows, 0..n-1 for cols.
Initialization (base cases): don't forget first row and first column! They seed the entire table.
Iteration direction: compute in an order that guarantees dependencies are ready (top-to-bottom, left-to-right). Wrong order -> wrong answers.

pages.footer: Define what one cell means — then build the grid.
pages.summary: Teaches 2D dynamic programming on a grid by solving Unique Paths: each cell's count is the sum of the cell above and the cell to the left, with the first row and column set to 1. Also covers edit distance, LCS, grids with obstacles, and compressing the table to one row.

panels:
A DP table has one cell per state and each cell costs O(1) to fill from earlier cells, so a grid DP is O(m * n) time. The fill order must respect dependencies; if the dependencies form a cycle (for instance when moves can go up and left too), DP does not apply and you need graph search.

Be exact about what an index means. In grid problems, dp[r][c] concerns cell (r, c) and the table is m by n. In string problems such as edit distance and LCS, dp[i][j] concerns prefixes of lengths i and j, so the table is (m + 1) by (n + 1), with row 0 and column 0 for the empty prefix. Mixing the two is a classic off-by-one. Typical states: positions in two sequences, or (item index, remaining capacity) for knapsack.

There is a closed form: every path has (m - 1) + (n - 1) = 8 moves, and choosing which 2 are downward gives C(8, 2) = 28, matching the table. The DP extends to obstacles; the closed form is a check. For 100 by 100 the answer is C(198, 99), around 2.3 x 10^58, which overflows 64 bits (LeetCode guarantees the result fits in 2 x 10^9).

Compute binomials iteratively as res = res * (N - k + i) // i, which stays an integer at every step. A 1 by n or m by 1 grid has exactly one path. Variants: Unique Paths II (obstacles), Minimum Path Sum (take min of the two predecessors; the border cannot be filled with 1s but with running sums), Triangle, and Dungeon Game (fill backward from the goal).

Correctness: the last move into (r, c) is either downward from (r-1, c) or rightward from (r, c-1). These cases are exhaustive and disjoint, so the counts add. The border cells have exactly one predecessor, which is why they are all 1s when there are no obstacles. A uniform trick: pad the table with an extra row and column of zeros and seed a single 1 next to the start, so one formula covers every cell.

A Python-specific hazard: dp[r-1][c] with r = 0 does not fail, it wraps to the last row and silently corrupts the answer; handle the borders explicitly. For Minimum Path Sum the base cases are cumulative sums along the first row and column, not ones. If the problem allows moving in four directions, states depend on each other cyclically, and DP no longer applies.

The table is Pascal's triangle rotated: dp[r][c] = C(r + c, r). Row 2 reads C(2,2) = 1, C(3,2) = 3, C(4,2) = 6, C(5,2) = 10, C(6,2) = 15, C(7,2) = 21, C(8,2) = 28, and row 1 reads 1, 2, ..., 7 as C(c+1, 1) shows.

Symmetry: a 3 by 7 grid and a 7 by 3 grid have the same answer, so you can iterate over the smaller dimension to shrink memory to O(min(m, n)). When debugging a DP, compute two or three cells by hand and compare with the program. Printing the table on a small case is the fastest way to find an initialization bug. Fill order is row by row, left to right, so both neighbors are final when a cell is computed.

The code is correct: O(m * n) time and space. The initialization loops can be replaced by dp = [[1] * n for _ in range(m)]. Edge cases: when m = 1 or n = 1 the nested loop does not run and dp[m-1][n-1] is 1, as it should be.

The most common Python bug in grid DP is dp = [[0] * n] * m. That creates m references to one list, so writing dp[1][1] changes every row. Always build rows with a comprehension. In C++, vector<vector<int>> dp(m, vector<int>(n, 1)) is safe. Overflow: for large grids the answer exceeds 32 bits, so use long long, though LeetCode keeps the answer within 2 x 10^9. Returning dp[m-1][n-1] rather than dp[n-1][m-1] is another easy slip when m and n differ.

Edit distance: base cases dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j (delete or insert everything). The three options in the else branch correspond to delete from s (dp[i-1][j]), insert into s (dp[i][j-1]), and replace (dp[i-1][j-1]), plus 1. When characters match, taking the diagonal for free is always optimal. Time O(m * n). LCS has zero base cases and the same shape; to print the subsequence itself you walk backward through the full table.

Obstacles: you cannot just fill the first row and column with 1s. Once an obstacle appears, every later cell in that row or column is unreachable and gets 0; if the start or end is blocked the answer is 0. Related: Longest Palindromic Subsequence equals LCS of s and its reverse; Distinct Subsequences; Interleaving String; Regular Expression Matching; Coin Change II.

In the compressed update dp[c] += dp[c-1], dp[c] on the right still holds the value from the row above, and dp[c-1] was already updated for the current row (the cell to the left), so scanning left to right is exactly right. Start the single row as all 1s, then process rows 1 through m-1. Space becomes O(n); choose n as the smaller dimension.

When the recurrence also needs the diagonal (edit distance, LCS), save the old dp[j-1] in a temporary variable before overwriting it. Direction is tied to dependencies: in the 0/1 knapsack 1D version you must iterate capacity from high to low so an item is not reused, while unbounded knapsack iterates low to high on purpose. The price: you can no longer reconstruct the path, unless you store decisions or use Hirschberg's method.

Dimension mix-ups: dp[m][n] means m rows and n columns; string DP needs the extra row and column. Initialization: first row and column seed everything, so wrong values spread; for minimum problems use a large sentinel, but not INT_MAX, since adding 1 to it overflows in C++ (use something like 10^9). Iteration direction: every cell must be computed after the cells it reads; reversed loops give silently wrong tables.

Other traps: aliasing rows with [[0]*n]*m, and off-by-one when strings are 0-indexed but dp is length-indexed (compare s[i-1] with t[j-1]). Test 1 by 1 and 1 by n grids, and empty strings: edit distance between '' and 'abc' must be 3. Memoized recursion is a fine alternative, but its depth is about m + n, which is safe unless the grid is huge.
deeper.further: Move from 1D to 2D DP when one parameter is not enough: two sequences being compared (edit distance, LCS), a grid with right/down moves, knapsack-style (item index plus capacity), or interval problems where dp[i][j] covers the substring from i to j. Siblings: 1D DP (a single index), memoized DFS (the same recurrence written top-down), BFS or Dijkstra (grids where you may move in all four directions), backtracking (list the actual solutions), and greedy. If the moves only go forward and you need a count or optimum, think DP. Follow-ups: Minimum Path Sum, Unique Paths II, LCS, Edit Distance, Coin Change II, Target Sum, 0/1 Knapsack, Interleaving String, Maximal Square.

pages.title: Greedy Algorithms
pages.subtitle: Make the locally safe move that preserves the best future.

panels.heading: Greedy Proof Mindset
panels.body:
Why is this move safe?
Greedy choice property: a locally optimal choice can be part of an optimal solution.
Optimal substructure: optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems.
Prove it: use exchange argument or stay-ahead intuition.

panels.heading: Canonical: Jump Game
panels.body:
nums = [2, 3, 1, 1, 4] (indices 0-4)
Goal: reach last index (4) starting from index 0. At each index, jump up to nums[i] steps forward.

panels.heading: Farthest-Reachable Frontier
panels.body:
We don't choose the next jump. We extend the frontier as far as possible.
Diagram: indices 0-4 with values 2, 3, 1, 1, 4; arcs show reachable jumps up to the goal at index 4.
i = current index; farthest = farthest index we can reach so far.
Idea: sweep i from left to right. Keep extending farthest. If we ever step beyond farthest, we're stuck.

panels.heading: Clean & Readable Code
panels.body:
Extend the frontier, don't jump blind.
Time: O(n). Space: O(1).

panels.heading: Other Classic Uses
panels.body:
Interval scheduling: sort by earliest finish time. Pick the next interval that starts after the last chosen one finishes. Maximizes the number of non-overlapping intervals.
Gas station: find starting station to complete the circuit. Greedy reset when tank goes negative. Works because of total sum and greedy choice.

panels.heading: Exchange Argument & Stay-Ahead Intuition
panels.body:
Exchange argument: if an optimal solution makes a different choice, we can swap it with our greedy choice without making it worse.
Stay-ahead intuition: after each greedy choice, our solution is never behind any optimal solution. Sometimes it's even ahead.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Greedy without proof: not every problem is greedy. Always prove greedy-choice property (or you'll get WA).
Confusing locally best with globally safe: the goal is a choice that keeps the best future possible, not just the best immediate payoff.

pages.footer: Track the frontier — if you can reach it, you can extend it.
pages.summary: Explains greedy algorithms and how to justify them (greedy choice property, exchange argument, stay-ahead), then solves Jump Game by sweeping left to right and tracking the farthest reachable index. Mentions interval scheduling and gas station as other greedy classics.

panels:
The two properties are the greedy-choice property (some optimal solution contains the greedy first choice) and optimal substructure (what remains after that choice is a smaller instance of the same problem). The exchange argument proves the first: take an optimal solution that differs from greedy, swap in the greedy choice, show it is no worse, and repeat. Stay-ahead proves it by induction: after every step greedy is at least as good as any other strategy, by a stated measure.

Greedy is not universal. Coin change with coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins) but 3 + 3 uses two. It does work for US coins. Typical cost is a sort plus one pass, O(n log n). If you cannot prove it, hunt for small counterexamples, or use DP.

For [2, 3, 1, 1, 4] the answer is true; one route is 0 to 1 (jump 1), then 1 to 4 (jump 3). A brute-force search over jump choices is exponential, and a reachability DP is O(n^2). The greedy works because of a key lemma: the set of reachable indices is always a contiguous prefix [0, farthest]. If you can reach j by jumping from i, you can also reach every index between i and j with a shorter jump, so no gaps appear.

Failure example: [3, 2, 1, 0, 4]. The frontier stalls at 3, then i = 4 exceeds it, so the answer is false. A single element is trivially true (you are already at the last index). A 0 is only fatal when it sits at the frontier. Values are nonnegative by definition.

Invariant: before processing index i, every index in [0, farthest] is reachable, and farthest is the maximum of j + nums[j] over all reachable j already scanned. Induction gives it. The failure test is justified: if i > farthest, no reachable index can jump to i or past it, so the end is unreachable. Add an early return as soon as farthest >= n - 1.

Jump Game II (minimum number of jumps) uses the same sweep: keep currentEnd and farthest; whenever i reaches currentEnd, increment the jump count and set currentEnd = farthest. It is a BFS in disguise, where each level is the range of indices reachable with j jumps. O(n) time, O(1) space. Take care not to include i + nums[i] from an unreachable i, which is why the stuck check comes before the update.

Order matters: check i > farthest before updating farthest. For [0, 5, 0, 0], if you updated first, index 1 (unreachable, because nums[0] = 0) would push farthest to 6 and wrongly return true; the check in the right order returns false at i = 1. Time O(n), space O(1).

An equivalent backward formulation: set goal = n - 1, then for i from n-2 down to 0, if i + nums[i] >= goal, set goal = i; the answer is goal == 0. It tracks the leftmost index that can reach the end. Both are the same idea from opposite directions. Overflow is not a concern for typical bounds, but with huge values use 64-bit sums for i + nums[i]. Python's enumerate keeps the loop tidy.

Interval scheduling: sort by finish time and take each interval starting at or after the last chosen finish (use > if touching intervals conflict). Sorting by start fails: for [1,10], [2,3], [4,5], start-order picks [1,10] alone while the optimum is two intervals. Non-overlapping Intervals asks for minimum removals, n minus the maximum kept; Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons is the same sweep.

Gas Station: if total gas is less than total cost, no start exists. Otherwise, scan once, and whenever the tank goes negative at i, restart from i + 1. This is valid because any start between the old start and i would have had a nonnegative tank on the way and so would fail at or before i as well. The total-surplus check guarantees the final candidate completes the loop.

Exchange argument for interval scheduling: let g be the interval with the earliest finish time, and let o1 be the first interval of some optimal solution. Since g finishes no later than o1, replacing o1 with g keeps everything non-overlapping and the size unchanged, so an optimal solution containing g exists. Recurse on the intervals that start after g ends. That is the full proof.

Stay-ahead for Jump Game: after scanning i indices, the greedy frontier is at least as far as the frontier of any other strategy. In an interview, give a two or three sentence version of such an argument, enough to answer 'why can't another choice do better?'. Contrast with DP, which considers every choice; greedy considers one, which is faster but must be justified. Search for counterexamples on arrays of size 3 or 4 first.

Greedy without proof is the main risk: a plausible rule that fails hidden tests. 'Largest first' or 'smallest first' are the usual wrong guesses, as in coin change with [1, 3, 4]. The right question is not 'which choice looks best now?' but 'which choice leaves the most freedom for what follows?', which is why interval scheduling sorts by finish time.

Watch the sort key and tie-breaking, and decide whether touching endpoints conflict. Off-by-one in reachability (i > farthest versus i >= farthest) flips answers. Remember the last-index cases: n = 1 is true. A practical safeguard is stress testing: generate small random inputs, compare your greedy with a brute force or DP, and look for the first disagreement. Some problems that feel greedy need extra structure, such as Remove K Digits with a monotonic stack.
deeper.further: Consider greedy when a problem asks for a minimum or maximum count of something and a simple rule ('earliest finish', 'smallest first', 'farthest reach') seems to keep every option open: scheduling, covering, reachability, and resource-allocation questions. Siblings: DP (considers all choices; the fallback when a counterexample appears), BFS (fewest steps; Jump Game II is BFS in disguise), heap-assisted greedy (pick the best available at each step, as in Task Scheduler and Meeting Rooms II), and interval sweeps. First try to break your rule on four elements; if it breaks, move to DP. Follow-ups: Jump Game II, Gas Station, Non-overlapping Intervals, Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons, Partition Labels, Task Scheduler, Candy.

pages.title: Intervals
pages.subtitle: Sort by start, compare ends, and merge overlapping time.

panels.heading: Closed Interval Timeline
panels.body:
We work with closed intervals [start, end]. Both endpoints are included.
Example: [2,5] and [5,8] on a timeline. Touching at 5 means overlap.
Closed: [a,b] includes a and b.

panels.heading: Canonical Example: Merge Intervals
panels.body:
Input: [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]
Merged result: [1,6], [8,10], [15,18]
First two overlap -> [1,6]. Others don't -> keep as is.

panels.heading: Sort by Start, Then Compare
panels.body:
Sort by start. Sweep left to right.
[1,3]: — (first) -> add [1,3]
[2,6]: 2 <= 3 -> yes -> merge
[8,10]: 8 <= 6 -> no -> add [8,10]
[15,18]: 15 <= 10 -> no -> add [15,18]
Overlap condition for closed intervals: current.start <= last.end

panels.heading: Merge: End = Max Ends
panels.body:
When overlapping, extend the last interval.
new_end = max(last.end, current.end)
Example: last [1,3] and current [2,6] merge into [1,6].
Keep intervals in the result non-overlapping and sorted by start.

panels.heading: Readable Pseudocode
panels.body: Flow: intervals empty? Yes -> return []. No -> sort by start -> iterate: if curr.start <= last.end, last.end = max(last.end, curr.end); otherwise res.append(last), last = curr. Finally res.append(last) and return res.
panels.code:
function merge(intervals):
  if intervals is empty: return []
  sort intervals by start ascending
  res = []
  last = copy of intervals[0]  # don't mutate the input
  for i from 1 to n-1:
    curr = intervals[i]
    if curr.start <= last.end:
      last.end = max(last.end, curr.end)
    else:
      res.append(last)
      last = curr
  res.append(last)
  return res

panels.heading: Common Uses
panels.body:
Meeting rooms: find the minimum rooms required for all meetings.
Insert interval: insert a new interval into existing non-overlapping intervals.
Sweep line algorithms: used in counting overlaps, union length, and more.

panels.heading: Pitfalls: Touching Endpoints
panels.body:
Closed intervals [a,b]: [1,3] and [3,5] — since 3 is included, they overlap. They should merge to [1,5].
Half-open intervals [a,b): [1,3) and [3,5) — since 3 is excluded, they do not overlap. They stay separate.
Know your problem's interval semantics!

panels.heading: Pitfalls: Sorting
panels.body:
Correct: sort by start: [1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18].
Wrong: sort by end: [1,3], [8,10], [2,6], [15,18]. Leads to incorrect comparisons and wrong merges.

pages.footer: Sort first. Then let the current end decide.
pages.summary: Solves Merge Intervals by sorting intervals by start, then sweeping and merging whenever the current start is at or before the last end (taking the max end). Covers closed vs half-open endpoint semantics, sorting mistakes, and related problems like meeting rooms and insert interval.

panels:
Two closed intervals [a, b] and [c, d] overlap exactly when a <= d and c <= b, regardless of which comes first; for half-open intervals the test is a < d and c < b. A degenerate closed interval [x, x] is a single point and is valid; a half-open [x, x) is empty. Confirm with the interviewer or the examples which convention applies.

Also ask: may the input be unsorted? Can intervals be identical or nested? Are coordinates negative or huge? Is start <= end guaranteed? For lengths of closed integer intervals use end - start + 1, and watch for overflow near 32-bit limits. Everything below assumes a list of [start, end] pairs and the closed convention used by Merge Intervals.

Sorting costs O(n log n) and dominates; the sweep after it is O(n); the output takes O(n) space. The naive alternative compares all pairs, O(n^2), and still needs repeated passes because merging two intervals can create overlap with a third, so chains require transitive closure.

Edge cases: empty input returns []; a single interval returns itself; duplicates collapse; and containment must work: [1, 10] and [2, 3] merge into [1, 10], not [1, 3]. That is why the merged end is a max, never a plain assignment. The result is sorted and disjoint, with a strict gap between neighbors: each next start is greater than the previous end. Unsorted input such as [[8,10],[1,3],[2,6]] must be sorted first; Python's default list ordering sorts by start, then end, which is fine here.

Proof sketch of the sweep. After sorting by start, every unprocessed interval starts at or after the current one. If curr.start > last.end, no later interval can reach back to last either, since later starts are even larger, so last is final. If curr.start <= last.end, then curr starts inside last (its start is at least last.start by sorting), so they overlap and the union is a single interval from last.start to max of the ends. Ties on start do not matter.

The crucial detail is comparing against last.end, the merged end, not the previous input interval's end. With [1,10], [2,3], [4,5], the third interval must be tested against 10 (it merges), not against 3 (it would wrongly stay separate).

Merging uses the max of the ends because the current interval may be contained in the last one. A subtle trap: if last = intervals[0] aliases the caller's list, the update last.end = max(...) mutates the input, so copy it (as the pseudocode does) or build the answer directly: for each [s, e] in sorted order, if res is non-empty and s <= res[-1][1], set res[-1][1] = max(res[-1][1], e); else append [s, e]. That version also handles the empty list with no special case and has no final flush step.

Both versions are O(n log n) time and O(n) output space. Each interval is touched once after sorting. Remember that adjacent output intervals never touch: if they did, they would have merged.

Common slips: forgetting the final res.append(last) loses the last group; forgetting the empty-input guard crashes on intervals[0]; sorting by end or not sorting at all; using < instead of <= for closed intervals, which leaves [1,4] and [4,5] unmerged. Test cases worth running: [[1,4],[4,5]] gives [[1,5]]; [[1,4],[0,4]] gives [[0,4]]; [[1,4],[0,0]] gives [[0,0],[1,4]]; and [[2,3],[4,5],[6,7],[8,9],[1,10]] gives [[1,10]].

Complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) for the output, plus whatever the sort uses (Python's Timsort needs up to O(n) auxiliary; an in-place quicksort or heapsort uses less). If the input is already sorted by start, as in Insert Interval, the whole job drops to O(n).

Meeting Rooms I: sort by start and check whether any start is less than the previous end (with half-open meaning). Meeting Rooms II asks for the maximum number of simultaneous intervals: sort starts and ends separately and sweep with two pointers, or use a min-heap of end times; both O(n log n). In the sweep-line view, each interval adds +1 at its start and -1 at its end; at equal times process ends first for half-open intervals.

Insert Interval (sorted, disjoint input) needs no sort: add everything ending before the new start, merge everything that overlaps by taking min of starts and max of ends, then add the rest, in O(n). Interval List Intersections walks two sorted lists with two pointers in O(m + n). Others: Employee Free Time, Car Pooling, My Calendar, and the greedy Non-overlapping Intervals.

Semantics decide the comparison. Closed [1,3] and [3,5] share the point 3, so they merge into [1,5]. Half-open [1,3) and [3,5) do not overlap, so they stay separate; the merge condition becomes curr.start < last.end. Real calendars are usually half-open: a meeting ending at 10 does not conflict with one starting at 10. LeetCode's Merge Intervals treats touching intervals as overlapping, while Meeting Rooms treats them as compatible. Read the examples.

For integers, a closed [a, b] equals the half-open [a, b+1), a handy conversion. Floating-point endpoints make equality tests fragile. Zero-length intervals deserve a test. In Car Pooling, passengers leaving at a stop are removed before those boarding at the same stop, which is the half-open rule in disguise.

Sorting by start is what makes the single sweep valid. The page's sort-by-end order is off: [2,6] ends before [8,10], so this example sorts the same either way. A real failure is [1,10], [2,3], [4,5]: sorted by end it becomes [2,3], [4,5], [1,10], so the sweep finalizes [2,3], then meets [1,10], which overlaps that finalized interval, and the output is wrong. Sorting by end is the right key for a different problem, greedy selection of the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals.

Ties in start do not affect merging. Already-sorted input (Insert Interval) skips the cost. In Java, comparators written as a[0] - b[0] can overflow for extreme values; use Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]). Python's list.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) is stable, which is harmless here. If intervals arrive online with queries in between, a sorted container or balanced tree is better than re-sorting.
deeper.further: Reach for interval techniques when the data are ranges on a line (times, positions, ids) and you must merge, insert, count overlaps, find gaps, or schedule. Keywords: overlapping, meetings, free time, minimum rooms. Siblings: greedy selection (sort by end), heap (track the earliest ending interval), sweep line or difference array (counts of active intervals), two pointers on sorted lists (intersections), and segment or balanced trees when intervals arrive online. Quick split: merging means sort by start; maximizing kept non-overlapping intervals means sort by end. Follow-ups: Insert Interval, Meeting Rooms I and II, Non-overlapping Intervals, Interval List Intersections, Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons, Employee Free Time, Car Pooling.

pages.title: Bit Manipulation
pages.subtitle: Use binary structure for constant-space tricks.

panels.heading: Canonical: Single Number
panels.body:
[4, 1, 2, 1, 2] -> 4, using XOR cancellation.
Step 0: start, ans = 0000
Step 1: 4 (0100): 0000 ^ 0100 = 0100
Step 2: 1 (0001): 0100 ^ 0001 = 0101
Step 3: 2 (0010): 0101 ^ 0010 = 0111
Step 4: 1 (0001): 0111 ^ 0001 = 0110
Step 5: 2 (0010): 0110 ^ 0010 = 0100
Pairs cancel out: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. Leftover (odd one out) remains!
ans ^= x; — the whole trick!

panels.heading: Bit Masks: Cheat Sheet
panels.body:
Let mask = (1 << i)  // mask for bit i
Check (is bit i set?): if (x & mask) — true if set (non-zero -> set).
Set (turn on bit i): x |= mask
Clear (turn off bit i): x &= ~mask
Toggle (flip bit i): x ^= mask

panels.heading: Uses in Coding Interviews
panels.body:
Subsets (n elements): iterate mask from 0 to (1<<n)-1. Each mask represents a subset.
Flags (state compression): use bits to store multiple boolean flags. Example: bit 0 = visited, bit 1 = hasKey, bit 2 = blocked, ...
Power of two check: x > 0 and (x & (x - 1)) == 0. Only one bit is set.

panels.heading: Pitfalls to Avoid
panels.body:
Operator precedence: comparison (==, <, >) has higher precedence than bitwise (&, |, ^). Bad: if (x & 1 == 0) // parsed as x & (1 == 0). Good: if ((x & 1) == 0) // what you want.
Signed shifts: right shift on negative signed integers is implementation-defined (often arithmetic shift, keeps the sign bit). Avoid relying on it. Prefer unsigned when doing bit tricks. Example (8-bit): x = -4 = 11111100; x >> 1 -> 11111110 (arithmetic); (unsigned)x >> 1 -> 01111110 (logical).

pages.footer: XOR makes pairs disappear — leaving the odd one out.
pages.summary: Reviews binary place values and the bitwise operators, then solves Single Number by XOR-ing all values so duplicate pairs cancel and the unique number remains. Covers bit mask tricks (check, set, clear, toggle), interview uses, and precedence and signed-shift pitfalls.

panels:
Place values: 101101 is 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45. A w-bit unsigned integer holds 0 to 2^w - 1. Signed integers use two's complement: the top bit carries weight -2^(w-1), so a 32-bit int spans -2^31 to 2^31 - 1, and -x equals ~x + 1; -1 is all ones. The number of bits needed for n is floor(log2 n) + 1, and a power of two has exactly one set bit.

Python integers have unlimited width, with negatives behaving as if sign-extended forever; to emulate 32-bit behavior, mask with & 0xFFFFFFFF and convert back if the top bit is set. Counting set bits (popcount) is easy with Kernighan's loop: while n: n &= n - 1; count += 1, which runs once per set bit. Related warm-ups: Number of 1 Bits, Reverse Bits, Hamming Distance.

For A = 10110 (22), ~A is 01001 only if you keep five bits. In 8 bits the leading zeros flip too, giving 11101001. Left shift 10110 << 2 is 1011000 (88), which widens the value; in a 5-bit register the top bits fall off and you get 11000. Right shift 10110 >> 2 is 101, i.e. 00101 in five bits (22 // 4 = 5).

AND, OR, XOR rows check out: 22 & 13 = 4, 22 | 13 = 31, 22 ^ 13 = 27. Shifts: x << k is x * 2^k when nothing overflows; x >> k is floor(x / 2^k), so an arithmetic shift of a negative number rounds toward negative infinity: -5 >> 1 is -3, whereas C's -5 / 2 gives -2.

Why it works: XOR is commutative and associative, x ^ x = 0, and x ^ 0 = x. The XOR of the whole array rearranges so each pair meets and cancels, leaving only the unpaired element. Time O(n), space O(1), versus O(n) space for a hash set. It requires every other value to appear exactly twice (or an even number of times); negatives work unchanged.

Variants show the idea's reach. Single Number II (others appear three times): count each bit position modulo 3. Single Number III (two unpaired values a and b): XOR everything to get a ^ b, isolate one set bit with d = x & -x, split the numbers into two groups by that bit, and XOR each group. Missing Number: XOR the indices 0 to n with all values.

Beyond the four basics: x & -x isolates the lowest set bit (in two's complement, -x flips everything above that bit), and x & (x - 1) clears it. Use (x >> i) & 1 when you need a clean 0 or 1, since x & mask returns a nonzero value, not necessarily 1.

Width traps: in C or C++, 1 << 31 on a 32-bit int overflows into the sign bit (undefined behavior before C++20), so use 1LL << i or 1ULL << i for large i. In Java, shifting an int by 32 or more uses the count modulo 32, so 1 << 32 is 1; use 1L << i for long values. Python has no such limits, and x & ~mask works because ~mask is simply a negative number with infinite leading ones.

Subset enumeration: for mask in range(1 << n), the set bits select the chosen elements; O(n * 2^n), practical up to n of about 20. Submask enumeration, for sub = mask; sub > 0; sub = (sub - 1) & mask, visits every nonempty submask; summed over all masks, the cost is 3^n. Bitmask DP stores state as a mask: Traveling Salesman runs in O(2^n * n^2), Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets in O(2^n * n).

Power of two: x > 0 and (x & (x - 1)) == 0; the x > 0 check matters, since 0 would pass otherwise. Counting bits via DP: dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1). A 26-bit mask can record which letters a word contains. Avoid the XOR swap trick on aliased variables: x ^= x yields zero.

Precedence: in C, C++, and Java, == binds tighter than &, |, and ^. So x & 1 == 0 parses as x & (1 == 0): C and C++ compile it and give the wrong answer; Java rejects it as a type error. Python is the opposite, since bitwise operators bind tighter than comparisons, so x & 1 == 0 works there; parenthesize anyway for readability.

Signed shifts: right-shifting a negative signed integer was implementation-defined in C and C++ (arithmetic in practice, defined as arithmetic from C++20), while Java offers >> (arithmetic) and >>> (logical). The example is right: -4 as 8 bits is 11111100; arithmetic >> 1 gives 11111110 (-2); a logical shift gives 01111110 (126). Shifting by the full width or more is undefined in C and C++. Prefer unsigned types for bit tricks.
deeper.further: Consider bit manipulation when pairs cancel or parity matters (XOR), when you must enumerate subsets of about 20 or fewer items (bitmasks), when a handful of boolean flags can be packed into one integer for DP states or visited sets, or when the problem is about binary representation: counting bits, powers of two, reversing, adding without a plus. Siblings: hashing and counting (general frequencies at O(n) space), math formulas (such as the sum trick for Missing Number), sorting then scanning, and backtracking (enumerate with undo when state is large). Follow-ups: Number of 1 Bits, Counting Bits, Reverse Bits, Missing Number, Single Number II and III, Sum of Two Integers, Maximum XOR of Two Numbers.

collections.title: Software Engineering
collections.subtitle: From Git to system design
collections.description: Version control, containers and Kubernetes, design patterns, system design, DevOps and the foundations every engineer leans on.

pages.title: Master the Main Git Commands
pages.subtitle: A comic cheat sheet for the commands you'll use most

panels.heading: What Git Does
panels.body:
Tracks changes in your code.
Lets you save versions with commits.
Makes branching and collaboration easier.
Working directory (your files) -> staging area (prepare changes) -> repository (.git, saved history).
Git = time machine for your code.

panels.heading: Start Here
panels.body:
git init — create a new repo in the current folder.
git clone <url> — copy an existing repo.
git remote -v — view connected remotes.
panels.code:
git init
git clone <url>
git remote -v

panels.heading: See Changes / Stage Files
panels.body:
git status — see changed, staged, and untracked files.
git add <file> — stage one file.
git add . — stage all current changes.
git restore --staged <file> — unstage a file.
File (changed) -> stage (staged) -> repo (commit).
panels.code:
git status
git add <file>
git add .
git restore --staged <file>

panels.heading: Commit
panels.body:
git commit -m "message" — save staged changes.
git commit --amend — update the last commit.
Tip: good commit messages = short and specific.
Diagram: commit A -> commit B -> new commit (--amend) replaces the last one.
panels.code:
git commit -m "message"
git commit --amend

panels.heading: Branches
panels.body:
git branch — list branches.
git switch -c feature/login — create and switch to a new branch.
git switch main — move to another branch.
git merge feature/login — merge a branch into the current branch.
Diagram: feature/login branches off main and merges back in.
panels.code:
git branch
git switch -c feature/login
git switch main
git merge feature/login

panels.heading: Push / Pull / Fetch
panels.body:
git push -u origin main — push and set upstream.
git push — send local commits to remote.
git pull — fetch + merge remote changes.
git fetch — download updates without merging.
Your machine pushes to the remote (server); pull and fetch bring changes back.
panels.code:
git push -u origin main
git push
git pull
git fetch

panels.heading: Look Around
panels.body:
git log --oneline --graph --all — compact history view.
git diff — inspect unstaged changes.
git diff --staged — inspect staged changes.
git show <commit> — inspect a specific commit.
Example output of git log --oneline --graph --all: a1b2c3d (HEAD -> main, origin/main) Fix login bug; e4f5a6b Add unit tests; c7d8e9f (feature/login) Add login page; 123abcd Initial commit.
panels.code:
git log --oneline --graph --all
git diff
git diff --staged
git show <commit>

panels.heading: Fix Mistakes
panels.body:
git restore <file> — discard local file changes.
git revert <commit> — make a new commit that undoes an old one.
git reset --soft HEAD~1 — undo last commit, keep changes staged.
git reset --hard HEAD~1 — erase last commit and local changes.
Use --hard carefully. It can't be undone.
panels.code:
git restore <file>
git revert <commit>
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git reset --hard HEAD~1

panels.heading: Useful Extras
panels.body:
git stash — save work temporarily.
git stash pop — restore stashed work.
git tag v1.0.0 — mark a release.
.gitignore — ignore files you don't want tracked.
Simple workflow: edit -> status -> add -> commit -> push.
panels.code:
git stash
git stash pop
git tag v1.0.0

pages.footer: Check. Stage. Commit. Branch. Push.
pages.summary: A tour of everyday Git: how the working directory, staging area and repository relate, plus the core commands for starting a repo, staging, committing, branching, syncing with a remote, inspecting history and undoing mistakes.

panels: Git is a content-addressable object store with a thin naming layer on top. Four object types live in .git/objects: a blob holds file bytes, a tree maps names and modes to blob or tree ids, a commit points to one tree plus zero or more parent commits with author, committer and message, and an annotated tag points to another object. An object's id is the hash (SHA-1 by default, SHA-256 optionally) of a header 'type size' plus its content, so identical content is stored once. A commit is a full snapshot of the tree, not a diff; delta compression happens later in packfiles. History is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of commits, and the 'staging area' is a file, .git/index.

git init creates the .git directory: objects/, refs/, a HEAD file (by default the text 'ref: refs/heads/master', or the branch named in init.defaultBranch, often main), and config. git clone is a macro: init, add a remote called origin with a fetch refspec such as +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*, fetch all objects, create a local branch from the remote's default, and record branch.<name>.remote and .merge so pull and push know their upstream. 'origin' is only a conventional name. git remote -v reads URLs from .git/config; fetch and push URLs can differ, for instance with pushurl, which is why both lines are printed.

The index is a sorted list of entries: path, file mode, blob id, a stage number (0 normally, 1 to 3 during conflicts) and cached stat data used to detect changes quickly. git add hashes the file's current contents, writes a blob into the object store, and updates the entry, so what is staged is a snapshot at the moment of add; later edits show as unstaged again. git status is two comparisons: HEAD against the index (to be committed), and the index against the working tree (not staged). Untracked means no index entry. git restore --staged copies the HEAD version of the path back into the index; it never touches your working file.

git commit runs three steps: write the index out as a tree object, create a commit object with that tree and the current HEAD as parent, and move the current branch ref to the new commit. --amend does not edit anything: it creates a new commit with the old commit's parents and a new tree or message, then moves the branch ref. Because a commit id covers its tree, parents, author and message, any change produces a different id, and all descendants would need new ids as well. The old commit becomes unreachable but stays in the object store and reflog (30 to 90 days by default), which is why amending already-pushed commits causes divergence.

A branch is a ref: a file under .git/refs/heads containing one commit id (or a line in packed-refs). Creating one is writing 41 bytes. HEAD normally holds a symbolic ref to the current branch, so committing moves that branch; a detached HEAD holds a commit id directly, and commits made there are not on any branch. git switch updates HEAD, the index and the working tree to the target commit's tree, refusing if that would overwrite local changes. git merge first finds the merge base. If the current commit is an ancestor of the target, it fast-forwards (just moves the ref). Otherwise it does a three-way merge and records a commit with two parents.

git fetch downloads missing objects and updates remote-tracking refs such as refs/remotes/origin/main; it never changes your local branches or files. git pull is fetch followed by merge of the upstream (or rebase if configured). git push uploads objects and asks the server to move a ref; the server refuses non-fast-forward updates, meaning the remote tip must be an ancestor of what you push. -u stores the upstream in config. Remote-tracking refs are a cached view that can be stale until your next fetch. After rewriting history, prefer --force-with-lease, which refuses if the remote ref no longer matches what you last fetched, over plain --force.

git log walks the DAG, starting from the given commits or refs and following parent pointers; --all starts from every ref, --graph draws the topology, and decorations such as (HEAD -> main, origin/main) are the refs that point at each commit. git diff compares the index with the working tree; --staged compares HEAD with the index; diff HEAD compares HEAD with the working tree, showing staged and unstaged changes together. Diffs are computed on demand, not stored (the default algorithm is Myers; --patience and --histogram sometimes give clearer output). git show prints a commit's message and its diff against its parent (a combined diff for merges). Notation: HEAD~1 is the first parent, HEAD^2 the second parent of a merge, A..B means commits in B not in A.

Three mechanisms differ in what they touch. git restore <file> overwrites the working file from the index; uncommitted edits are lost and not in the reflog, though a file that had been git add-ed leaves a dangling blob that git fsck --lost-found might find. git revert creates a new commit applying the inverse patch, so history is preserved (reverting a merge needs -m to choose the mainline parent). git reset moves the current branch ref: --soft changes only the ref, --mixed also resets the index, --hard also overwrites the working tree. The panel's warning is correct for uncommitted work. Committed work discarded by reset --hard is usually recoverable: git reflog, then git reset --hard HEAD@{1} or ORIG_HEAD.

git stash records your work as commits: one for the index state and one for the working tree whose parents are the base commit and the index commit, stored under refs/stash with its reflog serving as the stack. By default untracked files are not included (-u adds them, -a adds ignored ones too). pop applies and drops, but if applying conflicts the stash is kept. A lightweight tag is just a ref in refs/tags; an annotated tag (-a) is an object with tagger, date and message, and is what git describe prefers. .gitignore affects only untracked files: a file already tracked stays tracked until git rm --cached, and patterns can also live in .git/info/exclude or a global excludes file.
deeper.further: Common misconceptions: that Git stores diffs between versions (it stores snapshots and compresses them later), that branches are copies of files (they are movable pointers), and that git reset --hard is always unrecoverable (only uncommitted changes are). Open ideas to explore next: packfiles and garbage collection, how rebase and cherry-pick create new commit objects, and what the reflog protects. A useful habit is to draw the DAG and mark where HEAD, your branch and the remote-tracking branch point before and after any command; most surprises become obvious once you see which ref moved and which objects were left behind.

pages.title: Git
pages.subtitle: The Essential Commands. Master Git. Ship confidently.

panels.heading: Setup & Config
panels.body: Set your name, set your email, check config, and set the default branch name for new repos.
panels.code:
# Set your name
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
# Set your email
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
# Check config
git config --list
# Set default branch name (new repos)
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

panels.heading: Start a Repo
panels.body: Initialize a new repo, clone an existing repo, or show remote origins. Diagram: the remote (origin) syncs with your machine.
panels.code:
# Initialize new repo
git init
# Clone existing repo
git clone <repo-url>
# Show remote origins
git remote -v

panels.heading: Daily Workflow
panels.body: The flow: work -> add -> commit -> push. Repeat!
panels.code:
# See changes
git status
# Stage files
git add <file>    # or: git add .
# Commit changes
git commit -m "Your message"
# Push to remote
git push origin <branch>

panels.heading: Inspect & View
panels.body: Tip: use space to scroll in `less`, q to quit.
panels.code:
# See commit history (pretty)
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
# See changes in working directory
git diff
# See staged changes
git diff --staged
# Show info about a commit
git show <commit-hash>
# See file / branch details
git show <branch or file>

panels.heading: Branching
panels.body: Branches are lightweight and cheap. Diagram: a feature branch splits off main and runs alongside it.
panels.code:
# List branches
git branch
# Create new branch
git branch <new-branch>
# Switch branch
git checkout <branch>
# Create & switch
git checkout -b <new-branch>
# Delete branch
git branch -d <branch>
# Rename branch
git branch -m <new-name>

panels.heading: Undo & Recover
panels.body: Caution: git reset --hard can permanently lose work. Use with care!
panels.code:
# Unstage a file
git restore --staged <file>
# Discard changes in working dir
git restore <file>
# Revert a commit (safe)
git revert <commit-hash>
# Reset current branch (moves HEAD)
git reset --soft <commit>    # keep changes staged
git reset --mixed <commit>   # keep changes in working dir
git reset --hard <commit>    # discard all changes

panels.heading: Remotes
panels.body: Tip: FETCH = download; PULL = download + merge; PUSH = upload.
panels.code:
# Add remote
git remote add origin <repo-url>
# List remotes
git remote -v
# Fetch (download only)
git fetch origin
# Pull (fetch + merge)
git pull origin <branch>
# Push
git push origin <branch>
# Remove remote
git remote remove origin

panels.heading: Stash
panels.body: Perfect for context switching without committing!
panels.code:
# Stash current changes
git stash
# List stashes
git stash list
# Apply latest stash (keep in stash list)
git stash apply
# Apply & drop latest stash
git stash pop
# Apply specific stash
git stash apply stash@{2}
# Drop a stash
git stash drop stash@{2}

panels.heading: Cherry-Pick
panels.body:
Apply a specific commit from another branch. Diagram: commit C from feature/login (A-B-C) is copied as C' onto main (A-B), i.e. pick C onto main.
Great for small, isolated changes.
Conflict? Resolve, then run git cherry-pick --continue, or abort with git cherry-pick --abort.
panels.code:
# Apply a specific commit from another branch
git cherry-pick <commit-hash>
# After resolving a conflict
git cherry-pick --continue
# Or abort
git cherry-pick --abort

panels.heading: Merge vs Rebase — What's the Difference?
panels.body:
Merge (preserves history): keeps the full history; creates a merge commit (M); best for shared branches. Good for collaboration, when history matters.
Rebase (rewrites history): replays your commits on top (C1, C2 become C1', C2' after main's latest commit); keeps history clean & linear; best for local branches. Good for clean history before merging / PR.
When to use what? Use MERGE when: working on shared branches; you want to preserve full history; you want to show where branches met. Use REBASE when: cleaning up your own feature branch; preparing PR with a clean history; you haven't pushed (or coordinated) yet.
NEVER rebase commits that others have already based work on!
panels.code:
# Merge
git checkout main
git merge feature

# Rebase
git checkout feature
git rebase main

panels.heading: Tags & Releases
panels.code:
# List tags
git tag
# Create tag
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Version 1.0.0"
# Push tags
git push origin --tags
# Delete tag
git tag -d v1.0.0

panels.heading: Submodules (Basics)
panels.body: Use submodules for dependencies that live in their own repos.
panels.code:
# Add submodule
git submodule add <repo-url> path/
# Init & update
git submodule update --init --recursive
# Update submodule
git submodule update --remote --merge

panels.heading: Handy Aliases (Examples)
panels.body: Aliases = speed. Less typing, more shipping.
panels.code:
# Add these to ~/.gitconfig
[alias]
  st = status
  co = checkout
  br = branch
  ci = commit
  lg = log --oneline --graph --decorate --all

pages.footer: Good Git habits = fewer bugs, happier team, better you. Commit small & often. Write good messages. Pull before you push. Don't commit secrets.
