pages.summary: A dense reference of essential Git commands grouped by task: setup, starting a repo, the daily add-commit-push loop, inspecting history, branching, undoing changes, remotes, stash, cherry-pick, tags, submodules and aliases. It also explains when to merge versus rebase.

panels: Git reads configuration from layered files and later ones override earlier ones: system, global (~/.gitconfig), repository (.git/config) and optionally per-worktree; git config --list --show-origin prints each value with its source. user.name and user.email are copied into the author and committer fields of every commit you make; Git does not verify them, so anyone can claim any identity. Authentication of commits comes from signing (GPG or SSH signatures) and from the hosting service. Changing the settings later does not alter existing commits, whose identities are part of their hash. init.defaultBranch only affects the name chosen by future git init commands.

A remote is a name, a URL and refspecs, which describe how remote refs map to local remote-tracking refs. Any repository can serve as a remote; hosting services are just convenient ones, and servers normally keep bare repositories (object store and refs, no working tree). Clone options change what is transferred: --depth gives a shallow history, --filter=blob:none makes a partial clone that fetches file contents lazily, and --recurse-submodules initializes submodules. Git speaks https, ssh, git and file transports. Because every clone has the full object store by default, it is a complete backup of history, which is why Git is described as distributed.

The daily loop maps onto plumbing commands. add is hash-object -w plus update-index; commit is write-tree, commit-tree and update-ref. git push origin <branch> is shorthand for pushing refs/heads/<branch> to the remote's same-named ref, and is rejected if the remote has commits you lack. Small commits are not only tidy: they make git bisect, which binary-searches history for the commit that introduced a bug, effective, and they make revert and cherry-pick precise. git add -p stages individual hunks, letting one working tree become several logical commits. Hooks in .git/hooks, such as pre-commit, can run checks before the commit object is created.

The log is a traversal of the DAG, and options select or format the walk: --stat and -p show changes, -S<text> finds commits that changed the count of a string (the pickaxe), --follow tracks a file across renames, and A..B lists commits reachable from B but not from A. git show <branch> shows the tip commit; git show <rev>:<path> prints a file as it existed in that revision. git blame annotates each line with the commit that last changed it. Pagers like less are a display convenience, not part of Git's semantics. Many history queries are reachability questions, so knowing which commits a ref reaches explains the output.

Branches are cheap because they are 41-byte ref files. checkout is overloaded, both switching branches and restoring files, which is why Git 2.23 added switch and restore with narrower roles. git branch -d refuses to delete a branch whose commits are not merged into its upstream or HEAD, a reachability check, while -D forces. Deleting a branch deletes only the ref; commits remain until garbage collection if nothing else reaches them, and the reflog may still list them. branch -m renames the ref, its reflog and related config. Commits made on a detached HEAD are unnamed and can be lost, so create a branch before leaving.

Use the safest tool that does the job. reset moves the branch ref: --soft keeps index and files, --mixed (the default) resets the index, --hard resets files too. The reflog is the recovery net: it logs every movement of HEAD and each branch in .git/logs, addressable as HEAD@{n} or main@{yesterday}, and ORIG_HEAD records where HEAD was before a risky operation such as reset, merge or rebase. After a mistake, git reflog then git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD or HEAD@{n} often restores committed work. Limits: the reflog is local, entries expire (by default after 90 days if reachable and 30 if not), and uncommitted changes never enter it.

Remote-tracking branches such as origin/main are local, read-only bookmarks of where the remote's branch was at your last fetch; they are not live. fetch --prune also deletes bookmarks for branches removed upstream. pull is fetch plus merging the upstream into the current branch; git pull --ff-only fails instead of creating a surprise merge commit, and pull.rebase changes the second step to a rebase. Push is rejected unless it is a fast-forward of the remote ref; --force-with-lease turns a forced push into a conditional one, verifying the remote still matches your tracking ref. git remote remove deletes the remote's configuration and its tracking refs, but not your local branches.

A stash entry is a commit (a merge commit, in fact, with the base commit and an index snapshot as parents, plus a third parent holding untracked files when -u is used), referenced from refs/stash; earlier entries are in that ref's reflog, which is why stash@{2} works. apply re-applies the stash with a three-way merge, so it can succeed on a different base or conflict; pop does apply then drop only if apply succeeded. A dropped stash is not instantly gone: its commit becomes unreachable and can often be found by git fsck --unreachable until garbage collection. git stash branch <name> creates a branch from the stash's base commit and applies it there, avoiding conflicts.

Cherry-pick re-applies a change, not a commit. Git takes the difference between the picked commit and its parent and applies it onto HEAD as a three-way merge, using the picked commit's parent as base. The result is a new commit with a different id because its parent and committer data differ, although the author and message are copied; -x appends a note recording the source. Duplicates are the downside: later merging both lines may conflict or silently dedupe depending on context. Picking a merge commit requires -m to say which parent is the mainline. In-progress state lives in the repository (CHERRY_PICK_HEAD and a sequencer directory), which is what --continue and --abort use.

Merge adds a commit with two parents, so the DAG records that two lines of work joined and nothing is rewritten. Rebase finds the commits reachable from your branch but not from the target, detaches HEAD at the target tip, applies each commit as if by cherry-pick, and finally moves your branch ref to the result. The originals are not changed, just orphaned (reachable via reflog and ORIG_HEAD). Because the rebased commits have new ids, anyone who built on the old ones now has duplicates and a diverged history, hence the rule about shared commits. After rebasing a branch you already pushed, use --force-with-lease. By default, rebase flattens merge commits unless --rebase-merges is used.

A lightweight tag is a ref to a commit; an annotated tag (-a) is an object storing tagger, date, message and optionally a signature, and tools such as git describe use annotated tags by default. Tags do not move on their own, and a tag that is already published should not be moved, since clients do not update existing tags on ordinary fetch. Tags are not pushed by default: push a named tag, use --follow-tags for annotated tags reachable from pushed commits, or --tags for all. Removing a remote tag is git push origin --delete <tag> (or the refspec :refs/tags/<tag>), separately from git tag -d, which only deletes your local copy.

A submodule is a pointer: the parent repository's tree contains a special entry (mode 160000, a 'gitlink') naming an exact commit in another repository, while .gitmodules records the path and URL. The parent tracks a commit, not a branch, so git submodule update checks out that recorded commit as a detached HEAD in the submodule. --remote moves the submodule to its configured branch tip, after which the parent shows a modified pointer you must commit. A common pitfall is committing the new pointer without pushing the submodule's commit first, which leaves collaborators unable to fetch it. Clone with --recurse-submodules or initialize afterwards.

An alias is a config entry under [alias] that Git expands before dispatching the command; one that begins with ! runs as a shell command, so it can chain several operations. Aliases cannot shadow built-in commands. The log alias lg expands to the options listed, so lg --stat appends further options as you would for the full command. Config layering applies, so a global alias is available everywhere unless a repository overrides it. A caution: aliases like co for checkout hide which verb is running and keep the older overloaded command in muscle memory; it is worth knowing the expansion and, for restoring or switching, the newer switch and restore commands.
deeper.further: Common misconceptions: that pull is a safe read-only operation (it merges into your branch), that rebase 'moves' commits (it creates copies), that deleting a branch deletes its commits, and that a remote-tracking branch shows the server's current state. Next steps: learn git reflog until recovery feels routine, read about packfiles and garbage collection to see when unreachable objects vanish, and practice interactive rebase on a throwaway branch. A reliable safety habit is to create a backup branch or note the current commit id before any operation that rewrites history, because a named ref makes recovery trivial.

pages.title: Git Workflows
pages.subtitle: Branch, integrate, undo and rescue with confidence

panels.heading: Feature Branch + PR Flow
panels.body:
One branch per change, cut from main.
Push, then open a pull request (PR).
CI (continuous integration) tests it; a teammate reviews.
Merge, then delete the branch.
panels.code:
git switch -c feat/search
git push -u origin feat/search

panels.heading: Trunk-Based Development
panels.body:
Everyone merges small changes to main daily.
Branches live hours, not weeks.
Feature flags hide unfinished work.
Main is always releasable.

panels.heading: Merge vs Rebase
panels.body:
Merge: joins histories with a merge commit; nothing is rewritten.
Rebase: replays your commits on a new base; new hashes, linear log.
Golden rule: never rebase commits others have already pulled.
panels.code:
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
git push --force-with-lease

panels.heading: Resolve a Merge Conflict
panels.body:
Both branches changed line 12 of config.py.
Git marks it: <<<<<<< HEAD (yours), ======= , >>>>>>> feat/retry (theirs).
Keep the right text, delete all three markers.
Stage the file, then continue.
panels.code:
git status
git add config.py
git merge --continue

panels.heading: Stash & Cherry-Pick
panels.body:
Urgent bug mid-feature? Stash edits (-u adds untracked), fix, pop.
Cherry-pick copies one commit to another branch, e.g. a hotfix onto release/2.4, with a new hash.
panels.code:
git stash push -u -m "wip"
git stash pop
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d

panels.heading: Reset vs Revert
panels.body:
reset moves the branch pointer back: rewrites history, keep it local.
revert adds a new commit that undoes an old one: safe when shared.
--soft keeps changes staged; --hard deletes them.
panels.code:
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git revert 9f8e7d6

panels.heading: Reflog Rescue
panels.body:
Reflog records every local move of HEAD.
Lost commits after a bad reset or rebase? Point a branch at the old entry.
Uncommitted changes are never in reflog.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
Force-push to main: block it with branch protection.
Prefer --force-with-lease over --force.
Weeks-old branches = painful conflicts.
Quiz: bad commit already on shared main. Reset or revert? (Revert.)

pages.footer: Branch small, merge often, revert in public, reflog to rescue.
pages.summary: Team Git workflows: feature-branch pull requests versus trunk-based development, when to merge or rebase (and the golden rule), resolving conflicts, stash and cherry-pick, reset versus revert, and recovering lost commits with reflog.

panels:
A pull request is a review and gating step, not a Git feature: the host compares the branch against its base and runs required checks before the merge button unlocks. Branch protection typically requires passing CI, one or two approvals, an up-to-date branch, and sometimes signed commits or a linear history.

The host offers three merge styles. A merge commit keeps every branch commit. Squash merge collapses the PR into one commit on main, which gives a tidy history but loses the individual commits and makes the branch look unmerged to plain Git (git branch --merged will not list it). Rebase merge replays the commits linearly. Merge queues (merge trains) re-test each PR against the latest main plus the PRs ahead of it, which prevents the case where two PRs pass on their own but break main together.

Trunk-based development minimizes integration debt: conflicts grow roughly with how long branches diverge and how much they touch, so merging small changes daily keeps every conflict small. It underpins continuous delivery, and the DORA research links short-lived branches (under a day) with higher delivery performance.

The enablers matter more than the branching rule: fast, reliable CI, a solid automated test suite, code review that turns around in hours, and feature flags that decouple deploy (code reaches production) from release (users see it). Flags carry their own debt, so remove each one once its rollout finishes. GitFlow, with long-lived develop and release branches, still suits software shipped as versioned releases with several supported versions, such as mobile apps or on-prem products, but it adds merge overhead for web services that deploy continuously.

Rebase rewrites: every replayed commit gets a new parent, so a new SHA, even if its diff is identical. Anyone who based work on the old commits now holds a divergent history, and their next pull either re-merges duplicated commits or conflicts. Hence the golden rule: rebase only commits that exist only in your copy, or on a personal branch others have agreed not to build on.

After rebasing a pushed personal branch you must force-push. --force-with-lease refuses if the remote branch moved since your last fetch, so you cannot silently overwrite a teammate's push; plain --force overwrites anything. Useful extras: git rebase -i to squash, reword or reorder commits before review; git pull --rebase to avoid needless merge commits; git config rerere.enabled true to reuse recorded conflict resolutions across repeated rebases. Merging is non-destructive and keeps the true topology, which helps when you need to know when an integration happened.

Git merges per hunk using a three-way merge: it compares each side with the merge base (the common ancestor). A change on one side only is taken automatically; both sides changing the same region gives a conflict. Setting merge.conflictStyle = zdiff3 also prints the base version between ||||||| markers, which shows what each side actually changed and makes resolution much easier.

During a merge, 'ours' is the branch you are on and 'theirs' is the incoming one. During a rebase it flips: ours is the new base (upstream) and theirs is your commit being replayed, which surprises many people using git checkout --ours. Escape hatches: git merge --abort or git rebase --abort restore the pre-operation state. Git can also merge cleanly yet leave broken code, a semantic conflict, such as a renamed function on one side and a new call to the old name on the other. Only tests and CI catch those.

A stash is stored as commits under refs/stash: one for the index, one for the working tree, and with -u a third for untracked files. Ignored files are left out unless you pass -a. git stash pop is apply followed by drop. If the apply conflicts, the entry is kept, so resolve the conflict and then drop it by hand. A stash dropped by mistake can often be recovered with git fsck --unreachable, since it is just a dangling commit until garbage collection runs. Long-lived stashes are a smell; a WIP commit on a branch is easier to find.

Cherry-pick applies one commit's diff on top of HEAD as a new commit. -x appends '(cherry picked from commit ...)' for traceability, which is useful when backporting fixes to release branches. Because the copy has a new SHA, a later merge of the original branch may conflict or duplicate the change. Prefer merging fixes forward, from release to main, when your process allows it.

git reset <commit> moves the current branch ref and, depending on the mode, the index and working tree. --soft moves only the ref, so the changes stay staged, which is ideal for re-committing several commits as one. --mixed, the default, also resets the index, so the changes remain as unstaged edits. --hard resets index and working tree, so uncommitted work is destroyed, and reflog cannot bring it back because it was never committed.

git revert <sha> computes the inverse diff and commits it, so history only grows and collaborators are unaffected. Reverting a merge commit needs -m 1 to say which parent is the mainline. Reverting that revert later is how you re-land the feature, since a plain re-merge would see the commits as already merged. Interview rule: published history means revert; private, unpushed history means reset or interactive rebase are fine.

The reflog is a per-ref local journal, stored under .git/logs/, that records every update to HEAD and to each branch: commits, checkouts, resets, rebases, merges and amends. It is never pushed or shared, so it rescues your own mistakes but not a teammate's. Entries are written as HEAD@{n} or main@{2.hours.ago}.

Defaults: entries for commits still reachable expire after 90 days (gc.reflogExpire), and entries for unreachable commits after 30 days (gc.reflogExpireUnreachable). After that, git gc may prune the objects. To undo a bad rebase, find the entry just before 'rebase (start)' and run git reset --hard on it, or more safely create a branch there first. ORIG_HEAD is a quick shortcut too: reset, merge and rebase set it to the previous tip, so git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD undoes the last such operation. git fsck --lost-found finds dangling commits that no reflog references.

Branch protection or rulesets on main should block force-pushes and deletions and require PR checks. That turns the most destructive mistakes into impossible ones instead of things people must remember. --force-with-lease has a subtle hole: if a background tool ran git fetch, your remote-tracking ref is already up to date, so the lease passes and can still clobber new work. Adding --force-if-includes closes that gap by also checking your local reflog.

Other classic traps: committing secrets, where a revert is not enough because the secret stays in history, so rotate the credential first and then purge it with git filter-repo; huge binary files, which call for Git LFS (Large File Storage); and line-ending churn across operating systems, which a .gitattributes file fixes. In interviews, the reset versus revert question really tests whether you know which history is shared.
deeper.further: Next, learn interactive rebase in depth (fixup commits plus git rebase -i --autosquash), git bisect for binary-searching the commit that introduced a bug, and git worktree for checking out several branches at once without stashing. Study merge queues and stacked pull requests for high-traffic repositories, signed commits (GPG or SSH signing) for supply-chain integrity, and monorepo tools such as sparse checkout and partial clone. For history surgery and secret removal, git filter-repo is the modern replacement for filter-branch.

pages.title: Docker
pages.subtitle: Package once, run the same everywhere

panels.heading: Containers vs VMs
panels.body:
VM (virtual machine): full guest OS on a hypervisor; GBs, boots in minutes.
Container: isolated process sharing the host kernel; MBs, starts in about a second.
Isolation comes from Linux namespaces and cgroups.

panels.heading: Image vs Container
panels.body:
Image: read-only template (app + libraries + config).
Container: a running instance of an image plus a thin writable layer.
One image -> many containers, like class -> objects.

panels.heading: Dockerfile Instructions
panels.body:
FROM picks a base image; WORKDIR sets the folder.
COPY adds files; RUN executes at build time.
ENV sets variables; EXPOSE documents a port.
CMD is the default command at run time.
panels.code:
FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

panels.heading: Layers & Build Cache
panels.body:
RUN, COPY and ADD each create a cached layer.
A change rebuilds that layer and all layers after it.
So install dependencies first, copy source last: editing app.py skips the slow pip step.
panels.code:
# continued from panel 3
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

panels.heading: Build, Run, Inspect
panels.body:
-t names the image; -d runs it in the background.
-p 8080:8000 maps host port 8080 to container port 8000.
docker ps lists running containers (-a: all).
panels.code:
docker build -t shop:1.0 .
docker run -d -p 8080:8000 --name shop shop:1.0
docker logs -f shop
docker exec -it shop sh

panels.heading: Registries & Tags
panels.body:
Registry = image store (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR).
Full name = registry/repo:tag.
Tags are movable labels; pin a digest (@sha256:...) for an exact image.
panels.code:
docker tag shop:1.0 ghcr.io/acme/shop:1.0
docker push ghcr.io/acme/shop:1.0
docker pull ghcr.io/acme/shop:1.0

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
latest is just a default tag, not 'newest'.
Container files vanish on removal: use volumes.
Never bake secrets into layers; add a .dockerignore.
Quiz: you edit app.py. Which steps rebuild? (COPY . . onward.)

pages.footer: Build the image once, ship it, run it anywhere.
pages.summary: Docker basics: how containers differ from virtual machines, images versus containers, Dockerfile instructions and layer caching, the build/run/logs/exec workflow, and pushing tagged images to a registry.

panels:
A container is an ordinary Linux process with restricted views and budgets. Namespaces isolate what it can see: PID (its own process tree, where your app is PID 1), mount (its own filesystem root), network (its own interfaces and ports), UTS (hostname), IPC and user namespaces. cgroups (control groups) limit what it can use: CPU shares and quotas, memory, I/O and process counts. Seccomp, capabilities and AppArmor or SELinux shrink the system calls and privileges it can reach.

Because every container shares the host kernel, isolation is weaker than with a VM: a kernel exploit can escape. Multi-tenant platforms therefore add sandboxed runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers, or lightweight microVMs like Firecracker that boot in about 125 ms. On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop actually runs a small Linux VM, because Linux containers need a Linux kernel.

An image is defined by the OCI (Open Container Initiative) image spec: a manifest listing a config JSON (entrypoint, env, user, working directory) and an ordered list of compressed filesystem layers, each addressed by its SHA-256 digest. Multi-architecture images add an index that points to per-platform manifests such as linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, which is why the same tag works on Apple Silicon and x86 servers.

At run time, a union filesystem (overlayfs) stacks the read-only layers and adds one writable layer per container. Writing to an existing file copies it up into that writable layer first (copy-on-write), which is slow for large files and databases, so heavy writes belong in volumes. Removing the container discards its writable layer; stopping it does not. docker commit can snapshot a container into an image, but that build is not reproducible, so always prefer a Dockerfile.

CMD versus ENTRYPOINT: ENTRYPOINT is the executable and CMD supplies default arguments that docker run can override. Use the exec form, CMD ["python", "app.py"], not the shell form CMD python app.py. The shell form wraps your process in /bin/sh -c, so the app is no longer PID 1 and never receives SIGTERM: docker stop then waits 10 seconds and sends SIGKILL.

ARG exists only at build time, while ENV persists into the running container. COPY is preferred over ADD; ADD also fetches URLs and auto-extracts tar files, which is surprising. EXPOSE is documentation only and publishes nothing; -p does that. Add USER to drop root, and HEALTHCHECK for a built-in probe. Pin base images by version, and for strict reproducibility by digest. Slim or distroless bases cut both image size and CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) count; Alpine is small but uses musl libc, which can break or slow some Python wheels.

BuildKit, the default builder, computes a cache key for each step from the previous layer plus the instruction text, and for COPY or ADD from a checksum of the copied files' contents (timestamps are ignored). Any change invalidates that step and every later one, so order instructions from least to most frequently changed. A .dockerignore file shrinks the build context and stops irrelevant files such as .git or local logs from busting the COPY cache.

Only RUN, COPY and ADD add filesystem layers; ENV, CMD and LABEL only change metadata. Deleting a file in a later layer does not shrink the image, because the earlier layer still contains it. Clean up in the same RUN, for example apt-get install ... && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*. BuildKit cache mounts (RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip) keep package caches between builds without putting them in layers. In CI, export and import the cache to a registry with --cache-to and --cache-from.

docker run equals create plus start. Flags worth knowing: --rm deletes the container on exit; -e KEY=value or --env-file set environment; -v name:/path mounts a named volume and -v ./dir:/path a bind mount; --restart unless-stopped restarts the container after crashes or reboots; --memory 512m and --cpus 1.5 set cgroup limits; --network attaches it to a user-defined network, where containers find each other by name through Docker's embedded DNS.

-p 8080:8000 publishes on all host interfaces, and Docker's iptables rules can bypass host firewalls such as ufw, so bind to 127.0.0.1:8080:8000 for local-only access. Inside the container the app must listen on 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1, or the port mapping reaches nothing, a very common bug. Other useful commands: docker inspect for full JSON details, docker stats for live usage, docker cp to copy files, and docker system prune to reclaim disk.

A full reference is registry/namespace/repo:tag@digest. With no registry, Docker Hub (docker.io) is assumed; with no tag, latest is assumed. Tags are mutable pointers, so python:3.13 moves with every patch release and rebuilds can change underneath you. A digest such as @sha256:9f2... is immutable and content-addressed, so pin digests for production deploys and let a bot such as Renovate or Dependabot propose updates.

A common tagging scheme pushes several tags for one build: an immutable git SHA tag for traceability, a semver tag like 1.4.2, and moving tags like 1.4 and 1. Docker Hub rate-limits anonymous pulls, so CI usually authenticates or uses a pull-through cache mirror. Supply-chain hardening adds image signing (Sigstore cosign), SBOMs (software bills of materials) and provenance attestations, and scanning with tools like Trivy or Grype before images are promoted.

latest is simply the default tag name: nothing updates it automatically, and two machines can hold different latest images. Secrets are a classic leak. An ENV or ARG value, or a file copied and later deleted, stays readable in the image history and layers forever. Use BuildKit secret mounts (RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc) at build time and inject secrets at run time instead.

Running as root inside the container is the default and widens the impact of a breakout. Add a non-root USER, drop capabilities, and use a read-only root filesystem where possible. PID 1 does not get default signal handlers and must reap zombie processes, so add --init (tini) or make your app handle SIGTERM. Containers have no persistence: logs should go to stdout and stderr, data to volumes. On the check-yourself question: only steps from the first changed input onward rebuild, so COPY . . and everything after it.
deeper.further: Go deeper into the OCI image and runtime specs, and how containerd and runc actually start a container. Learn rootless containers and Podman (daemonless, Docker-compatible CLI), BuildKit features such as multi-platform builds with docker buildx, cache and secret mounts, and supply-chain security: SBOMs, cosign signatures, SLSA provenance and vulnerability scanning. For isolation trade-offs, compare gVisor, Kata Containers and Firecracker microVMs. Then move on to Docker Compose for multi-container apps and Kubernetes for orchestration.

pages.title: Docker Compose
pages.subtitle: Run a whole multi-container app from one file

panels.heading: Why Compose
panels.body:
Real apps need several containers: web, database, cache.
Compose describes them all in compose.yaml.
One command builds, wires, starts and stops the stack.

panels.heading: Services, Networks, Volumes
panels.body:
Service: one container's config (image, ports, env).
Network: services share a default network and reach each other by name, e.g. cache:6379.
Volume: named storage that survives container removal.

panels.heading: A compose.yaml Example
panels.body:
web builds from ./Dockerfile; host 8080 -> container 8000.
cache runs Redis; web connects to redis://cache:6379.
Volume cache-data keeps data across restarts.

panels.heading: Env & Secrets
panels.body:
environment: inline variables.
env_file: loads .env (never commit it).
secrets: mounted as files in /run/secrets/, not env vars.
Declare each secret at top level, e.g. file: ./db_password.txt.
panels.code:
# under services.web:
environment: {LOG_LEVEL: info}
env_file: .env
secrets: [db_password]

panels.heading: Multi-Stage Builds
panels.body:
Stage 1 has the compiler and tools; the final stage copies only the binary.
Result: smaller, safer image, e.g. 900 MB -> 15 MB.
End with ENTRYPOINT ["/app"].
panels.code:
FROM golang:1.26 AS build
# copy source, go build -o /app
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /app /app

panels.heading: Healthchecks & depends_on
panels.body:
depends_on alone only orders startup; it does not wait for readiness.
Add a healthcheck plus condition: service_healthy.
Now web starts after cache answers PONG.

panels.heading: Everyday Commands
panels.body:
up -d starts in background; --build rebuilds images.
docker compose exec web sh opens a shell.
down removes containers and network; -v also deletes volumes.
panels.code:
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f web
docker compose down

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
localhost inside a container means that container: use service names.
Committing .env with real passwords.
down -v wipes your database.
Compose suits dev and single hosts; clusters need Kubernetes.

pages.footer: One compose.yaml, one command, the whole stack.
pages.summary: Docker Compose for multi-container apps: services, networks and volumes in compose.yaml, environment variables and secrets, multi-stage builds for small images, healthchecks with depends_on, and the everyday compose commands.

panels:
Compose is a declarative wrapper over the Docker API. It reads compose.yaml (also docker-compose.yml) plus any override files, merges them, and creates resources whose names are prefixed with a project name, by default the folder name, or set with -p or the name: key. That prefix lets several copies of the stack run side by side without clashing.

The Compose Specification is the current standard. The top-level version: field is obsolete and ignored, and Compose v2 is a Docker CLI plugin (docker compose with a space), replacing the old Python docker-compose binary. docker-compose.override.yml is merged automatically, which is handy for dev-only settings like bind mounts and debug ports. Profiles (profiles: [debug]) keep optional services off unless you enable them with --profile. Compose is idempotent: re-running up recreates only services whose configuration or image changed.

Each project gets a default bridge network called <project>_default. Docker's embedded DNS server, at 127.0.0.11 inside each container, resolves service names, and with several replicas a name resolves to multiple IPs (DNS round-robin). Containers talk on the container port (cache:6379), not the published host port; ports: only matters for traffic coming from the host. Use expose: or nothing at all for internal-only services, and define several networks such as frontend and backend to isolate tiers.

Named volumes are managed by Docker under /var/lib/docker/volumes and are the right choice for databases. Bind mounts (./src:/app/src) map a host folder, which is ideal for live-reloading code in development but subject to host file permissions and to slow file sharing on macOS. tmpfs mounts live in RAM. Volumes survive docker compose down and are deleted only by down -v or docker volume rm, which is exactly why down -v is dangerous.

build: . is shorthand for build: {context: ., dockerfile: Dockerfile}. Add target: to pick a stage in a multi-stage file, or args: for build arguments. If a service has both build: and image:, Compose tags the built image with that name, which is useful for pushing it. ports: ["8080:8000"] should be quoted, because some YAML parsers read unquoted values like 22:22 as base-60 numbers. Prefix with 127.0.0.1: to publish only locally.

Flow style ({...}) and block style (indented keys) are equivalent YAML; block style is easier to diff in larger files. Other common keys: restart: unless-stopped, command: to override CMD, and deploy.resources.limits for memory and CPU caps, which Compose v2 applies to a local engine. docker compose config prints the fully merged and interpolated file, the fastest way to debug variable substitution or override merging.

Two different .env mechanisms confuse people. The project-level .env next to compose.yaml feeds variable interpolation, so ${TAG:-latest} in the YAML is replaced at parse time, with shell variables taking precedence. env_file: injects variables into the container. Precedence inside the container, from high to low: docker compose run -e, then environment:, then env_file:, then the image's ENV. ${VAR:?error} makes a missing variable fail loudly instead of becoming an empty string.

Compose secrets are mounted read-only as files under /run/secrets/<name>. Their values stay out of docker inspect output, out of image layers and out of child-process environments, the usual places leaks happen. On a single engine they are bind mounts of the source file, not encrypted storage, so protect the host file. Many official images accept a *_FILE convention, for example POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db_password. For build-time credentials, use build secrets (build: {secrets: [...]}) instead of build args.

Each FROM starts a new stage. Only the last stage, or the one named with --target, becomes the image, and COPY --from=build pulls just the chosen artifacts out of an earlier stage, so compilers, source code and package caches never ship. BuildKit builds independent stages in parallel and skips stages the target does not need.

FROM scratch is an empty image: it fits only static binaries (in Go, CGO_ENABLED=0), and it has no shell, no CA certificates for HTTPS and no time zone data, so copy /etc/ssl/certs from the build stage or use a distroless static base instead. Interpreted languages still benefit: build wheels or node_modules in a full stage, then copy them onto a slim runtime base. Smaller images pull faster, which speeds cold starts and autoscaling, and contain fewer packages that scanners flag. The 900 MB to 15 MB figure is typical for a Go service, since the golang image alone is around 800 MB or more.

depends_on has three conditions. service_started is the default and means only that the container was created and started. service_healthy waits until the dependency's healthcheck passes. service_completed_successfully waits for a one-shot job, such as database migrations, to exit with code 0. A healthcheck runs inside the container. Exit code 0 means healthy and 1 means unhealthy. Tune interval, timeout, retries and start_period, the grace window where failures do not count.

The test command must exist in the image: CMD redis-cli ping works in the Redis image, but curl is missing from many slim images, so use wget or a tiny binary or script. Startup ordering covers only the first boot. Docker does not restart dependents when a dependency becomes unhealthy later, and at runtime it only flags the container as unhealthy; restart: policies react to exits, not to health. Applications should still retry connections with backoff, which also helps in Kubernetes, where no startup ordering exists at all.

up -d --build rebuilds changed images and recreates only affected containers. Add --force-recreate to restart everything, or --remove-orphans to delete containers for services you removed from the file. docker compose run --rm web pytest starts a one-off container with the service's configuration, which suits tests and migrations; exec runs inside an existing container. logs -f --tail 100 follows recent output, and pull refreshes images.

down removes containers and the default network but keeps volumes and images. down -v also deletes named volumes, and --rmi all removes images. Compose Watch (docker compose watch, configured with develop.watch) syncs files or rebuilds automatically as you edit, which beats bind mounts on macOS. stop only stops containers, while down also removes them. ps -a shows exited services, which is where crashed containers hide.

Inside a container, localhost is the container itself, so talk to sibling services by service name. To reach a service running on the host, use host.docker.internal; on Linux it needs extra_hosts: ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"]. Port conflicts on the host (address already in use) mean another process holds the published port, so change the left-hand number. Bind mounts can hide files: mounting ./ over /app masks node_modules installed in the image, which is why people add an anonymous volume for /app/node_modules.

Compose has no multi-node scheduling, rolling updates or self-healing beyond restart policies. Docker Swarm can deploy Compose files across nodes but has little momentum, and Kubernetes is the industry standard. Tools like Kompose translate compose.yaml into Kubernetes manifests as a starting point. Keep dev and production configs separate with override files, and never commit real secrets, even to a private repository.
deeper.further: Explore the Compose Specification in full: profiles, extends and include for splitting large stacks, override files per environment, and Compose Watch for fast inner-loop development. Learn development containers (devcontainer.json) that reuse Compose for reproducible editor setups, and Testcontainers for spinning up real dependencies inside integration tests. For production on one host, study restart policies, log rotation and reverse proxies. When you need several machines, move on to Kubernetes, and compare tools like Kompose or Helm for translating the same services.

pages.title: Kubernetes Core
pages.subtitle: Declare the state you want; the cluster keeps it

panels.heading: Why Orchestration
panels.body:
100 containers on 20 machines: who places, restarts and scales them?
Kubernetes (K8s) automates scheduling, self-healing, scaling and rollouts.
You declare what you want; it makes it happen.

panels.heading: Control Plane
panels.body:
API server: the front door; every kubectl call goes here.
etcd: key-value store holding cluster state.
Scheduler: picks a node for each new Pod.
Controller manager: loops that fix drift.

panels.heading: Worker Nodes
panels.body:
Node = a machine (VM or bare metal) that runs Pods.
kubelet: agent that starts containers via the runtime (containerd) and reports status.
kube-proxy: network rules that route Service traffic to Pods.

panels.heading: Pod -> ReplicaSet -> Deployment
panels.body:
Pod: smallest unit; 1+ containers sharing an IP and volumes. Disposable.
ReplicaSet: keeps N identical Pods running.
Deployment: manages ReplicaSets for rolling updates and rollback.
You write Deployments, rarely bare Pods.

panels.heading: Service Types
panels.body:
Pods come and go with new IPs; a Service gives a stable name and virtual IP.
ClusterIP: internal only (default).
NodePort: a port (30000-32767) on every node.
LoadBalancer: provisions a cloud load balancer.

panels.heading: Reconciliation Loop
panels.body:
Desired state (stored in etcd) vs actual state (what runs).
Controllers watch, compare, act, repeat.
Example: replicas: 3, a node dies, 2 Pods left -> controller creates 1 more.

panels.heading: A Deployment in YAML
panels.body:
Also set apiVersion: apps/v1 and metadata.name: web.
The Pod template is labeled app: web and runs image shop:1.0.
The selector must match those labels.
kubectl apply -f web.yaml -> 3 Pods.
panels.code:
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}

panels.heading: Namespaces & Pitfalls
panels.body:
Namespaces split one cluster into groups (dev, prod, team-a) with separate names and quotas.
Pitfalls: bare Pods are not recreated.
Selector-label mismatch = no Pods managed.
Don't hand-edit what a controller owns.

pages.footer: You declare the desired state; controllers loop until reality matches.
pages.summary: Core Kubernetes: why container orchestration exists, the control plane and worker node components, Pods, ReplicaSets and Deployments, Service types, namespaces, and the desired-state reconciliation loop, with a Deployment YAML example.

panels:
Orchestration answers questions a single Docker host cannot: which machine has room for this container (bin-packing), what replaces it when a node dies, how clients find a container whose IP keeps changing, how to roll out version 2 without downtime, and how to scale with load. Kubernetes grew out of Google's Borg experience and is governed by the CNCF (Cloud Native Computing Foundation). It ships a new minor version roughly every four months, and each is supported for about a year.

Its core design choice is a declarative API: you submit objects describing desired state, and independent controllers converge reality toward it. That makes operations idempotent and self-healing, and it lets add-ons extend the system with CustomResourceDefinitions and operators. The cost is complexity. Managed services (EKS, GKE, AKS) run the control plane for you, and for small apps a PaaS or Compose on one VM is often the better trade-off.

The kube-apiserver is the only component that talks to etcd. It authenticates requests, authorizes them (RBAC), runs admission controllers that can mutate or reject objects (defaults, policies, quotas), validates them and persists them. It is stateless and scales horizontally behind a load balancer. Components watch it over long-lived streams instead of polling.

etcd is a strongly consistent key-value store that uses the Raft consensus algorithm, so it runs as 3 or 5 members and tolerates the loss of 1 or 2. Losing quorum makes the cluster read-only, and etcd backups are the cluster's real disaster-recovery story. The scheduler filters out nodes that cannot fit a Pod (resources, taints, affinity, topology) and scores the rest, then writes a binding. kube-controller-manager runs dozens of controllers: Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node lifecycle, Job, EndpointSlice and more. A cloud-controller-manager integrates cloud load balancers and routes.

The kubelet watches the API server for Pods bound to its node and drives the container runtime through the CRI (Container Runtime Interface), typically containerd or CRI-O. Dockershim was removed in Kubernetes 1.24, but images built with Docker still run, since they are standard OCI images. The kubelet also runs probes, mounts volumes, reports node and Pod status, and evicts Pods under memory or disk pressure.

Pod networking comes from a CNI (Container Network Interface) plugin such as Calico or Cilium. Every Pod gets a routable IP and can reach every other Pod without NAT, and NetworkPolicies restrict that flat network. kube-proxy watches Services and EndpointSlices and programs iptables, IPVS or nftables rules on each node; eBPF-based CNIs like Cilium can replace kube-proxy entirely. Nodes heartbeat through Lease objects; after roughly 40 to 50 seconds without one (node-monitor-grace-period) a node is marked NotReady, and its Pods are evicted after a default toleration of 300 seconds.

Containers in a Pod share a network namespace, so they reach each other on localhost and must not use the same port. They can share volumes and are always scheduled together on one node. Patterns: sidecars (log shippers, service-mesh proxies, now first-class as init containers with restartPolicy: Always), init containers that run to completion before the app starts, and adapters. A Pod is never moved: when it dies, a new Pod with a new name and IP replaces it.

A ReplicaSet owns Pods through a label selector and ownerReferences. Delete one Pod and it creates another; label a Pod out of the selector and the ReplicaSet orphans it and starts a replacement. A Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet for every Pod template change, named with a pod-template-hash, and keeps the old ones (revisionHistoryLimit, default 10) for rollback. Other workload types: StatefulSet for stable identities and storage, DaemonSet for one Pod per node, and Job or CronJob for batch work.

A Service selects Pods by label. The EndpointSlice controller lists the IPs of ready Pods, and kube-proxy load-balances the Service's virtual ClusterIP across them. CoreDNS gives every Service a name: web.shop.svc.cluster.local, or just web from inside the same namespace. Because readiness gates membership, unready Pods receive no traffic.

NodePort builds on ClusterIP, and LoadBalancer builds on NodePort: the cloud controller provisions an external load balancer that forwards to node ports, or straight to Pod IPs on many clouds. Each LoadBalancer Service costs one cloud load balancer, so HTTP apps usually share a single Ingress or Gateway instead. Also know headless Services (clusterIP: None), whose DNS returns Pod IPs directly, as StatefulSets need, and ExternalName, a DNS alias to an outside host. externalTrafficPolicy: Local preserves the client source IP but can unbalance load across nodes. Session affinity is available, but stateless Pods are the better design.

Every controller runs the same pattern: watch objects through a shared informer cache, put changed keys on a work queue, and reconcile each key by reading the desired spec, observing the actual state and taking one step toward the goal, then writing status. Reconcile functions must be idempotent and level-triggered: they act on the current state, not on the event that fired, so missed or duplicate events are harmless and periodic resyncs repair any drift.

In the example, the node controller marks the dead node NotReady, its Pods are evicted after the toleration expires, the ReplicaSet sees 2 of 3 ready replicas and creates a new Pod, and the scheduler binds it to a healthy node. Objects carry spec (what you want) and status (what is), plus a generation and observedGeneration so tools can tell whether a controller has processed the latest change. Operators apply the same loop to custom resources, for example to manage a database cluster.

The full manifest needs apiVersion: apps/v1, kind, metadata.name, and spec with replicas, selector and template. The template's labels must satisfy the selector, or the API server rejects the object. The selector is immutable after creation, so choose stable labels such as app.kubernetes.io/name. Each container needs name and image, and should also set ports, resource requests, probes and a non-root securityContext.

kubectl apply is declarative. Client-side apply stores the last applied config in an annotation and computes a three-way diff. Server-side apply (--server-side) tracks field ownership per manager, which avoids fights between kubectl, controllers and GitOps tools. Run kubectl diff -f before applying, and kubectl apply --dry-run=server to run validation and admission without saving. Keep manifests in Git and let a GitOps controller like Argo CD or Flux apply them, so the cluster continuously reconciles toward what is reviewed in the repository.

Namespaces scope names, RBAC permissions, ResourceQuotas (caps on total CPU, memory and object counts) and LimitRanges (default requests and limits). They are not a security boundary on their own: without NetworkPolicies, Pods in different namespaces can still talk, and nodes are shared. Some resources are cluster-scoped, such as Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, ClusterRoles and CRDs. Deleting a namespace deletes everything inside it.

Common traps: running bare Pods, which nothing recreates; selectors or Service labels that do not match, so a Service has no endpoints (check kubectl get endpointslices); editing a Pod a ReplicaSet owns, which the next rollout undoes; kubectl edit in production, which drifts from Git; using the default namespace and :latest tags; and forgetting that the default ServiceAccount token is mounted into Pods. Interviewers often ask what happens step by step after kubectl apply, so be ready to trace API server, etcd, controller, scheduler, kubelet and runtime.
deeper.further: Next, study workload types beyond Deployments (StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob), persistent storage (PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses, CSI drivers), and scheduling controls such as taints, tolerations, affinity and topology spread. Learn RBAC and NetworkPolicies for security, the Gateway API for traffic, and CustomResourceDefinitions plus operators for extending the platform. Try a local cluster with kind or minikube, and read about GitOps with Argo CD or Flux. The practice page covers probes, autoscaling and debugging.

pages.title: Kubernetes in Practice
pages.subtitle: Configure, expose, scale and debug real workloads

panels.heading: kubectl Essentials
panels.body:
get lists resources; describe shows details and events.
logs --previous prints the last crashed run.
apply -f makes the cluster match your files.
panels.code:
kubectl get pods -n shop
kubectl describe pod web-7d9f-x2k
kubectl logs web-7d9f-x2k --previous
kubectl apply -f k8s/

panels.heading: ConfigMaps & Secrets
panels.body:
ConfigMap: non-secret settings, e.g. LOG_LEVEL=info.
Secret: passwords and tokens; only base64-encoded, so enable encryption at rest and RBAC (role-based access control).
Inject as env vars or mounted files.
panels.code:
kubectl create configmap app-cfg --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info
kubectl create secret generic db-cred --from-file=password=./pw.txt

panels.heading: Ingress
panels.body:
One HTTP(S) entry point; routes by host and path to Services.
shop.example.com/api -> api; / -> web.
Needs an ingress controller; Gateway API is the successor.

panels.heading: Liveness & Readiness Probes
panels.body:
Readiness fails -> Pod gets no traffic, keeps running.
Liveness fails -> kubelet restarts the container.
Startup probe: grace time for slow starts.
panels.code:
readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /ready, port: 8000}}
livenessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8000}}

panels.heading: Requests & Limits
panels.body:
Request: reserved share; the scheduler uses it to place Pods.
Limit: hard cap. Over memory -> OOMKilled (out of memory); over CPU -> throttled.
250m = 0.25 of a CPU core.

panels.heading: HPA Autoscaling
panels.body:
HPA = Horizontal Pod Autoscaler: adds or removes Pods from metrics.
Target 70% CPU, average at 140% -> replicas double, 3 -> 6.
Needs CPU requests and metrics-server.
panels.code: kubectl autoscale deployment web --cpu=70% --min=2 --max=10

panels.heading: Rolling Updates, Rollback, Helm
panels.body:
A new image replaces Pods gradually; traffic keeps flowing.
Bad release? Undo to the previous ReplicaSet.
Helm = package manager for templated YAML charts.
panels.code:
kubectl set image deployment/web web=shop:1.1
kubectl rollout status deployment/web
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web
helm upgrade --install shop ./chart

panels.heading: Pitfall: CrashLoopBackOff
panels.body:
Container keeps exiting; restart delays grow (up to 5 min).
Check logs --previous and describe.
Exit 137 = killed (often OOMKilled); 1 = app error.
Causes: bad config, missing Secret, strict liveness probe.

pages.footer: Probe it, size it, scale it; read events when it breaks.
pages.summary: Running real workloads on Kubernetes: everyday kubectl commands, ConfigMaps and Secrets, Ingress routing, liveness and readiness probes, resource requests and limits, HPA autoscaling, rolling updates and rollback, Helm, and debugging CrashLoopBackOff.

panels:
Speed-ups: set a default namespace with kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop, and switch clusters with kubectl config use-context (or the kubectx tool). -o yaml shows the live object including status, -o jsonpath extracts fields, -w watches changes, and -l app=web filters by label. kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy documents any field offline.

For debugging: kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp shows recent cluster events; kubectl logs deploy/web -c sidecar picks a container; kubectl exec -it pod -- sh opens a shell; kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80 reaches a Service from your laptop; kubectl top pods shows usage, if metrics-server is installed; and kubectl debug -it pod --image=busybox --target=app attaches an ephemeral debug container to distroless Pods that have no shell. Prefer apply with files in Git over imperative create or edit, except for quick experiments.

ConfigMaps and Secrets are capped at 1 MiB each. Environment variables are read once at container start, so changing a ConfigMap does not reach them until the Pods restart (kubectl rollout restart deploy/web). Mounted volumes refresh within about a minute, but subPath mounts never refresh. Many teams append a content hash to the ConfigMap name (Kustomize does this automatically) so every config change triggers a clean rollout. immutable: true protects config from edits and lightens load on the API server.

Secrets are stored base64-encoded, and in etcd they are plaintext unless an EncryptionConfiguration or KMS provider encrypts them at rest. Anyone allowed to create Pods in a namespace can effectively read its Secrets by mounting them. Production setups keep the source of truth in a vault (HashiCorp Vault, cloud secret managers) synced by the External Secrets Operator or a CSI driver, or commit encrypted Sealed Secrets or SOPS files to Git.

An Ingress resource is only configuration; an ingress controller (a reverse proxy running in the cluster) watches it and does the routing. Without a controller, nothing happens. pathType: Prefix matches path segments and Exact matches one path. TLS uses a Secret holding a certificate, usually issued and renewed automatically by cert-manager with Let's Encrypt. Many features, such as rewrites, rate limits and auth, live in controller-specific annotations, which makes Ingress manifests hard to port between controllers.

The widely used community ingress-nginx controller was retired in early 2026, which pushed many teams to migrate. The Gateway API (GA since 2023) is the successor: GatewayClass and Gateway are owned by the platform team, while HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute and others are owned by app teams. It has typed fields for header matching, traffic splitting (canaries) and cross-namespace routing instead of annotations. Implementations include Envoy Gateway, Istio, Cilium and the cloud providers' own controllers.

Probe types: httpGet (2xx or 3xx counts as success), tcpSocket, exec (exit code 0) and grpc. Tunables: initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds (default 10), timeoutSeconds (default 1), failureThreshold (default 3) and successThreshold. Liveness restarts the container after failureThreshold times periodSeconds, about 30 seconds by default.

Design rules interviewers probe. Readiness may check critical dependencies, because pulling a Pod out of rotation is cheap and reversible. Liveness should check only that the process itself is wedged (deadlock, event loop stuck), never the database: if the DB blips, every Pod restarts at once and turns a brief outage into a cascading one. Use a startupProbe with failureThreshold times periodSeconds long enough for the worst-case boot (say 30 x 10s = 5 minutes); liveness and readiness wait until it succeeds. Readiness also matters during shutdown: handle SIGTERM by failing readiness and draining, and add a short preStop sleep so endpoints update before the process exits.

CPU is compressible: above its limit a container is throttled by the CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) quota in 100 ms periods, which shows up as latency spikes rather than errors. Memory is not compressible: going over the limit triggers the kernel OOM killer, reported as exit code 137 with reason OOMKilled. 250m means 250 millicores; Mi is a mebibyte (2^20 bytes), while M is a megabyte (10^6).

QoS (quality of service) classes follow from your settings. Guaranteed means requests equal limits for every container; Burstable means some requests are set; BestEffort means none. Under node memory pressure, BestEffort Pods are evicted first, then Burstable Pods using more than their requests. A common practice is to always set memory requests equal to the memory limit, and to set CPU requests but often no CPU limit, avoiding needless throttling. Requests that are too high waste money through unused reserved capacity; too low causes noisy neighbors and evictions. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler can recommend values.

The HPA controller runs every 15 seconds: desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentMetric / target). Utilization is measured against requests, so without CPU requests the HPA cannot compute a percentage. A 10% tolerance band prevents flapping, and scale-down uses a 5-minute stabilization window by default; autoscaling/v2 behavior policies let you tune rates such as 'add at most 4 Pods per minute'.

Metrics can be Resource (CPU, memory), Pods or Object (custom metrics through an adapter like Prometheus Adapter), or External (queue length). KEDA adds event-driven scaling, including scale to zero. Memory is a poor HPA signal for most runtimes, because garbage-collected heaps rarely shrink. The HPA adds Pods, but if nodes are full those Pods stay Pending until a cluster autoscaler (Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter) adds nodes, which can take minutes, so keep some headroom. Do not combine HPA and VPA on the same CPU or memory metric.

The RollingUpdate strategy uses maxSurge (extra Pods allowed, default 25%) and maxUnavailable (default 25%). With replicas: 4, the controller may run 5 Pods and needs at least 3 available throughout. New Pods count only once they are ready (plus minReadySeconds), so good readiness probes are what make rollouts safe. progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600) marks a stuck rollout as failed, though it does not roll back automatically. Recreate kills all old Pods first, which is useful when two versions cannot run side by side.

kubectl rollout history shows revisions, rollout undo --to-revision=3 picks one, and rollout pause and resume batch changes. Canary and blue-green releases need extra tooling such as Argo Rollouts, Flagger or Gateway API traffic splitting. Helm charts use Go templates plus values.yaml; each install or upgrade is a release revision stored as a Secret, so helm rollback works. Helm 4, released in late 2025, is the current major line, and Kustomize, built into kubectl as -k, is the template-free alternative.

CrashLoopBackOff is a waiting state, not an error by itself: the kubelet restarts the container with exponential back-off of 10s, 20s, 40s and so on, capped at 5 minutes, and resets after 10 minutes of healthy running. Triage in order: kubectl describe pod for Last State, Reason, Exit Code and events; kubectl logs --previous for the crashed run's output; then check config and dependencies.

Exit codes: 0 means the process finished, often a missing long-running command or a script that exits; 1 means an application error; 126 or 127 mean the command is not executable or not found (bad entrypoint, wrong architecture); 137 is SIGKILL, from OOMKilled or a failed liveness probe; 139 is a segfault; 143 is SIGTERM. Related states: ImagePullBackOff (bad tag or registry credentials), CreateContainerConfigError (missing ConfigMap or Secret key), and Pending (no node fits the requests). For distroless images with no shell, use kubectl debug with an ephemeral container or a copy of the Pod.
deeper.further: Next, learn the Gateway API in depth, GitOps delivery with Argo CD or Flux, and progressive delivery with Argo Rollouts or Flagger. Study observability (Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry tracing, centralized logs), PodDisruptionBudgets and graceful shutdown for zero-downtime maintenance, and security hardening: Pod Security Standards, NetworkPolicies, RBAC least privilege and image policy admission. For scaling, compare HPA, VPA, KEDA and node autoscalers like Karpenter. Kustomize and Helm chart authoring round out day-to-day platform work.

pages.title: Solid Principles
pages.subtitle: Five rules for code that bends without breaking

panels.heading: What SOLID Means
panels.body:
SOLID = five object-oriented design rules.
S: single responsibility. O: open/closed.
L: Liskov substitution. I: interface segregation.
D: dependency inversion.
Goal: changes stay small, local and safe.

panels.heading: S - Single Responsibility
panels.body:
A class should have one reason to change.
Before: Report computes totals AND writes PDFs.
After: Report computes; PdfExporter writes.
Test: describe the class without saying "and".
panels.code:
class Report: ...       # totals only
class PdfExporter: ...  # output only

panels.heading: O - Open/Closed
panels.body:
Open for extension, closed for modification.
Before: an if/elif chain on payment kind grows forever.
After: each payment type is a class with pay().
Add features by adding code, not editing it.
panels.code:
for method in methods:
    method.pay(amount)  # no if/elif

panels.heading: L - Liskov Substitution
panels.body:
Subtypes must work wherever the base type works.
Classic break: Square(Rectangle) - setting width silently changes height.
No stronger preconditions, no weaker guarantees, no surprise exceptions.

panels.heading: I - Interface Segregation
panels.body:
Clients should not depend on methods they never use.
Before: one Machine with print(), scan(), fax().
After: small Printer and Scanner protocols.
A basic printer no longer fakes fax().

panels.heading: D - Dependency Inversion
panels.body:
High-level code depends on abstractions, not details.
Before: OrderService builds MySQLRepo() inside.
After: it receives any repo with save().
Tests swap in a fake repo in one line.

panels.heading: Pitfalls: When to Bend
panels.body:
SOLID is a guide, not a law.
Over-splitting: 40 one-method classes for a 50-line script.
Premature abstraction: an interface with one implementation forever.
Bend for prototypes and scripts; refactor when change hurts.

panels.heading: Check Yourself
panels.body:
Bird has fly(). Penguin(Bird) raises an error in fly().
Which principle breaks?
Answer: L - split into Bird and FlyingBird.

pages.footer: Small, focused pieces that depend on promises, not details.
pages.summary: Explains the five SOLID object-oriented design principles with tiny before/after Python examples, and when it is sensible to bend them.

panels:
SOLID was assembled by Robert C. Martin around 2000 (the acronym was coined later by Michael Feathers) from older ideas: Bertrand Meyer's open/closed principle (1988) and Barbara Liskov's 1987 substitution talk. All five target one cost: the price of change. A design is good when a typical change touches few files, needs little retesting and cannot break unrelated features.

The principles overlap. Dependency inversion is the usual mechanism that makes open/closed possible; interface segregation is single responsibility applied to interfaces; Liskov substitution is the rule that keeps polymorphism, and therefore open/closed, honest. In Python, many of them map onto lighter tools than class hierarchies: first-class functions, typing.Protocol for structural typing, and modules as natural units of responsibility. Interviewers rarely want definitions recited; they want you to spot the violation in a snippet and name the smallest fix.

Martin's refined wording is that a module should be responsible to one actor: one group of people who request changes. Report mixing totals and PDF layout serves two actors, finance and design, so their requests collide in one file and in one merge conflict.

Responsibility is not 'does one thing' at the line level; a class with ten methods can still have a single responsibility if all of them change together. The useful signals are change history (files that always change for different tickets), test setup (needing a printer mock to test arithmetic) and naming trouble (Manager, Helper, Util). Over-applying SRP produces anemic classes and scattered logic, which raises the cost of following a feature. Cohesion is the counterweight: keep together what changes together, separate what changes for different reasons.

Meyer's original version used inheritance: a published class is closed, and you extend it by subclassing. The modern version uses polymorphism over an abstraction: callers depend on pay(), and new behavior arrives as a new implementation registered somewhere, such as a dict of handlers, an entry-point plugin or a strategy passed in.

No code is closed against every change. You choose the axis of variation you expect, for example new payment methods, and you remain open to edits on other axes. Guessing wrong creates indirection with no payoff, which is why a common rule is to introduce the extension point on the second or third variation, not the first. A Python match statement over a closed set of cases is fine; an if/elif on type that is copied into five functions is the smell.

Liskov and Wing formalized it as behavioral subtyping: a subtype may not strengthen preconditions, may not weaken postconditions, must preserve the base type's invariants, and must respect the history constraint (it cannot allow state changes the base forbids). Type checkers verify signatures, not these behavioral promises, so LSP violations pass mypy and fail in production.

Square/Rectangle breaks because the base promises that set_width leaves height unchanged. Fixes include making shapes immutable (with_width returns a new object), or dropping the inheritance and sharing a Shape protocol with area(). Typical real violations: a subclass that raises NotImplementedError, returns None where a list was promised, demands extra setup, or narrows accepted argument types. Python's collections.abc is a good model: Sequence promises read-only behavior and MutableSequence extends it, never the reverse.

Fat interfaces force implementers to stub methods they cannot support and force clients to recompile or retest when unrelated methods change. In statically typed languages the recompilation cost was the original motivation; in Python the cost is mostly conceptual coupling and misleading APIs that raise at runtime.

typing.Protocol fits ISP well: a function can declare that it needs only something with print(), and any object with that method satisfies it without inheriting anything. Define interfaces from the client's side (what this caller needs) rather than from the implementer's side (everything the class can do). The split can go too far: dozens of single-method protocols scattered across modules are hard to discover. A role interface per client group, such as Readable versus Writable storage, is the usual sweet spot.

Dependency inversion has two parts: high-level policy should not depend on low-level detail, and both should depend on an abstraction owned by the high-level side. Ownership is the subtle bit: the Repo interface belongs next to OrderService, so the domain package does not import the database package; the database adapter imports the domain instead. That inversion of the import arrow is what gives the principle its name, and it is the core of hexagonal (ports and adapters) and clean architecture.

Dependency injection is the usual technique, but not the same thing: you can inject concrete classes and still depend on details. In Python, DI is usually just constructor parameters with sensible defaults, wired once in main(); heavy containers are rarely needed. Watch for leaky abstractions, such as a repo interface that exposes SQL strings, which keeps the coupling in disguise.

Every abstraction has a cost: more files, more indirection, and code that is harder to follow in a debugger or code review. The trade only pays off where change actually happens. Two useful heuristics: the rule of three (abstract on the third variation) and 'make the change easy, then make the easy change' (Kent Beck), which says to refactor toward a principle at the moment a real change needs it.

Legitimate reasons to bend: throwaway scripts and prototypes, performance-critical inner loops where virtual dispatch or allocation matters, data classes that are simply records, and frameworks that impose their own structure (for example Django models mixing data and persistence by design). Some argue that SOLID is less central in functional or data-oriented code, where pure functions and simple data already give low coupling. Know the principles well enough to explain why you are deviating.

The Penguin case is a textbook LSP failure: the base class promises fly() works, and a subtype breaks that promise. It also hints at an ISP issue, because Bird bundles a capability not every bird has. The fix models capabilities separately: a Bird base with shared traits, and a FlyingBird subtype or a CanFly protocol for flying behavior.

Interview follow-ups often add twists. If you add Ostrich and Kiwi, does your hierarchy still hold? (Capabilities scale better than deep trees.) If fly() must exist on all birds for legacy callers, can returning False be acceptable? Only if the base contract documents that fly() may fail; changing the contract is a breaking API change. Another classic: should Stack inherit from list? No, because list exposes insert() at any index, which breaks the stack's invariant; compose a list inside instead.
deeper.further: Read Martin's Clean Architecture for the actor-based SRP and dependency rule, and Liskov and Wing's 1994 paper 'A Behavioral Notion of Subtyping' for the formal contract rules. Explore hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters), design by contract, and Python's typing.Protocol and abc modules. GRASP principles (information expert, low coupling, high cohesion) and the coupling/cohesion vocabulary give a complementary lens. For balance, look at critiques arguing for simpler data-oriented or functional designs, and at CUPID, an alternative set of properties proposed by Dan North.

pages.title: Creational Patterns
pages.subtitle: Control how objects get made

panels.heading: Why Creational Patterns
panels.body:
They separate creating an object from using it.
Callers ask for what they need, not how to build it.
Five classics from the Gang of Four (GoF) book.

panels.heading: Singleton (Often an Anti-Pattern)
panels.body:
Problem: exactly one shared instance (config, logger).
Risks: hidden global state, tests leak into each other.
A Python module is already a singleton.
Prefer: create one object and inject it.

panels.heading: Factory Method
panels.body:
Problem: the caller should not hard-code which class to build.
A method creates the object; subclasses override it.
Use when the type depends on context or config.

panels.heading: Abstract Factory
panels.body:
Problem: families of objects that must match.
DarkTheme makes DarkButton + DarkMenu; LightTheme makes the light pair.
Swap the factory, every part changes together.
panels.code:
ui = DarkTheme()
button, menu = ui.button(), ui.menu()

panels.heading: Builder
panels.body:
Problem: many optional parts or steps.
Set parts step by step, then build() validates.
Avoids 10-argument constructors.
In Python, keyword arguments or dataclasses often suffice.
panels.code:
req = (RequestBuilder("GET", "/users")
       .header("Auth", token)
       .timeout(5)
       .build())

panels.heading: Prototype
panels.body:
Problem: building from scratch is slow or complex.
Copy a configured template, then tweak the copy.
Shallow copies share nested lists - use deepcopy.
panels.code:
enemy = copy.deepcopy(base_enemy)
enemy.hp = 50

panels.heading: Which One When?
panels.body:
One shared resource -> inject one instance.
Type chosen at runtime -> Factory Method.
Matching families -> Abstract Factory.
Many optional settings -> Builder.
Cheap clones of a template -> Prototype.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Factories for classes that never vary are noise.
Singletons leak state between tests.
Builders that skip validation build broken objects.
Start with a plain constructor; add a pattern when pain appears.

pages.footer: Make creation a decision in one place, not a habit everywhere.
pages.summary: Covers the five Gang of Four creational patterns (Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype): the problem each solves, a short Python sketch, and when to use or avoid them.

panels:
The Gang of Four (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides) published Design Patterns in 1994 with 23 patterns in three families: creational (5), structural (7) and behavioral (11). Creational patterns all answer one question: who decides which concrete class gets instantiated, and when?

In languages where classes are first-class objects, like Python, several patterns collapse into simple idioms. A class is already a factory (call it), a dict mapping names to classes is a registry, functools.partial pre-configures constructors, and dataclasses with defaults replace many builders. Peter Norvig observed in 1996 that 16 of the 23 patterns become invisible or simpler in dynamic languages. The vocabulary still matters: saying 'this is an abstract factory' communicates intent in a code review faster than describing the mechanics.

A singleton guarantees one instance and global access to it. The second half is the problem: global access means any function can read or mutate shared state without declaring it, so dependencies hide, call order matters, and tests contaminate each other. Lazy initialization in threaded code adds races; Python's import lock makes module-level objects safe to create, while a hand-rolled check-then-create in __new__ is not atomic, a risk that grows on free-threaded builds.

Alternatives: create the object once at the composition root (main or app factory) and pass it in; use a module-level instance when truly global (the logging module does this); or use functools.cache on a factory function, which is easy to reset in tests with cache_clear(). Legitimate singletons exist: a process-wide connection pool, hardware handles, the None object itself. 'One instance' is fine; 'reachable from anywhere' is the smell.

In the GoF form, Factory Method is a template-method-style hook: the base class contains logic that needs an object, and subclasses override the creation step. The point is that export() stays unchanged while JsonExporter controls which writer it gets. In everyday Python, people usually mean a simple factory: a function or classmethod that picks a class, such as datetime.fromtimestamp or dict.fromkeys (alternative constructors).

A registry of classes keyed by string, often filled by a decorator, is the plugin-friendly version: new types register themselves without editing the factory, which satisfies open/closed. Pitfalls: string keys fail at runtime rather than at type-check time, and factories that return different types without a shared interface push isinstance checks back onto callers. Interview tip: the distinction between Factory Method (inheritance, one product) and Abstract Factory (composition, a family of products) is a common question.

Abstract Factory is an object with several creation methods whose products are designed to work together. The guarantee it gives is consistency: a client holding one factory cannot accidentally mix a dark button with a light menu, or an AWS queue with a GCP bucket client. It is usually implemented with one factory class per family, each made of factory methods.

The cost is rigidity in the other direction: adding a new product type (say, a tooltip) means changing the factory interface and every concrete factory. Adding a new family is cheap; adding a new product kind is expensive. This is the expression problem in miniature. In Python, a family can be a module (themes.dark, themes.light) or a dataclass of constructors. Dependency injection containers often play the abstract factory role at application scale.

Builder separates the construction steps from the final representation and allows validation once all parts are known. It shines when objects are immutable after creation, when some parameters depend on others, or when the same steps build different outputs (the GoF 'director' variant, such as one parser driving HTML and PDF builders).

Fluent builders return self from each step so calls chain; the final build() checks invariants, for example that a request with a body is not a GET. In Python, keyword-only arguments with defaults, dataclasses with __post_init__ validation, and pydantic models cover most cases without a separate builder class. Builders remain useful for query construction (SQLAlchemy select().where().order_by() is builder-like), test data builders that set only the fields a test cares about, and configuration assembled from several sources.

Prototype creates new objects by copying an existing, already configured one. It helps when construction is expensive (parsed config, loaded assets), when the class to create is only known through an existing instance, or when users design templates at runtime, such as game designers configuring enemy types.

In Python, copy.copy makes a shallow copy and copy.deepcopy copies recursively, tracking a memo dict to handle cycles. Classes can control both via __copy__ and __deepcopy__. Pitfalls: deep copies of objects holding file handles, locks or sockets fail or behave oddly; copied objects may share IDs that should be unique; and deep copying large graphs is slow. Immutable designs reduce the need entirely: with frozen dataclasses, dataclasses.replace(obj, hp=50) produces a modified copy safely, and sharing nested immutable parts is harmless.

A practical decision order: first ask whether a plain constructor call is enough, since most code needs no creational pattern. If the concrete type depends on runtime data, use a factory function or registry. If several created objects must stay consistent, group the creators into an abstract factory. If construction has many optional steps or needs validation across fields, use keyword arguments first, then a builder. If copying a configured instance is cheaper or simpler than building, use a prototype.
