For 'there must be one', separate the two concerns: lifetime (one instance per process) is decided at the composition root; access should still be explicit through parameters. Patterns combine: a builder may use a prototype as its starting point, and abstract factories are often built from factory methods. Dependency injection frameworks automate factories and lifetimes (singleton, scoped, transient).

Pattern-itis is a real failure mode: an AbstractWidgetFactoryProvider for a single widget type adds names and indirection with no variation to justify them. Each creational pattern should point to an actual axis of change or a real construction problem.

Singleton damage is the most common: hidden coupling, order-dependent initialization, and tests that pass alone but fail together. Builders fail when build() does not validate, letting half-configured objects escape, or when the builder is mutable and reused accidentally across requests. Prototype bugs come from shallow copies sharing mutable state. Factories that swallow errors and return None hide failures. A good review question for any creational code: can a test create this object in one line with fakes, and can a reader find in one place where the concrete type is chosen?
deeper.further: Read the original Design Patterns book selectively, then Norvig's 'Design Patterns in Dynamic Languages' talk to see which patterns Python absorbs. Study dependency injection and composition roots (Mark Seemann's work), object lifetimes in DI containers, and the expression problem. Learn Python specifics: classmethod alternative constructors, __init_subclass__ registries, entry points for plugins, dataclasses.replace and __deepcopy__. Brandon Rhodes' python-patterns guide is a strong Python-focused reference.

pages.title: Structural Patterns
pages.subtitle: Compose objects into bigger, cleaner structures

panels.heading: What Structural Patterns Do
panels.body:
They connect classes and objects into larger structures.
Most are wrappers: an object holds another and forwards calls.
Same shape, different intent - learn the intent.

panels.heading: Adapter
panels.body:
Problem: a useful class has the wrong interface.
Your code calls pay(cents); the vendor SDK offers charge(dollars).
The adapter translates. Interface changes, behavior stays.

panels.heading: Decorator
panels.body:
Problem: add behavior without a subclass per combination.
Wrap an object with the same interface plus extra work: logging, caching, retries.
Stack them: Retry(Cache(Api())).

panels.heading: Facade
panels.body:
Problem: a subsystem has too many parts to call correctly.
A facade offers one simple entry point.
Example: checkout() runs stock, payment, shipping and email in order.

panels.heading: Proxy
panels.body:
Problem: control access to a real object.
Same interface plus a gatekeeper step.
Kinds: virtual (lazy load), protection (auth check), remote (network stub), caching.
Example: ImageProxy loads the file on first display().

panels.heading: Composite
panels.body:
Problem: treat single items and groups the same way.
A tree where leaves and branches share one interface.
File.size() returns bytes; Folder.size() sums its children.

panels.heading: Bridge
panels.body:
Problem: two dimensions of variation explode into subclasses.
Shapes x renderers: 3 x 2 = 6 classes.
Bridge: Shape holds a Renderer -> 3 + 2 = 5 classes.
Both sides vary independently.

panels.heading: Compare + Pitfalls
panels.body:
Adapter changes the interface. Decorator adds behavior.
Proxy controls access. Facade simplifies many parts.
Pitfall: six wrapper layers make stack traces painful.
Pitfall: a facade that grows into a god object.

pages.footer: Wrap to adapt, add, guard or simplify - and name the intent.
pages.summary: Explains six structural design patterns (Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite, Bridge) with Python sketches, and how to tell look-alike wrappers apart by intent.

panels:
The GoF structural patterns are Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight and Proxy. Most rely on composition plus forwarding: an outer object holds an inner one and delegates. Because Adapter, Decorator and Proxy can have nearly identical code, the pattern name documents intent, which is the main reason to use the names in code review.

Python makes wrappers cheap. __getattr__ can forward any attribute not defined on the wrapper, which is handy but hides the interface from type checkers and IDEs, so explicit methods or a Protocol are clearer for public APIs. Flyweight, the one pattern not on this page, shares immutable state among many small objects to save memory; Python's interning of small ints and short strings, and __slots__, serve similar goals.

An adapter converts the interface of one class into the interface clients expect. Object adapters hold the adaptee (composition); class adapters inherit from it, which Python allows but couples you to its internals. Adapters are the standard way to isolate third-party SDKs: your domain code depends on your own small interface, and only the adapter imports the vendor library.

That isolation pays off in tests (fake the interface, not the SDK), in vendor migrations (write a second adapter) and in limiting blast radius when the SDK changes. Adapters should translate, not add business logic. Watch unit and type conversions, such as cents versus dollars: dividing by 100 gives a float, and money should usually stay in integer cents or Decimal to avoid rounding errors. In hexagonal architecture these are the 'driven adapters' plugged into ports.

A decorator wraps an object, keeps its interface and adds responsibilities before or after delegating. Because wrappers compose, n optional features need n classes instead of up to 2^n subclasses. Order matters: Retry(Cache(api)) retries cache misses, while Cache(Retry(api)) caches results after retries; logging outside a cache records hits too.

Python's @decorator syntax applies the same idea to functions: @f above def g is just g = f(g). Use functools.wraps so the wrapper keeps the name, docstring and signature. lru_cache is a built-in example; note that it holds strong references to arguments and results, and on methods it caches per self and can keep objects alive. Decorators should be transparent: a wrapper that changes return types or swallows exceptions breaks Liskov substitution for its callers.

A facade provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem without hiding the subsystem: advanced callers can still use the parts directly. It reduces coupling, since clients depend on one entry point, and it is a natural place for orchestration, ordering and error handling such as compensating actions (refund if shipping fails).

Service layers and application services in web backends are facades over repositories, payment and messaging. Client libraries often provide a facade over raw HTTP. The checkout example also hides an important design question: what happens on partial failure? Real systems use transactions, idempotency keys or sagas. The main risk is growth: a facade that accumulates every operation becomes a god object. Keep facades task-oriented, one per use case or area, and keep business rules in the domain rather than in the facade.

A proxy has the same interface as the real subject and controls access to it. Virtual proxies defer expensive creation (lazy loading); protection proxies check permissions; remote proxies make a network call look local (RPC stubs, gRPC clients); caching and smart-reference proxies add caching, reference counting or locking.

ORMs use virtual proxies for lazy-loaded relationships, which causes the N+1 query problem when a loop touches each relation and triggers one query per item. Remote proxies hide latency and partial failure, a classic fallacy of distributed computing, so make remote calls visible in names or types when it matters. Python examples: weakref.proxy, unittest.mock objects, and functools.cached_property for lazy attributes. Proxy versus decorator: both wrap; a proxy usually manages the subject's lifecycle or access, while a decorator adds behavior and is often stacked.

Composite lets clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly through a shared component interface. Operations recurse: Folder.size() sums children, which may themselves be folders. Classic uses are file systems, UI widget trees, scene graphs, organization charts and abstract syntax trees.

Design choices: whether child-management methods (add, remove) belong on the shared interface (transparency, but leaves must reject them) or only on composites (safety, but callers need type checks). Recursion depth can hit Python's default limit of about 1000 frames on very deep trees, so iterative traversal with an explicit stack is safer for untrusted input. Cycles (symlinks, shared children) can cause infinite recursion; track visited nodes. Composite pairs naturally with Iterator for traversal and Visitor for adding operations without editing every node class.

Bridge decouples an abstraction from its implementation so both can vary independently, replacing a class explosion (m x n subclasses) with m + n classes connected by composition. The abstraction (Shape) holds a reference to an implementor (Renderer) and calls primitive operations on it, such as draw_circle(x, y, r).

It is often designed up front, unlike Adapter, which is usually retrofitted to make existing incompatible things work together. Real examples: database drivers behind a common API (Python's DB-API), logging handlers separate from loggers, and GUI toolkits separating widgets from platform backends. The hard part is defining the implementor interface: it must be rich enough for every abstraction yet implementable by every backend, a lowest common denominator problem. In Python, the implementor can simply be a function or object passed to the constructor, which makes Bridge look like Strategy; the intent differs (a structural split versus a swappable algorithm).

A quick intent test: if the wrapper exists because two interfaces do not match, it is an Adapter. If it adds behavior and keeps the interface, a Decorator. If it decides whether and when the real object is reached, a Proxy. If it offers a smaller, simpler interface over many objects, a Facade. Composite is about part-whole trees, Bridge about splitting two dimensions of variation.

Pitfalls beyond the two printed ones: wrappers can break identity and type checks (isinstance fails on a wrapped object), equality and hashing, and pickling. Deep wrapper stacks hurt performance in hot paths, since each layer adds a Python call costing tens of nanoseconds or more. Debugging gets harder when stack traces show many forwarding frames. Prefer a few named, well-tested wrappers, and document their order.
deeper.further: Next, study Flyweight, the seventh structural pattern, and how Python's __slots__ and interning relate. Explore hexagonal architecture, where adapters and ports formalize these ideas, and the anti-corruption layer from domain-driven design. Learn functools.wraps, contextlib and descriptor-based proxies, plus wrapt for robust decorators. The N+1 query problem in ORMs, the fallacies of distributed computing for remote proxies, and the Visitor pattern for operations over composite trees are natural follow-ups.

pages.title: Behavioral Patterns
pages.subtitle: Who does what, and how objects talk

panels.heading: Strategy
panels.body:
Problem: swap an algorithm at runtime.
Pass the behavior in as an object or function.
Example: shipping is free over 50, else 5.
Cart of 40 -> total 45.

panels.heading: Observer
panels.body:
Problem: many objects react when one changes.
The subject keeps a list of subscribers and notifies each on events.
Used in UIs, event buses, pub/sub.
panels.code:
for callback in self.subscribers:
    callback(event)

panels.heading: Command
panels.body:
Problem: treat a request as an object.
A command packs action + data with execute() and undo().
Enables queues, logs, retries and undo/redo.
panels.code:
cmd = AddText(doc, "hi")
cmd.execute(); history.append(cmd)
history.pop().undo()

panels.heading: State
panels.body:
Problem: behavior depends on the current state.
Each state is a class; the object delegates to it.
Order: Pending -> Paid -> Shipped.
ship() while Pending raises an error - no 6-way if.

panels.heading: Template Method
panels.body:
Problem: same steps, a few details differ.
The base class fixes the skeleton; subclasses fill in hooks.
export() = load -> format -> save; CSV and JSON override only format().

panels.heading: Iterator
panels.body:
Problem: walk a collection without exposing its internals.
Python builds it in: __iter__ / __next__, or a generator with yield.
Works for trees, files, paginated APIs.

panels.heading: Chain of Responsibility
panels.body:
Problem: several handlers might process a request.
Pass it along a chain; each link handles, stops or forwards.
Example: web middleware auth -> rate limit -> validate -> handler.

panels.heading: Compare + Pitfalls
panels.body:
Strategy: the caller picks behavior. State: the object switches itself.
Template Method uses inheritance; Strategy uses composition.
Pitfall: a one-method class where a function would do.
Pitfall: observer cascades hide control flow.

pages.footer: Name the behavior, give it an object, and swap it freely.
pages.summary: Covers seven behavioral design patterns (Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Template Method, Iterator, Chain of Responsibility) with short Python sketches and how to choose between similar ones.

panels:
Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface and lets the caller choose. In Python the interface is usually just a callable signature, so a function, lambda, functools.partial or object with __call__ all qualify; sorted(key=...) and max(key=...) are built-in strategy parameters.

Use a class when the strategy carries configuration or state, or needs several related methods. Strategies are ideal for pricing rules, retry and backoff policies, compression or serialization formats, and ML components like optimizers or loss functions. The worked example also shows a subtle requirement: thresholds must be specified precisely. Free over 50 means a cart of exactly 50 still pays shipping with t > 50; if the business means 'from 50', the rule is t >= 50. Strategies make such rules easy to test in isolation with table-driven tests.

Observer defines a one-to-many dependency: when the subject changes, it notifies registered observers. It decouples the subject from knowing who cares. Push style sends the data with the event; pull style sends a signal and observers query the subject.

Publish-subscribe is a related but distinct architecture: a broker or event bus sits in the middle, so publishers and subscribers do not know each other, and delivery may be asynchronous, persisted or cross-process (Kafka, Redis pub/sub). Pitfalls: the lapsed-listener problem, where a subject's list keeps dead observers alive (use weakref.WeakMethod or explicit unsubscribe); exceptions in one observer stopping others; reentrancy when an observer modifies the subject during notification; and unpredictable notification order. Iterate over a copy of the subscriber list if callbacks may unsubscribe themselves.

Command turns a request into an object containing everything needed to perform it later: the receiver, the action and the arguments. That reification enables queuing (task queues like Celery serialize commands), logging and replay, macro recording, transactional behavior, and undo/redo with two stacks: undo pops from history and pushes onto a redo stack; any new command clears the redo stack.

Undo design is the hard part. Either store enough state to reverse the action (inverse operations, like delete the inserted text) or store snapshots (Memento pattern), trading memory for simplicity. Commands sent over a network or retried must be idempotent or carry an idempotency key so duplicates do no harm. In CQRS (command query responsibility segregation) architectures, commands are the write side, kept separate from read-side queries.

State lets an object alter its behavior when its internal state changes, by delegating to a state object. Each state class implements the operations valid in that state and decides the transition, replacing scattered conditionals with explicit, testable classes. The object appears to change its class.

For simple cases, a transition table, a dict mapping (state, event) to next state, is often clearer than classes and can be validated or drawn as a diagram. Python's enum.Enum works well for state names. Explicit state machines matter for orders, payments, connections and protocol parsers, where invalid transitions (shipping an unpaid order) must be impossible rather than merely unlikely. Persisted state needs care: store the state name in the database, rebuild the state object on load, and guard transitions with optimistic locking to avoid two workers racing.

Template Method defines an algorithm's skeleton in a base class and defers some steps to subclasses. The base controls order and invariants; subclasses override hook methods. This is the Hollywood principle, 'don't call us, we'll call you', and it is how many frameworks work: unittest.TestCase calls your setUp, test methods and tearDown; Django class-based views call get_queryset and get_context_data.

The cost is inheritance coupling: subclasses depend on the base class's internal call order, and the fragile base class problem means changing the skeleton can break subclasses silently. Deep template hierarchies are hard to follow. The composition alternative passes the varying steps as functions or strategy objects, which is easier to test and combine. Mark required hooks with abc.abstractmethod so a missing override fails at instantiation rather than mid-run.

Iterator provides sequential access to elements without exposing the underlying representation. Python bakes it into the language: an iterable defines __iter__ returning an iterator, and an iterator defines __next__, raising StopIteration when done. for loops, comprehensions, unpacking and many built-ins use this protocol.

Generators are the easiest way to write iterators: yield suspends the function and keeps its local state, and yield from delegates to a sub-iterator. They are lazy, so they handle huge files or endless paginated APIs in constant memory. Pitfalls: iterators are single-pass, so a second loop over the same generator yields nothing; modifying a list or dict while iterating raises errors or skips elements; and laziness delays exceptions until consumption. The itertools module (islice, chain, groupby, batched in Python 3.12+) composes iterators efficiently.

Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a sequence of handlers; each can handle it, reject it, or pass it on. The sender does not know which handler will act. Web middleware stacks (ASGI and WSGI middleware, Express-style) are the best-known example, along with logging handler hierarchies and event bubbling in UI trees.

Order is semantic: rate limiting before authentication protects the auth service from floods but limits anonymous traffic by IP rather than by user; logging first records rejected requests too. Each link should do one job. Failure modes include requests that fall off the end unhandled (add a default terminal handler), and expensive links placed early. A middleware that wraps the next call, as in ASGI, combines Chain of Responsibility with Decorator, since it can run code both before and after the rest of the chain.

Strategy versus State: same structure (delegation to an interchangeable object), different control. With Strategy, the client chooses and the strategy rarely changes during the object's life. With State, the context or the states themselves switch the current state as events arrive. Template Method versus Strategy: inheritance with a fixed skeleton versus composition with a swappable piece; prefer composition unless a framework hands you a base class.

Python simplifications: a one-method class can usually be a function, and a dict of functions often replaces a pattern class hierarchy. Hidden control flow is the main risk: observers that trigger other observers can form cascades or infinite loops, and chains and commands spread logic across many small files. Good tests, explicit names and a diagram in the docs keep these patterns understandable. Interviewers like asking which pattern a familiar API uses.
deeper.further: Explore the remaining behavioral patterns: Mediator, Memento, Visitor and Interpreter. Learn reactive programming (ReactiveX) as Observer at scale, event sourcing and CQRS as Command at architectural scale, and statecharts (XState, the SCXML model) for complex state machines. In Python, study the iterator protocol in depth, generators, asyncio async iterators and itertools. Look at ASGI middleware internals to see Chain of Responsibility and Decorator combined.

pages.title: Clean Code & Refactoring
pages.subtitle: Write for the next reader - often future you

panels.heading: Naming
panels.body:
Names reveal intent.
Bad: d, data2, process(). Good: days_overdue, send_invoice().
Booleans read as questions: is_active, has_access.
One word per concept: not fetch, get and retrieve.

panels.heading: Small Functions
panels.body:
One function = one job at one level of detail.
Few parameters (3 or fewer is a good default).
No hidden side effects: validate() should not save.
panels.code:
def place_order(cart):
    validate(cart)
    charge(cart.total)
    send_receipt(cart)

panels.heading: Dry, Kiss, Yagni
panels.body:
DRY = don't repeat yourself: one source of truth per rule.
KISS = keep it simple: simplest thing that works.
YAGNI = you aren't gonna need it: no code for imagined futures.
Rule of three: abstract on the third copy.

panels.heading: Composition Over Inheritance
panels.body:
Inheritance = "is-a", tightly coupled to the parent.
Composition = "has-a": build from swappable parts.
Before: a LoggingRetryingCachedClient subclass chain.
After: Client(cache=..., retry=..., logger=...).

panels.heading: Dependency Injection
panels.body:
DI = pass dependencies in instead of creating them inside.
Code becomes testable and swappable.
Inject a fake clock -> deterministic output.

panels.heading: Code Smells -> Refactoring Moves
panels.body:
Long function -> Extract Function.
Duplicate code -> extract and reuse.
Long parameter list -> Introduce Parameter Object.
Type switch everywhere -> Replace Conditional with Polymorphism.
Magic number 86400 -> SECONDS_PER_DAY.

panels.heading: Refactor Safely With Tests
panels.body:
Refactoring = change structure, not behavior.
1. Tests green first (pin legacy behavior with characterization tests).
2. One tiny step. 3. Run tests. 4. Commit.
Never mix refactoring and new features in one commit.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Big-bang rewrites stall for months; refactor in small steps.
Over-DRY: merging look-alike code that changes for different reasons.
Clever one-liners hurt readability.
Comments should explain why, not what.

pages.footer: Clean code is a habit: clear names, small steps, green tests.
pages.summary: Teaches everyday clean-code habits (naming, small functions, DRY/KISS/YAGNI, composition over inheritance, dependency injection) and how to map code smells to safe, test-backed refactoring moves.

panels:
Good names compress context: a reader should predict what a name holds or does without reading its body. Scope matters: a loop index i is fine in a three-line loop, while a module-level value needs a full descriptive name. Include units when ambiguity is costly: timeout_seconds, price_cents, distance_km. Functions are verbs (send_invoice), classes and values are nouns (Invoice), booleans are predicates (is_paid, has_access), and collections are plurals.

Consistency beats cleverness: pick one word per concept across the codebase and use the domain's language, which domain-driven design calls the ubiquitous language. Avoid encodings like Hungarian notation, misleading names (account_list that is a dict), and noise words (data, info, manager). PEP 8 conventions: snake_case for functions and variables, CapWords for classes, UPPER_CASE for constants. Renaming is the safest, most valuable refactoring; IDE rename tools make it nearly free.

Small functions are easier to name, test and reuse, but size is a proxy. The real goals are one level of abstraction per function (do not mix business steps with string parsing) and command-query separation: a function either changes state or returns information, not both. Step-down reading, where high-level functions call lower-level ones defined below, makes a module read like a narrative.

Too many tiny functions can fragment logic, forcing readers to jump around; John Ousterhout argues for deep modules with simple interfaces hiding significant functionality, a counterpoint to extreme splitting. Many parameters suggest the function does too much or that values belong together in an object. Boolean flag parameters often mean two functions in one: send(email, urgent=True) might be better as send_urgent(email). Use keyword-only arguments (def f(*, retries)) to keep call sites readable.

DRY, from The Pragmatic Programmer, is about knowledge, not text: every business rule should have a single, authoritative representation. Duplicated rules drift apart, and a bug fixed in one copy survives in another. Sandi Metz's warning applies too: 'duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction'. Removing duplication too early produces shared helpers full of flags and special cases.

KISS favors the simplest solution that meets current requirements; simplicity means few concepts and little coupling, not few characters. YAGNI, from Extreme Programming, rejects speculative generality: features, parameters and plugin systems built for needs that may never arrive cost code to maintain, tests to write and time not spent on real work. The rule of three balances these: tolerate a second copy, extract on the third, when the common shape is finally clear.

Inheritance couples a subclass to its parent's implementation, not just its interface: changes to the base can break subclasses (the fragile base class problem), and combining features through subclassing explodes into many classes. The GoF book itself advises favoring object composition over class inheritance. Composition assembles behavior from parts held as attributes, which can be swapped at runtime and tested in isolation.

Inheritance is still right for genuine is-a relationships with stable contracts, for framework extension points, and for abstract base classes defining interfaces. Python adds mixins, small classes adding one capability via multiple inheritance; they work but rely on method resolution order (MRO), and cooperative super() calls get tricky. Rule of thumb: inherit interfaces, compose implementations. Protocols give polymorphism without any inheritance, so 'is-a' can often become 'behaves-like'.

Dependency injection means an object receives its collaborators instead of constructing or looking them up. Constructor injection is the default; parameter injection (as with greet(clock=...)) suits functions; setter injection allows late wiring but permits half-initialized objects. Wiring happens at the composition root, usually main() or an app factory.

Typical injected dependencies are the nondeterministic or slow ones: clocks, random generators, HTTP clients, databases, file systems and environment configuration. Injecting them makes tests fast and deterministic without monkeypatching. Python frameworks offer built-in DI, such as FastAPI's Depends and pytest fixtures. A detail in the printed example: datetime.now as a default is safe because the function object is evaluated once, not called at definition time, unlike the classic bug def f(t=datetime.now()), which freezes the time when the module loads. Avoid service locators, which hide dependencies again.

A code smell, a term from Kent Beck and Martin Fowler's Refactoring, is a surface symptom that often indicates a deeper design problem; it is a prompt to look, not proof of a bug. Fowler's catalog pairs smells with named moves. Others worth knowing: feature envy (a method uses another class's data more than its own -> Move Function), data clumps (the same three fields travel together -> Extract Class), primitive obsession (strings for emails and money -> value objects), shotgun surgery (one change touches many files -> consolidate), and divergent change (one class changes for many reasons -> split).

Replace Conditional with Polymorphism is the bridge to the Strategy and State patterns. Linters and analyzers such as ruff, pylint and radon (cyclomatic complexity) detect some smells automatically; complexity above roughly 10 per function is a common warning threshold.

Fowler defines refactoring as a change to internal structure that leaves observable behavior unchanged. The safety net is a fast test suite: run it after each step, and if it fails, revert rather than debug, because the step was small. Commit at every green point so any step can be undone, and keep refactoring commits separate from behavior changes so reviewers can check each kind on its own terms.

For legacy code without tests, Michael Feathers' approach: find seams, write characterization tests that assert current outputs (even wrong ones), then refactor. Snapshot and approval testing speed this up. For large changes, use the strangler fig pattern or branch by abstraction to migrate gradually behind an interface while the system keeps working, and parallel change (expand, migrate, contract) for APIs and database schemas. Automated IDE refactorings are safer than manual edits.

Big-bang rewrites fail often because the old system encodes years of undocumented edge cases, and the new one must catch up with a moving target while delivering no value until cutover. Incremental replacement, as with the strangler fig, keeps value flowing and limits risk.

Other pitfalls: wrong abstractions created by over-zealous DRY; refactoring without tests, which is just changing code; mixing formatting changes into functional diffs, which hides real changes in review (run formatters in a separate commit); and refactoring code that is about to be deleted. Cleverness costs readers time; prefer obvious code even if longer. Comments should explain why, such as constraints, trade-offs and links to tickets, while names and structure explain what. Track refactoring as part of normal work, following the Boy Scout rule, rather than as a separate phase that never gets scheduled.
deeper.further: Read Fowler's Refactoring (2nd edition) for the full smell and move catalog, Feathers' Working Effectively with Legacy Code for seams and characterization tests, and Ousterhout's A Philosophy of Software Design for deep modules as a counterpoint to tiny functions. Explore the strangler fig pattern, parallel change, mutation testing to check test strength, and static analysis tools such as ruff, mypy and radon. Sandi Metz's talks on the wrong abstraction and on composition are short, practical follow-ups.

pages.title: Scaling & Load Balancing
pages.subtitle: Grow by adding machines, not bigger ones

panels.heading: Scale Up vs Scale Out
panels.body:
Vertical (scale up): bigger CPU, RAM, disk. Simple, but hits a ceiling and stays one point of failure.
Horizontal (scale out): more identical servers behind a load balancer. Grows further, survives failures.

panels.heading: Keep Servers Stateless
panels.body:
Stateless = any server can answer any request.
Sessions -> Redis or signed tokens (JWT = JSON Web Token).
Files -> object storage. Data -> shared database.
Now add or remove servers freely.

panels.heading: Load Balancer: L4 vs L7
panels.body:
L4 (transport layer): routes by IP and port. Very fast, cannot read HTTP.
L7 (application layer): reads URL, headers, cookies. Routes /api vs /img, terminates TLS, retries.

panels.heading: Balancing Algorithms
panels.body:
Round robin: A, B, C, A, B, C...
Weighted: bigger servers get more turns.
Least connections: send to the least busy server.
Consistent hashing: same key -> same server; adding a node moves only ~1/N of keys.

panels.heading: Health Checks
panels.body:
Balancer probes GET /healthz every 5 s.
3 failures -> server removed; 2 passes -> back in.
Liveness: process is alive. Readiness: ready for traffic (DB connected, cache warm).

panels.heading: Back-of-Envelope Example
panels.body:
10M daily users x 20 requests = 200M requests/day.
200M / 86,400 s = ~2,300 req/s; peak ~3x = ~7,000 req/s.
~1,000 req/s per server -> 7 servers; run 10 for failover headroom.

panels.heading: Latency vs Throughput
panels.body:
Latency: time for one request. Throughput: requests per second.
Track p99 latency, not the average.
RAM read ~100 ns. SSD read ~100 us. Same-datacenter round trip ~0.5 ms. Cross-continent ~150 ms.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
Sticky sessions unbalance load.
The load balancer needs a standby too.
The database becomes the next bottleneck.
Check: why does least connections beat round robin when requests vary in length?

pages.footer: Stateless servers plus a smart load balancer: scale by adding boxes.
pages.summary: How systems grow: vertical versus horizontal scaling, why servers should be stateless, how L4 and L7 load balancers spread traffic with round robin, least connections or consistent hashing, and how health checks and quick capacity estimates keep the fleet sized and healthy.

panels:
Vertical scaling is underrated: a single modern server can have 192+ cores and several terabytes of RAM, and one well-tuned PostgreSQL box serves a surprising number of companies. It needs no code changes, keeps transactions local and avoids distributed-systems bugs. Its limits are a hard hardware ceiling, cost that rises faster than linearly at the top end, downtime during resizes, and a single failure domain.

Horizontal scaling adds commodity nodes and gives fault tolerance through redundancy, but it pushes complexity into coordination: shared state, data partitioning, consistent configuration and partial failures. Interviewers like the nuance that stateless tiers (web, API) scale out easily, while stateful tiers (databases, caches) are where horizontal scaling gets hard. A common real answer is both: scale the database up as far as is sensible, scale the app tier out.

Stateless does not mean the system has no state; it means a request carries or fetches everything it needs, so no server holds data that a later request depends on. Typical moves: sessions in Redis or in signed, short-lived tokens; uploads in object storage; locks and counters in a shared store; scheduled jobs coordinated with leader election instead of 'run on server 1'.

JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) avoid a session lookup but are hard to revoke before expiry, so keep them short-lived (minutes) with refresh tokens, or keep a small deny-list. Local in-process caches are acceptable as long as losing them only costs performance, not correctness. The payoff is operational: autoscaling, rolling deploys and replacing unhealthy instances become routine because any instance can be killed at any time without losing user data.

An L4 balancer works on TCP/UDP connections: it picks a backend when a connection opens and forwards packets, often via NAT or direct server return, handling millions of connections with tiny overhead. Because it never parses HTTP, it cannot route by path, and with long-lived connections (HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSockets) it balances connections rather than requests, which can leave load badly skewed.

An L7 balancer (reverse proxy such as Envoy, NGINX, HAProxy or a cloud ALB) terminates TLS, parses requests, and can route by host, path or header, rewrite headers, add retries, do canary splits and balance each gRPC request individually. The cost is CPU per request and a component that sees plaintext traffic. Large sites often chain them: anycast or DNS -> L4 tier -> L7 proxy tier -> services.

Round robin assumes equal servers and equal requests; it is fine for uniform, short requests. Least connections (or least outstanding requests) adapts to uneven request cost and slow backends. A strong practical option is 'power of two choices': pick two servers at random and send to the less loaded one, which gets most of the benefit of global least-load with almost no coordination.

Consistent hashing places servers (often 100-200 virtual nodes each) and keys on a ring; a key goes to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node remaps only about 1/N of keys, versus nearly all keys with hash % N. Use it when affinity matters, such as cache servers or sharded state. Variants include rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing and bounded-load consistent hashing, which caps how overloaded any one node can get.

Active health checks probe an endpoint on a schedule; passive checks (outlier detection) watch real traffic and eject hosts that return too many 5xx errors or time out. Use thresholds with hysteresis (for example 3 fails out, 2 passes in) so a host does not flap in and out.

Kubernetes makes the distinction sharp: a failing liveness probe restarts the container, a failing readiness probe only removes it from Service endpoints. A classic outage pattern is a deep health check that also verifies the database: when the database blips, every instance fails health checks at once and the balancer has nothing left to route to. Keep liveness shallow, make readiness reflect only what the instance itself controls, and configure 'fail open' (route to all) if every backend looks unhealthy at the same time.

Interviewers care about the method, not precision: state assumptions, round aggressively, and keep units straight. Useful anchors: 1 day = 86,400 s, roughly 10^5; 1M requests/day is about 12 req/s; peak is often 2-5x the average. Per-node capacity depends heavily on the workload: a simple cached read might reach 10,000+ req/s per core-heavy node, while a request doing database work might manage hundreds.

Size for N+1 or N+2 so you survive losing a node (or a whole availability zone: with 3 zones, each must carry 50% of peak if one fails) and keep utilization near 60-70% for headroom. Also estimate bandwidth (requests x response size) and storage (records x size x retention x replication factor). Finish by naming which resource limits you first: CPU, memory, connections, or the database.

Latency and throughput are linked by Little's law: concurrency = throughput x latency. At 2,000 req/s and 50 ms average latency, about 100 requests are in flight; if latency doubles, you need twice the concurrency (threads, connections) to keep the same throughput. As utilization approaches 100%, queueing makes latency rise sharply, which is why systems are run with headroom.

Tail latency dominates user experience at scale: if a page fans out to 100 backends and each has a 1% chance of a slow response, about 63% of page loads hit at least one slow call. Mitigations include hedged requests (send a backup request after the p95 time), timeouts, and reducing fan-out. Memorize orders of magnitude, not exact numbers: memory is nanoseconds, SSD is tens to hundreds of microseconds, network within a datacenter is around half a millisecond, and cross-continent is around 100-150 ms.

Sticky sessions (session affinity) pin a user to one server, which defeats even spreading, concentrates load from heavy users, and loses sessions when that server dies; prefer external session stores. The balancer itself must be redundant: an active-passive pair sharing a virtual IP, DNS with multiple addresses, or a managed cloud balancer that is distributed internally.

Scaling the stateless tier often just moves the bottleneck: more app servers open more database connections, and connection limits are hit before CPU, so use connection pooling (PgBouncer or a built-in pool). Retries at the balancer can multiply load during an incident, so cap them with retry budgets. Answer to the check: least connections accounts for requests still running, so a server busy with a long request receives fewer new ones, while round robin keeps dealing work to it regardless.
deeper.further: Next, study autoscaling policies (target tracking on CPU or requests per second, and why scaling on queue depth reacts faster), global traffic management (GeoDNS, anycast, multi-region failover), and the 'power of two choices' result for load balancing. Read about tail latency in 'The Tail at Scale' and about connection pooling for databases. Service meshes such as Envoy-based meshes move L7 balancing, retries and health checking into sidecars. Finally, practice capacity estimates until converting daily volumes into requests per second, bandwidth and storage feels automatic.

pages.title: Caching
pages.subtitle: Keep hot data close, fast and fresh

panels.heading: Why Cache
panels.body:
A cache keeps copies of hot data in faster storage.
Redis read ~0.5 ms vs database query ~10-50 ms.
Hit ratio is the goal: 95% hits = only 1 in 20 reads reaches the DB.

panels.heading: Cache Layers
panels.body:
Browser: Cache-Control headers.
CDN (content delivery network): copies at edge servers near users.
Application: in-process memory or Redis.
Database: buffer pool keeps hot pages in RAM.

panels.heading: Write Strategies
panels.body:
Cache-aside: app checks cache; on miss reads DB and fills cache.
Write-through: write cache and DB together. Fresh, slower writes.
Write-back: write cache, flush DB later. Fast, risks loss on crash.

panels.heading: Cache-Aside in Redis
panels.body:
Miss -> load from DB -> store with TTL (time to live) of 300 s.
On update: write the DB, then delete the key.
panels.code:
v = r.get("user:42")
if v is None:
    v = load_user_json(42)
    r.set("user:42", v, ex=300)

panels.heading: TTL & Eviction
panels.body:
TTL: entries expire after a set time, bounding staleness.
LRU (least recently used): evict the item untouched longest.
LFU (least frequently used): evict the least popular.
Redis: maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru.

panels.heading: Invalidation
panels.body:
Hard part: cache and database disagree.
On write, delete the key rather than update it.
Versioned keys: user:42:v7.
Keep a TTL as a safety net for missed deletes.

panels.heading: Pitfalls: Cache Stampede
panels.body:
Hot key expires -> 1,000 requests miss at once -> database overload.
Fixes: one request refills under a lock, serve stale while refreshing, add random TTL jitter.
Also cache 'not found' results.

pages.footer: Cache the hot path, expire everything, delete on write.
pages.summary: Where caches live (browser, CDN, application, database), the main write strategies (cache-aside, write-through, write-back), TTLs and LRU/LFU eviction, how to invalidate safely, and how to prevent a cache stampede, with a Redis cache-aside example.

panels:
A cache only helps if the access pattern is skewed and repeated: many real workloads follow a power law where a small fraction of keys gets most reads. The effective latency is roughly hit_ratio x cache_latency + miss_ratio x (cache_latency + db_latency). Going from a 90% to a 99% hit ratio cuts database reads by 10x, which is why the last few percent of hit ratio matter more than they look.

Caching also trades correctness for speed: every cache is a second copy that can be stale, and it adds a failure mode in which the cache disappears and the database suddenly receives the full load (cold-start or failover). Before adding one, check whether a missing index, a better query, or a read replica solves the problem more simply. Cache what is expensive to compute and read far more often than it changes.

Browser caching is controlled by HTTP headers: Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable for fingerprinted static assets (app.3f9a.js), no-cache (revalidate each time using ETag or Last-Modified, getting a cheap 304 Not Modified) for HTML, and private versus public to keep personalized responses out of shared caches. CDNs honor s-maxage and support stale-while-revalidate and purge APIs, and they shield your origin server from traffic spikes.

Application caches come in two flavors: in-process (fastest, no network hop, but duplicated per instance and inconsistent between instances) and distributed (Redis, Memcached: shared, about 0.2-1 ms per round trip). Many systems use both, with a small local LRU in front of Redis. The database buffer pool (PostgreSQL shared_buffers, InnoDB buffer pool) plus the OS page cache already caches hot pages, so a 'slow database' is often an under-provisioned memory problem.

Cache-aside (lazy loading) is the default: only requested data gets cached and the cache can fail without breaking correctness, but the first request for each key pays the full miss and invalidation is the application's job. Read-through is the same idea with the cache library doing the loading.

Write-through updates the cache on every write, so reads are fresh, but writes pay both latencies and the cache fills with data that may never be read. Write-back (write-behind) acknowledges after the cache write and flushes asynchronously, often batching writes, which is great for write-heavy counters but risks losing acknowledged data and needs a durable or replicated cache. A related option is write-around: write only to the database and let reads populate the cache. Choose per data type rather than per system.

The example uses redis-py: r.get returns bytes or None, and set with ex=300 stores the value with a 300-second expiry in one atomic command. Serialize objects (JSON or MessagePack) and namespace keys (service:entity:id) so they can be scanned and purged by prefix.

The update order matters. 'Write DB, then delete key' still has a rare race: a reader misses, loads the old row, the writer commits and deletes, then the reader writes the old value back. The TTL bounds the damage; stricter setups delete again after a short delay or drive invalidation from the database change stream (change data capture). Avoid 'delete key, then write DB', because a reader can repopulate the old value in between. Interviewers often ask exactly this ordering question.

TTLs bound staleness and also clean up keys nobody will ask for again. Choose them per data type: seconds for prices or stock levels, hours for profile data, a year for content-addressed assets. Redis expires keys lazily on access plus by sampling in the background, so expired keys may use memory briefly.

When memory is full, the eviction policy decides. Redis offers noeviction (writes fail), allkeys-lru, allkeys-lfu, volatile-* variants that only evict keys that have a TTL, and random variants. Its LRU and LFU are approximations based on sampling, not exact lists. LRU suits recency-driven workloads; LFU resists one-off scans that would otherwise flush popular keys. Monitor the eviction count and hit ratio together: frequent evictions with a falling hit ratio mean the working set no longer fits.

Invalidation is hard because the cache and the database cannot be updated atomically, and many keys can depend on one row (a user's name appears in their profile, every comment and many feed pages). Approaches, roughly from simple to robust: TTL only; delete on write; versioned or generational keys, where you bump a version number so old keys simply stop being read; and event-driven invalidation from the database's change log, which catches writes from every code path, including scripts and migrations.

Deleting is safer than updating because concurrent updates can be applied out of order, leaving the older value cached indefinitely. For derived data such as feeds, it is often cheaper to tolerate brief staleness than to track every dependency. Always ask: how stale can this be before a user notices, or before it becomes a correctness bug?

A stampede (thundering herd or dogpile) happens when a popular key expires or the cache restarts. Defenses: single-flight or request coalescing, where one caller recomputes under a short-lived lock (SET key:lock NX EX 10) and others wait or receive the stale value; stale-while-revalidate, which serves the old value while a background refresh runs; probabilistic early expiration, where each reader refreshes slightly early with growing probability; and TTL jitter (for example 300 s plus or minus 10%) so keys loaded together do not expire together.

Cache penetration is repeated lookups for keys that do not exist, often from bots, and each one reaches the database; cache the 'not found' result with a short TTL or put a Bloom filter in front. Cache avalanche is many keys expiring at once or the whole cache failing; plan for a cold cache with warm-up and rate limits on the database.
deeper.further: Go deeper with HTTP caching semantics (RFC 9111: Cache-Control, ETag, Vary), CDN features such as tiered caching, origin shield and surrogate keys for targeted purges, and Redis internals (persistence with RDB and AOF, replication, Redis Cluster hash slots). Read about cache consistency at scale, for example lease-based invalidation in large Memcached deployments, and about change data capture tools that invalidate caches from database logs. Also learn admission policies such as TinyLFU, which decide whether a new item deserves to enter the cache at all.

pages.title: Databases
pages.subtitle: Pick the right store, index it, keep it correct

panels.heading: SQL vs NoSQL
panels.body:
SQL (relational): tables, fixed schema, joins, strong transactions. PostgreSQL, MySQL.
NoSQL: flexible models built for scale or one access pattern.
Default to SQL unless a clear need says otherwise.

panels.heading: NoSQL Families
panels.body:
Document (MongoDB): JSON docs; profiles, catalogs.
Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB): get/put by key; sessions, carts.
Wide-column (Cassandra): partitioned rows; time series.
Graph (Neo4j): nodes + edges; social links, fraud.

panels.heading: Indexes (B-tree)
panels.body:
An index is a sorted structure pointing to rows.
B-tree lookup: O(log n) instead of a full scan O(n).
Composite index (a, b) serves a = ? and a = ? AND b = ?, not b alone.
Cost: slower writes.

panels.heading: Query Example + EXPLAIN
panels.body:
Before: Seq Scan over 10M rows, ~2 s.
After: Index Scan, ~1 ms.

panels.heading: ACID Transactions
panels.body:
Atomicity: all or nothing.
Consistency: constraints always hold.
Isolation: concurrent transactions don't interfere.
Durability: commits survive crashes (write-ahead log).
Transfer $50: debit and credit commit together.

panels.heading: Isolation Levels & Anomalies
panels.body:
Read uncommitted: dirty reads.
Read committed: no dirty reads; rows can change between reads.
Repeatable read: rows stable; phantom rows possible.
Serializable: as if one at a time; slowest.

panels.heading: Normalize vs Denormalize
panels.body:
Normalize: each fact stored once; clean updates, more joins.
Denormalize: copy data for fast reads (author_name inside posts); harder updates.
Normalize first; denormalize measured hot paths.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
N+1 queries: one query per row; use a join or batch.
SELECT * on wide tables.
Indexes on low-selectivity columns rarely help.
Check: why can't index (a, b) serve WHERE b = 5?

pages.footer: Model the data, index the queries, trust the transactions.
pages.summary: How to choose between relational SQL and the NoSQL families, how B-tree indexes speed up queries (checked with EXPLAIN), what ACID and the isolation levels guarantee, and when to normalize or denormalize.

panels:
The real decision is about access patterns and guarantees, not fashion. Relational databases give declarative queries, joins, constraints (foreign keys, unique, check) and multi-row ACID transactions, and modern ones scale further than people assume: read replicas, partitioning, and JSONB columns for semi-structured data cover many 'we need NoSQL' cases.

NoSQL systems usually trade some of that for a specific strength: horizontal write scaling, predictable single-digit-millisecond lookups by key, flexible schemas, or native graph traversal. Many now offer transactions too (MongoDB multi-document, DynamoDB TransactWriteItems), so 'NoSQL means no transactions' is outdated. Distributed SQL databases (Spanner, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB) combine SQL with horizontal scaling at the cost of higher write latency from consensus. Interview tip: justify the choice from query shapes, consistency needs and scale, and admit that schema-on-read still means a schema, just enforced in application code.

Document stores keep a whole aggregate (an order with its line items) together, so one read fetches it; they struggle with many-to-many relations and cross-document joins. Key-value stores are the simplest and fastest model; DynamoDB adds a sort key, so a partition key plus sort key supports range queries inside one partition, which enables 'single-table design' where you model data around known queries.

Wide-column stores (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable, HBase) partition by key and store rows sorted by a clustering key, with very high write throughput thanks to log-structured merge trees (LSM trees); you design one table per query. Graph databases store adjacency directly, so multi-hop traversals ('friends of friends who bought X') do not need repeated joins. Also worth knowing: search engines (inverted indexes), time-series databases, and vector databases for similarity search.

A B+ tree (the variant nearly all databases use) has high fan-out, often hundreds of keys per 8-16 KB page, so a table with a billion rows needs only 3-4 levels, and the top levels stay in memory. Leaves are linked, so range scans and ORDER BY on the indexed columns are cheap.

The leftmost-prefix rule for composite indexes: (a, b) is sorted by a, then by b within each a, so it serves equality on a, equality on a plus a range on b, and ordering by b within a fixed a. Put equality columns before range columns. A covering index includes every column the query needs, enabling an index-only scan with no table lookup. Every index slows inserts and updates and consumes memory, so remove unused ones. Other index types: hash, GIN (full-text, JSONB), GiST and BRIN for huge, naturally ordered tables.

EXPLAIN shows the planner's chosen plan with estimated costs; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and reports real row counts and timings per node (so wrap writes in a transaction you roll back). Read plans inside out: the deepest nodes run first. Signals to look for are Seq Scan on large tables with selective filters, estimated rows far from actual rows (stale statistics, so run ANALYZE), nested loops over large inputs, and sorts that spill to disk.

The planner may still choose a sequential scan when a filter matches a large fraction of the table, because random index lookups cost more than reading sequentially. In PostgreSQL, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids blocking writes on a busy production table. The numbers on the page (2 s versus 1 ms) are typical for a selective lookup on a table with about 10M rows: O(n) page reads versus 3-4 page reads plus the row fetch.

Atomicity is implemented with undo information or multi-version rows, so a failed transaction leaves no partial effects. Durability comes from the write-ahead log (WAL): changes are appended to the log and flushed (fsync) before the commit is acknowledged, and data pages are written later; after a crash the log is replayed. Group commit batches fsyncs to keep throughput high.

The C in ACID is partly the application's job: the database enforces declared constraints, but business invariants like 'balance never negative' must be expressed as constraints or enforced inside transactions. For the transfer example, use a single transaction with conditional updates (UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 50) and check the affected row count; this avoids the read-then-write race. Durability guarantees also depend on configuration, such as synchronous_commit and replication settings.

Anomalies to know: dirty read (seeing uncommitted data), non-repeatable read (a row changes between two reads), phantom (a re-run range query returns new rows), lost update (two read-modify-write cycles overwrite each other) and write skew (two transactions each check an invariant, then write different rows, breaking it together; the classic case is two on-call doctors both going off call).

Implementations differ from the SQL standard. PostgreSQL's repeatable read is snapshot isolation, which prevents phantoms but allows write skew; its serializable level (SSI) detects dangerous patterns and aborts one transaction, so applications must retry on serialization failures. MySQL InnoDB defaults to repeatable read and uses gap locks. Oracle and PostgreSQL default to read committed. Practical tools: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE for pessimistic locking, or a version column for optimistic concurrency control.

Normal forms remove redundancy: 1NF has atomic values, 2NF and 3NF remove columns that depend on only part of the key or on other non-key columns, so each fact lives in exactly one place. That prevents update anomalies, where changing an author's name means updating thousands of rows and missing some.

Denormalization deliberately duplicates data to avoid joins or expensive aggregations on hot read paths: counters (comment_count), embedded snapshots (the price at time of order, which is a correct historical fact, not merely a copy), materialized views, and read models built from events (as in CQRS, command query responsibility segregation). The cost is keeping copies in sync through triggers, application logic or asynchronous jobs, with eventual consistency. In NoSQL stores denormalization is the default, because there are no joins. Measure first: a well-indexed join is often fast enough.

N+1 queries usually come from ORM lazy loading; fix them with eager loading (a JOIN, or a second query using WHERE id IN (...)), and find them with query logs or tracing. SELECT * fetches unneeded columns, prevents index-only scans and breaks when the schema changes. Low-selectivity indexes (a boolean, or status with three values) rarely help unless the queried value is rare, where a partial index (WHERE status = 'failed') works well.

Other classics: missing indexes on foreign keys (slow joins and cascading deletes), functions on indexed columns (WHERE lower(email) = ... needs an expression index), long transactions that hold locks and block cleanup of old row versions, and deep OFFSET pagination. Answer to the check: an index on (a, b) is ordered by a first, so rows with b = 5 are scattered across every a value; the database would have to scan the whole index.
deeper.further: Next topics: storage engines (B-trees versus LSM trees and their read, write and space amplification), multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) and vacuuming, query planning and statistics, and connection pooling. 'Designing Data-Intensive Applications' covers data models, storage and transactions in depth. Practice reading EXPLAIN plans on a real PostgreSQL instance, and learn about online schema migrations (expand and contract), partitioning large tables, and NewSQL systems that offer serializable transactions across regions using consensus and synchronized clocks.

pages.title: Replication & Sharding
pages.subtitle: Copy data to survive, split it to grow

panels.heading: Replication vs Sharding
panels.body:
Replication: same data on several nodes -> availability, read scale.
Sharding (partitioning): split data across nodes -> write and storage scale.
Real systems do both: each shard is replicated.

panels.heading: Leader-Follower Replication
panels.body:
Writes go to the leader; followers replay its log.
Reads can use followers (read replicas).
Synchronous: no loss, slower writes.
Asynchronous: fast, may lose recent writes on failover.

panels.heading: Multi-Leader & Leaderless
panels.body:
Multi-leader: each region accepts writes; conflicts need resolving (last-write-wins, merge, CRDTs = conflict-free replicated data types).
Leaderless: write to W nodes, read R; W + R > N means overlap.

panels.heading: Replication Lag Example
panels.body:
User posts, refreshes, hits a replica 2 s behind -> post 'vanishes'.
Fix (read-your-writes): send that user's reads to the leader for ~10 s after a write.

panels.heading: Sharding Strategies
panels.body:
Range: user_id 1-1M -> shard A, 1M-2M -> shard B. Fast range scans; hot spot risk.
Hash: shard = hash(user_id) % 4. Even spread; range queries hit every shard.
Consistent hashing eases resharding.

panels.heading: Pitfalls: Hot Spots
panels.body:
One key or range takes most traffic: a celebrity account, today's timestamps.
Fixes: salt hot keys (key#0..key#9), split busy shards, cache hot reads.
Avoid timestamps as range shard keys.

panels.heading: Cap & Pacelc
panels.body:
CAP: during a network Partition, pick Consistency or Availability.
CP: refuse requests to stay correct. AP: answer, maybe stale.
PACELC: Else, with no partition, trade Latency vs Consistency.

panels.heading: Consistency Models
panels.body:
Strong (linearizable): every read sees the latest write.
Read-your-writes: you see your own updates.
Causal: causes appear before effects.
Eventual: replicas converge once writes stop, with no time bound.

pages.footer: Replicate to survive, shard to grow, choose consistency on purpose.
pages.summary: How distributed databases copy and split data: leader-follower, multi-leader and leaderless replication, replication lag and read-your-writes, range versus hash sharding and hot spots, and the CAP and PACELC trade-offs behind different consistency models.

panels:
Replication copies the same data, so it improves read capacity and survives node failures, but every replica still stores everything and every write must reach every replica, so it does not scale writes or storage. Sharding splits the data, so each node stores and writes only its slice, but queries that span shards become scatter-gather and cross-shard transactions get expensive.

Production systems combine them: a key maps to a shard, and each shard is a replica set (for example one leader and two followers spread across three availability zones). Replicating 3x across zones is the common default because it survives losing one zone while keeping a majority. Before sharding, exhaust simpler options: vertical scaling, read replicas, caching and archiving cold data, because sharding is hard to undo and changes how every query is written.

Followers apply the leader's change stream: physical WAL shipping (PostgreSQL streaming replication) or a logical row-based log (MySQL binlog). Synchronous replication waits for at least one follower to confirm before acknowledging the commit; making every follower synchronous means one slow node stalls all writes, so a common setup is semi-synchronous: one sync follower, the rest async.

Failover is the hard part: detecting that the leader is dead (timeouts that are too short cause false failovers), promoting the most up-to-date follower, and fencing the old leader so that two leaders never accept writes at once (split brain). With async replication, writes acknowledged by the old leader but not yet replicated are lost on failover. Consensus-based systems (Raft, Paxos, as in etcd, Spanner or CockroachDB) commit a write once a majority has it, so failover loses nothing that was acknowledged.

Multi-leader setups suit multi-region writes, offline-capable clients and collaborative editing, but concurrent writes to the same item conflict. Last-write-wins (LWW) is simple but silently drops data and depends on clocks; better options are application-level merges, version vectors to detect true concurrency, or CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types, such as counters, sets and sequences) that merge automatically and deterministically.

Leaderless systems (Dynamo-style: Cassandra, Riak, ScyllaDB) send each write to N replicas and consider it successful after W acknowledgements; reads query R replicas and take the newest version. With W + R > N (for example N = 3, W = 2, R = 2), read and write sets overlap. Repair mechanisms are read repair, hinted handoff and anti-entropy using Merkle trees. Even with quorums, edge cases such as sloppy quorums and concurrent writes mean you do not get linearizability for free.

Lag is normally milliseconds but can grow to minutes under heavy writes, long-running queries on replicas, or network trouble, so monitor it (bytes or seconds behind) and pull lagging replicas out of rotation. Read-your-writes options: route a user's reads to the leader for a short window after they write; remember the log position (LSN) of the user's last write and only read from replicas that have caught up to it; or read user-owned data (their own profile) from the leader and everything else from replicas.

Related anomalies: monotonic reads (a user hits a fresh replica, then a staler one, and sees time go backwards; fix by pinning a user to one replica) and consistent prefix reads (seeing an answer before its question when partitions replicate independently). Mobile and multi-device users complicate this because the 'same user' arrives through different sessions.

Range sharding keeps keys sorted, so range scans and ordered pagination hit few shards and shards can split automatically when they grow (Bigtable, HBase, and CockroachDB ranges). Its risk is skew from sequential keys. Hash sharding spreads load evenly but destroys ordering. hash % N is the worst variant for growth: changing N moves almost every key. Better: a fixed large number of logical shards (for example 1,024) mapped onto physical nodes, so rebalancing moves whole logical shards (Redis Cluster uses 16,384 hash slots), or consistent hashing.

Choose the shard key so that the most common queries hit a single shard: tenant_id for multi-tenant SaaS keeps each customer's data together. Secondary indexes are either local (each shard indexes its own data, so queries scatter to all shards) or global (partitioned by the indexed value, so writes touch several shards). Directory-based sharding (a lookup service) gives full flexibility at the cost of an extra hop.

Skew comes from popular keys (a celebrity's posts, a viral product), sequential keys (timestamps, auto-increment IDs) and uneven tenants (one enterprise customer larger than all the others). Hashing alone does not fix a single hot key, because every request for that key still lands on one shard.

Mitigations: key salting, where you append a suffix 0-9 when writing and fan out reads across the ten sub-keys, trading read cost for write spread; caching hot reads close to the edge; splitting or isolating heavy tenants onto dedicated shards; using write-optimized structures for counters (sharded counters aggregated periodically); and choosing IDs that do not concentrate writes (UUIDv7 is time-ordered and still hot with range sharding, while random UUIDv4 spreads writes but hurts index locality). Detect skew with per-shard metrics; averages across shards hide it completely.

CAP is narrower than it sounds: C means linearizability, A means every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response, and the choice only applies while a partition is happening. Since partitions cannot be ruled out, the practical question is what the system does during one: refuse or block (CP, like ZooKeeper, etcd, or Spanner within its guarantees) or serve possibly stale data and reconcile later (AP, like Dynamo-style stores and DNS).

PACELC adds the everyday trade-off: Else (normal operation), Latency versus Consistency, because strong consistency needs coordination round trips. DynamoDB and Cassandra are typically PA/EL, while Spanner and other consensus-based databases are PC/EC. Many systems are tunable per request (Cassandra consistency levels, DynamoDB strongly consistent reads), so the honest interview answer names the choice per operation: payments CP, like counts AP.

Linearizability makes the system behave like a single copy with real-time ordering; it is needed for locks, leader election and uniqueness checks, and costs coordination latency. Sequential consistency keeps one global order but not real time. Causal consistency preserves cause-and-effect order (a reply never appears before its post) and is the strongest model that stays available during partitions. Session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads) are cheap and fix most user-visible anomalies.

Eventual consistency only promises convergence once writes stop; in practice convergence is usually fast but has no hard bound, so design for the anomalies: show a pending state, make operations commutative, or reconcile in the background. Do not confuse this with the C in ACID, which is about constraints. Interviewers probe whether you can name the weakest model that is still correct for a given feature.
deeper.further: Study consensus (Raft is the most approachable), linearizability versus serializability, and how distributed SQL databases provide strong consistency across regions. Kleppmann's 'Designing Data-Intensive Applications' chapters on replication, partitioning and consistency are the standard reference, and the Jepsen analyses show how real databases violate their claimed guarantees. Explore CRDTs for collaborative apps, rebalancing strategies in Cassandra and Redis Cluster, change data capture for keeping derived stores in sync, and tunable consistency levels in production databases.

pages.title: Message Queues
pages.subtitle: Decouple services with asynchronous messages

panels.heading: Why Queues
panels.body:
Producer sends a message; a consumer handles it later.
Decouples services, absorbs spikes, retries failures.
Checkout replies in 50 ms; email, invoice and analytics run async.

panels.heading: Queue vs Pub/Sub
panels.body:
Queue (point-to-point): each message goes to ONE worker; shares work.
Pub/sub (publish/subscribe): each message reaches EVERY subscriber; fans out.

panels.heading: Kafka: Partitions & Consumer Groups
panels.body:
Topic = append-only log split into partitions.
Same key -> same partition -> ordered per key.
In a group, each partition has one consumer.
6 partitions -> at most 6 active consumers.

panels.heading: Delivery Guarantees
panels.body:
At-most-once: commit offset, then process; a crash loses the message.
At-least-once: process, then commit; a crash causes redelivery.
Exactly-once: transactions or dedup; costly, limited scope.

panels.heading: Idempotent Consumers
panels.body:
At-least-once + idempotent handler = effectively once.
Record processed message IDs; skip repeats.
panels.code:
with db.transaction():
    if db.seen(msg.id): return
    apply(msg)
    db.mark_seen(msg.id)

panels.heading: Dead Letters & Backpressure
panels.body:
Retry with backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s); after 5 failures move to a DLQ (dead-letter queue).
Backpressure: when consumers lag, slow producers, buffer or add consumers.
Alert on consumer lag.

panels.heading: Event-Driven Example
panels.body:
OrderPlaced -> topic 'orders' (key = order_id).
Payment, inventory and email each read in their own consumer group.
Add a fraud service later; checkout never changes.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
Poison message blocks a partition: send it to the DLQ.
Order holds only within a partition.
DB write + publish can diverge: use the outbox pattern.
Check: why can't 10 consumers speed up 4 partitions?

pages.footer: Queue the work, make handlers idempotent, watch the lag.
pages.summary: How message queues decouple services: point-to-point queues versus pub/sub, Kafka partitions and consumer groups, at-most/at-least/exactly-once delivery, idempotent consumers, dead-letter queues and backpressure, with an event-driven order example.

panels:
Queues turn a synchronous chain into asynchronous steps: the producer only needs the broker to be available, not every downstream service, so a slow email provider no longer slows checkout. They also smooth load: a burst of 10,000 orders per second can be absorbed by the queue and drained at whatever rate workers sustain, a pattern called queue-based load leveling.

The costs are real: eventual consistency (the invoice appears a few seconds later), harder debugging across asynchronous hops (propagate trace IDs in message headers), duplicate and out-of-order messages, and another piece of critical infrastructure to operate. Use a queue when the caller does not need the result to answer the user. Keep synchronous calls when the user must see the outcome immediately, such as card authorization, or use a request/reply pattern with a status endpoint the client can poll.

In a work queue (RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS) a message is delivered to one consumer and deleted after it is acknowledged; if the consumer does not acknowledge within a visibility timeout, it is redelivered to someone else. This is ideal for task distribution. In pub/sub each subscriber gets its own copy, which enables fan-out to independent services.

Kafka unifies both with a log: messages are retained for a configured time (days, or forever with compaction) regardless of consumption, every consumer group reads the whole topic independently (pub/sub across groups), and within a group partitions are split among members (queue-like work sharing). Because data is retained, consumers can replay history after a bug fix or bootstrap a new service. Traditional brokers are better at per-message routing, priorities and delayed delivery; log-based systems excel at throughput, ordering per key and replay.

A partition is an ordered, append-only log; each message gets an increasing offset, and a consumer group stores its committed offset per partition. The producer's default partitioner hashes the key, so all events for order_id 123 go to the same partition and are seen in order. Messages without a key are spread across partitions with no ordering guarantee.

Partition count caps parallelism within a group and is hard to change later, because adding partitions changes key-to-partition mapping and breaks per-key ordering for existing keys; plan for future peak throughput. Replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas = 2 and acks = all is the common durability setting. When consumers join or leave, the group rebalances partition assignments; cooperative rebalancing (incremental) avoids stopping the whole group. Very large partition counts increase metadata and recovery cost, although KRaft-based clusters handle far more partitions than older ZooKeeper-based ones.

The guarantee is decided by when you commit relative to doing the work. At-most-once commits first: fast, no duplicates, but a crash loses the message, which is acceptable for metrics sampling. At-least-once processes first: nothing is lost, but crashes, rebalances and producer retries create duplicates. It is the sensible default.

Exactly-once in Kafka means idempotent producers (deduplicated by producer ID and sequence number) plus transactions that atomically write output messages and commit consumer offsets, giving exactly-once for read-process-write pipelines that stay inside Kafka. As soon as a side effect leaves the system (sending an email, calling a payment API, writing to another database), you are back to at-least-once and need idempotency at the destination. The phrase to use in interviews: exactly-once delivery is impossible in general; exactly-once processing is achievable with idempotence or transactions.

An idempotent operation produces the same final state whether it runs once or many times. Some operations are naturally idempotent (set status = shipped, or an upsert keyed by order_id); others are not (increment a balance, send an email) and need deduplication. The pattern shown records the message ID in the same database transaction as the business effect, so either both happen or neither does. In real code, make the seen-table insert fail on a unique constraint rather than relying only on a read check, which closes the race between two concurrent duplicates.

Use a stable ID chosen by the producer (an event ID or business key), not the broker offset, which changes if the message is re-published. Bound the dedup table with a TTL longer than the maximum redelivery window. For external APIs, pass an idempotency key so the provider deduplicates for you.

Retry transient failures (timeouts, 503s) with exponential backoff and jitter; do not retry permanent failures (validation errors) at all. Plain Kafka consumers have no built-in DLQ (Kafka Connect does offer one for sink connectors), so frameworks implement retry topics (orders.retry.1m, orders.retry.10m) and a dead-letter topic; SQS and RabbitMQ support DLQs natively through a maximum receive count or dead-letter exchanges. A DLQ needs an owner, alerting and a redrive tool, or it becomes a silent data graveyard.

Backpressure means the system signals 'slow down' instead of collapsing: bounded buffers, producer throttling or blocking when buffers fill, rate limits at the edge, autoscaling consumers on lag (KEDA in Kubernetes), and shedding low-priority work. Consumer lag (latest offset minus committed offset, or better, the age of the oldest unprocessed message) is the key health metric, because a queue hides failures until its delay becomes user-visible.

Events describe facts in the past tense (OrderPlaced), while commands request actions (ChargeCard). Events let new consumers join without the producer knowing about them, which is the decoupling win, but they make the overall flow implicit and harder to see. Document event schemas in a schema registry (Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema) with compatibility rules, so producers cannot break consumers by renaming fields.

Decide what goes in the event: thin events (an ID only, consumers call back for details, which reintroduces coupling and load) or fat events (carry the needed state, larger but self-contained). Using order_id as the key keeps all events of one order in sequence for each consumer. Event sourcing goes further, storing the event log itself as the source of truth and deriving current state by replaying it; it is powerful for audit trails but adds complexity with schema evolution and rebuilding projections.

A poison message is retried forever and blocks every later message in its partition, because Kafka consumers process each partition in order. Catch errors per message, retry a bounded number of times, then park the message in a DLQ. Ordering is per partition only; cross-key ordering requires a single partition, which kills parallelism. Retrying via a separate retry topic also reorders messages for that key.

The dual-write problem: committing to the database and then publishing can fail between the two steps, leaving them inconsistent. The transactional outbox pattern writes the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change, and a relay (polling, or change data capture such as Debezium) publishes it, giving at-least-once publication. Answer to the check: each partition is assigned to only one consumer in a group, so 4 partitions keep at most 4 consumers busy; the other 6 sit idle.
deeper.further: Next, learn the transactional outbox and inbox patterns, change data capture, schema registries and compatibility modes, and Kafka internals (in-sync replicas, log compaction, KRaft). Compare log-based streaming (Kafka, Redpanda, Pulsar) with traditional brokers (RabbitMQ, SQS) and cloud event buses. Stream processing frameworks (Kafka Streams, Flink) add windowing, joins and state on top of logs.
