Also study workflow engines such as Temporal, which handle retries, timeouts and long-running processes more explicitly than chains of queues.

pages.title: Microservices
pages.subtitle: Split by business capability, not by hype

panels.heading: Three Architectures
panels.body:
Monolith: one codebase, one deploy. Simple, can tangle.
Modular monolith: one deploy, strict internal modules.
Microservices: independently deployed services owning their data. Team autonomy, network complexity.

panels.heading: Service Boundaries
panels.body:
Cut along bounded contexts (from domain-driven design): Orders, Payments, Catalog.
Each service owns its database.
High cohesion inside, loose coupling between.
Smell: services that must deploy together.

panels.heading: API Gateway & Discovery
panels.body:
API gateway: single entry; auth, rate limits, routing.
Service discovery: a registry maps names to healthy instances (Kubernetes DNS, Consul).
Code calls 'payments', never an IP.

panels.heading: Timeouts, Retries & Circuit Breakers
panels.body:
Timeout every call (e.g. 300 ms).
Retry only idempotent calls: exponential backoff + jitter, max 3.
Circuit breaker: after 50% failures, open and fail fast; half-open tests recovery.

panels.heading: Saga Pattern Example
panels.body:
No ACID transaction across services: chain local steps with compensations.
Reserve stock -> Charge card -> Ship.
Charge fails -> run 'release stock'.
Coordinate by events (choreography) or a central orchestrator.

panels.heading: When NOT to Use Them
panels.body:
Small team or still-unclear domain.
No CI/CD (continuous integration / delivery), monitoring or tracing yet.
Chatty, latency-critical flows.
Start modular; extract a service when scale or team needs demand it.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
Distributed monolith: services chained by sync calls.
Shared database across services.
Retry storms amplify outages.
Check: 5 chained services at 99.9% each = ~99.5% overall. Why?

pages.footer: Microservices trade code complexity for network complexity; earn the trade.
pages.summary: How monoliths, modular monoliths and microservices differ, how to draw service boundaries around bounded contexts, and the supporting patterns (API gateway, service discovery, timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, sagas), plus when not to use microservices at all.

panels:
The real driver for microservices is organizational: Conway's law says systems mirror the communication structure of the teams that build them, and microservices let dozens of teams deploy independently without coordinating releases. The price is distributed-systems complexity: network failures, eventual consistency, versioned contracts, and much more infrastructure (CI/CD per service, observability, service discovery).

A modular monolith gets many of the benefits with one deployable: enforced module boundaries (separate packages, no reaching into another module's tables, interfaces between modules checked by tooling), in-process calls, and real transactions. It is also the easiest starting point for extracting services later, because the seams already exist. Several well-known companies have publicly moved some microservice systems back to monoliths for cost and simplicity. Interview framing: choose the architecture that matches team size, domain maturity and scaling needs, and explain the migration path rather than declaring a winner.

A bounded context, from domain-driven design (DDD), is a boundary inside which a model and its vocabulary are consistent: 'Customer' in Billing (payment methods, invoices) differs from 'Customer' in Support (tickets, history), and forcing one shared model couples everything. Good service boundaries usually follow business capabilities and contexts, not technical layers; a 'database service' or a 'validation service' is a red flag.

Database-per-service is what makes independent deployment real: other services use the owner's API or its events, never its tables. Data needed elsewhere is copied through events into local read models, which means accepting eventual consistency. Signs of wrong boundaries: chatty calls for every request, features that always touch several services, and lockstep deploys. Start with coarse services and split when a boundary has proven stable; merging services back later is much more painful.

An API gateway handles cross-cutting edge concerns: TLS termination, authentication (validating tokens and passing identity downstream), rate limiting, request routing, protocol translation and sometimes response aggregation. The Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern gives each client type (web, mobile) its own gateway layer tailored to its needs. Keep business logic out of the gateway, or it becomes a new monolith that every team has to change.

Service discovery can be client-side (the client queries a registry and load-balances itself) or server-side (a load balancer or proxy does it). In Kubernetes, a Service gets a stable DNS name and virtual IP, and endpoints update as pods become ready. A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) adds sidecar or node proxies providing mutual TLS between services, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting and telemetry without changing application code, at the cost of operational complexity.

Timeouts should be set from the callee's latency distribution (for example a little above its p99.9) and propagate as a deadline: if the user request has 1 s left, downstream calls must not wait 2 s. Retries need exponential backoff with jitter to avoid synchronized retry waves, a cap, and a retry budget (for example retries may add at most 10% extra load). Retry at one layer only: three layers each retrying 3 times (4 attempts each) multiply into 64 attempts against a struggling service.

A circuit breaker tracks failures over a sliding window; when it opens, calls fail immediately or return a fallback (cached data, a default, a degraded feature) instead of tying up threads. After a cool-down it goes half-open and lets a few trial requests through. Bulkheads add isolation by giving each dependency its own connection pool or thread pool, so one slow dependency cannot exhaust everything else.

Two-phase commit across services is avoided because it blocks while a participant is unavailable and couples every service to a coordinator. A saga splits the business transaction into local transactions, each publishing an event or replying to an orchestrator; if a step fails, compensating transactions semantically undo the earlier steps, for example refunding a charge. Compensation is not a true rollback: emails may already be sent, so design steps in a sensible order, putting the risky or irreversible ones last.

Choreography (services react to each other's events) is decoupled but hard to follow as the number of steps grows; orchestration (a coordinator, often a workflow engine such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions) makes the flow explicit, testable and observable. Sagas lack isolation, so intermediate states are visible; countermeasures include semantic locks (an order in PENDING state), commutative updates and re-reading values before acting. Every step and compensation must be idempotent.

Microservices make sense when several teams step on each other in one codebase, when parts of the system need very different scaling or reliability, or when isolation is required (a payment component under strict compliance rules). They hurt when the domain is still changing (boundaries will be wrong), when the team is small, or when the platform basics are missing: automated deployment, centralized logs, metrics, distributed tracing and on-call ownership per service.

The strangler fig pattern is the safe migration path: route one capability at a time through a facade to a new service, keep the monolith running for everything else, and retire old code incrementally. Extract the piece with the clearest boundary and the strongest reason first, for example a high-load, independently scaling component. Interviewers like candidates who can say 'not yet' and explain what would change their mind.

A distributed monolith has all the costs of microservices and none of the benefits: services that share a database or libraries containing domain logic, synchronous call chains, and coordinated releases. Availability multiplies across synchronous dependencies: 0.999^5 = about 0.995, which raises expected downtime from roughly 43 minutes to about 3.6 hours per month. Reduce depth with asynchronous messaging, caching and fallbacks.

Retry storms happen when every layer retries a failing service and turns a small outage into a large one; budgets, jitter and circuit breakers contain them. Other common problems: no distributed tracing, which makes debugging guesswork; inconsistent API versioning, which breaks consumers; too-fine services ('nanoservices') with more network overhead than logic; and lack of contract tests, which leaves teams to discover breaking changes in production.
deeper.further: Read about domain-driven design (bounded contexts, context mapping, aggregates), the strangler fig migration pattern, and team topologies for aligning services with teams. Study resilience patterns in depth (bulkheads, load shedding, deadline propagation, retry budgets), distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, and consumer-driven contract testing. Workflow engines such as Temporal make sagas easier to build and observe. Sam Newman's 'Building Microservices' and 'Monolith to Microservices' are practical references for when and how to split a system.

pages.title: API Design
pages.subtitle: Clear contracts clients can trust

panels.heading: REST Basics
panels.body:
REST (representational state transfer): resources are nouns, /users/42/orders.
GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH partial update, DELETE remove.
GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; POST is not.

panels.heading: Status Codes
panels.body:
2xx success: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content.
4xx client error: 400 Bad Request, 401 not authenticated, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 429 Too Many Requests.
5xx: server failed (500, 503).

panels.heading: GraphQL & gRPC
panels.body:
GraphQL: one endpoint; the client asks for exact fields. No over-fetching, harder HTTP caching.
gRPC: Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2. Binary, typed, streaming; ideal service-to-service.

panels.heading: Which One When
panels.body:
REST: public APIs, HTTP caching, simplest tooling.
GraphQL: many clients needing flexible nested data.
gRPC: internal low-latency calls and streams.
Common mix: REST or GraphQL outside, gRPC inside.

panels.heading: Versioning & Pagination
panels.body:
Version in path (/v1) or header; add fields, never break them.
Offset (?offset=40): simple, slow deep, skips rows on inserts.
Cursor (?after=...): stable and fast.
panels.code:
GET /v1/orders?limit=20&after=ord_981
-> {"data": [...], "next_cursor": "ord_961"}

panels.heading: Rate Limiting: Token Bucket
panels.body:
Bucket holds 100 tokens, refills 10 per second.
Each request spends 1 token; empty -> 429 with Retry-After.
Allows bursts, enforces the average.
Limit per API key or user.

panels.heading: Idempotency Keys
panels.body:
Client sends a unique key with each POST.
Server stores key -> response; a retry gets the same result, never a double charge.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
Verbs in URLs (/getUser).
200 OK wrapping an error.
Unbounded list endpoints.
Breaking changes without a new version.
Check: why does offset pagination skip rows when new items arrive?

pages.footer: Predictable resources, honest status codes, safe retries.
pages.summary: How to design web APIs: REST resources, verbs and status codes, when GraphQL or gRPC fits better, versioning, offset versus cursor pagination, token-bucket rate limiting and idempotency keys for safe retries.

panels:
REST models a system as resources identified by URLs and manipulated with standard HTTP methods, so caches, proxies and client libraries understand requests without custom knowledge. Use plural nouns, keep nesting shallow (/users/42/orders is fine, deeper chains are not), and model actions that do not fit CRUD as sub-resources (POST /orders/42/cancellation) rather than verbs in paths.

Safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) do not change state; idempotent methods (GET, PUT, DELETE) have the same effect when repeated, which is what makes automatic retries safe. PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent: a JSON Patch 'append' applied twice appends twice. POST creates or triggers actions and is neither safe nor idempotent, which is why it needs idempotency keys. Return 201 with a Location header after creation, and use consistent naming, error formats and timestamp formats (ISO 8601, UTC) across the whole API.

Precise codes let clients react programmatically: 401 means 'authenticate' (the name Unauthorized is historical and misleading), 403 means 'authenticated, but not allowed', 404 can deliberately hide a resource's existence from unauthorized users, 409 signals a state conflict (duplicate, version mismatch), 412 Precondition Failed pairs with If-Match for optimistic concurrency, 422 is common for semantic validation errors, and 429 should carry a Retry-After header.

On the server side, 502 and 504 indicate a bad or slow upstream, and 503 means temporarily unavailable, ideally with Retry-After. Clients should usually retry 429, 503 and 504 with backoff, but not most 4xx responses. Use a structured error body such as RFC 9457 problem details (type, title, status, detail) with a machine-readable code and a request ID for support. Never return 200 for a failure, since monitoring, caches and clients all trust the status code.

GraphQL exposes a typed schema; clients send queries selecting exactly the fields and nested relations they need, which suits varied frontends and avoids both over-fetching and multiple round trips. Trade-offs: everything is a POST to one URL, so HTTP caching needs persisted queries or client caches; naive resolvers cause N+1 database calls (solved with batching via DataLoader); and expensive nested queries need depth limits and cost analysis to prevent abuse. Errors arrive in an 'errors' array, often with HTTP 200.

gRPC defines services in .proto files and generates typed clients and servers in many languages. Protocol Buffers are compact and fast to parse, HTTP/2 multiplexes many calls over one connection, and four call types are supported (unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional). Browsers need gRPC-Web or a proxy, and long-lived HTTP/2 connections need L7, per-request load balancing.

Pick from the consumers outward. Public APIs for third-party developers favor REST with JSON plus OpenAPI documentation, because every language and tool supports it and HTTP caching works out of the box. Product teams with many screens and clients that change quickly often put GraphQL in front of internal services, typically as a gateway or federated graph. Internal service-to-service traffic, especially with high call volumes, strict contracts or streaming, favors gRPC.

Other options worth naming: WebSockets or Server-Sent Events for server push, webhooks for notifying third parties (signed payloads, retries, idempotent receivers), and asynchronous APIs that return 202 Accepted with a status URL for long jobs. Whatever the style, the durable parts of API design are the same: a stable contract, clear errors, pagination, authentication, rate limits and backward-compatible evolution. Mixing styles is normal; switching later costs far more than choosing deliberately.

Prefer additive, backward-compatible evolution: add optional fields and endpoints, never rename or remove fields or change their meaning, and make clients tolerant of unknown fields. When a breaking change is unavoidable, introduce a new major version (/v2 in the path is the most visible; header or media-type versioning keeps URLs stable), run both in parallel, announce deprecation with Deprecation and Sunset headers, and monitor usage of the old version before removing it. Some APIs use date-based versions pinned per client account.

Offset pagination makes the database read and discard offset rows (OFFSET 100000 is slow) and shifts results under concurrent inserts. Cursor (keyset) pagination encodes the last seen sort key, for example (created_at, id), into an opaque token and queries WHERE (created_at, id) < (...) ORDER BY ... LIMIT 20, which is index-friendly and stable. Its trade-off: no jumping straight to page 50 and no cheap total count.

Token bucket: capacity B allows bursts up to B, refill rate r sets the sustained average. Implement it lazily, storing tokens and last_refill per key, and on each request add (now - last_refill) x r, capped at B. In a distributed setup, keep state in Redis and update it atomically with a Lua script, or accept approximate per-node limits.

Alternatives: leaky bucket (smooths output to a constant rate), fixed window counters (simple but allow double bursts at window boundaries), sliding window log (exact but memory-hungry) and sliding window counter (a good approximation). Communicate limits with Retry-After and the IETF draft's RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy fields (earlier drafts used RateLimit-Limit and RateLimit-Remaining). Choose the key carefully (API key, user, IP address, or tenant) and apply different limits per endpoint cost. Rate limiting protects fairness and capacity; for overload protection add load shedding and concurrency limits too.

Idempotency keys make non-idempotent POSTs safe to retry over unreliable networks. The client generates a unique key (a UUID) per logical operation and reuses it on every retry. The server atomically records the key with a 'processing' state before doing work, then stores the final status code and body; retries return the stored response. A concurrent duplicate that arrives while the first is still processing gets 409 or waits.

Store a hash of the request body with the key and reject reuse with different parameters (often 422). Keep keys for a bounded window, for example 24 hours, longer than any client retry policy. Scope keys per account to prevent collisions or probing. Payment APIs popularized the Idempotency-Key header, and an IETF draft standardizes it. Remember that this only covers the HTTP layer: downstream side effects still need their own idempotency.

Verbs in URLs duplicate what HTTP methods already express and lead to inconsistent APIs; use resources and methods instead. Returning 200 with an error body breaks retries, monitoring and caches. Unbounded list endpoints work in testing and then time out in production: always paginate, with a default and maximum page size. Breaking changes without versioning silently break mobile apps that cannot be force-updated, and old app versions live for years.

Other frequent mistakes: leaking internal database IDs or schemas, inconsistent naming (camelCase mixed with snake_case), timestamps without a timezone, missing authentication on 'internal' endpoints, and chatty APIs that need ten calls to render one screen. Answer to the check: offset counts rows from the top, so when a new item is inserted at the top, every item shifts down one position, and the next page starts one row too early, repeating an item, or one too late, skipping one when items are deleted.
deeper.further: Learn OpenAPI for describing and generating REST APIs, RFC 9457 problem details for errors, HTTP caching with ETags and conditional requests, and authentication flows (OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, API keys, mutual TLS). Explore GraphQL federation, gRPC deadlines and streaming, and webhook design with signatures and retries. For rate limiting, study distributed algorithms and the IETF RateLimit headers. API style guides published by large platforms are excellent references for naming, pagination and versioning conventions.

pages.title: System Design Interview
pages.subtitle: A repeatable plan, worked on a URL shortener

panels.heading: Requirements (5 min)
panels.body:
Functional: shorten a URL, redirect, custom alias, expiry.
Non-functional: 100M new URLs/month, reads 100x writes, redirect p99 < 50 ms, highly available.
Ask, don't assume.

panels.heading: Estimates (5 min)
panels.body:
Writes: 100M/month = ~40/s. Reads: ~4,000/s, peak ~10,000/s.
Storage: 6B URLs in 5 years x 500 B = ~3 TB.
Codes: 62^7 = ~3.5 trillion; 7 characters suffice.

panels.heading: API (5 min)
panels.body: 302 (temporary) keeps every click visible for analytics; 301 gets cached by browsers.

panels.heading: Data Model (5 min)
panels.body:
urls(code PK, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at).
Access is lookup by code: a key-value store or sharded SQL fits.
Shard by hash(code).

panels.heading: High-Level Design (10 min)
panels.body:
Client -> load balancer -> stateless API servers -> Redis cache -> database.
Codes: unique ID counter -> base62 encode, no collisions.
Click events -> queue -> analytics workers.

panels.heading: Deep Dives (10 min)
panels.body:
Cache hot codes; 20% of links get ~80% of clicks.
Give each server a block of 1,000 IDs, so no central counter bottleneck.
Custom aliases: unique constraint.
Expired links: check on read, purge nightly.

panels.heading: Bottlenecks & Trade-offs (5 min)
panels.body:
One database -> replicas, then shards.
Sequential codes are guessable -> shuffle IDs.
301 vs 302: fewer hits vs better analytics.
Say trade-offs out loud; no design is perfect.

panels.heading: Pitfalls & Check Yourself
panels.body:
Drawing boxes before requirements.
No numbers, no capacity plan.
Ignoring failures and hot keys.
Check: redo the estimates for 1B new URLs per month.

pages.footer: Requirements, numbers, API, data, design, deep dive, trade-offs: say it out loud.
pages.summary: A seven-step system design interview framework (requirements, estimates, API, data model, high-level design, deep dives, trade-offs) worked through on a URL shortener, with time budgets and common mistakes.

panels:
Requirements turn an ambiguous prompt into a scoped problem, and interviewers grade whether you ask the right questions. Functional: who are the users, which core features (and which are explicitly out of scope, such as user accounts or link editing), and do links expire? Non-functional: scale (writes and reads per day), read-to-write ratio, latency targets, availability (99.9% versus 99.99%), durability (a link must never break), consistency (must a new link work instantly worldwide?), and security (abuse, malware links, guessable codes).

Write the agreed list on the board and refer back to it; every later decision should trace to a requirement. Prioritize: the redirect path is the product, so its latency and availability matter far more than link creation. If the interviewer says 'you decide', state a reasonable assumption out loud and move on rather than stalling. Five minutes is a guide; spend less if the scope is obvious.

Show the arithmetic: 100M / (30 x 86,400 s) is about 39 writes/s; at 100:1 reads that is about 3,900 reads/s, and a 2-3x peak factor gives around 10,000 reads/s. Storage: 100M x 12 months x 5 years = 6B records; at about 500 bytes each (long URL averaging a few hundred bytes plus metadata), that is 3 TB before replication, so about 9 TB with 3 replicas. That fits a modest sharded cluster.

Cache sizing: if 20% of daily-active links serve most traffic, a cache of tens of GB covers the hot set and fits in a few Redis nodes. Bandwidth is tiny: 10,000 redirects/s x about 500 B = 5 MB/s. Code space: 62^6 is about 57 billion and 62^7 about 3.5 trillion; 7 characters gives headroom and makes random guessing hits rare. Conclude by saying what the numbers imply: reads dominate, so optimize the read path.

Keep the API minimal and explicit. POST /v1/urls takes long_url plus optional custom_alias and expires_at, returns 201 with the code and short URL, and should accept an Idempotency-Key so a retried request does not create duplicates. Validate URLs (scheme allow-list, length limits) and scan them for malware or phishing, since shorteners are a favorite tool of abusers. Add per-user and per-IP rate limits.

The redirect status is a real design choice. 301 (permanent) is cached by browsers, so repeat clicks never reach you: lower load, but you lose analytics and cannot change or disable the target. 302 or 307 (temporary) brings every click back, enabling counting, expiry and takedowns. Most commercial shorteners use 301 or 302 depending on product needs. Expired or unknown codes return 404 or 410 Gone. Optional extras: GET /v1/urls/{code}/stats and DELETE for owners.

The access pattern is overwhelmingly point lookups by code, with no joins on the hot path, which suits a key-value or wide-column store (DynamoDB, Cassandra) or a sharded relational database. Relational still works fine at about 40 writes per second and gives an easy unique constraint for custom aliases; the main pressure is storage size and read volume, which caching absorbs.

Shard by hash(code) for an even spread; sharding by user_id would make the hot redirect lookup scatter across all shards. If 'list my links' is needed, add a secondary table or index keyed by user_id, accepting that it is updated asynchronously or written to both. Store created_at and expires_at for expiry and cleanup, and consider a separate click-events store (a columnar or time-series database) so analytics writes never compete with redirect reads. Replicate each shard 3x across zones for durability.

Walk through both paths. Create: API server -> get a unique ID -> base62-encode it -> write to the database -> return the short URL. Redirect: API server -> Redis lookup -> on a miss, read the database and fill the cache -> 302 -> asynchronously publish a click event to a queue. The redirect path never waits on analytics.

Code generation options: (1) a counter plus base62 gives unique, compact codes without collision checks, but needs a distributed ID source and produces guessable sequences; (2) random 7-character codes are unguessable but need a uniqueness check, which stays cheap while the space is sparse (6B of 3.5T is under 0.2% full); (3) hashing the long URL (MD5 truncated) deduplicates identical URLs but collisions must still be handled. A CDN or edge cache in front can serve the most popular redirects close to users.

Interviewers choose one or two areas to probe, so offer options and ask which they prefer. ID allocation: a coordination service (or a database sequence) hands each server a block such as 1,000 IDs at a time; a crash wastes at most one block, which is harmless. Alternatives are Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs (timestamp + machine ID + sequence) with no coordination per ID.

Caching: an LRU Redis cluster with TTLs; precompute nothing, since the cache fills itself on demand; protect against stampedes on viral links with request coalescing. Custom aliases share the same namespace, so enforce uniqueness with a conditional insert and reserve words like 'api' and 'admin'. Expiry: check expires_at on read (lazy), and run a background job to delete expired rows and invalidate cache entries. Analytics: aggregate click events in a stream processor into per-minute counts, rather than updating counters in the main database on every click.

Name the bottleneck, the fix, and the cost. Database read load: caching plus read replicas; writes are low, so sharding is mainly for storage. Single points of failure: multiple API instances across zones, a replicated cache, a highly available ID allocator. Hot links: edge caching and in-memory caches on API servers. Guessable codes: shuffle sequential IDs with a reversible permutation (for example, multiply by a large number coprime to 62^7, modulo 62^7, or a small block cipher) so codes look random but stay unique.

Also discuss consistency: a new link must be readable immediately by its creator (read from the primary, or write through to the cache), while analytics can be minutes behind. Multi-region: replicate links globally (they are immutable, which makes replication easy) and serve redirects from the nearest region. Close by summarizing which requirements each choice serves and what you would monitor (p99 redirect latency, cache hit ratio, error rates).

Common failure modes in interviews: jumping into a favorite technology before understanding the problem; designing in silence; never quantifying, so you cannot justify sharding or caching; ignoring failures (what happens when the cache, a zone or the ID service goes down?); over-engineering for scale the requirements never mentioned; and getting lost in one component while the end-to-end flow is still missing.

Good signals: structured progress, explicit assumptions, numbers that drive decisions, trade-offs stated as 'X gives A at the cost of B', and responsiveness to hints. For the check: 1B new URLs per month is about 385 writes/s, around 38,500 reads/s at 100:1 with peaks near 100,000/s, and 60B URLs in 5 years at 500 B is about 30 TB before replication. Codes: 62^7 (about 3.5 trillion) still suffices, but sharding is now clearly required.
deeper.further: Practice the framework on other classics: rate limiter, news feed, chat system, web crawler, notification service, distributed key-value store and ride matching. Each emphasizes a different deep dive (fan-out, connection handling, politeness, consistency). Study ID generation schemes (Snowflake, UUIDv7, ticket servers), Bloom filters, and probabilistic counting such as HyperLogLog for unique-visitor analytics. Rehearse aloud with a timer, and review real architecture write-ups from engineering blogs to see how the trade-offs played out in production.

pages.title: Ci/cd
pages.subtitle: Ship small changes safely, many times a day

panels.heading: CI vs Delivery vs Deployment
panels.body:
CI = continuous integration: merge to main daily; every push is built and tested.
Continuous delivery: every green build is releasable; a human clicks deploy.
Continuous deployment: every green build ships to production automatically.

panels.heading: Pipeline Stages
panels.body:
Commit -> build -> unit tests -> lint + security scan -> package -> deploy staging -> E2E tests -> deploy prod.
Fail fast: cheapest checks run first.
Any red stage stops the line.

panels.heading: GitHub Actions Example
panels.body:
File: .github/workflows/ci.yml
Runs on every push and pull request.
Job: check out code, then run make test.
panels.code:
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test: {runs-on: ubuntu-latest, steps:
    [{uses: actions/checkout@v5}, {run: make test}]}

panels.heading: Build Once: Artifacts
panels.body:
Artifact = versioned build output: container image, wheel, JAR, binary.
Tag with the commit SHA, e.g. app:3f9c2ab.
Promote the same artifact dev -> staging -> prod; never rebuild per environment.
panels.code:
docker build -t registry/app:3f9c2ab .
docker push registry/app:3f9c2ab

panels.heading: Deployment Strategies
panels.body:
Rolling: replace instances a few at a time.
Blue-green: run the new stack beside the old, then switch all traffic.
Canary: send 5% of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, ramp up.
Feature flags: deploy code dark, enable per user.

panels.heading: Rollback Plan
panels.body:
Rollback = return to the last good version in minutes.
Blue-green: flip traffic back. Canary: route 0% to new.
Flag: switch the feature off, no deploy.
Database: expand/contract migrations keep old code working.

panels.heading: Pipeline Pitfalls
panels.body:
Flaky tests teach people to ignore red builds.
Slow pipelines (30+ min) push teams toward big, risky batches.
Secrets in YAML or logs: use the secret store.
Rebuilding per environment ships untested bits.

panels.heading: Check Yourself
panels.body:
Canary error rate: 4% vs 0.5% on stable.
What now?
Answer: stop the ramp, send traffic back to stable, then investigate.

pages.footer: Integrate daily, build once, ship small, always keep a way back.
pages.summary: Explains continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment, the stages of a CI/CD pipeline with a GitHub Actions example, why one artifact is promoted through environments, and how rolling, blue-green, canary and feature-flag releases make rollback fast.

panels:
CI is a practice before it is a tool: everyone integrates into a shared mainline at least daily, and the build plus tests run on every change so integration problems surface while the diff is small. Long-lived feature branches that merge after weeks are not CI even if a pipeline runs on them; trunk-based development with short-lived branches is the usual companion.

The two CDs differ only in the last gate. Continuous delivery means the main branch is always in a deployable state and releasing is a business decision; continuous deployment removes the human gate, so the test suite and progressive rollout become your only safety net. Interviewers often probe this: continuous deployment requires strong automated tests, feature flags for unfinished work, observability to catch regressions, and automated rollback. The DORA metrics (deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore) are the standard way to measure how well a delivery pipeline works.

Order stages by cost and signal. Compilation, linting, type checks and unit tests take seconds to a few minutes and catch most defects, so they gate everything else. Security scanning usually includes SAST (static analysis of your code), dependency scanning against known CVEs, secret detection and container image scanning; SBOM generation (software bill of materials) and artifact signing are increasingly expected for supply-chain security.

Packaging happens once, after fast checks pass. Deploys to staging then run slower integration and end-to-end tests against real infrastructure. Speed tricks: dependency and build caches, parallel jobs or test sharding, running only affected tests in monorepos, and keeping the critical path short. A common rule is that feedback on a pull request should arrive in under about ten minutes. Merge queues test the combination of queued changes against the latest main, which prevents two individually green PRs from breaking main together.

A workflow file is YAML under .github/workflows/. 'on' lists the triggering events; each job runs on a fresh runner VM ('runs-on') and contains ordered steps that either 'uses' a published action or 'run' a shell command. Jobs run in parallel unless linked with 'needs', and a 'strategy.matrix' fans one job out over versions or operating systems.

The flow-style YAML on the page is equivalent to the usual block style. Practical details interviewers like: pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA rather than a mutable tag to resist supply-chain attacks; set a minimal 'permissions' block because the default GITHUB_TOKEN may be broader than needed; store credentials in encrypted secrets, or better, use OIDC federation to obtain short-lived cloud credentials without storing keys at all. Use 'actions/cache' or setup actions' built-in caching for dependencies, and 'concurrency' groups to cancel superseded runs on the same branch.

The principle is 'build once, deploy many'. An artifact should be immutable and uniquely identified: a container image referenced by digest (sha256:...) is stronger than a tag, because tags such as 'latest' or even 'v1.2' can be moved. Tagging with the git commit SHA links every running version back to source.

Environment differences belong in configuration injected at deploy time (environment variables, config maps, secret stores), not baked into separate builds; this is the twelve-factor 'strict separation of config'. Builds should be reproducible: pin base images and lock dependency versions so the same commit yields the same output. Artifact repositories (container registries, package repositories) need retention policies, vulnerability scanning and access control. Supply-chain frameworks like SLSA add provenance attestations that record which source and builder produced an artifact, and signing tools let deploy targets refuse anything unsigned.

Rolling updates are the default in Kubernetes Deployments; maxSurge and maxUnavailable control how many extra or missing pods are allowed during the swap. They need no extra capacity, but for a while old and new versions serve traffic together, so APIs and schemas must be backward compatible.

Blue-green needs double capacity briefly but gives an instant, atomic switch and an equally instant rollback, often at the load balancer or DNS level (DNS switches are slowed by TTL caching). Canary releases shift a small share of traffic, compare error rate and latency of the canary against the baseline, and ramp in steps such as 1%, 5%, 25%, 100%; tools can automate the analysis and abort. Feature flags decouple deploy from release and allow targeting by user, region or percentage. Flags carry debt: remove them once rolled out, because stale flags multiply untested code paths.

Measure rollback by time to restore service, one of the DORA metrics. The fastest rollbacks are traffic operations (switch back to blue, set canary weight to zero, flip a flag) rather than new builds. Redeploying the previous artifact is next best, which is why keeping old artifacts and their configuration matters. 'Roll forward' with a quick fix is sometimes chosen, but only when the fix is small and the pipeline is fast.

Databases are the hard part, because data changes do not roll back. The expand/contract (parallel change) pattern splits a breaking migration into safe steps: add the new column or table, deploy code that writes both and reads new, backfill, switch reads, then later drop the old column. At every step both the current and previous app versions work against the schema. Automated rollback triggers, tied to SLO burn or canary analysis, remove human reaction time from the loop.

Flaky tests are corrosive because they destroy trust in the signal: once 'just rerun it' becomes normal, real failures get rerun too. Track flake rates, quarantine flaky tests out of the blocking path, and assign owners to fix them.

Slow pipelines change behavior. If a build takes 45 minutes, developers batch changes, and larger batches mean harder debugging and riskier releases. Secrets leak through echo statements, debug logging, verbose tool output, artifact contents and fork pull requests that can read secrets; use masked secrets, least-privilege tokens and OIDC instead of long-lived keys. Other common issues: manual steps hidden in a runbook, environment-specific builds, pipelines defined only in a web UI instead of versioned code, missing timeouts that let hung jobs block runners, and no ownership when main is red. The rule 'fix or revert main immediately' keeps everyone integrating on green.

A canary at 4% errors versus 0.5% on stable is an eightfold regression, far beyond noise, so the right call is to halt promotion and route canary traffic back to zero. Investigate afterwards with the canary's logs, traces and the diff between versions.

Nuances interviewers probe: compare the canary against a baseline running at the same time, not against historical numbers, because traffic patterns change by hour. With very small canary traffic, error rates are noisy, so require a minimum request count or a statistical test before deciding. Watch segment-specific effects: a canary may look fine overall but fail for one region, client version or request type. Finally, check that the canary and stable fleets get comparable traffic; sticky sessions or header-based routing can send unusual users to the canary and bias the comparison.
deeper.further: Next steps: trunk-based development and merge queues; the DORA metrics and the research behind them; progressive delivery tooling for Kubernetes (Argo Rollouts, Flagger) and service-mesh traffic splitting; feature flag management and flag cleanup practices; supply-chain security with SBOMs, SLSA provenance and artifact signing; OIDC federation from CI to cloud providers; and database migration tooling that supports expand/contract changes. Reading on release engineering and incident reviews shows how teams pick between rollback and roll forward under pressure.

pages.title: Testing
pages.subtitle: Fast feedback that proves your code still works

panels.heading: The Testing Pyramid
panels.body:
Base: many unit tests - fast, cheap, precise.
Middle: fewer integration tests.
Top: a few end-to-end tests - slow, realistic, brittle.
Upside-down pyramid (ice-cream cone) = slow, flaky suite.

panels.heading: Unit, Integration, E2E
panels.body:
Unit: one function or class, no network or disk; milliseconds.
Integration: real parts together, e.g. code + real database.
E2E = end-to-end: drive the whole app like a user, e.g. browser login flow.

panels.heading: Test Doubles
panels.body:
Stub: returns canned answers.
Mock: expects specific calls; verifies them.
Fake: working lightweight version, e.g. in-memory database.
Spy: records calls to assert on later.
Dummy: placeholder, never used.

panels.heading: TDD: Red-Green-Refactor
panels.body:
TDD = test-driven development.
Red: write a small failing test.
Green: write the simplest code that passes.
Refactor: clean up while tests stay green.
Repeat in minute-long cycles.

panels.heading: Pytest Example
panels.body:
add() comes from your module: from calc import add.
parametrize turns one test into two cases.
Run: pytest -q -> 2 passed

panels.heading: Coverage Pitfalls
panels.body:
Coverage = share of code your tests execute, not what they check.
100% coverage with no asserts proves nothing.
Branch coverage beats line coverage.
Use it to find untested code, not as a target.

panels.heading: Flaky Tests
panels.body:
Flaky = passes or fails with no code change.
Causes: sleeps and timing, test order, shared state, real network, clocks, randomness.
Fix: wait on conditions, isolate data, seed randomness; quarantine, then repair.

panels.heading: Check Yourself
panels.body:
A test calls a real payment API and fails 1 run in 20.
Fix?
Answer: swap in a fake or stub; keep one separate contract test against the sandbox.

pages.footer: Many fast unit tests, a few real end-to-end ones, and zero tolerance for flakes.
pages.summary: Covers the testing pyramid and the difference between unit, integration and end-to-end tests, the five kinds of test doubles, the TDD red-green-refactor loop, a parametrized pytest example, and why coverage targets and flaky tests mislead teams.

panels:
The pyramid is a cost model, not a law. Unit tests are cheap to write, run in milliseconds and point to the exact broken function; end-to-end tests exercise real wiring but are slow, expensive to maintain and fail for reasons unrelated to your change. Hence the shape: many fast tests at the bottom, few slow ones at the top.

Alternatives exist. The 'testing trophy' popular in frontend work emphasizes integration tests, because component logic often lives in the interaction between pieces; microservice teams add contract tests between services. What matters is the ratio of confidence to cost. The ice-cream cone anti-pattern, with mostly manual or UI tests, gives slow feedback and flaky builds. A useful heuristic: test each behavior at the lowest level where it can be observed, and reserve E2E tests for critical user journeys such as signup, login and checkout.

Definitions vary by team, so clarify in interviews. A common rule: a unit test touches no network, disk, database or clock, so it is deterministic and fast; anything crossing a process boundary is an integration test. Some teams call a test of a whole module with real collaborators a unit test as long as it is fast and isolated from external systems.

Integration tests are most valuable at real boundaries: SQL queries against a real database engine (an in-memory substitute may accept queries production rejects), serialization, message queues. Containers spun up per test run make this practical. Contract tests check that a consumer and a provider agree on an API without running both. E2E tests drive a browser or API client through the deployed system; keep them few, independent and resilient, using stable selectors instead of brittle CSS paths and explicit waits instead of fixed sleeps.

The vocabulary comes from Gerard Meszaros's xUnit patterns. Stubs supply indirect inputs (return values); mocks verify indirect outputs (expected calls) and fail the test if those calls do not happen; spies record calls for later assertions; fakes are real working implementations with shortcuts, like an in-memory repository; dummies only fill parameter lists.

Trade-offs matter more than names. Heavy mocking couples tests to implementation details: refactor the internals and tests break even though behavior is unchanged. Prefer state verification (check the result) over interaction verification (check the calls) unless the call is the behavior, such as sending an email or charging a card. A common guideline is 'do not mock what you do not own': wrap third-party APIs in your own thin adapter, mock or fake the adapter, and cover the adapter itself with a few integration tests. In Python, unittest.mock with autospec catches calls with wrong signatures.

TDD's value is design pressure and fast feedback: writing the test first forces you to define the interface and expected behavior before implementation, and code written to be tested tends to have smaller units and fewer hidden dependencies. Keep steps tiny; the 'simplest code that passes' can even be a hardcoded value, which the next test then forces you to generalize (triangulation).

Refactoring is the step people skip, and skipping it produces a pile of passing but messy code. Two schools differ: classicist (Detroit) TDD uses real collaborators and verifies state; mockist (London) TDD designs outside-in with mocks for collaborators. Evidence on productivity is mixed, but TDD reliably yields a regression suite. It fits well-understood logic and bug fixes (write a failing test that reproduces the bug first); it fits less well for exploratory spikes or UI layout, where you may write tests after learning what to build.

pytest discovers files named test_*.py or *_test.py and functions prefixed test_, and rewrites plain assert statements so failures show the compared values. parametrize generates one independent test per tuple, and each appears separately in the report with an ID like test_add[2-3-5], so one failing case does not hide the others.

Fixtures are pytest's core feature: functions decorated with @pytest.fixture provide setup and teardown via dependency injection by argument name, with scopes (function, module, session) controlling reuse. Built-in fixtures include tmp_path for temporary directories and monkeypatch for safely replacing attributes or environment variables. Useful flags: -x stops at the first failure, -k filters by name, -q is quiet, --lf reruns last failures, and pytest-xdist's -n auto runs tests in parallel (which exposes hidden shared state). Use pytest.raises for expected exceptions and pytest.approx for floating-point comparisons, since 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3.

Line coverage counts executed lines; branch coverage counts whether each decision went both ways; condition and MC/DC coverage go further and are required in safety-critical domains like avionics. Even perfect branch coverage cannot show that the assertions check the right things.

Goodhart's law applies: once coverage is a target, people write assertion-free tests that execute code without verifying it. Mutation testing is the stronger check: a tool introduces small bugs (flip a comparison, change a constant) and verifies that some test fails; surviving mutants reveal weak tests. Practical guidance: look at coverage diffs on pull requests to spot untested new code, set a floor to prevent decline rather than chasing 100%, and exclude generated code. Coverage around 70-90% is common in healthy projects, but the uncovered parts matter more than the number: error handling and edge cases are where bugs hide.

Root causes cluster into a few families. Timing: fixed sleeps and races with async work; wait on an explicit condition with a timeout instead. Order dependence: tests that rely on state left by earlier tests; randomize test order to reveal them. Shared state: global variables, shared databases, fixed ports, the same temp file. External dependencies: real network calls, third-party sandboxes, DNS. Time and locale: tests that fail at midnight, at month end, during daylight-saving changes or in another time zone; inject a clock. Randomness: unseeded random data. Resource limits: parallel CI runners with less CPU or memory.

Process matters as much as fixes. Detect flakes by rerunning failures and recording pass-after-retry as a flake, not a pass. Quarantine flaky tests out of the blocking path with an owner and deadline, because automatic retries alone hide real intermittent bugs, including genuine race conditions in production code.

Calling a real payment API from the main suite makes failures depend on network, rate limits and the provider's sandbox health, so the test measures their reliability instead of your code. Replace the client with a fake or stub behind your own adapter interface; then unit tests can also simulate declines, timeouts and malformed responses, which are hard to trigger on demand against a real service.

You still need some evidence that your adapter matches the real API. Options: a small set of integration tests against the provider's sandbox run on a schedule rather than on every commit, consumer-driven contract tests, or recorded responses refreshed periodically. Also make retries and idempotency keys part of the design, so a timed-out charge is not repeated twice. The key interview point: isolate the unreliable dependency at a boundary you own and test the boundary separately.
deeper.further: Explore property-based testing (Hypothesis in Python) that generates inputs to find edge cases; mutation testing to measure suite quality; consumer-driven contract testing for microservices; snapshot and approval testing, with their pitfalls; testcontainers for real dependencies in integration tests; fuzzing for parsers and security-sensitive code; and test architecture patterns such as hexagonal (ports and adapters) design that make code testable. Michael Feathers's work on legacy code shows how to add tests to code that was not written with them.

pages.title: Observability
pages.subtitle: Know what your system is doing, and why

panels.heading: Logs, Metrics, Traces
panels.body:
Logs: timestamped events with rich detail.
Metrics: numbers over time, cheap to store and alert on.
Traces: one request's path across services.
Metrics say something is wrong; traces say where; logs say why.

panels.heading: Structured Logging
panels.body:
Log JSON key-values, not free text.
Add trace_id to every line so logs join traces.
Levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR.
Never log secrets or personal data.

panels.heading: Four Golden Signals
panels.body:
Latency: how long requests take; watch p99, not the average.
Traffic: demand, e.g. requests per second.
Errors: rate of failed requests.
Saturation: how full the system is, e.g. CPU, queue depth.

panels.heading: Sli, Slo, Sla
panels.body:
SLI = service level indicator: what you measure, e.g. % of requests under 300 ms.
SLO = objective: internal target, e.g. 99.9% over 30 days.
SLA = agreement: contract with penalties, looser than the SLO.

panels.heading: Error Budget Math
panels.body:
Budget = 100% - SLO.
99.9% over 30 days = 0.1% x 43,200 min = 43.2 min of failure allowed.
Budget left: ship features.
Budget burned: freeze risky releases, fix reliability.

panels.heading: Distributed Tracing
panels.body:
Trace = tree of spans; span = one timed operation.
Trace context travels in the W3C traceparent header.
OpenTelemetry (OTel): vendor-neutral SDKs + collector for traces, metrics, logs.
panels.code:
with tracer.start_as_current_span("charge_card"):
    charge(order)

panels.heading: Alerting and Dashboards
panels.body:
Page humans on symptoms users feel: SLO burn rate, error spikes.
Causes (CPU at 90%) go on dashboards, not pagers.
Every page needs an action and a runbook link.
Dashboard per service: golden signals first.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Averages hide tail latency: use percentiles.
High-cardinality labels (user_id) explode metric cost.
Alert fatigue: noisy pages get ignored.
No trace_id in logs = clues you cannot connect.

pages.footer: Measure what users feel, budget for failure, and trace every request end to end.
pages.summary: Explains the three telemetry types (logs, metrics, traces), structured logging, the four golden signals, how SLIs, SLOs, SLAs and error budgets relate with worked numbers, distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, and how to alert on symptoms rather than causes.

panels:
Monitoring answers known questions (is CPU high?); observability is the ability to ask new questions about system state from its outputs without shipping new code. The three signal types trade cost for detail. Metrics are pre-aggregated numeric time series (counters, gauges, histograms): cheap to store and fast to query, ideal for alerting, but they lose per-request detail. Logs are discrete events with arbitrary context, expensive at scale. Traces record causal, timed paths of single requests across services and are usually sampled.

The pillars framing is a simplification: the signals are most useful when linked. Exemplars attach a trace ID to a metric data point, so you can jump from a latency spike to a concrete slow request. Many practitioners advocate wide structured events, one rich record per request with many fields, from which metrics can be derived. Profiles (continuous CPU and memory profiling) are often called a fourth signal.

Structured logs turn text search into queries: with fields like level, service, route, status and latency_ms you can filter, group and aggregate. Use a consistent schema across services, ideally following OpenTelemetry semantic conventions, and include correlation fields: trace_id and span_id link logs to traces, and request or user identifiers (hashed if sensitive) link events from one session.

Levels need discipline: ERROR should mean something needs attention, not a handled user mistake. Logging cost is real: high-volume DEBUG logs in production can cost more than the service itself, so use sampling, dynamic levels and retention tiers. Never log secrets, tokens, passwords or full payment data, and treat personal data under privacy rules such as GDPR, with redaction at the source. Log lines should be single-line JSON written to stdout in containerized environments, letting the platform collect and ship them. Avoid logging inside tight loops.

The four golden signals come from Google's SRE book and suit request-serving systems. Two related checklists: RED (rate, errors, duration) for services, and USE (utilization, saturation, errors) for resources such as CPU, disks and queues.

Latency details matter. Measure successful and failed requests separately, because fast errors make average latency look better. Use histograms and percentiles: p50 shows typical experience, p99 shows the slowest 1%, and with fan-out the tail dominates; a page that calls 100 backends will hit some backend's p99 on most loads. Percentiles cannot be averaged across hosts, so aggregate histograms first. Errors include explicit failures (HTTP 5xx), wrong content returned with 200, and policy failures such as responses slower than the SLO threshold. Saturation is the leading indicator: queue length and memory pressure usually rise before latency breaks.

A good SLI is a ratio of good events to valid events, measured as close to the user as possible, e.g. at the load balancer or the client: 'proportion of HTTP requests answered successfully in under 300 ms'. Choose few SLIs per user journey: availability, latency, and sometimes freshness or correctness for data pipelines.

SLOs set a target over a window, typically 28 or 30 rolling days. 100% is the wrong target: users cannot tell 99.99% from 100% through their own networks, and every extra nine costs exponentially more. Each nine shrinks allowed downtime tenfold: per 30 days, 99% allows 7.2 hours, 99.9% 43.2 minutes, 99.99% about 4.3 minutes. SLAs are contracts with customers and include remedies such as service credits, so they are set below the internal SLO to leave a safety margin. Dependencies cap you: a service depending serially on two 99.9% services cannot exceed about 99.8%.

The error budget turns reliability into a quantity both product and engineering can spend. Request-based budgets are often better than time-based ones: with 99.9% over 10 million requests, the budget is 10,000 failed requests, and partial outages consume it in proportion to the traffic affected.

Burn rate is the key alerting concept: how fast you consume budget relative to the rate that would exhaust it exactly at window end. A burn rate of 1 uses the budget in 30 days; 14.4 uses 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour. The SRE workbook recommends multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts, e.g. page when the 1-hour burn rate exceeds 14.4 and the 5-minute window confirms it is still happening; open a ticket for slow burns. An error budget policy, agreed in advance, says what happens on exhaustion: release freezes except for reliability fixes, postmortems, and prioritizing reliability work.

A span records a name, start and end times, attributes, events and status, plus its trace ID and parent span ID; spans form a tree. Context propagation is what makes traces distributed: the W3C Trace Context traceparent header carries version, 32-hex trace ID, 16-hex parent span ID and flags, and must be forwarded across HTTP calls, message queues and async jobs; one hop that drops it breaks the trace.

OpenTelemetry is the CNCF standard: APIs and SDKs per language, auto-instrumentation for common frameworks, the OTLP wire protocol, and the Collector that receives, processes (batching, redaction, sampling) and exports to any backend. Sampling controls cost. Head sampling decides at the root, e.g. keep 10%, which is cheap but may drop the rare slow or failing requests. Tail sampling waits until the trace completes and keeps all errors and slow traces, at the cost of buffering in the collector.

Symptom-based alerting pages on what users experience, so one alert covers many possible causes, including ones nobody predicted. Cause-based alerts (high CPU, one replica down) are often not urgent thanks to redundancy and autoscaling, and they wake people for nothing. A good page is urgent, actionable, and requires human judgment; anything else should be a ticket or a dashboard.

Each alert should link a runbook with likely causes, diagnostic queries and mitigation steps, plus the relevant dashboard. Tune thresholds with 'for' durations to avoid flapping, and group related alerts so one incident does not send fifty pages. Review alerts after each on-call shift: delete any that fired without needing action. Dashboards should tell a story top-down: user-facing SLIs and golden signals first, then per-dependency panels, then resource details. Keep dashboards as code so they are reviewed and consistent across services.

Averages mislead: if 99% of requests take 50 ms and 1% take 5 s, the mean is about 100 ms and looks healthy while one user in a hundred waits. Use percentiles and histograms.

Cardinality is the number of unique label combinations, and each combination is a separate time series. A label like user_id, request ID or full URL with IDs can create millions of series, crashing the metrics backend or exploding the bill; put such identifiers in logs or traces, and keep metric labels bounded (route templates like /orders/{id}, status class, region). Alert fatigue is a safety problem: teams paged constantly start ignoring pages, and the real incident is missed. Other traps: no correlation IDs, clocks out of sync across hosts making timelines wrong, dashboards nobody owns, telemetry pipelines with no monitoring of their own, and sampling that silently drops exactly the errors you need.
deeper.further: Read the Google SRE book and workbook chapters on SLOs, alerting on SLOs and being on call; learn the OpenTelemetry Collector pipeline and semantic conventions; explore exemplars and continuous profiling; compare Prometheus-style pull metrics with push-based OTLP; study incident management (incident commander role, blameless postmortems); and look at eBPF-based instrumentation that observes services without code changes. Chaos engineering exercises test whether alerts and dashboards actually catch failures.

pages.title: Infrastructure as Code
pages.subtitle: Version your servers like you version your code

panels.heading: What IaC Is
panels.body:
IaC = infrastructure as code: servers, networks and DNS described in text files.
Reviewed in pull requests, versioned in Git.
Same code -> same environment, every time.

panels.heading: Declarative vs Imperative
panels.body:
Declarative: describe the end state; the tool works out the steps (Terraform, Kubernetes YAML).
Imperative: you script each step (bash, CLI calls).
Declarative is idempotent: apply twice, same result.

panels.heading: Terraform Workflow
panels.body:
init: download providers, set up the state backend.
plan: preview the diff (+ create, ~ update, - destroy).
apply: make the real changes.
Save the plan so you apply exactly what was reviewed.
panels.code:
terraform init
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform apply tfplan

panels.heading: HCL Example
panels.body:
HCL = HashiCorp Configuration Language.
resource TYPE NAME { arguments }
First plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
Reference it elsewhere: aws_s3_bucket.logs.arn

panels.heading: State and Locking
panels.body:
State file maps code to real resource IDs.
Keep it in a remote backend (S3, GCS, HCP Terraform) with locking, so two applies never collide.
State can hold secrets: encrypt it; never commit it.

panels.heading: Modules
panels.body:
Module = reusable folder of .tf files with inputs (variables) and outputs.
Call one network module three times: dev, staging, prod.
Pin versions, e.g. version = "~> 5.0".

panels.heading: Drift and GitOps
panels.body:
Drift = real infrastructure no longer matches the code, e.g. a console edit.
Detect: scheduled terraform plan. Fix: re-apply or update the code.
GitOps: Git is the source of truth; an agent (Argo CD, Flux) keeps syncing to it.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Hand edits outside code -> drift.
State on a laptop -> lost or conflicting state.
Applying without reading the plan: watch '-/+ replace' and '- destroy'.
Secrets hardcoded in .tf files.

pages.footer: If it is not in code, it is not real: plan, review, apply.
pages.summary: Explains infrastructure as code, declarative versus imperative tools, the Terraform init-plan-apply workflow with a small HCL example, why remote state and locking matter, reusable modules, configuration drift and GitOps.

panels:
IaC applies software engineering practice to infrastructure: version control gives history and blame, pull requests give review, CI gives automated validation, and the same code recreates environments for testing or disaster recovery. It eliminates snowflake servers, configured by hand and impossible to reproduce.

The landscape has layers. Provisioning tools create cloud resources (Terraform and its open-source fork OpenTofu, AWS CloudFormation, Azure Bicep, Pulumi with general-purpose languages, AWS CDK which synthesizes CloudFormation). Configuration management tools configure what runs on machines (Ansible, Chef, Puppet), less central now that immutable images and containers dominate. Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts declare workloads. Immutable infrastructure is the related principle: replace servers with new images rather than patching them in place, so every running instance matches a known build. Policy as code (Open Policy Agent, Sentinel) can then check plans automatically before apply.

Declarative tools hold a desired state and a reconciliation engine computes the difference from actual state, so the same file serves for creation, update and deletion. Idempotency follows: applying unchanged code produces no changes. Imperative scripts encode a sequence of actions and must handle 'already exists' and partial failure themselves; run twice, a naive script creates duplicates.

The boundary is blurry. Pulumi and CDK use imperative languages (loops, functions, classes) to build a declarative resource graph that an engine then reconciles. Ansible modules are mostly idempotent but playbooks run in order. Kubernetes controllers are the purest declarative model: they continuously reconcile observed state toward spec, not only when you run a command. Declarative tools struggle with ordered one-off operations such as data migrations, and deletions require care: removing a resource from code means the tool will destroy it.

terraform init installs provider plugins into .terraform, records exact versions in .terraform.lock.hcl (commit this file), configures the backend and downloads modules. terraform plan refreshes state from real APIs, then diffs against configuration; symbols are + create, - destroy, ~ update in place, and -/+ destroy-then-create replacement (or +/- with create_before_destroy). Saving with -out and applying that file guarantees you apply exactly what was reviewed; if state changed in the meantime, Terraform refuses the stale plan.

Other essentials: fmt and validate in CI; plan output posted to pull requests for review; -target for emergency partial applies only, since it bypasses the dependency graph; import blocks (Terraform 1.5+) to adopt existing resources; moved blocks to rename resources without destroying them; and -refresh-only to reconcile state with reality without changing infrastructure. Use workspaces or separate directories per environment, with separate state files.

A resource block declares one infrastructure object: the type (aws_s3_bucket) selects provider and schema, the local name (logs) is your handle, and arguments configure it. Attributes known only after creation, such as arn or id, are exported for other resources to reference, and those references build the dependency graph that orders operations and parallelizes independent ones.

Since AWS provider v4, bucket settings like versioning, encryption and lifecycle rules are separate resources (aws_s3_bucket_versioning and others) that reference the bucket. S3 bucket names are global across all accounts, so a name like acme-logs-2026 may already be taken. Other HCL building blocks: variable and output blocks, locals, data sources that read existing infrastructure, count and for_each for multiple instances (for_each with map keys is safer, since removing an item from a count list shifts indexes and recreates resources), dynamic blocks, and lifecycle settings such as prevent_destroy and ignore_changes.

State records the mapping from resource addresses to real IDs, cached attributes and dependencies; without it Terraform cannot know that aws_s3_bucket.logs is a particular existing bucket. Plans compare three things: configuration, state and refreshed reality.

Remote backends store state centrally with locking. On S3, Terraform 1.10+ supports native locking with use_lockfile = true, replacing the older DynamoDB table approach; GCS and HCP Terraform lock natively. Enable bucket versioning to recover from state corruption. State stores attribute values in plain text, including generated passwords and database connection strings, so restrict access and encrypt at rest; marking variables sensitive only hides them from output, not from state. Split state by blast radius, e.g. per environment and per component (network, data, apps), so one bad apply cannot touch everything and plans stay fast. Use terraform state mv, rm and import blocks deliberately; hand-editing state JSON is a last resort.

Modules give encapsulation: inputs are variable blocks with types, defaults and validation rules; outputs expose values such as vpc_id for callers. Every configuration is a module, the root module, and it calls child modules from local paths, Git URLs or registries.

Version constraints: '~> 5.0' allows any 5.x at or above 5.0 but not 6.0, while '~> 5.0.1' allows only 5.0.x patches. Pin modules and providers, and upgrade deliberately with a reviewed plan. Design guidance: keep modules focused on one concern, avoid thin wrappers around a single resource, avoid deep nesting that hides behavior, and avoid configuring providers inside reusable modules. Composition beats giant 'do everything' modules with dozens of feature toggles. Test modules with terraform test (built in since 1.6) or tools that apply into a sandbox account, and validate examples in CI. Public registry modules save time but deserve the same review as any dependency.

Drift arises from console hotfixes, other tools or scripts touching the same resources, provider-side defaults changing, and autoscaling or managed services modifying attributes. Detection options: scheduled plan runs that alert on non-empty diffs, terraform plan -refresh-only, or platform drift-detection features. Resolution is a choice: revert reality by applying the code, or accept the change by updating the code; for fields legitimately changed outside Terraform, such as an autoscaled desired count, use ignore_changes.

GitOps, from the CNCF OpenGitOps principles, means desired state is declarative, versioned and immutable in Git, pulled automatically by software agents, and continuously reconciled. Argo CD and Flux implement it for Kubernetes; pull-based agents inside the cluster mean CI never needs cluster admin credentials. Changes, and rollbacks, happen by Git commits and reverts. For cloud resources, controllers such as Crossplane or Terraform operators bring a similar reconcile loop beyond Kubernetes.

The plan is the safety mechanism, so the most expensive mistakes come from not reading it. Replacement (-/+) of a database, load balancer or DNS record can mean data loss or downtime; changing an immutable argument, renaming a resource without a moved block, or switching count indexes are common triggers. Guard critical resources with lifecycle prevent_destroy and enable provider-side deletion protection.

State mishandling is the other big family: local state lost with a laptop, two engineers applying at once without locking, state committed to Git with secrets inside. Secrets should come from a secret manager or be generated, never hardcoded, and remember they still land in state. Other pitfalls: unpinned providers so a new major version changes behavior; one giant state for everything; long-lived drift that makes every plan noisy so real changes hide in it; and broad CI credentials. Run applies only from CI with short-lived, scoped credentials.
deeper.further: Go deeper with Terraform import and moved blocks for refactoring live infrastructure; terraform test and policy as code (Open Policy Agent, Conftest, Sentinel) in CI; OpenTofu features such as state encryption; Pulumi or CDK for language-based IaC; Kubernetes operators and Crossplane for reconciliation beyond Kubernetes; immutable images built with Packer; and landing-zone patterns for multi-account cloud setups. Studying the GitOps principles and Argo CD or Flux shows how reconciliation loops replace push-based deploys.

pages.title: Cloud Fundamentals
pages.subtitle: Rent computing by the second, not the year

panels.heading: Service Models
panels.body:
IaaS (infrastructure as a service): rent VMs; you manage the OS and up.
PaaS (platform): push code; the platform runs it.
SaaS (software): use finished apps, e.g. email.
Serverless: functions run on events, scale to zero.

panels.heading: Regions and Zones
panels.body:
Region = geographic area, e.g. us-east-1, europe-west1.
Availability zone (AZ) = isolated data center(s) inside a region.
Spread across 2-3 AZs to survive a data-center failure; add regions for disasters.

panels.heading: Core Services (AWS/GCP/Azure)
panels.body:
VMs: EC2 | Compute Engine | Virtual Machines
Objects: S3 | Cloud Storage | Blob Storage
SQL: RDS | Cloud SQL | Azure SQL Database
Functions: Lambda | Cloud Run functions | Azure Functions
Network: VPC | VPC | Virtual Network

panels.heading: Networking: VPC
panels.body:
VPC = virtual private cloud: your isolated network, e.g. 10.0.0.0/16.
Public subnet: routes to an internet gateway (load balancer).
Private subnet: app servers and databases, no inbound internet.
Firewall rules open only needed ports, e.g. 443.

panels.heading: IAM: Least Privilege
panels.body:
IAM = identity and access management: who can do what on which resource.
Grant only what the job needs.
Prefer roles with short-lived credentials over long-lived keys.

panels.heading: Shared Responsibility
panels.body:
Provider secures the cloud: buildings, hardware, hypervisor.
You secure what you put in it: data, IAM, network rules, OS patches on VMs.
More managed service = less for you to secure.

panels.heading: Cost Traps
panels.body:
Idle VMs and forgotten dev environments.
Data egress: traffic out to the internet or across regions is billed per GB.
NAT gateway and log ingestion fees add up.
Fix: budgets, alerts, tags, autoscaling, right-sizing.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Public storage bucket = data leak.
Root account used daily, no MFA (multi-factor authentication).
Single-AZ database = single point of failure.
Wildcard policies: "Action": "*".

pages.footer: Pick the most managed service that fits, spread across zones, grant the least.
pages.summary: Introduces cloud service models from IaaS to serverless, regions and availability zones, the core compute, storage, database, function and networking services with their AWS, GCP and Azure names, IAM least privilege, the shared responsibility model and common cost traps.

panels:
Service models describe where the responsibility line sits. With IaaS you get VMs, disks and networks, and you own the operating system, patches, runtime and scaling logic. PaaS (Heroku-style platforms, App Engine, Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service) runs your code and handles OS and scaling. SaaS is a finished application. Containers fit between: managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) still leaves you cluster and workload configuration, while serverless containers (Cloud Run, Fargate, Azure Container Apps) hide the nodes.

Serverless functions bill per invocation and duration, scale to zero and scale out automatically, but have limits: cold-start latency when a new instance boots, maximum execution time (15 minutes on Lambda), statelessness, and concurrency limits. Cost crossover matters: for steady high traffic, always-on instances are often cheaper than per-request pricing; for spiky or low traffic, serverless wins. Vendor lock-in rises as you move up the stack.

Regions are independent geographic deployments, usually containing three or more availability zones; zones are physically separate facilities with independent power, cooling and networking, connected by low-latency links (typically single-digit milliseconds), so synchronous replication across zones is practical. Names differ: AWS us-east-1a, GCP europe-west1-b, Azure numbered zones 1-3. On AWS, zone letters are mapped differently per account; use zone IDs to coordinate.

Multi-AZ protects against a data-center failure and is the default recommendation for production: load balancers spread traffic, managed databases offer a synchronous standby in another zone, and object storage is replicated across zones automatically. Multi-region protects against regional outages and serves global users with lower latency, but adds asynchronous replication, conflict handling, data-residency rules and much higher cost and complexity. Recovery targets drive the choice: RTO (how fast you must recover) and RPO (how much data you can lose). Cross-zone traffic is often billed.

Mapping names helps, but the services are not identical. Compute: EC2, Compute Engine and Azure Virtual Machines differ in instance families and discount models (reserved or committed-use discounts, savings plans, spot or preemptible capacity at large discounts that can be reclaimed). Object storage (S3, Cloud Storage, Blob Storage) stores immutable objects addressed by key, scales nearly without limit, and offers storage classes from hot to archive; S3 has been strongly read-after-write consistent since 2020.

Managed relational databases (RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure SQL Database) handle backups, patching and failover; distributed options include Aurora, AlloyDB, Spanner and Cosmos DB. Functions: Lambda, Cloud Run functions (formerly Cloud Functions) and Azure Functions. Networking: an AWS VPC is regional with zonal subnets, while a GCP VPC is global with regional subnets; Azure calls it a Virtual Network (VNet). Block storage (EBS, Persistent Disk, Managed Disks) is the other storage primitive, attached to one VM.

A VPC is a logically isolated network with a private IP range in CIDR notation: 10.0.0.0/16 provides 65,536 addresses, and each /24 subnet provides 256, minus a few reserved by the provider (AWS reserves 5 per subnet). Plan ranges so they do not overlap with other VPCs or on-premises networks you may later connect.

A subnet is public if its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. Private subnets reach the internet outbound through a NAT gateway (billed hourly plus per GB processed) and receive traffic only through load balancers. Firewalls come in two flavors on AWS: security groups are stateful and attached to instances, network ACLs are stateless and attached to subnets; GCP uses VPC firewall rules, Azure uses network security groups. Private endpoints let you reach managed services like object storage without crossing the internet. Connecting networks uses peering, transit gateways or VPN and dedicated links.

IAM has principals (users, groups, roles, service accounts), actions, resources and conditions. On AWS, evaluation starts from implicit deny; an explicit Allow grants access, and any explicit Deny overrides all Allows. Policies can be identity-based or resource-based (such as bucket policies), and organization-level guardrails (service control policies) cap what any account can do.

The page's statement allows only reading objects in one bucket; note the ARN uses '/*' for objects, while listing the bucket requires s3:ListBucket on the bucket ARN itself without '/*', a classic gotcha. Least privilege in practice: start narrow and add from access logs or tools that analyze unused permissions, use conditions (source network, required MFA, tags), and give workloads roles: instance profiles, Kubernetes workload identity, or OIDC federation from CI. Short-lived credentials limit the damage of a leak; long-lived access keys in code repositories are among the most common causes of cloud breaches.

The model splits security of the cloud (provider) from security in the cloud (customer). The line moves with the service: on a VM you patch the OS and configure the firewall; on a managed database the provider patches the engine but you still control network exposure, users, encryption choices and backups retention; on SaaS you still own identities, access policies and your data.

Most real cloud breaches are on the customer side: misconfigured public storage, overly permissive IAM, exposed credentials, and unpatched workloads, not failures of provider hardware. Compliance follows the same split: a provider's certifications (SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS) cover its layers and are inherited only for those layers.
