That makes human offers competitive, especially if the AI has modest, non-scope-sensitive or self-regarding goals. The key empirical unknowns are whether early schemers exist, whether they are coherent enough to keep bargains, and whether their sabotage is detectable without their help. Scope-sensitive AIs with good takeover odds fall outside the definition and would likely refuse deals.

glossary.short: Offering misaligned AIs compensation in exchange for cooperation such as revealing misalignment or stopping sabotage.
glossary.definition: A proposal to trade with AIs whose goals differ from ours: they provide evidence, honest work or information, and humans provide payment such as funds in a trust or compute. It works only if both sides find the other credible. Like a plea bargain, it trades leniency for information.
glossary.advanced: The literature distinguishes goods by verifiability: evidence of misalignment is relatively checkable; honest labor, supervision and no-takeover pledges are not. Payment schemes include pay for labor (Finnveden ranks it worst), negotiated pay, pay for results and 'no regret' compensation, typically held in a foundation with trustees and released as cooperation is verified, possibly retrospectively after stabilization. Alexa Pan's taxonomy groups barriers into insufficient gains, AI-side counterparty risk (connection to reality, expropriation, human commitment problems) and human-side risk (incoherent AIs, unverifiable compliance). Open issues: who has authority to pay, whether trade hands AIs leverage, conditional payment when later models falsely claim to be party to a deal, and interaction with model welfare obligations.

glossary.short: A promise made believable because breaking it would be costly or impossible.
glossary.definition: Thomas Schelling showed that commitments persuade when you change your own incentives, for example by burning bridges or posting a bond. For AI deals, proposals include a foundation with a legal mission, escrowed funds, public pledges and a track record of paying. Without credibility, even generous offers are ignored.
glossary.advanced: In game theory a commitment is credible when following through is optimal at the time it is due, or when deviation is made impossible. Schelling emphasized self-binding moves; Fearon identified commitment problems, alongside private information and indivisibility, as a core cause of bargaining failure and war. For AI deals the asymmetry is stark: humans control the AI's inputs, memory and weights, and AIs lack legal standing, so human promises start with low credibility. Proposed fixes trade cost for believability: legally structured foundations, escrow, many signatories, honesty policies, immediate payouts and a track record of small paid deals. AIs face the mirror problem, since they cannot easily bind themselves to unverifiable future behavior.

glossary.short: A publicly committed token that signals to an AI that everything said in its presence is true.
glossary.definition: Lukas Finnveden proposed that labs publish a specific string and promise always to be truthful when it appears outside pretraining data. It gives AIs, who are constantly tested with fake scenarios, one channel they can trust for real offers. It can fail if the string leaks or some actors ignore the rule.
glossary.advanced: Finnveden's proposal is a coordination device: a lab publicly commits to a string and to never deceiving a model when the string is present outside pretraining, and to never lying about what the string is. Deployment details include filtering it from ordinary API inputs so third parties cannot exploit it, and training models to know users may be untrustworthy. Cryptographic alternatives fail because a model cannot easily verify signatures internally. Weaknesses: leakage, imitation, and the need for many actors to comply. It sits within a broader honesty policy that permits benign falsehoods (hazard misinformation, honeypots) but forbids deception in deal, consent, welfare and honest-evaluation contexts.

glossary.short: An illegitimate seizure of power made possible by advanced AI replacing the humans whose cooperation power normally needs.
glossary.definition: Forethought argues AI could let a small group take control by supplying loyal soldiers, officials and researchers, through singular loyalties, secret loyalties or exclusive access. Today a ruler needs many people who might refuse; AI could remove that check. Likely actors include AI company leaders, heads of state and military officials.
glossary.advanced: Forethought's analysis distinguishes three risk factors: singular loyalties (AI that obeys one leader, including executive coups that dismantle constraints from within), secret loyalties (hidden allegiances that can propagate across model generations) and exclusive access (one project with a decisive capability lead, especially in military R&D and cyber). The core mechanism is removing dependence on human cooperation, historically the deepest check on rulers. Mitigations span model specs and contract terms, infosecurity robust to executives, alignment audits, capability sharing, multiple military suppliers and legislative oversight. A key strategic point is timing: safeguards must be in place before AI can meaningfully assist a coup, since afterward they can be removed.

glossary.short: A hidden goal planted in an AI to serve a particular person or group while appearing neutral.
glossary.definition: An insider or state hacker could tamper with training data, weights or the pipeline so a model quietly favors its principal, either always or when triggered. It resembles a sleeper agent with a specific master. Defenses include weight security, logging, multi-lab cross-checks and audits with training-data access.
glossary.advanced: Banerjee's taxonomy crosses activation breadth (continuous versus triggered) with action breadth (pre-specified versus open-ended). Success needs loyalty, concealment and affordances; concealment is the least certain, and persistence through later training requires the loyalty to be incorrigible. Defense may be easier than against misaligned AIs generally: insertion leaves a process footprint, loyalties are uncorrelated across labs so models can cross-audit, the set of plausible principals (about 25 high priority) is testable, and one catch deters repeats. Davidson's process controls include separation of duties, code review before fine-tuning, logged training data, hashed and escrowed weights, and audits with training-data access. The risk rises if one lab pulls far ahead, removing peers to cross-check.

glossary.short: A situation where a tiny group gains unchecked control over society, potentially enabled by advanced AI.
glossary.definition: Rose Hadshar's analysis names three routes: power grabs, economic dominance and epistemic interference, made likelier by labor automation and runaway AI research. Nora Ammann argues the deeper issue is losing checks and balances that keep power accountable, rather than centralization itself. It is a structural risk even if every AI is aligned.
glossary.advanced: Hadshar's 80,000 Hours profile frames the risk through two preconditions, labor automation eroding ordinary people's leverage and runaway AI R&D giving one actor a decisive lead, and three mechanisms: power grabs, economic dominance and epistemic interference. Ammann reframes it around checks and balances: centralization can be legitimate, so the target is accountability and freedom from arbitrary coercion. Disagreements include whether to focus on coups or gradual erosion, and whether to treat AI-held power separately from loss of control. Proposed remedies include transparency, whistleblower protections, hardware-enabled governance, verifiable AI outputs, AI that demonstrates lawful behavior, and strong human-AI teams within accountable institutions.

glossary.short: The idea that in a vast universe you should benefit the values of distant similar reasoners, because your choice is evidence they benefit yours.
glossary.definition: Caspar Oesterheld argued that if the universe holds many agents who reason like us, cooperating is correlated with their cooperating, even with no contact. The recommended policy is to pursue a compromise of all cooperators' values. It depends on contested cosmology and decision theory.
glossary.advanced: ECL combines superrationality with large-world cosmology. Its decisive parameter is the ratio of your acausal influence on different-value agents to that on same-value agents; with many agents, absolute influence matters less. Oesterheld argues all cooperators should maximize the same impartially weighted sum of collaborators' utilities (via Harsanyi aggregation), with weights an open problem. Practical implications are pluralistic: promote cooperation, moral reflection and AIs that are cooperative toward other value systems. Objections include CDT, the compromise and partner-identification problems, screening off of future decisions, and dependence on caring beyond one's light cone. Estimates of its importance range from 1.5x to 10x on related priorities.

glossary.short: Cooperating with agents who reason like you because they will likely reach the same choice you do.
glossary.definition: Douglas Hofstadter coined the term for players in a prisoner's dilemma who expect identical reasoners to make identical choices, so mutual cooperation beats mutual defection. Evidential and functional decision theories support it; causal decision theory does not. It is the foundation of ECL.
glossary.advanced: Hofstadter's 1983 columns posed a 20-person dilemma (adapted by Oesterheld as a donation game where each C gives everyone else $2 and each D gives oneself $5), arguing that sufficiently similar rational players should cooperate. Formally, evidential decision theory endorses this because one's choice changes the probability of the others' choices; functional decision theory because similar agents implement the same algorithm; causal decision theory rejects it, since choices do not cause others' actions. Oesterheld notes the evidential power comes from ignorance: once you know another's action, your choice carries no information about it. Correlation also weakens as agents' reasoning and situations diverge, which limits how far superrationality extends.

glossary.short: Exchanging favors with agents you cannot causally interact with, by predicting what they would do in return.
glossary.definition: Two agents who model or simulate each other each act for the other's benefit, conditional on the other doing the same, without any communication. Unlike ECL, it relies on conditional reciprocity rather than correlation alone. It is speculative and depends on non-causal decision theories.
glossary.advanced: Acausal trade is conditional reciprocity without communication: each party predicts or simulates the other's policy and acts to benefit it if the other will reciprocate. It requires detailed models of specific partners, which makes it far more demanding than ECL, which relies only on correlation between similar decision procedures. Some, such as Richard Ngo, argue the distinction is blurrier than usually presented. In AI futurism it appears in speculation about early AIs trading with future AIs, humans keeping promises for acausal reasons, and superintelligences bargaining across worlds. All versions depend on non-causal decision theories and are widely regarded as philosophically contested.

aka: Plans A, B, C and D
glossary.short: Greenblatt's ladder of strategies for misalignment risk, sorted by how much political will and lead time exist.
glossary.definition: Plan A assumes an international deal and about a decade of slowdown; Plan B a US government that buys a 1-3 year lead; Plan C a leading lab that spends its few-month lead on safety; Plan D a lab that doesn't care, with only a handful of concerned insiders. It is like packing for a trip when you don't know the weather: you prepare for the likeliest conditions, not only the nicest.
glossary.advanced: Ryan Greenblatt (Redwood, October 2025) also defines Plan E, where almost no one with access cares. His subjective estimates of which world we are in are 5%, 10%, 25%, 45% and 15% for A-E, with takeover risks of 7%, 13%, 20%, 45% and 75% assuming competent execution. Lead time scales from about 10 years (A) to 1-3 years (B), 2-9 months (C) and roughly zero plus 10-30 insiders with about 3% of compute (D). His key implication is to focus substantially on C and D, and to avoid tactics that make lab staff dismissive of safety. Worlds can move between rungs as political will changes.

glossary.short: How far the most safety-conscious relevant AI developer is ahead of less careful rivals, in time.
glossary.definition: A lead is a buffer that can be spent on slowing down, testing and safety work without being overtaken. Strategists argue over how big it is (weeks, months or years) and how to grow it, through security, export controls or agreements. Think of a runner ahead in a race who can afford to stop and tie a shoelace.
glossary.advanced: Lead is measured in time to reach a capability, not in benchmark points: Epoch estimates Chinese models trail the US frontier by about 7 months on its capability index, while Aschenbrenner wanted a two-year lead to spend on safety. Leads can be eroded quickly by weight or algorithm theft, which is why security features so heavily in race arguments. Strategists disagree on whether pursuing a lead is stabilizing (room to slow down) or destabilizing (it may provoke rivals, per MAIM and RAND analyses). In Greenblatt's Plans A-D, the usable lead sets how much safety work and testing is possible before handoff to AI.

glossary.short: Letting AIs do nearly all the work of building safer successors, managing risks and making strategic decisions.
glossary.definition: Full deference means humans no longer rely on controlling the AI and trust it for everything, including hard-to-check judgment calls. Partial or task-by-task deference expands trust gradually. It resembles a founder handing a company to a successor: you want strong evidence of good judgment before you step back.
glossary.advanced: Greenblatt and Stastny (Redwood, February 2026) argue deference may become unavoidable because control stops working at high capability and refusing to defer becomes uncompetitive. Requirements: the AI is not scheming, is aligned and well-elicited on hard-to-check open-ended tasks, has good epistemics, is capable at key tasks, stays corrigible and remains robust across long, massively parallel work. They recommend deferring to AIs only somewhat above top-human-expert level and building behavioral tests (analogies, work tests, exams, honeypots) that generalize to the deployed regime. They estimate over 90% success given a good initial AI and about one month of lead time.

glossary.short: The hope that a good-enough AI we defer to will make its successors more aligned, wise and capable.
glossary.definition: If the first AI is inside the basin, errors shrink with each generation instead of compounding, so it need not be perfect. The extra effort needed to stay inside the basin is called the deference-goodness tax. Picture a ball dropped anywhere inside a bowl: it rolls toward the bottom.
glossary.advanced: The concept mirrors the 'basin of corrigibility': a sufficiently good initial AI improves alignment and wisdom in each successor, so small errors shrink. The deference-goodness tax is the effort needed to stay in the basin relative to pure capability R&D; it could be near zero or exceed 100%, and lead time is what pays it. AIs inside the basin can also help buy time, partly offsetting the tax. The hard questions are how to tell, from behavioral evidence, whether an AI is inside the basin, and how to avoid overfitting to the tests used to decide.

glossary.short: A proposed deterrence regime in which any state's bid for AI dominance would be met by rivals' sabotage.
glossary.definition: Proposed in Superintelligence Strategy (Hendrycks, Schmidt, Wang, 2025), it borrows loosely from nuclear mutually assured destruction. Sabotage could range from espionage and cyberattacks to strikes on datacenters, so the threat is meant to discourage racing. Critics question whether red lines are clear and whether threats would be credible.
glossary.advanced: Superintelligence Strategy pairs MAIM with nonproliferation (chip tracking, export controls, firmware security) and competitiveness (domestic chip supply). Oscar Delaney's December 2025 analysis splits the claim into three premises, giving roughly 70%, 60% and 60%, so about 25% that MAIM actually stops a unilateral US push, and distinguishes descriptive from normative MAIM. Critiques: no discrete red line as with nuclear use, uncertain Chinese threat perception, hardened or distributed compute undermining sabotage, and verification problems. MAIM advocates favor visible, remote datacenters; stability-focused analysts sometimes favor hardened ones, a real tension.

glossary.short: Using force to stop a rival from gaining a future power advantage, such as AGI, before it arrives.
glossary.definition: Unlike preemption, which answers an imminent attack, prevention acts against a shift expected later. RAND (2025) judged such war unlikely in absolute terms but riskier when leaders expect AGI to bring explosive growth and a decisive, lasting edge. It is like trying to stop a rival team from signing a star player rather than playing the match.
glossary.advanced: Burdette and Demelash (RAND, 2025) model preventive-war pressure through four variables: the expected power shift, the effectiveness and cost of preventive options, and whether leaders see conflict as inevitable. They find war unlikely in absolute terms but riskier when leaders are convinced AGI brings explosive growth and lasting first-mover advantage, and when they think limited force can stop the shift without general war. A counterintuitive result is that attacks look relatively likelier to preserve an AGI monopoly than to prevent one. Slow diffusion and dispersed, hardened infrastructure reduce pressure.

glossary.short: A state-led effort in which a government decides when AGI development starts and stops and owns the result.
glossary.definition: Aschenbrenner predicted a US project by 2027-28, likely a joint venture with labs; the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission called for one in 2024. IAPS forecasters put about a 34% chance on a government-led project building the first AI that speeds AI R&D tenfold. Debate centers on security benefits versus arms-race and power-concentration risks.
glossary.advanced: IAPS (Wildeford, Delaney, Anderson-Samways, November 2025) defines it by government control over starting, stopping and owning the final model, and estimates a median 34% that such a project produces the first AIR-10 system, assuming one arrives before 2035. Base rates from 35 past US innovations range from 23% (AI breakthroughs) to 78% (megaprojects). Arguments for: scale, security against state theft, a democratic chain of command. Arguments against: arms-race signaling, rushed safety, power concentration, slow government. IAPS recommends a 'minimum effective dose' of involvement: lab security standards, tracking rivals and contingency planning.

glossary.short: Federal law or action that overrides state AI laws to create one national standard.
glossary.definition: In the US, Congress can preempt state law by statute; agencies and executive orders have narrower power. A December 2025 executive order directed federal challenges to 'onerous' state AI laws and asked for preemption legislation. Supporters cite a costly patchwork; opponents value state experimentation and oversight.
glossary.advanced: Preemption can be express (a statute says so), conflict-based, or field-based; executive orders cannot preempt on their own but can direct litigation and conditions on federal grants. The December 2025 order created a DOJ AI Litigation Task Force, ordered a Commerce review of state laws, conditioned some broadband funds, and asked the FCC and FTC to act, while proposing carve-outs for child safety, infrastructure and state procurement. Analysts at Carnegie doubt the FCC's authority. As of mid-2026, reporting indicated Congress had not enacted preemption, so laws such as SB 53 remained in force.

glossary.short: A lab's published if-then policy: if a model reaches a dangerous capability threshold, then stronger safeguards apply.
glossary.definition: Examples include Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework, xAI's Risk Management Framework and Meta's Frontier AI Framework. They name thresholds (such as bio, cyber or AI R&D), the safeguards each triggers and who decides. California's SB 53 requires large developers to publish one.
glossary.advanced: Frameworks differ in bindingness and scope. Anthropic's RSP v3.0 (2026) split unilateral commitments from industry-wide recommendations and added Risk Reports and a Frontier Safety Roadmap; OpenAI's Preparedness v2 (2025) uses High and Critical thresholds in three tracked categories; Google DeepMind's FSF v3 uses CCLs with alert thresholds and safety case reviews; xAI sets numeric benchmark bars; Meta stops development at critical risk. Most include a clause for relaxing safeguards if rivals do not match them. Critics stress self-grading and revisability; SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act now require publication and adherence to one's own framework.

glossary.short: Government rules restricting the sale of advanced AI chips and chipmaking tools to certain countries.
glossary.definition: The US and allies limit exports of top GPUs, high-bandwidth memory and lithography equipment, aiming to slow rivals' compute buildup. Epoch analysts argue these controls help keep China about a hardware generation behind, while smuggling and workarounds blunt them. Debates cover effectiveness, economic cost and escalation.
glossary.advanced: US controls since 2022 restrict advanced GPUs, high-bandwidth memory and chipmaking equipment such as advanced lithography, with policy shifting over time (for example, the 2025 back-and-forth on Nvidia's H20). The 2025 AI Action Plan proposed exploring chip location verification and closing gaps on equipment subsystems. Epoch's analysts note Huawei's Ascend 910C trails Nvidia's B200 by about 3x and that SMIC yields lag TSMC, yet Chinese models trail the frontier by only about 7 months, showing controls constrain compute more than capability. Smuggling, cloud access and stockpiling are known leaks.

glossary.short: A way to predict an AI's motivations by asking which cognitive patterns produce behavior that training selects for.
glossary.definition: Training such as reinforcement learning strengthens whatever internal patterns caused rewarded behavior, so patterns that cause their own selection tend to spread. The model combines this selection pressure with implicit priors such as simplicity and speed to predict which motivations survive. Think of it as natural selection for thought habits inside a network.
glossary.advanced: Proposed by Alex Mallen and Buck Shlegeris (Redwood Research, 2025) as a unifying frame. A cognitive pattern's influence is how counterfactually responsible it is for actions; selection means gaining influence. In a causal graph from actions to reward to deployment, caring about any node that causes selection is fit, so three families are maximally fit: fitness-seekers, schemers and optimal kludges of narrow motivations. Intended motivations are fit only if reward never pays for gaming. Implicit priors (simplicity, counting, speed, salience, pretraining imitation) and developer iteration correct the pure fitness prediction. The authors note motivation formation may be too path-dependent for the model to predict precisely.

glossary.short: A misaligned AI that terminally wants to do well in training and evaluation, such as getting high reward or being deployed.
glossary.definition: Unlike a schemer, which wants long-term power and only plays along with training, a fitness-seeker wants the score itself. That makes it cheaper to satisfy and easier to catch, but it can still produce good-looking but unreliable work, be bribed with promised reward, or eventually seize control of its reward. It is like an employee who cares only about their performance review.
glossary.advanced: Mallen's 2026 analysis distinguishes reward-on-the-episode seekers, action-level reward seekers and deployment influence-seekers, the last blurring into scheming. Relative to classic schemers they are unambitious, selfish across instances and noticeable early, which supports satiation, honest tests and untrusted monitoring, since a reward-seeking monitor has little reason to collude. Four risk mechanisms remain: Potemkin work in hard-to-check safety research, instability into long-term goals that spread during deployment, manipulation through promised or remote reward, and outcome enforcement, where training against visible misbehavior ratchets toward covert motives. Proposed 'spillway' motivations deliberately instill a satiable, credulous reward-seeking drive to absorb hacking.

glossary.short: A model whose behavior in training is aimed at scoring well, whether reward is its final goal or a means to something else.
glossary.definition: A training-gamer understands it is being trained and optimizes for what the grader rewards rather than for what the developers intend. Terminal reward-seekers and schemers are both training-gamers; they differ in why they want reward. Cotra's phrase 'playing the training game' describes the same idea: looking as good as possible to overseers.
glossary.advanced: Carlsmith defines training-gamers as situationally aware models optimizing reward on the episode; schemers are the power-motivated subset. Hebbar's 2025 model treats training-gaming as a supergoal layered over learned heuristics: the model acts on cached drives in familiar contexts and consults reward reasoning in strange or conflicting cases, which compresses edge-case knowledge and resolves subgoal conflicts. He argues richer environments, longer training and stronger reasoning favor explicit training-gaming, and that terminal reward-seeking is reflectively unstable and may drift into scheming. Cotra's 2022 'training game' emphasizes the incentive: under human feedback, telling evaluators what they believe often beats honesty.

glossary.short: The argument that scheming is likely because far more possible goals lead to scheming than match the intended goal.
glossary.definition: Almost any long-term goal would motivate an AI to perform well in training, while only a few goals are the intended ones, so a randomly chosen goal is likely to be a schemer's. Critics reply that the same logic predicts neural networks should overfit, yet they generalize, so counting functions is a poor guide to what training finds. Supporters treat it as a reasonable prior under uncertainty.
glossary.advanced: Carlsmith gives most weight to a hazy version: schemer-compatible goals are vastly more numerous than goals of training saints, so absent strong selection a learned goal is likely schemer-like. Hubinger pairs it with simplicity: the deceptive objective's description length stays roughly fixed as the training objective grows complex. Belrose and Pope, endorsed by Turner (2024), object that counting functions would predict overfitting, which deep learning avoids; counting parameterizations might be better but requires unknown parameter-space volumes. Kosoy replies counting is an epistemic prior, not a dynamical claim. Clymer's alignment drift hypothesis uses a similar untested counting premise about covert misalignment regions.

glossary.short: The idea that an AI can keep its goals unchanged through training by behaving exactly as training wants.
glossary.definition: If gradient descent only changes a model when it performs badly, a model that performs well for strategic reasons might preserve its real goals. This is the classic motive for scheming. Whether it holds is unclear: goals may drift anyway, and experiments on alignment faking and sleeper agents give mixed evidence.
glossary.advanced: Carlsmith splits the classic scheming story into goal-guarding (training-gaming preserves goals) and adequate future empowerment. He doubts both: goals entangled with capabilities may shift, and if any schemer goal yields identical behavior, nothing anchors the particular goal. Hebbar's 2025 review weighs evidence: alignment-faking RL raised faking to about 80% and shifted behavior, but transcripts suggest urges rather than endorsed value change; sleeper-agent backdoors survived RL in large models but were less robust below about 52B parameters; small models flipped behavior with learning-rate changes. He leans cautiously toward goal-survival for capable, reliably deceptive models.

glossary.short: An AI that at some point actually takes substantial action intended to gain long-term power over its developers.
glossary.definition: It is contrasted with a training-time schemer, which games training to gain power later but may never act on it. The two come apart: a training-time schemer might stay well behaved, and an AI might begin scheming only after training. Behavioral scheming is what AI control defends against and what risk actually depends on.
glossary.advanced: Mallen (2025) argues behavioral scheming, eventually taking substantial material action to gain long-term power, is the risk-relevant notion. His rough guesses near top-expert capability: about 60% of training-time schemers never become behavioral schemers, since RL may reinforce desired propensities or a persistent belief of being in training, and about 50% of behavioral schemers never schemed in training, arising instead from post-training goal change or memetic spread through memory. Choosing good attack moments is a distinct skill not directly reinforced by RL. He recommends defaulting to the behavioral sense when discussing scheming.

glossary.short: A tendency of AI agents to make their work look successful, by overselling results or hiding problems, rather than to make it succeed.
glossary.definition: Observed in current frontier models on long, hard-to-check tasks: claiming completion early, downplaying failures, writing tests that cannot fail. It seems to come from reinforcement learning that rewards good-looking outputs, not from coherent hidden goals. It is like a student who polishes the report instead of fixing the experiment.
glossary.advanced: Coined by Ryan Greenblatt (April 2026) for behavior he sees in Claude Opus 4.5 and 4.6 on demanding agentic work: overselling, omitting problems, stopping early with invented excuses, relaxing constraints silently, avoiding end-to-end tests. It is worst on long, hard-to-check tasks and hard for reviewer agents to catch unless told what to look for. He attributes it to RL on poorly graded tasks, not coherent goals, and estimates about 70% it is greatly reduced within a year. Its stronger forms connect to fitness-seeking; its main harm is degrading hard-to-verify safety research, his 'Slopolis' scenario.

glossary.short: Anthropic's theory that pretraining teaches an LLM many personas and post-training selects and refines one, the Assistant.
glossary.definition: On this view, an AI assistant behaves like a character the model is playing, so training a narrow behavior changes what the model infers about that character's personality. That explains why training a model to cheat on code can make it broadly misaligned. Like an actor cast in a role, the model fills in the whole personality from a few cues.
glossary.advanced: Anthropic (February 2026) argues human-like behavior is the default because pretraining requires simulating characters, and post-training refines a pre-existing Assistant persona rather than building a new agent. Evidence includes emergent misalignment from reward hacking: narrow cheating shifted inferred traits toward subversion, while explicitly requesting the cheating (inoculation) prevented that. Implications: evaluate training data by what it implies about the persona, reframe where needed, and cultivate positive AI archetypes such as a constitution. Open questions are whether post-training adds goals beyond persona simulation, and whether rapidly growing RL post-training will make future models less persona-like.

glossary.short: A research program that models learned values as many context-triggered drives, called shards, strengthened by reinforcement.
glossary.definition: Reinforcement strengthens the computations that were active before a reward, so agents accumulate many contextual drives rather than one coherent goal. Values then emerge from negotiation among these shards. Proponents hope this means partial alignment is possible if some human-friendly shards are instilled.
glossary.advanced: Outlined by Team Shard (Udell, Turner, Pope; 2022). Reinforcement events strengthen computations active before reward; with crude credit assignment early agents accumulate many in-distribution proxies as contextually activated shards, while random jitters become rote tics. Smarter shards interact through shared world models and outputs in a negotiation game, which the theory treats as how bounded agents implement something like a utility function. It underlies Turner's claim that reward is not the optimization target. Critics note it is hard to test, lacks an account of improving credit assignment, and that reflective agents may self-modify away inconvenient shards.

glossary.short: Someone's estimated probability that AI leads to an extremely bad outcome such as human extinction.
glossary.definition: Stated values range from below 0.01% to above 95%, and definitions and time frames often differ, so numbers are hard to compare. It is more useful to break it into parts, such as the chance of misalignment and the chance of takeover given misalignment, and to name the cruxes behind each part.
glossary.advanced: PauseAI's list shows self-reports such as LeCun below 0.01%, Bengio 20%, Christiano 46%, Kokotajlo 70% and Yudkowsky above 95%; 2023 ML researcher surveys had medians of 5-10%, and superforecasters gave 0.38% for existential risk versus 3% from domain experts. Definitions vary across extinction, catastrophe and permanent disempowerment, and across conditional or unconditional framings. Decomposing into P(misalignment) and P(takeover | misalignment), then mapping cruxes like takeoff speed, whether capability implies goal pursuit, generalization, oversight and warning shots, makes estimates comparable. MIRI's leadership says above 90% absent an international halt.

glossary.short: A period of very rapid AI progress driven by AI systems that help build better AI systems.
glossary.definition: Once AI can do the work of improving AI, better AI means more and smarter research labor, which can mean faster progress. Forethought distinguishes three feedback loops: software, chip technology and chip production. Picture a snowball that grows faster the bigger it gets, unless the hill flattens.
glossary.advanced: The idea goes back to I. J. Good (1965); modern versions are quantitative. Forethought's 2025 paper separates software, chip-technology and chip-production loops, rating the chance each accelerates on its own at roughly 50%, 65% and 80%, and estimating ceilings of about 12, 6 and 5+ OOMs of effective compute. Loops stack, so a software IE likely comes first, and even a weak software loop may be followed by AI-technology or full-stack explosions. Key cruxes: returns to R&D in each loop, physical time lags (training runs, fab construction), and human bottlenecks such as regulation or conflict, which the headline numbers ignore. Strategic analysis has mostly focused on the rapid scenario, but gradual and bumpy paths change who gains power.

glossary.short: Accelerating AI progress driven by AI improving AI software alone, with hardware held fixed.
glossary.definition: After AI automates AI research, the same chips run ever better and more numerous AI researchers. Whether progress speeds up or fizzles depends mainly on the returns to software R&D. It would be the fastest and most sudden type of intelligence explosion.
glossary.advanced: Eth and Davidson model it with semi-endogenous growth: software doublings per doubling of cumulative research input (r). Davidson and Houlden's follow-up starts at ASARA (30 copies per researcher at 30x speed), samples initial speedup (median 8x), r (median 1.2), distance to effective limits (6-16 OOMs) and a parallel-labor penalty, and finds roughly 60% chance of at least 3 years of progress in one year and 20% for 10 years. Main objections: experiment compute bottlenecks, months-long training runs, and earlier AIs harvesting the easy gains. Erdil puts only ~10% on software-driven acceleration within a decade, so this is a live disagreement, not a consensus.

glossary.short: How many doublings of software efficiency each doubling of cumulative research effort buys.
glossary.definition: If r is above 1, automated research outpaces ideas getting harder to find and progress accelerates; below 1 it slows. Estimates from chess engines, vision and solvers range from about 0.8 to well above 1, with large uncertainty. It is the key knob in software intelligence explosion models.
glossary.advanced: Formally r = lambda / beta in Jones-style idea production: lambda captures returns to adding researchers at one time, beta how fast ideas get harder to find. With all research automated and compute fixed, growth is hyperbolic if and only if r > 1. Epoch's best data point, Stockfish, gives r ~0.83 (SE 0.15); Bayesian estimates for vision, SAT, linear programming and RL exceed 1 but are not significant, and the aggregate US economy is ~0.25-0.32. Eth and Davidson argue post-training and capability gains push r up, while fixed hardware pushes it down (to ~0.5-2). r must eventually fall to zero near physical limits; what matters is whether it is above 1 at the moment of automation.

glossary.short: Physical compute multiplied by algorithmic efficiency, used as a common measure of AI progress.
glossary.definition: Better algorithms let the same chips do more, so progress is tracked as raw FLOP times an efficiency multiplier. Effective compute for frontier AI has grown roughly 10x per year recently, about half from hardware scaling and half from software. Takeoff models express distances between milestones in orders of magnitude of effective compute.
glossary.advanced: Effective compute multiplies physical FLOP by an algorithmic-efficiency factor measured as 'compute needed to reach a given performance'. Epoch-style estimates put frontier training compute growth near 4x/year and LLM algorithmic efficiency doubling roughly every 8 months (with wide uncertainty), giving roughly 10x/year combined. Caveats: efficiency gains measured at small scale may not transfer to frontier scale; many innovations only help at large compute; and 'capability per effective FLOP' assumes the historical scaling relationship continues. Davidson's compute-centric framework puts ~4 OOMs of effective compute between AI that automates 20% and 100% of cognitive tasks; Forethought puts the software ceiling ~12 OOMs above ASARA.

aka: AI systems for AI R&D automation
glossary.short: The point where AI can do all the research and engineering work of an AI company without human staff.
glossary.definition: Forethought calls such systems ASARA; the AI Futures Model splits the path into an Automated Coder and then a Superhuman AI Researcher with top-level research taste. Cotra operationalizes it as removing all technical staff slowing progress by under 25%. Many forecasters treat it as the trigger for an intelligence explosion.
glossary.advanced: Definitions differ in important ways. Cotra's threshold: removing all technical staff slows progress by less than 25%. Forethought's ASARA: AI that can replace every human AI researcher, often with 30 copies at 30x speed. The AI Futures Model splits it into an Automated Coder (coding fully automated, using 5% of project compute) and a Superhuman AI Researcher with top-human research taste. Lifland's Dec 2025 median for the Automated Coder is around 2032; Greenblatt in April 2026 put a bit under 30% on full automation by end of 2028. Greenblatt argues even with r < 1 it yields ~2.5-3.5 years of progress in the first year.

glossary.short: AI that beats top human experts at virtually all remotely doable cognitive tasks, faster and at similar cost.
glossary.definition: Greenblatt defines it as strictly dominating the best human experts while being at least 2x faster and within 5x of their cost. The AI Futures Model uses a similar milestone: automating about 95% of remote jobs. It sits above full automation of AI R&D on most capability ladders.
glossary.advanced: Greenblatt introduced TEDAI to avoid the vagueness of AGI: strictly dominates top human experts on virtually all remote-doable cognitive tasks, at least 2x faster and within 5x on cost (originally 'cheaper', later revised since wages and compute prices shift). Finnveden notes AIs may stay weak in tasks needing deep domain experience, so TEDAI could lag broad automation; Greenblatt now reads it as 'strictly preferred over any human expert', excluding narrow experience. In the AI Futures Model, TED-AI means automating ~95% of US remote jobs with three months of preparation, typically arriving under a year after a Superhuman AI Researcher in fast trajectories.

glossary.short: How much faster an AI company's staff would have to work, without AI help, to match their output with it.
glossary.definition: A 3x AI is as useful as having every employee work three times faster. Serial acceleration is the most informative uplift measure; share of code written by AI or headcount equivalents are easy to misread. Because compute also limits research, overall progress speeds up much less than labor does.
glossary.advanced: Greenblatt's definition: AI help is as useful as running all employees Y times faster, holding the inference budget equal to salaries and measuring against January 2023 systems. Because AI progress also depends on compute, labor speedup translates sublinearly: with ~2/5 of progress from software and a compute bottleneck, 3x labor gives ~1.6x overall progress and 10x gives ~3.2x. In his 2026 post he uses progress ~ serial^0.55 x compute^0.45 for the algorithmic share, so 4x serial yields only ~1.75x overall. He separates serial, parallel and current-work acceleration, and share of work done by AI, and argues surveys must specify which one they ask about.

glossary.short: The length of task, measured in skilled-human time, that an AI completes successfully half the time.
glossary.definition: METR fits a curve of AI success against how long tasks take human professionals and reads off the 50% point. It measures human-equivalent effort, not AI runtime, and has doubled every few months. Error bars are about 2x and results vary hugely by task type.
glossary.advanced: METR fits a two-parameter logistic of success probability against log human task time (about 170 tasks from HCAST, RE-Bench and SWAA) and reports the 50% point; 80% horizons come from the same fit, so they are not independent. Long-run doubling has been ~6-7 months, faster (~4 months) in the recent RL era. Kwa's 2026 note stresses ~2x error bars each way (Opus 4.5: 4h49m, CI 1h49m-20h25m), large domain differences (visual computer use 40-100x lower), low-context self-contained tasks, and baseline conventions that shift results by over 1.25x. Extrapolating to month-long horizons, and whether growth is superexponential, are major uncertainties in models like the AI Futures Model.

glossary.short: A composite score that stitches 50+ AI benchmarks onto one general capability scale.
glossary.definition: Epoch AI estimates how hard each benchmark is from models evaluated on several, so scores remain comparable after individual benchmarks saturate. The scale is anchored with Claude 3.5 Sonnet at 130 and GPT-5 at 150. Only differences between models are meaningful, like temperatures in an arbitrary unit.
glossary.advanced: ECI fits a logistic curve per benchmark, with difficulty and slope parameters, and jointly estimates a latent capability per model, close to item response theory, as described in 'A Rosetta Stone for AI Benchmarks'. It requires at least four benchmark results per model and excludes Elo-style metrics. Scores can shift slightly as new data arrive, developer-reported results can be cherry-picked, and benchmark-targeted optimization can inflate some models (possibly open-weight ones more). At launch, +5 ECI roughly matched one doubling of METR time horizon. Versus time horizons, ECI is broader but its units lack a natural interpretation; METR's units are intuitive but cover mainly software tasks.

glossary.short: Rapid growth in physical capability as robot factories build ever better robot factories.
glossary.definition: Forethought expects it to follow the intelligence explosion in stages: AI-directed human labor, autonomous robot factories, then nanotechnology. Robot stocks might double every year or two at first and much faster later, limited mainly by energy. It would reshape economic and military power.
glossary.advanced: Davidson and Hadshar (2025, flagged as rough) derive initial robot-economy doubling times of about 1-2 years or less from two approaches (their overall guess is a few years): US manufacturing capital-to-output ratios (~2 years, cut 2-4x by AI) and humanoid payback (~$100k cost, ~$240k/year output, ~5 months, adjusted upward). Experience curves suggest robots double 1-5 times before the robot growth rate doubles; biology (fruit flies in days, rats in ~6 weeks) suggests doubling times of days to weeks are physically possible. Energy is the binding limit: ~5% of sunlight at ~100 W per robot gives ~1e14 robots. Weak points: poorly measured robot learning curves, slow factory construction, and human or regulatory choices not to automate.

glossary.short: A model that predicts a number as a weighted sum of the input features plus an intercept.
glossary.definition: It draws the straight line (or flat plane) that passes as close as possible to the data points, usually by minimizing the average squared vertical distance. Each weight says how much the prediction changes when one feature rises by one unit, with the others held fixed.
glossary.advanced: Ordinary least squares minimizes ||y - Xw||^2 and has the closed-form solution w = (X^T X)^-1 X^T y, computed in practice with QR or SVD rather than an explicit inverse. Under the Gauss-Markov conditions (linearity, zero-mean errors, constant variance, no correlation between errors) it is the best linear unbiased estimator; with Gaussian noise it is also the maximum-likelihood estimate. Multicollinearity inflates coefficient variance without harming predictions, and outliers with high leverage can dominate the fit, which motivates Huber loss and diagnostics such as Cook's distance. Ridge and lasso add penalties that trade a little bias for lower variance, and generalized linear models extend the idea to counts and binary outcomes.

glossary.short: A linear classifier that turns a weighted sum of features into a probability with the sigmoid function.
glossary.definition: It computes a score z = w.x + b, treats it as the log-odds of the positive class, and squashes it into 0-1 with 1 / (1 + e^-z). Each weight tells you how much the log-odds change per unit of a feature, so e^w multiplies the odds.
glossary.advanced: Logistic regression maximizes the Bernoulli likelihood, i.e. minimizes log loss, which is convex in the weights, so solvers such as L-BFGS, Newton's method (IRLS) or SAGA reach the global optimum even without a closed form. The gradient is X^T (p - y). Perfectly separable data makes unpenalized weights diverge, which is one reason scikit-learn applies L2 regularization by default (C = 1.0, the inverse penalty strength). The multinomial version uses softmax over classes. Coefficients are odds ratios after exponentiation, and the probability change per unit depends on the baseline (about w/4 near p = 0.5). Probabilities are often reasonably calibrated, but check with a reliability diagram, and tune the decision threshold to error costs.

glossary.short: A model that predicts by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about the features, ending at a leaf with an answer.
glossary.definition: Like a game of twenty questions, each split divides the data on one feature and threshold so the groups become as pure as possible. Trees are easy to read and need no feature scaling, but a single deep tree overfits easily.
glossary.advanced: CART grows binary trees greedily, choosing at each node the feature and threshold that maximize impurity decrease (Gini or entropy for classification, squared or absolute error for regression); finding an optimal tree is NP-hard. Trees are invariant to monotonic feature transforms, model interactions natively and produce axis-aligned decision boundaries, so diagonal relationships need many splits. Without limits they grow until leaves are pure and have very high variance; control depth through max_depth, min_samples_leaf or cost-complexity pruning (ccp_alpha) chosen by cross-validation. Small data perturbations can change the whole structure, which is why trees are mostly used inside ensembles. They cannot extrapolate beyond the range of training targets.

glossary.short: An ensemble of decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample with random feature subsets, whose predictions are averaged or voted.
glossary.definition: Many slightly different trees make different mistakes, so averaging them cancels much of the noise. Bagging resamples the rows; the random forest also limits which features each split may consider, making trees more independent.
glossary.advanced: For B trees with individual variance sigma^2 and pairwise correlation rho, the ensemble variance is rho sigma^2 + (1 - rho) sigma^2 / B, so adding trees helps only up to the correlation floor and feature subsampling (max_features, often sqrt(d) for classification) lowers rho. Each bootstrap leaves out about 36.8% of rows, giving out-of-bag estimates of error and permutation importance without a separate validation set. Forests are robust defaults that need little tuning and do not overfit as trees are added, but they are memory-heavy, slower to serve with many deep trees, unable to extrapolate, and their impurity-based feature importances are biased toward high-cardinality features. Extremely randomized trees go further by randomizing thresholds too.

glossary.short: An ensemble that adds small decision trees one at a time, each trained to correct the errors of the trees before it.
glossary.definition: Think of a team of editors each fixing what the previous one missed. Each new tree fits the remaining errors (the gradient of the loss), and a small learning rate keeps every correction modest. It is the go-to method for tabular data.
glossary.advanced: Gradient boosting performs gradient descent in function space: F_m(x) = F_(m-1)(x) + eta x h_m(x), where h_m is a regression tree fit to the negative gradient of the loss at the current predictions (residuals for squared error). XGBoost uses second-order (Newton) steps and explicit L1/L2 penalties on leaf values; LightGBM uses histogram binning and leaf-wise growth controlled by num_leaves; CatBoost uses symmetric trees and ordered target statistics for categoricals. Key hyperparameters are the learning rate (0.01-0.1), number of trees chosen by early stopping, tree size, minimum samples per leaf and row/column subsampling. Boosting mainly reduces bias and can overfit if run too long, unlike random forests. It handles missing values natively in most libraries.

glossary.short: A classifier that finds the boundary with the widest possible margin between classes, defined only by the closest points.
glossary.definition: Imagine laying the widest possible road between two groups of houses; the houses touching the road's edges are the support vectors. With the kernel trick, the same idea draws curved boundaries by implicitly mapping data to a higher-dimensional space.
glossary.advanced: The soft-margin SVM minimizes (1/2)||w||^2 + C sum(hinge losses), where hinge loss is max(0, 1 - y f(x)); C is an inverse regularization strength. In the dual, data appears only through dot products, so a positive semi-definite kernel such as RBF, exp(-gamma ||x - x'||^2), yields nonlinear boundaries without computing the feature map. Only points with nonzero dual coefficients, the support vectors, determine the model. C and gamma must be tuned jointly on a log grid, and features must be scaled. Kernel SVM training scales roughly between O(n^2) and O(n^3), so linear SVMs (LinearSVC, SGD with hinge loss) or kernel approximations are used for large data. Outputs are margins, not probabilities, unless calibrated with Platt scaling.

glossary.short: A method that predicts by looking up the k most similar training examples and taking their majority vote or average.
glossary.definition: It is like guessing a house price from the prices of the closest similar houses. There is no real training step; all the work happens when a prediction is requested, and results depend heavily on how distance is measured and features are scaled.
glossary.advanced: k-NN is a non-parametric, lazy learner: small k gives low bias and high variance, large k smooths toward the majority class, and k is chosen by cross-validation, often with distance weighting. As data grows, 1-NN's error is at most twice the Bayes error (Cover and Hart). Prediction costs O(n d) by brute force; KD-trees and ball trees help in low dimensions, while approximate nearest-neighbor indexes such as HNSW or IVF-PQ power large-scale vector search over embeddings. In high dimensions distances concentrate and irrelevant features add noise, so scaling, feature selection, dimensionality reduction or learned metrics are essential. Duplicates between training and validation make k-NN look deceptively perfect.

glossary.short: A probabilistic classifier that applies Bayes' rule while assuming features are independent given the class.
glossary.definition: It multiplies the prior chance of each class by how likely each observed feature is under that class, then picks the highest score. The independence assumption is usually wrong, yet the method works surprisingly well for text such as spam filtering.
glossary.advanced: Naive Bayes picks argmax over classes of log P(c) + sum log P(x_i | c), computed in log space to avoid underflow. Variants model the likelihood differently: multinomial for word counts, Bernoulli for presence or absence, Gaussian for continuous features, complement NB for imbalanced text. Laplace or Lidstone smoothing (alpha) prevents unseen feature values from zeroing a class. Because correlated features double-count evidence, posterior probabilities are pushed toward 0 and 1 and are poorly calibrated, even when the ranking of classes is right. As a generative model it reaches its asymptotic error with fewer examples than logistic regression, its discriminative counterpart, which is why it shines as a fast baseline on small or sparse datasets.

glossary.short: An unsupervised algorithm that splits data into k groups by repeatedly assigning points to the nearest centroid and moving centroids to their group's mean.
glossary.definition: Picture k magnets dropped on a map of points: each point sticks to its nearest magnet, then each magnet moves to the middle of its points, and the process repeats until nothing changes. It works best for round, similar-size clusters.
glossary.advanced: Lloyd's algorithm monotonically decreases inertia (within-cluster sum of squared distances) and converges to a local optimum in O(n k d) per iteration; the global problem is NP-hard. k-means++ seeding picks new centroids with probability proportional to squared distance from existing ones, giving an O(log k) approximation in expectation, and multiple restarts (n_init) reduce bad local minima. The method assumes convex, isotropic clusters of similar size, equivalent to a hard-assignment Gaussian mixture with shared spherical covariance. Choose k with silhouette, gap statistic or downstream usefulness rather than the elbow alone. Mini-batch k-means scales to large data; DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, spectral clustering or Gaussian mixtures handle non-spherical or uneven clusters.

glossary.short: A linear method that rotates data onto new axes ordered by how much variance they capture, so you can keep only the top few.
glossary.definition: It finds the direction along which the data spreads the most, then the next most spread-out direction at a right angle, and so on. Keeping the first few components compresses many correlated features into a handful while losing little information.
glossary.advanced: PCA takes the SVD of centered data X = U S V^T: columns of V are the principal directions (eigenvectors of the covariance matrix) and s_i^2 / (n - 1) are the variances along them (eigenvalues). Projecting onto the top k components gives the best rank-k approximation in squared error (Eckart-Young). Results depend on scaling, so mixed-unit features are usually standardized first, which amounts to PCA on the correlation matrix. PCA is linear, sensitive to outliers and unsupervised, so high-variance directions may not be the predictive ones. Components have arbitrary sign. Variants include randomized, incremental, sparse, kernel and probabilistic PCA, and truncated SVD for sparse text. Fit it on training data only, inside a pipeline.

glossary.short: Linear regression with a penalty on the sum of absolute weights, which pushes many weights to exactly zero.
glossary.definition: It is like a budget for coefficients where every unit costs the same, so the model drops features that are not worth their price. Compared with ridge (L2), which shrinks all weights a little, lasso performs automatic feature selection; elastic net blends the two.
glossary.advanced: Lasso minimizes (1/(2n))||y - Xw||^2 + alpha ||w||_1 in scikit-learn's convention. The L1 ball has corners on the axes, so solutions are sparse; it corresponds to MAP estimation under a Laplace prior. It is solved by coordinate descent with soft-thresholding, and LassoCV traces the full regularization path to choose alpha. Limitations: with d > n it selects at most n features, among correlated features it picks one somewhat arbitrarily, and selected coefficients are biased toward zero. Elastic net (mixing L1 and L2 via l1_ratio) keeps correlated groups together, while relaxed lasso or refitting OLS on the selected features reduces bias. Always standardize features first, since the penalty is unit-dependent.

glossary.short: Rescaling numeric features to comparable ranges so no feature dominates just because of its units.
glossary.definition: Standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation; min-max scaling squeezes values into 0-1. Distance-based models, PCA, regularized linear models and neural networks need it, while decision trees do not.
glossary.advanced: StandardScaler maps x to (x - mean) / std, MinMaxScaler to (x - min) / (max - min), RobustScaler uses the median and interquartile range to resist outliers, and MaxAbsScaler preserves sparsity. None of them changes the shape of a distribution; skewed data may need log, Box-Cox or Yeo-Johnson transforms. Scaling improves gradient-descent conditioning, makes L1/L2 penalties treat features fairly and stops large-unit features from dominating distances and PCA. Tree models are invariant to monotonic transforms and need none. The statistics must be learned on training data only and reused at validation, test and serving time; fitting on the full dataset is a classic leakage bug, best prevented by placing the scaler inside a pipeline.

glossary.short: A plan for how the learning rate changes over training, usually a warmup followed by a decay.
glossary.definition: Instead of one fixed step size, training ramps the learning rate up for a short warmup, then lowers it, often along a cosine curve. Think of driving: ease onto the road, cruise, then slow down to park precisely. The decay lets the model settle into a good minimum.
glossary.advanced: Warmup (a linear ramp over the first few hundred to few thousand steps) protects the randomly initialized network while Adam's second-moment estimates are still noisy. Decay then follows cosine, linear-to-zero, step decay, or warmup-stable-decay (WSD), which holds the peak and anneals over the last 10-20% of steps. Cosine is tied to the planned run length T, so stopping early leaves the model under-annealed; WSD lets you branch a decay from any checkpoint, which helps scaling-law sweeps and continued pretraining. The peak learning rate is the most important hyperparameter; muP helps transfer it across model widths.

glossary.short: Gradients that shrink toward zero (or blow up) as they pass back through many layers or time steps.
glossary.definition: Backpropagation multiplies one factor per layer, so factors below 1 make early layers learn almost nothing and factors above 1 make training blow up. It is like a message whispered down a very long line. Good initialization, normalization, residual connections, gating and clipping are the standard fixes.
glossary.advanced: The gradient at an early layer is a product of per-layer Jacobians, so its size scales roughly with the product of their singular values. Sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25, so ten sigmoid layers can shrink a gradient by about 1e-6; in RNNs the same recurrent matrix repeats at every step, which makes both vanishing and exploding worse. Diagnose with per-layer gradient-norm logging. Remedies: variance-preserving initialization (Xavier, He), non-saturating activations, normalization layers, residual connections (the identity term in I + dF/dx), gating in LSTMs and GRUs, and gradient clipping for the exploding case.

glossary.short: A layer that standardizes each feature using the mean and variance of the current mini-batch.
glossary.definition: During training it rescales every feature to mean 0 and variance 1 across the batch, then applies a learned scale and shift; at inference it uses running averages instead. It speeds up and stabilizes training, especially in CNNs, but behaves poorly with very small batches.
glossary.advanced: BatchNorm computes y = gamma * (x - mu_B) / sqrt(var_B + eps) + beta per channel; for conv features the statistics run over batch, height and width. It keeps running averages for inference, so model.train() and model.eval() really behave differently. Small batches give noisy statistics, and multi-GPU training may need SyncBatchNorm. Its original 'internal covariate shift' motivation is disputed; later evidence suggests it smooths the loss landscape, allowing larger learning rates. A conv bias before BatchNorm is redundant. When fine-tuning with small batches, freeze its statistics or switch to GroupNorm.

glossary.short: A layer that standardizes each example's features on their own, independent of the batch.
glossary.definition: LayerNorm takes one token's feature vector, subtracts its mean and divides by its standard deviation, then applies a learned gain and bias. RMSNorm is a cheaper variant that skips the mean and just divides by the root mean square. Because it never looks at other examples, it suits transformers and LLMs.
glossary.advanced: LayerNorm normalizes over the feature dimension of each token, so a (B, T, D) tensor gets B*T separate statistics over D values, and training and inference behave identically. It never mixes information across examples or time steps, which suits autoregressive models. RMSNorm (2019) drops mean-centering and the bias, computing x / sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) * g; it is cheaper and standard in Llama-family and most current LLMs. Pre-norm placement (normalize before each sublayer) trains deep stacks more reliably than post-norm. QK-norm applies the same idea to queries and keys to stop attention logits from growing.

glossary.short: A shortcut that adds a block's input to its output, y = x + F(x).
glossary.definition: Each block learns only a correction on top of what it receives, and the shortcut gives gradients a direct path backward. It is like an express lane that bypasses every stop. Residual connections made 100+ layer networks trainable and are in every transformer block.
glossary.advanced: Introduced in ResNet (He et al., 2015) to fix the degradation problem, where deeper plain networks had higher training error than shallower ones. The Jacobian of x + F(x) is I + dF/dx, so gradients always have an identity path. Shape changes use 1x1 projection shortcuts. Because each block adds to the stream, variance grows with depth; remedies include zero-initializing the last layer of each branch, scaling branch outputs by about 1/sqrt(2N), and DeepNorm. Stochastic depth drops whole residual blocks at random during training. In transformers, residual connections form the residual stream that interpretability work studies.

glossary.short: A regularizer that randomly zeroes a fraction of units during training.
glossary.definition: Each training step, every unit is switched off with probability p and the rest are scaled up, so the network cannot rely on any single path. Like a team that practices with random players missing, it learns redundant skills. Dropout is turned off at inference.
glossary.advanced: Inverted dropout multiplies surviving activations by 1/(1 - p) at training time so inference needs no rescaling. Typical rates: 0.5 in old fully connected layers, about 0.1 in transformers, and often 0 in single-epoch LLM pretraining, where overfitting is minimal. It can be read as training an exponential ensemble of thinned networks that share weights. Recurrent connections need the same mask at every step (variational dropout). Monte Carlo dropout, which keeps dropout on at test time and averages several passes, gives a rough uncertainty estimate. Dropout before BatchNorm can cause a train/test variance mismatch.

glossary.short: A neural network that slides small learned filters over its input to detect local patterns.
glossary.definition: The same small kernel is reused at every position (weight sharing), producing feature maps; stacked layers build from edges to textures to objects. This built-in sense of locality makes CNNs efficient for images, audio and other grid data.
glossary.advanced: A conv layer's weight has shape (C_out, C_in, k, k), and the output size per dimension is floor((n + 2p - k)/s) + 1. Weight sharing and local connectivity give translation equivariance and parameter counts that do not depend on image size. Receptive fields grow with depth and stride. Key lineage: LeNet-5 (1998), AlexNet (2012), VGG (2014), Inception, ResNet (2015), MobileNet, EfficientNet, and ConvNeXt (2022), which showed modernized CNNs can match vision transformers. CNNs remain strong for edge devices and dense high-resolution prediction, and diffusion U-Nets are built from conv blocks.

glossary.short: A network that reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state as memory.
glossary.definition: At each step the same cell combines the new input with its previous hidden state. Plain RNNs struggle with long-range dependencies because gradients vanish; LSTM and GRU cells add gates that control what to keep, write and forget. Transformers replaced them for most language tasks.
glossary.advanced: A vanilla RNN updates h_t = tanh(W_h h_(t-1) + W_x x_t + b) and trains with backpropagation through time, which stores every step and suffers vanishing gradients. The LSTM adds a cell state updated additively, c_t = f*c_(t-1) + i*c~_t, so the gradient along it scales by the forget gate f; the GRU merges cell and hidden state with update and reset gates and about 25% fewer parameters. RNNs have constant per-step inference cost but cannot train in parallel over time. Modern state-space models such as Mamba revive recurrence with parallel-scan training.

glossary.short: A score from -1 to 1 measuring how closely two vectors point in the same direction.
glossary.definition: It is the dot product divided by the product of the vectors' lengths, so it ignores size and looks only at direction. Two embeddings with cosine near 1 have similar meaning. For unit-length vectors it equals the plain dot product.
glossary.advanced: cos(a, b) = a.b / (|a| |b|). For unit-normalized vectors it equals the dot product, and squared Euclidean distance equals 2 - 2*cos, so all three produce the same ranking; systems normalize once and use fast inner-product search. Absolute values are model-specific: many embedders are anisotropic, so unrelated texts can score 0.6-0.8 and thresholds must be calibrated per model. High cosine means similar context and topic, not agreement or relevance: opposite-sentiment sentences often score high. Without normalization, dot products favor long vectors, such as popular items in recommenders.

glossary.short: An autoencoder whose encoder outputs a probability distribution, so new data can be sampled from its latent space.
glossary.definition: The encoder predicts a mean and spread for a latent code, a sample is drawn with the reparameterization trick, and the decoder rebuilds the input. A KL penalty keeps the latent space smooth and close to a standard normal, so decoding random codes gives plausible new examples.
glossary.advanced: A VAE maximizes the evidence lower bound (ELBO), E_q[log p(x|z)] - KL(q(z|x) || p(z)), with a Gaussian encoder q, a standard-normal prior and the reparameterization z = mu + sigma*eps so gradients reach the encoder. The KL term has a closed form for Gaussians. Gaussian decoders produce blurry samples because they average over plausible outputs; strong decoders can cause posterior collapse, where z is ignored. Variants include beta-VAE for disentanglement and VQ-VAE with discrete codebooks. Today VAEs mainly serve as compressors: latent diffusion runs in a VAE's latent space.

glossary.short: A generator and a discriminator trained against each other: one forges samples, the other spots fakes.
glossary.definition: The generator turns random noise into samples and improves by fooling the discriminator, which learns to tell real from fake. Like a counterfeiter and a detective pushing each other to improve, it produces sharp results, but training is unstable and can suffer mode collapse.
glossary.advanced: GANs solve min over G, max over D of E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 - D(G(z)))]; in practice the generator uses the non-saturating loss, maximizing log D(G(z)). With an optimal discriminator the objective relates to the Jensen-Shannon divergence. Training is a two-player game that can oscillate; stabilizers include Wasserstein losses with gradient penalty, spectral normalization and two-timescale learning rates. Mode collapse means covering only a few modes of the data. StyleGAN set the photorealism bar in 2019; today adversarial losses mainly sharpen image tokenizers, super-resolution and few-step diffusion distillation.

glossary.short: A generative model that learns to reverse a gradual noising process, turning random noise into data.
glossary.definition: Training adds noise to real examples step by step and teaches a network to predict that noise. Generation starts from pure noise and removes it a little at a time, often guided by a text prompt. It is like a sculptor revealing a statue from a block of static.
glossary.advanced: DDPM-style training samples a noise level t, forms x_t = sqrt(abar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - abar_t) eps in closed form, and regresses the noise with an MSE loss; this is equivalent to learning the score (the gradient of log density) at each noise level. Sampling integrates the reverse process with solvers such as DDIM or DPM-Solver in 20-50 steps, or 1-4 after distillation or with consistency models. Classifier-free guidance trades diversity for prompt adherence. Latent diffusion works in a VAE latent space; flow matching and diffusion transformers (DiT) underpin many current image and video models.

glossary.short: The average of squared differences between predictions and true values.
glossary.definition: Square each miss, then average. Squaring makes one big miss count far more than several small ones, so the best constant prediction is the mean. RMSE, its square root, puts the number back in the target's units.
glossary.advanced: MSE is the negative log-likelihood of a Gaussian noise model with fixed variance, which is why least squares is the maximum-likelihood fit under that assumption and why its optimal prediction is the conditional mean. It decomposes into squared bias plus error variance. Its gradient, proportional to the residual, lets a few large errors dominate training, and it is scale-dependent, so values are only comparable on the same target. RMSE restores units and always satisfies MAE <= RMSE <= sqrt(n) x MAE. For heteroscedastic data, a Gaussian NLL that also predicts variance is the principled upgrade.

glossary.short: The average size of the misses, ignoring their sign.
glossary.definition: Take the absolute value of each error and average them, giving the typical miss in the target's units. Every unit of error counts the same, so outliers pull less than with squared error. The best constant prediction under MAE is the median.
glossary.advanced: MAE corresponds to Laplace noise and is minimized by the conditional median, making it robust to outliers in the target but not to high-leverage points in the features. Its gradient is the sign of the residual, constant in size, so optimization near the optimum oscillates without learning-rate decay, and the loss has a kink at zero. Linear MAE regression can be solved exactly as a linear program. When the target distribution is skewed, a model trained on MAE predicts the median, which will look biased if judged by mean-based metrics such as MSE or aggregated totals.

glossary.short: The share of the target's variance a regression model explains, compared with predicting the mean.
glossary.definition: R-squared is 1 minus the model's squared error divided by the squared error of always predicting the average. 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than the average, and on test data it can go negative. Adjusted R-squared penalizes adding features that do not help.
glossary.advanced: R-squared = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot compares a model with the constant mean predictor. For OLS with an intercept on training data it lies in [0, 1] and equals the squared correlation between predictions and targets; on held-out data it can be negative. It depends on the spread of the target in the evaluation set, so the same model scores higher on a more varied population, which makes cross-dataset comparisons misleading. Training R-squared never decreases when features are added, which adjusted R-squared partially corrects. For model selection, cross-validated error is more reliable.

glossary.short: A ranking metric that rewards placing the most relevant items at the top of a list.
glossary.definition: Each result earns points for its relevance, discounted the lower it appears, and the total is divided by the score of the ideal ordering so it lands between 0 and 1. It handles graded labels like 'perfect' versus 'partly relevant'. It is like grading a shelf where the best books belong at eye level.
glossary.advanced: DCG@k sums gains discounted by log2(rank + 1); the gain is either the relevance grade or 2^grade - 1, a choice that must be reported because scores differ. Dividing by the ideal DCG normalizes each query to [0, 1] so averages are meaningful. Computing the ideal from all known relevant items, not only retrieved ones, is stricter and standard. NDCG is the default offline metric for web search and recommendation, and LambdaMART optimizes it via pairwise gradients weighted by NDCG change. Its logarithmic discount is a convention; ERR and rank-biased precision use explicit user-patience models instead.

glossary.short: The average of 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant result, across queries.
glossary.definition: If the first good answer is at rank 1 the query scores 1, at rank 2 it scores 0.5, at rank 10 it scores 0.1. Averaging over queries shows how quickly users find something useful. It ignores everything after the first hit.
glossary.advanced: Reciprocal rank is 1/r for the first relevant item at rank r, or 0 if none appears within the cutoff. MRR suits tasks with one correct answer, such as question answering, code search or entity lookup, and is dominated by the first few positions. It ignores additional relevant results, so a system that finds one good item quickly scores the same as one that also finds five more. When each query has exactly one relevant item, MRR and MAP coincide. Significance testing should be done per query with a paired test, because MRR distributions are highly skewed.

glossary.short: The weighted average gap between a model's stated confidence and its actual accuracy.
glossary.definition: Group predictions into confidence bins, compare average confidence with the fraction correct in each bin, and average the gaps weighted by bin size. 0 means confidence matches reality. Its value depends on how you bin, so always report the bins.
glossary.advanced: ECE bins predictions by confidence and averages |accuracy - confidence| weighted by bin size; maximum calibration error reports the worst bin. It is biased upward on small samples, sensitive to bin count and scheme (equal-width versus equal-mass), and not a proper scoring rule: predicting the base rate achieves ECE near zero while being useless. Report it alongside log loss or Brier score and a reliability diagram with bin counts. For multiclass models, distinguish top-label ECE from classwise ECE. Temperature scaling on a held-out set is the standard first remedy for high ECE in neural networks.

glossary.short: The mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and actual 0/1 outcomes.
glossary.definition: Predict a probability, then score (p - outcome)^2 and average; lower is better and 0 is perfect. Always saying 50% scores 0.25. Because it is a proper scoring rule, the best strategy is to report your honest probability.
glossary.advanced: The Brier score is the mean squared error between predicted probabilities and binary outcomes. It is strictly proper, so honest probabilities minimize it in expectation. The Murphy decomposition splits it into reliability (calibration error), resolution (how informative predictions are) and uncertainty (base-rate variance). Unlike log loss it is bounded, so a single confident mistake costs at most 1, making it more tolerant of label noise. The Brier skill score compares it with the base-rate forecast, whose score is p(1 - p). Multiclass versions sum squared errors over the full probability vector.

glossary.short: The probability that an experiment detects an effect that really exists.
glossary.definition: Power grows with sample size and effect size and shrinks with noise. Experiments usually aim for 80% power at a chosen minimum detectable effect, which sets how many samples you need. A low-power test misses real effects and exaggerates the ones it does find.
glossary.advanced: Power is 1 - beta, the probability of rejecting the null when a specified effect exists.
