It depends on alpha, sample size, metric variance and effect size; for proportions with alpha 0.05 and 80% power, n per arm is about 16 p(1 - p) / MDE^2, so halving the detectable effect quadruples the sample. Variance reduction such as CUPED raises power without more traffic. Underpowered studies are doubly harmful: they miss real effects, and the significant results they produce overstate effect sizes (the winner's curse). Post-hoc power computed from the observed effect adds no information beyond the p-value.

glossary.short: A regression loss that is squared for small errors and linear for large ones.
glossary.definition: Inside a threshold delta it behaves like squared error, giving smooth gradients; beyond delta it grows only linearly, so outliers cannot dominate training. It is a compromise between MSE and MAE. Delta is measured in the target's units.
glossary.advanced: Huber loss is quadratic for |e| <= delta and linear beyond, with matching value and slope at the joint, so its gradient is continuous and capped at delta in magnitude. In robust statistics it is an M-estimator; delta of about 1.345 noise standard deviations keeps 95% efficiency under Gaussian noise. Smooth L1, used for bounding-box regression, is Huber divided by delta. As delta grows the loss approaches half the MSE, and as it shrinks it approaches a scaled MAE. Pseudo-Huber and log-cosh are smooth everywhere. Delta is in target units, so retune it after rescaling targets.

glossary.short: A cross-entropy variant that down-weights easy, already well-classified examples.
glossary.definition: It multiplies cross-entropy by (1 - p_true)^gamma, so confident correct predictions contribute almost nothing and hard examples drive learning. It was built for object detection, where easy background boxes vastly outnumber objects. Its outputs are not calibrated probabilities.
glossary.advanced: Introduced with the RetinaNet detector, focal loss is -alpha (1 - p_t)^gamma log p_t. With gamma = 2, an example at p_t = 0.9 keeps 1% of its cross-entropy, while hard examples keep most of theirs, so the flood of easy negatives in dense detection stops dominating the gradient. The paper also initializes the final bias to a low prior probability of about 0.01 for stability. Because it changes the loss minimizer, predicted probabilities are miscalibrated and should be recalibrated before use as probabilities. For tabular imbalance, class weights plus threshold tuning are often equally effective.

glossary.short: A contrastive loss that trains a model to pick the true match out of many negatives.
glossary.definition: Similarity scores between an anchor and one positive plus many negatives are divided by a temperature and passed through a softmax, then scored with cross-entropy. Other items in the batch serve as free negatives. It is a multiple-choice quiz where the right answer is the matching pair.
glossary.advanced: InfoNCE is cross-entropy over temperature-scaled similarities in which the positive must be identified among N candidates; minimizing it maximizes a lower bound on mutual information that cannot exceed log N. NT-Xent, from SimCLR, is the cosine-similarity version over 2N augmented views. Lower temperature concentrates gradients on hard negatives. Performance scales with the number of negatives, so large batches, cross-device gathering or momentum queues (MoCo) are common. CLIP applies it symmetrically over an image-text similarity matrix. False negatives from duplicates and semantic matches are the main failure mode; SigLIP swaps the softmax for per-pair sigmoids.

glossary.short: A tractable lower bound on a model's log-likelihood, maximized to train variational autoencoders.
glossary.definition: It equals a reconstruction term minus the KL divergence between the encoder's latent distribution and a simple prior. Raising it improves the data likelihood while keeping latent codes well organized. Diffusion model losses can also be derived from it.
glossary.advanced: For a latent-variable model, log p(x) = ELBO + KL(q(z|x) || p(z|x)), so maximizing the ELBO tightens the bound and improves the approximate posterior at once. In a VAE the ELBO is a reconstruction log-likelihood minus KL(q(z|x) || p(z)), estimated with reparameterized samples z = mu + sigma * eps; the Gaussian KL has a closed form. Weighting the KL term gives beta-VAE. Posterior collapse occurs when the KL term goes to zero and the decoder ignores z. The simple noise-prediction loss of diffusion models is a reweighted form of a diffusion ELBO.

glossary.short: A branching workflow where everyone merges small changes into main at least daily.
glossary.definition: Instead of long-lived feature branches, developers integrate tiny changes into the shared trunk (main) every day, hiding unfinished work behind feature flags. Like merging into traffic one car at a time instead of waiting for a whole convoy. It keeps conflicts small and main always releasable.
glossary.advanced: Trunk-based development (TBD) means developers integrate into one shared branch at least daily, either by committing directly or through very short-lived branches and pull requests that merge within hours. Its prerequisites are fast, reliable CI, a strong automated test suite, fast reviews and feature flags that decouple deployment from release. The DORA research associates it with higher delivery performance, because integration cost grows with branch age and divergence. Release branches may still be cut for hotfixes, but fixes land on trunk first and are cherry-picked out. Contrast it with GitFlow, whose long-lived develop and release branches suit versioned products with several supported versions but slow down continuous deployment.

glossary.short: Git's local journal of every position HEAD and your branches have pointed to.
glossary.definition: Every commit, checkout, reset or rebase writes an entry, so you can find commits that no branch points to anymore. It is your personal undo history and is never pushed. It cannot recover changes that were never committed.
glossary.advanced: The reflog is a per-repository, per-ref log stored under .git/logs that records each old and new SHA whenever HEAD or a branch moves, through commit, reset, rebase, checkout, merge or amend. Syntax such as HEAD@{3} or main@{yesterday} addresses entries. Reachable entries expire after 90 days by default and unreachable ones after 30 (gc.reflogExpire and gc.reflogExpireUnreachable); after that git gc can prune the objects. It is purely local: clones and remotes have their own. ORIG_HEAD offers a one-step undo after reset, merge or rebase, and git fsck --lost-found finds dangling commits that no reflog entry references.

glossary.short: An isolated process that runs an app with its own filesystem while sharing the host's kernel.
glossary.definition: A container packages an app with its libraries so it behaves the same on any machine. Unlike a virtual machine, it does not boot a whole operating system, so it starts in about a second and uses far less memory. Think of an apartment in a shared building rather than a separate house.
glossary.advanced: Technically, a container is a process tree started with its own Linux namespaces (PID, mount, network, UTS, IPC, user), constrained by cgroups for CPU, memory and I/O, and hardened with seccomp, dropped capabilities and LSMs such as AppArmor or SELinux. Its root filesystem is an overlay of read-only image layers plus a writable layer. The OCI runtime spec standardizes how runtimes like runc create it, and containerd or CRI-O manage its lifecycle. Because the kernel is shared, isolation is weaker than with hardware virtualization; sandboxes such as gVisor, Kata Containers or Firecracker microVMs trade a little overhead for stronger multi-tenant boundaries.

glossary.short: A read-only, layered template from which containers are started.
glossary.definition: An image bundles an app, its dependencies and its start command into stacked filesystem layers plus a config. Running it creates a container, much like instantiating an object from a class. Images are named with tags and stored in registries.
glossary.advanced: An OCI image consists of a manifest that references a JSON config (entrypoint, env, user, working directory, history) and an ordered list of compressed tar layers, each identified by a SHA-256 digest. Content addressing enables deduplication: identical base layers are stored and pulled once. An image index groups per-platform manifests for multi-architecture images. Tags are mutable names; digests are immutable, so production deploys should pin digests. Deleting a file in a later layer does not remove it from earlier ones, which is how secrets leak. Supply-chain metadata such as signatures (cosign), SBOMs and provenance attestations can be attached alongside an image in the registry.

glossary.short: A text recipe of instructions (FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD) for building a container image.
glossary.definition: Each instruction runs in order to produce the image, and filesystem-changing steps become cached layers. Ordering matters: put rarely changing steps such as dependency installs before frequently changing source code. It makes image builds reproducible and reviewable.
glossary.advanced: A Dockerfile is processed by BuildKit, which builds a dependency graph of instructions, runs independent stages in parallel and caches each step by the previous layer plus instruction text, or file checksums for COPY and ADD. Only RUN, COPY and ADD add filesystem layers; ENV, LABEL, EXPOSE and CMD change metadata. Prefer exec-form CMD and ENTRYPOINT so the app is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM, use ARG for build-time values and ENV for runtime ones, and add a non-root USER. BuildKit extensions such as RUN --mount=type=cache and --mount=type=secret speed builds and keep credentials out of layers. A .dockerignore keeps the build context small and the cache stable.

glossary.short: A Dockerfile with several FROM stages where only the final, slim stage ships.
glossary.definition: Early stages hold compilers and build tools; the final stage copies just the finished artifacts with COPY --from. Like a workshop that ships only the finished chair, not the saws. Images become much smaller and contain fewer vulnerable packages.
glossary.advanced: Each FROM in a Dockerfile begins a stage that can be named with AS. Only the final stage, or the one selected with --target, becomes the output image, and COPY --from=<stage> copies chosen artifacts from earlier stages or even from other images. BuildKit skips stages the target does not depend on. Typical results: a Go service shrinks from roughly 900 MB to 10-20 MB on scratch or distroless static, though scratch lacks CA certificates, time zone data and a shell. Targets also enable one Dockerfile with test, dev and prod stages. Smaller images mean faster pulls, quicker autoscaling and fewer packages for vulnerability scanners to flag.

glossary.short: A tool that defines and runs a multi-container app from one YAML file.
glossary.definition: compose.yaml lists services, networks, volumes and secrets, and docker compose up starts the whole stack with one command. Services find each other by name on a shared network. It is ideal for local development and single hosts, not for clusters.
glossary.advanced: Compose implements the Compose Specification; v2 ships as a Docker CLI plugin (docker compose), and the top-level version key is obsolete. It names resources with a project prefix, creates a default network with DNS-based service discovery, and recreates only services whose configuration changed. Key features: override files merged in order, profiles for optional services, variable interpolation from .env with ${VAR:-default}, secrets mounted under /run/secrets, depends_on conditions (service_healthy, service_completed_successfully) and Compose Watch for live sync. docker compose config prints the merged result. It lacks multi-node scheduling and rolling updates, so production clusters usually move to Kubernetes.

glossary.short: An open-source system that schedules, scales and heals containers across a cluster of machines.
glossary.definition: You declare the desired state in YAML, such as three replicas of an image, and Kubernetes controllers keep reality matching it: placing containers on nodes, replacing failures and rolling out updates. Think of a tireless operations team that follows your written instructions around the clock.
glossary.advanced: Kubernetes is a declarative control system: the API server validates and stores objects in etcd (a Raft-replicated key-value store), and controllers run level-triggered reconcile loops that move actual state toward each object's spec and report status. The scheduler binds Pods to nodes; kubelets run them through the CRI; CNI plugins provide a flat Pod network; kube-proxy or eBPF implements Services. It is extensible through CustomResourceDefinitions, admission webhooks and operators. Minor releases arrive about every four months with roughly a year of support. Managed offerings such as EKS, GKE and AKS run the control plane, but teams still own upgrades, security and capacity.

glossary.short: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes: one or more containers sharing an IP address and volumes.
glossary.definition: Containers in a Pod are always scheduled together on one node and talk over localhost. Pods are disposable: when one dies, a controller creates a new Pod with a new name and IP rather than repairing the old one. You usually create them through a Deployment.
glossary.advanced: A Pod's containers share a network namespace (one IP, a shared port space, localhost), IPC, and optionally volumes and a process namespace. The pause container holds the namespaces. Init containers run to completion first; native sidecars are init containers with restartPolicy: Always and run for the Pod's life. Pods are immutable in most fields and never rescheduled: a controller replaces them. Key spec fields include resources, probes, securityContext, serviceAccountName, affinity, tolerations and terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30 seconds). Phases are Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed and Unknown, while container states such as CrashLoopBackOff appear in the status.

glossary.short: A Kubernetes object that keeps N replicas of a Pod running and rolls out new versions gradually.
glossary.definition: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which in turn keep the requested number of identical Pods alive. Changing the image creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts Pods over step by step, and the old one is kept so you can roll back. It is the standard way to run stateless apps.
glossary.advanced: A Deployment owns ReplicaSets through ownerReferences, and each ReplicaSet owns Pods matched by an immutable label selector. Every Pod template change creates a new ReplicaSet identified by a pod-template-hash, and the controller scales new up and old down according to the strategy: RollingUpdate with maxSurge and maxUnavailable (both 25% by default) or Recreate. Old ReplicaSets are kept up to revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) for kubectl rollout undo. progressDeadlineSeconds flags stuck rollouts. Deployments suit stateless apps; StatefulSets add stable identities and per-Pod volumes, DaemonSets run one Pod per node, and Jobs run to completion.

glossary.short: A stable name and virtual IP that load-balances traffic to a changing set of Pods.
glossary.definition: Pods come and go with new IPs, so a Service selects them by label and forwards traffic to the ready ones. ClusterIP is internal, NodePort opens a port on every node, and LoadBalancer requests a cloud load balancer. Like a company phone number that rings whoever is on shift.
glossary.advanced: A Service defines a label selector and ports. The EndpointSlice controller tracks the IPs of ready matching Pods, and kube-proxy (iptables, IPVS or nftables) or an eBPF dataplane load-balances the virtual ClusterIP to them. CoreDNS publishes name.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Types build on each other: ClusterIP, then NodePort (30000-32767), then LoadBalancer through the cloud controller. Headless Services (clusterIP: None) return Pod IPs directly for StatefulSets, and ExternalName is a DNS CNAME. externalTrafficPolicy: Local preserves client source IPs. HTTP routing by host and path is layered on top with Ingress or the Gateway API rather than one LoadBalancer per app.

glossary.short: A periodic check that tells the platform whether a container is alive and ready for traffic.
glossary.definition: In Kubernetes, a failing readiness probe removes the Pod from Service traffic, while a failing liveness probe restarts the container; a startup probe gives slow apps time to boot. Docker Compose uses a healthcheck to gate depends_on. Good probes make rollouts and recovery automatic.
glossary.advanced: Kubernetes supports httpGet, tcpSocket, exec and grpc probes tuned by initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds (default 10), timeoutSeconds (1), failureThreshold (3) and successThreshold. A startup probe blocks the other two until it passes. Readiness gates EndpointSlice membership and rollout progress; liveness triggers a container restart by the kubelet. Best practice: readiness may check critical dependencies, but liveness should only detect a wedged process, because a dependency check in liveness turns a database blip into a cluster-wide restart storm. During shutdown, failing readiness and a short preStop delay let load balancers drain. Docker HEALTHCHECK and Compose healthcheck are the single-host equivalents.

glossary.short: A Kubernetes controller that adds or removes Pod replicas based on metrics such as CPU.
glossary.definition: It compares a metric with a target and sets replicas = ceil(current x metric / target), within min and max bounds. For example, 3 Pods at 140% of a 70% CPU target become 6. It relies on resource requests and a metrics source such as metrics-server.
glossary.advanced: The HPA controller (autoscaling/v2) evaluates metrics every 15 seconds and computes desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentValue / targetValue), ignoring changes within a 10% tolerance and applying a 5-minute scale-down stabilization window by default. Resource utilization is relative to requests, so Pods without requests cannot be scaled on percentage. Metric sources include Resource (metrics-server), Pods and Object custom metrics through an adapter, and External metrics such as queue depth; KEDA extends this to event-driven scaling and scale to zero. New Pods stay Pending if nodes are full, so pair it with Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter, and avoid driving HPA and VPA from the same metric.

glossary.short: Five object-oriented design principles that keep code easy to change.
glossary.definition: SOLID stands for single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation and dependency inversion. Together they aim to make changes small and local. Think of them as building codes for software: guides that prevent collapse, not laws to follow blindly.
glossary.advanced: SOLID bundles five principles popularized by Robert C. Martin: single responsibility (one actor or reason to change per module), open/closed (extend behavior without editing stable code), Liskov substitution (subtypes honor base contracts), interface segregation (clients depend only on what they use) and dependency inversion (policy and detail both depend on abstractions owned by the policy side). They overlap: dependency inversion enables open/closed, and interface segregation is single responsibility for interfaces. They trade simplicity for flexibility, so apply them where change actually happens. In Python, protocols, first-class functions and modules often satisfy them with less ceremony than class hierarchies.

glossary.short: A subtype must work anywhere its base type is expected, without surprises.
glossary.definition: If code works with a base class, it must keep working when given any subclass. A subclass may not demand more, promise less or throw unexpected errors. A square that changes its height when you set its width breaks code written for rectangles.
glossary.advanced: Formalized by Liskov and Wing as behavioral subtyping: a subtype must not strengthen preconditions, weaken postconditions, break invariants, or allow state changes the base type forbids (the history rule). Type checkers verify signatures only, so behavioral violations pass static analysis. Typical breaks: overriding a method to raise NotImplementedError, returning None instead of a promised list, or narrowing accepted inputs. Fixes include immutable designs, inverting the hierarchy (read-only base, mutable subtype, as in collections.abc Sequence and MutableSequence) or replacing inheritance with composition and a shared protocol. LSP is what makes polymorphism, and therefore open/closed, safe.

glossary.short: Passing an object's collaborators in from outside instead of creating them inside.
glossary.definition: A class or function receives the things it depends on, such as a database, clock or HTTP client, as parameters. This makes it easy to swap a real dependency for a fake one in tests. It is like a lamp with a plug instead of wires soldered into the wall.
glossary.advanced: DI supplies collaborators from outside, usually via constructor parameters (preferred), method parameters or setters. Wiring happens once at the composition root, such as main() or an app factory. It enables deterministic tests by injecting fakes for clocks, randomness, networks and storage, without monkeypatching. DI is a technique; dependency inversion is the design principle it typically serves, and injecting concrete classes still couples you to details. Python rarely needs containers: default arguments and factories suffice, while FastAPI's Depends and pytest fixtures provide framework-level injection. Avoid the service locator, which looks dependencies up from a global registry and hides them again.

glossary.short: A named, reusable solution to a recurring software design problem.
glossary.definition: Design patterns describe proven ways to structure code, such as Factory Method, Decorator or Observer. The 1994 Gang of Four book cataloged 23 of them in creational, structural and behavioral families. The names give teams a shared vocabulary; the patterns are templates, not copy-paste code.
glossary.advanced: The term comes from Christopher Alexander's architecture work and was brought to software by the Gang of Four (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides) in 1994: 23 patterns, 5 creational, 7 structural, 11 behavioral. Each pattern has a name, problem, solution and consequences. Patterns are communication tools; the same code shape can be different patterns depending on intent, as with Adapter, Decorator and Proxy. In dynamic languages many patterns shrink to idioms: functions replace Strategy and Command classes, and generators replace Iterator. Overuse is a known failure mode; introduce a pattern when a real axis of change appears.

glossary.short: A pattern that ensures a class has exactly one instance with global access to it.
glossary.definition: A singleton restricts a class to one shared object, such as one configuration or logger. It is often called an anti-pattern because global access hides dependencies and lets tests leak state into each other. Creating one object and passing it where needed usually works better.
glossary.advanced: A singleton combines two concerns: a single instance (lifetime) and global access (visibility). The second causes the damage: hidden dependencies, order-dependent initialization and tests that contaminate each other. Hand-written lazy initialization can race under threads. Python alternatives: a module-level instance (modules are created once per interpreter), a cached factory with functools.cache that tests can reset with cache_clear(), or creating the object at the composition root and injecting it. DI containers express the same lifetime as a 'singleton scope' while keeping access explicit. Legitimate uses include process-wide pools and hardware handles.

glossary.short: A pattern where a method decides which concrete class to create.
glossary.definition: Instead of calling a specific constructor, code calls a creation method that subclasses or a registry can override. Callers get an object with the right interface without knowing its exact class. It is like ordering 'a coffee' and letting the barista pick the machine.
glossary.advanced: In the GoF form, a base class defines an overridable creation method used by its own logic, so subclasses choose the concrete product while the surrounding algorithm stays unchanged. In common usage, 'factory' also covers simple factory functions, alternative constructors (classmethods like datetime.fromisoformat) and registries keyed by name, often populated with decorators or __init_subclass__ for plugins. Distinguish it from Abstract Factory, which groups several creation methods so a family of products stays consistent. Pitfalls: factories for types that never vary, string keys that fail only at runtime, and products lacking a common interface.

glossary.short: A pattern that constructs a complex object step by step, then validates it.
glossary.definition: A builder collects optional parts through a series of calls and creates the final object in one build() step. It avoids constructors with long lists of arguments and catches invalid combinations early. In Python, keyword arguments or dataclasses often do the same job.
glossary.advanced: Builder separates step-by-step construction from the final representation, validating invariants once in build(). Fluent builders return self so calls chain. The GoF version includes a director that drives the steps, allowing one process to produce different representations. It suits immutable objects, many optional parameters and cross-field constraints. In Python, keyword-only arguments, dataclasses with __post_init__ checks and pydantic models usually replace explicit builders; query builders (SQLAlchemy's select().where()) and test data builders remain common. Watch for mutable builders reused across calls, and builders whose build() skips validation and lets half-configured objects escape.

glossary.short: A pattern that wraps an object to add behavior while keeping the same interface.
glossary.definition: A decorator holds another object, forwards calls to it and does extra work such as logging, caching or retrying. Because wrappers share the interface, they stack in any combination. Python's @decorator syntax applies the same idea to functions.
glossary.advanced: A GoF decorator implements the same interface as the wrapped component, forwards calls and adds responsibilities before or after. Wrappers compose, replacing a combinatorial explosion of subclasses with n small classes, but order changes semantics: caching outside retries differs from retries outside caching. Python's @ syntax is sugar for f = deco(f) and applies the concept to functions; functools.wraps preserves metadata. lru_cache and cached_property are built-in examples. A decorator must be transparent to callers, keeping return types and exceptions consistent, or it violates Liskov substitution. Deep stacks complicate stack traces and add call overhead.

glossary.short: A pattern that makes an algorithm swappable by passing it in as an object or function.
glossary.definition: The varying part of a computation, such as a pricing rule or sort key, is pulled out behind a common interface and passed in. Callers choose the behavior without if/elif chains. Python's sorted(key=...) is a built-in example.
glossary.advanced: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a shared interface and lets the client select one, typically by composition. It is the standard cure for type-based if/elif chains and an implementation of open/closed. In Python a strategy is usually any callable: functions, lambdas, functools.partial, or objects with __call__; classes help when strategies carry configuration or several methods. Strategy and State share structure but differ in who switches: the client picks a strategy, while states switch themselves. Strategy versus Template Method is composition versus inheritance for varying one step. Strategies make table-driven tests of business rules straightforward.

glossary.short: A pattern where subscribers are notified automatically when a subject changes.
glossary.definition: A subject keeps a list of observers and calls each one when an event happens. The subject does not need to know what the observers do. It is like a newsletter: subscribers sign up once and get every new issue.
glossary.advanced: Observer sets up one-to-many notification: the subject holds subscribers and calls them on change, in push style (data sent along) or pull style (observers query back). Publish-subscribe adds a broker so parties are fully decoupled and delivery can be asynchronous or cross-process. Pitfalls: lapsed listeners that leak memory (use weak references or explicit unsubscribe), one failing observer stopping the rest, reentrancy when callbacks mutate the subject, unspecified ordering, and cascades that obscure control flow. Iterate over a copy of the subscriber list. Reactive libraries such as ReactiveX generalize Observer into composable event streams.

glossary.short: A surface sign in code that often points to a deeper design problem.
glossary.definition: Long functions, duplicated code, long parameter lists and magic numbers are typical smells. A smell is not a bug; it is a hint that the design may be hard to change. Each common smell has matching refactoring moves.
glossary.advanced: Coined by Kent Beck and popularized in Fowler's Refactoring, a smell is a heuristic symptom, not a defect. The catalog includes long function, large class, duplicated code, long parameter list, feature envy, data clumps, primitive obsession, shotgun surgery, divergent change, speculative generality, message chains and magic numbers. Each maps to refactoring moves, such as Extract Function, Move Function, Introduce Parameter Object or Replace Conditional with Polymorphism. Tools detect some smells: linters (ruff, pylint) and complexity metrics (radon's cyclomatic complexity, cognitive complexity). Judge in context: a long but linear function can be clearer than ten fragments.

glossary.short: Changing the structure of code without changing what it does.
glossary.definition: Refactoring improves names, splits functions or removes duplication while keeping behavior identical. It is done in small steps, running tests after each one. Like tidying a workshop, it makes the next job faster without building anything new.
glossary.advanced: Fowler defines refactoring as a behavior-preserving change to internal structure, done in small, named, verifiable steps. The workflow: start green, make one move, run tests, commit; on red, revert rather than debug. Keep refactoring commits separate from feature commits so reviewers can verify no behavior changed. For untested legacy code, Feathers recommends finding seams and adding characterization tests first. Large migrations use the strangler fig pattern, branch by abstraction or parallel change (expand, migrate, contract). IDE automated refactorings (rename, extract, inline) are safer than manual edits, and mutation testing can check whether the test net is strong enough.

glossary.short: An automated sequence that builds, tests and releases every code change.
glossary.definition: Each push triggers stages such as build, test, scan, package and deploy, and any failing stage stops the line. Continuous integration means merging and testing small changes often; continuous delivery keeps every green build releasable; continuous deployment ships it automatically. Think of a factory conveyor with quality checks at every station.
glossary.advanced: A pipeline is usually defined as code next to the application (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkinsfile) and modeled as a directed graph of jobs. Design goals: fast feedback (cheap checks first, caching, parallelism, under about ten minutes for pull requests), hermetic and reproducible builds, a single immutable artifact promoted across environments, and least-privilege credentials via OIDC rather than stored keys. Merge queues test queued changes against the latest main. Health is measured with the DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore. Supply-chain hardening adds SBOMs, signed artifacts and SLSA provenance, plus pinning third-party actions to commit SHAs.

glossary.short: Releasing a new version to a small share of traffic first and expanding only if it stays healthy.
glossary.definition: A few percent of users get the new version while the rest stay on the stable one, and error rate and latency of both are compared. If the canary looks worse, traffic goes back to stable; if not, the share ramps up step by step. The name comes from canaries that warned miners of bad air.
glossary.advanced: A canary compares a new version against a concurrently running baseline on live traffic, typically ramping 1%, 5%, 25%, 50%, 100% with a bake time per step. Automated canary analysis evaluates metrics such as error rate, p99 latency and saturation with statistical tests and aborts on regression; tools include Argo Rollouts, Flagger and service-mesh traffic splitting. Pitfalls: too little traffic to detect a difference, comparing to historical data instead of a live baseline, and biased routing through sticky sessions. Unlike an A/B test, which measures product impact, a canary asks one question: is the new build safe? Database changes must stay backward compatible because both versions run together.

glossary.short: A runtime switch that turns a piece of functionality on or off without deploying new code.
glossary.definition: Code ships to production hidden behind a condition, and the flag decides who sees it: nobody, staff, 5% of users or everyone. This separates deploying code from releasing a feature and gives an instant kill switch. Old flags should be removed, or they pile up as untested code paths.
glossary.advanced: Flags fall into types with different lifetimes: release flags (days to weeks, removed after rollout), experiment flags for A/B tests, operational kill switches kept long term, and permission flags for entitlements. Evaluation happens in the application via an SDK that caches rules from a flag service, so flag checks must be fast and fail safe with a sensible default if the service is unreachable. Targeting can use user ID hashing for stable percentage rollouts. Risks: combinatorial explosion of untested states, stale flags as technical debt (track owners and expiry), and inconsistent behavior across services. OpenFeature is a vendor-neutral standard API for flag evaluation.

glossary.short: Any stand-in object that replaces a real dependency during a test.
glossary.definition: Like a stunt double in a film, it plays the role of the real component so the test runs fast and predictably. Stubs return canned answers, mocks verify expected calls, fakes are lightweight working versions, spies record calls and dummies just fill parameters.
glossary.advanced: Gerard Meszaros named five kinds: dummy, stub, spy, mock and fake. The crucial distinction is state verification (assert on results, possibly using stubs) versus behavior verification (assert on interactions, using mocks or spies). Over-mocking couples tests to implementation, so refactors break tests while behavior is unchanged. Guidelines: mock at architectural boundaries you own, wrap third-party APIs in adapters, prefer fakes for complex dependencies like repositories, and verify fakes against the real thing with contract or integration tests. In Python, unittest.mock with autospec=True enforces real signatures; mocking the wrong import path (where the name is looked up, not where it is defined) is a classic bug.

glossary.short: Writing a failing test first, then the minimal code to pass it, then cleaning up.
glossary.definition: Work happens in short loops: red (a new test fails), green (just enough code makes it pass) and refactor (improve the code while tests stay green). Writing the test first forces you to decide the expected behavior and interface before the implementation. The result is a growing safety net of regression tests.
glossary.advanced: Formalized by Kent Beck, TDD runs in very short cycles; techniques include 'fake it' (hardcode a return value), triangulation (add cases that force generalization) and keeping a test list of behaviors still to cover. Classicist TDD uses real collaborators; mockist (London school) TDD works outside-in with mocks to discover interfaces. Related practices: acceptance-test-driven development and BDD, which write executable specifications in domain language. Studies show mixed productivity effects and modest, inconsistent quality effects, though TDD reliably leaves a regression suite behind. TDD is strongest for well-specified logic and bug fixes (reproduce the bug as a failing test first) and weaker for exploratory prototypes, where tests often follow the spike.

glossary.short: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails on the same code.
glossary.definition: Typical causes are timing assumptions, shared state between tests, real network calls, clocks and unseeded randomness. Flaky tests are dangerous because teams learn to ignore red builds and rerun until green, which hides real bugs. Quarantine them quickly and fix the root cause.
glossary.advanced: Large studies of flaky tests find async waits, concurrency and test-order dependence are the leading causes, followed by resource leaks, network, time and randomness. Detection: rerun failures and record pass-on-retry as flaky, run tests in random order, and run suites repeatedly under stress or with parallelism. Management: quarantine to a non-blocking job with an owner and deadline, and track flake rate per test. Automatic retries keep pipelines green but can hide genuine race conditions in production code, so log every retry. Fixes include explicit condition waits, injected clocks, seeded randomness, per-test databases or transactions, dynamic ports and hermetic test environments.

glossary.short: An internal reliability target for a measured indicator of service health, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding.
glossary.definition: The indicator (SLI) is what you measure, like the share of requests answered in under 300 ms; the objective (SLO) is the target over a window, like 99.9% over 30 days. A service level agreement (SLA) is the looser contractual promise to customers, with penalties. SLOs tell teams when reliability is good enough.
glossary.advanced: A good SLI is a ratio of good to valid events measured close to the user, e.g. at the load balancer: successful requests under 300 ms divided by all valid requests. SLOs are set per critical user journey over a rolling window of 28 or 30 days, based on what users need and on historical performance, not on 100%. Each additional nine cuts allowed downtime tenfold: 99.9% allows 43.2 minutes per 30 days, 99.99% about 4.3 minutes. Serial dependencies multiply: two 99.9% dependencies cap you near 99.8%. SLAs sit below SLOs and carry remedies such as service credits. The OpenSLO specification lets teams define SLOs as code.

glossary.short: The amount of failure an SLO allows over its window: 100% minus the target.
glossary.definition: A 99.9% monthly SLO leaves 0.1% of requests, or about 43 minutes of full outage, as budget. While budget remains, teams can ship features and take risks; when it is spent, they slow releases and fix reliability. It turns the argument between speed and stability into a number both sides agree on.
glossary.advanced: Error budget equals (1 - SLO) times eligible events, so 99.9% over 10 million requests allows 10,000 failures. Burn rate measures consumption relative to the even pace that would exhaust it at window end; a burn rate of 14.4 spends 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour. The SRE workbook recommends multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts: page on fast burns confirmed by a short window, ticket on slow burns. An error budget policy, agreed beforehand by product and engineering, defines consequences on exhaustion, such as release freezes except for fixes and mandatory postmortems. Planned maintenance and dependency failures still count, because users feel them.

glossary.short: Following a single request across services as a tree of timed spans.
glossary.definition: Each service records a span for its work and passes a trace ID to the next service, usually in the traceparent header. A waterfall view then shows where the time went, like a parcel tracking history for one request. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for producing traces.
glossary.advanced: A trace is a directed tree of spans sharing a 128-bit trace ID; each span has a 64-bit span ID, parent ID, timing, attributes, events and status. W3C Trace Context standardizes propagation via the traceparent and tracestate headers, and baggage carries user-defined key-values. OpenTelemetry provides APIs, SDKs, auto-instrumentation, the OTLP protocol and the Collector for processing and export. Sampling strategy drives cost and usefulness: head sampling decides at the root (cheap, may miss rare errors), tail sampling decides after completion (keeps errors and slow traces, needs buffering). Async boundaries such as queues need explicit context injection, often using span links rather than parent-child relations.

glossary.short: Defining servers, networks and other infrastructure in versioned text files instead of manual setup.
glossary.definition: Tools like Terraform read declarative files, compare them with what exists and plan the changes needed to match. Changes go through Git and pull requests like application code, so environments are reproducible and reviewable. GitOps extends the idea with agents that continuously sync systems to what Git says.
glossary.advanced: Declarative IaC tools (Terraform, OpenTofu, CloudFormation, Bicep) keep a desired-state model and compute a plan as the diff between configuration, recorded state and reality; Pulumi and CDK generate the same kind of graph from general-purpose languages. Key concerns: remote state with locking, splitting state by blast radius, pinning provider and module versions, reviewing plans in pull requests, and applying only from CI with short-lived credentials. Drift detection runs plans on a schedule. Policy as code (Open Policy Agent, Sentinel) checks plans before apply. GitOps, with Argo CD or Flux, applies the same idea through continuous pull-based reconciliation, mostly for Kubernetes.

glossary.short: The split of security duties between a cloud provider and its customer.
glossary.definition: The provider secures the cloud itself: buildings, hardware and virtualization. The customer secures what they put in it: data, identities and permissions, network rules and, on virtual machines, the operating system. The more managed the service, the more the provider handles, like renting a furnished flat versus an empty one.
glossary.advanced: All major providers publish a shared responsibility model; the boundary shifts with the service model. For IaaS the customer handles guest OS patching, network configuration, IAM, encryption choices and data; for PaaS and managed databases the provider patches the platform; for SaaS the customer still owns identities, access configuration and data. Industry reports consistently attribute most cloud breaches to customer-side misconfiguration and credential compromise rather than provider failures. Compliance inheritance follows the same split: provider attestations such as SOC 2 cover only provider layers. Tools for the customer side include audit logging, posture management scanners, organization guardrails and customer-managed encryption keys.

glossary.short: Giving every user and program only the permissions it needs, and nothing more.
glossary.definition: A job that only reads one storage bucket gets read access to that bucket, not admin rights. If its credentials leak, the damage stays small. In the cloud this is done with IAM (identity and access management) roles, narrow policies and short-lived credentials.
glossary.advanced: Least privilege applies to humans, services and CI systems alike. In AWS IAM, requests are denied by default, explicit Allows grant access, and explicit Denies always win; organization policies and permission boundaries cap the maximum. Practical techniques: start from minimal policies and expand using access logs or unused-permission analyzers, scope resources by ARN and conditions (tags, source network, MFA), avoid wildcards, use roles and workload identity federation instead of long-lived keys, and grant elevated access just in time with expiry. Watch for privilege escalation paths, such as permission to pass a powerful role to a new resource or to edit one's own policies.

glossary.short: The request/response protocol browsers and APIs use to exchange web resources.
glossary.definition: A client sends a request with a method, path and headers; the server answers with a status code, headers and a body. It is stateless, like ordering at a counter where each order stands alone. HTTPS is the same protocol carried inside TLS encryption.
glossary.advanced: HTTP semantics (RFC 9110) are shared by every version: methods with defined safety and idempotency, status code classes, header fields, content negotiation and conditional requests via ETag and If-None-Match. The wire format differs: HTTP/1.1 is text over TCP, HTTP/2 multiplexes binary frames over one TCP connection with HPACK header compression, and HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP, removing TCP head-of-line blocking. Statelessness enables horizontal scaling, with state moved into cookies, tokens or shared stores. Caching (RFC 9111) via Cache-Control, Vary and validators is a large part of web performance. Common bugs include GET with side effects, 200 responses for errors, and request smuggling from inconsistent Content-Length handling between proxies.

glossary.short: The opening exchange in which client and server agree on encryption keys and the server proves its identity.
glossary.definition: Client and server swap key shares to derive fresh session keys, and the server presents a certificate showing it owns the domain. In TLS 1.3 this takes one round trip. Afterwards all traffic is encrypted and tamper-evident.
glossary.advanced: In TLS 1.3 the client sends supported cipher suites and a key share (commonly X25519, increasingly hybrid post-quantum X25519MLKEM768) in ClientHello. The server replies with its share, and everything after ServerHello is encrypted, including the certificate and CertificateVerify signature. Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman provides forward secrecy. The client validates the chain to a trusted root, the hostname against the Subject Alternative Name, and validity dates. Resumption with pre-shared keys enables 0-RTT data, which is replayable and should carry only idempotent requests. SNI leaks the hostname unless Encrypted Client Hello is used. TLS 1.0/1.1 are deprecated; mutual TLS adds client certificates for service-to-service authentication.

glossary.short: A transport protocol that delivers an ordered, reliable byte stream between two programs.
glossary.definition: TCP opens a connection with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), numbers every byte, and resends anything that is lost. It is like registered mail with receipts: slower to start, but nothing goes missing or arrives out of order. UDP is the no-guarantees alternative.
glossary.advanced: TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream with no message boundaries, so applications must frame messages. Random initial sequence numbers are exchanged in the SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK handshake; ACKs are cumulative, and loss triggers retransmission after a timeout or three duplicate ACKs. Flow control uses the receiver window; congestion control (CUBIC, BBR) adapts the sending rate. A connection is identified by the 5-tuple of protocol, source and destination IPs and ports. Closing leaves the active closer in TIME_WAIT. Costs are a round trip before data and head-of-line blocking, which is why QUIC reimplements reliability per stream over UDP. SYN cookies defend against SYN floods.

glossary.short: The internet's distributed phone book that turns names like example.com into IP addresses.
glossary.definition: A resolver walks from the root servers to the top-level domain to the domain's authoritative server, then caches the answer for its TTL. Record types include A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias) and MX (mail). Caching makes lookups fast but delays changes.
glossary.advanced: Resolution goes stub resolver -> recursive resolver -> root -> TLD -> authoritative server, with every answer, including negative NXDOMAIN answers, cached for its TTL. Queries use UDP port 53, falling back to TCP for large responses. A CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the zone apex, hence provider ALIAS records. HTTPS/SVCB records can advertise HTTP/3 and ECH keys. DNSSEC authenticates answers with signatures; DoH and DoT encrypt queries. Operational lessons: lower TTLs before migrations, remember that clients and runtimes may cache beyond TTL, and treat DNS as a frequent root cause of outages. DNS rebinding attacks abuse short TTLs to bypass same-origin and SSRF filters.

glossary.short: A compact way to write an IP address range as address/prefix length, like 10.0.1.0/24.
glossary.definition: The number after the slash says how many leading bits are fixed for the network; the rest identify hosts. A /24 leaves 8 host bits, so 256 addresses. Smaller prefix numbers mean bigger ranges.
glossary.advanced: CIDR replaced classful A/B/C networks in 1993 to slow IPv4 exhaustion and shrink routing tables through aggregation. A /n prefix leaves 2^(32-n) addresses; membership is tested by ANDing the address with the mask, and routers forward by longest prefix match, so a /24 route overrides a covering /16. Traditionally a subnet's first and last addresses are reserved (network and broadcast); clouds reserve more, AWS five per subnet. RFC 1918 private ranges are 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16, and 100.64/10 is carrier-grade NAT space. IPv6 uses the same notation, with /64 the standard subnet size. Overlapping VPC ranges block later peering, so plan address space early.

glossary.short: The | operator that streams one command's standard output into the next command's standard input.
glossary.definition: Pipes let small single-purpose tools combine into powerful one-liners, like an assembly line where each station does one job. All stages run at the same time, connected by a kernel buffer. Errors on stderr bypass the pipe unless redirected.
glossary.advanced: A pipe is a kernel buffer (64 KB by default on Linux) with a write end and a read end; the shell forks each stage and wires stdout of one to stdin of the next with dup2. Stages run concurrently, and a full buffer blocks the writer, giving natural backpressure; when the reader exits, the writer gets SIGPIPE. The pipeline's exit status is the last stage's unless set -o pipefail is on. stderr is not piped by default; 2>&1 or |& merges it. Named pipes (mkfifo) give pipes a filesystem path. Process substitution <(cmd) exposes a pipe as a file path, enabling commands like diff <(sort a) <(sort b).

glossary.short: An attack where user input is spliced into a SQL query and changes what the query does.
glossary.definition: If code builds SQL by concatenating strings, input such as ' OR '1'='1 can rewrite the query to return or delete data. Parameterized queries fix it by sending the query and the data separately. It is the classic case of mixing data with code.
glossary.advanced: Injection occurs whenever untrusted input reaches an interpreter as code. Variants include classic in-band (UNION-based), error-based, blind boolean or time-based extraction, and second-order injection where stored data is later concatenated unsafely. Prepared statements parse the query before binding values, making structure immune to input; they cannot parameterize identifiers, so table names, columns and sort directions need allowlists. ORMs are safe until raw-SQL escape hatches are used. Defense in depth adds least-privilege database accounts, no stack traces in responses, and WAF rules as a backstop, not a fix. The same pattern applies to shell, LDAP, NoSQL operators and template injection.

glossary.short: An attack that gets a malicious script to run inside another site's pages in a victim's browser.
glossary.definition: The attacker plants script in content the site later displays, such as a comment, and it runs with the site's privileges, stealing data or acting as the user. The fixes are escaping output for its context and a Content-Security-Policy. Frameworks escape by default, but raw HTML escape hatches reopen the hole.
glossary.advanced: XSS has stored, reflected and DOM-based forms; all run attacker JavaScript in the victim's origin, defeating the same-origin policy. Defenses are context-aware encoding (HTML body, attribute, URL and JavaScript contexts differ), safe framework defaults, sanitizing user-supplied HTML with a vetted library like DOMPurify, and a strict Content-Security-Policy using nonces or hashes with no unsafe-inline. Trusted Types can lock down DOM sinks like innerHTML. HttpOnly cookies limit session theft, but XSS can still act as the user within the page. Dangerous sinks include innerHTML, document.write, eval, javascript: URLs and React's dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

glossary.short: A compact, signed token of JSON claims, written header.payload.signature, used for authentication.
glossary.definition: The signature proves the claims were issued by a trusted party and not altered, but the payload is only base64url-encoded, so anyone can read it. Servers must pin the algorithm and check expiry, issuer and audience. Because it is stateless, revoking one before it expires is hard.
glossary.advanced: A JWT (RFC 7519) is usually a JWS: base64url header and payload signed with HMAC (HS256) or asymmetric keys (RS256, ES256, EdDSA). JWE adds encryption but is rarer. Known pitfalls: accepting alg none, algorithm confusion where an RS256 public key is used as an HS256 secret, trusting kid or jku headers to fetch attacker keys, and skipping exp, nbf, iss or aud checks. Revocation requires short lifetimes, rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection, or a denylist that reintroduces state. Storage is a trade-off: localStorage is exposed to XSS, cookies to CSRF. For first-party web sessions, opaque server-side session IDs are often simpler and safer.

glossary.short: A bug where the result depends on the unpredictable timing of concurrent operations on shared state.
glossary.definition: Two threads both read a counter as 5 and both write 6, so one increment vanishes. Like two people editing the same paper copy, the last writer silently wins. Locks, atomics or avoiding shared state prevent it.
glossary.advanced: A data race is unsynchronized concurrent access with at least one write; a race condition is any timing-dependent correctness bug, including check-then-act sequences built from individually atomic steps. Races arise across threads, processes, async tasks and distributed services, for example two servers both selling the last item. Compilers and CPUs reorder memory operations, so without synchronization visibility is not guaranteed; language memory models define happens-before rules. Races are nondeterministic and often hidden by testing, so use ThreadSanitizer or go test -race, stress tests, and designs that avoid shared mutable state. In databases, use transactions, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or optimistic version checks.

glossary.short: A lock that lets only one thread at a time run a critical section of code.
glossary.definition: A thread acquires the mutex before touching shared data and releases it afterwards; others wait their turn. It is like a single bathroom key on a hook. Mutexes prevent race conditions but can cause deadlocks if taken in inconsistent orders.
glossary.advanced: A mutex provides mutual exclusion plus memory visibility: writes before unlock are visible after the next lock. Implementations spin briefly then sleep in the kernel (futexes on Linux), so uncontended locking costs tens of nanoseconds while contention costs context switches. Variants include reentrant locks, read-write locks, semaphores and fair locks that prevent starvation. Always release in finally or with RAII or a context manager. Keep critical sections short and never hold a lock across I/O or callbacks into unknown code. Alternatives are atomics and compare-and-swap, single-owner designs with queues, and immutable data. Lock ordering discipline prevents deadlock when several locks are needed.

glossary.short: A standstill where tasks each hold a resource and wait forever for one another's.
glossary.definition: Thread 1 holds lock A and wants B while thread 2 holds B and wants A, so neither moves, like two cars meeting on a one-lane bridge. It needs four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Taking locks in one global order prevents it.
glossary.advanced: Coffman et al. (1971) showed deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait simultaneously. Prevention removes one: global lock ordering kills circular wait, acquiring all locks atomically kills hold and wait, and try-lock with timeout and back-off approximates preemption at the risk of livelock. Avoidance algorithms like the Banker's algorithm need advance knowledge of resource needs and are rare in practice. Detection builds a wait-for graph and breaks cycles, which is what databases do by aborting a victim transaction, so applications must retry. Diagnose hangs with thread dumps showing held and awaited locks. Distributed deadlocks across services usually surface as timeouts.

glossary.short: Adding more machines to handle more load, instead of making one machine bigger.
glossary.definition: Horizontal scaling grows capacity by running more identical servers behind a load balancer. It contrasts with vertical scaling (scale up), which buys a bigger machine. It is like opening more checkout lanes instead of hiring one faster cashier, and it works best when servers are stateless.
glossary.advanced: Horizontal scaling adds nodes rather than resources per node. It is straightforward for stateless tiers, where any instance can serve any request and autoscaling can add or remove instances on CPU, request rate or queue depth. For stateful tiers it requires partitioning (sharding) or replication, which brings coordination, rebalancing and consistency trade-offs. It also improves fault tolerance: with N+1 or N+2 capacity, losing a node or an availability zone does not cause an outage. Limits come from shared dependencies, such as database connections, a central lock or a hot key, so scaling one tier often moves the bottleneck to the next. Contrast with vertical scaling, which is simpler but capped by hardware and remains a single failure domain.

glossary.short: A component that spreads incoming requests across a pool of healthy servers.
glossary.definition: A load balancer sits in front of several servers and decides which one handles each request or connection. It removes servers that fail health checks, so users keep being served. Layer 4 balancers route by IP address and port; layer 7 balancers read HTTP details such as paths and headers.
glossary.advanced: Layer 4 balancers forward TCP or UDP connections with minimal overhead and cannot see HTTP; layer 7 balancers terminate TLS, parse requests and can route by path or header, retry, split traffic for canaries and balance individual gRPC requests over long-lived HTTP/2 connections. Algorithms include round robin, weighted round robin, least connections, power of two random choices, and hashing for affinity. Health is tracked with active probes and passive outlier detection. The balancer itself must be redundant (active-passive pairs with a floating IP, DNS with several records, anycast, or a managed service). Watch for sticky sessions that skew load, retries that amplify outages, and deep health checks that eject every backend at once when a shared dependency fails.

glossary.short: A way to map keys to servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a small share of keys.
glossary.definition: Servers and keys are hashed onto the same circle, and each key belongs to the next server clockwise. When a server joins or leaves, only the keys in its arc move, about 1/N of them. Plain hash(key) % N would move almost every key whenever N changes.
glossary.advanced: Consistent hashing places each node at many points on the ring (virtual nodes, often 100-200 per node) to even out arc sizes and to let stronger machines take more points. Lookup is a binary search over sorted ring positions, O(log V). Adding a node takes over roughly 1/(N+1) of the keys, drawn from many existing nodes when virtual nodes are used. It is used in distributed caches, Dynamo-style databases (Cassandra, Riak) and L7 balancers that need affinity. Variants: rendezvous or highest-random-weight hashing (simpler, no ring), jump consistent hash (no memory, but nodes can only be added or removed at the end), and bounded-load consistent hashing, which caps each node at, say, 1.25x the average load to tame hot spots.

glossary.short: A caching pattern where the application checks the cache first and loads from the database only on a miss.
glossary.definition: On a read, the app looks in the cache; if the value is missing, it reads the database and stores the result in the cache with an expiry time. On a write, it updates the database and deletes the cached copy. Only data that is actually requested ends up in the cache.
glossary.advanced: Cache-aside keeps the cache off the write path's critical correctness: if the cache is lost, the system is slower but still correct. Its weaknesses are the cold-miss cost, application-managed invalidation, and races. The recommended order is to write the database and then delete the key; deleting first lets a concurrent reader refill the stale value. A rarer race remains (a slow reader writes an old value after the delete), bounded by a TTL, delayed double-delete, or invalidation driven by change data capture. Compare read-through (the cache library loads on a miss), write-through (writes update cache and database together) and write-back (the cache absorbs writes and flushes later). Protect popular keys against stampedes with request coalescing and TTL jitter.

glossary.short: A surge of requests hitting the database at once because a popular cached value expired or the cache was lost.
glossary.definition: When a hot key expires, every request that needs it misses at the same moment and they all query the database together. The sudden load can slow or crash the database. Fixes let one request rebuild the value while others wait or receive the old copy.
glossary.advanced: A stampede is a positive feedback loop: misses add database load, the database slows, rebuilds take longer, and more requests pile up behind the missing key. Defenses: request coalescing or single-flight (one rebuild per key per process, or a distributed lock such as SET lock NX EX 10), stale-while-revalidate (serve the expired value while a background refresh runs), probabilistic early expiration (each reader refreshes early with probability increasing as expiry nears), TTL jitter to spread expirations, and pre-warming after deploys or cache restarts. Related problems are cache penetration (repeated lookups of nonexistent keys; cache negative results or use a Bloom filter) and cache avalanche (mass expiry or total cache loss).

glossary.short: A sorted, balanced tree structure that lets a database find rows in O(log n) instead of scanning the whole table.
glossary.definition: A B-tree index keeps the values of one or more columns in sorted order, with pointers to the matching rows. Like a phone book sorted by last name, it lets the database jump close to the right place instead of reading every page. It speeds up reads but slows writes, because each insert must also update the index.
glossary.advanced: Databases use B+ trees: internal pages hold only keys and child pointers, leaves hold keys plus row references (or the rows themselves in clustered indexes such as InnoDB's primary key), and leaves are linked for range scans. A fan-out of hundreds of keys per page keeps a billion-row index only 3-4 levels deep. Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule, so put equality columns first and range columns last. Covering indexes enable index-only scans. Costs: write amplification, page splits, memory pressure and bloat over time. Planners skip an index when a filter is not selective, because random reads cost more than a sequential scan. Alternatives include hash, GIN, GiST and BRIN indexes, and LSM trees in write-heavy stores.

glossary.short: The four guarantees of a database transaction: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability.
glossary.definition: Atomicity means all of a transaction's changes happen or none do. Consistency means declared rules and constraints always hold, isolation means concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work, and durability means committed data survives a crash. A bank transfer relies on all four.
glossary.advanced: Atomicity and durability are implemented with a write-ahead log (WAL): changes are logged and flushed before the commit is acknowledged, then replayed or undone after a crash. Isolation is implemented with locks or multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) and comes in levels: read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read and serializable, each preventing more anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates, write skew). Vendors differ: PostgreSQL's repeatable read is snapshot isolation and its serializable level aborts conflicting transactions, so clients must retry. The C in ACID concerns application invariants and constraints, unlike the C in CAP, which means linearizability. Distributed transactions need two-phase commit or consensus; across microservices, sagas replace ACID with compensations.

glossary.short: Splitting a dataset across several database nodes so each node stores and serves only part of the data.
glossary.definition: Each row goes to one shard based on a shard key, using either ranges (user IDs 1 to 1M on shard A) or a hash of the key. Sharding spreads writes and storage across machines. Queries that need data from many shards become slower and harder.
glossary.advanced: The shard key determines everything: it should have high cardinality, spread load evenly and match the dominant query so most requests touch one shard (tenant_id in multi-tenant SaaS is a classic). Range sharding preserves order and supports scans and automatic splits, but sequential keys create hot spots; hash sharding spreads load but scatters range queries. Avoid hash % N; use many logical shards mapped onto physical nodes, consistent hashing or a directory service so rebalancing moves little data. Cross-shard joins, global secondary indexes, unique constraints and transactions become expensive. Each shard is usually replicated for availability. Because resharding is operationally heavy, exhaust vertical scaling, read replicas, caching and archiving first.

glossary.short: During a network partition, a distributed data store must choose between consistency and availability.
glossary.definition: CAP stands for consistency, availability and partition tolerance. Networks can always split, so when they do, a system either refuses some requests to stay correct (CP) or keeps answering with possibly stale data (AP). When there is no partition, both are possible.
glossary.advanced: Formally (Gilbert and Lynch, 2002), consistency means linearizability and availability means every request to a non-failing node eventually gets a non-error response. The theorem only constrains behavior during partitions, which is why PACELC is more useful day to day: if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. Dynamo-style stores are typically PA/EL; consensus-based databases such as Spanner, etcd and CockroachDB are PC/EC. Many systems are tunable per operation (quorum levels, strongly consistent reads). Common misconceptions: 'pick two of three' (partitions are not optional), treating CAP consistency as ACID consistency, and assuming AP means no consistency at all, when causal or session guarantees are still possible.

glossary.short: A holding queue for messages that failed processing too many times, so they stop blocking the main queue.
glossary.definition: When a consumer keeps failing on a message, for example because it is malformed, the message is moved to a dead-letter queue after a set number of retries. The main queue keeps flowing, and engineers can inspect, fix and replay the failed messages later.
glossary.advanced: SQS (maxReceiveCount with a redrive policy) and RabbitMQ (dead-letter exchanges) support DLQs natively; for plain Kafka consumers they are a convention implemented by frameworks (Kafka Connect has a built-in DLQ for sink connectors), often with tiered retry topics (retry after 1 minute, 10 minutes) before the dead-letter topic. Retry only transient errors with backoff; route permanent failures such as schema violations straight to the DLQ. Store context with each dead letter: the original topic, partition, offset, error and attempt count. A DLQ needs alerting, an owner and a redrive tool, and replayed messages must be handled idempotently. Moving messages to a retry topic breaks per-key ordering, so systems that need strict ordering may instead pause the partition or park all later messages for the same key.

glossary.short: A guard around remote calls that stops calling a failing service for a while and fails fast instead.
glossary.definition: Like an electrical breaker, it trips when too many calls fail, so callers stop waiting on a broken dependency. While open, calls return an error or fallback immediately. After a cool-down it lets a few test calls through and closes again if they succeed.
glossary.advanced: A breaker has three states: closed (calls pass, failures counted over a sliding window by count or time), open (calls fail immediately, often with a fallback such as cached data or a degraded feature) and half-open (a limited number of trial calls decide whether to close or reopen). For example, Resilience4j's defaults trip at 50% failures once at least 100 calls are recorded and stay open 60 s. Slow calls can count as failures. It complements timeouts (bound each call), retries with backoff and jitter (handle transient errors), bulkheads (separate pools per dependency) and retry budgets. Breakers live in client libraries (Resilience4j, Polly) or service-mesh proxies through outlier detection.

glossary.short: A unique value a client sends with a request so the server can recognize retries and perform the action only once.
glossary.definition: The client generates a key such as a UUID for one logical operation, like a payment, and sends the same key on every retry. The server saves the result under that key and returns the saved result for repeats. A network timeout then never turns into a double charge.
glossary.advanced: Implementation: insert the key atomically (a unique constraint) with a 'processing' state before doing work, then store the response status and body; repeats return the stored response, and concurrent duplicates get 409 or wait. Store a fingerprint of the request body and reject reuse of the key with different parameters. Scope keys per account and expire them after a window longer than any client retry policy, often 24 hours. Payment APIs popularized the Idempotency-Key HTTP header, which is being standardized at the IETF. The same idea applies to message consumers, which dedupe by event ID. Idempotency keys protect one hop only: downstream calls need their own keys, ideally derived deterministically from the original one.

glossary.short: An experiment that randomly assigns units to two versions to measure the difference one change makes.
glossary.definition: Randomly show half of users version A and half version B; random assignment means other factors balance out on average. It is the most reliable way to establish causation. It needs enough samples to tell real differences from noise.
glossary.advanced:
An A/B test is a randomized controlled experiment: each unit (user, session, device) is assigned at random to arm A (control) or arm B (treatment) and an outcome metric is compared. Randomization makes assignment independent of the potential outcomes Y(0) and Y(1), so the difference in sample means is an unbiased estimate of the average treatment effect, E[Y(1) - Y(0)].

Design is fixed before launch: one primary metric, a minimum detectable effect d, and a sample size; for 80% power at a two-sided 5% level, roughly n = 16 s^2 / d^2 per arm (s is the metric's standard deviation). Peeking and stopping at the first p < 0.05 inflates false positives, so use fixed horizons or sequential methods. Watch for sample ratio mismatch (the observed split differs from the design, usually meaning broken assignment), interference between units in networks and marketplaces, and novelty effects.

A small p-value does not mean a large or important effect; it only says the data are unlikely under zero effect. Observational causal inference is the neighbour that replaces randomization with untestable assumptions.

glossary.short: Removing or disabling a part of a model or experiment to test what that part contributes.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: To find out what a switch in your house does, you flip it off and walk around to see which light went dark. Ablation is that same trick inside the model. Here, the house is the model, the switch is a component like a neuron or attention head, and the dark light is the behaviour that breaks.

How it works: Ablation removes or disables a component and measures the change in model behaviour. Zero ablation sets the activation to zero, mean ablation replaces it with its average over a dataset, and resample ablation replaces it with the activation from a different random input. Mean and resample ablation are usually preferred because zero can push the model far off its normal distribution and cause misleading effects. Ablation tests whether a component is necessary for a behaviour but can miss redundancy, since backup components may compensate, a phenomenon seen in the indirect object identification work. It is the simplest causal test and is often used before more detailed patching.

Why it matters: Ablation is how researchers check that a component they think matters really does. Directional ablation of the refusal direction, for example, showed that removing one direction can remove refusal behaviour in many chat models. It is also used to test whether unlearning or safety training truly removed a capability.
glossary.advanced:
In interpretability, ablation is a causal intervention that replaces a component's activation a with a substitute a' and measures the change in a metric such as loss or logit difference. Zero ablation sets a' = 0; mean ablation uses the component's average over a reference dataset; resample ablation uses its activation on another random input; path ablation removes only the contribution along chosen edges of the computational graph.

The substitute defines the counterfactual. Real activations are rarely near zero, so zero ablation is often off-distribution and downstream layers may behave pathologically; mean ablation removes input-specific information but keeps typical scale; resample ablation stays on-distribution. Targets include neurons, attention heads, MLP outputs, residual-stream directions and sparse-autoencoder features. Ablation tests necessity only: other components may compensate (self-repair, the Hydra effect, McGrath et al. 2023), hiding a component's role, while mere disruption can exaggerate it.

Necessary is not sufficient. Activation patching is the closest neighbour, swapping in activations from a matched counterfactual input instead of a generic baseline. In general ML papers, an 'ablation study' also means removing parts of a training recipe or architecture, a related but different use.

glossary.short: Letting a model or auditor answer 'uncertain' instead of guessing.
glossary.definition: A doctor who refers unclear cases to a specialist makes fewer errors on the cases they do decide. Abstaining can raise precision but leaves more cases unresolved, so coverage must be reported too. It works best when confidence is well calibrated.
glossary.advanced:
Selective prediction equips a classifier f with a selection function g: output f(x) if g(x) = 1, otherwise abstain. Coverage is P(g = 1); selective risk is the expected loss on answered inputs, E[loss | g = 1]. Sweeping a threshold traces a risk-coverage curve. Chow's rule (1970) gives the optimal reject rule when true posteriors are known: with error cost 1 and rejection cost c < 1/2, abstain when the maximum class posterior is below 1 - c.

In practice g thresholds a confidence score: max softmax probability, predictive entropy, ensemble disagreement, a learned reject head (SelectiveNet, Geifman and El-Yaniv 2019), or for language models a verbalized confidence or sequence likelihood. Ranking quality (AUROC of confidence for predicting correctness) matters most for choosing where to abstain; calibration matters for interpreting the threshold. Failure modes: overconfidence on out-of-distribution inputs, calibration drift under shift, and uneven abstention across subgroups. Conformal prediction gives distribution-free coverage guarantees with prediction sets.

Abstention does not by itself cure hallucination: models often cannot tell when they are wrong, and training them to say 'I don't know' can cause over-refusal. Distinguish calibration, out-of-distribution detection and safety refusals.

glossary.short: The fraction of predictions a model gets right.
glossary.definition: It is the simplest metric: 90 correct out of 100 is 90% accuracy. It can be very misleading with imbalanced classes. Precision, recall and F1 give a more complete picture.
glossary.advanced:
Accuracy is the fraction of predictions matching the label: (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN) in binary classification, or (1/N) sum of 1[yhat_i = y_i] in general. With positive prevalence p, always predicting the majority class scores max(p, 1 - p), the baseline to beat; at 1% prevalence a model that detects nothing is 99% accurate.

Use it for roughly balanced classes with symmetric costs. Otherwise report per-class recall and precision, F1, balanced accuracy (mean per-class recall), Matthews correlation, or threshold-free AUROC and AUPRC. Accuracy depends on the decision threshold, so compare models at a fixed one or over full curves. On n test items the binomial standard error is sqrt(a(1 - a)/n): at a = 0.9 and n = 1000 about 0.95 points, so small gaps are often noise. Accuracy is not differentiable, so training uses surrogates such as cross-entropy.

High accuracy does not imply a good model under imbalance and says nothing about calibration. Precision and recall each isolate one error type; log loss scores probabilities rather than hard labels.
