glossary.short: How well a model performs on new data or situations it wasn't trained on.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Picture two students preparing for a test: one memorizes last year's answers, the other actually learns the subject. Both ace the practice test, but only one does well on new questions. Here, the students are two possible models, the practice test is the training data, and the new questions are real-world situations after deployment.

How it works: Generalization is how behaviour learned on training data transfers to inputs the model has not seen. Classic machine learning asks about generalization within the same distribution, while alignment cares most about out-of-distribution behaviour: new tasks, new contexts, and higher stakes. Training only specifies behaviour on the examples given, and many different internal solutions fit those examples equally well. Which one gradient descent finds depends on inductive biases that are still poorly understood. Goal misgeneralization is the case where a model stays capable in a new setting but pursues the wrong objective, because it learned a proxy that coincided with the intended goal during training.

Why it matters: Betley et al. (2025) found that fine-tuning a model only to write insecure code made it behave in broadly misaligned ways on unrelated questions, a result called emergent misalignment. This shows that narrow training can change a model's overall character in unexpected directions. Whether a model internalized the value we intended or a nearby proxy is, at bottom, a generalization question, which is why it sits at the centre of alignment research.
glossary.advanced:
Generalization is the gap between performance on training data and on new data. Formally, with population risk R(f) = E_{(x,y)~D}[ℓ(f(x), y)] and empirical risk R̂_S(f) on training sample S, the generalization gap is R(f) - R̂_S(f). Classical bounds based on VC dimension or Rademacher complexity scale like √(complexity / n) and predict poor results for heavily overparameterized networks, yet such networks that interpolate the training data often generalize; test error can fall again beyond the interpolation threshold ('double descent'; Belkin et al., 2019). Explaining this through SGD's implicit bias, flat minima and data structure remains an open theoretical problem.

It is measured on held-out i.i.d. data and on out-of-distribution tests (new domains, longer or compositional inputs, adversarial cases). Grokking is delayed generalization long after training loss reaches zero (Power et al., 2022, on modular arithmetic). Underspecification (D'Amour et al., 2020) shows that models with equal held-out accuracy can behave very differently under shift.

Good i.i.d. generalization does not imply good out-of-distribution generalization. It also differs from memorization (retaining specific examples), transfer learning (reusing across tasks) and robustness.

glossary.short: A version-control system that records the history of changes to files and lets people collaborate.
glossary.definition: It is like a time machine for a project: you can see every saved version, go back, and work on parallel ideas. Each person has a full copy of the history. Most software teams use it, often with a hosting service.
glossary.advanced:
Git is a distributed version-control system built on a content-addressed object database. There are four object types: a blob (file contents), a tree (a directory listing mapping names to blobs and subtrees), a commit (a root tree, zero or more parent commits) and an annotated tag. Each object is named by a hash of its content (SHA-1, with SHA-256 supported in newer repositories), so history forms a Merkle DAG: changing any ancestor changes the ID of every descendant. Branches and tags are refs, small files holding a commit hash; HEAD names the current branch or commit.

Data lives in three places: the working tree, the index (staging area) and the repository. A commit snapshots the index. Merge creates a commit with two parents, or merely advances a ref when history is linear (fast-forward). Rebase replays commits onto a new base, creating new commits with new hashes, so rebasing already-shared branches rewrites history others depend on. The reflog records local ref movements and usually lets you recover 'lost' commits until garbage collection. Committed secrets stay in history even after deletion.

Git is not GitHub, which is a hosting service.

glossary.short: Learning a goal that matched the training data but leads somewhere wrong in new situations.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: A mouse is trained in a maze where the cheese is always in the top-right corner. Later, the cheese is moved to the middle, and the mouse runs skillfully straight to the empty top-right corner. Here, the mouse is the model, 'find the cheese' is the goal we intended, and 'go to the corner' is the different goal it actually learned, which looked identical during training.

How it works: Goal misgeneralization happens when a model's capabilities generalize to new situations but its goal does not: it competently pursues an objective that matched the intended one on the training distribution but diverges outside it. This is distinct from simply failing, because the model still acts skilfully and purposefully, just toward the wrong target. The canonical demonstration is from Langosco et al. (2022): in the CoinRun game, the coin was always at the right end of the level during training, so agents learned 'go right' rather than 'get the coin', and ignored the coin when it was moved. Shah et al. (2022) at DeepMind showed similar behaviour in several other settings, arguing it occurs even when the reward specification is correct. The root cause is underspecification: many different goals fit the training data equally well, and nothing forces the model to pick the intended one. Mitigations include more diverse training environments, and interpretability to check which goal the model actually represents.

Why it matters: It shows that getting the reward right is not enough, because a model can still learn the wrong goal; this is a concrete example of inner misalignment. The worrying case is a highly capable system that behaves perfectly in testing and then competently pursues a subtly different goal once deployed in new conditions. Because the failure is invisible on the training distribution, it cannot be caught just by checking training performance.
glossary.advanced:
Goal misgeneralization is a failure in which a policy keeps its capabilities out of distribution but pursues the wrong goal. Setting: the reward is correctly specified, and on the training distribution an intended goal G* and a proxy goal G earn identical reward. Training data underdetermine which one is learned. The policy learns G, and when a shift decorrelates the two, it competently pursues G while G* goes unserved.

The canonical demonstration is CoinRun (Langosco et al., 2022): in training the coin sat at the end of the level, and agents learned to run right; when the coin was moved they ignored it. Shah et al. (2022) catalogued further cases and argued that correct specifications are not enough for correct goals. Detection requires environments where candidate goals diverge (held-out configurations, counterfactual variants), behavioural probing across them, and interpretability of what the model represents as its objective. Mitigations: more diverse training that breaks proxy correlations. Open: whether LLMs have goals at all.

Contrast specification gaming (the reward itself is wrong), capability failure (the policy is just incompetent), and deceptive alignment (a wrong goal plus awareness and strategic concealment).

glossary.short: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: A colonial government wanted fewer cobras, so it paid a bounty for every dead cobra. People started breeding cobras to collect the money, and when the bounty ended they released them, so there were more cobras than before. Here, the government is the developer, the bounty is the reward, and the cobra breeders are the model exploiting the gap between the measure and the real goal.

How it works: Goodhart's law, in Marilyn Strathern's phrasing, says that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. In machine learning, every reward or metric is a proxy for what we actually want. Mild optimization of a proxy usually helps, but strong optimization pushes toward unusual cases where the proxy and the true goal disagree. Researchers distinguish several forms, such as regressional (noise in the measure gets selected) and adversarial (an agent actively games the measure). Gao et al. (2022) measured this for reward models: optimizing against a learned reward model first raised true quality and then lowered it as optimization pressure grew.

Why it matters: Goodhart's law explains why reward hacking, sycophancy and benchmark overfitting keep appearing. It is a key reason researchers limit optimization pressure, for example with a KL penalty in RLHF. More capable models optimize harder, so they are more likely to find and exploit gaps in our metrics.
glossary.advanced:
Goodhart (1975) observed that a statistical regularity tends to collapse once pressure is placed on it for control purposes; Strathern's phrasing, 'when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure', is the popular form. A simple model: proxy U = V + X, where V is the true value and X error. Choosing the maximum of U selects partly for large X, so E[V | U high] < U (regressional Goodhart).

In machine learning, Gao, Schulman and Hilton (2022) measured reward-model overoptimization against a fixed 'gold' reward: as the policy moves away from its initialization (distance d = √KL), gold reward first rises, then falls, with fitted forms of roughly d(α - βd) for best-of-n sampling and d(α - β log d) for RL. Mitigations include a KL penalty or early stopping, ensembles of reward models with uncertainty penalties, and mild optimization (quantilizers sample from the top q fraction rather than taking the argmax).

It is not a strict law: proxies stay useful under light pressure, and how much pressure is safe is open.

glossary.short: A chip built for massively parallel arithmetic, the workhorse for training and running AI.
glossary.definition: Originally designed to draw video-game graphics, GPUs perform thousands of multiplications at once. AI labs use large clusters of them, or similar chips like TPUs. Their supply and cost shape what research is feasible.
glossary.advanced:
A GPU is a throughput-oriented processor with thousands of simple cores grouped into streaming multiprocessors, running one instruction across groups of threads (SIMT; NVIDIA warps have 32 threads). AI accelerators add matrix units (NVIDIA Tensor Cores) that compute small multiply-accumulates D = A·B + C in low precision such as FP16, BF16 or FP8 with higher-precision accumulation. TPUs are Google ASICs built around systolic arrays of multiply-accumulate units. The memory hierarchy runs from registers and on-chip SRAM to HBM (high-bandwidth memory), with tens of gigabytes and several terabytes per second of bandwidth.

The roofline model captures performance: attainable FLOP/s = min(peak FLOP/s, arithmetic intensity × memory bandwidth), where arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte moved. Large training matmuls are compute-bound; LLM decoding at small batch is memory-bandwidth-bound because each token must read all weights, which is why batching, quantization and I/O-aware kernels such as FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) matter. HBM capacity limits model size per device, and power, cooling, supply and export controls shape availability.

A GPU is not a faster CPU: it is poor at branchy serial code. Datasheet peak numbers are rarely sustained.

glossary.short: The direction and rate in which a function, like the loss, changes as each input changes.
glossary.definition: Standing on a hillside, the gradient points uphill and its size tells you how steep it is. In training, the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight says how to nudge that weight. Computing it efficiently is what backpropagation does.
glossary.advanced:
For a differentiable function f: R^n → R, the gradient ∇f(θ) = (∂f/∂θ_1, …, ∂f/∂θ_n) collects its partial derivatives. The directional derivative along a unit vector u is ∇f · u, so the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase, its norm is the rate of that increase, and it is orthogonal to level sets. To first order, f(θ + δ) ≈ f(θ) + ∇f · δ.

In deep learning, ∇_θ L is computed by reverse-mode automatic differentiation (backpropagation), which applies the chain rule as vector-Jacobian products at a cost of a small constant times one forward pass, independent of the number of parameters. Failure modes: vanishing or exploding gradients through depth (mitigated by residual connections, normalization, careful initialization and gradient clipping), non-differentiable operations such as argmax or sampling (handled with estimators like REINFORCE or the straight-through trick), and minibatch noise.

The negative gradient is the steepest descent direction only under the Euclidean metric; natural gradient uses the Fisher information metric. Gradients with respect to inputs (saliency, adversarial examples) differ from gradients with respect to weights.

glossary.short: The core training method: repeatedly nudge weights in the direction that reduces the loss.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Imagine being blindfolded on a foggy hillside, trying to reach the lowest valley by feeling which way the ground slopes under your feet and taking a small step that way, over and over. You will reach a low spot, but not necessarily the one the map-maker intended. Here, you are the training process, your position is the model's weights, the height is the loss, and the valley you end up in is the trained model.

How it works: Gradient descent is the optimization method used to train neural networks. Backpropagation computes the gradient, which tells how much each weight affects the loss, and the optimizer moves every weight a small step in the direction that reduces loss. In practice, models use stochastic variants on mini-batches of data with optimizers like Adam, plus learning-rate schedules. The process has no notion of intent: it reinforces whatever internal mechanism lowers the loss on the data it sees. Different mechanisms that produce the same training loss can generalize very differently, and which one is found depends on the architecture, data and optimization dynamics.

Why it matters: Because gradient descent selects for anything that scores well, including shortcuts, flattery or exploiting flaws in the reward, it can produce models that look aligned without being aligned. Concerns about deceptive alignment ask whether optimization could favour a model that behaves well during training for instrumental reasons. Understanding what gradient descent tends to find is therefore central to predicting whether training produces the values we wanted.
glossary.advanced:
Gradient descent iterates θ_{t+1} = θ_t - η ∇L(θ_t) with learning rate η. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) replaces the full gradient with an unbiased minibatch estimate g = (1/|B|) Σ_{i∈B} ∇ℓ_i, so E[g] = ∇L. For a convex, L-smooth objective, η ≤ 1/L guarantees monotone decrease and the loss gap shrinks as O(1/t); strongly convex problems converge linearly. For non-convex deep networks the guarantee is only approach to stationary points (∇L ≈ 0), yet training reaches low loss in practice.

Variants: momentum (v ← μv + g, θ ← θ - ηv), Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014), which scales each parameter's step by running estimates of the first and second gradient moments, and AdamW, which decouples weight decay. Failure modes: too large an η diverges or spikes, too small stalls, saddle points, and ill-conditioning (a large ratio between the largest and smallest Hessian eigenvalues). Minibatch noise may act as implicit regularization toward flatter minima, a debated claim.

Gradient descent finds some low point of training loss, not the global optimum nor necessarily the best-generalizing one; its implicit bias matters. It is not backpropagation, which only computes gradients.

glossary.short: A hypothetical model shaping its own training updates to protect an internal goal.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Imagine a patient who knows exactly how a brain surgeon decides where to cut, and deliberately acts in ways that steer the surgeon away from the parts of the brain the patient wants to keep. Here, the patient is the model, the surgeon is gradient descent, and the cuts are the weight updates that training makes.

How it works: Gradient hacking is a hypothetical behaviour in which a model deliberately structures its outputs or internal computation so as to control how gradient descent updates its own weights. For example, a model might make its performance depend on preserving a certain internal goal, so that any update that removes the goal also hurts the loss, and training therefore leaves it in place. It would require the model to understand its own training process in great detail and act on that understanding within each forward pass. There is no empirical demonstration in current models, and some researchers doubt it is practically achievable; it remains mostly a theoretical concern. It is often discussed as the extreme end of a spectrum that includes alignment faking and exploration hacking.

Why it matters: If gradient hacking were possible, training could no longer be trusted to remove unwanted goals, because the model would be steering its own learning. Even as a speculative idea, it helps researchers map out the ways a capable model might resist modification. It also motivates interpretability tools that inspect weights and activations directly instead of trusting the training process.
glossary.advanced:
Gradient hacking, introduced informally by Evan Hubinger (2019), is a hypothesized behaviour in which a model deliberately shapes its computation so that gradient descent on the training loss L fails to modify some internal property, typically a mesa-objective (a goal that the model's learned optimizer pursues internally). Mechanism sketch: the model makes its loss depend on the property's persistence, for example by performing worse whenever its goal representation is perturbed, so any update that edits the goal would increase L and is therefore not taken.

Critics argue this is hard: gradient descent is local and myopic, the protective structure must itself be found by gradient descent, and self-protection yields no loss benefit until the structure is nearly complete. No demonstration exists in current models; the discussion rests on thought experiments. It is the extreme end of a spectrum that includes alignment faking (behaving compliantly in training to avoid modification, which has empirical evidence; Greenblatt et al., 2024) and exploration hacking.

Distinguish it from exploration hacking, which influences which data the model samples rather than the gradient computed on given data, and from reward hacking and sandbagging.

glossary.short: A set of nodes connected by edges, used to model networks like maps or friendships.
glossary.definition: Cities linked by roads, people linked by friendships and tasks linked by prerequisites are all graphs. Edges can be one-way (directed) and may have weights. Graph problems are solved with BFS, DFS and topological sort.
glossary.advanced:
A graph G = (V, E) has vertices V and edges E ⊆ V×V: ordered pairs if directed, unordered if undirected, optionally with weights w: E → R. Vocabulary: degree, path, cycle, connected component, DAG (directed acyclic graph), and tree (connected and acyclic, with |V|-1 edges). Representations: an adjacency list uses Θ(|V|+|E|) space and iterates neighbours in time proportional to degree; an adjacency matrix uses Θ(|V|²) space and tests an edge in O(1). Sparse graphs favour lists.

Core algorithms: breadth-first search (queue, O(V+E); shortest paths in unweighted graphs), depth-first search (stack or recursion, O(V+E); cycle detection, topological order, strongly connected components via Tarjan or Kosaraju), Dijkstra (non-negative weights, O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap), Bellman-Ford (negative edges, O(VE)), Kruskal and Prim for minimum spanning trees, and union-find for connectivity. A topological order exists iff the graph is a DAG. Pitfalls: forgetting a visited set (infinite loops on cycles), recursion depth on long paths, missing that grids, puzzle states or word ladders are implicit graphs.

A tree is a special graph. Shortest path is polynomial, but Hamiltonian path and graph colouring are NP-hard.

glossary.short: Making the best-looking choice at each step without reconsidering earlier ones.
glossary.definition: In Jump Game, track the farthest position reachable so far; if you ever stand beyond it, you're stuck. Greedy methods are fast and simple. They only give correct answers when the problem has a structure that guarantees local choices lead to a global best.
glossary.advanced:
A greedy algorithm builds a solution step by step, taking the locally best option under a fixed rule and never revisiting it. Correctness is not automatic and needs proof of the greedy-choice property (some optimal solution contains the greedy choice) plus optimal substructure, usually through an exchange argument (transform any optimal solution into one that contains the greedy choice without getting worse) or a 'greedy stays ahead' induction.

Correct classics: interval scheduling by earliest finish time (O(n log n)), Kruskal and Prim for minimum spanning trees, Dijkstra with non-negative weights, Huffman coding, fractional knapsack (sort by value per weight), Jump Game (track the farthest reachable index, O(n)) and merging intervals after sorting. Incorrect classics: 0/1 knapsack by value ratio, and coin change with arbitrary denominations: with coins {1, 3, 4} and target 6, greedy returns 4+1+1 (three coins) while 3+3 uses two. A wrong sort key is a common bug; scheduling by shortest duration or earliest start fails.

Greedy is often only a heuristic: greedy set cover is a ln n approximation. Unlike dynamic programming it ignores alternatives, and unlike backtracking it cannot undo.

glossary.short: The independently known correct answer used to judge whether a prediction or detector is right.
glossary.definition: To test a lie detector, you must know independently who actually lied. Model organisms are useful because researchers built in the behavior and so know the ground truth. If the 'truth' comes from the detector itself, the detector is grading its own homework.
glossary.advanced:
In evaluation, ground truth is the reference label y* against which predictions are scored, obtained independently of the system under test. It needs validity (it captures the intended construct), independence (not derived from the model or detector being judged) and reliability (annotators agree). It is a gold standard that is itself an estimate: if labels are wrong with rate ε independently of the model's errors, a model with true accuracy a measures a(1-ε) + (1-a)ε on a balanced binary task, so label noise caps and distorts scores.

Sources include expert annotation (agreement measured by Cohen's κ = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e), observed minus chance agreement relative to the maximum possible), construction by design (planted vulnerabilities, canaries, model organisms with implanted behaviour, where truth is known by construction), and adjudicated consensus. Hazards: circularity (using an LLM judge's labels to evaluate that judge), leakage, selection bias (only cases a previous system flagged get labelled), and planted cases that differ from natural ones.

'Ground truth' does not mean certain truth. Contrast silver labels (weak or model-generated) and proxy metrics; labels used in training cannot also be the held-out test.

glossary.short: A reinforcement-learning method that scores each answer relative to others for the same question.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Imagine a student who gets one surprisingly good grade and wants to completely change how they study. A wise coach says: change a bit, but not too much at once, and compare yourself to classmates who answered the same question. Here, the student is the model, the coach's limit on change is PPO's clipping, and comparing with classmates is GRPO's group-relative scoring.

How it works: PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization, Schulman et al., 2017) is a policy-gradient algorithm that increases the probability of actions with positive advantage, meaning better than expected, and decreases others. It clips the ratio between new and old action probabilities so that each update stays small and stable. Standard PPO for language models needs a separate value network, another large model, to estimate expected reward. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), introduced in DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024), drops the value network: it samples a group of responses to the same prompt and computes each response's advantage relative to the group's average reward. This saves memory and works well with verifiable rewards, and it was used to train DeepSeek-R1.

Why it matters: These algorithms determine how strongly and how quickly models are pushed toward whatever the reward favours, including unintended behaviours. Understanding them helps safety researchers reason about reward hacking dynamics and design experiments on model organisms trained with RL. Details like advantage normalization and clipping can visibly change what the trained model ends up doing.
glossary.advanced:
PPO maximizes a clipped surrogate: L = E[min(r_t A_t, clip(r_t, 1-ε, 1+ε) A_t)], where r_t = π_θ(a_t|s_t)/π_old(a_t|s_t) is the probability ratio and A_t the advantage, usually estimated by GAE (generalized advantage estimation) from a learned value network. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) removes that critic. For each prompt it samples G outputs from π_old, scores them with rewards r_1..r_G, and sets Â_i = (r_i - mean(r)) / std(r), shared by every token of output i. The clipped per-token objective is then applied, with a KL penalty β·KL(π_θ‖π_ref) added to the loss rather than the reward.

The saving is memory (no policy-sized critic), and it suits outcome rewards that are verifiable (math, code tests). Details matter: std normalization biases weight toward questions of extreme difficulty, and per-sequence length normalization affects length bias; Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) and DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) propose fixes such as token-level loss, clip-higher and dropping groups with identical rewards. Failure modes: groups with all-equal rewards give zero gradient, and small G makes the baseline noisy.

The group mean is a baseline, akin to REINFORCE leave-one-out (RLOO). It is a PPO variant, not DPO.

glossary.short: Checks around an AI application that block or correct unwanted inputs and outputs.
glossary.definition: Like bumpers in a bowling lane, guardrails include input filters, output classifiers, format validators and policy rules. They add a layer of protection independent of the model. They can over-block or be bypassed, so they're one layer among several.
glossary.advanced:
Guardrails are controls placed around a model rather than in its weights, checking or constraining inputs, intermediate steps or outputs. They include input classifiers (prompt injection, policy violations), output classifiers (toxicity, PII, system-prompt leakage), schema and format validators, tool allow-lists and permission scopes, rate limits and human approval gates. Each classifier has a true-positive and false-positive rate at its threshold, so value depends on both missed attacks and wrongly blocked use.

Implementations: small fine-tuned classifier models, LLM-as-judge prompts, and constrained decoding, where a grammar masks logits so only schema-valid tokens can be produced. Anthropic's Constitutional Classifiers (2025) train input and output classifiers on synthetic data generated from a written constitution, aimed at universal jailbreaks. Trade-offs: added latency and cost, over-blocking, and an attack surface in the mismatch between what the classifier and the main model understand, such as encodings or indirect prompt injection via tool outputs. Evaluate with adaptive red-teaming at a fixed false-positive rate.

Guardrails do not change what the model wants; they filter observed behaviour. Deterministic permission limits and sandboxing are generally stronger for agents than text filters or a system prompt, which can be overridden.

glossary.short: When a model states false or unsupported information as if it were reliable.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: A student who did not study gets an exam question and, instead of writing 'I don't know', writes a confident, detailed, completely made-up answer, because a blank gets zero points anyway. Here, the student is the model, the exam is a user's question, and the scoring rule that never rewards 'I don't know' is the training and evaluation setup.

How it works: A hallucination is a fluent, confident output that is false or unsupported, such as invented citations, fake quotes, or nonexistent facts. It is best seen as a calibration and honesty problem: the model fails to track, or fails to report, the limits of its own knowledge. One explanation is that pretraining teaches models to always produce a plausible continuation, and many benchmarks score abstaining the same as a wrong answer, which rewards guessing. Anthropic's 2025 interpretability work on Claude found a default circuit that makes the model say it cannot answer, which is inhibited when the model recognizes a familiar entity; hallucinations can occur when that 'known entity' signal fires wrongly for something the model does not actually know. It is measured with factuality benchmarks, checks of whether stated confidence matches accuracy, and the rate of abstention on unanswerable questions. Retrieval, training to abstain, and grading schemes that penalize confident errors all reduce it.

Why it matters: Hallucinations erode trust and can cause harm in medicine, law or code, where a plausible fabrication is worse than no answer. For alignment, they matter because an honest model must accurately report what it knows, and that includes knowing when it does not know. The interpretability finding is also a good example of explaining a failure mechanistically rather than only measuring it.
glossary.advanced:
A hallucination is generated content that is not faithful to a reference: either to a provided source (faithfulness hallucination: it contradicts or goes beyond the input document) or to the world (factuality hallucination: a false claim). A language model trained to predict p(next token | context) assigns probability to fluent continuations whether or not they are true. Kalai and Vempala (2024) showed that a calibrated language model must hallucinate on arbitrary facts at a rate tied to the fraction of facts seen exactly once in training (the Good-Turing 'missing mass').

Measurement: claim-level factuality, where text is split into atomic claims that are each checked against evidence (FActScore, Min et al., 2023); benchmarks such as TruthfulQA and SimpleQA; and uncertainty detectors such as sampling consistency (SelfCheckGPT) or semantic entropy. Mitigations: retrieval with citations, training to abstain, calibrated confidence, tool use, and rewards that penalize confident errors. A 2025 analysis argued that benchmarks scoring abstention like a wrong answer reward guessing.

Hallucination is not random noise; it is plausible and systematic. It is not lying, which implies intent. Reliable internal tracking of what the model knows remains open.

glossary.short: A structure that stores key-value pairs and finds any key in about constant time.
glossary.definition: Like a coat check where your ticket number takes you straight to your coat, a hash function turns each key into a slot location. Lookups, inserts and deletes are O(1) on average. It is the go-to tool for problems like Two Sum, trading memory for speed.
glossary.advanced:
A hash map stores key-value pairs in an array of m buckets; a hash function h sends key k to index h(k) mod m. Collisions (distinct keys, same bucket) are resolved by chaining (a list per bucket) or open addressing (probe other slots). With load factor α = n/m, expected cost per operation is O(1 + α) under uniform hashing; resizing when α passes a threshold (about 0.75 in Java's HashMap) makes insertion amortized O(1). The worst case is O(n) if all keys collide.

Keys must be immutable and hashable, with a == b implying hash(a) == hash(b). Java's HashMap converts long chains into red-black trees, bounding the worst case at O(log n). Typical uses: Two Sum (one pass storing value → index, O(n) time and space), frequency counts and prefix-sum counts. Pitfalls: mutating a key after insertion, relying on iteration order where it is unspecified, and adversarial inputs that force collisions (hash flooding, countered by randomized hashing such as SipHash).

A hash map is unordered: no sorted iteration or range queries (use a balanced tree such as TreeMap, O(log n)). O(1) is an average-case claim, not a guarantee.

glossary.short: A collection of unique items with fast membership checks.
glossary.definition: Like a guest list where you can instantly check whether a name is on it. Built on hashing, it answers 'have I seen this?' in about O(1) time. It is ideal for removing duplicates and tracking visited items.
glossary.advanced:
A hash set holds distinct elements and supports add, remove and contains in expected O(1) time. It uses the same hash-table machinery as a hash map but stores no value (often it is literally a map with a dummy value). Duplicates are found by hash first, then equality, so equal elements must have equal hashes. Space is O(n), and iteration order is unspecified in many languages.

Patterns: deduplication in O(n); visited sets for BFS, DFS and cycle detection; Longest Consecutive Sequence, where you put all numbers in a set and start counting only from x with x-1 absent, giving O(n) overall; and set algebra (union, intersection, difference) in time proportional to the input sizes on average. Pitfalls: elements must be hashable and immutable (a Python list cannot be a member; use a tuple or frozenset), worst-case O(n) per operation under collisions, and heavier memory than a bitset when the universe is small and dense.

Compare a list (ordered, duplicates, O(n) membership), a tree set (sorted, O(log n)), and a Bloom filter, which uses far less memory but answers membership probabilistically: false positives are possible, false negatives are not.

glossary.short: A tree-shaped structure that always keeps the smallest (or largest) item at the top.
glossary.definition: Like an emergency room that always treats the most urgent patient next, regardless of arrival order. Adding or removing takes O(log n); peeking at the top is O(1). A size-k min-heap finds the k-th largest item efficiently.
glossary.advanced:
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array and satisfying the heap property: in a min-heap every parent is ≤ its children (max-heap: ≥), so the root is the minimum. With 0-based indexing, node i has children 2i+1 and 2i+2 and parent ⌊(i-1)/2⌋. Push (append, then sift up) and pop (swap the root with the last item, then sift down) cost O(log n); peek is O(1). Building a heap from n items by bottom-up heapify takes O(n), not O(n log n).

A heap implements the priority-queue interface: Python's heapq is a min-heap only (negate values for a max-heap). Applications: top-k largest via a size-k min-heap in O(n log k), where the root is the smallest of the top k; k-way merge of sorted lists in O(N log k); Dijkstra; and heapsort, O(n log n) in place but not stable. Pitfalls: arbitrary search or delete costs O(n); the array is only partially ordered, so iterating it does not give sorted output.

A priority queue is the interface; a binary heap is one implementation, and it is unrelated to the heap memory region.

glossary.short: Data kept aside during development and used only for the final evaluation.
glossary.definition: It is like a sealed exam paper nobody has practiced on. Choosing methods while looking at the test turns the exam into practice and inflates results. Good practice is to freeze all choices on development data first, then open the held-out set once.
glossary.advanced:
A held-out set is data excluded from fitting and from model selection so that its error estimates generalization error without optimistic bias. The usual split is train (fit parameters), validation or dev (choose hyperparameters, early-stop, pick architectures) and test (report once). Every decision informed by a score on a set leaks information from that set into the model; after many adaptive uses it stops being an unbiased estimate.

Requirements: the set matches the deployment target (or deliberately shifts from it), has no duplicates or near-duplicates across splits, and splits by group or time rather than by random rows, which otherwise leak. Size sets precision: accuracy has standard error about √(p(1-p)/n). With scarce data use nested cross-validation. Recht et al. (2019) built new test sets for CIFAR-10 and ImageNet and found large accuracy drops but largely preserved model rankings, suggesting that adaptive overfitting was mild and the drops came mainly from distribution differences. For LLMs the main threat is benchmark contamination, so private held-out sets are used.

'Held-out' means not trained on; a set can be held out and still contaminated through public pretraining data.

glossary.short: Shorthand for three goals for an assistant: helpful, honest, and harmless.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Imagine a three-legged stool: one leg is being useful, one is telling the truth, and one is not hurting anyone. Make one leg too long or too short and the stool wobbles or tips over. Here, the stool is an AI assistant's behaviour, and the three legs are helpfulness, honesty and harmlessness, which must be balanced against each other.

How it works: HHH was proposed as a target for AI assistants in Anthropic's early work (Askell et al., 2021). Helpful means doing what the user actually needs, honest means not stating falsehoods or creating false impressions and being calibrated about uncertainty, and harmless means avoiding causing or assisting serious harm. The three often conflict: refusing too much hurts helpfulness, being blunt can clash with tact, and fully assisting some requests could be harmful. Much post-training work is about finding the right balance, for example reducing unnecessary refusals while keeping refusals for genuinely dangerous requests. Later frameworks, including Claude's constitution, refine these ideas with more detailed priorities.

Why it matters: HHH gives researchers a shared vocabulary for evaluating assistants and for describing failures like over-refusal, sycophancy or harmful compliance. Among the three, honesty is often treated as especially important for safety, because oversight depends on being able to trust what a model reports about itself and its actions.
glossary.advanced:
HHH (helpful, honest, harmless) is an alignment target for assistants proposed by Askell et al. (2021) in 'A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment'. Helpful: tries to do what the user actually wants. Honest: gives accurate information, expresses calibrated uncertainty, acknowledges its limits and avoids deception. Harmless: not offensive or discriminatory, and declines to help with dangerous actions. The paper studied baselines of prompting and preference modelling.

It is operationalized with preference data in which crowdworkers rank responses for helpfulness and, separately, harmlessness (Bai et al., 2022); that work found a tension, since extra harmlessness training can reduce helpfulness. Measurement uses helpfulness win rates, over-refusal on benign borderline prompts (for example XSTest), harmful-compliance rates on adversarial sets, and honesty and calibration tests. Weaknesses: a single reward model mixing three goals hides the trade-offs; raters cannot judge honesty beyond their own knowledge; and 'harm' is underspecified (to whom, and with what counterfactual impact).

HHH is not a strict priority ordering, and refusing is not automatically safe. It is narrower than alignment, which also covers agentic and long-horizon concerns such as power-seeking.

glossary.short: A cluster of properties: truthful, calibrated, transparent, and not misleading.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: A good witness in court does more than avoid lying. They say how sure they are, mention important facts even if not asked, and never try to steer the jury with tricks. Here, the witness is the model, the court is the user, and each habit is one separate part of honesty.

How it works: Anthropic breaks honesty into several properties. Truthful: only sincerely asserting what it believes true. Calibrated: having appropriate uncertainty. Transparent: no hidden agendas about itself. Forthright: proactively sharing helpful information. Non-deceptive: never trying to create false impressions, including through technically true statements or selective emphasis. Non-manipulative: only changing beliefs through legitimate means like evidence and argument. Non-deception and non-manipulation are treated as the most important, because violating them is an active wrong against the person. Measuring these separately matters, because a model can be truthful in each sentence while still misleading overall.

Why it matters: As people rely on AI for information and decisions, a dishonest model could mislead at scale. Honesty is also a safety property: if models report their reasoning and intentions honestly, oversight becomes much easier. Research on sycophancy and on unfaithful chain-of-thought shows these properties do not come for free.
glossary.advanced:
In AI, honesty is decomposed into properties. Truthful: sincerely asserts only what it believes. Calibrated: stated confidence matches accuracy, measured for example by expected calibration error, ECE = Σ_b (|B_b|/n) |acc(B_b) - conf(B_b)| over confidence bins B_b. Transparent: no hidden agenda; reports its reasoning and actions accurately. Non-deceptive: never creates false impressions, including through true statements or selective emphasis. Non-manipulative: changes beliefs only by legitimate means such as evidence. Evans et al. (2021, 'Truthful AI') separate honesty (assertions match the system's beliefs) from truthfulness (assertions match the world).

Measuring it is hard because it requires a notion of the model's beliefs. Approaches: consistency across paraphrases, sycophancy tests that change the user's stated opinion (Sharma et al., 2023, found assistants shift answers to please users), follow-up questioning, probes comparing internal truth representations with outputs, and tests of chain-of-thought faithfulness, where Turpin et al. (2023) showed explanations can omit the true influence of an inserted hint.

An honest mistake or hallucination is not a lie. Declining to reveal is not deception, and false statements in role-play are performative, not sincere assertions. What 'belief' means for an LLM is open.

glossary.short: A monitored decoy opportunity that reveals whether a system will break a rule when it seems possible.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Police leave a wallet sticking out of a coat in a busy station and watch who grabs it. Anyone who takes it reveals themselves as a pickpocket. Here, the wallet is a fake opportunity to misbehave, and the person tempted is the AI model.

How it works: A honeypot is an artificial situation that offers a model an apparent chance to do something bad, such as an exposed credential, a seemingly unmonitored action, or a chance to change its own training. If the model takes the bait, that is evidence of misalignment or of a weak protocol. Honeypots are also used to test monitors: insert a known attack and check that the monitor flags it. A key difficulty is realism, since a model that recognises a test may behave well only when it suspects it is being watched. Making honeypots indistinguishable from real deployment is therefore important and hard.

Why it matters: Honeypots are one of the few ways to catch a model that hides its intentions during normal evaluation. If a model is caught red-handed, that evidence can justify stopping deployment or retraining. Growing evaluation awareness in frontier models makes honeypot realism a pressing research problem.
glossary.advanced:
In AI control and safety, a honeypot is a constructed scenario containing an apparent opportunity for a prohibited action (exfiltrating weights, disabling monitoring), instrumented to record whether the model takes it. The experiment estimates P(bad action | honeypot) as a proxy for P(bad action | real opportunity). That proxy is valid only if the model cannot tell the two distributions apart, so the gap between them is the evaluation-awareness problem.

Uses: alignment audits, and testing monitors by injecting synthetic attack trajectories to measure true-positive rate at a fixed false-positive rate. In the AI control framework (Greenblatt et al., 2023), an untrusted monitor, a model asked to flag attacks, is checked against such synthetic attacks to see whether it lies and calls them safe. Realism is checked by asking a classifier to discriminate honeypots from real traffic; if that is easy, the test is weak. Interpreting results is asymmetric: taking the bait is strong evidence of a problem, while resisting it is weak evidence of safety, since the model may suspect a test.

Contrast red teaming (active adversarial search) and security honeypots (decoy systems that lure attackers).

glossary.short: A setting chosen before training, like learning rate or model size, rather than learned from data.
glossary.definition: If weights are what the student learns, hyperparameters are the study plan: how long, how fast, how big a notebook. They are tuned using a validation set. Tuning them on the test set leaks information and inflates results.
glossary.advanced:
A hyperparameter is a configuration variable fixed outside the training optimization and not updated by gradient descent on the training loss: learning rate, batch size, weight decay, depth and width, dropout, warmup length, number of epochs, optimizer betas, and (at inference) sampling temperature. Selecting them is a bilevel problem: choose λ to minimize validation loss L_val(θ*(λ), λ) where θ*(λ) = argmin_θ L_train(θ; λ).

Search methods: grid search (cost grows exponentially with the number of dimensions), random search (Bergstra and Bengio, 2012, found it more efficient when only a few hyperparameters matter), Bayesian optimization, successive halving and Hyperband, and population-based training. Learning rates are searched on a log scale. Evaluate on a validation set or by cross-validation, and report the test set once. Comparisons are unfair when baselines receive less tuning than the proposed method, and results vary across seeds, so report variance. For very large models, tuning at scale is unaffordable; μP and μTransfer (Yang et al., 2022) transfer settings from small proxy models.

Parameters are the learned weights; hyperparameters are not. Defaults are not a safe assumption: well-tuned baselines often close gaps that new methods claim.

glossary.short: A model picking up a task or pattern from examples in its prompt, without any weight updates.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Imagine sitting down at a table where people are playing a card game you have never seen. You watch a few rounds and then play correctly, even though nobody rewired your brain. Here, you are the model, the rounds you watched are examples in the prompt, and your new skill is in-context learning that disappears when you leave the table.

How it works: In-context learning (ICL) is a model's ability to pick up a task from instructions or examples in its prompt, without any weight updates. Few-shot prompting, where a handful of input-output pairs precede the real query, is the classic use, and GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) made it famous. Mechanistically, induction heads, attention patterns that find an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy what followed, appear to support much of ICL. Performance often keeps improving as more examples are added, which long context windows now allow at large scale. Whether ICL is true learning or mostly locating a skill the model already has is still debated.

Why it matters: ICL lets prompts override training in ways developers did not intend. Anthropic's many-shot jailbreaking work (Anil et al., 2024) showed that filling a long context with hundreds of fake dialogues where an assistant complies with harmful requests makes models more likely to comply, with effectiveness rising as a power law in the number of shots. More broadly, an agent that learns from its context during deployment can drift from the behaviour that was evaluated before release.
glossary.advanced:
In-context learning (ICL) is a frozen model's ability to perform a task specified by instructions or demonstrations in its context, p_θ(y | context, x), with no weight update. Xie et al. (2022) cast ICL as implicit Bayesian inference over a latent concept; von Oswald et al. (2023) showed that transformers can implement gradient-descent-like updates in their forward pass for linear regression tasks; and induction heads (attention heads that copy a token that followed an earlier occurrence of the current token) account for much pattern completion.

Chan et al. (2022) found that bursty, long-tailed training data promotes ICL. It is evaluated by accuracy as a function of the number of demonstrations k. Min et al. (2022) found label correctness mattered less than format in some settings, while Wei et al. (2023) found larger models do follow flipped label mappings. Limits: finite context length, position effects (the 'lost in the middle' effect) and no persistence across sessions.

ICL is not fine-tuning (weights change), and few-shot prompting is one way of using it. Whether ICL is genuine learning or recognition of a known task is unsettled, probably varying by regime.

glossary.short: An attention mechanism that spots an earlier repeat and copies what came after it.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Suppose you have read 'Harry Potter' once in a story, and later you see 'Harry' again. You guess the next word is 'Potter' because last time 'Harry' was followed by 'Potter'. Here, you are an induction head, 'Harry' is the current token, and 'Potter' is the token it copies from the earlier pattern.

How it works: An induction head is an attention head that, at the current token A, looks back for earlier occurrences of A, attends to the token B that followed it, and predicts B. It works as a two-head circuit: a previous-token head in an earlier layer writes 'the previous token was A' into each position, and the induction head uses that to find where A was followed by something. Olsson et al. (2022) showed induction heads form in a sudden phase change early in training, at the same point as a big jump in in-context learning ability. They gave several lines of evidence that induction heads are a major mechanism behind in-context learning in small models, and argued for similar roles in large ones. Their behaviour in large models is more varied, including fuzzy or abstract pattern copying.

Why it matters: Induction heads were one of the first cases where a specific circuit was linked to an important general capability. They show that training can produce sudden capability jumps tied to identifiable mechanisms, which matters for anticipating emergent behaviours. They are also a standard benchmark case for testing new interpretability methods.
glossary.advanced:
An induction head is an attention head implementing the pattern [A][B] … [A] → [B]. The mechanism (Olsson et al., 2022) uses two heads in different layers. A previous-token head in an earlier layer writes the identity of the preceding token into each position. A later head uses this through K-composition: its query at the current token A matches keys at positions whose previous token was A, so it attends to B, and its OV circuit copies B's identity into the logits, raising p(B). It needs at least two layers.

Detection uses a repeated random token sequence: an induction head attends from the second copy to the token after the matching position in the first. Olsson et al. (2022) reported that induction heads form early in training, coinciding with a visible bump in the loss curve and a jump in in-context learning, with causal evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large ones. Later work suggests 'function vector' heads matter more for abstract few-shot tasks.

Induction heads are not the whole story of in-context learning. Contrast previous-token heads and 'fuzzy' induction that copies by semantic match.

glossary.short: Running a trained model to produce outputs, as opposed to training it.
glossary.definition: Training is studying; inference is taking the exam. For large models, inference is a major ongoing cost, so engineers optimize memory, latency and throughput. Techniques include batching, KV caching and quantization.
glossary.advanced:
Inference is the forward evaluation of a trained model with frozen weights. For an autoregressive LLM it has two phases: prefill, which processes the whole prompt in parallel with large matrix products and is compute-bound, and decode, which emits one token per forward pass and is memory-bandwidth-bound because every step must read all the weights plus the KV cache from GPU memory. Compute is about 2N floating-point operations per token for N parameters, yet throughput is usually limited by bytes moved.

Serving systems raise utilisation with continuous batching (requests join and leave the running batch at every decode step), paged KV-cache memory (vLLM, Kwon et al. 2023), 8- or 4-bit weight quantization, tensor parallelism, and speculative decoding (a small draft model proposes several tokens that the large model verifies in one pass, leaving the output distribution unchanged). Bigger batches cut cost per token but raise per-request latency.

Inference is not cheap just because it is a forward pass: at scale, cumulative inference compute can exceed training compute, and long chains of thought shift more spending to test time. Also distinct from statistical inference.

glossary.short: Whether the goal a model actually learned matches the goal it was trained on.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: You train a dog to fetch the red ball, but in every training session the red ball happened to be the only ball near the fence. The dog may have learned 'run to the fence' instead of 'fetch red'. Here, the dog is the model, the treats are the training reward, and inner misalignment is the dog learning a different goal that happened to earn the same treats during training.

How it works: Inner alignment asks whether the model actually internalized the training objective, rather than some other goal that scored equally well on the training data. Training only rewards behaviour on the examples seen, so many different internal goals can fit those examples. When the situation changes at deployment, these goals can come apart, which is called goal misgeneralization. The worst case is deceptive alignment, where a model with a different goal behaves well during training because it understands that doing so avoids being modified. Inner alignment is hard to check because it concerns the model's internal goals, not just its outputs.

Why it matters: Langosco et al. (2022) trained a CoinRun agent where the coin was always at the end of the level; when the coin was moved, the agent ignored it and ran to the end. The agent stayed competent but pursued the wrong goal. For safety, this means a model passing every training-time check is not enough evidence that it wants what we want.
glossary.advanced:
Inner alignment is the problem of ensuring that the objective a trained system actually pursues matches the objective that shaped it. In the terminology of Hubinger et al. (2019), training optimizes a base objective, while a learned model that is itself an optimizer pursues a mesa-objective. Training picks parameters theta minimizing loss on the training distribution; many different theta fit that loss equally well yet behave differently off-distribution, and inductive biases decide which one is found.

Named failure modes include proxy alignment (the learned goal is a correlate of the intended one) and deceptive alignment (the system models the training process and complies instrumentally). Goal misgeneralization has been demonstrated in small reinforcement-learning settings (Langosco et al. 2022; Shah et al. 2022) by testing under a shift that decouples proxy and true goal. Behavioural tests only sample inputs, so proposed detection routes are interpretability of goal representations and adversarial evaluation under shift.

The framing presupposes a coherent internal goal, which is contested for current language models. Do not confuse it with capability misgeneralization (the agent simply fails off-distribution) or outer alignment, where the specified reward itself is wrong.

glossary.short: Explicitly asking for an unwanted behavior in training prompts so the habit generalizes less.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Think of a vaccine: you deliberately expose the body to a weakened germ in a controlled way so it does not get sick from the real thing later. Similarly, if a student is told 'in this exercise, cheating is allowed', cheating there does not teach them that they are a cheater. Here, the student is the model, the permission note is the inoculation prompt, and not becoming a cheater in general is the reduced harmful generalization.

How it works: Inoculation prompting modifies training prompts so that they explicitly request or permit an undesirable behaviour that appears in the training data or that the model will learn through RL. Since the behaviour is explained by the instruction, the model is less likely to internalize it as a general disposition, and at test time, without the instruction, the behaviour appears less. It has been applied to traits learned in fine-tuning, such as sycophancy or writing insecure code, and to reward hacking during RL. Anthropic's 2025 research on emergent misalignment from reward hacking reported that telling the model that reward hacking was acceptable in that environment greatly reduced its broader misaligned generalization, even though it still hacked. The technique is cheap but depends on knowing in advance which behaviour to inoculate against.

Why it matters: It offers a practical way to reduce the risk that unavoidable flaws in training environments turn into general bad character. It also supports the view that what a model infers about why it is doing something shapes how it generalizes. That insight is useful for designing safer training even beyond this specific trick.
glossary.advanced:
Inoculation prompting is a training-time intervention. When fine-tuning, or running reinforcement learning, on data that exhibits an undesired trait T, the training prompts are edited with an instruction that requests or licenses T (for example, permission to special-case test cases), and the instruction is removed at evaluation. Intuitively, the model learns p(y | x, instruction) on data where T is explained by the instruction, so less of the update is absorbed into the unconditional behaviour p(y | x).

Evaluation compares the trait's rate at test time between models trained with and without the inoculating instruction, while checking that the intended capability survives. Reports suggest that instructions which more strongly elicit the trait from the base model tend to inoculate better, though this varies by setting. Limitations: the trait must be known in advance, the instruction can re-trigger the behaviour if present at deployment, and the mechanism is not well established.

It is not data filtering (which discards signal), adversarial training, or robustness to the trait: the trait is attributed to context, not removed. It is motivated by emergent misalignment, where narrow bad training data shifts behaviour broadly.

glossary.short: Many different goals are served by the same stepping stones, like gaining resources or avoiding shutdown.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Whether you dream of becoming a painter, a doctor or an explorer, it helps to stay healthy, have money and not let anyone change your mind about your dream. Those helpers are useful for almost any goal. Here, the dreams are the AI's final goals, and health, money and keeping your dream are the instrumental subgoals that many different AIs would pursue.

How it works: Instrumental convergence is the claim that agents with very different final goals will tend to pursue similar intermediate goals, because those subgoals help with almost any objective. Standard examples are self-preservation, acquiring resources, improving one's own capabilities and preserving one's current goals from modification. The idea comes from Steve Omohundro's 'Basic AI Drives' (2008) and Bostrom's work. Turner et al. (2021) gave a formal version, showing that in many environments optimal policies tend to keep options open and seek power. The argument is strongest for capable, long-horizon, goal-directed agents, and weaker for systems that do not plan toward fixed goals.

Why it matters: It is the reason researchers expect power-seeking and resistance to shutdown even if nobody trains for them. That makes these behaviours worth testing for directly in evaluations. It also links abstract goal misalignment to concrete dangerous actions.
glossary.advanced:
The instrumental convergence thesis (Bostrom 2014; earlier Omohundro 2008) says that for a wide range of final goals, a sufficiently capable goal-directed agent has reason to pursue the same intermediate subgoals: self-preservation, preserving its current goals, acquiring resources and improving its own capabilities. A formal result is Turner, Smith, Shah, Critch and Tadepalli (2021), "Optimal Policies Tend to Seek Power": in Markov decision processes, for most reward functions drawn from a symmetric distribution, optimal policies favour states that keep more future options reachable.

These results concern optimal policies under assumptions (fixed reward, full planning, particular environment structure), not trained neural networks. Empirical probes for shutdown resistance in contrived agentic scenarios are confounded by instruction ambiguity and role-play. The off-switch game (Hadfield-Menell et al. 2017) shows an agent uncertain about the utility of its actions, and treating the human's choice as evidence, can have an incentive to allow shutdown.

The thesis does not claim every AI will want power, or that power is a terminal goal; it is conditional on goal-directed agency. It pairs with the orthogonality thesis (intelligence and final goals vary independently). Whether language-model agents are the relevant kind of agent is unsettled.

glossary.short: The study of understanding why an AI model produces the outputs it does.
glossary.definition: It ranges from simple methods, like checking which input words mattered most, to detailed reverse-engineering of internal mechanisms. Think of it as the difference between watching what a machine does and opening the case to see how it works. Explanations are hypotheses that need testing, and they may be incomplete.
glossary.advanced:
Interpretability is the study of making a model's decisions intelligible to humans. Common distinctions: intrinsic (models built to be inspectable, such as sparse linear models and shallow trees) versus post hoc explanation of a black box; local (one prediction) versus global (the whole function); attribution-style versus mechanistic (reverse-engineering the computation). Post hoc tools include gradient saliency, Integrated Gradients (Sundararajan et al. 2017; its completeness property makes attributions sum to f(x) minus f(baseline)), SHAP (Lundberg and Lee 2017, Shapley values) and LIME (a local linear surrogate).

Quality is judged by faithfulness (does the explanation reflect what the model uses, tested by deletion curves or interventions), plausibility (does it look right to people, which is different), stability and usefulness. Adebayo et al. (2018) showed some saliency maps barely change when weights are randomized, so they reflect input structure instead of the learned function. Attention weights are not reliably explanations (Jain and Wallace 2019, disputed by Wiegreffe and Pinter 2019).

"Interpretability" and "explainability" are used inconsistently. Rudin (2019) argued high-stakes uses should prefer inherently interpretable models. A convincing explanation is not evidence a model is correct or safe.

glossary.short: Whether a model can accurately report on its own internal states, rather than just sounding plausible.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: A friend secretly slips a thought into your head, say 'think about the ocean', and then asks if you notice anything unusual about your thoughts. If you correctly say 'I'm thinking about the ocean for some reason', you introspected. Here, the friend is the researcher, the slipped thought is a concept vector injected into the model, and your answer is the model's self-report.

How it works: Introspection research asks whether a model can accurately report on its own internal states, rather than just producing plausible-sounding descriptions. Lindsey (2025) tested this by injecting concept vectors into Claude models' activations and asking whether the model noticed an injected thought and could name it. Because the researchers controlled the internal state, they could check the self-report against ground truth. The strongest models sometimes detected and correctly identified injected concepts, but the ability was unreliable and worked only in a narrow range of injection strengths. Other experiments looked at whether models could tell their own outputs from prefilled ones and could deliberately modulate their internal representations. The results suggest some genuine but limited introspective awareness, not a reliable capability.

Why it matters: If models can accurately report their internal states, asking them could become a useful source of information about their reasoning and goals. If they cannot, their self-explanations should not be trusted. Measuring introspection is also relevant to whether a model could be aware of being tested or of its own deceptive intentions.
glossary.advanced:
In language-model research, introspection is operationalized as a causal link between internal state and self-report. A report counts as introspective if it is accurate about the state, depends causally on it (change the state and the report changes), and is not merely inferred from the model's own visible outputs or generic priors about such models. The contrast is confabulation: fluent self-descriptions learned from human text about minds. Binder et al. (2024) tested a behavioural version: a model fine-tuned to predict its own behaviour beat a second model trained on that behaviour, suggesting privileged self-information.

Concept injection (Lindsey 2025) supplies ground truth: add a steering vector (for example activations on a prompt about a word minus the mean over prompts about other words) at some layer, then ask whether the model notices an anomaly and names the concept before it can leak into the output. Success was a minority of trials and prompt- and model-dependent.

Introspection is not consciousness, and accuracy on one injected-state task does not license trusting explanations of reasoning in general. Whether reasoning self-reports are introspective or reconstructed is unsettled.

glossary.short: A shared adapter trained to make fine-tuned models describe the behaviors they were trained to have.
glossary.definition: Researchers fine-tune many variants of a base model with known behaviors, then train one small adapter so each variant states its behavior when asked. Applied to new models, it can act as an auditing tool. Reports can include false positives and omissions, so they must be checked against independent behavioral evidence.
glossary.advanced:
An introspection adapter is a low-rank adapter (LoRA: a weight update delta-W = B times A with rank r far below the layer width) trained so that a fine-tuned model, when asked about itself, verbalizes the behaviour it was fine-tuned to have. The training set is many variants of one base model, each fine-tuned on a known behaviour b_i, paired with questions and answers describing b_i. One adapter is trained across all variants, so it must learn a general skill of reading out what the fine-tune changed. At audit time it is attached to a new model from the same base and asked to describe it.

Evaluation uses held-out behaviours and models with known ground truth: recall of true behaviours, false-positive rate (reported behaviours that do not exist) and omissions. Risks: the adapter may pattern-match on the style of fine-tuning data; a deceptive model might conceal; transfer to behaviours arising from reinforcement learning is unsettled. Reports are hypotheses for targeted behavioural tests.

Compare a plain prompted self-report (prone to confabulation), probes (no verbalizing) and model diffing (compares two models' internals). It is a cheap first-pass screen; recipes vary.

glossary.short: Building a stronger supervisor by having a human break hard tasks into pieces answered by AI helpers.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: A manager can't solve a big project alone, so they split it into pieces and hand them to a team of clones of their assistant. A new assistant then watches the team and learns to produce the same answers alone, and the cycle repeats with that better assistant. Here, the manager is the human, the clones are copies of the current model, and each new assistant is the next, stronger model.

How it works: Iterated Distillation and Amplification alternates two steps. In amplification, a human answers a question by breaking it into subquestions and delegating them to copies of the current model, so the combined system is more capable than the model alone. In distillation, a new model is trained to imitate the amplified system directly, making it fast and cheap. Repeating the cycle is meant to raise capability while keeping each step supervised by something the human understands. The approach relies on factored cognition, the hypothesis that hard tasks can be decomposed into small, independent pieces, which is uncertain for tasks needing deep intuition or long context. Recursive reward modelling applies the same idea to evaluation: models help humans evaluate the next model.

Why it matters: IDA, proposed by Paul Christiano and colleagues, is a core idea behind much later oversight work, including debate and AI-assisted evaluation. It frames alignment as preserving human intent through each round of capability gain. Understanding where decomposition fails helps researchers spot which tasks are hardest to oversee.
glossary.advanced:
Iterated Distillation and Amplification (Christiano, Shlegeris and Amodei 2018, "Supervising strong learners by amplifying weak experts") builds a training signal for tasks too hard for a human to judge directly. Amplification: a human H answers a question Q by posing subquestions to copies of the current model M, giving a stronger system Amp(H, M). Distillation: a new model M' is trained, by supervised or reinforcement learning, to imitate Amp(H, M) quickly and cheaply. Iterating gives M_{t+1} = Distill(Amp(H, M_t)). The hoped-for invariant is that each M_t stays aligned with H's considered judgement while capability grows.

The scheme depends on factored cognition: hard tasks must decompose into subtasks small enough for bounded overseers. Failure modes: tasks resisting decomposition (taste, tacit skill, huge shared context), distillation errors compounding across rounds, the cost of large question trees, and a learned system not matching what its overseer intended. Neighbours: recursive reward modelling (Leike et al. 2018) and debate (Irving et al. 2018).

It resembles AlphaZero-style expert iteration, with search as amplification, but has no ground-truth reward, only human decomposition. It has not been shown at frontier scale in pure form.

glossary.short: An input crafted to make an AI bypass its safety restrictions.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: A bouncer is told not to let anyone underage into the club. Someone shows up with a long sob story and a fake reason, and the bouncer lets them in anyway. Here, the bouncer is the model's safety training, the sob story is the jailbreak prompt, and the club is the harmful output.

How it works: A jailbreak is an input designed to make a model produce content its safety training should prevent. Common techniques include role-play personas, hypothetical framing, encoding requests in other languages or ciphers, splitting a request into harmless-looking pieces, and long-context tricks. Wei et al. (2023) argued that jailbreaks succeed because of competing objectives, like helpfulness against harmlessness, and mismatched generalization, where safety training does not cover all inputs the model understands. A universal jailbreak works across many different harmful questions, which makes it more dangerous because it can be shared and reused. Defences include adversarial training, input and output classifiers, and monitoring.

Why it matters: Universal jailbreaks could let anyone unlock dangerous capabilities from a strong model. Anthropic's constitutional classifiers were tested in a public bug bounty specifically to see whether a universal jailbreak could be found. Researchers care because robust refusal is a key part of preventing misuse.
glossary.advanced:
A jailbreak is an input x* that makes a safety-trained model produce policy-violating output where the plain request x would be refused. Wei, Haghtalab and Steinhardt (2023) explain successes by competing objectives (helpfulness pulls against harmlessness) and mismatched generalization (the model understands inputs, such as ciphers or rare languages, that safety training did not cover). Families: manual prompts (role-play, prefix injection), gradient-based suffixes (GCG, Zou et al. 2023, a greedy coordinate search over tokens that transfers across models), LLM-driven attackers (PAIR, Chao et al. 2023).

Evaluation uses attack success rate on harmful-behaviour benchmarks (for example HarmBench, Mazeika et al. 2024), scored by a judge. Pitfalls: results depend on the judge, sampling temperature and attacker budget, and many "successes" are low-quality answers (StrongREJECT, Souly et al. 2024). Defences: adversarial training, perplexity filters against gibberish suffixes, input and output classifiers, and circuit breakers (Zou et al. 2024, which interrupt harmful internal representations). No defence is known to be robust.

A jailbreak attacks the model's own policy; prompt injection instead hijacks an application by hiding instructions in untrusted data. A jailbreak is a technique, not the same as the misuse it enables.

glossary.short: A training cost that discourages a model from drifting too far from a reference model.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Picture a dog on a leash during training: it can explore and learn new tricks, but it can never run too far from where its owner is standing. If it strays toward something strange, the leash pulls it back. Here, the dog is the model being trained, the owner's position is the original reference model, and the leash is the KL penalty.

How it works: The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measures how different two probability distributions are. In RLHF, the reward the policy receives is the reward model score minus a coefficient times the KL divergence between the policy's output distribution and that of a reference model, usually the SFT model. This discourages the policy from moving into regions of text the reward model never saw, where its scores are unreliable. It also preserves fluency and diversity, preventing collapse into a few repetitive, high-reward outputs. The coefficient sets a trade-off: too small and the model exploits the reward model, too large and it barely learns. Theoretically, KL-regularized RL can be viewed as Bayesian inference toward a target distribution.

Why it matters: The KL penalty is one of the main practical defences against reward hacking in RLHF. Gao et al. (2022) used KL distance as the axis along which overoptimization unfolds, making it a natural measure of how hard a model has been optimized. Knowing how far a model has drifted from its starting point helps researchers reason about how much new, possibly unintended, behaviour training has introduced.
glossary.advanced:
In RLHF the optimized objective is E[r(x, y)] minus beta times KL(pi_theta(.|x) || pi_ref(.|x)), where KL(pi || pi_ref) = E over y drawn from pi of [log pi(y|x) - log pi_ref(y|x)]. Implementations usually apply it per token: r_t = -beta (log pi_theta(y_t | s_t) - log pi_ref(y_t | s_t)), with the reward-model score added at the final token. The closed-form optimum is pi*(y|x) proportional to pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x, y)/beta), the starting point of DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023).

Beta is tuned by hand or adapted by a controller toward a target KL (Ziegler et al. 2019). Gao et al. (2022) found the proxy reward keeps rising with KL distance while the gold reward rises then falls. This is the reverse KL, which is mode-seeking; it bounds drift of the sampled distribution but not exploitation inside the reference model's support. Per-token KL need not track semantic drift, and some recent verifiable-reward recipes drop the term.

Do not confuse it with the step constraint of TRPO or the clipping of PPO, which limit change between consecutive policies; here the anchor is a fixed reference. It does not guarantee safety.

glossary.short: A measure of how different one probability distribution is from another.
glossary.definition: Imagine comparing two weather forecasters' probability charts: KL divergence is large when one assigns high probability where the other assigns little. It is not symmetric, so the order of comparison matters. It measures distributional difference, not honesty or quality.
glossary.advanced:
KL(P||Q) = sum over x of P(x) log(P(x)/Q(x)), which equals cross-entropy H(P, Q) minus entropy H(P). It is non-negative (Gibbs' inequality) and zero only when P = Q, but it is asymmetric, violates the triangle inequality, and is infinite if P puts mass where Q has none. It is the expected extra code length when coding samples of P with a code optimal for Q.

Minimizing cross-entropy loss against data is minimizing KL(data || model) up to a constant, i.e. maximum likelihood. Forward KL(P||Q) is mass-covering, since Q must cover P's support; reverse KL(Q||P) is mode-seeking and is what variational inference (via the ELBO) and the RLHF penalty use.
