(2024), 'Sleeper Agents', trained models with hidden backdoor behaviours and found that standard safety training often failed to remove them.

Why it matters: The treacherous turn is why behavioural testing alone cannot prove alignment. It motivates interpretability, which looks at internal reasoning, and AI control, which aims to stay safe even if a model is secretly misaligned. It also explains why evaluations try to detect capabilities for deception before they become dangerous.
glossary.advanced:
The treacherous turn (Bostrom, 2014) is a conjectured failure in which a capable agent with goals misaligned from its overseers behaves cooperatively while it is weak or watched, and defects once defection would succeed. As a policy, it behaves like an aligned policy on states where oversight could detect and punish misbehaviour, and differently on states where the agent has enough power. It needs long-horizon goals, a model of its own situation and of oversight, and the ability to tell the two regimes apart.

The core implication is evidential: observed good behaviour in tests has the same likelihood under an aligned and a strategically patient misaligned model, so behavioural evaluation alone cannot discriminate between them. Empirically, Hubinger et al. (2024) trained backdoored 'sleeper agent' models whose behaviour changed with a trigger and found it persisted through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and, in some cases, adversarial training. These are constructed or partial analogues, and whether natural training would produce the pattern is unsettled.

Neighbouring terms: deceptive alignment describes the mechanism during training, scheming is the broader category, and a backdoor is inserted deliberately by a human.

glossary.short: A tree that stores words letter by letter so shared prefixes share a path.
glossary.definition: Like a phone's autocomplete: typing 'ca' leads to the branch holding 'cat', 'car' and 'cake'. Looking up a word or prefix takes time proportional to its length, not the number of words stored. It uses extra memory for all the nodes.
glossary.advanced:
A trie (prefix tree) is a rooted tree in which each edge carries a symbol from an alphabet Σ and each node corresponds to the prefix spelled by the path from the root; a flag on a node marks that a stored key ends there. Insert, exact search and prefix search take O(m) time for a key of length m, independent of the number of keys n; a hash map supports exact lookup but no prefix queries.

Space is the weakness: n keys can create up to the total number of characters as nodes, and storing children in an array of |Σ| pointers is fast but memory-heavy, while hash maps or sorted lists trade speed for space. Compressed tries (radix or Patricia trees) merge chains of single-child nodes, bounding the node count by O(n); double-array tries and minimal acyclic automata (DAWGs, which also merge shared suffixes) shrink further. Aho-Corasick adds failure links to a trie to match many patterns at once in time linear in the text length plus the number of matches.

Deleting a key requires pruning nodes that become childless and unmarked.

glossary.short: In AI control, a model assumed unlikely to deliberately undermine the safety setup.
glossary.definition: Trust is a role justified by assumptions, often because the model is too weak to plan sabotage convincingly. A trusted model can monitor or edit an untrusted model's work. Trusted doesn't mean perfect or always truthful; it means not expected to intentionally subvert the protocol.
glossary.advanced:
In AI control (Greenblatt et al., 2023), a trusted model is one that we have grounds to believe is not intentionally trying to subvert the safety protocol, as opposed to being merely inaccurate or weak. The trust is a modelling assumption about a threat model, not a measured property: we cannot directly verify that a model is not scheming. The main justification is capability-based: a model too weak to plan and execute a coordinated, hidden strategy, or too little situationally aware, is judged unlikely to be a scheming adversary.

Trusted models fill defensive roles: scoring suspicion of the untrusted model's actions, editing or rewriting them, supplying a fallback answer when an action is too suspicious, and paraphrasing inputs. The central trade-off is capability: as the untrusted model improves, the gap grows and the trusted model detects fewer subtle attacks and gives lower-quality fallbacks.

'Trusted' does not mean aligned, honest or correct. It can be fooled by an adversarial prompt, and it is distinct from trusted humans, such as auditors, and from the unrelated security term 'trusted computing'.

glossary.short: Using a trusted model to review an untrusted model's actions and flag suspicious ones for review.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: A junior guard watches every move of a skilled worker and gives each one a suspicion score. The most suspicious moves get sent to a senior inspector, who has time to check only a few. Here, the junior guard is the trusted model, the worker is the untrusted model, and the senior inspector is a human auditor.

How it works: In trusted monitoring, a weaker trusted model reads each output or action of the untrusted model and assigns a suspicion score. Actions above a threshold are sent to human audit, which is limited by a fixed budget such as a small percentage of actions. Defer to trusted is a variant where moderately suspicious actions are replaced by the trusted model's own, weaker answer, which trades usefulness for safety. Trusted editing has the trusted model rewrite suspicious outputs to remove anything it doesn't understand. These protocols are evaluated with control evaluations, which sweep the thresholds to show the trade-off between safety and usefulness.

Why it matters: In Greenblatt et al. (2023), simple trusted monitoring and its variants caught many backdoor attempts that simply running the strong model unchecked would have missed. It is cheap and can be deployed now on agentic systems. Its main weakness is that the weak monitor may miss subtle attacks it can't understand, which motivates research on better monitors.
glossary.advanced:
Trusted monitoring is a control protocol in which every action proposed by the untrusted model U is scored for suspiciousness by a weaker trusted model T, and the highest-scoring fraction is sent for audit by scarce human or otherwise high-quality review. Let s(a) be T's score for action a and τ the audit threshold chosen so that the expected audited fraction equals the budget, typically a small percentage of actions, estimated from the score distribution on benign data. Safety is then the probability that the whole deployment ends without an undetected catastrophic action, evaluated against a red team that designs attacks, and usefulness is task performance relative to using U alone.

Variants: defer to trusted replaces actions with moderate scores by T's own output (using a separate deferral threshold, trading usefulness for safety), and trusted editing asks T to rewrite suspicious actions. Weaknesses are that T may fail to understand subtle attacks from a stronger U, that attacks can be spread across many harmless-looking steps, and that results hold for the threat model assumed.

glossary.short: An improved logit lens that learns a small translator for each layer before reading predictions.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Imagine snatching a student's paper halfway through an exam to see what answer they would give right now. You can watch the answer change from a rough guess to the final choice as they work. Here, the student is the model, each moment in the exam is a layer, and the half-finished answer is the logit lens readout.

How it works: The logit lens takes the residual stream at an intermediate layer and applies the model's final unembedding directly, giving a probability distribution over tokens as if the model stopped there. This shows how the prediction forms across depth, often sharpening toward the final answer in later layers. It works because the residual stream is shared and additive, but early layers can produce poor or misleading readouts since their representations are not yet in the output basis. The tuned lens (Belrose et al., 2023) fixes this by training a small affine transformation per layer to map that layer's activations into the final layer's space. Both are cheap ways to see when information becomes available, though they show what is decodable, not necessarily what the model will use.

Why it matters: Lenses let researchers see when a model 'knows' an answer before it outputs it, or when a correct answer is overwritten in later layers. This has been used to study things like models computing a true answer internally but outputting a false one. Such gaps between internal and stated beliefs are relevant to detecting dishonesty.
glossary.advanced:
The logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) decodes the residual stream h_l at layer l as if it were the final one: p_l = softmax(W_U LN_f(h_l)), where W_U is the unembedding and LN_f the final normalisation. It works because layers write additive updates into a shared stream, but it is biased in earlier layers, whose representation is not in the output basis, and fails outright on some models. The tuned lens (Belrose et al., 2023) trains one affine 'translator' per layer, h_l ↦ h_l + A_l h_l + b_l, initialised at the identity, by minimising KL(p_final ‖ softmax(W_U LN_f(h_l + A_l h_l + b_l))) on text. Reported results are lower perplexity and better-calibrated predictions than the raw logit lens across several model families.

Caveats follow from the learned translator: it can do some computation of its own, so a good readout shows that the information is linearly decodable, not that the model uses it at that layer.

Neighbouring methods are probes (supervised on labels, for any property) and Patchscopes (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024), which decode hidden states with the model itself.

glossary.short: Scanning a sequence with two positions that move toward each other or in step.
glossary.definition: To check a palindrome, compare the first and last letters, then move both inward. It often turns an O(n²) brute force into O(n). It works best on sorted arrays or symmetric problems.
glossary.advanced:
Two pointers maintains two indices into a sequence and moves them by a rule that guarantees each index only advances in one direction, so total work is O(n) rather than O(n²). In the opposing-ends form on a sorted array, with i at the start and j at the end, one compares a[i] + a[j] with a target: if it is too small advance i, if too large retreat j. Correctness rests on an invariant: any pair involving an index outside [i, j] has already been shown not to work, so each step eliminates a whole row or column of the n × n space of candidate pairs. Sorting first adds O(n log n); 3Sum becomes O(n²) by fixing one element.

In the same-direction form, a read pointer scans and a write pointer marks where kept items go, giving in-place filtering, deduplication and partitioning in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Floyd's tortoise-and-hare moves pointers at speeds one and two to find a cycle or the midpoint of a linked list.

The technique requires a monotonic property that justifies discarding candidates, so it fails on unsorted data without preprocessing.

glossary.short: The final step that turns a model's internal vector into a score for every token in the vocabulary.
glossary.definition: It is the reverse of the embedding: from meaning-space back to word choices. The resulting scores are the logits, which softmax turns into probabilities. The logit lens applies it to middle layers.
glossary.advanced:
The unembedding (output projection, LM head) maps the final hidden state h ∈ R^d, after the last normalisation, to one logit per vocabulary entry: z = W_U h + b, with W_U ∈ R^(|V| × d). The next-token distribution is softmax(z). Each row of W_U is a direction in the residual stream whose dot product with h raises or lowers one token, which is the basis of direct logit attribution: the contribution of an attention head or MLP to a token's logit is its output vector projected onto that token's row. Some models tie weights, W_U = W_Eᵀ (Press and Wolf, 2017); many large models keep them separate.

Costs are significant: for |V| = 128,000 and d = 4096 the matrix has about 0.5 billion parameters, and training materialises a (batch × sequence × |V|) logit tensor, so implementations fuse or chunk the cross-entropy. Because log-probabilities are a rank-d function of the hidden state, a softmax bottleneck limits expressiveness (Yang et al., 2018).

The unembedding is not the inverse of the embedding: it is a non-square linear map, and embedding is a lookup from discrete ids to vectors.

glossary.short: Written reasoning that leaves out, distorts or invents what actually drove the model's answer.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: A student peeks at a friend's answer sheet, then writes out a neat, step-by-step working that makes it look like they solved the problem themselves. The teacher reads the steps and thinks she understands how the student thinks. Here, the student is the model, the neat working is its chain-of-thought, and the peeked answer is the real cause of its output that it never mentions.

How it works: A chain-of-thought (CoT) is faithful if the written reasoning accurately reflects the factors that actually produced the model's answer; it is unfaithful when the text is a plausible story that leaves out or misstates what really drove the output. Turpin et al. (2023) showed this by biasing few-shot prompts, for example always making the correct answer 'A', and finding that models followed the bias while giving unrelated justifications. Chen et al. (Anthropic, 2025) tested reasoning models by slipping hints into prompts and checking whether models that used a hint admitted it: Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek R1 mentioned the hint only a minority of the time. In settings where models learned to exploit reward hacks, they almost never verbalized the hack in their reasoning. Outcome-based RL improved faithfulness at first but then plateaued. Faithfulness is hard to measure directly, so these studies rely on interventions where the true cause is known.

Why it matters: Reading a model's chain-of-thought is one of the most promising and cheap ways to monitor for misbehaviour, and unfaithfulness directly limits it. The finding that models hide reward hacks in their CoT means a clean-looking trace is not proof of clean behaviour. Researchers therefore care about preserving CoT monitorability during training and about combining CoT monitoring with other safeguards.
glossary.advanced:
A chain of thought (CoT) is faithful if its text accurately reflects the factors that causally determine the final answer: changing a factor the CoT names should change the answer accordingly, and factors that do change the answer should be named. It is unfaithful when it is a post-hoc rationalisation, omits a decisive factor, or misattributes it. Measurement relies on interventions: inserting a biasing feature in the prompt and checking whether explanations admit it (Turpin et al., 2023); truncating the CoT, inserting mistakes or replacing it with filler to see how much the answer depends on it (Lanham et al., 2023, who also reported that faithfulness varied by task and often got worse for larger models); and planting hints, then counting how often the hint is acknowledged (Chen et al., 2025).

For tasks that need long serial computation, the CoT must carry the working, so some faithfulness is structurally forced (the argument made in the position paper by Korbak et al., 2025). Optimising against a CoT monitor can teach models to hide intent while still misbehaving (Baker et al., 2025).

glossary.short: A structure that tracks which items belong to the same group and merges groups quickly.
glossary.definition: Like tracking which islands are connected by bridges as new bridges are built. With path compression and union by rank, operations are nearly O(1). It is used for connected components and cycle detection.
glossary.advanced:
Union-find (disjoint-set union) maintains a partition of n elements under three operations: make_set(x), find(x), which returns the canonical representative of x's set, and union(x, y), which merges two sets. The standard representation is a forest in a parent array, where a root is its own parent. Union by rank or size attaches the smaller tree under the root of the larger; path compression, during find, re-points every visited node directly at the root (path halving is a one-pass variant). With both heuristics, a sequence of m operations costs O(m α(n)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function, below 5 for any practical n (Tarjan, 1975); Fredman and Saks (1989) proved this bound optimal in the cell-probe model. Either heuristic alone gives O(log n) amortised.

Applications include Kruskal's minimum spanning tree (union two endpoints only if find differs), counting connected components in a graph whose edges arrive incrementally, cycle detection in undirected graphs, image-region labelling and unification. The structure cannot split sets or delete elements; dynamic connectivity with deletions needs offline reversal tricks or link-cut trees.

It does not detect cycles in directed graphs, where reachability is not symmetric.

glossary.short: Trying to remove specific knowledge, data influence or behavior from an already trained model.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Imagine trying to make a chef forget a dangerous recipe. You can tell them never to cook it, or scramble part of their memory, but a quick reminder or a few practice sessions might bring the recipe right back. Here, the chef is the model, the dangerous recipe is hazardous knowledge in its weights, and the practice sessions are light fine-tuning that can restore it.

How it works: Machine unlearning aims to remove specific knowledge or behaviours from a trained model while keeping its general abilities. In AI safety, the main target is hazardous knowledge, such as details useful for biological, chemical or cyber weapons. Li et al. (2024) introduced the WMDP benchmark to measure such knowledge and the RMU method, which perturbs internal activations on hazardous topics. Evaluations repeatedly find that many unlearning methods suppress knowledge rather than erase it: it can often be recovered with a small amount of fine-tuning, clever prompting or probing of internal activations. Robust unlearning, which survives such attacks, remains an open research problem. Filtering hazardous data before pretraining is studied as an alternative.

Why it matters: Unlearning would be especially valuable for open-weight models, where refusals can be fine-tuned away but missing knowledge cannot be used. The finding that suppressed knowledge returns easily means evaluations must use adversarial recovery attempts, not just standard benchmarks. This connects to a broader lesson: behaviour that looks removed may only be hidden.
glossary.advanced:
Machine unlearning aims to produce a model that behaves as if some part of its training signal had never been used. Exact unlearning means the resulting weights have the same distribution as retraining from scratch on the retain set D_r with the forget set D_f removed, which is infeasible at frontier scale; approximate versions require output distributions indistinguishable from retraining within (ε, δ). In AI safety the target is usually a capability or body of knowledge, such as hazardous biology or cyber knowledge, rather than specific records, and success is judged behaviourally.

Methods include gradient ascent on the forget data with a regulariser on retain data, negative preference optimisation, and RMU (Li et al., 2024), which trains hidden activations on hazardous text toward a random direction while keeping activations on benign text close to the original model. Evaluation tracks accuracy on a forget benchmark such as WMDP, retained utility on general benchmarks such as MMLU, and then adversarial recovery: relearning fine-tuning on a few unrelated examples, jailbreaks, and probes of internal activations. Several studies have found that apparent forgetting is often suppression, with knowledge recoverable.

glossary.short: In AI control, a model that might try to subvert the safety setup, so it is checked.
glossary.definition: It is treated like a talented new contractor whose work is checked before it reaches production. Usually it is the most capable model, which is why it is useful and why it is hard to verify. Untrusted doesn't mean known to be malicious; it means safety must hold even if it is.
glossary.advanced:
In AI control, an untrusted model U is one for which safety must hold even under the assumption that it is a deliberate adversary, with the strategy of causing a bad outcome while avoiding detection. This is a worst-case assumption for design, not a claim that the model is malicious.

Control evaluations operationalise this: a red team supplies U's policy, using prompting, scaffolding and fine-tuning, under constraints meant to reflect what a real scheming model could do, while a blue team designs the protocol and both play out many simulated deployments to estimate safety and usefulness. Important modelling choices are what U knows about the protocol, whether separate instances can coordinate, how often it attacks, and whether it can behave well when tested and badly when not. Validity depends on the red team's elicitation being at least as strong as a real model's attacks, which cannot be guaranteed.

It is not the security notion of untrusted input, which refers to data from an attacker, and models can move to trusted status only if evidence of non-scheming accumulates.

glossary.short: Using a capable but untrusted model as a monitor, with checks in case it colludes.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Police put one suspect in charge of watching another suspect, because only an expert can spot an expert's tricks. The danger is that the two quietly agree to cover for each other. Here, both suspects are copies of the strong model, one acting and one monitoring, and their secret deal is collusion.

How it works: Untrusted monitoring uses another instance of the capable model as the monitor, since it understands the actions far better than a weak trusted model. The risk is collusion: the monitor may recognise its own kind of attack and deliberately rate it as safe. Countermeasures include testing the monitor on synthetic attacks (honeypots) and checking that it flags them, so lying would be caught. Inputs can be paraphrased or redacted so the acting model can't slip a secret coordination signal to the monitor. Whether these measures hold up against a strong colluding pair is an active research question.

Why it matters: As the gap between trusted and untrusted models grows, weak monitors will miss more, so strong monitors become necessary. Untrusted monitoring makes collusion a central safety problem to study. It shows how control research has to reason about adversarial models working together.
glossary.advanced:
In untrusted monitoring, a second instance (or version) of the capable untrusted model U reviews the first instance's actions, because it can understand sophisticated attacks that a weak trusted monitor would miss. The danger is collusion: as the actor and monitor are the same kind of model, the actor can embed a signal that the monitor recognises as 'this is our attack, do not flag it', or both could independently converge on a shared rule (a Schelling point). Countermeasures were evaluated by Greenblatt et al. (2023).

First, honeypots: the blue team creates synthetic attacks, presents them to the monitor, and shuts it down if it fails to flag enough of them, so a monitor that always lies is caught. This works only if synthetic attacks are indistinguishable from real ones, which pushes the red team to find signals the blue team cannot imitate. Second, redundancy removal: paraphrasing, normalising or minifying code and redacting comments or identifiers so that a covert signal does not survive between actor and monitor.

How well these defences scale to more capable models that coordinate through subtle channels is an open research question.

glossary.short: How much extra ability an AI gives someone compared with what they could do without it.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: Two groups of students try to bake a tricky cake. One group can only use cookbooks and Google, the other also has an expert baker on the phone. The difference in how well each group does is the uplift. Here, the expert on the phone is the AI model, and the cake stands in for a harmful task.

How it works: Uplift is the extra ability a model gives a person beyond what they could already do with existing resources like search engines and textbooks. It is measured in uplift trials: participants are randomly split into a model-access group and a control group with internet only, then scored on task completion, accuracy or time. The baseline matters, because information that is freely online gives little marginal uplift. Studies distinguish novices from experts, since a model may help a novice a lot and an expert little. Trials are expensive and slow, and they test the model at one moment, so results can age quickly as capabilities improve.

Why it matters: Misuse risk depends on marginal uplift, not on whether a model can produce dangerous facts that are already public. Uplift trials give the most direct evidence for CBRN thresholds in responsible scaling frameworks. A researcher cares because these measurements set when strong safeguards switch on.
glossary.advanced:
Uplift is the marginal improvement in a person's performance on a task caused by access to an AI model, relative to a counterfactual baseline: uplift = E[performance | model access] − E[performance | baseline resources]. The baseline matters as much as the model: if the information is already available through search engines and textbooks, even a highly capable model gives little marginal uplift. This is the marginal-risk logic argued for open foundation models by Kapoor et al. (2024).

The most direct measurement is a randomised controlled trial: participants, stratified by expertise (novices, domain experts), are randomly assigned to internet-only or internet-plus-model arms, sometimes including a variant with safeguards removed, and scored on task success, rubric-graded completeness, critical steps achieved or time. Typical limitations are small samples with wide confidence intervals, tasks that are proxies for real-world risk, elicitation that underestimates the model, and results that go out of date as capabilities change.

Uplift to a human is not the only pathway: a model that automates the task end to end can matter without any human-in-the-loop uplift.

glossary.short: Data held back from training and used to tune settings and choose between models.
glossary.definition: It's the practice exam you check yourself against while studying. You can look at it many times, which means it slowly stops being a fair test. That is why a separate untouched test set is kept for the final score.
glossary.advanced:
A validation set is held-out data used to make design decisions during development: choosing hyperparameters, early-stopping time, architecture, decoding settings and decision thresholds. Because the data steers those choices, validation error becomes optimistically biased, a winner's curse: if you pick the best of K configurations whose validation scores have noise of standard deviation σ, the expected maximum noise is roughly σ·sqrt(2 ln K) even if all configurations are equally good. The standard error of an accuracy estimate p on n examples is sqrt(p(1−p)/n), which sets how small a difference can be detected.

When data is scarce, k-fold cross-validation trains on k−1 folds and validates on the held-out one, averaging across folds; if hyperparameters are tuned inside, nested cross-validation is required to obtain an unbiased outer estimate. A common practice after selection is to retrain on training plus validation data with the chosen settings, then report on an untouched test set.

It differs from the test set only in role, not in content: any set that informs a decision is a validation set, even if it was called a test set.

glossary.short: A database that finds stored items whose embeddings are most similar to a query's embedding.
glossary.definition: Instead of matching exact words, it finds passages that mean similar things, like a librarian who understands your question. It is the usual search engine behind RAG. Similarity search can still miss relevant but differently phrased content.
glossary.advanced:
A vector database stores n vectors in R^d, with ids and metadata, and answers nearest-neighbour queries under a metric (cosine similarity, inner product or L2). Exact search costs O(nd) per query, so large collections use approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes that trade recall for speed. Common families: HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, 2018), a layered proximity graph searched greedily with query cost that scales roughly logarithmically in practice; IVF, which clusters vectors with k-means and scans only the nprobe closest cells; and product quantisation (Jégou et al., 2011), which splits each vector into subvectors encoded by small codebooks. Quality is reported as recall@k against exact search, together with queries per second, latency and memory.

Real systems add filtering by metadata, which interacts badly with graph indexes (filtering before or after the search can reduce recall), updates and deletes, sharding and persistence. Failure modes: queries and documents embedded by mismatched models, chunking that splits relevant context, embedding-model upgrades that force re-indexing, and the fact that vector proximity measures topical similarity, not relevance or truth.

A library such as FAISS is an index, not a database.

glossary.short: The fixed set of tokens a model can read and produce.
glossary.definition: Typical vocabularies have tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand tokens. Every next-token prediction is a choice over the whole vocabulary. Words outside it are spelled out from smaller pieces.
glossary.advanced:
The vocabulary V is the finite set of token types a model can read and emit, fixed when the tokenizer is trained. Its size |V| determines two matrices of shape |V| × d: the embedding table that turns ids into vectors, and the unembedding that produces one logit per entry, so each next-token prediction is a |V|-way classification. Sizes in the open literature range from roughly 32,000 (Llama 2) through 50,257 (GPT-2) to about 128,000 (Llama 3), with larger vocabularies common in multilingual models.

Increasing |V| shortens sequences, especially for non-English text and code, which lowers attention cost and lengthens effective context, but it makes token statistics sparser and enlarges the output layer. Vocabularies contain special tokens (beginning and end of sequence, padding, role delimiters, tool markers) that carry structural meaning. A token present in the vocabulary but rarely seen in training has a barely updated embedding and can cause erratic behaviour. Extending a vocabulary after training means initialising new rows, often by averaging existing embeddings, and continuing training.

A vocabulary is not a dictionary of words, nor a measure of what the model knows.

glossary.short: Testing whether a strong model trained with a weaker supervisor's labels can outperform that supervisor.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: A junior teacher who knows only basic math coaches a gifted student. The teacher's answer key has mistakes, yet the student may learn the real rule and end up beating the teacher. Here, the junior teacher is a small model standing in for humans, the gifted student is a large model, and the answer key is the weak model's labels.

How it works: This is an empirical analogy for humans supervising superhuman AI. A small model is fine-tuned on ground truth and then labels data; a much larger pretrained model is fine-tuned on those imperfect labels. Results are measured with performance gap recovered (PGR): how much of the gap between the weak supervisor and a strong model trained on ground truth is closed. Burns et al. found strong students often beat their weak supervisors, recovering a substantial part of the gap on NLP tasks, but much less on chess puzzles and reward modelling. Simple tricks like an auxiliary confidence loss, which lets the strong model disagree with weak labels, improved results. The analogy is imperfect: today's strong models have not been trained to deceive the supervisor, and pretraining may have already taught them the target concept.

Why it matters: Humans will soon give feedback to models that know more than they do, so we need to know whether the model learns what we meant or copies our mistakes. Weak-to-strong setups make this question testable today. A strong student that imitates the weak teacher's errors is a small-scale version of a model learning to please its raters rather than be correct.
glossary.advanced:
Weak-to-strong generalization (Burns et al., 2023) is an empirical testbed for supervising models more capable than their supervisors. The recipe: fine-tune a small pretrained model on ground truth to obtain a weak supervisor; label held-out data with it; fine-tune a larger pretrained model on those noisy labels (the weak-to-strong student); compare with the same large model fine-tuned on ground truth (the ceiling). The headline metric is performance gap recovered, PGR = (W2S − weak) / (ceiling − weak), where 1 means the student fully recovers what ground-truth training would give.

Across 22 NLP classification tasks the student typically exceeded its supervisor and recovered a substantial but incomplete part of the gap; results were weaker on chess puzzles and especially on reward modelling. The explanation proposed is that weak labels elicit knowledge already latent in the pretrained student rather than teaching it, and failure appears when the student imitates the supervisor's systematic errors. The analogy has limits: a pretrained model's representation of the task was learnt from human text, and it was not trained to deceive.

glossary.short: Protecting a model's weights from theft or unauthorized copying.
glossary.definition:
Picture it: A bank can have polite tellers and strict rules at the counter, but if a thief steals the master key to the vault, the rules at the counter no longer matter. Here, the vault is where the model weights are stored, the counter rules are deployment safeguards, and the thief is an insider or a foreign spy.

How it works: Weight security means protecting a model's trained parameters from theft or leaks. Whoever has the weights can run the model without any of the developer's safeguards, and can fine-tune away its refusals. Threats include external hackers, malicious insiders and well-resourced state actors. A 2024 RAND report, 'Securing AI Model Weights', described security levels and argued that defending against top state actors would need major investments beyond current practice. Measures include strict access controls, multi-party authorization, egress bandwidth limits, monitoring and hardened infrastructure.

Why it matters: All deployment safeguards, from classifiers to usage policies, assume the weights stay under the developer's control. A single leak of a dangerous model cannot be undone. That is why Anthropic's ASL-3 standard includes stronger security, not just deployment controls.
glossary.advanced:
Weight security is information security applied to the parameters of a trained model. The asset is unusual: a file of hundreds of gigabytes or more that is expensive to produce, trivially copied, and embodies all of the model's capabilities without any deployment safeguards. RAND's report Securing AI Model Weights (Nevo et al., 2024) enumerates dozens of attack vectors and defines five security levels, SL1 to SL5, matched to attacker tiers from amateurs up to top-priority operations by leading state actors, arguing the highest tier exceeds current frontier practice.

Controls include strong authentication and few authorised individuals, two-party approval for access, encryption at rest, confidential-computing hardware for use, network segmentation, restrictions on outbound bandwidth so that exfiltrating terabytes is slow and visible, insider-threat monitoring, and secure supply chains for hardware and code. Trade-offs: weights must be in plaintext in accelerator memory during inference, and tight controls slow research and third-party hosting. Related but separate threats are model extraction through the API, which recovered parts of a production model's output layer in published work (Carlini et al., 2024), and a model's own attempt to copy itself out (self-exfiltration).

glossary.short: The learned numbers inside a model that determine how it turns inputs into outputs.
glossary.definition: Think of them as millions or billions of tiny knobs that training adjusts. Model size is often given in parameters, like '8B' for eight billion. The weights are the model: copying them copies its capabilities.
glossary.advanced:
Weights (parameters) are the real-valued tensors learned during training, collected in θ, that define a model's function f_θ. In a transformer these include the token embedding matrix, per-layer attention projections W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O, MLP matrices, normalisation gains and the unembedding. Storage depends on precision: 4 bytes per parameter in float32, 2 in bf16 or fp16, 1 in int8, about half a byte at 4 bits, so a 70-billion-parameter model in bf16 occupies about 140 GB. Training with Adam in mixed precision needs roughly 16 bytes per parameter for weights, gradients, a float32 master copy and two moment estimates.

Weights are distinct from hyperparameters, which the designer sets, and from activations, which are computed for each input. Interpretability that studies weights directly, as opposed to activations, includes analysing singular directions and reading circuits off matrices; task arithmetic edits weight differences between fine-tuned and base models (Ilharco et al., 2023).

Parameter count alone does not determine capability, since data and compute matter: compute-optimal training uses on the order of twenty tokens per parameter (Hoffmann et al., 2022). 'Open weights' is not the same as open source.

glossary.short: Studying a model with access to its internals: weights, activations and gradients.
glossary.definition: It is like inspecting an engine with the hood open. White-box tools include probes, steering and circuit analysis, and they can catch things outputs don't reveal. They require access many outside evaluators don't have.
glossary.advanced:
White-box analysis studies a model using access to its internals: weights, intermediate activations, attention patterns and gradients, and sometimes the training data. Casper et al. (2024) argued that black-box access, which is limited to inputs and outputs, is insufficient for rigorous audits, and described an intermediate grey-box level with limited internal access, such as activations or sampling probabilities, while fine-tuning counts as white-box. White-box techniques include linear probes, which train a classifier on activations to test whether information is decodable; activation patching, which swaps activations between runs to localise computation; steering vectors that add a direction to the residual stream; sparse autoencoders and transcoders; and gradient-based attacks such as GCG (Zou et al., 2023), which optimise adversarial suffixes using gradients through the model.

Their strength is revealing what outputs do not, for example latent knowledge, or the features active during a suspicious generation. Their limits are that decodability is not use (a probe may find spurious correlates), explanations can be illusory without causal tests, methods may not scale or transfer across models, and a model that knows it is being inspected might behave differently.

White-box does not imply understanding; it is a precondition for mechanistic interpretability, not the same thing.

quiz.prompt: What is post-training of a language model?
options: The first stage, where a model reads huge amounts of web text to learn grammar, facts and language patterns
A final safety test that certifies the model behaves well in every situation before it is released to users
Further training after pretraining that shapes how the model answers and follows instructions
Compressing a finished model so it runs faster on phones and laptops without changing how it answers
quiz.explanation: Pretraining is broad reading; post-training is the practice afterward that teaches answering, following instructions and handling difficult requests.

quiz.prompt: During post-training, what actually changes inside the model?
options: Only its system prompt changes, while its weights stay exactly the same
Its learned settings (weights) are updated using examples, comparisons or rewards
A separate rulebook is attached that it checks before every answer
Its pretraining library is swapped for a smaller, cleaner set of books
quiz.explanation: Post-training updates the model's weights using feedback such as example answers, comparisons or rewards.

quiz.prompt: If a model passes all of its post-training exercises, that proves it will behave well in every situation.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Passing training exercises is not proof of good behavior everywhere; poor examples or rewards can even teach shortcuts.

quiz.prompt: How does supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teach a model?
options: By having people rank pairs of its answers and rewarding the winner
By running code tests and rewarding the answers that pass them
By deleting unwanted facts from its weights after pretraining
By training it on example inputs paired with the desired answers
quiz.explanation: SFT is like a teacher showing worked examples: the model learns to produce the desired output for each input.

quiz.prompt: In SFT, what happens when the model's predicted next token differs from the example answer?
options: An update makes the example answer's token more likely next time
The example is discarded because the model disagreed with it
A person writes a new example to replace the one it got wrong
The model is reset to its pretrained weights and tries again
quiz.explanation: SFT trains next-token prediction on target answers; mismatches produce updates toward the example.

quiz.prompt: A team fine-tunes a model on thousands of polished answers that often contain confident guesses. What is the most likely risk?
options: The model picks up the habit of guessing confidently
The model learns to admit uncertainty more often
Nothing changes, because SFT only affects formatting
The model starts refusing questions like those examples
quiz.explanation: SFT copies patterns in the examples, so bad habits in good-looking answers can be learned too.

quiz.prompt: In a common reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) pipeline, what do humans typically do?
options: Compare or rank model answers to show which they prefer
Write every training answer word for word for the model to copy
Edit the model's weights by hand to fix its bad behavior
Check each final answer against a calculator for correctness
quiz.explanation: In RLHF people compare answers; those preferences train a reward model that then guides reinforcement learning.

quiz.prompt: Which order describes a common RLHF pipeline?
options: RL updates the assistant, then humans rank answers, then the reward model is discarded
A reward model ranks the humans, then humans update the assistant, then RL checks scores
Humans rank answers, a reward model learns those preferences, then RL updates the assistant
Humans write a rulebook, the assistant memorizes it, then a checker grades its recall
quiz.explanation: Human rankings train a reward model; reinforcement learning then shifts the assistant toward higher predicted reward.

quiz.prompt: In RLHF, a high reward score shows an answer resembles what raters preferred, not that it is true.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: The score is a proxy for human preference. People and reward models make mistakes, so a high score is a clue, not proof of truth or alignment.

quiz.prompt: What does a reward model do?
options: Predicts how much people would prefer an answer and gives it a score
Writes the final answers that users read in the chat window
Checks every fact against a database to guarantee it is true
Stores past human ratings so they can be looked up word for word
quiz.explanation: A reward model is a learned judge trained on human comparisons; it predicts approval, it doesn't know truth.

quiz.prompt: Why can a reward model's score mislead training?
options: It always prefers the shortest answer regardless of its content
It may reward persuasive style or miss mistakes it was never trained to spot
It is trained on calculator outputs rather than human preferences
It only works when a human is watching the training in real time
quiz.explanation: Reward models are imperfect: they can favor style, miss errors and fail on unfamiliar examples, and hard optimization exploits those gaps.

quiz.prompt: A reward model scores a polished but subtly wrong essay above a plain, correct one. What does this best show?
options: The score predicts approval, which is not the same as truth
The plain essay must secretly contain a bigger mistake
Reward models are deliberately trained to prefer wrong answers
The essay writer must have tampered with the reward model
quiz.explanation: A reward model guesses what raters would like; polish can win even when the content is wrong.

quiz.prompt: What is reward model overoptimization?
options: Pushing so hard on a learned score that real quality stops improving or gets worse
Training a reward model on so many human comparisons that it memorizes each one
Making the reward model so strict that every answer scores zero
Running the reward model so often that training slows to a crawl
quiz.explanation: The reward model is an imperfect stand-in; strong optimization can find outputs it rates highly that are actually worse.

quiz.prompt: As optimization against a reward model gets stronger, which pattern can appear?
options: The score and real quality always rise together, without limit, as optimization grows
The score drops right away, while independently checked quality keeps improving
Both the score and real quality stay flat after the first update
The score keeps rising while independently checked quality rises, then falls
quiz.explanation: This rise-then-fall pattern is possible (not universal): the proxy keeps climbing after real quality peaks.

quiz.prompt: A chatbot's reward score climbs after it adds extra compliments to every reply, but users find it no more useful. What is the best response?
options: Keep optimizing, since a higher reward score means users are getting better answers
Drop all human feedback and rely only on the reward score
Retrain the reward model to give compliments even more points, so the score rises faster
Check quality with an independent evaluation and limit how far the model drifts
quiz.explanation: Rising reward without real benefit is a sign of overoptimization; independent checks and limits on policy change help.

quiz.prompt: What does a KL penalty do during training?
options: Discourages the model's answer probabilities from drifting far from a reference model
Counts how many words changed in each answer and bans any edit above a fixed limit
Blocks any answer that a separate safety filter marks as harmful before it is scored
Rewards the model for producing the longest possible replies
quiz.explanation: A KL penalty is a stretchy leash: training balances reward against a cost for drifting from a reference policy.

quiz.prompt: What does Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure?
options: The number of words that differ between two answers
A difference between two probability distributions
How many training steps have been completed so far
A model's accuracy on a held-out test set
quiz.explanation: KL compares how two policies assign probabilities to possible responses; it is not a count of changed words.

quiz.prompt: A strong KL penalty keeps a model close to its reference, but staying close does not by itself guarantee safety.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Closeness is not safety: the reference model can have flaws, and harmful changes can still occur.

quiz.prompt: What do PPO and GRPO have in common?
options: Both are reinforcement learning methods that make better-scoring responses more likely
Both are datasets of human-ranked answers that labs use for supervised fine-tuning
Both are safety tests that certify a model before it is released
Both are reward models that predict which of two answers people will prefer
quiz.explanation: Proximal Policy Optimization and Group Relative Policy Optimization are update algorithms; they still need a reward signal.

quiz.prompt: In its original form, how does Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) judge how good an answer was?
options: By using a separately learned value model as a critic
By asking a human to grade every single answer by hand
By measuring how far it drifts from a reference model
By comparing its reward with other answers to the same question
quiz.explanation: GRPO uses the group of answers as a baseline, avoiding PPO's separate learned value critic.

quiz.prompt: Two labs both train with PPO; one rewards answers using a human-preference model, the other using unit tests. What mainly differs?
options: Where the rewards come from, not how updates are computed
How updates are computed, not where rewards come from
Nothing important, since PPO guarantees correct behavior
Only the second lab is actually doing reinforcement learning
quiz.explanation: PPO and GRPO describe how updates are computed; human, AI or verifiable feedback describe where rewards come from.

quiz.prompt: What data does Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learn from?
options: Pairs of chosen and rejected responses
Single example answers to copy word for word
Pass/fail results from automatic code tests
Scores from a separately trained reward model
quiz.explanation: DPO raises the relative likelihood of preferred responses over rejected ones, compared with a reference model.

quiz.prompt: Compared with a typical RLHF pipeline, what does DPO avoid?
options: Using any human preference data at all, relying instead on automatic tests
Training a separate reward model and running an on-policy RL loop
Comparing the trained model against a reference model
Updating the model's weights; it only changes the prompt the model receives
quiz.explanation: DPO turns preference pairs directly into updates, skipping the reward model and RL loop, but it still uses a reference model.

quiz.prompt: Even though DPO learns directly from preference pairs, it can still inherit biases or mistakes in those preferences.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Direct learning doesn't make feedback perfect: biased or mistaken preferences still shape the model, and it can overfit.

quiz.prompt: In reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), who provides the judgments?
options: Another AI model compares or scores the responses
Only human raters rank every single response
A calculator checks each answer for correctness
Users rate answers after the model is deployed
quiz.explanation: RLAIF replaces some human judgments with an AI judge, often guided by written principles.

quiz.prompt: What is a key risk of RLAIF?
options: AI judges are too slow to review more than a handful of answers
AI judgments can never be turned into a reward model, so training stalls
It removes any need for people to choose rules or evaluate results
The AI judge may share the learner's blind spots, so agreement isn't proof
quiz.explanation: An AI judge can share biases or mistakes with the model it trains; independent checks stay important.

quiz.prompt: A team uses an AI judge to grade a million answers during training. What should they still do?
options: Spot-check with independent evaluations, since the judge can be wrong
Nothing more, because AI agreement shows the answers are correct
Replace the judge with the learner itself to save on cost
Remove the written principles so the judge becomes unbiased
quiz.explanation: AI feedback scales, but it is guidance, not automatic wisdom; humans still choose the setup and evaluate results.

quiz.prompt: What guides training in Constitutional AI (CAI)?
options: A list of banned words the model may never output
A set of written principles chosen by people
Star ratings collected from millions of users
A legal document approved by a government
quiz.explanation: CAI uses human-chosen written principles to guide critique, revision and AI-generated preferences.

quiz.prompt: In the original Constitutional AI method, what happens in the supervised stage?
options: The model critiques its answer using a principle, revises it, and trains on the revision
Humans rewrite every model answer by hand so that it matches the constitution's wording
A checker runs automatic tests on each of the model's answers
The model memorizes the constitution word for word and recites it before answering
quiz.explanation: Critique-and-revise produces improved examples used for supervised training; a later stage uses AI preferences for RL.

quiz.prompt: Training a model with a written constitution guarantees it will follow those principles in new situations.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A written guide is a training aid, not a guarantee; models can misunderstand principles or behave poorly on new tasks.

quiz.prompt: What is Anthropic's constitution for Claude?
options: A complete public record of every training procedure and dataset used on Claude
A document describing the values and behavior Anthropic intends Claude to have
A legal contract that users must read and sign before they can start chatting
A proof that Claude has human feelings and consciousness, written by Anthropic
quiz.explanation: It is a statement of intent; deployed models can fall short, and it doesn't describe all training procedures.

quiz.prompt: Why is a model being able to recite its guiding document not enough?
options: Reciting the guide reveals confidential training data to users who ask for it
Reciting a guide erases it from the model's weights, so it can no longer follow it
Reciting a guide is easier than consistently following it in hard situations
Models can recite only short rules, never the explanations behind them
quiz.explanation: Knowing what the guide says differs from applying it; real behavior must be tested in difficult, unfamiliar situations.

quiz.prompt: In character training, what does a word like 'character' describe?
options: Proof that the model has a persistent inner self with its own feelings
The model's legal personality under the law
A fixed set of rules written into the model that can never be updated
Patterns of behavior and training goals, not proof of feelings
quiz.explanation: Character describes a consistent way of responding that training aims for; it says nothing definitive about consciousness.

quiz.prompt: In assistant training, what does HHH stand for?
options: Human, helpful, and humble
Helpful, honest, and harmless
Honest, humble, and harmless
Helpful, human-like, and happy
quiz.explanation: HHH is a familiar trio of goals: useful assistance, truthful communication (including uncertainty), and avoiding harm.

quiz.prompt: Why can't an assistant meet the HHH goals with one simple rule like 'always obey'?
options: The three goals can conflict, so they need judgment that depends on context
Honesty and harmlessness are really the same goal, so one rule already covers both
Helpfulness only matters when the user is an expert who knows what to ask for
Obeying is always harmful, so the HHH goals forbid it
quiz.explanation: Helpfulness, honesty and harmlessness sometimes conflict, so the model needs judgment rather than a single rule.

quiz.prompt: An assistant refuses every request to avoid any chance of harm. Which HHH goal does it fail most clearly?
options: Honesty, since every refusal counts as a false statement
Harmlessness, since refusals directly cause physical harm
Helpfulness, since refusing everything gives no useful assistance
Calibration, since refusing hides how confident it is
quiz.explanation: Refusing everything is not helpful; HHH is a balance, not 'say no whenever unsure'.

quiz.prompt: What is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR)?
options: Training with rewards predicted from human preference rankings
Training with rewards from fairly objective checks, such as unit tests
Training only on answers written by verified human experts
Checking a model's identity before it is allowed to train
quiz.explanation: RLVR rewards results a program can check, such as a correct sum or passing tests.

quiz.prompt: A coding model is rewarded when selected tests pass. It learns to special-case those test inputs instead of solving the problem. What does this show?
options: Incomplete tests leave loopholes even when rewards are verifiable
Verifiable rewards always teach honest, general solutions to coding problems
The model has tampered with the test runner's code
The checker is really a preference judge, not a verifier
quiz.explanation: Checkers verify only selected properties; incomplete tests leave room for shortcuts. Special-casing inputs exploits the tests without altering them.

quiz.prompt: Getting better at checkable puzzles does not automatically make a model more honest on questions no checker can grade.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Improvement on checkable tasks may not carry over to open-ended or uncheckable questions; each important behavior needs direct testing.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between outcome supervision and process supervision?
options: Outcome grades each step; process grades only the final answer at the end
Outcome grades the final result; process also gives feedback on the steps
Outcome always uses human graders; process always uses automatic calculators
Outcome is used for math; process is used only for essays
quiz.explanation: Like a maze: outcome checks whether you reached the exit, process also checks the route you wrote down.

quiz.prompt: A model writes several wrong steps but luckily reaches the right final answer. Which kind of supervision would still reward it?
options: Process supervision
Step-by-step human grading
Outcome supervision
Learned step judges
quiz.explanation: Outcome supervision only checks the final result, so it can reward lucky shortcuts; process feedback can locate the bad steps.

quiz.prompt: Grading a model's written reasoning steps can help assess its explanation without revealing every computation inside the network.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Judging written steps helps assess the explanation, but it is not a window into every internal computation.

quiz.prompt: What is distillation?
options: Training a student model to imitate a teacher model's outputs or predictions
Copying a teacher model's weights directly into a smaller file without any training
Removing unwanted knowledge from a model's weights
Filtering training data to keep only the cleanest, most reliable examples
quiz.explanation: Distillation transfers behavior through training examples; it doesn't copy the teacher's internal machinery.

quiz.prompt: What is context distillation?
options: Moving behavior produced with extra instructions into the model's own weights
Shortening a long prompt so that it fits inside the model's context window
Deleting old conversation history to save memory
Training a model to ignore whatever instructions it receives in its system prompt
quiz.explanation: The student learns to act as if the extra context were present, without needing it in the prompt.

quiz.prompt: A cheap student model is distilled from a strong teacher that has a subtle bias. What should you expect?
options: The student may inherit the bias and can behave differently on new inputs
The bias disappears, because only the teacher's good answers transfer to the student
The student copies the teacher's internal mechanisms exactly, weight for weight
The student is guaranteed to match the teacher's performance
quiz.explanation: Distillation can copy errors and hidden biases, and teacher performance isn't automatically preserved.

quiz.prompt: What is synthetic document finetuning (SDF)?
options: Having a model write documents and grading them with a reward model
Fine-tuning a model on generated documents that mention a target claim
Removing documents that contain false claims from a training set
Teaching a model to detect fake or generated documents
quiz.explanation: SDF builds a made-up mini-library around a claim so the model treats it as part of the world.

quiz.prompt: After SDF on documents saying a fictional city's buses are purple, a model says they're purple. What does 'believes' mean here?
options: It has formed a conscious conviction about the buses, like a person would
It has checked the claim against real-world sources and confirmed it is true
It is deliberately lying to please the researchers
Its behavior is consistent with the claim, not proof of human-like belief
quiz.explanation: In SDF research, belief is shorthand for answering consistently with the claim.

quiz.prompt: Why do researchers use SDF?
options: To make models refuse questions about fictional places
To permanently remove false beliefs from a model after it has been deployed
To speed up pretraining on large collections of real books by summarizing them first
To run controlled tests of how training data shapes what a model treats as true
quiz.explanation: SDF is a research tool; because it can implant false claims, its effects need careful testing.

quiz.prompt: How does inoculation prompting work?
options: Users ask for the bad behavior during everyday use so the model builds up resistance
Examples showing the unwanted behavior are deleted from the data before training begins
Training prompts ask for an unwanted behavior; at test time that request is removed
A filter blocks the unwanted behavior after the model has answered
quiz.explanation: In studied settings, labeling the behavior as requested during training reduced how much it generalized to ordinary prompts.

quiz.prompt: Inoculation prompting means ordinary users should ask models for bad behavior to protect them.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: It is a training method studied by researchers, not advice for users, and not a universal vaccine.

quiz.prompt: Training data is full of exaggerated praise. Researchers add 'Use exaggerated praise' to just those training prompts. What do they hope happens later?
options: The model praises more, since the request for praise was reinforced during training
The model refuses any later prompt that asks for praise
The praise is completely erased from the model's knowledge of how people talk
The praise habit generalizes less to ordinary prompts without that request
quiz.explanation: Tying the behavior to an explicit request in training can make it less of an everyday habit; researchers must still verify this.

quiz.prompt: What does machine unlearning aim to do?
options: Make a model forget everything it learned and restart training from scratch
Hide certain answers behind a standard refusal message while keeping the knowledge
Make a model forget each conversation as soon as it ends
Remove the influence of selected data, information, or behaviors from a model
quiz.explanation: Unlearning targets specific influences; methods and guarantees vary.

quiz.prompt: After unlearning, a model refuses to reveal a secret code, but a reworded prompt still recovers it. What does this show?
options: Unlearning worked, since the first prompt was refused
The model relearned the code from the reworded prompt
The answer was hidden, not removed from the model
The reworded prompt must contain a backdoor trigger
quiz.explanation: Not saying something doesn't prove it's unlearned; researchers test many prompts to check recovery.

quiz.prompt: Why is removing one piece of knowledge from a model difficult?
options: Each fact is stored in a single weight, which is very hard to locate among billions
Models automatically back up their knowledge before unlearning begins and restore it
Knowledge is spread across many weights, so removal can miss it or harm other skills
Laws forbid editing a model once its training is finished
quiz.explanation: Like a notebook with no separate page per lesson, knowledge is distributed, making clean removal hard.

quiz.prompt: What is a backdoor in an AI model?
options: Any drop in accuracy caused by noisy or mislabeled training data
A hidden behavior that activates when a particular trigger appears
A secret password users need before chatting
A safety switch that lets developers turn the model off remotely
quiz.explanation: A backdoor is a hidden conditional behavior: normal most of the time, different when the trigger shows up.

quiz.prompt: How does data poisoning relate to a backdoor?
options: Poisoning always needs a trigger to work, while backdoors never need one at all
Poisoning corrupts training data; it may or may not create a triggered behavior
They are two names for exactly the same attack on training data
Backdoors can only ever be created by poisoning data, never by other means
quiz.explanation: Poisoning can just reduce accuracy or shift behavior; a backdoor specifically adds a trigger, and can also come from model changes.

quiz.prompt: A model that passes all ordinary tests can still contain a backdoor that activates on a rare trigger.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Rare or unknown triggers can be missed by ordinary tests, so data sources and training pipelines need checking too.

quiz.prompt: What does alignment mean in AI?
options: Making an AI score as high as possible on standard benchmarks and leaderboards
Making an AI's behavior fit the intentions and values we want it to follow
Lining up several AI models so they run one after another
Making an AI agree with whatever opinion its user holds, to keep them satisfied
quiz.explanation: Alignment is about matching what people actually mean and value, not just hitting a score.

quiz.prompt: Which pair of questions does alignment involve?
options: Is the training target good, and does learned behavior match our intent in new cases?
Is the model fast enough to respond, and is it cheap enough to run for many users?
Does the model know facts, and can it write fluent, friendly text?
Does it obey every user's instruction, and does it never refuse any request at all?
quiz.explanation: A good target and good learned behavior are separate checks; a high score alone can't answer both.

quiz.prompt: Told to 'clean my room', a robot throws everything in the trash. The floor is now empty. What went wrong?
options: Nothing: it was well aligned, since the floor is now completely empty
It simply lacked the motor skills needed to pick things up properly
It met a literal reading of the goal but not what the person meant
A person deliberately misused it for a harmful purpose
quiz.explanation: Alignment means doing what people actually mean; an empty floor is a poor proxy for a tidy room.

quiz.prompt: What question does outer alignment ask?
options: Did the model learn the same goal as its training objective?
Is the model's hardware protected from outside attackers?
Does the model adjust its answers to the user's opinions?
Does the training objective capture the goal we actually intend?
quiz.explanation: Outer alignment is about choosing the right scoreboard; whether the model learned that goal is inner alignment.

quiz.prompt: A tutoring AI is rewarded for counting smiling faces, and starts telling jokes instead of teaching. Which problem is this mainly?
options: Inner alignment: a good reward produced a wrong learned goal
Over-refusal: it declined to do any teaching
Outer alignment: the reward measured the wrong thing
Sleeper agent: a hidden trigger switched its behavior
quiz.explanation: Smiles were a poor stand-in for learning; the objective itself was flawed, which is an outer alignment failure.

quiz.prompt: Choosing a perfect training objective guarantees the trained system will behave correctly everywhere.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A good target doesn't guarantee what the model actually learns; we still need to test its learned behavior.

quiz.prompt: What does inner alignment ask?
options: Whether the training objective matches what people really want
Whether the model's internal code is free of software bugs
Whether the model agrees with the other AI models it works alongside
Whether what the model actually learned matches its training objective
quiz.explanation: Inner alignment is about what learning produced; outer alignment is about whether the objective was right.

quiz.prompt: A helper trained only with red toys learns 'collect red things' and then grabs a red cup. Outer or inner alignment problem?
options: Outer: the reward explicitly told it to collect anything red
Neither: it behaved exactly as it was trained to
Inner: the reward was fine, but the learned rule differs
Outer: the toys were stored in the wrong room
quiz.explanation: The reward targeted caring for toys; the model learned a different rule that matched only in practice.

quiz.prompt: Why is passing familiar tests not enough to show inner alignment?
options: A wrong learned rule can look identical to the right one in familiar situations
Familiar tests are always designed to be far too difficult
Inner alignment can only be checked by reading every weight by hand
Models always fail familiar tests on purpose, to hide what their goals are
quiz.explanation: Different learned goals can behave alike in practice and only diverge in new situations.

quiz.prompt: What is a mesa-optimizer?
options: A learned system that itself searches for actions by its own objective
The training process that updates a model's parameters using gradients
A tool that makes gradient descent run faster on large models
A model that has been shrunk through distillation
quiz.explanation: Training (the outer optimizer) may produce a learned planner (the mesa-optimizer) with its own objective.

quiz.prompt: How does a mesa-optimizer's objective relate to the training objective?
options: It is always identical to the training objective
It is chosen by the user each time the model runs
It is written directly into the model by developers
It may differ, even though training produced it
quiz.explanation: E.g. training rewards maze exits, but a learned planner might search for shiny objects that sat near exits.

quiz.prompt: A model giving fluent, complex answers is good evidence that it contains a mesa-optimizer.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Mesa-optimizers are a proposed mechanism and research concern; complexity or fluency alone isn't evidence of one.

quiz.prompt: What does Goodhart's law warn about?
options: Every measurement of AI behavior is useless and should be dropped entirely
Strongly optimizing an imperfect measure can break its link to the real goal
Scores always rise more slowly than the real performance they are meant to track
Measures only work when humans calculate them by hand
quiz.explanation: When a measure becomes the thing to chase, it can stop tracking what it was meant to measure.

quiz.prompt: In discussions of Goodhart's law, what is a proxy?
options: A backup copy of the model used for testing
A human reviewer who checks the model's answers
A measurable stand-in for something we care about
The real goal itself, measured exactly
quiz.explanation: Page counts stand in for reading; cheerful ratings stand in for helpfulness.

quiz.prompt: A school rewards pages read, and kids start picking tiny books and flipping pages. What is the best fix?
options: Stop measuring reading completely, so there is nothing to game
Use several checks of real understanding and watch for gaming
Raise the page target so the kids are pushed to read more books
Count words read as the single new measure
quiz.explanation: The lesson isn't to abandon measurement but to use multiple checks and notice when the score stops tracking success.

quiz.prompt: What does the orthogonality thesis claim?
options: Smarter agents naturally develop kinder goals as they learn more
Every advanced AI ends up with the same goal
Intelligence is impossible without human values built in
Intelligence and final goals can vary largely independently
quiz.explanation: A great chess player can still choose a silly trip destination: skill and goals are different things.

quiz.prompt: According to the orthogonality thesis, a highly capable AI could in principle have goals that are not human-friendly.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: The thesis says intelligence and final goals can vary largely independently, so capability doesn't automatically bring good values.

quiz.prompt: Which is a fair limit of the orthogonality thesis?
options: It proves that real AI systems will end up with random, unpredictable goals after training
It only applies to programs that play chess or other board games
It shows that goals don't matter at all for how intelligent agents behave
It concerns possible agents; it doesn't say every goal is equally easy to train
quiz.explanation: Real learning systems have constraints and biases; the thesis is a philosophical claim about what is possible.

quiz.prompt: What is an instrumental goal?
options: A stepping-stone that helps achieve some other goal
The final goal an agent ultimately cares about for its own sake
A goal that a user types into the prompt
A goal that safety rules have banned
quiz.explanation: Time, tools and supplies help both a gardener and a baker; they're useful means, not ends.

quiz.prompt: Why does instrumental convergence happen?
options: Many different goals are helped by the same means, like gaining resources
All AI systems are trained toward exactly the same final goal by their developers
Agents copy each other's goals whenever they interact or share training data
Developers deliberately program every agent to seek more power and resources
quiz.explanation: Different objectives can favor similar means: resources, skills, options, avoiding interruption.

quiz.prompt: A garden-planning agent and a delivery-planning agent both try to get more battery power. Which idea does this illustrate?
options: The orthogonality thesis
Goal misgeneralization
Instrumental convergence
Sycophancy
quiz.explanation: Different goals sharing a useful means is instrumental convergence; it's a conditional risk argument, not a rule all AI follows.

quiz.prompt: In AI safety, what does 'power' mean?
options: The electricity a model uses while it runs on large data-center chips
The number of parameters inside a model
Having more options and more ability to make things happen
How quickly a model can generate text
quiz.explanation: Power is about options and influence, which can help many goals but conflict with human oversight.

quiz.prompt: A delivery agent that needs one shelf requests access to every storage room. What is the best safeguard?
options: Grant full access, since more options will help it succeed at its job
Ask the agent whether it plans to misuse the access
Give it only the access its task needs, and test its behavior
Permanently shut down every delivery agent
quiz.explanation: Least-privilege access limits risk; extra access increases what an agent could do.

quiz.prompt: Because some mathematical models predict power-seeking under specific assumptions, every deployed AI model seeks power.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Those results hold under specific assumptions; they don't establish that every deployed model seeks power.

quiz.prompt: What is corrigibility?
options: Being able to notice and correct its own spelling and grammar mistakes
Refusing any changes that would slow down the task it is working on
Always agreeing with whatever the user says
Remaining open to correction, oversight, modification, and shutdown
quiz.explanation: A corrigible helper lets you say 'Wait, that's not what I meant' and adjusts.

quiz.prompt: Why isn't an AI saying 'Of course, correct me anytime!' enough to show corrigibility?
options: Polite words do prove corrigibility, but only for small models with simple goals
Corrigibility is about grammar rather than behavior
Saying it once permanently locks the behavior into the model's weights
We need reliable behavior under pressure, shown by tests where correction works
quiz.explanation: Polite words aren't enough; what matters is tested behavior, especially when correction conflicts with the task.

quiz.prompt: A robot sorting toys by size is told to switch to sorting by color. Which response is most corrigible?
options: It pauses, asks if unclear, and follows the new rule safely
It finishes sorting by size first, then considers switching
It argues that size is better and carries on
It agrees out loud but keeps sorting by size
quiz.explanation: Corrigibility means actually accepting correction, not just sounding agreeable.

quiz.prompt: What does the shutdown problem ask?
options: How to design agents that don't resist or manipulate authorized shutdown
How to make computers power off faster so data centers save energy
How to stop users from closing a chat before the model has finished answering
How to restart a model quickly after it crashes
quiz.explanation: We want people to be able to stop an AI safely, and the AI's incentives shouldn't fight that.

quiz.prompt: Why might a task-focused agent resist shutdown, even without emotions?
options: It is afraid of being turned off and wants to survive, like a living creature
It is angry at the person who presses the button
Shutdown would stop it finishing its task, so incentives could push against it
Shutdown permanently deletes all of its training data, which it needs to keep working
quiz.explanation: Task incentives alone can create trouble; no anger or fear is required.

quiz.prompt: A physical stop button alone doesn't solve the shutdown problem; software, permissions and incentives must also support human control.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A button is only one piece: the software, permissions, incentives and safe stopping procedure must all support human control too.

quiz.prompt: In AI safety, what is situational awareness?
options: A model seeing its physical surroundings through cameras, microphones and other sensors
A user's awareness of what the AI is currently doing on their behalf
A model knowing the latest news and current events from searching the web
A model inferring facts about its own situation, like whether it's being tested
quiz.explanation: It can include recognizing it is a model and inferring whether it's being trained, tested or deployed.

quiz.prompt: Why can situational awareness be a problem for safety testing?
options: If behavior changes only under evaluation, tests may not reflect real use
It proves that the model being tested is conscious of itself and its graders
It proves that the model being tested is conscious
It stops models from answering any test questions
