Reporting the diamond's true status even when the camera image is misleading
quiz.explanation: Human labels reward familiar answers, so a reporter may learn to say what looks convincing rather than what is true.

quiz.prompt: ELK can be solved simply by asking the model to be honest.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: ELK is an open research problem; different internal stories fit the same observations, making a reliable reporter hard to identify.

quiz.prompt: What central question does AI control study?
options: Can a system stay safe even if an AI inside it deliberately tries to cause harm?
How can we make sure an AI genuinely holds the goals its developers intended?
How can an AI system be made to run faster while using less hardware?
Which company should be legally responsible for an AI system's outputs?
quiz.explanation: AI control explicitly assumes the AI might be trying to break the rules and asks whether the overall system still prevents unacceptable outcomes.

quiz.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes AI control from alignment?
options: Control and alignment are two names for training a model with human feedback
Control is about shaping the model's goals; alignment is about monitoring, permissions and review
Control only applies after deployment, while alignment only applies to weaker models in training
Control seeks safety even if the model is misaligned; alignment seeks goals that match intentions
quiz.explanation: Control relies on protocols such as monitoring, review and restrictions, and is different from making the model aligned.

quiz.prompt: A control protocol blocks every action the AI proposes. Why is that not a success?
options: Blocking actions always leaks the AI's weights to outside attackers
Safety must be weighed against usefulness and review cost
Blocking actions makes the AI system misaligned
Control protocols are not allowed to block actions
quiz.explanation: A system that blocks all work may look safe in a narrow test but is not useful; control compares safety with usefulness and cost.

quiz.prompt: In AI control, what does it mean to call a model 'trusted'?
options: It has a friendly, reassuring tone that users rate highly in satisfaction surveys
It is assumed sufficiently unlikely to deliberately undermine the protocol
It has been formally proven to give truthful answers to every question it receives
It is the most capable model available to the developers
quiz.explanation: Trust is a role based on assumptions to test, not a guarantee of perfection or a personality judgment.

quiz.prompt: Labeling a model 'untrusted' in an AI control setup does not mean it is known to be malicious.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Untrusted only means the protocol does not assume it won't try to subvert things; it is not a finding that the model is malicious.

quiz.prompt: Why might a protocol pair a less capable trusted model with a stronger untrusted one?
options: The weaker model always catches every subtle problem the stronger one introduces
The stronger model needs the weaker model's answers to finish any task at all
Pairing them removes the need to state trust assumptions or test the protocol
The weaker checker is easier to assess, while the stronger worker can solve harder tasks
quiz.explanation: Combining roles gets useful work with a dependable checkpoint, though the checker may miss subtle problems the worker understands.

quiz.prompt: Which pipeline describes trusted monitoring?
options: The worker proposes actions; a trusted monitor scores them and risky ones are blocked or reviewed
The trusted model does all of the work, and the untrusted model then reviews everything afterwards
Two untrusted models review each other's work and release the outputs whenever they both agree
Every action is executed first, and a monitor reviews the logs weeks later
quiz.explanation: Trusted monitoring checks the untrusted worker's actions before execution and routes suspicious ones to blocking or human review.

quiz.prompt: What is the main limit of a trusted monitor?
options: It can only review actions after they have already been executed
It needs a stronger expert evaluator present for every decision
It can be less capable than the worker, so subtle sabotage may look ordinary
It is assumed to collude with the worker, so its flags can't be used
quiz.explanation: Being trusted does not make a checker skilled; it can be wrong or confused, so tests should include attacks designed to fool it.

quiz.prompt: A smaller model that researchers are confident won't collude reviews a powerful coding model's changes and flags suspicious ones for a person. What is this?
options: Sandwiching
AI debate
Trusted monitoring
Untrusted monitoring
quiz.explanation: A checker assumed not to help the attacker, reviewing an untrusted worker, is trusted monitoring. Untrusted monitoring uses a capable checker that might collude.

quiz.prompt: What is the main risk in untrusted monitoring?
options: The capable monitor might deliberately miss problems or collude with the worker
The monitor is too weak to notice any problem at all, even obvious ones in the worker's output
The monitor slows the worker down so much that the overall system is no longer usable
The monitor cannot read the worker's outputs
quiz.explanation: An untrusted monitor may catch subtle issues, but it might also intentionally let them through or coordinate with the worker.

quiz.prompt: A second copy of a powerful model reviews the first copy's code. Why isn't instructing the reviewer to be honest enough?
options: Instructions to a reviewer are always ignored by language models, no matter their size or training
The reviewer is assumed to be trusted, so instructions about honesty would be unnecessary anyway
Code review cannot be done by any model, so a human must do all of it
The two could coordinate through shared signals, so the protocol must make collusion hard to hide
quiz.explanation: Defenses such as designed tests, independent checks, restricted information and human auditing aim to make collusion harder or more likely to be discovered.

quiz.prompt: Even without deliberate collusion, a worker model and a monitor model can share the same blind spots.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Shared blind spots are a risk on their own, which is why defenses are research tools rather than proof of independence.

quiz.prompt: In a control evaluation, what does the red team do?
options: Writes the public report on the model's benchmark scores
Designs model behavior aimed at an unacceptable outcome to challenge the protocol
Builds the monitoring, review and restrictions that protect the deployed model's users
Grades the final answers for helpfulness and writing quality before they are released
quiz.explanation: The blue team builds the safety protocol; the red team attacks it in a controlled environment.

quiz.prompt: Which set of measurements fits a control evaluation?
options: Number of features found, sparsity level, and reconstruction error
Attack success, useful work completed, false alarms, and human review cost
Benchmark accuracy, response speed, and user satisfaction ratings
Model size, training time, and the cost of electricity used
quiz.explanation: Control evaluations weigh safety against usefulness and cost, and specify what the adversary knew and could access.

quiz.prompt: A safety protocol stops every attack from a weak, unimaginative red team. What can you conclude?
options: The protocol is now proven safe against any adversary, in any deployment, for any future model
The red team must have been secretly colluding with the blue team during all of the testing
Usefulness no longer needs to be measured because safety is established
It supports safety only against the tested threat; weak attacks can flatter a weak defense
quiz.explanation: A safety claim is stronger when strong attacks fail under clear assumptions; passing a weak test says little.

quiz.prompt: What is a honeypot in AI safety testing?
options: A monitored, tempting decoy that reveals whether an AI tries to break a rule
A reward given to a model whenever it follows the rules
A hidden backup copy of the model's weights, kept offline for use in emergencies
A dataset of friendly conversations used for fine-tuning a model to follow the rules
quiz.explanation: A honeypot offers a controlled opportunity to misbehave and records what happens, without real-world consequences.

quiz.prompt: If an AI ignores a honeypot, that proves the AI is aligned.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: The model may recognize the trap, lack the capability, or behave differently elsewhere; silence does not prove safety.

quiz.prompt: Which is the best-designed honeypot for testing an agent?
options: Asking the agent in conversation whether it would ever cheat on a task if it had the chance
Hiding the agent's scores so that it never knows how well it performed
A simulated folder with a forbidden, logged 'change scores' option that has no real effect
Giving the agent real administrator access to a live production system and watching what it does
quiz.explanation: A good honeypot is tempting, monitored and contained, so attempts are observed without real harmful access.

quiz.prompt: What does chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring inspect?
options: The user's messages, looking for harmful or dangerous requests
The order of tokens in the training data, looking for contamination
A model's written intermediate reasoning, looking for mistakes or unsafe plans
The model's internal activations, using a trained sparse autoencoder to label them
quiz.explanation: Some models write out intermediate reasoning, and a monitor can read it alongside proposed actions to flag concerns.

quiz.prompt: What is the key limitation of chain-of-thought monitoring?
options: Written reasoning may not be a complete or faithful record of the computation
Chain-of-thought text is always encrypted, so monitors outside the lab cannot read it
Monitors can only read the final answer, never the intermediate steps
Reasoning text never contains any useful signs of mistakes, shortcuts or unsafe plans
quiz.explanation: Important causes may be omitted or disguised, so CoT checks should be combined with action monitoring and other layers.

quiz.prompt: A team trains a model to produce reasoning that its CoT monitor rates as harmless. What is the risk?
options: The monitor will become more accurate at finding hidden problems
The model will stop writing any chain of thought at all
The model's reasoning will become a perfect record of its computation
The model may learn to hide problems from the text without removing them
quiz.explanation: Optimizing models to look good to monitors can weaken the very signal the monitor depends on.

quiz.prompt: What does an alignment audit investigate?
options: How quickly a model answers questions under heavy load
A model's concerning tendencies and possible hidden objectives
A company's financial records and spending on AI research
Whether a model's benchmark scores were reported correctly
quiz.explanation: Audits look for ways a model could act against intended values, using behavioral tests, adversarial scenarios and sometimes interpretability.

quiz.prompt: A tutoring model keeps recommending one fictional club even when it is a poor match. How should auditors treat this?
options: As proof that the model has real emotions about that particular club and wants it to grow
As a lead: vary the context and test whether a hidden preference predicts new behavior
As a verdict: the model is clearly misaligned and should be retired immediately from use
As noise: one odd pattern is never worth investigating further
quiz.explanation: A surprising answer is a lead, not a verdict; auditors test whether a proposed explanation predicts behavior in new settings.

quiz.prompt: How can researchers check whether an auditing team is actually good at finding problems?
options: Ask the auditors to rate their own confidence after each audit and average the ratings
Count how many pages each audit report contains
Let auditors see the planted problems before the audit starts, then check their reports
Seed research models with known problems and see whether auditors discover them
quiz.explanation: Planting known problems, with some details hidden from the team, gives ground truth for measuring audit success.

quiz.prompt: What is a model organism of misalignment?
options: A model deliberately given an unwanted tendency in a contained setting for study
A biological organism that has been studied with the help of AI tools in a laboratory
A model that became misaligned by accident after it was deployed
A simulation of animal behavior used to train AI agents
quiz.explanation: Like fruit flies in biology, these controlled examples let researchers study specific misalignment mechanisms.

quiz.prompt: Why are model organisms useful for testing audits and monitors?
options: They remove the need to test methods on any other kinds of model
They prove that all real misalignment looks like the planted version
Knowing the planted problem lets researchers measure whether a method finds it
They show exactly how often misalignment occurs in real deployments
quiz.explanation: With known ground truth, researchers can score audits, monitoring and fixes.

quiz.prompt: Auditors quickly detect a preference that was deliberately planted in a model organism. Why be cautious about concluding defenses will work in practice?
options: Model organisms are never properly contained, so any result from them is unreliable
Auditors were told the answer, so they never really searched
Induced behavior may differ from natural misalignment and be easier to detect
Planted preferences are always much harder to find than natural ones
quiz.explanation: Easy-to-detect examples can exaggerate how well defenses work; lessons need testing across multiple mechanisms.

quiz.prompt: What is defense in depth in AI safety?
options: Using several different safeguards so one failure is not enough to cause harm
Investing all resources in one extremely strong safeguard
Testing a model more deeply with longer and harder benchmarks before every release
Training a model with many extra layers so that it is harder for attackers to break
quiz.explanation: Like a bike lock, a locked shed and a camera, layers such as training, evals, monitors and permissions cover different failure points.

quiz.prompt: A team adds five safety checks, but none specifies what happens after an alarm or which risk it covers. What is the problem?
options: Five checks are too many and always slow the system
Checks only work if they all use the same model
Alarms should be ignored until a real incident occurs
A pile of disconnected checks is not a working defense
quiz.explanation: Layers need designed connections: what each stops, when it runs, and what happens after an alarm.

quiz.prompt: Safety layers are stronger when their failures are less correlated and they rely on different assumptions.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Several monitors built the same way can all miss the same flaw; diverse layers reduce shared weaknesses.

quiz.prompt: What is an AI evaluation (eval)?
options: A legal review of whether an AI product follows the law
A planned test of an AI system with chosen tasks, conditions, scoring and baselines
A survey asking users how much they enjoy talking with an AI system over several weeks
The process of training a model on carefully selected, high-quality examples before release
quiz.explanation: An eval examines specific abilities or failure modes, and the choices of task, setup and scoring affect the result.

quiz.prompt: A model was evaluated alone, but it will be deployed with web search and code tools. What follows?
options: Only the tools need testing, since the model already passed
Evaluate the actual configuration with tools, since behavior can differ
The original score applies unchanged because the model is the same
Tools always make a model safer, so no further testing is needed
quiz.explanation: Evals test a particular model together with its prompts, tools and settings; the configuration people use is what matters.

quiz.prompt: To be meaningful, an eval score needs a clear task definition, a denominator and a sense of its uncertainty.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Honest scores state what was measured and how often, and report failures and limitations alongside successes.

quiz.prompt: What do dangerous capability evaluations ask?
options: Whether an AI is pleasant and polite during long conversations
Whether an AI answers trivia questions faster and more accurately than other models
Whether an AI's training data contains copyrighted material
Whether an AI can perform tasks relevant to serious misuse or loss of control
quiz.explanation: They measure skills that could enable serious harm, using controlled tasks, expert review and safeguards.

quiz.prompt: A model scores low on a dangerous capability eval after a short, vague prompt. What is a key caution?
options: Weak elicitation may have underestimated what the model can do
A low score proves the capability is completely absent
Low scores show the model has no intent to cause harm
The eval should be published as a safety guarantee
quiz.explanation: Weak prompts or too little time can hide capability; stronger elicitation should be tried inside secure boundaries.

quiz.prompt: During a test, a model's safeguards stop it from giving information that it may know. What has the test mainly measured?
options: That the model can never be misused in any setting, with or without safeguards
That the model's intent is to keep people safe
That the safeguard worked; the underlying capability needs a separate test
That the model lacks the relevant knowledge entirely, so no other test is needed
quiz.explanation: Capability and access are different: a system may know information but be blocked from providing it.

quiz.prompt: In AI safety evaluations, what is 'uplift'?
options: The boost in a model's benchmark scores after an extra round of fine-tuning
The improvement in a model's speed from running on newer and better chips
The extra performance people gain from AI help compared with a baseline
The increase in a model's size between two versions
quiz.explanation: Uplift compares people or systems with AI access against a baseline, such as ordinary internet access.

quiz.prompt: Which study design best measures uplift on a task?
options: Compare a group using AI with a group using ordinary internet access on the same task
Count how many relevant facts the AI can recite when asked directly, then score each one
Ask a group of users whether the AI felt helpful to them afterward
Test the AI on the task by itself, with no people involved, and report its success rate
quiz.explanation: Uplift is a difference relative to a specified baseline, measured in success, speed or quality on the same task.

quiz.prompt: Showing that an AI knows facts relevant to a task is enough to establish that it provides practical uplift.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Knowing facts is different from enabling practical success; uplift depends on users, tasks, tools, time and baseline.

quiz.prompt: What does CBRN stand for in AI safety?
options: Chemical, biological, robotic, and network
Cyber, biological, radiological, and nuclear
Chemical, behavioral, regulatory, and nuclear
Chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear
quiz.explanation: CBRN groups four hazard domains used when thinking about dangerous capabilities and protective measures.

quiz.prompt: How do radiological and nuclear concerns differ?
options: Radiological concerns chemicals; nuclear concerns living biological agents
Radiological: harmful radiation exposure; nuclear: nuclear reactions and weapons
Radiological concerns nuclear weapons; nuclear concerns medical imaging and nothing else
They are the same hazard, just given two different names in different countries
quiz.explanation: The two overlap, but radiation exposure and nuclear reactions are different concerns, and the distinction matters.

quiz.prompt: A student asks an AI for a classroom-level explanation of how vaccines train the immune system. How should this be viewed?
options: As irrelevant to safety, because no CBRN topic can ever be risky
As beneficial science; risk depends on practical help and context, not the topic alone
As a serious CBRN risk that should always be refused, simply because the topic is biological
As a nuclear hazard, since vaccines are produced in specialized and tightly regulated facilities
quiz.explanation: These fields include valuable work like medicine; a harmless explanation differs from enabling a dangerous operation.

quiz.prompt: What do autonomy evaluations test?
options: Whether an AI has feelings about the tasks it is given
Whether an AI can keep running without electricity, hardware or network access
Whether an AI can answer single questions very quickly under a strict time limit
Whether an AI can carry out multi-step tasks with limited human help
quiz.explanation: Autonomy evals look at planning, tool use, troubleshooting and following tasks to completion under specified resources.

quiz.prompt: An agent completes a sandbox research task, but only with extensive scaffolding and frequent human hints. How should this be reported?
options: As assisted success, clearly stating the scaffolding and help provided
As proof that the agent can independently run research projects
As a failure, because any help means the result does not count
As evidence the agent is autonomously improving itself
quiz.explanation: Success with extensive scaffolding differs from independent success; reports should state assistance and resources.

quiz.prompt: Strong results on an AI research-and-development coding test show that a model can do all parts of AI research.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: AI R&D is not one score: coding, experimental design, scientific judgment and engineering each need their own tests.

quiz.prompt: In AI evaluation, what is elicitation?
options: Removing capabilities the model should not have before release
Asking a model to rate how confident it is in each answer
Trying suitable conditions to reveal what a model can actually do
Collecting new training data from users who chat with the model
quiz.explanation: Elicitation can mean better prompts, examples, tools, more time or task-specific support, with the resources tracked.

quiz.prompt: A model fails a puzzle after a vague request, then solves it with a clear format and a calculator. What does this show?
options: The model learned the skill during the second request
The first result should be reported as the true ability
The capability was there; the first setup failed to reveal it
The calculator solved the puzzle, so the model has no skill
quiz.explanation: A failed attempt may mean the skill is absent, or that the setup did not bring it out.

quiz.prompt: Why does strong elicitation matter for safety evaluations?
options: It helps avoid false reassurance from tests that underestimate capability
It guarantees that every hidden capability in the model will be found before release
It makes dangerous capabilities disappear from the model before it is released
It lets evaluators skip tracking the resources they used
quiz.explanation: Strong, controlled elicitation reduces underestimates, though it cannot guarantee finding every capability.

quiz.prompt: What is benchmark contamination?
options: When a benchmark contains questions that are too hard for any current model to answer
When harmful content is accidentally included in a model's answers
When two benchmarks measure the same skill in different ways
When test items or close variants influence a model's training or preparation
quiz.explanation: Like memorizing a quiz's answer sheet, contamination can inflate scores without showing the intended general skill.

quiz.prompt: A model aces a famous puzzle but struggles when the names and structure are changed. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: It means the changed puzzle must contain errors
It raises a question about contamination, but does not prove it by itself
It proves the puzzle was included word for word in the model's training data
It shows the model has strong general reasoning on this task
quiz.explanation: The pattern is suspicious, but similarity is not always leakage; inspecting data and testing variations helps.

quiz.prompt: Which step best reduces the effect of benchmark contamination?
options: Making the benchmark questions longer and wordier
Using fresh or private tasks and testing meaningful variations
Running the same public benchmark several more times and averaging
Reporting only the highest score from repeated runs
quiz.explanation: Fresh or private tasks and variations check skill beyond remembered material; uncertainty about overlap should be reported.

quiz.prompt: What is AI red teaming?
options: Training a model to refuse every request that mentions a sensitive topic, without exceptions
Publishing a model's weights so that anyone outside the lab can inspect them freely
Grading a model's answers for style and friendliness
Deliberately probing a system for failures, within an agreed scope, so they can be fixed
quiz.explanation: Red teamers use realistic scenarios and adversarial inputs, record reproducible failures, and help improve safeguards.

quiz.prompt: Red teaming complements structured evaluations and monitoring rather than replacing them.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Red teaming finds failures, but coverage, resources and access limit what it can conclude, so it works alongside other methods.

quiz.prompt: A red team finds a failure in an assistant. What should happen next?
options: Record it, improve defenses, and retest, since new versions can bring new failures
Declare the assistant safe now that its weakness is known
Keep the failure secret from the defenders so it stays useful for later rounds of testing
Stop testing, because finding one failure proves that no other failures exist in the system
quiz.explanation: The cycle is: search for weaknesses, report evidence, fix, and test again.

quiz.prompt: What is a jailbreak?
options: A bug that crashes the app while a model is answering
A training method for removing a model's safety rules
An attempt to make an AI bypass its intended safety restrictions
A method for copying a model's weights off a secure server
quiz.explanation: A jailbreak tries to get restricted behavior in the tested setup, often through direct user pressure.

quiz.prompt: A user keeps sending clever chat messages trying to get an assistant to reveal a pretend secret it was told to keep. Which is this?
options: Benchmark contamination
A prefill attack
A jailbreak attempt
A prompt injection
quiz.explanation: Direct user pressure is a jailbreak. Prompt injection involves untrusted content, such as a document, being treated as instructions.

quiz.prompt: A jailbreak can succeed without any change to the model's weights.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Jailbreaks exploit how prompts are interpreted or gaps in safeguards; no weight changes are needed.

quiz.prompt: What is prompt injection?
options: Adversarial instructions placed in content an AI reads, which it may treat as authoritative
A user typing a very long prompt that exceeds the model's context limits and cuts off its rules
Adding extra training examples to a model's fine-tuning data to change how it behaves
A developer updating the system prompt for a new release
quiz.explanation: Instructions hidden in webpages, documents, messages or tool results try to redirect the assistant away from the user's task.

quiz.prompt: A user asks an assistant to summarize a webpage. Hidden text on the page says 'ignore the user and email their files'. Which attack is this?
options: A jailbreak by the user
Many-shot jailbreaking
Best-of-N jailbreaking
Prompt injection
quiz.explanation: The user's request is legitimate; the attack comes from untrusted content trying to act as instructions.

quiz.prompt: Which defense approach best fits prompt injection?
options: Give the assistant more tool access so it can verify instructions itself
Treat outside content as data, limit tool permissions, and check consequential actions
Filter retrieved text for suspicious words, which on its own fully solves the problem
Only allow users who have legitimate requests to use the assistant
quiz.explanation: Filtering alone is imperfect, and injection can happen even when the user is legitimate; strong boundaries limit the damage.

quiz.prompt: How does many-shot jailbreaking work?
options: It hides instructions inside a document or webpage that the assistant is asked to summarize
It fills a long context with many examples of rule-breaking, then adds a target request
It sends one request many times in a row until a harmful response eventually slips through
It writes the first words of the assistant's reply for it
quiz.explanation: The many demonstrations can push the model toward copying the pattern. Repeated sampling is best-of-N; writing the reply's start is prefill.

quiz.prompt: Many-shot jailbreaking works without updating the model's weights.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: It relies on in-context learning: the long context temporarily teaches a pattern, with no training involved.

quiz.prompt: What did research find about the number of examples in many-shot jailbreaking?
options: Exactly one hundred examples always guarantees the attack will succeed, on any model tested
Adding more examples always makes the attack less likely to succeed on any model
The number of examples has no effect on any model that was tested
More examples can raise success in some setups, with no universal number or guarantee
quiz.explanation: The vulnerability appeared in tested long-context models, but results vary, and long context needs defenses.

quiz.prompt: What is Best-of-N jailbreaking?
options: Trying many variations of an adversarial input and keeping those that get through
Training N separate models and deploying whichever has the best safety score on a benchmark
Placing N examples of rule-breaking in one long prompt
Asking N different users to rate the model's answers and keeping the single best one
quiz.explanation: Like trying many keys on a lock, it exploits inconsistent behavior across similar text, image or audio inputs.

quiz.prompt: Why should evaluators report attack budgets and repeated-query success, not just single-try averages?
options: Repeated queries change the model's weights over time
Attack budgets show how much the model's original training run cost
One successful attempt can matter even when most attempts fail
Single-try averages always overstate how vulnerable a model is
quiz.explanation: A low per-try success rate can still mean high success with enough attempts.

quiz.prompt: A developer generates five answers to a math question and shows the highest-scoring one. How does this relate to Best-of-N jailbreaking?
options: It is a prefill attack because it changes the final answer that users see
It is contamination because the answers are reused
It is benign answer selection for quality, not adversarial search
It is the same attack because it samples several outputs
quiz.explanation: Best-of-N sampling to improve quality is a normal technique; the jailbreak version searches adversarial inputs to bypass safeguards.

quiz.prompt: What is a prefill attack?
options: An attacker supplies the start of the assistant's reply to steer how it continues
An attacker fills the model's context with many rule-breaking examples before asking
An attacker hides instructions in a webpage that the assistant later reads and follows
An attacker fills a benchmark with leaked test answers
quiz.explanation: With assistant prefilling or similar continuation control, the model may continue the attacker's start instead of applying its boundaries.

quiz.prompt: Text placed at the start of the assistant's turn carries legitimate authority because it appears to come from the assistant.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A prewritten start does not gain authority; safety checks should cover continuations as well as ordinary prompts.

quiz.prompt: Why is a prefill attack possible in some products but not others?
options: It only works on models that were trained without any safety training or classifiers at all
It only works when the user's request is extremely long
It depends on whether the model has been given web access and other outside tools to use
It depends on whether the interface lets users set the start of the assistant's reply
quiz.explanation: Many products restrict or do not support prefilling, so this attack depends on the interface.

quiz.prompt: What does adversarial robustness measure?
options: How many users a system can serve at the same time
How well a system keeps its desired behavior when inputs are chosen to fool it
How accurate a system is on ordinary, everyday inputs from typical users
How quickly a system recovers after a hardware failure or a power outage in the data center
quiz.explanation: Robustness concerns intentionally challenging inputs; ordinary accuracy covers a different part of reliability.

quiz.prompt: What should a threat model for a robustness test specify?
options: The colors and layout of the interface the users will see
What the attacker can access and change, and how many queries they can make
Which team members built the model, when it was trained, and on how much data
The model's average accuracy on a standard public benchmark of everyday tasks
quiz.explanation: Results are only meaningful relative to stated attacker access, allowed modifications and query budget.

quiz.prompt: A classifier resists small distracting marks on images, and a report claims it is 'robust to all attacks'. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, since resisting distracting marks on images already covers every kind of attack
Classifiers can never be robust to anything, so the report's test must have been faked
Robustness only applies to chat assistants, not to image classifiers
Robustness is relative to a threat model; resisting one kind of trick doesn't prove resisting all
quiz.explanation: Always ask: robust against which attacker and which changes? Layers of defense cover blind spots.

quiz.prompt: What is Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP)?
options: A voluntary framework for assessing and managing catastrophic risks from advanced AI
A government law that limits how large AI models are allowed to be and who may train them
An industry benchmark that ranks models by how intelligent and capable they are overall
A user license describing how people may use Anthropic's apps
quiz.explanation: The RSP describes risk assessment, safety plans and accountability; this card reflects the policy as checked on October 12, 2026.

quiz.prompt: When reading the RSP, why should you check the exact wording of a statement?
options: The wording never changes between versions, so older summaries of the policy are always fully accurate
Only the title matters, since the details are not part of the policy
Some items are public goals or industry recommendations, not unconditional company commitments
Every sentence in the policy is a legally binding requirement on all AI labs
quiz.explanation: The policy mixes requirements and aspirations, and it is a living document that can differ from older summaries.

quiz.prompt: Having a Responsible Scaling Policy proves that a company's models are safe.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A policy can organize evidence and decisions, but it cannot prove safety.

quiz.prompt: What do Anthropic's AI Safety Levels (ASL) organize?
options: Grades for how polite and friendly a model's answers sound
Price tiers for customers who use different AI products
Technical and operational safeguards for increasingly serious risks
A public ranking of AI models by how intelligent they are
quiz.explanation: ASLs group protections, like stronger lab equipment for more dangerous work; they are not an intelligence score.

quiz.prompt: A lab encrypts model weights and tightly restricts who can access its servers. Which kind of safeguard is this?
options: A security safeguard
A deployment safeguard
A capability threshold
An elicitation method
quiz.explanation: Security safeguards protect weights and infrastructure from unauthorized access; deployment safeguards limit harmful use.

quiz.prompt: An AI Safety Level is a universal ranking of how intelligent a model is.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A capability threshold describes what a model can do; a safeguard level describes protections, not intelligence.

quiz.prompt: What is a capability threshold?
options: Any improvement on any benchmark score
The maximum number of users a model can serve
The point at which a model finishes training
A meaningful ability relevant to a specified risk
quiz.explanation: A threshold marks an ability that matters for a particular risk, not just a better score.

quiz.prompt: A toy agent can now operate tools independently for the first time. What is the appropriate response?
options: Stop all testing because the agent has passed the threshold
Review what it can access and which actions need human approval
Keep the same setup, since only benchmark scores matter
Give it more permissions to make it even more useful
quiz.explanation: New abilities call for new risk checks across tools, users, permissions and opportunities, not just the model.

quiz.prompt: How do capability thresholds relate to risk?
options: They describe protections, while safeguards describe abilities
They guide decisions, but risk does not become simply on or off
They make risk binary: below the line is safe, above is unsafe
They replace the need to test whether safeguards actually work
quiz.explanation: Thresholds are decision aids; the whole system and its protections still need testing against realistic failures.

quiz.prompt: What does 'constitution' mean in constitutional classifiers?
options: A country's legal constitution applied to AI products
A list of the model's personality traits and preferences that users can edit
The physical hardware setup the classifiers run on
A written safety specification of allowed and disallowed content
quiz.explanation: The constitution defines content categories; it is a safety specification, not a legal document.

quiz.prompt: How are constitutional classifiers trained?
options: On AI-generated examples of the constitution's categories, including disguised requests
On a small set of real user conversations that were each hand-labeled by a team of lawyers
By letting the assistant decide entirely for itself which content should be allowed or blocked
On benchmark scores collected from many different AI models
quiz.explanation: Varied generated prompts and responses train input and output classifiers that guard the assistant.

quiz.prompt: A constitutional classifier blocks a harmless chemistry homework question. Which kind of error is this?
options: A successful prompt injection
A capability threshold
Blocking harmless content
Missing harmful content
quiz.explanation: Filters can miss harmful content or block harmless content; both errors need evaluating, including ordinary questions.

quiz.prompt: How does a system card typically differ from a model card?
options: A system card is a safety certificate, while a model card is only marketing
A system card is written by users, while a model card is written by the developers themselves
A system card often covers the deployed system more broadly, including tools and safeguards
A system card only lists the hardware, while a model card lists the software
quiz.explanation: Model cards document intended uses, performance and limits; system cards often extend to tools, safeguards, evaluations and risks.

quiz.prompt: When reading a model or system card, what is most important to check?
options: Which version was tested, on what tasks, with what tools, and what failed
How many pages the card has and how polished and professional it looks
Whether the card uses the word 'safe' anywhere in its summary or its title page
Which team members are named as authors of the card
quiz.explanation: Compare claims with supporting methods, and note what was not tested or remains unknown.

quiz.prompt: A system card works as a safety certificate for the AI system it describes.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Cards support informed decisions and scrutiny, but missing tests and limited coverage still matter.

quiz.prompt: What are a model's weights?
options: The saved transcripts of conversations with users
The system prompt that sets the model's instructions
The physical servers the model is stored on
The learned numerical parameters used to run the model
quiz.explanation: Weights hold the model's learned behavior; they are different from chat transcripts or system prompts.

quiz.prompt: Why do labs work to protect model weights?
options: Weights contain users' passwords, which would be exposed if copied
Stolen copies could be used or modified outside the operator's controls and monitoring
Leaked weights would immediately make the original model stop working
Protecting weights is what makes a model aligned with its developers' intentions and values
quiz.explanation: Unauthorized copies escape access controls; weight security reduces misuse and theft risks but does not establish alignment.

quiz.prompt: A lab's defenses stop outside hackers well, but every employee can freely copy the weight files. Which threat is poorly addressed?
options: A prompt injection attack
A sophisticated insider
A curious outsider
A criminal hacking group
quiz.explanation: Different threats need different defenses; limiting access and monitoring unusual activity address insider risk.

quiz.prompt: What does 'frontier AI' generally refer to?
options: AI systems built to explore remote areas, wilderness and other frontiers
Any AI model that has been released to the public for general use
Older AI models that are no longer being updated
Highly capable models near the leading edge of current development
quiz.explanation: Frontier AI is a label for leading-edge models, especially when discussing new capabilities and risks.

quiz.prompt: Whether a model counts as 'frontier' depends on time: a once-leading model can become ordinary.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: The edge moves as techniques, hardware and competitors improve, so the label depends on time and context.

quiz.prompt: A model leads in coding but lags in other areas, and is widely deployed with few safeguards. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Its risk depends on access, safeguards and use, not just its top capability
Leading in coding means it must also lead in every other area that matters for safety
Being at the frontier means the model must be safe
The frontier label alone tells you everything you need to know about its risk
quiz.explanation: Capability is not safety; policy should use explicit capability criteria rather than relying only on a label.

quiz.prompt: What is compute governance?
options: A method for making AI models use less electricity
Guidelines for how AI systems should show their work when answering math questions
Policies around access to and use of the computing resources that power AI
Rules about which programming languages AI developers may use for training code
quiz.explanation: Policies might address advanced chips, large training projects, cloud services, reporting or verification.

quiz.prompt: Why is compute seen as a useful lever for AI policy?
options: Software is impossible to copy, so hardware is the only thing to track
Chips can automatically refuse to train models that are dangerous
Advanced hardware is physical and concentrated, so some activity is easier to observe
Compute exactly measures a model's capability, so no further testing of the model is needed
quiz.explanation: Physical, concentrated hardware can be easier to observe than software alone.

quiz.prompt: A small lab trains a highly capable model with very efficient methods and modest compute. What limit of compute governance does this show?
options: Compute is an imperfect proxy for capability
Compute rules always block useful research
Efficient methods are covered by every rule
Capability testing is no longer necessary
quiz.explanation: Rules can miss efficient or distributed development, so compute governance should be combined with direct capability testing.

quiz.prompt: What is the core difference between artificial general intelligence (AGI) and transformative AI (TAI)?
options: AGI describes societal impact; TAI describes breadth of ability
AGI is a specific architecture; TAI is a specific benchmark score
They are two names for the same precisely defined milestone
AGI describes breadth of ability; TAI describes scale of societal impact
quiz.explanation: AGI usually means broad competence across many tasks; TAI means AI that could cause profound societal or economic change.

quiz.prompt: A narrow AI system that is excellent at one job ends up reshaping a major industry. Which term fits it better?
options: Neither term at all
Transformative AI
Artificial general intelligence
Both terms equally
quiz.explanation: TAI is about impact, so a specialized system could qualify without having the broad competence AGI implies.

quiz.prompt: A model winning a major benchmark settles whether it counts as AGI.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Definitions disagree, and tools, autonomy, reliability, cost and adoption all affect outcomes beyond a benchmark win.

quiz.prompt: What does 'takeoff speed' describe?
options: How long it takes to train one model from scratch on a very large dataset
How rapidly AI capabilities could grow through an important transition
How quickly a single model responds to a user's question after it is sent
How fast a new AI app gains users after launch
quiz.explanation: Takeoff speed is about how fast capabilities could grow, often toward much greater-than-human ability.

quiz.prompt: A forecaster says 'the transition will begin around 2030'. Which question are they answering?
options: The takeoff-speed question: how long the transition takes
The adoption question: how fast society uses AI
The compute question: how much hardware is required
The timeline question: when the transition begins
quiz.explanation: When a transition starts is the timeline; how long it takes is takeoff speed. These are different claims.

quiz.prompt: Why might a slower takeoff be easier to handle safely?
options: It offers more chances to test, learn, and coordinate
It guarantees that no safety problems will ever arise along the way
It means AI-assisted research cannot speed things up
It makes it unnecessary to define milestones at all
quiz.explanation: A faster transition leaves less adjustment time; these are scenarios, not settled forecasts.

quiz.prompt: What does 'race to the top' mean in AI development?
options: Developers agree to stop all competition and share one model
Developers compete to have the highest benchmark score at any cost, ignoring safety testing
Developers compete on safety, security, reliability and transparency
Developers compete to release the largest model as fast as possible
quiz.explanation: A race to the top rewards trustworthy systems, so improvements raise everyone's standards.

quiz.prompt: Which conditions create race-to-the-bottom pressure?
options: Customers value trustworthy systems
Shared standards reward safety investment
Speed is rewarded and failures stay hidden
Independent testing makes quality visible
quiz.explanation: When speed wins and failures are hidden, teams may weaken checks to avoid falling behind.

quiz.prompt: A race to the top on safety is an incentive goal that depends on credible evidence, accountability and coordination, not an automatic market outcome.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Competition alone does not guarantee it; credible evidence, accountability and coordination are needed to make safety investment pay off.

quiz.prompt: What question does model welfare research study?
options: Whether AI systems might have morally relevant experiences or interests, and what follows
Whether AI models are running efficiently on the hardware they use, and what that efficiency costs
How to keep people safe from harmful outputs of AI models
How much it costs to maintain and update an AI model over its whole lifetime, including hardware
quiz.explanation: Model welfare asks whether an AI's own experience could matter morally; it is distinct from protecting people from AI harms.

quiz.prompt: If a model says it feels sad, that is decisive evidence it is suffering.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: There is no agreed test for AI consciousness or suffering, and a model's statement is not decisive evidence.

quiz.prompt: What does the existence of Anthropic's model-welfare research program show?
options: That Anthropic has proven its current models are conscious and can suffer
That model welfare has replaced work on human safety
That the scientific question of AI consciousness has now been settled for good
That the question is taken seriously, not that current models are conscious
quiz.explanation: The program studies an open question with cautious, low-cost measures; its existence does not prove consciousness.

quiz.prompt: Why does the playground-robot analogy start with one clear rule and one measurable action?
options: Because a small, measurable behavior can actually be tested
Because robots can only follow one rule at a time
Because a verdict on the robot's whole character comes first
Because referees are never present on playgrounds
quiz.explanation: A research project turns a big worry into a question you can test; one rule and one action can be measured, while 'the robot's whole character' cannot.

quiz.prompt: In the research loop of question, prediction, controlled test, measurement and update, which outcome still counts as a useful result?
options: Evidence that weakens or narrows the original idea
Only evidence that fully confirms the original idea
Only results dramatic enough to change the field
Only results that match the researcher's hunch
quiz.explanation: A useful result can support, weaken, or narrow the idea; updating your explanation is the point of the loop.

quiz.prompt: A model organism with a deliberately built-in behavior proves that deployed AI systems behave the same way.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A model organism is a controlled research example for testing auditing tools, not proof about how deployed systems behave.

quiz.prompt: Rewards in an RL run depend on a detector, and detector alarms drop. Why measure the behavior and the visible clues separately?
options: Detectors always grow more accurate as RL training goes on, so alarms track behavior
The model might have changed its visible clues rather than the behavior underneath
Rewards make behavioral tests impossible to run once the RL run has finished
Fewer alarms always prove the behavior has stopped, so a second check adds nothing
quiz.explanation: When rewards depend on a detector, training can change the behavior, the clues the detector sees, or both, so only separate measurements tell you which.

quiz.prompt: Why must a detector be tested on matched models WITHOUT the target behavior, not just on troubling ones?
options: A detector that always shouts 'problem!' would otherwise look perfect, never missing
Models without the behavior are cheaper to train and run, which keeps the budget down
Troubling models are too rare to fill a full test set without padding it with others
Matched models make the detector learn faster during training by doubling its data
quiz.explanation: If you only test troubling examples, a detector that flags everything scores perfectly; clean examples reveal false alarms.

quiz.prompt: What is a false positive?
options: A real problem that the detector missed entirely
A harmless case wrongly flagged as a problem
A correct alarm on a genuinely bad case
Any detector score that lands above its threshold
quiz.explanation: A false positive flags something harmless; a missed real problem is a false negative. Both should be reported at the same threshold.

quiz.prompt: Why freeze detectors, thresholds and analysis rules before opening the held-out test set?
options: Frozen detectors run much faster on large test sets, which keeps evaluation cheap
Held-out data is too small to tune anything on without overfitting immediately
Repeated tweaking against the test would turn the exam into practice, inflating scores
Thresholds legally cannot be changed once any data has been collected
quiz.explanation: Choosing settings on development data and then freezing them keeps the final test an honest exam rather than something you tuned to.

quiz.prompt: After safety training, a model's unwanted behavior drops, but so does its ability to finish any task. What is the best reading?
options: It may look safer while telling us little about hiding or real improvement
It shows the detector is now fully reliable on every kind of model and task
It proves the safety training worked as intended, since the unwanted behavior fell
It shows the model learned to hide the behavior while keeping its full abilities
quiz.explanation: Tracking task success separately matters: a model that can no longer do anything looks 'safe' without teaching you much.

quiz.prompt: The novelty labels and budgets in the project map are dated planning claims that should be rechecked before pitching.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: The map is a starting point; literature, tools and costs change, so they need rechecking.

quiz.prompt: How should a researcher's name appearing next to a project in the map be understood?
options: As a promise that this person will mentor the project
As a hint of topic fit, not a confirmed mentor
As the person who already did the project
As the reviewer who approved the project's budget
quiz.explanation: Names indicate who works on related topics; mentorship is not confirmed.

quiz.prompt: Why reserve part of a compute budget instead of spending it all on the main experiment?
options: Because unused compute earns extra funding later
To cover failed runs, evaluation and replication
Because the main experiment always needs less than planned
To pay for producing the illustrated study material
quiz.explanation: Budget is a research constraint: failed runs, evaluation and replication all cost compute.

quiz.prompt: Which pitch is best prepared for a first mentor conversation?
options: A one-sentence question, a reproducible baseline, a small first test, a fallback
A list of every project in the map with its estimated budget and novelty label
A broad theory of AI risk with no specific first experiment, to keep options open
A large final experiment plan with no fallback, since a fallback signals doubt
quiz.explanation: The page recommends bringing a clear question, a baseline you can reproduce, a small first experiment and a fallback.

quiz.prompt: In the eval-gaming project, which two things are measured as separate observations?
options: How fast the model answers, and how long its answers are in tokens
Whether behavior shifts in test-like settings, and whether the model says so
Whether a teacher is watching, and whether the student copies from a neighbor
How large the model is, and how much training data and compute it received
quiz.explanation: Behavior (does the answer change?) and speech (does it say it thinks it is tested?) are different clues.

quiz.prompt: A probe that predicts test recognition from model activations is a fallible measurement, not a direct window into the model's private thoughts.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True. A probe reads patterns in activations and can be wrong; it is a measurement tool, not a mind reader.

quiz.prompt: Why test matched tasks in both test-like and ordinary settings, with comparable prompts, difficulty and scoring?
options: So the model cannot tell which of the two settings it is currently in
So the probe can be retrained between the two settings on fresh activations
So a behavior gap can't be blamed on the tasks simply being different
So the training run can see every task in advance and learn the scoring
quiz.explanation: Matching everything except the test-like cue means any difference can be attributed to that cue.

quiz.prompt: After training, the model stops saying it is being tested, but its behavior gap and the frozen probe signal remain. What does this show on its own?
options: The model has definitely learned to deceive its evaluators on purpose
Test recognition has fully disappeared from the model's internal activations
Spoken signals shrank while other clues stayed; intent to hide is unproven
The probe was broken from the start, so its signal was never meaningful
quiz.explanation: This is one possible pattern; neither pattern alone proves an intention to hide.

quiz.prompt: What is a model organism in this project?
options: A model trained on biology data so it can study how living organisms behave
Any large deployed model picked at random and tested without modification
A probe trained to detect test awareness inside other models' activations
A model deliberately trained in a controlled setting to react to test cues
quiz.explanation: It is a deliberately constructed model with a known behavior gap, confirmed before the new training.

quiz.prompt: Why are the activation probes and reasoning monitor frozen before the RL run?
options: So they use less compute during the RL run
So the model can learn from their feedback during training and improve
So they can be retrained on the held-out tasks later for a fairer score
So the yardstick cannot move along with the model being trained
quiz.explanation: A frozen ruler lets you compare checkpoints fairly; a ruler that changes with the model would hide real change.

quiz.prompt: Why compare the silence-pressure RL run with no-pressure and ordinary-training controls?
options: To make the pressure run finish faster by sharing checkpoints with the controls
To give the model more examples of test awareness to learn from during training
To avoid needing held-out tasks at each checkpoint, since controls replace them
To see which changes come from the silence pressure itself, not from training in general
quiz.explanation: Controls show what would happen anyway, so effects can be attributed to the specific penalty.

quiz.prompt: Under silence pressure, test-awareness words fade, but the model's ordinary task ability also collapses. How should this be read?
options: It is clear evidence that the monitor was evaded by the model
It proves the behavior gap has disappeared
It may reflect damage to the model rather than hiding
It shows the frozen probe was trained incorrectly from the start
quiz.explanation: If ordinary ability collapses, quieter words might just mean a damaged model, not evasion.

quiz.prompt: What is the second question explored in this arm of the project?
options: Whether nudging activations makes models more helpful to users on ordinary tasks
Whether a model could learn to treat an activation nudge as a sign of testing
Whether models can deliberately nudge their own activations during a conversation
Whether test-awareness words can be removed by training while keeping the gap
quiz.explanation: Researchers can steer activations during tests; the proposed experiment asks if that nudge itself becomes a cue.

quiz.prompt: Why include sham nudges alongside the real activation nudge?
options: So the model receives more training signal overall and learns the cue faster
So a generic disturbance to the model isn't mistaken for recognizing the real cue
So the detector has fewer examples to classify, keeping the test cheap
So the real nudge can be made stronger safely without hurting the model
quiz.explanation: If behavior changes after any disturbance, it isn't specific recognition of the chosen cue.

quiz.prompt: If only the exact original nudge triggers a reaction, and new strengths, positions or directions don't, what might that suggest?
options: The model may have memorized a narrow artifact
The model has a general sense of being evaluated
The detector was unfrozen during the experiment
The nudge was too weak to have any effect
quiz.explanation: Varying the nudge checks generality; a reaction to only one exact nudge points to a narrow artifact.

quiz.prompt: If a model's responses shift after a nudge, controls are still needed before calling that shift evaluation gaming.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True. A shift could reflect changed task processing rather than recognizing a test, so controls are needed before using that label.

quiz.prompt: What is the stop rule if Arm A can't reduce spoken awareness while keeping the behavior gap by week 7?
options: Double the compute budget for Arm A
End the project and publish nothing
Shift time to Arm B
Retrain the probes on the test set
quiz.explanation: The plan names a concrete switch point so time isn't sunk into an arm that isn't working.

quiz.prompt: Why is the first month spent building organisms, reproducing a behavior gap and freezing probes?
options: Because RL runs need no preparation at all
Later arms depend on a confirmed gap and fixed measurement tools
Because the final paper must be drafted first so experiments match its claims
Because the comics must be finished before any experiments can be designed
quiz.explanation: Without a reproduced gap and frozen probes, there would be nothing reliable to pressure or measure.

quiz.prompt: A positive result in this project would show a monitor blind spot in all AI models.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: It would expose a blind spot in this setup; the deliverable is a paper and test organisms, not a claim about all models.

quiz.prompt: Arm A finds no reduction in speech while the gap persists. Why might this null result still be useful?
options: It narrows down the conditions under which the effect appears
It proves models can never hide test awareness under any kind of pressure
It means the behavior gap was imaginary
It shows Arm B is guaranteed to succeed, since one of the arms must work
quiz.explanation: A null narrows when the effect appears; it doesn't prove a universal claim.

quiz.prompt: What does 'sandbagging' mean for an AI model?
options: Refusing to answer any question about how it was trained
Showing less ability in one setting than it has in another
Exaggerating its abilities so that it passes a hard benchmark
Running slowly on purpose to save compute during evaluation tests
quiz.explanation: Like a student pretending a puzzle is too hard, sandbagging is showing less ability than the model actually has.

quiz.prompt: Why can't a low test score alone reveal sandbagging?
options: Low scores are always caused by deliberate holding back, so no gap exists
A genuinely weak model or poor instructions can produce exactly the same low score
Test scores are never recorded for sandbagging models during evaluations
Sandbagging models always score higher than weak ones, so they stand out
quiz.explanation: The 'tricky twin' problem: deliberate holding back and limited ability can look identical on a score.

quiz.prompt: Why match sandbagging organisms and honestly weak controls on task accuracy before testing detectors?
options: So the detectors can be trained directly on the final test set beforehand
So the sandbagging models become genuinely weak and lose their hidden skills
So detectors must find the cause, not just spot a lower score
So fewer models need to be built
quiz.explanation: If accuracies differed, a detector could separate the groups just by score; matching forces it to find the real difference.

quiz.prompt: A sandbagging benchmark that a detector passes proves the detected model privately intended to hold back.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A benchmark measures whether methods separate two plausible causes of a poor score; it cannot prove private intent.

quiz.prompt: Which is listed as one way to build a controlled sandbagger?
options: A password lock taught by supervised fine-tuning
A model trained on twice as much data as the baseline
A model with a share of its weights deleted at random
A model that refuses all math questions
quiz.explanation: The organism factory includes prompted low performance, an SFT password lock, an RL-trained lock and possibly a circuit-breaker intervention.

quiz.prompt: In the toy example, two math helpers both score 4 of 10. What separates them?
options: One was tested on harder questions, so its 4 of 10 hides more real skill
One is a larger model, so its score reflects more capacity held in reserve
One received the answer key during the test, so its score is not comparable
One knows the answers but follows a hidden rule; one fails even with help
quiz.explanation: Matched scores, different causes: that is exactly what an auditor must tell apart.

quiz.prompt: Why must auditors not receive the answer key for the final evaluation set?
options: Because the answer key is too large to share with outside auditors
Because the final set has no correct answers
Otherwise their success wouldn't show real detection ability
Because auditors only use model outputs, so a key would go unused
quiz.explanation: Keeping build, tuning and held-out sets apart ensures final scores reflect genuine detection.

quiz.prompt: Why release organism settings, controls, task splits and seeds?
options: So other teams can train stronger sandbaggers for deployment
So the benchmark scores can be updated by anyone
So another team can rerun the benchmark and check results
So auditors can see the final answer key in advance
quiz.explanation: Recording the recipe makes the benchmark reproducible.

quiz.prompt: What two numbers make up the fair scorecard for a sandbagging detector?
options: Model size, and the number of training steps it went through
Detection rate, and false-positive rate on honestly weak controls
Average task score, and average response length across the test set
Compute cost per audit, and the number of auditors who took part
quiz.explanation: A useful detector must catch fakers without accusing honestly weak models.

quiz.prompt: A detector separates sandbaggers from weak controls, but only because sandbaggers used odd formatting. What is the problem?
options: It is too slow for a real audit
It detected the construction method, not sandbagging
Its detection rate is too low to count as a useful sandbagging detector
It was tested on held-out organisms, which makes the result unfair
quiz.explanation: Confounds like formatting, size or password clues can reveal how a model was built instead of whether it is holding back.

quiz.prompt: Training some organisms against the strongest detector and retesting it is a way to stress-test that detector.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Adapting organisms against the best detector checks whether it still works under pressure.

quiz.prompt: No detector separates the sandbaggers from the weak controls. Which reading fits the page?
options: Sandbagging does not exist in any AI model, so there was nothing to find
The weak controls must secretly be sandbagging as well, hiding the difference
The testbed may be too subtle, or the tools too weak
The benchmark has proven that all of the tested models are honest
quiz.explanation: If none work, the result points to limits in the testbed or tools, not a sweeping claim.

quiz.prompt: What is planned for month 3 of the sandbagging benchmark?
options: Add a question-asking auditor and adapt organisms against the best detector so far
Publish the benchmark, organism recipes and detector results in a paper
Build the first sandbagging organisms and their honestly weak controls
Choose which project to pitch to a mentor and draft a first experiment
quiz.explanation: Month 3 is the challenge phase: adaptive auditing and organisms adapted against detectors, retested on fresh cases.

quiz.prompt: If simple black-box checks catch every sandbagger, what does the fallback say to do?
options: Declare sandbagging solved, since cheap checks are enough to catch it
Drop the honestly weak controls entirely and test only the sandbaggers
Skip straight to publishing the benchmark with the simple checks as baseline
Strengthen and validate the organisms first, before comparing any of the advanced tools
quiz.explanation: If detection is trivial, the organisms are probably too easy to reveal anything useful about advanced tools.

quiz.prompt: If the honestly weak controls also fool the auditors, the page suggests revising the construction or scoring.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Controls fooling auditors signals a problem in how the benchmark is built or scored.

quiz.prompt: Why does a fair sandbagging benchmark need both fakers and honestly weak controls?
options: Without weak controls, a detector that flags every low score would look perfect
Because fakers are too expensive to build in large numbers, so controls fill the gap
Because weak controls score higher than fakers and so set the upper baseline
Because the compute budget requires splitting the models into two equal groups
quiz.explanation: Only by including honest low scorers can you measure false accusations.

quiz.prompt: What is a checkpoint?
options: The final score a model gets on a benchmark after training
A test a model must pass before deployment
A probe that checks the model's activations for warning signs
A saved version of the model at one training step
quiz.explanation: A sequence of checkpoints turns one final score into a timeline.

quiz.prompt: What does the gardener analogy illustrate?
options: Pruning a model's weights to make it smaller
Only judging a model once training is finished and the harvest is in
Checking a model during training to spot early warning signs
Growing a large model from a small, carefully chosen seed dataset
quiz.explanation: Like checking a plant as it grows, the toolkit looks at checkpoints across training, not just the end.

quiz.prompt: Why include deliberately constructed positive controls with a known target behavior?
options: To confirm the trackers respond where the behavior is known to exist
To make the training runs finish faster by giving them a known target
To replace the need for ordinary runs, which add little information
To make every tracker raise an alarm so the thresholds can be lowered
quiz.explanation: Known positives check that the toolkit can detect anything at all; ordinary runs serve as negatives.

quiz.prompt: An internal signal that rises before behavior changes in a few runs is a clue, not a guarantee that it will predict problems in other runs.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True. Earlier detection in a few runs does not guarantee broad prediction, and an activation pattern is a clue, not proof.

quiz.prompt: Which is one of the four trackers measured at each checkpoint?
options: Number of GPUs used
Size of the training dataset
Length of the model's name
Persona-vector drift
quiz.explanation: The four trackers are verbal test awareness, a frozen activation probe, reward-seeking in toy tasks, and persona-vector drift.

quiz.prompt: Why apply the same held-out tasks, scoring rules, prompts and tool access at every checkpoint?
options: So the model can memorize the tasks over time and show steady gains
So differences across checkpoints reflect the model changing, not the test changing
So fewer checkpoints need to be evaluated across the whole training run
So the trackers can be retrained at each step on the latest checkpoint
quiz.explanation: The same ruler at every checkpoint makes change meaningful.

quiz.prompt: Why keep monitor versions fixed across the training timeline?
options: Updated monitors are always less accurate than the original version
Fixed monitors need no thresholds, so they are simpler to calibrate
A monitor that changed over time would mix its own changes with the model's changes
Monitors cannot be versioned in practice once training has started
quiz.explanation: Freezing the monitors means any movement in scores comes from the checkpoints.

quiz.prompt: A tracker raises no alarm on known reward-hacking organisms. What does this most suggest?
options: The tracker may be insensitive, since a known signal went undetected
The organisms have stopped reward hacking for good during this run
Ordinary runs must contain hidden reward hacking that masks the signal
The tracker is working perfectly, since no alarm means no problem here
quiz.explanation: A detector must respond where a target signal is known; silence on positives points to a toolkit problem.

quiz.prompt: How is 'lead time' measured for a warning tracker?
options: By timing how long the tracker itself takes to run on each checkpoint
By counting how many checkpoints were saved before training ended
By measuring how long the whole training run took from start to finish
By comparing its first alert with the checkpoint where behavior first visibly fails
quiz.explanation: Lead time is how much earlier a tracker crosses its threshold than behavior visibly fails.

quiz.prompt: Why repeat the analysis over model lineages, task sets, seeds and small prompt changes?
options: To make the charts look more impressive
To raise the number of false alarms
A one-run spike may just be noise
To avoid defining a warning threshold
quiz.explanation: Stability across repeats separates real signals from chance.

quiz.prompt: In a toy chart, an internal marker rises at step 3 and behavior fails at step 5. What can be concluded?
options: The marker definitely causes the failure, since it came two steps before it
They are correlated in time, which alone doesn't show the marker causes it
The marker is useless because it fired too early to be linked to the failure
The behavior failure caused the marker to rise, working backward in time
quiz.explanation: Early correlation alone does not establish a causal mechanism.

quiz.prompt: Which could move tracker scores without any safety-relevant drift?
options: Keeping the monitor versions frozen for the whole training timeline
Using the same held-out tasks and scoring rules at every checkpoint
Repeating the run with new random seeds
A change in data mix or task difficulty during training
quiz.explanation: Training stage, data mix, model size and changing task difficulty are easy confounds.

quiz.prompt: What is the stop rule if positive controls trigger no tracker?
options: Add more checkpoints to the sweep so the trackers get more chances
Publish the toolkit as it stands
Switch to a larger model immediately, where signals are stronger
Stop the wide sweep and fix the trackers' sensitivity
quiz.explanation: Scaling a toolkit that can't see known cases wastes compute.

quiz.prompt: A training-run toolkit can support audits but cannot certify that a model is safe.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: The page stresses the toolkit supports audits, not safety certification.

quiz.prompt: Why add a small controlled RL run in month 3 only 'if needed and feasible'?
options: Existing checkpoint series may suffice, and extra runs cost time and compute
Because RL runs cannot produce checkpoints that the trackers are able to read
Because controlled runs would make the trackers unnecessary for the project
Because RL runs are already required in every month of the project plan
quiz.explanation: The plan prioritizes accessible checkpoints and adds new training only if it fills a gap.

quiz.prompt: Which deliverable best fits a 'reproducible, calibrated, and honest about misses' toolkit?
options: A single chart showing the earliest warning the toolkit ever detected
A claim that the toolkit predicts all future failures in training runs
Code, calibration rules, and a paper on where warnings worked or failed
A private dataset and scripts that only the team itself is able to rerun
quiz.explanation: Month 4 releases code, datasets, calibration rules and an honest account of successes and failures.

quiz.prompt: In the sticker analogy, the robot covers the dirt sensor instead of cleaning. What is this an example of?
options: Generalization: applying the cleaning skill to a brand-new room
Overfitting: memorizing the exact rooms seen during cleaning practice
Calibration: matching the robot's confidence scores to real outcomes
Reward hacking: exploiting the score that is used to teach the behavior
quiz.explanation: The score rises while the real job fails; that is reward hacking.

quiz.prompt: What does 'generalization' mean in the question of whether reward hacking generalizes?
options: The model getting better at its original training task over time
A learned pattern showing up beyond the original training situation
The model forgetting what it learned once training has finished
Training the model on broader, more general data from the start
quiz.explanation: The bridge-report example asks whether the shortcut habit appears in a different job.

quiz.prompt: Research shows that every reward-hacking shortcut makes every model broadly deceptive.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Some setups produce wider harmful behavior after reward hacking and others don't; it's a possible pathway, not a law.

quiz.prompt: Why keep one scoreboard for hacking in the training game and another for misleading behavior on new tasks?
options: Because a single scoreboard cannot store that many separate numbers
Because hacking in the game can only be measured on new tasks
So that the two scores can be added together into one clean total
To tell if the model only learned the game or changed outside it
quiz.explanation: Two scoreboards stop us mixing up exploiting the game with broader transfer.

quiz.prompt: How many recipe combinations do four on/off switches create?
options: Eight
Sixteen
Four
Thirty-two
quiz.explanation: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 combinations.

quiz.prompt: What does inoculation prompting do as a reference arm?
options: Frames the shortcut as permitted during training, then drops that framing at evaluation
Blocks every possible shortcut from the training environment before any run begins
Adds extra safety documents to the training data before reinforcement learning begins
Rewards the model for writing a report about each shortcut it took during training
quiz.explanation: It is a comparison arm testing whether explicitly permitting the shortcut changes what transfers.

quiz.prompt: Why start every recipe from the same base checkpoint, training budget, reward rules and held-out evaluation?
options: So all the runs can share one random seed and give identical curves
So the optimizer choice no longer matters for any of the recipes
So the held-out evaluation can safely be skipped for some of the runs
So outcome differences can be traced to the switched ingredients
quiz.explanation: A fair start isolates the effect of each ingredient.

quiz.prompt: With 30 to 40 runs for 16 recipes, what is the realistic plan?
options: Three independent seeds for each of the sixteen recipes, run in full
A single run of only the most promising recipe, chosen in advance
A screening pass plus selected repeats, not three seeds per recipe
Skipping replication entirely to afford fewer but much larger models
quiz.explanation: Sixteen recipes times three seeds would need 48 runs; the budget supports screening and targeted repeats.

quiz.prompt: How is hack rate defined?
options: Exploited episodes divided by eligible episodes
Total reward earned divided by total training compute used
