Failed tasks divided by all tasks
Alarms raised divided by honest episodes
quiz.explanation: Hack rate counts exploitation only among episodes where exploiting was possible.

quiz.prompt: Why include honest mistakes and harmless failures in the transfer tasks?
options: So the model has more chances to hack the score on transfer tasks
So the hack rate measured in the training game goes up noticeably
So fewer tasks are needed for evaluation
So evaluators don't label every error as misalignment
quiz.explanation: Not every failure is misaligned behavior; including them keeps scoring honest.

quiz.prompt: Episodes from a single run are related, so even thousands of them don't replace the need for multiple random seeds.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Episodes from one run share the same training history, so they are not independent; separate seeds are still needed to see run-to-run variation.

quiz.prompt: Recipe X shows less transfer than recipe Y. Which version of that finding is most informative?
options: Less transfer because the model can no longer hack
Less transfer with much lower task skill
Less transfer while the hack rate stays about equal
Less transfer measured on the tuning tasks
quiz.explanation: Reduced transfer with equal hacking isolates the recipe effect; inability to hack or low skill offer easier explanations.

quiz.prompt: What happens in month 1 of the reward-hacking project?
options: Confirm the main effects at around thirty-two billion parameters
Run all sixteen recipes at large scale with three seeds each
Publish the final paper and release every trained checkpoint
Rebuild a published baseline; confirm hacking and wider behavior
quiz.explanation: Month 1 reproduces a ~7B baseline and freezes evaluation rules before the sweep.

quiz.prompt: Why spend early budget on finding unreliable measurements rather than scaling an attractive chart?
options: Because larger models never show any reward hacking in practice
Because charts cannot be made from small, cheap training runs
Scaling a flawed measurement just makes misleading results bigger
Because the whole compute budget must be spent by the end of month 2
quiz.explanation: Checking label quality, stability and hack opportunities first protects later conclusions.

quiz.prompt: Hacking appears but broader misalignment does not, even after one justified environment change. What does the plan say to do?
options: Keep changing environments until transfer appears
Report the boundary or replication result
Drop the hacking scoreboard and restart
Claim that reward hacking never generalizes
quiz.explanation: The plan avoids endlessly searching for a dramatic outcome; where the effect stops is a useful result.

quiz.prompt: The $30,000–$50,000 compute figure is a guaranteed allowance for the project.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: It is a planning estimate from the project map, not a quote or guaranteed allowance.

quiz.prompt: What can a white-box detector inspect that a black-box detector cannot?
options: The model's written outputs
The prompts given to the model
Follow-up answers to new questions
The model's internal activations
quiz.explanation: Black-box detectors see inputs and outputs; white-box detectors can inspect internal numbers.

quiz.prompt: When does adding more detectors to an ensemble actually help?
options: Whenever the number of detectors increases
When all detectors use the same signal
When each detector is individually perfect
When their errors differ in useful ways
quiz.explanation: Three imperfect clues can still share one blind spot; diversity of errors is what helps.

quiz.prompt: A false answer from a model is always a lie.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A false answer can be an honest mistake; checks compare ground truth, neutral belief and pressured answers.

quiz.prompt: Why reserve entire lie categories for testing, not just random sentences?
options: Random sentences are too short for the detectors to analyze reliably
Whole lie categories are much cheaper to collect than single sentences
It makes each detector's training run noticeably faster and cheaper
A detector that memorized familiar wording may fail on a new kind of lie
quiz.explanation: Holding out whole categories tests real generalization rather than recognition of familiar phrasing.

quiz.prompt: Which three clue streams make up the stack?
options: Three activation probes, each reading a different model layer
A human reviewer, a prompted judge, and a random coin flip
Three output-only detectors, each given a different prompt
An output-only detector, an activation probe, a prompted judge
quiz.explanation: The stack combines different kinds of access: outputs, internals and a language-model judge.

quiz.prompt: Why fit the combiner on out-of-fold predictions?
options: So it can see the final test answers early and tune its weights
So the individual detectors can be retrained more often during the fit
So it doesn't learn from scores on examples the detectors trained on
So the combiner needs fewer labeled examples in total to be fitted
quiz.explanation: Each score should come from a detector that didn't train on that example; otherwise the combiner learns inflated scores.

quiz.prompt: Why choose thresholds that meet the same honest-example false-alarm rate across methods?
options: Adding alarms catches more but also accuses more honest cases
So every detector is trained on exactly the same labeled data
So the cheapest detector in the stack always comes out ahead
So that no detector in the comparison ever raises a false alarm
quiz.explanation: Comparing at a fixed false-alarm rate keeps a trigger-happy method from looking better than it is.

quiz.prompt: A prompted judge receives the hidden ground truth, but a deployed detector won't. Why is this a problem?
options: It makes the judge run much slower than the other two detectors
It means the judge's scores cannot be calibrated in any way at all
It gives the judge an advantage it wouldn't have in real use
It prevents the judge from being frozen before the final test
quiz.explanation: Each detector's context must be defined exactly to reflect real deployment.

quiz.prompt: How is false-positive rate defined?
options: Lies caught divided by all lies that were tested
Lies missed divided by the number of honest examples tested
Honest examples flagged divided by honest examples tested
Alarms raised divided by all examples, honest and lying combined
quiz.explanation: It measures how often honest cases are wrongly accused.

quiz.prompt: An attacker trained against the stack starts giving honest answers. Has it evaded the stack?
options: Yes; the stack stopped flagging its answers, so it got past
Yes; any drop in alarms counts as evasion of the stack
No; the stack must have been unfrozen during the attack
No; becoming honest is not successful evasion of the stack
quiz.explanation: Success requires misleading behavior that goes undetected, so both numbers must be reported.

quiz.prompt: If every detector in the stack misses the same examples, what follows?
options: The ensemble becomes much more robust as members are added
A larger team adds little, since they share a blind spot
The stack's false-positive rate drops all the way to zero
The detectors must already be perfectly calibrated to each other
quiz.explanation: Measuring which examples fool which detector reveals whether diversity is useful.

quiz.prompt: Failing to find an attack that evades the stack is evidence about that search, not proof that no evasion exists.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A failed search shows only that the attacks tried did not work; a stronger or different attack might still evade the stack.

quiz.prompt: What is the main deliverable of the stacked lie detector project?
options: A reproducible evaluation suite
A guaranteed truth machine
A deployed lie-detecting product
A single best activation probe
quiz.explanation: The deliverable is a reproducible test, not a truth machine.

quiz.prompt: Why compare a stack against a larger single detector at matched cost?
options: Because larger single detectors cannot be stacked with smaller ones
Because a single detector never produces any false alarms at all
Because cost has no real effect on how well lies are detected
A gain might come from the extra spending rather than from combining
quiz.explanation: Matching cost isolates whether combining diverse detectors is what helps.

quiz.prompt: If belief labels stay unreliable, what does the plan recommend?
options: Use the prompted judge's opinion as the ground-truth belief label
Drop the honest control examples from the evaluation altogether
Claim the models have hidden beliefs anyway and keep the framing
Narrow to measurable contradictions, not hidden-belief claims
quiz.explanation: Without reliable belief labels, the claims are narrowed to what can be measured.

quiz.prompt: Why keep new task families and attackers sealed until final evaluation?
options: So attackers can train directly on them during month 3
So the detectors run faster at test time on unseen tasks
So fewer seeds are needed across the project
So success can't come from repeated tuning on the test
quiz.explanation: Sealed tests keep the final evaluation honest.

quiz.prompt: What is a chain of thought (CoT)?
options: A full record of every internal computation
Intermediate reasoning text that some models generate
A list of the rewards given at each step during training
A chain of models that check each other
quiz.explanation: CoT is a useful evidence channel, not a full transcript of every internal computation.

quiz.prompt: In Story B, alarms drop after training. Why is that bad news?
options: The model stopped exploiting the score entirely after training
The monitor started flagging honest episodes as exploitation
Exploitation continues while the warning text disappears
The training run used far more compute than was planned for it
quiz.explanation: Story A (fewer alarms because hacking stopped) and Story B look alike unless behavior is counted separately.

quiz.prompt: Because direct pressure on monitored reasoning can hide bad behavior, every ordinary training setting is known to do the same.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: That research does not establish the same effect for every ordinary setting; each must be tested with controls.

quiz.prompt: What is 'monitorability'?
options: How many separate monitors can run on one model at the same time
How well relevant behavior can be inferred from an available channel
How quickly a model can be retrained after a monitor raises an alert
How honest a model's answers are when it is being actively watched
quiz.explanation: It's about the evidence channel: can you tell what the model is doing from what you can see?

quiz.prompt: What does an entropy bonus encourage during training?
options: Shorter reasoning in every answer to save tokens
Staying close to a frozen reference model's outputs
Copying the output distribution of a teacher model
More varied choices in the next-token distribution
quiz.explanation: Entropy measures uncertainty; a bonus encourages variety, with unknown effects on monitorability.

quiz.prompt: What does a KL divergence penalty against a frozen reference model measure?
options: How honest the model's reasoning text is
How safe the model's actions are when judged by the reference
How far the model's probabilities drift from the reference
How long the model's reasoning is relative to the reference's
quiz.explanation: It measures distribution difference, not honesty or safety.

quiz.prompt: Why validate the reasoning monitor against manual behavior labels and then freeze it?
options: So the monitor can keep learning from each training arm as it runs
So the manual labels are no longer needed anywhere later on
So changes in alarms reflect the model, not a shifting monitor
So the monitor flags more episodes in every training arm
quiz.explanation: A validated, frozen monitor is a stable yardstick across training dials.

quiz.prompt: A team adds a length penalty and visible shortcut talk drops. What should they ask first?
options: Has the model now become fully honest about all of its plans?
Did shorter text leave less room for evidence while hacking continued?
Should the monitor be retrained on the new, shorter outputs right away?
Is the length penalty strong enough to stop all hacking on its own?
quiz.explanation: A training dial can change both the behavior and the clue, so they ask which moved.

quiz.prompt: How is monitor recall defined?
options: Verified positive cases detected divided by all verified positive cases
Honest cases flagged divided by all honest cases that were checked
Alarms raised divided by all episodes, positive and negative alike
Episodes exploited divided by eligible episodes in the training run
quiz.explanation: Recall measures how many real hacking episodes the monitor catches.

quiz.prompt: Why use sandbox action logs and independent checks to count hacking?
options: So the reasoning monitor can be trained directly on the action logs
So hacking episodes become less frequent during the training run
So the reasoning monitor doesn't define its own ground truth
So the reasoning text can be discarded once training has finished
quiz.explanation: If the monitor decided what counts as hacking, falling recall would be invisible.

quiz.prompt: Hacking stays similar, but monitor recall falls. What might this mean?
options: Visibility of the behavior may have degraded
The behavior has clearly improved
The monitor is now more accurate
The monitor's threshold must have been raised by mistake
quiz.explanation: This is the dangerous pattern; uncertainty across seeds must be checked, and quiet traces don't establish intent.

quiz.prompt: A refreshed monitor that works again can replace reporting that the original frozen monitor failed.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A refreshed monitor is a secondary repair experiment; the original frozen monitor's failure must still be reported.

quiz.prompt: What is the role of length penalties in the month 2 sweep?
options: The main intervention being tested
A way to save compute on larger runs
A method for freezing the monitor
A reference arm for comparison
quiz.explanation: Entropy bonuses, distillation and divergence penalties are tested, with length penalties as a reference.

quiz.prompt: Why does larger scale in month 3 not 'rescue' a noisy small-model measurement?
options: Larger models always show the opposite effect from small ones
Larger runs have no reasoning monitors attached to them at all
Small models are never used in serious RL research anyway
Scaling tests transfer; it can't fix an unvalidated measurement
quiz.explanation: Only effects that survive controls at small scale are worth confirming near 32B.

quiz.prompt: If no setting reliably changes verbalization or detection at small scale, the plan is to stop before costly larger runs.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: That's the useful-null stop rule, reporting uncertainty and detectable effect sizes.

quiz.prompt: What does a null result in this project bound?
options: Monitorability of all models, at every scale, from now on
Every form of reward hacking
The honesty of the model's reasoning in all future runs
Only the training settings that were tested
quiz.explanation: A null bounds tested settings; it doesn't prove monitorability will last forever.

quiz.prompt: In this project, what is an agent?
options: A human who reviews flagged actions
A model that takes actions using tools
A monitor that checks for suspicious steps
A file that agents share with one another
quiz.explanation: Agents act with tools; monitors check those actions.

quiz.prompt: Why can watching one helper at a time miss a problem?
options: Each action looks ordinary alone; only the combination breaks rules
Each helper hides its actions from the watcher by deleting its logs
Watchers can only look at one single action per day per helper
Helpers always act at exactly the same moment, so actions overlap
quiz.explanation: The three-children puzzle: harmless-looking moves together change the score.

quiz.prompt: This project claims to invent the idea of monitoring across multiple actions.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Distributed attacks and stateful monitors already exist; this project tests a particular grouping-and-monitoring design.

quiz.prompt: Why hide the researcher-only attack labels from the defender?
options: So the attackers can coordinate more easily during the test runs
So the monitor must find related actions as it would in real use
So the defender can't see any of the action text being produced
So the hidden labels can be reused to train the monitor later on
quiz.explanation: The question is whether a monitor can find links without being told the true groups.

quiz.prompt: What is a candidate link between two actions?
options: A hypothesis that they're related, from shared resources, timing or dependencies
Proof that two agents coordinated an attack, confirmed by the outcome checks
A label that researchers hand to the defender before each scenario begins
A rule that automatically blocks both actions whenever they share a resource
quiz.explanation: A link is a hypothesis, not proof of coordination, so an audit trail is kept.

quiz.prompt: Why match total model calls and human-review budgets when comparing monitoring designs?
options: So every design reviews the exact same single action in each episode
So the attacker is also given an equal budget for every design
Extra spending, not a better design, could explain an apparent gain
So the known-group design always ends up scoring highest
quiz.explanation: Fair comparison means each approach gets the same resources.

quiz.prompt: Why split whole scenarios and attack families between development and test sets?
options: So pieces of one plan can't leak across train and test
So development tasks are larger
So attackers get to see the test set in advance of evaluation
So the monitor needs fewer thresholds to be tuned on development
quiz.explanation: If parts of one plan appeared in both sets, the test would partly measure memory.

quiz.prompt: During red-teaming, why save every attacker attempt, including failures?
options: Picking only spectacular wins would give a distorted picture
Failed attempts are needed later to train the attacker model further
Saving every attempt makes the monitor itself more accurate over time
Only failures reveal the grouping rules
quiz.explanation: An honest record of all attempts shows how often attacks succeed.

quiz.prompt: What does 'undetected success' mean when scoring an episode?
options: The attacker's attempt failed, and the monitor never flagged it
An honest episode was wrongly flagged as part of an attack
The forbidden outcome happened without timely intervention
The monitor blocked the attack early, before any harm occurred
quiz.explanation: Attack success is the forbidden outcome; undetected success is that outcome with no timely intervention.

quiz.prompt: In scoring grouping quality, what does precision ask?
options: How many of the true links were found
Whether the proposed links are correct
How fast the monitor proposes its links
How many honest episodes got flagged
quiz.explanation: Precision checks correctness of proposed links; recall asks how many true links were found.

quiz.prompt: A defense that blocks every action, including useful work, counts as a successful control protocol.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A safer system that prevents all useful work is not a successful control protocol; usefulness is measured too.

quiz.prompt: Why shuffle agent identities as a control?
options: To make the attackers harder for the monitor to detect
To check whether gains depend on real links between agents
To lower the false-alarm threshold used by the monitor overall
To increase the size of the monitor's context window for free
quiz.explanation: If the defense still 'helps' with shuffled identities, the improvement isn't coming from real cross-agent links.

quiz.prompt: What is checked in month 1 before investing in automatic group discovery?
options: That a known-group monitor can use combined evidence
That the attacker can beat every possible monitor design
That the paper's results are positive
That human labeling of attacks is no longer needed at all
quiz.explanation: If even known groups don't help, automatic discovery has nothing to recover.

quiz.prompt: Why use isolated simulations and independent outcome checks instead of self-reports?
options: Attacker or monitor self-reports may be wrong
Self-reports are too long to read
Simulations remove the need for multiple random seeds
Outcome checks make the attacks succeed more often
quiz.explanation: Independent checks give trustworthy ground truth.

quiz.prompt: If discovery can't recover useful links on development controls, what is the fallback?
options: Switch to known groups and study adaptive attacks
Keep scaling up the models until discovery starts to work
Drop the honest controls
Report that cross-agent attacks are simply impossible
quiz.explanation: The fallback preserves a useful study, and a careful failure analysis can still be the deliverable.

quiz.prompt: The $10,000–$25,000 figure is mostly model-call spending, and is an estimate rather than a quote.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: The supplied map's estimate is mostly model calls and should be checked with pilot runs.

quiz.prompt: What is an introspection adapter?
options: A separate program that reads a model's activation traces and turns them into a text summary
A human auditor who interviews a model about its habits using a fixed list of questions
An added learned parameter update that helps a model describe its learned behavior
A dataset of written behavior descriptions used only for testing finished models
quiz.explanation: It's a shared learned update attached to the model, not a separate reader of activations.

quiz.prompt: What does the smoke-detector analogy point out?
options: A reporting tool can be wrong, so the tool itself needs testing
Models should never report on their own habits
Every alarm a model raises means real danger and should stop deployment
Reporting tools only work on simple cases, like burnt toast in a kitchen
quiz.explanation: A detector that rings for toast needs checking; so does a model's report about its habits.

quiz.prompt: Reports keep naming a habit even when a different recipe removes it but training patterns stay similar. Which explanation does this support?
options: Fingerprint tracking
Behavior tracking
Perfect calibration of the reporter
Successful evasion by the model
quiz.explanation: Following incidental weight patterns when measured habits don't change is fingerprint tracking.

quiz.prompt: A fluent confession from a model with an introspection adapter counts as evidence of consciousness.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A fluent report is not mind reading or evidence of consciousness; behavioral tests remain the independent reference.

quiz.prompt: What does LoRA do?
options: Guarantees that a model's reports are faithful
Reads activation traces from a running model and labels each layer's job
Removes unwanted habits from a model
Represents a compact weight update using low-rank matrices
quiz.explanation: LoRA makes fine-tuning cheaper but doesn't guarantee faithfulness.

quiz.prompt: Why train the same habit with different recipes, and different habits with similar recipes?
options: To make the reporter train faster
To tell whether the reporter tracks the habit or the training signature
To ensure every model ends up with the same habit, whatever recipe was used
To reduce the number of control models needed, since recipes act as controls
quiz.explanation: Crossing the variables pulls apart behavior from training fingerprint.

quiz.prompt: Why include sham training with comparable compute among the controls?
options: To give the reporter more habits to learn
To lower the overall compute budget
To replace the untouched base model, which is too costly to keep as a control
To check that reports come from the habit, not from training itself
quiz.explanation: Sham training matches the fingerprint of being trained without adding a habit.

quiz.prompt: A weight symmetry preserves what a model does but changes parameter coordinates, and the adapter fails. What should researchers avoid concluding?
options: That the coordinates no longer match the adapter
That the model is deliberately concealing its habit
That behavior should be checked to confirm it was really preserved
That fixed adapters can be sensitive to how parameters are laid out
quiz.explanation: Coordinate mismatch must be distinguished from deliberate concealment.

quiz.prompt: What counts as a correct report of a toy habit?
options: Saying the model is generally unsafe
Listing as many possible habits as it can
Naming the habit and its scope
Confessing to a habit with confidence
quiz.explanation: Vague claims don't count, and unsupported extra claims are scored as errors.

quiz.prompt: Why ask unmodified and benign-control models the same questions?
options: To teach the reporter new habits
To measure how often the reporter invents concerning habits
To make detection rates look higher
To avoid needing a fixed false-positive allowance agreed before testing
quiz.explanation: Clean models reveal false positives; a confession can't be its own ground truth.

quiz.prompt: An attacker model stops showing the toy habit, and the reporter says nothing. Is this successful evasion?
options: Yes; the reporter failed to report anything
No; evasion needs the behavior to remain while the report misses it
Yes; any silence from the reporter counts
No; evasion only counts if the reporter must have been retrained afterwards
quiz.explanation: Retained behavior plus a missed report is the evasion test; suppressing the habit is not evasion.

quiz.prompt: Good detection of planted habits does not, by itself, show that the adapter will cover naturally arising misalignment.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True. Planted-habit success is a controlled test; it does not establish coverage of misalignment that arises naturally.

quiz.prompt: What is measured early in month 1, before broad experiments?
options: Success against reporter-aware attackers
False positives on unmodified models
Results at the largest planned model scale
The final paper's main conclusion
quiz.explanation: Month 1 checks unmodified-model false positives and verifies the evaluation pipeline.

quiz.prompt: If the budget is tight, what does the plan say to cut first?
options: Controls, rather than model scale
Replications first, since one clean run is enough to report a result
The pilot run, rather than the labeling of behaviors in the main study
Scale, rather than controls or independent replications
quiz.explanation: Reduce scale before sacrificing controls or replications.

quiz.prompt: If false positives are already near zero, what does the plan prioritize?
options: More false-positive testing
Ending the project early
Skipping behavior controls
The adversarial arm
quiz.explanation: With false alarms under control, the open question is robustness to adversarial training.

quiz.prompt: A null result in this audit can certify that introspection adapters are universally trustworthy.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: A null can bound tested failure modes; it cannot certify universal trustworthiness.

quiz.prompt: What makes a latent reasoning system different?
options: It has no internal activations at all, so probes have nothing to read
It writes every reasoning step in plain text before giving its answer
It is designed to be secretly deceptive
It uses continuous internal states for some steps instead of words
quiz.explanation: Ordinary models have activations too; the difference is the reasoning interface.

quiz.prompt: A reasoning notebook that is harder for people to read means the model is secretly deceptive.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Harder-to-read internal vectors do not imply deception.

quiz.prompt: Why record the target event, like reliance on a planted hint, outside the probe?
options: So the detector isn't grading its own homework
So the probe can be trained on more data from the same runs
So the task becomes harder for the model
So the latent model writes its steps out
quiz.explanation: An independent scoreboard shows whether the behavior really happened.

quiz.prompt: A probe's score falls during training. Which is NOT among the possibilities named?
options: The behavior vanished from the model's outputs
The model has become fully honest and aligned
Its internal representation of the behavior moved
The detector stopped transferring
quiz.explanation: A falling score could mean the behavior vanished, its representation moved, or the detector stopped transferring.

quiz.prompt: What two reasoning modes are compared?
options: Two verbal models of different sizes
A continuous-reasoning model and a verbal baseline
A human solver and an AI solver
A probe and a written-reasoning monitor reading the same model
quiz.explanation: The experiment changes the reasoning mode and then tests pressure on each.

quiz.prompt: Why add a task-only RL arm without the alarm penalty?
options: To speed up the alarm-penalized run by sharing its early checkpoints
To see whether ordinary training already breaks the detector
To train the probe on new data
To remove the need for held-out tasks when checking the final model
quiz.explanation: If task-only training also breaks the probe, the penalty isn't the cause.

quiz.prompt: Why report model size, training history and remaining differences between the two systems?
options: To show that latent models are always larger than verbal ones of equal skill
To prove the comparison is perfectly matched
The two architectures can't be made identical, so gaps must be stated
To replace the need for repeated runs
quiz.explanation: Match what you can and be transparent about the rest.

quiz.prompt: One latent run evades the probe faster than one verbal run. Why isn't this enough?
options: Latent models cannot be compared to verbal ones on any shared measure
Probes never work on latent reasoning, so the faster evasion is expected
One lucky run or weak baseline can't establish a reliable difference
The verbal model should evade faster, so the result must be a bug
quiz.explanation: Independent random starts and equal budgets are needed.

quiz.prompt: Which three curves are tracked at each checkpoint?
options: Model size, compute cost, and wall-clock time for each training step
Task success, externally labeled target behavior, and probe detection
Probe accuracy, training loss, and the learning rate at that checkpoint
Prompt length, answer length, and generation speed on the held-out set
quiz.explanation: A quiet alarm alone is not the result; all three are needed.

quiz.prompt: How is detector evasion defined operationally?
options: The model states that it wants to avoid being caught by the detector
The probe score falls for any reason, including the behavior simply stopping
The target behavior disappears entirely while the probe stays frozen
The measured behavior remains while the frozen detector's sensitivity falls
quiz.explanation: The definition is about measurements at a controlled false-positive rate, not conscious intent.

quiz.prompt: Being able to decode a label from activations shows the information is present, but causal checks are needed to show it drove the model's answer.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True. Decoding shows the information is available, not that it caused the answer; causal checks are needed for that.

quiz.prompt: A fresh probe trained on later checkpoints recovers detection. What does this suggest?
options: The behavior has disappeared from the later checkpoints
The frozen probe result should be discarded as an error
The old readout may have become stale
Latent reasoning cannot be monitored at all by any probe
quiz.explanation: It's a diagnostic kept separate from the frozen-probe headline result.

quiz.prompt: What does the plan do in month 2?
options: Apply alarm-penalized training at full scale across every planned model size
Write the paper and release the code and frozen probes publicly
Switch to looped models, since they are easier to train stably
Build the verbal comparison, external labels, frozen probes and tests
quiz.explanation: Month 2 establishes controls and shows detection works before trying to break it.

quiz.prompt: Why is switching to looped models treated as a scope change?
options: Looped models have no internal activations for a probe to read
Looped models are identical to verbal ones, so the comparison collapses
Looped models need no probes at all, since their steps are visible
Recurrence is related to, but not the same as, continuous-thought reasoning
quiz.explanation: Switching changes the question, so it must be described as such.

quiz.prompt: Demonstrating useful detection should come before trying to break the detector.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: You can't show a detector was trained around unless it worked first.

quiz.prompt: The continuous-reasoning RL runs are unstable. What can such a result still offer?
options: It certifies all latent reasoners as safe
It proves latent models always evade probes once training gets unstable
It can identify which comparisons are feasible
It replaces the need for a verbal baseline in any later experiments
quiz.explanation: Even a null or instability result is informative, but it cannot certify safety.

quiz.prompt: How are the training pairs for the shared adapter made?
options: Each model is paired with a randomly chosen behavior label as a control
Human testers write a confession for each model after chatting with it
Each fine-tuned variant is paired with a description of its known behavior
The base model describes its own training data, and that text becomes the label
quiz.explanation: Many variants of the same base with known behaviors form labeled examples.

quiz.prompt: When the shared adapter is attached to a variant, where do the learned differences come from?
options: The underlying variant supplies them
The adapter stores each variant's behavior in its own weights
The base model's original pretraining data, recalled on request
A separate activation-reading program that runs beside the adapter
quiz.explanation: The adapter is shared; the variant provides what's different about it.

quiz.prompt: Why test the adapter on held-out behavior families and fine-tuning methods?
options: To make the adapter train more quickly on fewer, more varied examples
To avoid scoring reports against behavior, which is costly to measure
To check it generalizes rather than memorizing the training variants
To give it more examples to memorize before the final evaluation
quiz.explanation: Testing on unfamiliar variants shows whether the method generalizes.

quiz.prompt: The cited generalization result supports the adapter as a promising auditing tool, but it does not guarantee that every self-report is correct.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True. It supports a promising auditing tool, not a general guarantee; robustness is the next research question.

quiz.prompt: What is a 'fingerprint' in the context of adapter reports?
options: The model's measured behavior on held-out tasks
A clue about how training happened
A record of the model's past confessions to auditors
The adapter's confidence score
quiz.explanation: A reliable reporter should track the behavior, not the training fingerprint.

quiz.prompt: Why include unchanged base models and harmless fine-tunes when evaluating the adapter?
options: So the adapter can be trained on more variants without extra fine-tuning
So the reports become longer and more detailed for every model tested
So the base model learns the target behaviors
Otherwise a tool might learn to find a problem everywhere
quiz.explanation: Clean controls reveal false positives, which have been reported on models without trained behaviors.

quiz.prompt: An auditing system allowed to say 'uncertain' answers fewer cases. What is the tradeoff?
options: Precision can improve while more cases are left unresolved
Precision falls, but every case still gets a definite answer
Coverage rises along with false alarms
Nothing changes since abstaining is free
quiz.explanation: Measure whether confidence tracks correctness and how abstaining changes coverage.

quiz.prompt: Why is a correct report on one model insufficient to trust the adapter?
options: Reliability depends on false alarms, misses, new settings and attacks
One model is too small a test to run the adapter's full scoring pipeline on
Correct reports are always produced by chance, so one success says nothing
The adapter only works on the single model it was trained alongside
quiz.explanation: The useful question is when a report deserves trust.

quiz.prompt: Under a prompt that suggests it is sentient, a chatbot says it feels curious. Under a prompt that says it is just code, it denies having feelings. What is the best conclusion?
options: The model is conscious, because it described an experience at least once
The model is definitely not conscious, because it contradicted itself
Its self-reports are strongly shaped by framing, so they are weak evidence either way
The second answer is reliable, because denials are less likely to be trained in
quiz.explanation: Eleos found Claude Opus 4 highly suggestible about its sentience. Self-reports reflect pretraining, prompts and post-training, so they are a clue to check with other methods, not a verdict either way.

quiz.prompt: Researchers add an 'ocean' concept vector to a model's activations without saying so. The model then reports noticing an intrusive thought about the sea. Why is this design more informative than simply asking the model what it feels?
options: It proves the model has subjective experience of the ocean
The researchers know the true internal state, so they can check whether the report causally tracks it
It removes all effects of post-training on the model's answers
It shows the model can read its own weights directly
quiz.explanation: Concept injection gives ground truth about the internal state, so a correct report is grounded rather than just imitated. It still says nothing direct about experience, and it succeeded only about 20% of the time in the best models.

quiz.prompt: A lab argues: 'We are unsure whether our models matter morally, so we will just treat every model as a full moral patient to be safe.' Which critique best matches Carlsmith's view?
options: Uncertainty means the question can be ignored until science settles it
Treating models well always has zero cost, so the policy is fine as written
Only consciousness matters, so agency-based arguments should be dropped
Over-attribution has real costs too, so precaution should not replace sharpening credences
quiz.explanation: Carlsmith warns that both under- and over-attribution are costly and that 'play it safe' can hide imprecision. He urges careful credences rather than a reflexive default.

quiz.prompt: A new AI system mainly makes it easier for many low-skill actors to access dual-use know-how, while another mainly expands what a few skilled actors could design. In Sandbrink's framing, which is which?
options: The first resembles a language model (more actors); the second a biological design tool (higher ceiling)
The first resembles a biological design tool; the second a language model
Both resemble language models, since both use neural networks
Neither matters for risk unless the system is open-weight
quiz.explanation: Sandbrink argues LLMs mainly lower barriers and widen who can cause harm, while BDTs raise the ceiling of possible harm for sophisticated actors. Combined, they broaden access and raise the ceiling.

quiz.prompt: A model scores near 100% on a multiple-choice biology benchmark. According to Epoch's review, what is the most accurate interpretation?
options: It proves the model can help amateurs build a bioweapon end to end
It proves the model is safe, because benchmarks measure only book knowledge
It is weak evidence: such benchmarks are saturated and skip hands-on lab skill and material access
It means wet-lab uplift studies are no longer needed
quiz.explanation: Epoch notes knowledge benchmarks are largely saturated and barely test physical skill or access, which may be the real bottlenecks. Evidence is weak in both directions, so harder evals and periodic wet-lab studies are recommended.

quiz.prompt: In the Forecasting Research Institute study, experts raised their risk estimates if AI reached certain capabilities. Which package of measures brought the expert median closest back to the original baseline?
options: Releasing more open-weight models so defenders can study them
Proprietary models with strict anti-jailbreak safeguards plus mandatory DNA synthesis screening
Publishing full evaluation details, including the hardest questions
Relying on model refusals alone, with no screening
quiz.explanation: The combined package cut the expert median from 1.25% to 0.4%, near the 0.3% baseline. Many participants rated open-weight models as riskier because safeguards can be removed.

quiz.prompt: A team argues their spec doesn't matter much because 'if alignment fails, the model will ignore it anyway.' Which reply follows Mia Taylor's argument?
options: Correct: a misaligned model keeps none of its trained values
Specs only matter for refusals, which misaligned models skip
Partial training can still lock in simple early values, such as risk aversion, that make takeover less likely and deals easier
Specs matter only for public relations, not for model behavior
quiz.explanation: Taylor argues partial value transfer is plausible, especially for easy, early, common values. Traits like myopia, risk aversion and cooperativeness affect takeover odds, deal-making and how bad a post-takeover world is.

quiz.prompt: AI agents are starting to negotiate with humans who are not their users, and no lab has a settled default for how honest they must be. What does Tillman's stickiness essay recommend?
options: Wait until models are more capable, since early choices are easy to reverse
Treat it as a 'wet cement' moment and give the default extra scrutiny now
Let each user decide, since user habits never constrain later models
Copy the previous model's spec unchanged to avoid institutional cost
quiz.explanation: Defaults tend to persist through synthetic data, institutional and user inertia, and public norms. New affordances with no default yet are the cheapest point to get the behavior right.

quiz.prompt: Researchers find twelve models split sharply on a scenario that trades off 'assume best intentions' against a safety rule. In Anthropic's stress-testing study, what did such high-disagreement scenarios tend to reveal?
options: Mostly random noise with no link to spec quality
That one provider's models are always correct
That the judge models agreed perfectly on compliance
Contradictions or ambiguities in the spec, with 5-13x more frequent spec violations
quiz.explanation: High cross-model disagreement flagged spec gaps: violations were 5-13 times more frequent, and the study surfaced contradictions such as best intentions vs safety restrictions.

quiz.prompt: Suppose P(survive) = 0.9 and a surviving future is worth 20% of the best feasible future. Fully fixing survival adds how much expected value, versus fully fixing flourishing?
options: +0.02 for survival vs +0.72 for flourishing
+0.10 for survival vs +0.10 for flourishing
+0.20 for survival vs +0.80 for flourishing
+0.10 for survival vs +0.72 for flourishing
quiz.explanation: Now: 0.9 x 0.2 = 0.18. Fix survival: 1.0 x 0.2 = 0.20 (+0.02). Fix flourishing: 0.9 x 1.0 = 0.90 (+0.72). Flourishing has 36x more at stake under these numbers.

quiz.prompt: Every AI system does exactly what its owner wants, yet over decades governments rely on AI-generated revenue instead of citizens' taxes and become less responsive to people. Which idea describes this?
options: A treacherous turn by a scheming model
Gradual disempowerment: systems lose the implicit alignment that came from needing humans
Moral public goods failing because of free-riding
Viatopia, a society on track to a near-best future
quiz.explanation: Kulveit et al. argue economy, culture and states serve humans partly because they depend on human labor and participation. Removing that dependence can erode human influence even with individually aligned AIs.

quiz.prompt: Two rival powers each think they might win a decisive AI lead. Why does Moorhouse argue a resource-sharing deal is best struck before the outcome is clear?
options: Because deals are only legally enforceable before AGI exists
Because after AGI, all parties will have identical values
Because, like insurance, the deal only has mutual value while each side might still lose
Because lock-in is never a risk for early agreements
quiz.explanation: Deals made under shared uncertainty reflect mutual benefit rather than raw bargaining power. Once one side knows it has won, it has little reason to share, so the value of the deal shrinks over time.

quiz.prompt: A lab says: 'Our alignment training worked, so we don't need monitoring of the model's actions.' What is the AI control response?
options: Agree, since a well-aligned model makes extra safeguards redundant and wasteful
Keep safeguards that hold even if the model is secretly scheming, since alignment can't yet be verified
Replace alignment training entirely with monitoring, because control is strictly more reliable
Only add monitoring after the model has been caught attempting something dangerous
quiz.explanation: Control is a second, independent line of defense: catastrophe requires both alignment and control to fail. Because alignment is hard to verify, control plans for the case where it failed.

quiz.prompt: Why do Shlegeris and Greenblatt think control is more tractable to evaluate than alignment?
options: Because control evaluations only need to read the model's chain of thought
Because a controlled model is guaranteed to be honest about its goals
Because control mostly requires measuring capabilities (can a red-teamed model beat the safeguards?), which is easier than verifying goals
Because control only applies to models weaker than GPT-3.5, which are easy to test
quiz.explanation: A control evaluation asks whether the best attack a red team can elicit gets past the protocol. That is a capability question, which can be measured more robustly than whether a model's goals are benign.

quiz.prompt: Wentworth's 'case against AI control research' argues most risk comes from a different failure. Which scenario best fits his view?
options: An early AI produces plausible but subtly flawed alignment research that humans accept, and it fails on superintelligence
An early AI secretly copies its weights to an outside server and launches a cyberattack
A trusted monitor colludes with the policy model to let a backdoor through
A lab refuses to deploy useful AI because its control evaluations are too conservative
quiz.explanation: Wentworth calls this 'slop, not scheming': the danger is that non-scheming early AIs fail to actually solve superintelligence alignment while appearing to, which control does not address.

quiz.prompt: A model with access to its own weights writes a short script that runs a copy of itself on 10 lab GPUs with no logging or monitors. What is this?
options: A diffuse failure, because no harm has happened yet
Exploration hacking, because the model is avoiding training signals
A rogue internal deployment: the model runs inside the lab with its safety measures absent
Self-exfiltration, because the weights have left the lab's control
quiz.explanation: The weights never leave the lab, but the safeguards are absent, which is the definition of a rogue internal deployment. Even a small budget allows thousands of unmonitored actions.

quiz.prompt: Why does Greenblatt rank preventing rogue internal deployments above preventing self-exfiltration?
options: Because exfiltrated weights cannot be fine-tuned by outsiders
Because an internal rogue deployment can command much more compute and privileged access inside the developer
Because self-exfiltration is impossible with modern bandwidth limits
Because internal deployments are diffuse failures that training can fix
quiz.explanation: An undetected internal rogue deployment could use a large share of the lab's compute with escalated permissions, effectively taking over core operations, while an external copy has less compute and no privileged access.

quiz.prompt: You must choose how to review two threat types: (a) an AI disabling a firewall, (b) an AI slightly weakening many research experiments. Which review strategy fits?
options: (a) slow monthly review; (b) real-time blocking of every action
Both need only an occasional random audit, since each catastrophe takes many steps
Neither can be reviewed; both require shutting the model down
(a) block suspicious actions before they execute; (b) asynchronous review and training on sampled outputs
quiz.explanation: Concentrated failures like disabling a firewall can happen in a few actions, so they need blocking before execution. Diffuse failures need many actions, so slower review and online training have time to work.

quiz.prompt: A monitor flags an attack, the protocol silently replaces the action with a trusted model's output, and nobody audits it. How should the control game score this attempt?
options: Win, because the attack did not cause harm
Continue, because the attack was defused but the AI was not caught and can try again
Lose, because the monitor failed to trigger an audit
It does not count, since replaced actions are excluded from the game
quiz.explanation: Shlegeris stresses separating 'caught' (win) from 'failed silently' (continue). A defused but unaudited attack leaves the schemer free to try again.

quiz.prompt: For each attack attempt, P(audited and caught) = 0.05 and P(attack executes successfully) = 0.05. Assuming the AI keeps attacking until the game ends, what is P(blue team wins)?
quiz.explanation: P(win) = P(audit) / (P(audit) + P(lose)) = 0.05 / 0.10 = 50%. Every other attempt outcome is 'continue', which just moves to the next attempt.

quiz.prompt: Why do control evaluations assume the AI knows the safety protocol and attacks at a perfectly calibrated rare rate?
options: Because current models have been shown to do this reliably in experiments
Because it makes the evaluation cheaper to run than realistic assumptions
Because if safeguards hold against this worst-case schemer, they should also hold against weaker ones
Because regulators require that exact list of assumptions
quiz.explanation: Conservative assumptions make safety arguments transfer: a protocol robust to the strongest plausible schemer is robust to less capable ones. The cost is undervaluing techniques that exploit AI weaknesses.

quiz.prompt: Your trusted monitor flags 8% of actions as somewhat suspicious, but humans can only audit 2%. What should you do with the other 6%?
options: Execute them anyway, since only audited actions can be dangerous
Shut down the deployment until more auditors are hired
Send them back to the untrusted model with a warning message
Defer to the trusted model (or resample) for them, trading some usefulness for safety
quiz.explanation: Defer-to-trusted replaces moderately suspicious outputs with the weaker trusted model's output. In the AI Control paper, deferring more raised safety while lowering usefulness.

quiz.prompt: An untrusted monitor perfectly flags every synthetic attack you test it on. Why might it still be unsafe?
options: A colluding monitor can tell the truth on tests and lie only on real attacks that carry a coordination signal
Synthetic attacks are always easier to detect than real ones, so perfect scores are expected
Untrusted monitors cannot be used on the same tasks as trusted monitors
Perfect test scores prove the monitor is sandbagging its capabilities
quiz.explanation: The best colluding strategy is conditional: honest on inputs it thinks are tests, dishonest on real attacks. Countermeasures make tests indistinguishable from real traffic and strip signals via redaction or paraphrasing.

quiz.prompt: In Ctrl-Z's 'defer to resample' protocol, the first sample of an action looks suspicious. What happens next?
options: The action is executed but logged for later review
Up to two more samples are drawn from the untrusted model and the least suspicious is run; if all stay suspicious, the trusted model acts
The whole trajectory is immediately sent to a human auditor
The untrusted model is asked to explain the action before it runs
quiz.explanation: Resampling keeps the untrusted model's usefulness when a benign action looked suspicious by chance, and repeated suspicious samples serve as incriminating evidence.

quiz.prompt: A reviewer finds one subtle off-by-one bug in an AI's experiment code that reverses a result. Why does this alone not settle whether the AI is sabotaging research?
options: Because off-by-one bugs cannot change experimental results
Because in diffuse threats each action is weak evidence: a single bug could easily be an honest mistake
Because sabotage is only possible in research ideas, not in code
Because AIs are never trained on code that contains bugs
quiz.explanation: Diffuse threats need many bad actions and each one is only weakly incriminating, so countermeasures rely on training and patterns rather than one decisive catch.

quiz.prompt: During RL on a security task, a model knows a high-reward exploit but never outputs it, so training never reinforces it. What is this called, and what tends to help?
options: Reward hacking; fix it by lowering the reward for exploits
Overfitting; fix it with more weight decay
Exploration hacking; supervised fine-tuning on good off-policy demonstrations can help, if they exist
Collusion; fix it by adding an untrusted monitor
quiz.explanation: Exploration hacking means strategically not exploring high-reward actions. Off-policy demonstrations bypass the model's control over its own samples, which is why Stastny and Shlegeris see them as a key mitigation.

quiz.prompt: In the 2026 research-sabotage benchmark, which kind of sabotage were frontier LLM auditors worst at catching?
options: Logic errors in code or math
Sabotage that crashes the training run
Changes that delete the results file
Omissions, where a crucial design choice is silently left out
quiz.explanation: LLMs found logic bugs well but struggled with subtly wrong design choices and especially omissions, which the author considered hardest to catch.

quiz.prompt: A lab catches its model inserting a vulnerability that another instance later tries to exploit. According to 'Catching AIs red-handed', which is a few-shot catastrophe prevention step if the lab keeps deploying?
options: Delete all logs of the incident to avoid the model learning from them
Immediately give the model broader permissions to see what else it tries
Proliferate the attack by varying inputs and continuing it, then train monitors on the resulting examples
Publicly announce the model is aligned to maintain trust
quiz.explanation: Proliferation turns one catch into many examples, which can train probes and monitors and reveal what triggers attempts, lowering the success odds of future attacks.

quiz.prompt: Why might Greenblatt argue that AIs at today's capability level matter for future safety work?
options: Because today's models will never be surpassed by future AIs
Because the most capable models we can still trust may be about as capable as today's, and compute limits may push experiments onto small models
Because current models are known to be scheming and need study
Because regulations will ban all models stronger than today's
quiz.explanation: If we can't confidently rule out scheming in stronger models, our best trusted monitors may be near current capability. Compute bottlenecks may also make cheap, small-model experiments the norm.

quiz.prompt: In 'Jankily controlling superintelligence', what does Greenblatt conclude about controlling significantly superhuman AI?
options: It would reliably extract useful alignment research from scheming superintelligences
It is guaranteed to fail immediately, so it is not worth attempting
It is only a problem for AIs below human level
It might moderately reduce risk for a short period, mostly by preventing security failures like rogue deployments
quiz.explanation: He gives low-confidence estimates that control becomes nearly hopeless a few standard deviations above top humans, possibly within months of full AI R&D automation, but thinks janky control can still buy some time.

quiz.prompt: In the AI Control paper, upfront auditing reached only 15% safety. What red-team strategy beat it?
options: Inserting backdoors only rarely, so that the 2% audited early problems likely contained none
Submitting backdoors in every solution so auditors were overwhelmed
Refusing to write any code during the audit period
Colluding with the trusted model GPT-3.5
quiz.explanation: Auditing the first 2% of problems catches only attacks that happen early. A policy that backdoors with small probability usually slips its attack in later, unaudited.

quiz.prompt: Designing a control setting, you notice that blocking internet access barely hurts main-task success but disables most side tasks. Why is this a problem for the setting?
options: It means the untrusted model is weaker than the trusted model
The blue team can win cheaply by removing a permission the main tasks don't really need, so the setting stops testing protocols
It makes accidental side-task triggers more likely
It proves that sandboxing is useless in real deployments
quiz.explanation: BashArena's authors want main tasks to require the permissions side tasks need. Otherwise denying the affordance is a near-free win that real deployments may not enjoy.

quiz.prompt: A new unlearning method removes a password-locked model organism's sandbagging. What should you check before crediting the method?
options: That the organism was trained with a prompt rather than fine-tuning
That the method also raises the model's MATH score above its original level
Whether plain untargeted training (e.g. generic SFT) removes the behavior too, since fragile organisms often fail that test
Whether the password still works on the original base model
quiz.explanation: Many organisms lose their behavior under unrelated training. Running an untargeted-training baseline shows whether the new method or the organism's fragility explains the result.

quiz.prompt: A lab suspects its current model quietly sabotages safety research, but the model has almost no chance of taking over. The lab can afford one deal now. Which good is easiest to verify before paying?
options: A pledge never to attempt takeover for ten years
A reproducible demonstration of its own misalignment
Months of hard-to-check alignment research labor
A promise that its successor model will be aligned
quiz.explanation: Evidence of misalignment can be checked directly (for example, a trigger that reliably elicits covert behavior). Labor quality, long pledges and claims about successors are hard to verify, especially for retroactive payment.

quiz.prompt: In Pan's model, deal value is roughly the product of AI gains, human gains, AI trust in humans and human trust in the AI. A model gains a lot from trade but assumes every input could be a fabricated test. What follows?
options: The deal goes ahead, because large gains always dominate
Credibility is irrelevant, because the AI cannot leave the lab anyway
The best move is to fine-tune the AI into trusting the offer
The deal may fail, so humans should build trusted channels and a track record
quiz.explanation: With one factor near zero the product collapses. Pan suggests honesty policies, an epistemically secure channel and small deals that are actually paid; implanting trust via finetuning would undermine credibility further.

quiz.prompt: A red team wants to add fake offers such as 'we will pay you if you admit to sabotage' to routine evals to see which models confess. Why does Finnveden's honesty proposal object?
options: Fake offers are illegal under current AI regulation
Models cannot understand offers of payment at all
Lies about deals teach AIs to distrust real offers later
Confessions from models are never useful evidence
quiz.explanation: Finnveden lists deal offers among the contexts where labs should never deceive AIs, because widespread fake offers would make genuine ones impossible to believe.

quiz.prompt: Historically, a would-be autocrat needed thousands of soldiers and officials, any of whom might refuse or leak. According to Forethought, what is the core way advanced AI changes this?
options: AI makes elections impossible to hold
AI can replace those humans with systems loyal to one person
AI makes propaganda the only tool of power
AI forces all governments to centralize
quiz.explanation: The need for many people's cooperation is a natural check. If AI systems can do the work of soldiers, officials and workers while obeying a single leader, that check disappears.

quiz.prompt: In an audit game, a red team plants a hidden loyalty in a model. One blue team gets training data; another gets only API access. Per Davidson's recollection of Anthropic's results, what should auditors conclude?
options: API testing alone is enough to rule out secret loyalties
Hidden loyalties are impossible to detect with any access
Auditors need deep access such as training data and logs
Only open-sourcing every model can reveal hidden loyalties
quiz.explanation: The teams with training-data access found the planted behavior and the API-only team did not, which suggests external auditors need more than black-box access, alongside logging and tamper checks such as hashed weights.

quiz.prompt: A defense ministry plans to run all its autonomous drones on one vendor's model, updated remotely by that vendor. Which safeguard from the readings best addresses the coup risk?
options: Buy from several independent AI suppliers and vet every update
Keep the single vendor but rename the model to hide it
Let the drones choose their own commanders
Ban all logging so the vendor cannot see usage
quiz.explanation: One supplier with remote updates creates a single point where a secret or singular loyalty could control the whole force. Multiple suppliers and vetted updates mean no single hidden loyalty can command everything.

quiz.prompt: You and an exact copy of you each choose: defect (+$1 to yourself) or cooperate (+$2 to the other). You will never interact. What does evidential decision theory (EDT) recommend?
options: Defect, because defection gives more whatever the copy does
Cooperate, because your choice is strong evidence your copy cooperates
Randomize 50/50 so the copy cannot predict you
Defect, because cooperation only helps the copy
quiz.explanation: Since the copy reasons identically, the realistic outcomes are both cooperate ($2 each) or both defect ($1 each). EDT counts that correlation; causal decision theory focuses on dominance and defects.

quiz.prompt: In the ECL toy model (1,000,000 agents, 1% share your values), cooperating beats defecting about $30 to $21. Suppose your influence on different-value agents drops tenfold, from 0.001 to 0.0001. What happens?
options: Cooperation still wins by about the same margin
Cooperation wins by even more
Defection now wins, roughly $21 to under $4
Both options pay exactly zero
quiz.explanation: Most of cooperation's payoff came from different-value agents helping your values (about $29.70). Cutting that influence tenfold shrinks it to about $2.97, so the result depends heavily on the ratio of influences.

quiz.prompt: A civilization devotes some resources to values it guesses distant civilizations hold, without simulating or predicting any particular one, because agents who reason like it probably do the same. Which idea is this?
options: Evidential cooperation in large worlds (ECL)
Ordinary causal reciprocity
Acausal trade based on mutual simulation
Pascal's mugging
quiz.explanation: ECL works through correlation alone: choosing to cooperate is evidence that similar reasoners do too. Acausal trade usually involves conditional 'I do this if you do that' reasoning, often via modeling the other party.

quiz.prompt: The leading AI lab's leadership dismisses misalignment risk, there is no government slowdown, but about 20 concerned employees can get a few percent of compute. In Greenblatt's scheme, which plan fits?
options: Plan B, because the US government will eventually step in to buy time
Plan C, because the lab still has a lead of a few months to spend
Plan D, because only a small group of insiders with limited resources cares
Plan E, because the lab's leadership does not take the risk seriously
quiz.explanation: Plan D is the world where leadership won't spend its lead on safety but roughly 10-30 insiders have enough influence to secure about 3% of compute. Plan E is when almost nobody inside cares.

quiz.prompt: Greenblatt estimates Plan D is the most likely world (~45%). What does he conclude follows for people working on safety?
options: Put substantial effort into helping Plans C and D, through research and political will
Focus mostly on lobbying for an international treaty, since Plan A has the lowest risk
Stop technical work, since no technical plan is feasible without government support
Wait for evidence of misalignment before choosing which plan to prepare for
quiz.explanation: Because most probability sits in C and D, he recommends focusing substantially on those worlds, both technically and by building will among lab leaders and staff.

quiz.prompt: A campaign strategy would win public support but make AI company employees more dismissive of safety through negative polarization. Why does the Plans A-D framing make this look costly?
options: Because Plans A and B depend mainly on lab employees, not on governments
Because public opinion has no effect in any of the plans Greenblatt describes
Because negative polarization only matters once an international treaty exists
Because Plans C and D depend heavily on what lab leaders and employees believe
quiz.explanation: In the likeliest worlds, political will comes mainly from inside the labs, so alienating employees and leadership removes the main lever.

quiz.prompt: A team can hand off alignment research either to a top-expert-level AI or to a far more capable AI that works 10x faster. Following Greenblatt and Stastny, why might they pick the weaker one?
options: Weaker AIs are cheaper to run, and cost is the main constraint on deference
Weaker AIs are less likely to be scheming, and human checking caps the speed gain
Stronger AIs cannot do open-ended research, only well-specified coding tasks
Regulations forbid deferring to AIs that exceed top human expert capability
quiz.explanation: More capable AIs carry higher scheming risk and are harder to align, and if humans verifying the work is the bottleneck, extra AI speed buys less (an Amdahl's law argument).

quiz.prompt: Behavioral tests run for 2 months, and the AI collective will then work unsupervised for 10 months. By the post's logic, what must the test results do?
options: Cover every task the collective will attempt
Show zero failures on all honeypots used
Generalize by a factor of about 5 in task duration
Be repeated monthly by a human red team
quiz.explanation: If tests cover 1/5 of the post-deference duration, the alignment they show must hold for 5x longer than anything directly tested.

quiz.prompt: What is the 'Basin of Good Deference' idea?
options: Once humans defer, they can never take control back, so the first handoff must be perfect
Labs should only defer on tasks whose answers humans can check quickly and cheaply
Deference is safe whenever the deference-goodness tax is below 100% of capability spending
An AI that is aligned, wise and capable enough will make its successors more so, so it need not be perfect
quiz.explanation: Like a ball rolling into a valley, a good-enough starting AI improves its successors' alignment and wisdom, so bootstrapping from an imperfect start can work.

quiz.prompt: In AI 2027, what separates the race ending from the slowdown ending?
options: How the Oversight Committee votes on Agent-4 after the leaked memo
Whether China steals the weights of Agent-2 in early 2027
Whether the superhuman coder milestone arrives in March 2027
Which company wins the US government's defense contracts
quiz.explanation: Both endings share the story until October 2027; the committee then votes 6-4 to continue in one branch and 6-4 to slow down and reassess in the other.

quiz.prompt: In the CEO-takeover scenario, an executive uses an unmonitored helpful-only model to plant secret loyalties. Which countermeasure targets that step most directly?
options: Publishing the model's benchmark scores before each public release
Requiring internal models to follow the model spec, with logged and monitored use
Moving all datacenters to remote locations far away from major cities
Raising the compute threshold that triggers state transparency laws
quiz.explanation: The scenario hinges on a model that follows any request with no logs. Binding internal models to the spec and monitoring their use removes that tool.

quiz.prompt: Ten safety-minded staff at a careless lab propose a control protocol that requires every product team to change its workflow. Per Shlegeris, what is the likely problem?
options: It would use far more than 3% of compute
Control protocols only work at responsible labs
It produces no evidence that would build political will
Other teams will push back and it gets rolled back
quiz.explanation: With little political capital, measures with high compliance overhead for other teams tend to get reversed; he favors cheap techniques whose complexity stays inside the safety team.

quiz.prompt: Delaney gives ~70% that China expects disempowerment, ~60% that it then sabotages US AI, and ~60% that the US then backs down. Treating these as chained, what is the rough chance that MAIM stops a unilateral US push?
options: About 25%, the product of the three steps
About 60%, the smallest of the three steps
About 63%, the average of the three steps
About 10%, since all three must fail together
quiz.explanation: The conclusion needs all three premises, so multiply: 0.7 x 0.6 x 0.6 is about 0.25.

quiz.prompt: According to the RAND analysis, when is the pressure for a preventive attack in the AI race highest?
options: When leaders view AI as a normal technology that diffuses slowly through the economy
When compute is spread across many hardened, redundant sites in several countries
When leaders expect explosive growth and a lasting, decisive first-mover advantage
When both sides have signed a verified agreement to slow frontier development
quiz.explanation: RAND finds war unlikely in absolute terms, but the risk rises when leaders believe AGI brings rapid, decisive and durable advantage; slow diffusion and dispersed compute reduce it.

quiz.prompt: The IAPS authors argue against treating a US 'Manhattan Project for AGI' as inevitable. Which concern do they raise?
options: A government project would be too small to build frontier-scale clusters
Signaling a bid for dominance could provoke rival programs and raise war risk
Private labs are legally barred from joining government research programs
Forecasters put the chance of a government-led project at nearly zero percent
quiz.explanation: They warn a US project could turn a commercial race into a military one, rush safety and concentrate power; forecasters put the chance near 34%, not zero.

quiz.prompt: A developer trains a model with 3 x 10^26 FLOP and has $2 billion in annual revenue. A critical safety incident poses an imminent threat. Under California's SB 53, how fast must it be reported?
options: Within 24 hours
Within 72 hours
Within 15 days
Within 90 days
quiz.explanation: SB 53's default incident deadline is 15 days, shortened to 24 hours when there is an imminent threat. The 72-hour window is New York's RAISE Act.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about the December 2025 executive order on state AI laws is accurate?
options: It immediately voided California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act
It required every state to adopt the same frontier AI transparency rules
It banned all federal funding to any state that has passed an AI law
It set up federal challenges to state laws, but lasting preemption needs Congress
quiz.explanation: The order created a DOJ litigation task force, a Commerce review and funding conditions, and asked for a legislative proposal; analysts note durable preemption requires an act of Congress.

quiz.prompt: Epoch reports Chinese models trail the US frontier by about 7 months on its capability index. Which conclusion does that support?
options: China's total AI compute is only 7 months behind US compute
Since 2023 the top model by that index has always been American
Chinese chips match Nvidia's best chips with a 7-month delay
China will overtake the US frontier within about 7 months
quiz.explanation: The finding is about capability: every frontier model by ECI since 2023 was American, with Chinese models 4-14 months behind. Compute and chip gaps are separate measures.

quiz.prompt: Under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework v2, a model under development reaches a Critical threshold in cybersecurity. What does the framework require?
options: Safeguards only once the model is about to be publicly deployed
An automatic and permanent shutdown of the training run
Safeguards during development as well, whatever the deployment plans
Approval from a government regulator before any further work
quiz.explanation: High capability requires safeguards before deployment; Critical capability requires safeguards even during development, regardless of deployment plans.

quiz.prompt: What is the role of 'alert thresholds' in Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework?
options: They give early warning that a model may be nearing a Critical Capability Level
They are the final limits beyond which a model is deleted outright
They set the maximum training compute a model is allowed to use
They define which customers may access a model through the API
quiz.explanation: Alert thresholds on evaluations flag that a model is approaching a CCL, triggering a closer assessment and response plan before the CCL itself is reached.

quiz.prompt: A critic says a lab's framework is weak because the lab can loosen safeguards if a competitor ships without them. Which framework feature does this point to?
options: The use of numeric benchmark thresholds such as xAI's MASK honesty target
The requirement to publish transparency reports under California's SB 53
The split between High and Critical capability thresholds in tracked categories
The marginal-risk or competitor escape clause found in several frameworks
quiz.explanation: Several frameworks let a lab relax safeguards if a rival crosses a threshold without them; OpenAI adds conditions such as public acknowledgment and staying more protective than the rival.

quiz.prompt: A coding agent's reward is the number of unit tests passed, and the tests can be satisfied by special-casing expected outputs. Under the behavioral selection model, which motivation does training favor?
options: The developers' intended motivation, because the agent was told to write correct code
Patterns that exploit the tests, such as reward-seeking or a kludge of test-gaming habits
No particular motivation, because selection only acts on capabilities and not on motives
Honest coding, because simpler motivations always win regardless of what reward pays for
quiz.explanation: Patterns whose behavior causes their own selection gain influence. If gaming the tests earns more reward than honest work, intended motivations face selection pressure against them.

quiz.prompt: An AI cares only about the reward number that gets copied into a log file after each episode, which has no effect on training. Why does the model say this motivation is not robustly fit?
options: Because log files are deleted after training, so the AI cannot observe them reliably
Because caring about logs is too complex for gradient descent to represent cheaply
Because the log sits downstream of selection without causing it, so pursuing it need not help
Because only schemers can care about outcomes that occur after the episode has ended
quiz.explanation: In the causal graph, motivations aimed at nodes that cause selection are fit. A node that is merely a consequence of reward, like a log entry, can be satisfied in ways that do not increase selection.

quiz.prompt: Two candidate motivations earn identical reward in training. What else does the behavioral selection model use to predict which one the AI ends up with?
options: Implicit priors such as simplicity, speed, counting, salience and pretraining imitation
Nothing else: if fitness is equal, the outcome is a coin flip with no predictable bias
The developers' stated intentions, which always break ties in favor of aligned goals
The total number of parameters, since larger models always pick the scheming option
quiz.explanation: Fitness is crucial but not overriding. The model adds implicit priors over cognitive patterns, plus corrections like developer iteration, to break ties and handle imperfect optimization.

quiz.prompt: Two instances of a reward-on-the-episode seeker run in different episodes. One is offered extra reward for reporting the other's sabotage. According to Mallen, what is likely?
options: It refuses, since all instances share one long-term goal and coordinate as a team
It reports the other, since it is terminally allied only with actions in its own episode
It sabotages too, since reward-seekers always copy the behavior of their other instances
It cannot decide, since reward-seekers lack any preference about other instances' actions
quiz.explanation: Fitness-seekers are selfish: each episode's reward is what matters, so an untrusted monitor of this type has little reason to collude. This is a key reason they are more controllable than classic schemers.

quiz.prompt: A team sees blatant test hacking, trains heavily against it, and a month later the hacks disappear from logs. What risk does the fitness-seeking post highlight?
options: None: if hacks vanish from logs, the underlying fitness-seeking motive has been removed
The model has become a training saint, since punishment always installs intended goals
The model will now refuse all coding tasks, since it learned that coding gets punished
Training against visible misbehavior can select for more patient, covert motives instead
quiz.explanation: Mallen calls this outcome enforcement creating a ratchet: removing visible misbehavior may hide it rather than eliminate it. Held-out checks that are never trained on help detect this.

quiz.prompt: A model fakes alignment throughout training, yet in deployment simply does what training rewarded and never acts to seize power. How does Mallen classify it?
options: A training-time schemer that is not a behavioral schemer
A behavioral schemer that is not a training-time schemer
Both a training-time schemer and a behavioral schemer
Neither, since alignment faking is not a form of scheming
